en.body_markdown:
Essay

Hassan Makaremi

2013

Incorporating the entirety of Khayyâm’s quatrains

Translated by: Charles Grolleau

Can We Free Ourselves from Prejudices to Better Understand Khayyâm [1]?

“Imitate, as far as lies within your power, the libertines
undermine the foundations of prayer and fasting
Listen to the word of truth from Omar Khayyâm
Get drunk, and rob upon the highways [2]”

Khayyâm is undoubtedly the most widely known Persian poet. Yet his existence and his presence as a poet remain obscured by clouds of mystery[3]. Becoming acquainted with his life, his works, his thoughts, and his contributions to the various fields of human knowledge and learning requires effort. The means and methods at our disposal to attain this understanding remain limited. Yet while we know his poems and his writings in Persian and Arabic, other ancient or more recent texts likewise inform us about him. Multiple translations of his quatrains[4] also exist, the introductions to which are often exceedingly valuable. Among the numerous contemporary studies devoted to his work, one may cite the studies of twentieth-century Iranian scholars such as Ghani[5], Foroughi, and Hedayat[6], who used Khayyâm’s original poems and certain of their interpretations as bases for enquiry.

How are we to characterise these scholars of ten centuries ago? Contemporary classifications seem so ill-suited to their intellectual trajectories. How would Khayyâm characterise himself? Is he a philosopher, a poet—in the literary sense of the term—a mystic, a man of science, all of these at once, or something else besides? And of what spirituality are we speaking in Khayyâm’s case? Is it metaphysics, that discipline which sets matter against spirit, or a certain aesthetic dimension of poetry? And if we speak of philosophy, to what kind of philosopher does he belong? What is his stance? Does he engage in a reflection upon the world, does he make use of his reason to grasp the meaning of life, or is it for him a matter of confronting the events of existence with patience? As for his status as a poet, should we understand him as one who possesses the art of combining words, sonorities, and rhythms in order to evoke images and suggest sensations and emotions?

Be that as it may, Khayyâm communicates his messages to us through words—words that must be heard within the context of his time. Khayyâm lived in the same geographical region as the poets Ferdowsi and Attâr[7]; he was Attâr’s contemporary for nearly seventy years, and lived half a century after Ferdowsi. One may therefore imagine that his vocabulary differs little from that of Ferdowsi and Attar.

To revisit Khayyâm’s poetry without prejudice and to grasp the core of his message, we must first attend to the meaning of his words placed back in their proper context, rather than attempting to attach to them adjectives belonging to our own era. Let us put it simply: Khayyâm is an exceptional being who delivers to us a singular message. That is what we shall retain.

Yet what is this message? It defines another universe, neither completely metaphysical nor purely epicurean. A universe at the border of time and of the space of symbolisation: of gestures and states (intoxication, dreaming, ...), of objects (the carafe, the wine, the cup, …), of practices (from those of shamans to those that gave birth to rock art), and of narratives (from mythology to the invention of metaphysics and of “spirit”). In other words, this message opens a path that leads us back, in a more fundamental and dizzying way, to the invention of humanity.

The birth of the concept of time itself took time. Let us recall that originally we had one and the same word to name time and space. Here, Khayyâm puts forward a genuine discovery, a powerful message. He puts his finger on the concept of time that we use today.

Yet we shall see this more precisely through the poems of the great Khayyâm. Khayyâm is an ambivalent figure. While he is the scholar, the mathematician, the philosopher, the pupil of the greatest savants of his age, leaving behind major scientific and philosophical works, and respected as such, he is also this poet writing quatrains. He is the first poet to bestow real significance upon this rather folkloric form of poetry. However, his contemporaries viewed him primarily as a scholar. It would take several decades after his death for him to be recognised as a poet—a poet to whom we owe dozens, indeed hundreds, of quatrains.

And his ambivalence does not stop there. While he is regarded as one of the figures most contested by the clergy, he is also the most famous Iranian figure following Edward FitzGerald’s translation.

How are we to reconcile these two Khayyâms? Should we overlook the first Khayyâm, the mathematician-scholar, respected as such by the authorities of his time? Can one focus solely on his poetry in order to understand his discourse and his message?

Rumour has it that there were two Khayyâms: on the one hand, the epicurean poet, without religion, an outlaw, running counter to the values of Iran and Islam; on the other hand, Khayyâm the scholar-poet. Should we believe it? How can we make these two figures, with their unresolved paradoxes, live within one and the same individual when we lack so much information?

What do we have in our possession to understand better? A series of poems in Persian whose authors we do not know, which we sign Anonymous, as though Anonymous were the name of a poet.

Sayings, proverbs, and set expressions can also help us hear the voice of a culture. Indeed, these sources are doubtless the truest mirror, devoid of any intermediary.

The quatrains attributed to Khayyâm—read, published, re-edited, translated, and sung in various languages—which have become subjects of philosophical and literary discussions, as well as various in-depth studies, are likewise at our disposal. These quatrains serve as the mirror of a certain dimension of Persian culture and of the culture of Humankind.

Let us posit the hypothesis that, like the Anonymous poems, sayings, and proverbs, these quatrains were composed by Persian culture over the course of centuries. One might compare this to the designs of Persian carpets, with their symbols, their colours, and their harmonies. Used as an educational medium—writing par excellence—these carpets served for centuries to transmit the elements of the Iranian language, both to settled villagers and to nomadic Iranians. One can doubtless read in their designs and symbols messages of hope, wishes, and aspirations. They remain testimonies to the life of an entire people. These Persian carpets are like hieroglyphs still undecoded to this day.

Yet let us return to Khayyâm: among the different translations and versions of his quatrains, to move forward in our task we have chosen the translation from Persian into French that Charles Grolleau published in 1902. While these quatrains reveal a genuine aesthetic sense, a finesse and delicacy of style, we shall endeavour above all here to draw closer to the content of their discourse. Deciphering the codes, understanding the mystery of this work, and finding the profound message of these poems—so close to folkloric discourse both in their form and in the richness of their message—are the tasks we set ourselves. Arduous tasks, yet with an accessible result, for they are always endowed with that proximity to everyday language and popular common sense.

First, it is necessary to understand what Islam altered two centuries after its arrival in Iran. The script was no longer the same, a new administration had been established in Baghdad, and a new religion had become widespread. Historians[8] have also termed these first two centuries the Centuries of Silence.

One must wait until the middle of the ninth century for Iranians to awaken and make themselves heard. Violent, military, and political protests—such as the movements of the Saffarids in 1003 and the Ziyarids in 1090—emerged. Iranians infiltrated the Baghdad administration and developed their positions in architecture, literature, and above all poetry. In the tenth century came the apogee of Persian culture, thanks to men such as Ferdowsi and Attar, each opening a path for the development of a culture resolutely oriented towards the future. Historians and bibliographers of the tenth and eleventh centuries speak of the presence, among poets and scholars, of a man born in 1048 and deceased in 1131, a disciple of Avicenna, highly respected in Nishapur (in north-eastern Iran) and notably by the Seljuk dynasty. To this day we know the titles of his major works[9]:

- Demonstration of Problems of Algebra.

- Treatise on Certain Difficulties in Euclid’s Definitions.

- The Zij-i Melik Shahi, astronomical tables.

- A Manual of Natural Science (title unknown).

- Lawazim ul Amkina, treatise on natural science.

- El Kawn Val Taklif.

- El Vajud.

- Mizan ul Hukm.

- Treatise on Indian Methods for the Extraction of Square and Cube Roots.

Time passes. A culture germinates. A branch of Islam establishes itself on Persian soil. The ancient language and culture continue to evolve in a relatively calm climate of cohabitation with the Islamic religion. The earliest traces of quatrains, in popular form, date from this period. The earliest traces of quatrains composed by Khayyâm date from around 1193[10]. The number of these quatrains varies between 158 and 637 pieces[11]. It was in 1859 that Edward FitzGerald (1809–1883) published the translation of these quatrains into English and attributed them without hesitation to the poet and scholar Khayyâm.

This act had two consequences. These quatrains were disseminated throughout the world and in several languages; Khayyâm became popular both as a poet and as a scholar. On the other hand, one notes a genuine dichotomy between the personality of the mathematician, astronomer, philosopher, and scholar respected by the city and that of the poet, author of the quatrains[12]. Even today, this dichotomy never ceases to puzzle and haunt minds[13]. Yet polemic is not our subject here. These quatrains form an integral part of Persian culture. They have traversed the centuries and today possess a quasi-universal dimension. Why this longevity? Why this popularity[14]? Where does it come from?

Proponents of the polemic stop at the conflict, at the opposition, at this contradiction within the same individual. For them, the individual is unitary and indivisible. Consequently, they do not accept that other part present within each of us—that depth, that buried stratum generating questions and extending beyond our conscious mind.

It was Sigmund Freud who discovered this stratum, termed the unconscious, on the basis of forgotten memories. He gave it a name: the unconscious. Poetry and the dream, for him, are the two royal roads to the manifestation of this unconscious. Our will can play no role in it.

Since then, it has become easy to accept that a scholar respected by the city and by the social, scientific, moral, and religious authorities—to the point that he is called Hojjat-al-hagh (Sign of the Presence of God)—could also be the author of poems profoundly calling into question the foundations of belief. The voice of the unconscious separates and frees itself from the control of the Subject. Ultimately, do these poems not find their path and their echo, after decades hidden in the shadows of oral and written culture, among the anonymous poets?

Be that as it may, it is now a matter of studying the poems themselves, dissecting them, and opening up lines of enquiry, by examining the signifiers and families of signifiers most frequently used in these poems.

First and foremost, however, within the perimeter of the Persian language, what was the cultural, political, and social climate of the era? Several legacies present this cultural identity to us today: on the one hand, the Book of Kings, with its staging of Persian mythology; on the other hand, the rise of the school of love, the esoteric mysticism of the Khorasan school, and the production of masterpieces such as “The Language of the Birds” by Farîd al-Dîn Attâr. Against this backdrop, there are quatrains signed Khayyâm:

“Since our stay in this monastery is not lasting
without the Cupbearer and without love, how bitter is life!
O philosopher, how long do beliefs old and new endure?
Since I must depart, what matters it to me whether the world be old or new?”

What was the pillar of Islam at that time in Nishapur, in Khorasan? The three fundamental pillars are: the Oneness of the Creator Allah, who has existed from all eternity and possesses absolute power and knowledge; His Prophet, the final prophet with the book of the Qur’an, transmitting a direct word come from Allah; and the reality of the Last Day, the day on which beings will awaken and be judged for the deeds committed during their life on earth. At the outcome of this judgement, two paths open: Paradise and Hell.

We shall be judged according to our deeds, according to prohibitions and obligations. Yet among the absolute, intolerable prohibitions is that of doubting these three pillars.

In practice, drinking wine is likewise regarded as a prohibition—that wine which makes us drunk and beside ourselves.

“Of that spirit which is called pure wine
they say, ‘It is the remedy of a devastated heart’
Then quickly bring me two or three brimming cups
why then do they call so fine a drink the accursed water?”

“Truly the wine in the cup is a gracious spirit
a delicate soul dwells within the resonant flanks of the jar
Nothing heavy is worthy of being the friend of wine
save the cup, for it is at once both heavy and delicate.”

“Since the world is perishable, I deal only in the artificial
I care only for gaiety and sparkling wine
They say to me, ‘May God grant you repentance!’
He does not grant it, and even if He were to grant it, I would not want it.”

If we call into question the prohibition of wine, calling the other prohibitions and obligations into question will become possible.

“Although I have come, most humbly, to the mosque
by God, I did not come here to pray
I came here to steal a prayer rug
which sin wears out… and I have returned there several times.”

“My heart can no longer distinguish between the bait and the snare
one counsel drives me towards the mosque, the other towards the cup
yet wine, the beloved, and I
are better cooked in a tavern than raw in a monastery.”

In Persian poetry, we encounter four types of wine:

The wine of ignorance, which takes one out of the state of questioning, renders one incapable of establishing relations of cause and effect, and makes one forget reason.

“Life passes by, a mysterious caravan
steal from it its minute of joy!
Cupbearer, why grieve over the morrow of your companions?
Pour wine… the night is slipping away.”

“I must rise to seek out the pure wine
You, give my cheeks the colour of the jujube tree
If reason still torments me, I shall spit in its face
a mouthful of wine so that it may sleep!”

The wine of astonishment; drinking then allows one to understand better and to be more sensitive to perception. This is wine understood as an intermediary. The first two verses of Ghazal Number 218 of the Divan of Hafez of Shiraz are good illustrations of this:

“Cupbearer, our discourse concerns the cypress, the rose, and the tulip,

And this exchange unfolds with three purifying cups!

Pour the wine, for our words, like a young bridegroom, are at the limits of beauty,

All this now holds sway through the mediation of wine![15]”

The wine that alters our state to allow us to enter another state, like a mystical experience. Let us cite the first two verses of Ghazal number 178 of the Divan of Hafez:

“Last night, at the break of dawn, I was delivered from anguish.

In that Darkness of the night I was given the Water of Life.

Beneath the radiance of the ray of the Essence I was taken away from myself,

From the Cup of the manifestation of the Attributes, wine was poured for me[16]”

The wine of pleasure:

“It is morning; let us inhale for a moment the rose-coloured wine
and shatter once again upon the stone this vessel of good repute and honour
Let us cease panting after what was for so long our hope
and play with the long locks and the carved neck of the lute.”

Drinking wine, speaking of it, and consuming it thus becomes the first step towards stepping out of a state of belief and practice.

I drink wine, and on my right and on my left they tell me:
“Do not drink wine, it is the enemy of religion!”
When I learnt that wine was the enemy of religion,
I said, “By Allah! Let me drink its blood—it is an act of piety.”

“We have returned to our accustomed debauchery
we have renounced the five prayers
Wherever a cup is found, you will see us
stretching out our necks like the neck of a bottle”

Even if the Creator exists, He takes no interest in the details of our carnal life; He keeps account of our acts and gestures:

“If two measures of wine are now given to you
drink wine in every assembly, in every gathering
for He who made the world concerns Himself
neither with your moustaches nor with my beard.”

Khayyâm is a pupil of Avicenna. The three foundational elements of Avicenna’s thought may be summarised thus: “He did not believe in the resurrection of bodies after death; God can know only the essence of the universe, and not particular points; and thirdly, God is simple and incorporeal, so He did not create things in their singular forms, but rather in their erroneous primary forms.[17]” These elements may be heard as forming an integral part of the messages of the quatrains—almost ironic messages, in the form of questions.

The three fundamental pillars of Islam are linked in such a way that each, in a sense, upholds the other two. If one of them is eliminated, the other two naturally collapse. The definition of Allah is in the Qur'an; it was pronounced by His prophet. And if there is neither a Last Day nor a Last Judgement, what guarantee is there for the observance of the bundles (prohibitions and obligations) proclaimed by the Prophet and the Qur'an? A tightly welded and closed system of thought? The Last Day (and its Judgement) is the interface, the passage between the triangles: "Allah, Prophet–Qur'an, the Last Day" and the two bundles. Once we are within the system of the triangle of belief, observance of the two bundles is naturally secured.

"The Qur'an, which men call the Supreme Word,
Is read from time to time, yet who reads it unceasingly?
Ah! Upon the lines of the Cup, an exquisite text is engraved
Which the mouth itself, for want of the eyes, knows how to read."

"We, and the wine, and the tavern bench, and our drunkards' bodies, we are
Heedless of the hope of mercy and of the terror of punishment;
Our souls and our hearts, our cups and our garments stained with lees
Are independent of earth, and of fire, and of water."

Full of desire, I placed my lips upon the lips of the jar
to ask it how long my life would be
It pressed its lips to mine and said to me
"Drink wine, you will not return to this world"

To delve more deeply into the quatrains and examine the fundamental questions raised within them, we must answer this question: Which signifiers and bundles of signifiers are used most frequently in the poems?

They might be catalogued as follows:

- Family of the environment, nature, the universe, space: sun, moon, clouds, box of nothingness, chessboard, workshop, curtain, old caravanserai, universe, …

- Family of time: morning, day, dawn, night, morning, Nowruz (first day of spring), spring, …

- Family of historical and mythological figures:

- Kay Khosrow, Kavoos, Jamshid, Bahram, Khosrô, Feridun, … [18]

- Mahmoud, Ayaz, [19]

- Family of wine: jar, wine, tavern, grape juice, glass, red, colours of flowers, …

- Family of out-of-the-ordinary figures: libertine, madman, drunkard, …

- Family of the beloved: angel, friend, companion, idol, …

- Family of the creator: heaven, solar, wheel, God, Yazdân[20], the one who gives, …

- Family of another world: paradise, hell, angel, angel of death, …

- Family of death: tomb, prison, underground, …

- Family of nature: nightingale, shore, flower…

The 158 quatrains translated by Charles Grolleau can be placed into certain categories inspired by these families of signifiers.

Within this initial classification, three types of quatrains stand out, each in turn offering:

· A Khayyâmian vision representing the foundation and essence of the message.

· A certain praise of a free way of life "outside the social framework", with mystical and Sufi tendencies, concerning rather the manner of living. (8 quatrains)

· A diversity, yielding what may be regarded as general messages produced and transmitted by each of us. (19 quatrains)

Yet how are these families of signifiers linked to one another? And what messages do they serve to announce to us? We shall attempt to reread and classify these quatrains through the themes that connect the aforementioned families of signifiers. They can be classified into 18 major groups:

1- Drinking wine, having a good time amidst the beauty of nature, with music in the presence of songs, celebrating as much as possible, savouring the present moment, not worrying about tomorrow, not questioning the past, and expecting nothing from Heaven.

"Do not expend yourself so much in senseless sorrow, but make merry
Give, along the path of injustice, the example of justice
since the end of this world is nothingness
suppose that you do not exist, and be free."

2- Before us, there were kings, others, fair ones, the rich and the poor. They have departed, and the wine we drink today is made from the earth derived from their bodies and their graves. (39 quatrains)

Pour the red wine, the colour of fresh tulips
draw the pure blood from the throat of the jar
for today, apart from the cup, I do not have
a single friend who possesses a pure heart

Look, just as I do, on every side
in the garden, there flows a branch of Kausar[21]
The desert becomes like Heaven; you may say that Hell is no more
Sit down, then, in Heaven with a friend of celestial countenance

A sip of old wine is better than a new kingdom
Avoid every path save that which leads to wine… it is better thus
A cup is worth a hundred times more than the kingdom of Feridun [i][22]
the tile covering the jar is better than the crown of Khosrô[23]

Though your life counts more than sixty years, do not yield
wherever you go, walk no other way than as a drunken man
Before a jar is fashioned from your skull
do not set the pitcher down from your shoulder, nor let go of the cup

It is better to abstain from everything, save drinking
and wine is best when beauties drunk upon it serve it to you in a pavilion
Nothing compares to being a drunkard, a qalandar, a vagabond
nothing is better than drinking from Mah to Mahi [24]

How much longer shall we be the slaves of daily troubles?
What matters it whether we live one year or one day in this world
Pour a cup of wine
before we become pots in the potter's workshop

Fill the cup—day is dawning, lily-white as snow
learn from the wine what the colour of the ruby is
Take two pieces of aloeswood and illuminate the gathering
fashion a lute from one, a torch from the other

Upon the face of the rose, a little mist ever floats
ever within me, in my heart, lives the desire for wine
Do not sleep! Who gave you the right to sleep?
Dear one, give me wine—the sun still shines

Drink of this wine, it is eternal life
it is what remains in you of youthful delights—drink!
It burns like fire, yet sorrows
it turns into a life-giving water—drink!

Bring me that ruby in a crystal glass
that companion, that intimate among the free
since you know that this world of dust
is but a passing breath… bring me wine

Arise! Bring the remedy for this oppressed heart
give the musk-scented wine, the rose-coloured wine
Do you wish for the antidote to sorrow?
Bring the wine, that ruby, and the silken-stringed lute

Friends, when you are gathered together
you must think tenderly of me
when you drink the generous wine together, and it comes to my turn
drain your glass to the very bottom

Friends, when at your gatherings
you delight in one another's charms
When the cupbearer takes the Maghâni wine in hand[25]
remember, in your toast, an unfortunate soul who was dear to you

A single cup of wine is worth a hundred hearts and a hundred religions
a draught of wine is worth the empire of China
Apart from wine, that ruby, there is nowhere on earth
a single sour thing worth a thousand sweet souls

Each drop the cupbearer lets fall upon the earth
extinguishes the fire of anguish in a saddened eye
Glory be to God! You acknowledge, then, that wine
is a balm that eases your heart of many sorrows

Do not let sorrow embrace you
nor absurd cares trouble your days
do not forsake the book, the lips of the beloved, and the fragrant lawns
before the earth takes you back into its bosom

Drink wine, so that it may drive far away all your miseries
and the troubling thought of the seventy-two sects
Do not flee the alchemist, for from him
if you take but a single sip, he will make a thousand cares vanish

Wine is forbidden, for everything depends on who drinks it
and also on its quality and the drinker's company
Once these three conditions are fulfilled, you may ask
who, indeed, drinks wine, if not the sage?

Take care to comfort me with a cup of wine
and to give my amber skin the colour of the ruby
When I die, wash me with wine
and make the planks of my coffin from vine-wood

Limit your desires for the things of this world and live content
Free yourself from the shackles of good and evil here below
take the cup and play with the beloved's curls, for very swiftly
all passes… and how many days remain to us?

Although wine has torn away my veil
as long as my soul lives, I shall not forsake it
Yet truly, those who sell wine astonish me:
what can they buy that is better than what they sell?

We shall be wiped away from the path of love
destiny will crush us beneath its heels
O sweet-faced cup-bearer, leave your languid pose
give me wine, for I shall turn to dust

Now, of happiness nothing remains to us but the name
apart from new wine, not one old friend remains
Do not turn your joyful gesture away from the cup
for today, it alone remains within our reach

Those who are slaves to the intellect and vain subtleties
Have died amidst quarrels over being and non-being.
Go! You simple soul, choose the juice of the grape
For the ignorant, from eating raisins, have become like unripe grapes.

Since life passes away: what are Baghdad and Balkh?
Once the cup is full, what matter its bitterness and its sweetness.
Drink wine, for often after your departure and mine, this very Moon
Will pass from the last day of the month to the first, from the first to the last.

Wherever a robe or a bed of tulips is seen,
Once the blood of a king was shed:
Each stem springing from the soil
Is the beauty-mark that adorned a fair one's cheek.

Wine is a liquid ruby, and the cup is its mine,
The cup is the body of which wine is the soul.
The crystal cup wherein the wine laughs
Is a tear in which the blood of the heart is hidden.

Drink wine… it is Eternal Life,
It is the treasure left to you from the days of your youth:
The season of roses and of wine, and of drunken companions!
Be happy for one instant—that instant is your life.

Give me wine, the remedy for my wounded heart,
Good companion of those whom love has wearied;
My spirit prefers drunkenness and its lies
To the vault of the heavens, the base of the world's skull

Since no one here can guarantee you a tomorrow,
Make your lovesick heart happy now.
In the moonlight, drink wine, for that orb
Will seek us tomorrow and see us no more.

Arise, give me wine—is this the moment for vain words?
Tonight your little mouth suffices for all my desires.
Give me wine, rosy as your cheeks…
My vows of repentance are as tangled as your curls.

Today the season of my youth blooms anew:
I have a longing for that wine from which all my joy comes.
Do not blame me—even harsh, it enchants me;
It is harsh because it has the taste of my life.

Spring gently fans the face of the rose;
In the shade of the garden, how sweet a beloved face is!
Nothing you can say of the past holds any charm for me;
Be happy with Today; speak not of Yesterday.

Like the water of the river or the wind of the desert,
Another day flees from my existence…
Sorrow never made my thoughts languish over two days:
The one that is not yet, the one that has passed.

Those atoms of a cup that he fashioned to fill with wine,
The drinker will not allow them to be scattered at random.
All those delicate ornaments that his fingers joined together…
For love of whom did he make them? Out of hatred for whom would he break them.

I was falling asleep and Wisdom said to me:
"Never in sleep has the rose of happiness bloomed for anyone.
Why surrender yourself to this brother of death?
Drink wine!… You have centuries in which to sleep."

In spring, upon the bank of a river or on the edge of a field,
With a few companions and a companion fair as a houri,
bring the cup… those who drink the morning draught
are independent of the mosque and free of the synagogue.

I saw a man, alone, upon the terrace of his house
who was trampling clay beneath his feet with contempt
and that clay, in its mystical language, said to him
"Be calm—one day, you too shall be trampled as you trample me"

3- Also the worship of pleasure and love as the supreme purpose of life. (4 quatrains)

Every vow of repentance we break once more
and close upon ourselves the door of good repute
Do not blame me if I act like one enraptured
for, once again, I am drunk on the wine of love

Love that is not sincere is worthless
like a fire nearly extinguished, it gives no warmth
The true lover, for years, months, nights, days
tastes neither rest, nor peace, nor food, nor sleep

Ah! Woe to the heart from which passion is absent,
Which is not under the spell of love, joy of the heart!
The day that you pass without love
Does not deserve that the sun should light it and the moon console it

Whoever waters in his heart the rose of Love
Does not have a single day of his life that is in vain,
Whether he seeks to go forward to meet the will of God,
Or seeks bodily well-being and raises his cup.

4- Changing the relationship between knowledge and official wisdom, and becoming aware of our presence in the universe—another state of wakefulness. (8 quatrains)

How long shall I grieve over what I have done or left undone
and over the care of leading my life with a light heart, or not?
Fill the cup, for I know not
whether I shall breathe out this breath that I draw in

This celestial vault is like a bowl fallen upside down
beneath which all the sages are held prisoner
As for you, imitate the love of the cup and the jar
they are lip to lip, though blood flows between the two of them

One cannot consume with sorrow a heart filled with joy
nor destroy the pleasure of living by testing it upon the touchstone
There is no one who knows the secret of the future
what is needed is wine, love, and rest at one's pleasure

When young, we attended a master for a while
For a while we were pleased with our progress
Look at the bottom of it all—what became of us?
We came like water, we departed like the wind

He who has not seen the fruit of Truth grow and ripen for him
Does not walk with a firm step upon the Path.
Whoever bent the tree of knowledge towards himself
Knows that today is like yesterday and tomorrow like the First Day

Know this: that from your soul you shall be separated,
You will pass behind the curtain of God's secrets.
Be happy… you know not whence you came;
Drink wine… you know not whither you will go.

No one can pass behind the curtain that hides the enigma;
No mind knows what lives beneath appearances.
Save in the heart of the earth, we are without refuge…
Drink wine! Do you not know that to such discourses there is no end?

None among those who have questioned the dark mystery
has taken a single step outside the circle of Shadow
O Woman, what ominously mute mouth did you kiss
that you created us all silent and powerless?

5- Others will come, and Heaven will turn. Above all, no one understood anything before us and no one will understand anything after us. Therefore one must drink wine and savour the present moment. Among those who have spoken, no one is right, and above all, a great doubt hangs over the Judgement of the Last Day. Consequently, the triangle (God, Prophet–Qur'an, Judgement of the Last Day) breaks. Heaven will take the place of this triangle. Not one dead person has returned to tell us what happens afterwards, or whether there is another side to life. (4 quatrains)

To speak plainly and without parables
we are the pieces in the game that Heaven plays
we are toyed with upon the chessboard of being
and then we return, one by one, into the box of nothingness

This vessel, just like me, was once a sorrowful lover;
Eagerly it leaned towards some dear face.
That handle which you see upon its neck
Is an arm that once embraced a beloved neck.

You have no power today over tomorrow;
Anxiety for the morrow is futile.
If your heart is not foolish, do not even worry about the present;
Do you know what the days left for you to live will be worth?

If, in the season of spring, a being with the form of a houri[26]
Pours me, upon the green bank of a field, a goblet full of wine,
Though this may seem strange to all:
A dog is better than I if I then utter the name of Heaven.

6- This calling into question of the Last Day can have several consequences:

First, the concept of time may lose its linearity, and thus the First Day will be called into question as the day of creation, and the Last Day as the day of the end of time. (5 quatrains)

Where, then, is the limit of eternity to come or that of eternity past?
Now is the hour of joy; nothing can replace wine
Theory and practice are beyond my reach
yet wine unties the knot of every enigma

Drink wine, your body will one day be dust
and from that dust cups and jars shall be made
be carefree of Heaven and of Hell
why should the sage trouble himself with such things?

Since my coming was not for me the day of Creation
And my departure is the subject of a sentence I know not,
Arise and gird your loins well, nimble cup-bearer,
I am going to drown the misery of this world in wine.

Drink wine, for you shall sleep long beneath the clay,
Without an intimate, a friend, a comrade, a woman;
Take care never to tell this secret to anyone:
Withered tulips will never bloom again.

This Intelligence that prowls along the paths of Heaven
Tells you a hundred times a day:
"At this very minute, understand then that you are not
Like those grasses that grow green again after being plucked.

Creation, as monotheistic belief proclaims it, will within a short time be called into question.

Next, Heaven will be an undefined, undetermined, and unrecognised actor, incapable of taking the place of the Creator. This Heaven is everywhere; it accompanies us from our birth, it exists and will exist… It will be the beating of our heart, taking the place of absolute time. (2 quatrains)

O heart, never shall you fathom the mystery,
never shall you unravel the subtleties of the philosophers.
Make yourself a heaven of wine and the cup,
for into true Heaven, do you know if you shall ever enter?

This celestial vault before which we stand astounded,
we know that it is but a kind of magic lantern:
the sun is the lamp, the universe the lantern,
and we, the images that turn.

7- Then the grand declarations, like the foundations of our understanding, become like the wind. (2 quatrains)

O Saki[27], those who departed before us
have fallen asleep in the dust of their vanity.
Go! Drink wine and learn the truth from my lips:
all that they have said, O Saki, is wind.

Do not surrender to the cares of this unjust world;
do not summon the mournful memory of the departed.
Give your heart only to the daughter of the Peris[28], with breasts of jasmine;
keep wine always by you, and do not cast your life to the passing winds.

8- There is neither a Last Day nor judgement nor obligation, hence neither Hell nor Paradise. (6 quatrains)

Go! Cast dust in the face of heaven,
drink wine, embrace beauty;
is this the time for prayer and supplication,
since, of all those who have departed, not one has returned?

Before destiny strikes you upon the head,
order that rose-coloured wine be brought to you.
Poor fool, do you think you are a treasure
and that you shall be unearthed after having been buried?

I have dreamt of heaven only as a place of rest,
for I have wept so much that I can scarcely see.
Hell is but a spark beside what my soul has endured,
and I believe in Paradise only when I taste a moment of peace.

They say the Garden of Eden enchants the houris;
I say the juice of the grape alone is delectable.
Hold fast to ready cash and renounce a promised gain,
for the sound of drums, brother, is fair only from afar.

I know not whether He who fashioned my being
has prepared me a dwelling in Heaven or in dreadful Hell;
but a little food, a beloved, and wine on the green slope of a plain—
that is cash in hand… keep for yourself the Heaven you take on credit.

A jug of wine, the lips of the beloved, at the edge of a lawn,
have drained my ready cash and ruined your credit…
The entire human race is bound for Heaven or Hell,
yet who ever went to Hell, who ever returned from Heaven?

9- We may then question the purpose of this Creation. The usefulness of bringing us into the world. (2 quatrains)

If I had been free to come, I would not have come;
if I could control my steps, where then would I go?
Would it not be better that in this world of dust
I had never had to come, to leave it… or to live there!

My coming was of no profit to the celestial sphere;
my departure will diminish neither its beauty nor its grandeur.
My two ears have never heard anyone tell
the why of this coming and the why of this departure.

10- We cannot hold anyone other than ourselves responsible, for heaven is without responsibility. (3 quatrains)

To my attentive heart, Heaven whispered in secret:
“Learn from me the commandments I have decreed;
had I any power over my own revolutions,
wine would have preserved me from dizziness.”

The good and the evil that are in human nature,
the happiness and the misfortune that destiny keeps in store for us…
do not blame Heaven for them, for, from the standpoint of Wisdom,
this Heaven is a thousand times more powerless than you.

The good and the evil that are in human nature,
the happiness and the misfortune that destiny keeps in store for us…
do not blame Heaven for them, for, from the standpoint of Wisdom,
this Heaven is a thousand times more powerless than you.

11- Human feelings, humours, are of our own making. There is no one responsible in an already written destiny. If from the very first day, from the Creation, everything is already written, for what can I be responsible? (4 quatrains)

Be happy, for yesterday your reward was fixed,
and yesterday is far away, beyond your reach.
Be happy, though all your efforts come to nothing:
yesterday, with certainty, what you will do tomorrow was inscribed.

O heart, since in this world even truth itself is a hyperbole,
why trouble yourself so much over this turmoil and this debasement?
Surrender your body to destiny, and your soul to the mercy of the hours:
what the Pen has written shall not be crossed out for you.

From the beginning was written what shall be:
tirelessly the Pen writes on, heedless of good or evil.
On the First Day, it inscribed all that shall be…
Our grief and our efforts are in vain.

What the Pen has written never changes;
grieving over it brings only deep sorrow.
Even by enduring anguish all your life,
you do not add a single drop more to it.

12- This system of a triangle and two bundles (prohibitions and obligations) doubtless requires guardians of the temple. These guardians can become irresponsible, cheats, hypocrites. (2 quatrains)

The bodies that populate this vault of heaven
baffle those who think.
Beware of losing the end of the thread of wisdom,
for the guides themselves suffer from dizziness.

To drink wine and embrace beauty
is better than the hypocrisy of the devout;
if the lover and the drunkard are bound for Hell,
then no one shall ever see the face of Heaven.

13- Thus, since we know very little, in the face of the pride and deceit of others, let us be humble and live among human beings. Let us return to social rules. Laws are made by human beings so that they may live together upon this earth, and have no divine origins. (7 quatrains)

Do not follow the Sunnat[29], leave the precepts aside;
refuse no one the morsel you possess;
slander no one, grieve not a single heart:
I guarantee you the world to come—bring wine!

Yesterday in the bazaar I saw a potter
who was fiercely trampling some clay,
and the clay said to him in its mystic tongue:
“Once I was alive, just like you—be less brutal!”

O you who think yourself wise, do not blame those who get drunk;
cast aside pride and imposture.
To taste triumphant calm and peace,
bow down towards those who are humiliated, towards the lowliest.

However assured and steadfast you may be, cause pain to no one;
let no one have to bear the weight of your anger.
If the desire for eternal peace is within you,
suffer alone, so that none, O victim, may call you an executioner.

The mystery must remain veiled from base minds,
and secrets impenetrable to fools.
Reflect upon your deeds towards other human beings;
we must hide our hopes from all humanity.

Be prudent: fortune is uncertain;
beware: the sword of destiny is sharp.
If fate places sweet almonds in your mouth,
do not swallow them; poison is mixed therein.

Since the whole mission of the human race in this desert
is only to suffer and then yield up the soul,
light of heart is he who departs swiftly from this world,
and he knows rest who never came into it.

14- A certain irony and a rather mocking point of view bring out paradoxes similar to the paradoxes of monotheistic fundamentals: an unresolved dilemma between our already written destinies and responsibility for our deeds.

Upon the road I walk, in a thousand places You set traps;
You say, “I shall seize you if you set foot therein.”
Not an atom of the world escapes Your power;
You ordain all things, and You call me a rebel!

O Heaven, in Your bounty all the wretched have their share;
You grant them the sustenance required for the torment of living.
Yet I ask You, O Heaven, if You were a man,
would You give even a fig for such felicity?

Lord! You have shattered my flask of wine;
Lord! You have shut upon me the door of happiness.
You have spilled my pure wine upon the ground—
may I die! Why, it is You who are drunk, O my Lord!

I drink wine, and whoever drinks as I do is worthy of it;
if I drink, it is a very slight thing before Him.
God knew from the very first day that I would drink wine;
if I did not drink, God’s knowledge would be in vain.

May my soul be haunted by the desire for idols fair as houris;
may my hand, all the year round, hold the brimming cup!
They say to me: “May God grant you repentance!”
He will not grant it to me, I want none of it—let us speak of it no more.

I have never strung into a necklace the pearls of Prayer,
nor hidden this dust of sins that soils my face;
therefore I do not despair of Your Mercy,
for I have never said that the One was Two.

Is it not better to tell You my secret thoughts in a tavern
than to prostrate myself without You before the Mihrab?
O You, the First and the Last of all beings,
give me Hell or Heaven, but do with me what You will.

Here now for the world is a little possible happiness;
every living heart yearns for solitude.
Upon every branch, one seems to glimpse the white hand of Moses;
every breeze seems quickened by the breath of Jesus.

Those who, for a time, adorn Heaven
come, go, and return, according to the hour.
In the shirt of heaven and in the pocket of the earth,
since God does not die, there are beings yet to be born.

I am not a man to fear non-being;
that half of destiny pleases me better than the other half.
This is a life that was lent to me by God;
I shall give it back when the time comes to return it.

In my old age, my love for you has led me into a trap;
else how comes it that my hand holds this cup of Nebid?
The beloved has slain the repentance to which reason gave birth;
she has torn the robe that patience sewed.

In the tavern, you can perform the Wuzu only with wine,
and there you cannot cleanse your tarnished name.
Be happy: the veil of our temperance
is so torn that no one can dream of stitching it back together.

15- In a system that does not have as its precise goal the perfection of creation, what is the use of making things disappear and recreating them? Perhaps there is here a certain conception of evolution. (2 quatrains)

What use the coming, what use the departure?
Where then is the warp of the weft of our life?
How many delicate bodies the world shatters—
where then has their smoke vanished?

Take the cup and the flask, O desire of my heart!
Joyfully stroll through the garden and along the banks of rivers.
How many charming beings has mocking Heaven
a hundred times turned into cups and a hundred times into flasks!

16- Khayyâm uses his own name and speaks of himself in these quatrains—quatrains that run in the same direction as the unsigned ones. This may perhaps prove their authenticity. (4 quatrains)

Be happy, Khayyâm, if you are drunk;
if you rest beside a tulip-cheeked beloved, be happy.
Since at the end of all you shall be nothingness,
dream that you are no more, and already be happy.

How long shall I cast stones into the sea!
I am sickened by the idolaters of the pagoda:
Khayyâm! Who can assure us that he will dwell in Hell?
Who then ever visited Hell? Who ever returned from Heaven?

Khayyâm, who laboured at the tents of wisdom,
fell into the furnace of sorrow and was consumed in a single stroke;
the shears of destiny cut the rope of his tent,
and the merchant of hope sold him for a song.

Khayyâm, why weep thus over your sins?
What do you gain by giving yourself over to such sorrow?
Since Mercy is not for the righteous,
and awakens only at the sound of our sins, why lament?

17- Here we find a certain mystical tendency in the search for truth. This series of quatrains allows us to put forward the idea of meditative retreat and reflection through mystical rituals. (12 quatrains)

So long as I have a little bread within reach of my hand,
a gourd of wine, and a morsel of meat,
and the two of us can sit together in solitude,
no sultan shall have me as a guest at his most sumptuous feasts.

What I desire is a drop of ruby-coloured wine and a book of verse,
and half a loaf of bread, enough to sustain my life;
and if I am then seated beside you, even in some deserted and desolate place,
I shall be happier than in a sultan’s kingdom.

O soul, if you can cleanse yourself of the dust of your body,
a naked spirit, you shall soar into the sky.
The Empyrean shall be your dwelling, yet may it be to your shame
if you come to it while still an inhabitant of the earth.

Last night I shattered my cup against a stone;
my head spun at having been able to do such a thing,
and the cup said to me in its mystic tongue:
“I was like you; you shall be like me one day.”

If you desire to journey towards Him, leave wife and children;
courageously part from your kinsfolk and your friends.
Whoever is upon your road delays you—
how can you travel with such obstacles?… Sweep them aside!

Beyond the day of Creation, beyond the heavens, my soul
sought the Tablet and the Kalam, and Heaven and Hell;
at last the master spoke to me, he whose mind is full of clarity:
“The Tablet and the Kalam, Heaven and Hell are within you.”

In the cell and the school, in the monastery and the synagogue,
take shelter those who dread Hell and seek Heaven.
He who knows the secrets of God
sows no such seeds in the heart of his heart.

O heart, leave for a while the company of those sick with love;
cease for a moment to be absorbed by these frivolous things;
go and haunt the threshold of the dervishes—
perhaps you too must be for a moment among the Accepted?

Those whose beliefs are founded on hypocrisy
seek to draw a distinction between the soul and the body.
As for me, I know that wine alone holds the answer to the riddle,
and that it gives awareness of a perfect unity.

We have preferred a quiet corner and two loaves of bread to the world,
and we have weaned ourselves from desire for its wealth and magnificence.
We have bought poverty with our heart and our soul;
we have, in poverty, discovered great riches.

For the one who understands the mysteries of the world,
joy and sorrow are identical.
Since good and evil must both come to an end,
what does it matter whether all is affliction or remedy?

Dervish, tear from your body this veil flowered with arabesques,
rather than sacrifice your body to that veil.
Go, cast over your shoulders the coarse robe of Poverty,
and drums shall beat royal marches for you within your heart.

Miscellaneous: these quatrains do not convey a particular message: (19 quatrains)

The wine has the red of roses, the glass is full of rosewater,
perhaps!
Within the crystal casket lies a purest ruby,
perhaps!
Within the water is a liquid diamond,
perhaps!
The moonlight is the veil of the sun,
perhaps!

So much generosity, so much tenderness at the start! Why?
And having drenched me in delights and caresses—why?
Now that you think only of tearing my heart apart,
what have I done to you? Once more, why?

Here below, it is better for you to make few friends;
step outside yourself only for brief encounters.
The one whose arm seems to you a support—
examine him closely, and beware.

My heart said to me: “I have an ardent desire for inspired knowledge:
instruct me, if you are able.”
I said “Alif”; my heart replied: “Say no more;
if the One is in the house, one letter is enough.”

O you whose cheek is fashioned after the pattern of wild roses!
You whose face is cast like that of the idols of China,
yesterday your amorous glance turned the King of Babylon
into a bishop whom the player manoeuvres upon the chessboard.

Of those who draw pure wine from dates,
and of those who spend the night in prayer,
not one stands on solid ground—all are drowning;
there is One who watches, the others are asleep.

The day is fair, the breeze is warm and pure;
the rain has washed away the dust that dulled the roses’ cheeks.
The nightingale says to the rose, in the ancient and sacred tongue:
“All your life, intoxicate yourself with sweet songs and perfumes!”

O Shah, the stars have destined you for the throne of Khosrô;
they have saddled for you the imperial steed.
When your golden-hooved courser stirs
and sets foot upon the ground, the soil is gilded.

From the bosom of the clouds, the heavens rain down flowers;
one would say they are scattering blossoms across the garden.
Into a lily-cup I pour rose-coloured wine,
just as the violet clouds shed jasmine.

Here is the season when the earth adorns itself beneath the spring breezes,
and lets eyes open, full of hope for the rain.
The hands of Moses seem to silver the young branches;
the breath of Jesus rises from the earth.

Every morning the dew pearls the tulips;
the violets bow their heads in the garden.
In truth, nothing delights me like the rosebud
that seems to gather its silken tunic around itself.

If you will listen to me, I give you this counsel:
for the love of God, do not put on the robe of hypocrisy.
The life to come is for ever, this world is but a moment;
do not sell the kingdom of eternity for a single second.

Look upon my merits one by one, forgive my sins by the ten;
forgive every past sin—the reckoning rests with God.
Let neither air nor wind fan your hatred;
forgive me, by the dust of the tomb of Mohamed!

I am not always master of myself… what can I do?
And I suffer for my deeds… what can I do?
Truly, I believe in Your generous forgiveness,
so ashamed am I to think that You have seen my deeds… yet, what can I do?

In loving you I incur reproach for a hundred sins,
and if I fail in this pledge, I pay a penalty.
If all my life I remain faithful to your cruelty, please God,
I shall have a lighter burden to bear until the Day of Judgement.

Look at the misdeeds of this celestial vault,
and see this empty world… since friends have departed.
As much as you can, live a moment for yourself;
taste only the present—the past has the odour of the Dead.

This celestial vault, for my ruin and yours,
takes aim at our pure souls, mine and yours.
Sit down upon the grass, my Idol—before long,
this very grass will grow from my dust and yours.

See, the breeze has torn the robe of the rose,
of the rose with which the nightingale was enamoured;
must we weep over it, must we weep over ourselves?
Death will come to strip our petals, and other roses will bloom again.

You feed only upon the Smoke from the kitchen of the World;
how long will you lament over being and non-being?
The capital you covet wears away in mending many breaches,
yet you waste your time reckoning up a treasure that does not belong to you.

18- Finally, there is a group of miscellaneous quatrains devoid of any particular message. (19 quatrains)

perhaps!

perhaps!
Within the water is a liquid diamond,
perhaps!

how long will you lament over being and non-being?
The capital you covet wears away in mending many breaches,
yet you waste your time reckoning up a treasure that does not belong to you.

In sum, these broad groupings provide sufficient elements to imagine that Khayyâm, poet and scholar, is one and the same person. He employs a poetic form of folkloric origin as a vehicle of culture and knowledge, integrates within it the philosophical viewpoints of his master Avicenna in the form of questioning and irony, and makes use of signifiers and concepts linked to astronomy. The themes found in the poems signed by his hand are wholly consistent with the body of work surmised to be from his pen. Everywhere, political power and religions are criticised.

Questions arise, however. Do so many signifiers impel us towards the stars and Heaven? Does this emphasis placed on the importance of reasoning, in place of beliefs, not constitute a bridge towards the thought of a mathematician, philosopher, and astronomer?

Yet this debate leads us astray from our path. We wish to devote ourselves to understanding a major work born of a culture, transmitted by anonymous poets as a heritage of humanity.

The profound message of these poems has aroused considerable attention and curiosity. Why, then, should we not believe that we find here a genuine vehicle of Persian culture, on a par with esoteric mysticism and the epic of the Book of Kings?

Perhaps here we may develop a new idea. The contemporary rise of a certain atheist and secular esotericism, following upon shamanic experiences several millennia old, might express an independent line—independent of religions on the one hand, and of philosophy on the other.

“Flee the study of all the sciences—that is better;
plait playfully the curls of the beloved—that is better;
before fate spills your blood,
spill the blood of the bottle into your cup—that is better.”

Here we find a declaration that urges us to abandon both worlds—the metaphysical and the physical—in favour of a third place.

“Ah! My beard has swept the threshold of the tavern!
I have bidden farewell to the good and evil of both worlds;
if they fall into my street like two balls,
you will find me, if you seek me, sleeping the drunkard’s sleep.”

This third form of existence in the universe struggles to survive, owing to the influence of science and institutions.

I know the outward aspect of being and non-being;
I know the inward depth of all that is high and low;
yet what shame upon my knowledge
if I recognised anything higher than drunkenness!

Last evening I went into a potter’s workshop;
I saw two thousand pots—some were speaking, others kept silent.
Suddenly, one of them cried out in an aggressive voice:
where, then, is the potter, the buyer, and the merchant?

In conclusion, one should retain from these quatrains a message of wisdom and common sense. Any single system produces futile wars between believers and non-believers. No one knows the truth—to such a point that discussion around the “system” becomes pointless.

With this method of analysis established, this work could be pursued further. A more meticulous study of movements of thought in Persian lands between the tenth and nineteenth centuries, and of the links between signifiers and literature, could serve as an avenue for deepening this work.

[1] Different ways of writing Khayyâm: khayyâm, Khayyām, Khayyam, Kháyyám, Khayam, Omar Khayyām; Omar Khayam; ʿUmar Khayyām; ´Umar-i-Khayyám; Omar Khèyam; Omar Kheyyam; Omar Keyyam; Omar Xayām; Omar Chajjám; Omar Alkhayyámí; Omar-i-Khajjam; Omar Qayyam; Omar Caiiam; Omar Chiam. …

[2] We use the poems of Khayyâm translated by Charles Grolleau, published in 1902 and reissued in 2008, translated from the Persian on the basis of the 1460 manuscript of the “Bodleian Library” in Oxford—amounting to 158 quatrains, translated into English by FitzGerald (1859).

[3] “There are few works that are, as much as the quatrains of Omar Khayam, admired, rejected, hated, slandered, condemned, dissected, and that attain universal renown while nonetheless remaining little known.”

[4] Chronological bibliography of translations of the quatrains of Khayyâm: http://biblioweb.hypotheses.org/5492

[5] Foroughi–Ghani; 1943; “Quatrains of Khayyâm”, Tehran,
[6] Ṣādiq Hidāyat; 1993; “Les chants d’Omar Khayam” [The Songs of Omar Khayyam]; critical edition, Paris; translated by M.-F. Farzaneh and J. Malaplate,
[7] Attar: born in 1059, died in 1146; Ferdowsi: born around 940, died around 1020; Khayyâm: born in 1048, died in 1131.
[8] Abd al-Ḥusayn Zarrīnʹkūb, 2000; “Dū qarn-i sukūt (Two Centuries of Silence)”, Sukhan; Tehran

[9] Monteil, Vincent – Mansour, 1983; “Khayyâm Quatrains…”; Sindbad; Paris
[10] La Revue de Téhéran, Iranian cultural monthly in the French language, Issue 59, October 2012: “Khayyâm, regarded during his lifetime as a scholar, is today famous for his poems. Few of his contemporaries knew his quatrains, and rare are the historians of the era who cite him in anthologies of poets. The first to do so was Emâdeddin Kâteb Esfahâni, in his anthology Farid al-Ghasr in 1193, nearly fifty years after Khayyâm’s death.”

[11] “Les quatrains du sage Omar Khayyâm de Nichâpour et de ses épigones” [The Quatrains of the Sage Omar Khayyâm of Nishapur and His Epigones], presentation, translation, and notes [by] Hassan Rezvanian. Paris: Imprimerie nationale, 1992. (La Salamandre) 637 robâyât translated.

[12] Avery, P. and Heath, J., 1979; “The Ruba’iat of Omar Khayyam”, Penguin Books, London, page 21: “the words ‘Authority in Truth’ are the translation of the title ‘Hujjatu’l-Haqq’, used only for very learned men. It was the title used for Avicenna; after Ali ibn Ziad, Khayyâm was the second, known as master prefect of the totality of the exact sciences and philosophy of his age…”

[13] Idem 9, Page 14: “A century after the death of Omar Khayyâm, … Muslims scarcely spared him: ‘an unfortunate philosopher, atheist and materialist,’ said Shaykh Najm ad-Dîn in 1223; ‘a detestable man, yet an astronomer without equal, …’”
[14] Idem 9, Page 14: “However, from the 14th and 15th centuries onwards, manuscript copies of the quatrains multiplied.”

[15] Fauchécour (de), C.-H.; 2006; “Le Divân; Hâfez de Chiraz” [The Divan; Hafez of Shiraz]; Verdier; Paris
[16] Idem 15

[19] Persian literature took as an exemplar the very strong bond between Mahmoud Ghaznavi—one of the major rulers of the Ghaznavid dynasty (975–1187), comprising the regions of Khorasan, Ghazni, and the Punjab—and his slave Ayaz.
