en.body_markdown:
## Introduction

Analysing the approach of mystics is an interesting endeavour, yet one that has very few references on which to rely, even though these phenomena exist across all cultures and since the most ancient times. Since the discovery of psychoanalysis and up to the present day, this subject has not been the occasion for extensive research. This text is therefore a plea for launching this multidisciplinary research, which touches equally upon psychology, literature, the arts, theology, etc.

This work is also useful insofar as the phenomenon of mystics is a mystery and represents a by no means negligible historical presence, one that can undoubtedly help us to understand a little "something" more about man.

This task proves very difficult, for we find ourselves facing a paradox: a psychoanalyst links the unconscious to his or her conception of the world—in other words, to the field of signifiers, to the field of speech. Yet mystics belong to a category that operates "outside speech".

They are very ancient and vary greatly across different civilisations; they mingle with traditions, myths, religions, sects, brotherhoods, abuses of power, and magic…

All the utterances of mystics are heavily coded because of their fear of others, problems of comprehension, and issues of interpretation. They are regarded as "mad", possessed, "outside the field", outside religion, outside systems, outside institutions. They are unsettling because they speak through metaphors. The Indian, Iranian, or Arabic literatures about them are very rich and have been translated, yet their cataloguing remains relatively recent.

In an attempt to articulate our definition of mystics, let us first examine their common characteristics. In every case, the mystic is one who is persuaded that he or she hears a voice or sees "other things". These things are communicated through him or her. There is no monopoly reserved for prophets; anyone can be a recipient of the message. It is no different for other subjects in their ways of being. Unlike with prophets, everyone can find his or her own path there.

Another common point: the source of the message resides within him or her (esoteric), and this inner world is linked with love and a state of well-being.

All mystics declare themselves different from others. Their "supreme" state of difference is to manage to live like others and in the midst of others, while remaining a "master". The term "mystic" ("mystique"), which appeared in the French language as early as the fourteenth century, comes from the Latin "mysticus", from the Greek "mustikos", and derives from "mystery", "mysterium", "mustérion", and ultimately from "mustès", which means "initiated into the mysteries".

In other cultures, mystics are named differently: knowers, sages, those "set apart", one "who abandons", one who is "beyond need" (he has everything, he is inwardly rich). In Western culture, this term "mystic" is often applied to women.

Similarities are also observed between the discourses of mystical subjects in the various situations in which they find themselves. Using different signifiers, they speak of love, of a state of well-being, of being "outside time", "outside space". They speak of union, of a certain type of absolute knowledge that has no need for research since they have already found everything. Mystical experiences, prophets, and the psychotic state all represent a path of no return.

As with an absolute passion, perseverance is indispensable here, as if there were another absolute reality already acquired and irreversible. Once the process is set in motion, they do not turn back.

Can one, within the field of speech, explain a state that is "outside the field"? Everything that lies outside the field of speech is expressed only with difficulty in words: colour, music, art, dance…

In the case of the "outside-the-field", dream and life have the same value, the same reality. The miracle or the hallucination, at the moment it is expressed, has always already taken place "before". Putting it into words comes afterwards; the voice is always in the past, "never present".

All of them declare themselves incapable of adequately explaining their experience through words, which makes receiving their speech and any possible interpretation very difficult. The richness of the texts in the literature concerning the various fields of our research is such that it is impossible for us to carry through a study equal to our ambition.

Moreover, a confusion is observed between the subject of our research—which analyses discourses—taking them as truth, and our faith: for we separate the words of prophets addressed to their disciples from what they say about their own state. The object of our study does not deal with socio-historical fields, nor with the knowledge of cults.

There also exist correlations between this mystical state and various other situations:

- Near-death experiences (NDE)

- Prophets

- Hallucinations of psychotics

- Drug addicts

- High-level athletes

- Patients returning from a comatose state

- Certain cases of hypnosis, or of an altered state.

For all those who have lived through these various experiences, there is "the moment when there is nothing" and "the moment when there is everything": "I hear nothing anymore, I forget everything", "I am everywhere, all-powerful, I see everything". The body image and its comfort are forgotten. The body no longer experiences real needs; it becomes empty. The experience unfolds with its message, beyond carnal life.

To better understand this quest for the mystical state, can we not draw a certain parallel between the approaches of the field of psychoanalysis and certain relatively advanced types of mystical schools?

Stages of the Mystics' Research — Stages of the Psychoanalytic Cure

1
"Does anything else exist?" Questioning
The analysand's demand

2
In both cases, the "driving force" is feeling for someone; Love
Transference

3
Knowledge; To be acquired through work
Unconscious knowledge

4
Independence; I am old enough to move forward alone
Counter-transference

5
Fusion into a whole, to the point of disappearance; Unity
Symbolic castration

6
Astonishment — Elucidation:
the encounter with "the unconscious"

7
Destitution and "death":
The outside exists, yet one is no longer subjected to it — Exchange of place between inside/outside, inversion of the torus

Although we have been able to draw this parallel, distinct elements nevertheless remain. Analysis does not address the question of the hereafter. It begins with the Law (continuation of the generations, prohibition of incest, of death…), whereas the mystic is "outside the law".

The mystic seeks jouissance, whereas the analysand seeks to identify and detach from the objet petit a ("A"), cause of his or her desire.

Yet in both approaches, the subject of study is the interior, the psyche of the subject, and it evolves within a predominantly oral culture. Transference operates between two individuals (Master/disciple and Analyst/Analysand). In both cases, the processes involve a long quest in which the subject's discourse is crucial, whereas on the side of the Master/Analyst words are few, dense, and significant. The interpretation of a gesture or a spoken word "awakens" the individual. In both approaches, the work is carried out upon oneself and is situated outside the social field and any institution. The method is rather that of apprenticeship; there is neither text, nor diploma, nor written record, and the aim is always to find a certain inner harmony.

Individual healing takes precedence over the relation to the social sphere and to society. If there is change, it is bound to the individual. Mythological elements are omnipresent (Oedipus, Narcissus, Eros…), and this field is linked to other fields such as poetry, literature, art, and psychology. Both undertakings of research into oneself serve rather as a set of waymarks: the subject searches, and the guide lets him or her know that he or she is on the right path, that he or she is "on the verge of knowing".

One can also compare mystical tendencies with other institutions, religions, sects, schools, and research units. The modes of learning are comparable. In scientific and religious experience, there is only one path: for science, it is the identification of a palpable "cause and effect" and the reproduction of clearly identified elements; for religion, the path passes through the voice of the prophet. Instead of saying "seek your own way", they say "follow me". Initiation and autonomy run counter to the principle according to which "the further you advance, the more you shall obey". Here, the message is individual; there is no group work. The first questions to ask oneself are "Who am I?", "What am I doing here?".

In religion, the definition of God is singular and already given. By contrast, the mystic has his or her own definition of God, with his or her own foundational signifiers. Thus, Ibn Arabi, in his quest for a "greatest name" for God, takes up his own signifiers of the "Name-of-the-Father".

Similarly, within a brotherhood, all uniformly renounce sex, money, and power… all things quite petty in view of the Absolute represented by "fana", absolute fusion.

Can mystical experience also be regarded as a drug? The initiate will generally reply that this is not the case at all, that the need he or she feels is linked to the "surplus" brought by his or her practice, and that omitting it would bring him or her back down from the qualitative plane to which this particular state of consciousness elevates him or her.

## The Mystics in Their Own Words

Let us cite a few ideas drawn from the Book of the Saints by Attar, the great eleventh-century Iranian mystic:

Fear is just as important as love, obedience, gratitude, asking for forgiveness of sins, fusion, guilt—"like a lost child before its parents"—and the renunciation of every possible pleasure. Why is a subject drawn to the mystical path? They call themselves mad for forsaking reason. Their teaching advocates killing the "ego" in the seven states cited in the previous chapter, attaining perfection by making oneself blind, deaf, and mute, and thus arriving, by closing the sensory doors to the outside, at fusion: "How long shall there be between you and me, the 'I' and the 'you'? Remove my 'I' from between us; make it become everything in your 'you' and no longer be my 'I'."

Another eleventh-century Iranian mystic, Mansur al-Hallaj, stated the following principle: "Whoever renounces this lower world sees his sensual person rise to asceticism. Whoever renounces himself, it is his soul that he sees rise to asceticism." A mystic perceives himself as unique, in fusion with God, with whom he forms a single whole.

This exclusive love leads to detachment from the world, despite the obstacles to be overcome, the pleasures of this world, associating with people to whom they do not become attached, and sensual appetites… They must attain humility.

Despite the differences observed in their paths, tools, languages, and vocabularies, there exists only one kind of mystic: "outside signifiers", "outside the system", "outside intuition". Ultimately, they name their goal "Him" or "the thing", as if to personalise the absence of any naming of that goal. They have already named the thing. The means employed are highly varied, yet can be grouped around a few types: physical practices (postures, breathing techniques, etc.), chemical practices (cannabis, alcohol, tea, etc.), practices linked to the psyche (use of sounds, prayers, mental imagery) such as the method of Zekr (repeating the same words or phrases for several hours), or finally what the medical literature calls "relaxation".

## Mysticism and Psychoanalysis

(In preparing this chapter, I drew upon the work of several Lacanian psychoanalysts, in particular those who were kind enough to allow us to benefit from the results of their research on the Internet. My thanks to them all.)

Mystical experiences interest us here on at least three counts:

- Experiences of a mystical appearance or nature occur in certain delusional individuals

- The great mystics themselves have at times lived through hallucinatory-type experiences

- They describe motives, means, stages, states of consciousness, and physiological effects of their practice.

For a comparison between these two fields, let us first quote S. Freud: "We can hope to arrive through the analysis of dreams at a knowledge of man's archaic heritage, to discover what is psychically innate (…). Psychoanalysis is entitled to claim a high place among the sciences that endeavour to reconstruct the earliest and most obscure phases of the origins of humanity."

"There is an instinctive knowledge in the child, notably sexual, which would constitute the nucleus of the unconscious, a sort of primitive mental activity, (…) of our psyche, which is formed in layers." He further cites "dream-material that does not derive from the dreamer's experience but from his archaic heritage", and asks further on: "Have you noticed that infantile theories of sexuality are indispensable for understanding myth? (…) the regressive archaic is what must be grasped in symbolism as well as in mythology and the development of language."

One can also find in various texts by S. Freud notions such as primal repression, primordial symbolisation, the unnameable thing, the drive, and sublimation—an activity of sensual origin, desexualised through narcissism, which itself is oriented towards the ego-ideal.

As for Jung, his status as a theorist of the unconscious and an experimenter lends quite particular weight to his opinion on the afterlife. Long before he himself experienced a Near-Death Experience, his conception of the unconscious and his interest in metapsychical phenomena led him to a break with Freud. It is well known that the latter, anxious to preserve an image of scientificity for psychoanalysis, judged Jung's conceptions to be wholly unrealistic and incompatible with the rational thought upon which he intended to establish his new science.

For S. Freud, there exists in the unconscious a "black box", the unnameable thing, yet he goes no further in his research.

Following this separation, Jung definitively abandoned the principle of an unconscious governed by the deterministic laws of a biological mechanics, which some then claimed would sooner or later be reduced to an equation. In his search for an alternative to this model, he took an interest very early on in Eastern philosophies and opted for a certain idea of reincarnation. At the end of his life, his judgement had not altered.

Psychoanalysis concerns itself with problems posed in language and by language; it therefore attends to the body insofar as it is a speaking body. "The body functions above all in language," says Lacan. Psychoanalysis institutes the body as language and treats the body in its enunciation. Yet in literature, what body is in question? It is a constructed and fictional body—that is to say, a body worked upon by language and offered to interpretation. Every reading is interpretative. And interpretation is fundamental in the constitution of the literary object. From the body of flesh to the body of fiction, there is more than one link, psychoanalysis teaches us. The real body and the textual body are constituted by language. And the body is of the same essence as writing: a written object.

We wish to reposition the notion of body image onto the terrain of psychoanalysis, which posits the lived body as belonging to the register of the signifier—a signifier that is subject to interpretation. In doing so, we situate ourselves within a Lacanian perspective. As is known, Lacan inscribed the subject within the problematic of the signifier (this is structural theory). More precisely, we wish to try to show what is at stake with the mystical body: the mystical body enables us to think through what is at stake with the sexed body—more particularly, desire, the Other, jouissance, suffering, language, and the Law. The mystical attitude finds in faith the means to exalt a sexuality, and yet more precisely an "erotics of the Body-God". The spiritualisation of the body asserts itself at the very same time as the vision of desire is emancipated. It is merely the reverse side of sexualisation. Let us quote J. Lacan: "the mystic is a lover. Love is an intoxication."

"It is like Saint Teresa: you need only go and look at Bernini's statue in Rome to understand immediately that she is experiencing jouissance—there is no doubt about it. And of what does she experience this jouissance? It is clear that the essential testimony of the mystics is precisely to say that they experience it, yet know nothing of it."

The gaze of the passionate lover and, to take up the paradigm of courtly love—that "meteor" which gave Lacan so much to think about, and this more particularly, that to sublimate is to put an object in the place of the Thing—what is the "nothing" on earth that he most desired, regarding courtly ideology. He remarks that, according to the latter, "love is the only feeling capable of disincarnating the body of its desire". The mystical body plays out in the register of the inside and the outside. Mystics express their experience through the senses of the body, and the outside of the body is what must be subdued. One of the mystical approaches, indeed, consists in controlling the senses.

More generally, there is a putting to death of whatever belongs to the order of the drives and desire: the sacrifice necessary to be brought into the presence of the Other (God), the inside, experienced as a positive interior. "Empty your interior so as to see within it the light of knowledge."

This mystical marriage consists in incorporating God right down to His effects: ecstasy. The carnal reality of the external body is therefore extremely important for this marriage to live. Thus, one might try to see whether the mystical grasp is not that of an "excentration"—that is to say, the experience of a being whose core might well lie at the periphery of the self, there where God envelops it. God is absent, yet He leaves traces, "touches", "impressions" upon the body. It is within these traces left by the Other that jouissance is inscribed. The human body, psychoanalysis teaches us, is primitively summoned by suffering. Suffering is part of the feast!

We know that the boundaries of body image are acquired during the process of the child's defusion from its mother. If this catastrophe of detachment enables the subject to come into being, it also forever seals the subject's lack-of-being in the Other. In his or her faith, the mystic relives something of the child's rupture with its mother… This jouissance translates into a particular style of writing, for there is no mystical discourse outside its own mode of expression.

Lacan brings phallic jouissance close to that of the mystics—or rather, he finds in mystical jouissance an idea of phallic jouissance. It is indeed beyond the phallic term embodied by a man that feminine jouissance is addressed, in a place where prohibition would no longer hold sway, where the truth of jouissance might be glimpsed. Mystics are those who have crossed that limit where love and jouissance can still be encumbered by sex.

Thus the supplementary jouissance experienced by a woman, beyond that which she derives from embodying a man's fantasy, presents itself in a total absence of signification. That is why it manifests equally through the cry, which delimits a boundary of the signifier and which, like a saying without words, makes a central void resound at the heart of language. It is the echo of the lost jouissance of God, which "makes it such that, starting from language, no relations can be established between sexed beings".

Yet according to J. Lacan: "saying it all is impossible, materially—the words are lacking; it is indeed through this impossible that truth holds to the Real" (the same holds true in jouissance). For J. Lacan, the jouissance of the other is lived, not spoken. That which excludes the Symbolic returns in the Real and, cast outside, reaches the ego without passing through repression (such is the case with the notion of the "curtain" perceived by mystics). The jouissance of being is equally and indistinctly called the jouissance of the other. Which other is this? The Body as other, a radical other, outside language, the seat of a jouissance bound to the Thing impossible to symbolise.

All jouissances are jouissances of the Other: the jouissance of the body outside language (the Real), the jouissance that passes through the Law (the Symbolic), and the third, supplementary jouissance, situated beyond castration and its symbol, which is feminine jouissance—the jouissance of the Other sex.

This is why we recognise, in a final synthesis, the jouissance of being (of the mythical thing), phallic jouissance (of the signifier, linguistic), the jouissance of the Other (feminine – ineffable), and the jouissance lost through castration—mythical and linked to the Thing prior to phallic signification, appreciable in certain forms of the Thing.

Because it is lost, it IS; because jouissance is lost, the Real—the impossible—is what one pursues. Speech separates and restores jouissance, yet by diminishing it, by marking it with a loss that is the insurmountable difference between the signifier and the referent, between speech and things. Jouissance will only be possible by traversing the field of words, yet it will be another jouissance: missed and evocative, nostalgic.

Originary jouissance is that of the Thing, a jouissance prior to the Law. It is a forbidden, accursed jouissance, which will have to be refused and replaced by a promise of phallic jouissance resulting from the acceptance of castration. "You cannot prove to yourself what you have lost."

Castration, for Lacan, is salvation, not the threat; the real threat would be for castration to be lacking. For the newborn, the ego and the world are indistinct, the world then being essentially the mother's body. This originary and mythical thing, prior to all differentiation, is designated by Freud by the name "real-ego". Speech is always the speech of the Law that prohibits jouissance.

fa.body_markdown:
## روان‌کاوی، روان‌کاو و لائیسیته

از لاکان نقل می‌کنم: «فروید از روان‌کاو چیزی بیش از ایمان به وجود ناخودآگاه (یعنی دانشی که گفتمانِ آن در بر دارد) و نه پالایشِ قدرتِ خویش، نمی‌خواهد. ایمان در اینجا به یک آیینِ راه‌یابی، یعنی روان‌کاوی، وابسته است که ناخودآگاه را به کنش درمی‌آورد و با گسستنِ آن از بدن، بدان عینیت می‌بخشد. این جداییِ میان ساحت نمادین و بدن که در ساحت واقعی تجربه می‌شود، به روی هر سوژهٔ زبان گشوده است، زیرا در آن جز گفتار چیزی به شمار نمی‌آید. این گشودگیِ هستی به روی محروم‌ترین کسان، به روی روان‌نژند‌ها و چه بسا دیوانگان، و این باور به وجود ناخودآگاه، خود همچنان یک آیینِ راه‌یابی است، اما این دسترسیِ همگان به گفتمانِ علم، سنتزی تازه از دانش و امر جهان‌شمول را پدید می‌آورد.

آیا نزد فروید، این از سرِ مهر و شفقت نیست که به درماندگیِ موجودات سخنگو رخصت داده است به خود بگویند که — از آن رو که ناخودآگاه وجود دارد — چیزی هست که استعلا می‌یابد، براستی استعلا می‌یابد، و چیزی نیست مگر همان که این گونه در آن مسکن دارد، یعنی زبان؟ آیا، آری، این از سرِ مهر و شفقت نیست که به او این مژده را بدهیم که در آنچه زندگیِ روزمرهٔ اوست، به واسطهٔ زبان از پشتوانه‌ای با عقلانیتی بیش از آنچه می‌نمود برخوردار است، و اینکه از هم‌اکنون در آنجا مایه‌ای از فرزانگی هست؟» (لاکان، «باز هم» [Encore]، ص ۸۸)

من از این گفتار سه عنصر کانونی را برمی‌گیرم: ایمانِ روان‌کاو، جایگاه زبان، و پدیدار شدنِ فرزانگی؛ تا آن‌جا که این مثلث به کارِ تحلیلی کالبد می‌بخشد.

نخستین برخورد‌های من با روان‌کاوانِ باورمند آسان نبود، زیرا خود به‌ژرفی لائیک بودم و برآمده از آموزش روان‌کاوانه و نشان‌دار از اصلِ لائیسیته توسط بنیان‌گذارِ آن و جانشینانش، و از این رو نمی‌توانستم راهِ برون‌رفتِ درخوری بیابم. با این حال، رفتار‌های آنان را سالم و کارِ بالینی‌شان را هم‌ترازِ روان‌کاوانِ خداناباور می‌یافتم. این پارادوکس آنگاه گشوده شد که در تجربهٔ کاریِ خویش دریافتم باور‌های روان‌کاو تا چه اندازه بیرون از پرانتزِ کاناپه و صندلیِ تحلیل باقی می‌مانند. در اینجا می‌کوشم مسیرِ فکریِ خود را بازپیموده، این دریافت را روشن‌تر بیان کنم: روان‌کاوی، در هستیِ خویش، تنها به دستِ آن سوژهٔ لائیک می‌تواند به اجرا درآید که روان‌کاو است.

به همین سان، انسان‌شناسی که با مطالعهٔ ساختار‌های گوناگونِ اجتماعیِ موجودات سخنگو، از کهن‌ترین آن‌ها تا به امروز و در سرتاسر کرهٔ زمین، می‌کوشد پاره‌ای نقاط مشترک بیابد، خود نیز به‌ژرفی لائیک است، زیرا هیچ ارزش‌های پایهٔ از پیش تعیین‌شده‌ای در کار نیست. روان‌کاوی نیز در این نکته در همان راستا گام برمی‌دارد و این امر از زمان فروید آغاز شده است؛ او میدانِ کاوش‌های خود را به روی نخستین انسان‌ها می‌گشاید و نظریه‌اش را دربارهٔ توتم‌ها و تابو‌ها، حیوان قربانی، خدای دادگر و سرشتاً نیک‌خواه — که والا‌ترین والایشِ عقدهٔ والدینیِ ماست —، پدر آغازین، و پیوند میان گناه نخستین، احساس گناه و خدا-پدر بسط می‌دهد. او نشان می‌دهد که خدا و شیطان، پدر را به‌عنوان الگوی آغازینِ خود دارند. پژوهش‌هایش او را به انسان‌شناسی رهنمون می‌شود. فروید بار‌ها خاستگاه دین را مبتنی بر حقیقت تاریخی تعریف می‌کند و آن را با حقیقت مادی و حقیقت واقعی می‌سنجد.

انسان‌شناسیِ معاصر که از نظر ریشه‌شناسی به‌عنوان «علمِ انسان» تعریف شده است، خاستگاه‌های فکری، الهام‌های ایدئولوژیک و الزام‌های عملیِ بسیار کهنی دارد. موضوع‌های آن از تنوعی گسترده برخوردارند: فرهنگ، ساختار‌های اجتماعی، عناصر پایدار و دگرگونی‌های جوامع انسانی، و پیوند‌های آن‌ها با محیط زیست طبیعی. این دانش از این پس به‌عنوان علم گوناگونی‌های فرهنگی و اجتماعی، و به‌طور کلی، به‌عنوان علم انسان در جامعه تعریف می‌شود. بدین سان، پروژهٔ انسان‌شناسی، مفصل‌بندیِ نسبت‌های میان امر بومی و امر جهانی، و اندیشیدن به «دیگری» و «همان» در گوناگون‌ترین وجوه آن‌هاست.

لائیسیته موضوعی مربوط به موجودِ سخنگو، یعنی فرزندِ انسان خردمند (هومو ساپینس-ساپینس) است: در تلقیِ آن هیچ تفاوتی میان مردمان وجود ندارد. احترام به زندگیِ این کودک در شهر، از بیش از ۴۰۰۰۰ سال پیش و در سرتاسر زمینِ ما، به‌خوبی ژرفای این لائیسیته را تعریف می‌کند. در حقیقت، تفاوت‌های اجتماعی، فرهنگی، زبانی، شیوه‌های زیست و باور‌ها... برای انسان‌های خردمند (هومو ساپینس-ساپینس) وجود نداشت. چنان‌که سعدی، شاعر ایرانی سدهٔ چهاردهم، می‌گوید:

> بنی‌آدم اعضای یک پیکرند / که در آفرینش ز یک گوهرند

موضوع مطالعهٔ روان‌کاوی نیز موجودِ سخنگوست. آن‌کس که سخن می‌گوید، ناخودآگاهِ خویش را شکل می‌دهد. ناخودآگاه ساختارمند است و از قاعده‌ای دقیق در شکل‌گیری و کارکرد تبعیت می‌کند که موضوع پژوهش روان‌کاوانه است. شکل‌گیری و کارکرد این ناخودآگاه بر پایهٔ میلِ سوژهٔ سخنگو و گنجینهٔ دال‌ها بنیان نهاده شده است.

با دریافت اینکه شرایط بنیادینِ اجرای لائیسیته و روان‌کاوی از نخستین روز‌های بشریت به یکدیگر می‌رسند، روان‌کاوی نمی‌تواند جز لائیک باشد. از فروید نقل می‌کنم: «روان‌کاوی از هیچ جهان‌بینی و از هیچ تلقی خاصی از زندگیِ نیک پشتیبانی نمی‌کند، و همین امر آن را به طرز شگفت‌انگیزی به دولتِ لائیک نزدیک می‌سازد، ... در عین حال که نظام فکری‌ای در پیوند با امر جهان‌شمول باقی می‌ماند.» روان‌کاوی به سوژه گونه‌ای دیگر از شنیدنِ خویشتن و دیگری (دگرشنیدن) می‌بخشد: رواداری...

حکایت: یک بانوی روان‌کاو در سال‌های پایانیِ کارش، در سمیناری، هنگام گفت‌وگو دربارهٔ «چیز فرویدی»، «فانتاسم آغازین» و «آنچه سبب می‌شود انسان سخن بگوید»، رشتهٔ سخن را به دست می‌گیرد و با تأکید بر نیازِ کودک به این چیز برای سخن گفتن و دست یافتن به دال، به شرح موضوع می‌پردازد. او در ادامه به وضعیت خویش می‌پردازد؛ نقل می‌کنم: «حتی اگر یک عمر گفته و تکرار کرده باشم که انسان، خدا را ابداع کرده است، زیرا به چیزی نیاز داشت تا خود را سر پا نگه دارد، امروز از خود می‌پرسم آیا من نیز همچون همان کودک نیستم که به چیزی نیاز دارد... برای نمونه، خدا.»

شما را به سفری کوتاه در مفاهیمِ بنیادِ نظریهٔ روان‌کاوانه و لائیسیته فرا می‌خوانم، تا سپس اثرِ این نظریه را بر کار بالینی، و سرانجام چند تحلیل از گفتارِ روان‌کاوانِ اهل ایمان را بنگریم.

## ناخودآگاه و باور

فروید در مکاتبه‌هایش با کشیش پفیستر می‌گوید: «روان‌کاوی به خودیِ خود، نه مذهبی است و نه ضدمذهبی. ابزاری است بی‌طرف که هم دینیان و هم لائیک‌ها می‌توانند از آن بهره ببرند، به شرط آنکه تنها در خدمت رهاییِ انسان‌های رنجور باشد.» فروید به تفصیل باورِ دینی را به پرسش کشیده است. او حتی امید داشت که جهان‌بینیِ علمی‌ای که در برابرِ آن می‌نهاد، بتواند «توهمِ دین» را بی‌فایده سازد.

استدلال‌های فروید در برابر نیاز به باور کردن به‌طور کلی، و باور دینی به‌طور خاص چه بود؟ از دیدِ فروید، باور دینی از جنس توهم است. منظور فروید از توهم، بازنمایی‌ای است که لزوماً نادرست نیست، اما از تأیید شدن به دستِ واقعیت چشم می‌پوشد، یعنی برای فردِ باورمند در فراسوی این تأیید جای می‌گیرد. از این رو، نقد فروید در اثباتِ بیهودگیِ دین نیست، بلکه در کشفِ انگیزه‌های ناخودآگاهِ آن است. زیرا نیروی توهم — که به آن امکان می‌دهد از تأیید واقعیت بی‌نیاز شود — از میلِ مهارناپذیری سرچشمه می‌گیرد که آن را در فانتاسم تحقق می‌بخشد. از نظر فروید، این میلی که بازنماییِ خدا را شکل می‌دهد، بنیاداً به بی‌پناهیِ انسان بازمی‌گردد که خود با نارس‌زاییِ زیست‌شناختیِ او پیوند دارد و انسان را تا دیرزمانی وابسته به مراقبت‌های مادرانه نگاه می‌دارد. بدین ترتیب، فروید ضمن آنکه دین را به‌عنوان یک توهم افشا می‌کند، همواره در لابه‌لای سطور، بر حضورِ گریزناپذیرِ نیاز به باور کردن پای می‌فشارد و آن را — دست‌کم در ادیانِ یکتاپرست — با نیاز به حمایت شدن از سوی پدر یکی می‌داند. او در مقام نظریه‌پرداز، از کتاب «توتم و تابو» در سال ۱۹۱۱ تا «مردِ موسی» (L’Homme Moïse) در سال ۱۹۳۸، همواره موضوع دین را در ذهن داشته است. متن‌های سترگی چون «ناخشنودی در تمدن» یا «آیندهٔ یک توهم» گواهِ این امرند. این درون‌مایه در واقع سراسرِ اندیشهٔ او دربارهٔ فرهنگ و پدیده‌های جمعی را درمی‌نوردد.

واژهٔ یونانیِ لائیکوس (laïkos) به معنای «مردم» است، در برابر کلریکوس (clericos) که بر «کسی که قدرتی دینی در دست دارد» (و به تعمیم، قدرتِ سیاسی یا اقتصادی) دلالت می‌کند. مفهوم لائیسیته که تعریف دقیق آن دشوار است، در غرب بیش از همه به وضعیتی اشاره دارد که در آن شهروندان و دولت از کلیسا‌ها مستقل‌اند. این مفهوم پیش از هر چیز بر یک نظام حقوقی و سیاسیِ جدایی میان دولت و ادیان و بی‌طرفیِ دینیِ دولت دلالت دارد.

بدین سان، کهن‌ترین لایهٔ آن دربردارندهٔ این ایده از لائیسیته به‌مثابه چارچوبی برای هم‌زیستیِ آرام میان چند دین، چند فلسفه و چند فرهنگ است. این چارچوب بی‌طرف می‌نماید. از این رو، لائیسیته را می‌توان در سه ارزش خلاصه کرد: آزادیِ وجدان، پذیرشِ دیگری، و رواداری.

به نوبهٔ خود، روان‌کاوی به استقرار لائیسیته در شهر کمک می‌کند، زیرا دسته‌بندی را بر پایهٔ ساختارِ روان انجام می‌دهد و نه بر پایهٔ معیاری دیگر همچون فقر یا ثروت مادی...

## کار بالینیِ روان‌کاوانه و لائیسیته

میلِ روان‌کاو چنین تعریف می‌شود: «آنچه می‌تواند روان‌کاو را در عملیاتش پشتیبانی کند — به‌عنوان تکیه‌گاهِ احتمالیِ رانه یا وجه فانتاسمیِ کنشِ او — این است که او بر حسبِ یک آرمان، بر پایهٔ بازنمایی‌ای از سرشتِ انسان یا یک رانهٔ فرضیِ درمان‌گری، عمل نمی‌کند؛ اینکه خویشتن را از چنگِ فانتاسم رها می‌سازد، و اینکه کمتر وابسته به این بزرگ‌دیگری است که هر کس در فانتاسم، خود را ابژهٔ آن می‌سازد.» بنابراین، می‌توان گفت: تحلیل‌گر باید به گونه‌ای بی‌طرفی پای‌بند بماند؛ او تحلیل‌شونده را هدایت نمی‌کند، بلکه درمان تحلیلی را هدایت می‌کند، و این بدان معناست که کتابِ تحلیل‌شونده را به دستِ خودِ تحلیل‌شونده بخواناند، زیرا بخش‌هایی بدشکل‌گرفته و نماد‌هایی ناجورچیده‌شده پیرامونِ تروما‌ها در آن وجود دارد. چنان‌که لاکان می‌گوید: «روان‌کاو، به‌عنوان تکیه‌گاهِ انتقال، در مقام سوژهٔ مفروض به دانایی، در پایانِ فرایند به جایگاهِ جانشینِ ابژه آ کوچک فروکاسته می‌شود؛ ابژه‌ای که سرنوشتش کنار نهاده شدن است و نه یک مفهوم است و نه یک دال.» سمینار ژ. لاکان، ۶۸-۱۹۶۷، «کنشِ روان‌کاوانه».

در مورد روان‌کاو، پرسش درست می‌تواند پرس‌وجو دربارهٔ کارکرد و جایگاهِ روان‌کاو باشد. او از یک سو هدایت‌گرِ درمانِ تحلیل‌شونده است و از سوی دیگر سوژهٔ مفروض به دانایی، یا به بیانی دیگر، ساختارِ یک ناخودآگاهِ پیش‌تر تحلیل‌شده و حساس به تفسیر.

درمانِ تحلیلی برای هر سوژه یگانه است، مسیری فردی و ویژه. دال‌هایش از آنِ خود اوست، امیالش، رؤیا‌هایش، و بی‌گمان عناصرِ تفسیر‌هایش نیز همین‌طور. این موضوعِ تعبیرِ رؤیا، که بر اندیشه‌های نهفته استوار است، تفاوتی ژرف با تفسیر‌هایی دارد که بر عناصر دینی، فرهنگی، اجتماعی و جز آن استوارند. نه ناخودآگاهِ جمعی‌ای در کار است، نه رؤیا‌های جمعی، و نه طرح‌های درمانِ جمعی.

لائیسیته، همچون ناخودآگاه، به زندگی معنا نمی‌دهد: هر دو به‌ژرفی بیرون از ایدئولوژی و باور قرار دارند. زیگموند فروید در نوشته‌های فنیِ خویش تصریح می‌کند که در نهایت روان‌کاو تنها با ناخودآگاهِ خود کار می‌کند. باورِ روان‌کاو نه در روشی که با آن درمان را هدایت می‌کند جایی دارد و نه در تفسیر‌هایش، زیرا تفسیر‌های او به دال‌های تحلیل‌شونده پیوند خورده‌اند و نه به دال‌هایِ خودِ او در مقام تحلیل‌گر.

در درمان تحلیلی، این روان‌کاو است که به جهانِ تحلیل‌شونده وارد می‌شود و می‌کوشد فضای روانیِ تحلیل‌شونده را بازسازی کند، نه برعکس. در آن هنگام، هیچ اثرِ باوری از سوی تحلیل‌گر به سوی تحلیل‌شونده وجود ندارد، زیرا تحلیل‌گر ناخودآگاهِ خویش را به امانت می‌سپارد و دست به تلقین نمی‌زند؛ تلقینی که مانع از شفافیتِ ناخودآگاهِ سوژهٔ تحلیل‌شونده می‌شد.

یک روان‌کاوی، کاراییِ خود را از رابطه‌ای می‌گیرد که بیرون از هرگونه مناسباتِ اقتدار میان روان‌کاو و تحلیل‌شونده برقرار می‌شود. یک روان‌کاوی در واقع عبارت است از پذیرشِ یک انسان در همان نقطه‌ای از زندگی‌اش که در آن قرار دارد، برای همراهی کردنِ او در آن بخش از راهی که به همراهیِ روان‌کاو بخواهد و بتواند بپیماید.

اگر تحلیل‌شونده به‌ندرت می‌داند به دنبال چه آمده است، روان‌کاو، اما، ایده‌ای در پسِ ذهن دارد. او از رهگذر تجربهٔ خویش در مقام تحلیل‌شونده و تجربهٔ کمابیش درازمدتش در مقام روان‌کاو می‌داند که اگر تحلیل‌شونده بتواند اندیشه‌ای دربارهٔ خود بسازد، گونه‌ای «دانش» دربارهٔ خویشتن، «دانشی» دربارهٔ آنچه او را تعیین می‌کند — یعنی تاریخِ خود و پیشینیانش (به معنای گستردهٔ واژه) — این امر اثر‌هایی بر جای خواهد نهاد.

تحلیل‌شونده نمی‌تواند در مقطعی از پیشبردِ کار احساس نکند که تحلیل‌گر از او، و برای او، انتظارِ تولیدِ این اندیشه، این شکل از «دانش»، و این «حقیقتِ» سوبژکتیو را دارد. این انتظار، بی‌هیچ پیش‌داوری دربارهٔ شکل‌های دگرگونی‌ای که ممکن است در تحلیل‌شونده برانگیزد، یکی از محرک‌های فرایند است.

قلبِ این فرایند در لحظه‌های پدیدار شدنِ شکلی از «حقیقت» جای دارد که تحلیل‌شونده را همچون محصولِ تاریخِ خویش برمی‌سازد. تحلیل‌شونده معنا می‌سازد؛ معنایی بازساخته و خیال‌پرداخته.

کارِ روان‌کاوی عبارت است از گوش‌سپاری‌ای که به بازشناسیِ تعین‌های ناخودآگاهِ حاکم بر گزینش‌ها، رفتار‌ها و همچنین شیوه‌های اندیشیدنِ یک سوژه نظر دارد. چه سخن بر سرِ لغزش‌های زبانی، کنش‌های خطا، رؤیا‌ها و نشانه‌هایی باشد که بر آنچه واپس‌رانده شده است گواهی می‌دهند، و چه سخن بر سرِ هذیان‌ها و دیگر نشانه‌هایی باشد که بازتابِ طردِ واقعیت‌اند، همهٔ این‌ها جلوه‌هایی از همان ناخودآگاهی هستند که فروید تعریف کرده است.

در صحنه‌پردازی‌هایی که سوژه در آن‌ها بازنمایی می‌شود، خویشتن را بازنمی‌شناسد. اگرچه ویژگیِ انسان است که در پاسخ به پرسش‌های بنیادینِ هستیِ خود گزاره‌هایی بسازد که معنا برمی‌انگیزند، اما هیچ پاسخی، همانند هیچ بازنمایی‌ای، وجود ندارد که سوژه بتواند خود را در آن تعریف کند.

سرشتِ تعارض‌آمیزِ زندگیِ روانی آنگاه به‌آشکار پدیدار می‌شود که مطالبهٔ بنیادینِ نگذاشتنِ هیچ مرزی برای گفتار — که در اصل و پایهٔ موقعیتِ تحلیلی قرار دارد — به نیرو‌های محافظه‌کار، موسوم به مقاومت، برخورد می‌کند که پیوسته در فرد و پیرامون او در کارند. آنچه نمی‌تواند به یاد آورده شود، گرایش به تکرار شدن دارد و به‌روزشدن‌های آن در انتقال، امکان تفسیرش را فراهم می‌آورد.

تفسیر روان‌کاوانه مستلزم آن است که تحلیل‌گر جایگاهی را که تحلیل‌شونده برای او تعیین می‌کند بازشناسد و بپذیرد، اما بی‌آنکه بگذارد در آن جایگاه مقید و تثبیت شود. آنچه اغلب انتقال متقابل نامیده می‌شود، اثرِ همین انتسابِ بیمار بر تحلیل‌گر است. تحلیل‌گر به مدد کار روانیِ خویش و تجربه‌اش، خود را در موضعی قرار می‌دهد که با یک کنشِ گفتاری بدان پاسخ گوید؛ کنشی که برآمدِ آن، پدیدار شدنِ برخی پیوند‌ها و تثبیت‌های ناخودآگاهِ میل است.

موضع تحلیل‌گر با دو مفهومِ فرویدیِ به یک اندازه بنیادین مشخص می‌شود: از یک سو، ضرورتِ تعلیقِ داوری که هم‌گام با پاسخ‌ندادن است (و گاه «بی‌طرفیِ خیرخواهانه» خوانده می‌شود)؛ و از سوی دیگر، قاعدهٔ موسوم به پرهیز یا «عمل نکردن»، که وامی‌دارد در جایی که کششِ خودانگیخته به سوی «انجام دادن» می‌برد، سخن گفته شود. از آنجا که این دو اصل شرطِ اجرای قاعدهٔ بنیادین به شمار می‌آیند، به همراهِ رعایتِ رازداری، به اخلاقِ حرفه‌ایِ تحلیل‌گر تعلق دارند.

کار تحلیلی تابع زمان‌مندی‌ای است که زمان‌مندیِ پردازشِ روانی است. بر عهدهٔ روان‌کاو است که این زمان‌مندی را پاس بدارد و در هدایتِ درمانِ تحلیلی، آن را در نظر بگیرد.

## تحلیل گفتارِ چند کشیشِ روان‌کاو

### ۱- تونی آناترلا:

تونی آناترلا روان‌کاو و متخصص روان‌پزشکی اجتماعی است. او همچنین کشیش است. تازه‌ترین کتاب‌های منتشرشده از او عبارت‌اند از: «میان بزرگسالان و نوجوانان: گاه‌نگارِ در گذرِ روز‌ها» (انتشارات لو سرْف، ۱۹۹۷)؛ «تفاوتِ ممنوع» (انتشارات فلاماریون، ۱۹۹۸).

از او نقل می‌کنم: «بر بستری فراهم‌شده از سوی انسان‌شناسی و معنویت مسیحی بود که فروید توانست مفاهیم و روشی را با هدفِ بازگویی و تبیین فرایند‌های ناخودآگاه بپروراند.» او به فرایند ناخودآگاه باور دارد. نمونه‌ای از یک فردِ مذهبی که به حضور ناخودآگاه ایمان دارد، اما بر این باور است که این اندیشهٔ مسیحی بوده که به فروید... داده است: این یک سازش است، اما نکتهٔ اساسی این است که او به حضور ناخودآگاه باور دارد.

بار دیگر نقل می‌کنم: «هنگامی که می‌خواهیم به کارِ پژوهشیِ روشمند دست بزنیم، منطق‌های روانی به خودیِ خود بازشناخته می‌شوند و از منطق‌های زندگیِ اخلاقی و زندگیِ دینی متمایز می‌گردند. اما این بر عهدهٔ سوژه و تلقیِ انسان‌شناختی‌ای است که از هستی به خویشتن می‌دهد تا وحدتِ خود را از رهگذرِ امورِ روان‌شناختی، اخلاقی، دینی، اجتماعی و سیاسی بسازد. در رویکردِ ‹همه‌چیز-روان‌شناختی› که امروزه چیره است، روان‌کاوی در خطرِ آن است که همچون ‹دینی› برای روانِ انسان جلوه کند، حال آنکه با توجه به اینکه یک فنِّ روان‌درمانگرانه و مجموعه‌ای از دانش‌ها دربارهٔ روان‌شناسیِ انسانی است، ادعای معنابخشیدن به هستی را ندارد. بی‌چشم‌انداز‌های انسان‌شناختی که روان‌شناسیِ انسانی را تغذیه کنند، این روان‌شناسی در نفرت و خشونت به هرز می‌رفت و روان‌کاوی هیچ کمکی نمی‌توانست بکند؛ روان‌کاوی به تنهایی نمی‌تواند انسانیت ببخشد.»

درمی‌یابیم که حتی یک کشیشِ روان‌کاو نیز برای یافتن نقطهٔ هم‌زیستی میان دین و روان‌کاوی، به انسان‌شناسی ارجاع می‌دهد.

### ۲- پدر دویگو:

دربارهٔ مصاحبه‌ای که پدر دویگو در ماه فوریهٔ ۲۰۰۱ با مجلهٔ «لاکتوالیته ده رولیژیون» (L’Actualité des religions) انجام داده است

نقل می‌کنم: «... برای من، زندگی خود یک مدرسهٔ علوم دینی است. روزنامه‌نگار و تحلیل‌گر شدم و این دو فعالیت را ادامه می‌دهم. این شیوهٔ من است برای جست‌وجوی درکِ بهتر و مشارکتِ بهتر در ماجراجوییِ انسانی، تا بتوانم خدا را بهتر بگویم و بهتر بشارت دهم، که رسالتِ کشیش است. اما در چهل و چند سالگی، با این همه با خود گفتم:

«راست است که جمع کردنِ سمت‌های روزنامه‌نگار، روان‌کاو و کشیش چندان متداول نیست. ... این نخستین پله برای آموزشِ من در مقام تحلیل‌گر بود. اما در روزنامه‌نگار، روان‌کاو یا کشیش بودن، پیش از هر چیز باید در من یک باورمند را دید. یعنی کسی که به زندگی باور دارد، آن را دوست می‌دارد و می‌خواهد آن را با تمام وجود زندگی کند.»

«در مقام تحلیل‌گر، باور دارم که درمانِ تحلیلی، تحلیل‌شونده را به سوی بهبودی هدایت می‌کند. در مقام کشیش، باور دارم که خدای کتاب مقدس، که خدایی پنهان است، فرد را در رویداد‌های زندگی‌اش فرا می‌خواند و او را دعوت می‌کند تا در تاریخِ خویش، یعنی تاریخِ رهاییِ انسان، زندگی کند.»

فروید در سخن گفتن از هدفِ روان‌کاوی می‌گفت که «بهبودی خود به‌عنوانِ افزوده‌ای جانبی از پی می‌آید.»

از فروید نقل می‌کنم: «باور‌ها و انگاره‌های دینی، که مدعیِ جزم‌بودن‌اند، نه ته‌ماندهٔ تجربه و نه دستاوردِ نهاییِ اندیشه‌ورزی‌اند: آن‌ها توهم‌اند؛ تحققِ کهن‌ترین، نیرومند‌ترین و مبرم‌ترین امیالِ بشریت؛ رازِ نیروی آن‌ها در نیروی همین امیال نهفته است. ما پیشاپیش این را می‌دانیم: اثرِ هراس‌انگیزِ درماندگیِ دوران کودکی، نیاز به حمایت شدن — حمایت شدن از راهِ دوست‌داشته‌شدن — را بیدار کرده بود؛ نیازی که پدر بدان پاسخ گفت؛ دریافتِ این واقعیت که این درماندگی سراسرِ زندگی به درازا می‌کشد، سبب شد که انسان به پدری، این بار به پدری بس نیرومند‌تر، چنگ بیفکند... و این تسکین و سبک‌باریِ سترگی برای روانِ فردی است که ببیند تعارض‌های کودکی — تعارض‌هایی که هرگز به‌تمامی حل‌وفصل نمی‌شوند — به یک معنا از دوش او برداشته شده‌اند و راه‌حلی مورد پذیرشِ همگان یافته‌اند.»

چنان‌که فروید می‌گوید: «تعارض‌های کودکی» را باید به هر دو معنا شنید: هم تعارضِ کودکیِ بشریت، و هم کودکی به‌مثابه نمونه‌ای از جوانیِ بشریت.

## سرانجام

به عنوانِ ردّی از این گفتار، در گشودگیِ شنودِ خیرخواهانه و روادارانهٔ شما نسبت به من، می‌خواهم از اودون واله (Odon Vallet)، دکترای حقوق و علوم ادیان، مدرس دانشگاه سوربن و نویسنده، نقل کنم: «... به یک معنا می‌توان کنش‌های خویش را تحلیل کرد و دریافت، و از این رو، بودا شاید نخستین روان‌کاوِ جهان بود، زیرا دریافت که کنش‌ها هنگامی که از زاویه‌ای دیگر نگریسته شوند، ارزشی دیگر می‌یابند.»

تنها تصریح می‌کنم که شاید تعریفِ این فرزانگیِ بسیار طلب‌شده برای انسان، به سادگی آن باشد که بتواند گزینش‌های روزمرهٔ خویش را در چشم‌اندازِ زمین، این کرهٔ خاکیِ ما، و در فرهنگی با پیشینهٔ ۴۰۰۰۰ سال جای دهد؛ امری که لائیسیته و روان‌کاوی به‌تمامی در آن اشتراک دارند.

به سهم خویش، درهم‌آمیزیِ فزایندهٔ انسان‌شناسی در شناختِ انسان را نشانه‌ای از تکاملِ مجموعهٔ رشته‌های دانش می‌دانم. و چرا حضورِ اندیشمندانِ فرزانه (با این تعریف) به روند‌های تصمیم‌گیریِ قانون‌گذاران و دستگاه‌های دولتی راه نیابد؟

## Psychoanalysis, Psychoanalyst, and Secularism

I quote Lacan: “Freud asks no more of the psychoanalyst than faith in the existence of the unconscious (that is, the knowledge implied by its discourse) and not the purification of his power. Faith therein depends upon an initiation—psychoanalysis—which puts the unconscious into act and objectifies it by unbinding it from the body. This separation of the Symbolic and the Body experienced in the Real is open to every subject of language, since speech alone counts therein. This opening of being to the most destitute, to neurotics if not to the mad, this belief in the existence of the unconscious is still an initiation, yet this access to the discourse of science by anyone whatsoever brings about a new synthesis of knowledge and the universal.

Is it not charity, in Freud, to have allowed the misery of speaking beings to tell itself that there is—since there is the unconscious—something that transcends, truly transcends, and which is nothing other than what it inhabits, this species, namely language? Is it not, yes, charity to announce to it this news that in what constitutes its everyday life, it has with language a support of greater reason than might have appeared, and that some wisdom… is already there?” (Lacan, Encore, p. 88)

I retain three key elements from this discourse: the faith of the psychoanalyst, the place of language, and the emergence of wisdom—to such an extent that this triangle gives substance to analytic practice.

My first encounters with believing psychoanalysts were not easy, for being deeply secular, shaped by psychoanalytic training and marked by the principle of secularism instilled by its inventor and his successors, I could not find a satisfactory way out. However, I found their behaviour sound and their practices on a par with those of atheist psychoanalysts. This paradox was resolved the moment I observed in my own practice the extent to which the psychoanalyst’s beliefs remain outside the parentheses of the couch and the armchair. Here, I attempt to retrace my trajectory in order to clarify this observation more fully: psychoanalysis, in its very existence, can only be practised by the secular subject that the psychoanalyst is.

Likewise, anthropology—which, by studying the different social structures of speaking beings from the earliest times to our own day and across the entire globe, endeavours to identify certain common points—is itself also deeply secular, for there are no predefined foundational values. Psychoanalysis, on this point too, moves in the same direction, and has done so since Freud, who opened the field of his investigations to early humans and developed his theory of totems and taboos, the sacrificial animal, and the God who is just and benevolent by nature—who is the noblest sublimation of our parental complex, primal father, and the link between original sin, the sense of guilt, and God the Father. He shows that both God and the devil have the father as their primal model. His studies lead him to anthropology. On several occasions, Freud defines the origin of religion as founded upon historical truth, and compares it with material truth and real truth.

Etymologically defined as the “science of man”, contemporary anthropology has very ancient intellectual origins, ideological inspirations, and pragmatic constraints. Its objects are of great diversity: culture, social structures, the stable elements and the changes of human societies, and their relationships with the natural environment. It is henceforth defined as the science of cultural and social diversities and, in general, as the science of man in society. Thus, the project of anthropology is to articulate the relations between the local and the global, and to think the other and the same in their most diverse aspects.

Secularism is a matter for the speaking being, the child of Homo sapiens sapiens: there is no difference between peoples in its conception. Respect for the life of this child in the city, for more than 40,000 years and across the entirety of our earth, clearly defines the depth of this secularism. Indeed, differences—social, cultural, of languages, ways of life, beliefs…—did not exist for Homo sapiens sapiens. As the fourteenth-century Persian poet Saadi says:

> Human beings are organs of the same body, for they were created of the same essence.

The object of study of psychoanalysis is likewise the speaking being. The one who speaks forms his unconscious. The unconscious is structured, and it obeys a precise rule of formation and functioning—the subject of psychoanalytic study. The formation and functioning of this unconscious are grounded in the desire of the speaking subject and the treasury of signifiers.

Observing that the basic conditions for the exercise of secularism and of psychoanalysis converge from the earliest days of humanity, psychoanalysis can only be secular. I quote Freud: “Psychoanalysis upholds no worldview, no conception of the good life, which brings it rather singularly close to the secular state, … while remaining a system of thought in relation to the universal.” Psychoanalysis gives the subject a way of listening differently to oneself and to the other: tolerance…

Anecdote: A psychoanalyst at the end of her career, during a seminar, at the moment of discussion concerning “the Freudian thing”, the “primal fantasy”, and “what makes man speak”, takes the floor and comments on the subject by emphasising a child’s need for this thing in order to speak and to have the signifier. She goes on to speak of her own situation; I quote: “Even though I have said and repeated throughout an entire lifetime that man invented God because he needed something to hold onto, today I wonder whether I am not like that child who needs something… for example, God.”

I invite you to take a brief journey through the foundational concepts of psychoanalytic theory and secularism, and then to examine the effect of this theory upon practice, and finally several analyses of the discourse of psychoanalysts who are men of faith.

## The Unconscious and Belief

In his correspondence with Pastor Pfister, Freud states: “In itself, psychoanalysis is neither more religious nor more irreligious. It is a non-partisan instrument that both the religious and the secular may use, provided it is solely in the service of the deliverance of suffering beings.” Freud questioned religious belief at great length. He even hoped that the scientific worldview he set against it might be capable of rendering “the illusion of religion” unnecessary.

What were Freud’s arguments regarding the need to believe in general, and religious belief in particular? For Freud, religious belief belongs to the order of illusion. By this, Freud means a representation that is not necessarily erroneous, yet which forgoes confirmation by reality—that is to say, which is situated, for the believer, beyond such confirmation. Accordingly, Freud’s critique consists not in demonstrating the futility of religion, but in uncovering its unconscious motivations. For the strength of the illusion—which enables it to dispense with confirmation by reality—derives from the irrepressible desire that it realises in fantasy. For Freud, this desire which shapes the representation of God fundamentally refers back to the dereliction of man, itself linked to his biological prematurity, which renders the human being dependent for a long time upon maternal care. Consequently, while denouncing religion as an illusion, Freud never ceased, between the lines, to emphasise the imperious presence of the need to believe, which he identifies with the need to be protected by the Father—at least in monotheistic religions. As a theoretician, from Totem and Taboo in 1911 to Moses and Monotheism in 1938, he always kept the subject of religion in mind. Major texts such as Civilisation and Its Discontents and The Future of an Illusion bear witness to this. This theme in fact runs throughout his reflection on culture and collective phenomena.

The Greek word laïkos means “people”, as opposed to clericos, which designates “one who holds religious power” (and by extension, political or economic power). Difficult to delineate with precision, the notion of secularism (laïcité) most commonly refers in the West to a situation in which citizens and the State are independent of the churches. Above all, it designates a legal and political regime of separation between the State and religions, and of the religious neutrality of the State.

Thus, the oldest stratum encompasses this idea of secularism conceived as a framework for peaceful coexistence among several religions, several philosophies, and several cultures. This framework appears as neutral. Thus, secularism may be summed up in three values: freedom of conscience, welcoming the other, and tolerance.

In turn, psychoanalysis aids in establishing secularism in the city, for it classifies according to the structure of the psyche and not by any other criterion such as poverty or material wealth…

## Psychoanalytic Practice and Secularism

The desire of the psychoanalyst is defined thus: “What can sustain the psychoanalyst in his operation—a possible drive-based or fantasmatic support for his act—is that he does not act according to an ideal derived from a representation of human nature or from a hypothetical drive to cure, that he frees himself from the grip of fantasy, and that he is less dependent upon that Other of whom, in fantasy, each person makes himself the object.” One may therefore say: the analyst must adhere to a certain neutrality; he does not direct the analysand, he directs the cure—which means having the analysand read the analysand’s own book, for there are poorly formed passages and poorly arranged symbols around traumas. As Lacan says: “the psychoanalyst, support of the transference, as subject supposed to know, is reduced at the end of the process to being the stand-in for objet a, an object destined to be rejected, which is neither a concept nor a signifier.” JL Seminar, 1967–68, The Psychoanalytic Act.

With regard to the psychoanalyst, the right question may be the enquiry into the function and place of the psychoanalyst. He is, on the one hand, the director of the analysand’s cure and, on the other hand, the subject supposed to know—or, in other words, the structure of an unconscious already analysed and receptive to interpretation.

The analytic cure for each subject is unique—an individual and particular path. His signifiers are his own, his desires, his dreams, and of course the elements of his interpretations as well. This subject of dream interpretation, based on latent ideas, differs profoundly from interpretations based upon religious, cultural, social, and other elements. There is no collective unconscious, there are no collective dreams, and there are no collective cure projects.

Secularism, like the unconscious, does not bestow meaning upon life: both lie profoundly outside ideology and belief. Sigmund Freud, in his technical writings, specifies that ultimately the psychoanalyst works solely with his own unconscious. The psychoanalyst’s belief has no place either in the method with which he conducts the cure or in his interpretations, for his interpretations are tied to the analysand’s signifiers and not to his own signifiers as an analyst.

In the cure, it is the psychoanalyst who enters into the analysand’s world and endeavours to recreate the analysand’s psychic environment, and not the reverse. At that moment, there is no effect of belief from the analyst towards the analysand, for the analyst lends his unconscious and does not engage in suggestion, which would impede the transparency of the analysand subject’s unconscious.

A psychoanalysis derives its efficacy from the relationship established outside any relation of authority between the psychoanalyst and the analysand. A psychoanalysis effectively consists in welcoming a person where they are in their life, in order to accompany them along the stretch of the way that they will want and be able to cover in the company of the psychoanalyst.

While the analysand rarely knows what he has come seeking, the psychoanalyst, for his part, has an idea at the back of his mind. He knows, from his own experience as an analysand and his more or less extensive experience as a psychoanalyst, that if the analysand succeeds in constructing a thought about himself—a kind of “knowledge” about himself, “knowledge” about what determines him, namely his history and that of his forebears (in the broad sense of the term)—this will produce effects.

The analysand cannot fail to sense, at one moment or another in the unfolding of the work, that the analyst expects from him, and for him, the production of this thought, of this form of “knowledge”, of this subjective “truth”. This expectation, without presuming the forms of change that this may induce in the analysand, is one of the driving forces of the process.

The heart of this process lies in the moments when a form of “truth” emerges, constituting the analysand as the product of his history. The analysand constructs meaning—a reconstructed, imagined meaning.

The practice of psychoanalysis consists in a mode of listening aimed at recognising the unconscious determinations governing a subject’s choices and conduct as well as his ways of thinking. Whether in the form of slips of the tongue, bungled actions, dreams, and symptoms bearing witness to what has been repressed, or delusions and other symptoms expressing the rejection of reality, these are all manifestations of the unconscious as defined by Freud.

In the stagings in which he is represented, the subject does not recognise himself. While it is characteristic of human beings to produce utterances that foment meaning in response to the essential questions of their existence, there is no answer, just as there is no representation, in which the subject can define himself.

The conflictual character of psychic life appears manifestly as soon as the radical demand to place no limit upon speech—which lies at the foundation of the analytic situation—collides with the conservative forces, known as resistance, ceaselessly at work within the individual and his surroundings. What cannot be remembered tends to repeat itself, and its actualisations in the transference allow for its interpretation.

Psychoanalytic interpretation implies that the analyst recognises and accepts the place that the analysand designates for him, yet without allowing himself to be assigned to it. What is often termed counter-transference is the effect upon the analyst of this attribution by the patient. Through his own psychic work and his experience, the analyst places himself in a position to respond to it by an act of speech, whose effect is the emergence of certain unconscious connections and fixations of desire.

The position of the analyst is characterised by means of two equally fundamental Freudian notions: on the one hand, the necessity of suspending judgement, which goes hand in hand with non-response (and which is sometimes called “benevolent neutrality”); on the other hand, the so-called rule of abstinence or of “non-action”, which commits one to speaking where the spontaneous impulse would lead one to “act”. Given that they condition the implementation of the fundamental rule, these two principles—to which respect for confidentiality must be added—belong to the deontology of the analyst.

Analytic work is subject to a temporality that is that of psychic elaboration. It is incumbent upon the psychoanalyst to respect this temporality and to take it into account in the conduct of the cure.

## Analysis of the Discourses of Several Priest-Psychoanalysts

### 1. Tony Anatrella:

Tony Anatrella is a psychoanalyst and specialist in social psychiatry. He is also a priest. Latest published works: “Entre adultes et adolescents : chronique au fil des jours” [Between Adults and Adolescents: A Day-to-Day Chronicle] (Le Cerf, 1997); “La Différence interdite” [The Forbidden Difference] (Flammarion, 1998).

I quote him: “It is upon ground prepared by anthropology and Christian spirituality that Freud was able to forge concepts and a method aimed at accounting for unconscious processes.” He believes in the process of the unconscious. An example of a clergyman who has faith in the presence of the unconscious, yet thinks that it was Christian thought that gave it to Freud…: it is a compromise, but the essential point is that he believes in the presence of the unconscious.

I quote again: “When one seeks to carry out a methodical work of investigation, psychic logics are recognised in their own right and are distinguished from those of moral life and religious life. Yet it falls to the subject, and to an anthropological conception of existence that the subject adopts for himself, to forge his unity out of the psychological, the moral, the religious, the social, and the political. Within the ‘all-psychological’ mindset that currently prevails, psychoanalysis risks appearing as a ‘religion’ of the human psyche, whereas, being a psychotherapeutic technique and a body of knowledge about human psychology, it makes no claim to give a meaning to existence. Without anthropological perspectives to nourish human psychology, the latter would spin in a void amid hatred and violence, and psychoanalysis would be of no help; psychoanalysis alone cannot humanise.”

We observe that even a priest-psychoanalyst makes reference to anthropology in order to find the point of cohabitation between religion and psychoanalysis.

### 2. Father Duigou:

Regarding the interview given by Father Duigou to the magazine “L’Actualité des religions” in February 2001

I quote: “…for me, life is a seminary. I became a journalist, an analyst, and I continue these two activities. It is my way of seeking to understand better and participate better in the human adventure—in order to speak of and proclaim God better, which is the mission of the priest. Yet around forty-something years of age, I nevertheless said to myself:

‘It is true that combining the roles of journalist, psychoanalyst, and priest is scarcely common. …That was the first step towards my training as an analyst. Yet in my being a journalist, psychoanalyst, or priest, one must first see in me a believer—that is to say, someone who believes in life, who loves it, and who wishes to live it to the full.’”

“As an analyst, I believe that the cure leads the analysand to healing. As a priest, I believe that the God of the Bible, who is a hidden God, addresses the individual in the events of his life, calling him to live within his history, the history of the liberation of man.”

Freud, speaking of the aim of psychoanalysis, said that “healing comes as an added bonus.”

I quote Freud: “Religious ideas, which profess to be dogmas, are not the residue of experience or the final result of reflection: they are illusions, the realisation of the oldest, strongest, and most pressing desires of humanity; the secret of their strength is the strength of these desires. We already know this: the terrifying impression of infantile helplessness had awakened the need to be protected—protected through being loved—a need which the father satisfied; the recognition that this helplessness lasts throughout life caused man to cling to a father, this time a more powerful father…… And it is an enormous relief for the individual soul to see the conflicts of childhood—conflicts which are never entirely resolved—removed from it, as it were, and given a solution accepted by all.”

As Freud says, “the conflicts of childhood” are to be understood in both senses: the conflict of the childhood of humanity, and childhood as a specimen of the youth of humanity.

## Finally

By way of leaving a trace of this discourse within the openness of your benevolent and tolerant listening towards me, I wish to quote Odon Vallet, Doctor of Law and Religious Studies, lecturer at the Sorbonne, and writer: “…..One can, in a certain sense, analyse and understand one’s acts, and in this respect the Buddha was perhaps the world’s first psychoanalyst, for he understood that when acts are viewed from another angle, they take on another value.”

I simply clarify that, perhaps, the definition of this wisdom so eagerly sought for the human being is simply to succeed in placing one’s daily choices within the setting of the earth, our globe, and within a culture 40,000 years old—something that Secularism and psychoanalysis fully share.

For my part, the growing integration of anthropology into the knowledge of humankind is an indicator of the evolution of all disciplines. And why should the integration of wise scholars (by this definition) not enter into the decision-making procedures of legislators and State apparatuses?

Hassan Makaremi

fr.executive_summary: https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/24139031947668587699907894813691614777941046n.jpg https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/2414005214766858753324124849846745053256144n.jpg Il ne sera pas inutile de vous transmettre également une copie de la lettre que j'ai adressée aujourd'hui à la galeriste…
fr.body_markdown:
https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/241390319_4766858769990789_4813691614777941046_n.jpg https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/241400521_4766858753324124_849846745053256144_n.jpg

Il ne sera pas inutile de vous transmettre également, chers amis, une copie de la lettre que j'ai adressée aujourd'hui à la galeriste présentant mes œuvres à Chiraz. Peut-être qu'avec le concours de tous, en ces temps très difficiles de pandémie et d'instabilité, pourrons-nous ensemble organiser une exposition en Iran et dans les pays voisins.

« Bonjour et tous mes vœux de santé et de succès.

Je souhaitais prendre de vos nouvelles. Par la même occasion, je voulais vous faire part d'une bonne nouvelle. Récemment, la Fondation Toos au Royaume-Uni a présenté les grands peintres iraniens depuis le début de l'époque safavide jusqu'à nos jours, et m'a inscrit parmi les artistes vivants aux côtés de maîtres éminents tels que : Ali-Shir Nava'i, Kamal al-Din Behzad, Reza Abbasi, Sani al-Molk, Kamal al-Molk, Hossein Kazemi, Alivandi, Mahmoud Farshchian, Hannibal Alkhas, Parviz Kalantari, Bahman Mohassess, Afjehei, Tanavoli, Aydin Aghdashloo et Hassan Makaremi.

De même, ma présentation au Musée de la calligraphie moderne de Moscou avec sept œuvres.

Peut-être ces deux nouvelles nous donneront-elles, à vous et à moi, une motivation accrue pour organiser une exposition en Iran et dans les pays voisins.

Avec toute ma gratitude pour vos efforts et dans l'espoir de vous revoir, ainsi que votre vénérable père, à Paris.

Portez-vous fièrement. »

[https://toosfoundation.com/fa/category/iranian-painters-fa/](https://toosfoundation.com/fa/category/iranian-painters-fa/?fbclid=IwAR20iTD42tLl5EpkPvMh0Wgn2ehjtNmkcTLUD6L4oQQI7-SVOaHIJYXWfbA)

en.title: A Letter for an Exhibition in Shiraz
en.executive_summary: https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/24139031947668587699907894813691614777941046n.jpg https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/2414005214766858753324124849846745053256144n.jpg It will not be without value to share with you a copy of the letter I sent today to the gallery owner…
en.body_markdown:
https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/241390319_4766858769990789_4813691614777941046_n.jpg https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/241400521_4766858753324124_849846745053256144_n.jpg

It will not be without value to share with you, dear friends, a copy of the letter I sent today to the gallery owner presenting my works in Shiraz; perhaps, through everyone's collective endeavour in these very difficult times of coronavirus and instability, we may together arrange an exhibition in Iran and neighbouring countries.

"Greetings, and wishing you health and success.

I wanted to enquire after you, and at the same time share some good news with you. Recently, the Toos Foundation in England presented distinguished Iranian painters from the beginning of the Safavid era to the present day, and included me among the living artists alongside luminous figures such as: Ali-Shir Nava'i, Kamal al-Din Behzad, Reza Abbasi, Sani al-Molk, Kamal al-Molk, Hossein Kazemi, Alivandi, Mahmoud Farshchian, Hannibal Alkhas, Parviz Kalantari, Bahman Mohassess, Afjehei, Tanavoli, Aydin Aghdashloo, and Hassan Makaremi.

And likewise, my introduction at the Contemporary Museum of Calligraphy in Moscow with seven works.

Perhaps these two pieces of news will give both you and me greater incentive to organise an exhibition in Iran and neighbouring countries.

With gratitude for your efforts and hoping to see you and your esteemed father in Paris.

Remain proud and triumphant."

fr.body_markdown:

C'est tellement amer, tellement

… et toi tu es douceur,

et toi tu chantes,

dans le froid de l'amertume de la séparation,

et toi tu sais ce que veut dire être femme,

et ton salut est ivresse,

et ton passage est de verre et ton corps d'un bleu pur,

et tu viendras à l'heure où mon cœur,

cherche le témoin sublime de ton désir.

Ah, cette ombre-canari de mon cœur,

ah, cet oiseau captif à l'envol lointain,

dont le salut est ivresse.

Hassan Makaremi

Été 1400 (2021), France

en.body_markdown:
https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/241763786_4784700384873294_6258596699936031133_n-1.jpg

It is so bitter, so very bitter

… and you are sweetness,

and you sing,

in the chill of separation's bitterness,

and you know what it means to be a woman,

and your greeting is intoxication,

and your passage is glass and your body pure blue,

and you shall come at a time when my heart

seeks the lofty witness of your longing.

Ah, this shadow-canary of my heart,

ah, this captive of distant flight,

whose greeting is intoxication.

Hassan Makaremi

Summer 1400 (2021), France

Quand je lui ai demandé pourquoi sa femme détournait sans cesse le regard, il a répondu : “parce qu'elle est atteinte de la maladie d'Alzheimer.” Je lui ai alors demandé : “votre femme s'inquiétera-t-elle si vous la lâchez ?” Il m'a répondu : “elle ne se souvient de rien, elle ne sait plus qui je suis, elle ne me reconnaît plus depuis des années.” Surpris, je lui ai dit : “et vous continuez à la guider chaque jour, même si elle ne vous reconnaît pas ?” Le vieil homme a souri, m'a regardé droit dans les yeux et m'a dit : “elle ne sait peut-être pas qui je suis, mais moi je sais qui elle est, et elle est l'amour de ma vie.” »

“He is 85 and insists on taking his wife’s hand everywhere they go. When I asked him why his wife kept looking away, he responded, ‘because she has Alzheimer's.’ I then proceeded to ask him, ‘will your wife worry if you let her go?’ He then replied, ‘she doesn't remember anything, she doesn't know who I am anymore, she hasn't recognised me for years.’ Surprised, I said, ‘and you have continued to guide her every single day even though she doesn't recognise you?’ The elderly man smiled, looked into my eyes, and said, ‘she may not know who I am, but I know who she is, and she is the love of my life.’”

fr.body_markdown:
Enfant de l'exil, Masrour Makaremi, 44 ans, a choisi le Bergeracois, sa terre d'adoption, pour faire renaître l'élixir banni par les mollahs iraniens. Un acte de résistance et de résilience.

Exfiltrés de Chiraz, au sud de l'Iran, en 1986 à l'âge de 9 et 11 ans, Masrour Makaremi et sa sœur Chowra n'ont rien emporté de leur terre natale. Rien, si ce n'est la certitude que personne ne pourrait jamais leur enlever leur identité iranienne. Pas même les Gardiens de la révolution islamique, qui ont emprisonné, torturé et assassiné leur mère, Fatemeh, soupçonnée d'être une opposante politique au régime. « Vos bourreaux peuvent tout vous prendre, sauf la liberté de penser que votre pays vous appartient autant qu'il leur appartient. Ces gens-là ont du pouvoir, mais ils n'ont pas le monopole de l'iranité », confie Masrour Makaremi, enfant de l'exil devenu orthodontiste spécialiste en orthopédie dento-faciale à Bergerac, en Dordogne, où vivent avec lui sa femme, Sandie, et ses trois enfants, Leila, 12 ans, Myriam, 8 ans, et Kyan, 6 ans.

en.title: Dordogne: He Revives Persian Wine in the Bergerac Vineyard
en.executive_summary: A child of exile, Masrour Makaremi, aged 44, chose the Bergerac region, his adopted homeland, to bring back to life the elixir banned by the Iranian mullahs. An act of resistance and resilience. Smuggled out of Shiraz, in southern Iran, in 1986 at the ages of 9 and 11…
en.body_markdown:
A child of exile, Masrour Makaremi, aged 44, chose the Bergerac region, his adopted homeland, to bring back to life the elixir banned by the Iranian mullahs. An act of resistance and resilience.

Smuggled out of Shiraz, in southern Iran, in 1986 at the ages of 9 and 11, Masrour Makaremi and his sister Chowra carried nothing away from their native land. Nothing, save the certainty that no one could ever strip them of their Iranian identity—not even the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, who imprisoned, tortured, and murdered their mother, Fatemeh, suspected of being a political opponent of the regime. "Your torturers can take everything from you, except the freedom to believe that your country belongs to you just as much as it belongs to them. Those people hold power, but they do not hold a monopoly on Iranianness," confides Masrour Makaremi, a child of exile who has become an orthodontist specialising in dentofacial orthopaedics in Bergerac, Dordogne, where he lives with his wife, Sandie, and their three children, Leila, 12, Myriam, 8, and Kyan, 6.

fr.body_markdown:
Cours sur les fondements essentiels des enseignements de Jacques Lacan

Dr Hassan Makaremi

Recueillis et édités par : Dr Narges Sharifzadeh

Téhéran, Éditions Neshaneh : 1399 (2020)

Présentation de l'ouvrage

La singularité de ces enseignements réside dans le rapport de notre vérité individuelle à la réalité extérieure. Au cours des vingt-cinq dernières années, à travers ma propre psychanalyse, la formation analytique de personnes issues de langues diverses d'une part, la tenue de nombreuses conférences, l'enseignement de la doctrine lacanienne en différentes langues et la formation de psychanalystes dans des idiomes variés, je puis affirmer avoir intériorisé les enseignements lacaniens et les avoir transmis vers l'extérieur.

Naturellement, cette intériorisation et cette extériorisation ont traversé le filtre de ma propre culture. En ce sens, ces cours s'efforcent de traduire les enseignements de Lacan dans la langue culturelle de leurs auditeurs, ce qui diffère de l'enseignement de Lacan au sein de sa culture et de sa langue maternelle.

Dans ces cours, chaque fois que cela s'est avéré possible, il a été fait appel à la richesse de la culture persane afin de rendre plus accessible le langage ardu, scientifique et clinique de Lacan. Autant que faire se peut, nous nous sommes efforcés de préserver à la fois la vivacité orale de l'enseignement et la correction de l'écriture persane.

Nous formons l'espoir de mettre progressivement à la disposition des lecteurs intéressés d'autres cycles de cours, principalement fondés sur les séminaires de Lacan et de ses disciples.

Book introduction: The defining feature of these teachings is the relation of our individual truth to external reality. Over the past twenty-five years, through my own psychoanalysis, training…
en.body_markdown:
Lectures on the Foundational Principles of Jacques Lacan's Teachings

Dr Hassan Makaremi

Compiled and edited by: Dr Narges Sharifzadeh

Tehran, Neshaneh Publishing: 1399 (2020)

Book Introduction

The defining feature of these teachings is the relation of our individual truth to external reality. Over the past twenty-five years, through my own psychoanalysis, training individuals in psychoanalysis across diverse languages on the one hand, delivering various lectures, teaching Lacan's doctrines in different languages, and training psychoanalysts in varied tongues, one may claim that I have internalised Lacanian teachings and transmitted them outward.

Naturally, this internalisation and externalisation have entered and emerged through my cultural filter. From this perspective, these lectures endeavour to render Lacan's teachings into the cultural language of their listeners, which differs from teaching Lacan's doctrines within the culture of his mother tongue.

In these lectures, wherever possible, the rich Persian culture has been drawn upon so that Lacan's complex, scientific, and clinical language may become more intelligible. As far as feasible, effort has been made to preserve both the oral cadence of teaching and proper written Persian.

It is hoped that, gradually, further lecture series—chiefly grounded in the seminars of Lacan and his students—will also be made available to those interested.

fr.executive_summary: https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/19639695444948816605218362303611268463398444n.jpg Je veux la paix. Je veux la paix et une brûlure sans douleur, mon âme ne peut plus consentir à une autre séparation, et j'abandonnerai l'éloignement à la plus lointaine branche du pin. Je veux la paix et un sommeil…
fr.body_markdown:
https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/196396954_4494881660521836_2303611268463398444_n.jpg

Je veux la paix.

Je veux la paix et une brûlure sans douleur,

mon âme ne peut plus consentir à une autre séparation,

et j'abandonnerai l'éloignement à la plus lointaine branche du pin.

Je veux la paix et un sommeil sans lieu,

mon esprit, dans la sérénité de mon âge,

déploie ses ailes,

et mon corps, dans tous les parfums de ma patrie,

cherche le matin.

Je veux la paix et un lendemain plein d'allégresse et créateur,

et des femmes et des hommes qui croient en mes yeux :

car je veux la paix et un savoir qui bâtisse le monde...

Je veux la paix,

la paix.

Hassan Makaremi.

France, printemps 1400 (2021)

en.title: I Want Peace
en.executive_summary: https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/19639695444948816605218362303611268463398444n.jpg I want peace. I want peace and a burning without pain; my soul can bear no further parting, and I shall consign separation to the farthest bough of the pine. I want peace and a sleep…
en.body_markdown:
https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/196396954_4494881660521836_2303611268463398444_n.jpg

I want peace.

I want peace and a burning without pain;

my soul can bear no further parting,

and I shall consign separation to the farthest bough of the pine.

I want peace and a placeless sleep;

my spirit, in the ease of my years,

flutters its wings,

and my body, amidst all the fragrances of my homeland,

searches for the morning.

I want peace and a vibrant, constructive tomorrow,

and women and men who believe in my eyes:

for I want peace and a knowledge that builds the world...

I want peace,

peace.

Hassan Makaremi.

France, Spring 1400 (2021)

fr.title: Viens toi aussi
fr.executive_summary: Viens toi aussi, viens toi aussi, ô le plus bel être humain que je connaisse ! Ton parfum sans rien d'autre est beau comme toi-même, comme ton vêtement, comme ton visage, comme l'événement des nuits passées, que je reconstruis, et je m'apaise : tel le chant d'un ange montant au paradis et disant d'une voix douce et emplie de désir : viens toi aussi, viens…
fr.body_markdown:
Viens toi aussi, viens toi aussi

Ô le plus bel être humain que je connaisse !

Ton parfum sans rien d'autre,

est beau comme toi-même,

comme ton vêtement,

comme ton visage,

comme l'événement des nuits passées,

que je reconstruis,

et je m'apaise :

tel le chant d'un ange qui monte au paradis et

dit d'une voix douce et emplie de désir :

viens toi aussi,

viens toi aussi…

Hassan Makaremi

Été 1400 (2021)

en.title: Come Too
en.executive_summary: Come too, come too, O most beautiful human being I know! Your scent, with nothing else, is beautiful like yourself, like your attire, like your face, like the happening of past nights, which I reconstruct, and grow serene: like the hymn of an angel ascending to paradise and saying in a gentle voice full of longing: come too, come…
en.body_markdown:
Come too, come too,

O most beautiful human being I know!

Your scent, with nothing else,

is beautiful like yourself,

like your attire,

like your face,

like the happening of past nights,

which I reconstruct,

and grow serene:

like the hymn of an angel ascending to paradise and

saying in a gentle voice full of longing:

come too,

come too…

Hassan Makaremi

Summer 1400 (2021)

fr.body_markdown:
Bonjour et salutations respectueuses aux chers membres.

Lors de la séance de cette semaine, nous aurons l'honneur d'accueillir la présentation du livre « Un autre regard sur le secret de Hafez » par son distingué auteur, l'éminent maître, Monsieur le Docteur Makaremi.

Date et heure : jeudi 27 Khordad à 13 h

[https://youtu.be/b9gOqeDIbKo](https://youtu.be/b9gOqeDIbKo?fbclid=IwAR09ei0YPW9rdEENwZi3ZDwTO9nNnsbtvMYo4SdpCQbS9ZkVKusPAUIIIfw)

Hafez met sans aucun doute le doigt sur la mémoire collective (mémoire collective, mémoire historique, âme populaire, génie de la langue, substance historique partagée, substance ethnique partagée) de l'Iranien persanophone, de telle sorte qu'après des siècles, sa poésie demeure toujours intimement tissée à cette mémoire. C'est en « Hafez » qu'ils trouvent leur parole vive, et d'une certaine manière Hafez est le médiateur entre la mémoire collective-imaginaire des peuples iraniens et leur mouvement historique. Tel est le secret que Hafez porte en son sein, et tel est le secret de la présence profonde et pérenne de Hafez pour les Iraniens.

« J'ai tracé ces lettres de telle sorte que nul étranger ne les comprît ; / Toi aussi, par grâce, lis-les ainsi que toi seul le sais. »

en.body_markdown:
Greetings and respect to all esteemed members.

In this week's session, we shall have the honour of presenting the book "Another Perspective on the Secret of Hafez" by its distinguished author, the esteemed master Dr Makaremi.

Time: 1:00 p.m., Thursday, 27 Khordad

[https://youtu.be/b9gOqeDIbKo](https://youtu.be/b9gOqeDIbKo?fbclid=IwAR09ei0YPW9rdEENwZi3ZDwTO9nNnsbtvMYo4SdpCQbS9ZkVKusPAUIIIfw)

Hafez undoubtedly places his finger upon the collective memory (collective memory, historical memory, national spirit, spirit of language, shared historical essence, shared ethnic essence) of the Persian-speaking Iranian, in such a way that even after the passage of centuries his poetry remains inextricably woven into this memory. They find their eloquent voice in "Hafez", and in a sense Hafez serves as a mediator between the collective-imaginary memory of Iranian peoples and their historical movement. This is the secret Hafez carries within his breast, and this is the secret of Hafez's profound and enduring presence for Iranians.

I wrote these letters such that no stranger might know;
You too, out of grace, read them as only you know how.
