en.body_markdown:
Last week in Tehran, the book *Writing in Exile: Essays on Iranian Literature in Today's World*, compiled by Shahrokh Tondro-Saleh, was published by Gostareh Publishing. This book is the first volume of a three-volume series that seeks in a way to provide a general report on the achievements of Iranian intellectuals, literary figures, and specialists outside Iran and to examine the problematisation of Iranian literature of migration and exile. From pages 392 to 418, across 26 pages, an interview with me appears under the title *Once Again, Longing for My Homeland*.

Once Again, Longing for My Homeland

A written interview with

Professor Hassan Makaremi

Thinker and theorist in the psychoanalysis of literature and art, poet, painter, and calligrapher

Dr Makaremi, I am delighted to have this opportunity to converse with you about Iranian literature and its life across the countries of the world. Undoubtedly, your perspectives on this subject will be most valuable. On this topic, my first question is: how do you review the history of Iranian literature of migration and exile?

In our rich and ancient history, in the matter of separation from our beloved homeland, migration plays the largest role. After that comes seeking refuge, and then exile in the sense of being forced to leave the homeland; for political punishment was not especially prominent. However, here the difficulty we encounter with the word "literature" lies in defining its scope. Does it mean the production of short stories, novels, and poetry, or can one go further and consider any piece of writing in any field to be literature? As is customary in academia when we say that much has been written in the psychoanalytic literature on this or that subject*.

*What is meant here is specifically the production of short stories, novels, poetry, and texts in the realm of pure literature.

Very well, then let us agree on this convention and speak of a new concept called the written output of Iranians living outside Iran who also write in Persian. These productions can be traced from distant times right up to the present day, whether in the achievements of poets in India or in the travels of Persian-speaking mystics across the length and breadth of Islamic lands. Yet it is roughly from the beginning of the period of the Iranian Awakening that, with the presence and emergence of intellectuals such as Akhundzadeh, Mostashar al-Dowleh, and others, Constitutionalist literature took shape—and did so remarkably outside the country. This chain has never been broken since, and today, with around four million expatriate migrants possessing an average education of "secondary diploma plus two years", one may say that written production has reached its peak. Of course, it would be unfair not to mention the exceedingly rich scholarly output of Iranians abroad in the field of literature. Let me give an example: Homa Katouzian, as a researcher in the political economy of Iran, publishes an authoritative book entitled *The Political Economy of Iran: From the Constitutional Era to the End of the Pahlavi Dynasty*, translated [into Persian] by Mohammad-Reza Nafisi and Kambiz Azizi. Yet the same scholar later became interested in studying the works of Saadi, Jamalzadeh, and Sadegh Hedayat, and indeed wrote valuable and noteworthy works. Thus we see that separating intellectual, literary, and artistic achievements is no simple task.

Another point is the language of composition. In this respect, among Iranians outside the homeland, we can distinguish several spectra from one another: the first spectrum consists of those who have written solely in Persian, their mother tongue. Another spectrum consists of those who write solely in the language of the host country; and finally, one can name those who write in both languages. On the other hand, one may also note that there is a group of writers who have written their works abroad and published them only abroad, and those whose works have been and continue to be published in both places. In France, in the 1960s and 1970s (1340s and 1350s in the Iranian solar calendar), we have an eminent writer and painter such as Cyrus Rezvani [1], who writes exclusively in French.

Of course, today, with the expansion of modern means of communication, all these concepts have assumed a new form. Virtually any book, regardless of where and by which publisher it is issued, has its PDF edition accessible everywhere. One might say that this is precisely why the number of online publishers of Persian books in America and Europe is on the rise.

This distinction and categorisation is exceedingly important. Moreover, it is this very distinction that reveals the breadth of knowledge and the power of insight of the Iranian writer and thinker in today's world—a domain whose functional sphere can be expanded through intercultural exchanges and among people of literature and thought.

Categorising contemporary Iranian writers outside the country is by no means simple. One could say that the generation of migrant writers following the events of 1953 (1332) came to an end with the passing of Bozorg Alavi. The end of the migrant generation of 1977 to 1982 (1356 to 1361)—such as figures like Iraj Pezeshkzad—is also on the wane, whereas the flourishing of the second generation and of the migrants from 2001 (1380) onwards is now arriving.

Generational divisions are a convention, and conventions have always had their limitations and flaws; yet the essence of literature is the core of civilisational life and the vital strivings of world cultures, and the clearest exemplars of the life and continuity of civilisational life are borne by a country's literature. In the clime of Persian culture, Ferdowsi is forever Ferdowsi, Hafez is Hafez, and Saadi will remain Saadi until the eternity of the world. What can reveal to us the wonder of their thought and works is the kind of inspiration we are able to draw from Hafez, Saadi, Ferdowsi, Mowlana (Rumi), Khayyam, and Attar in the present age. In other words, what connection does today's pupil and university student forge with these literary figures? Alongside this very endeavour, one may name Akhavan, Forough, Simin Behbahani, Shamloo, Parvin, Bahar, Eshghi, Dehkhoda, Aref, and Iraj, and add dozens of other figures to the creators of Persian literature. Well, these transcend generational divisions, part of whose characteristics can be seen in the intellectual achievements and literature of Iranian migrants. You yourself are among the thinkers and writers who possess deep and precise experience in the field of Lacanian psychoanalysis, psychological literature, and charting the clime of the human soul and the inner exploration of contemporary humanity. Your experiences as a psychoanalyst, psychologist, and artist—and, above all, as a creator of literary text—are something else altogether. I would like us to speak somewhat more broadly about this subject. One can also look at humanity's "written achievement" in another way: form and content. Let us call the form poetry, short story, research, screenplay, play, monograph… and call the content that very message intended to pass from the author to the other in its broadest sense. The achievements of these thirteen billion *Homo sapiens* [2] who have gradually come into the world—of whom only some seven billion are alive today—have, since the invention of writing sometime between seven thousand and four thousand years ago, been preserved vertically and horizontally by means of this very writing. Writing transmits messages from one generation to the next (vertical transmission) and from one culture to another (translation—horizontal transmission). Today we know that the functioning of our psyche relates differently to writing and to oral discourse. In other words, writing is inscribed within us, whereas speech enjoys greater freedom. You are right: "Literature is the essence of the life of a civilisation and a culture," and if we sum up your phrase, the totality of human writing is our cultural life.

Now let us go a step further and look qualitatively at this treasure. This vast treasure encompasses everything from the smallest vowel mark—a *zammah* or *kasrah* that transforms the meaning of a word from "the lote-tree (*konār*)" to "by the side of the beloved (*kenār-e yār*)"—to the pivotal discourse that is the product of all human research and inquiry, such as "energy is the product of mass multiplied by the speed of light squared". Here, perhaps, we can categorise writings according to their significance in the history of cognition of the totality of human cultural achievement: writings that stand at the summit of our archaeology of knowledge. It is through them that other productions come to life. These are the summits that can not only represent each culture, but also serve as an index of general human culture. To produce works standing at such a summit, the author must himself stand upon the summit and gaze from there upon the human presence in being. Fortunately, we live in a culture in which we have abundant examples of summits and summit-climbers; we need only appreciate their worth. Sometimes the combination of form and content reaches such a pinnacle together that it enchants us for a lifetime. Attending to the human psyche—there where the human being separates himself from the trunk of his tree of life, the four families of tailless apes—has accompanied us from the very first day of humanity's fundamental questions. With the approach of the twentieth century, several branches of knowledge that had drifted apart converged once again. Friedrich Nietzsche [3], like a giant in philosophy, called himself a psychologist; Sigmund Freud [4], the discoverer of the unconscious and inventor of the stages of clinical psychoanalysis, for the first time placed the human body and psyche within culture—like a fish in water: *"Whosoever, like a fish, has had his fill of its water…"*—and from there invited us to reread the entirety of human knowledge; read it again: "the human being is divided [split]".

Humanity possesses an unconscious that laments and clamours within our weary hearts. At that same time, Wittgenstein [5] placed the knowing subject alongside what he knows and called the mutual interaction between the two hermeneutics. Michel Foucault [6] joined sociology and anthropology to the historical trajectory of the words employed, and in the twentieth century the structuralists, for the first time, equipped humanity with an effective and indispensable instrument: Saussure [7] linked structuralism to linguistics, Lévi-Strauss [8] in sociology [anthropology], and Jacques Lacan [9] in understanding the human psyche. It is precisely here that a revolution occurs. The symbolisation of *Homo sapiens* over hundreds of thousands of years down to the present day gradually civilises us. Grasping precisely and stage by stage the evolutionary trajectory of symbolisation requires immense labour. One day, the "fruitful tree of the archaeology of knowledge", like the Darwinian tree of the evolution of life, will reveal itself to us. On that day, comprehensive human culture will recognise the path of the strivings of cultures, and we shall attain the root of our "becoming".

If we view writing—and Persian writing in particular, which is the fruit of several millennia of continuity and evolution—in this light, every text takes on a different colour and savour. Then the *Shâhnâmeh* becomes "the King of Kings of Books"; the *Divân* of Hafez becomes the distilled essence of the human gaze upon one's own being; the *Masnavi-ye Ma'navi* becomes the chronicle of striving and fervour, of tearing away husks and extracting kernels; *The Conference of the Birds* (*Mantiq al-Tayr*) becomes the revolution and transformation of the relationship of servant and master into that of lover and beloved; and the quatrains of Khayyam become the grammar of human doubt…

With this brief introduction, if I wish to apply such words to what I myself have produced and continue to produce, I would say that I strive to situate every piece of writing within the totality of human knowledge—to hear every human being against his thirteen-billion-strong background, and to behold every achievement against the backdrop of its million years of symbolisation. The human being dwells in the ocean of his culture, and culture rests upon his symbolisation.

What, in your view as a psychoanalyst, writer, and social sciences researcher, are the principal characteristics of the literature of migration and exile?

By the very fact of migration—that is, daily life in another culture—the migrant becomes attuned to the category of culture and the richness of cultural difference. His angle of vision in the shared sphere of cultures widens. He both tastes other cultures and gains greater awareness of the dimensions of his own culture. After his departure, he keeps his written language steady while infusing it with colours from other languages. His gaze upon humanity, history, and even being and his own presence in being deepens as well.

If the migrant writer is able to maintain contact, even occasionally, with his own people and culture, return to the country, and engage directly with other cultural figures, he is less prone to idealising his own culture and becomes better acquainted with contemporary culture in Iran. Otherwise, in the depths of his being, Iran and Iranian culture grow more distant and ever more idealised, while his connection to the reality of Iranians' everyday lives diminishes. On the other hand, the values and beliefs of the migrant writer are challenged by what may represent the novelties of other global values. This challenge can become a kind of quiet inner war between the migrant's internalised cultural identity and his newly discovered values. All of us harbour a divided human being within ourselves, such that at times, caught between identity and everyday life, we must weather many unwanted and heavy storms. To put it more simply: migration is a kind of psychological trauma that lives within the migrant and becomes institutionalised. In short, today's Iranian literature of migration is moving towards completing the breadth of domestic literature, which remains under constraint. The day travel becomes normal and restrictions are lifted, we shall witness the blossoming of an era of cultural growth in our beloved Iran that may well be unprecedented in our country's history.

In your remarks I see two points that merit further elucidation. The first is the challenges. Tell us about these challenges. Undoubtedly, given your expertise, you have more precise case studies than the usual second-hand quotations, which could form the basis for continuing our dialogue.

The migrant becomes bicultural and simultaneously both leans more heavily upon the culture of his mother tongue and knows it more deeply. He attains mastery over his presence in being from both within and without. It is as though another human being is born alongside him, enlarging him. On the other hand, in everyday life the migrant's link with his own self, with the culture of his mother tongue, and with his tradition and way of life is intermittently severed:

The chief challenge is not to fall prey to splitting [fragmentation]. The migrant writer writes with two right hands (two cultures), yet sees with one eye—unless he is aware of that deficiency and consciously lets his self-observing cultural eye, his eye for the everyday, roam across all the possibilities available in his homeland and among his compatriots.

I recall thirty-five years ago: the late Gholam-Hossein Sa'edi wasted away from heartbreak in separation from the homeland; he melted himself down. At that very same time, Bozorg Alavi used to travel to Iran and speak with such vigour of how piped drinking water, electricity, and roads had reached the villages that it seemed he had not merely paid a brief visit to beloved Iran, but possessed a world-reflecting mirror in which he beheld Iran and knew more than all of us who had recently emerged from the heart of that society. As another example, the total page count of Bagher Momeni's works over these thirty-five years amounts to more than double his output during the first thirty-five years of his life in Iran, and is twofold in maturity and depth.

The question of Iranian human identity in the Iranian text is a fundamental issue, and it would be well if you could analyse it transparently for us. When one speaks of identity, we are confronted with a chain of issues and states without attending to which one cannot speak of identity. As you know, our literature is one infused with mysticism—or, to put it better, with lofty aspiration and the symbol-creating powers of the human mind. This symbolising mind has a literature of its own. Yet in confronting other cultures of the world, it becomes breathless and exhausted. Why does this happen? Why do we Iranians, in terms of identity, upon encountering other cultures of the world, fall into self-doubt and pessimism towards ourselves, our traditions, and our heritage, and experience frustration and disillusionment? Can this stance of identity be analysed with the aid of the psychoanalysis of the migrant writer's literary works?

Speaking more broadly, migration—especially forced migration—from one culture to another, particularly after adolescence and youth, after our unconscious has formed its structure through our maternal culture, is like the migration of a fish from saltwater sea to a freshwater lake. An old poem expresses this beautifully: *"This house is lovely, yet it is not my house!"*

Henri Corbin, an astute researcher who has played the greatest role in excavating and understanding Iranian culture from the remotest times down to the present day, speaks of our distinctive Iranian cultural world and relates it to our cultural presence in a parallel world—neither this world nor the other world envisioned by the three monotheistic religions, but a world like an Eighth Clime that exists yet remains inaccessible to everyone, the very place where Mount Qaf and the Simurgh dwell. This imaginal, Hurqalya world is the foundation of the imaginary and dream-laden world of Iranian culture.

Here lies the stage of the Iranian human being's presence in existence, from whose mythological foundation the grounds of Iranian mysticism also emerge; a vantage point that the noble Ferdowsi and Attar draw upon in the deep structure of their two masterpieces, the *Shahnameh* and *The Conference of the Birds* (*Mantiq-ut-Tayr*). There is also another stage: this world, knowledge, technology, and construction—the empirical global reality that must be precisely understood and utilised for welfare, progress, construction, and the future of life on planet Earth. In this arena, our culture is currently undergoing training, learning, and experimentation. If we look at either of the two stages in isolation, we fall prey either to unwarranted pride or to futile depression. We, too, need one or two generations of intensive work to overcome this exaggerated perspective.

In your view, what are the spiritual and psychological coordinates of the geographical realm of migration and exile for a writer?

With your permission, I will respond only to its psychological aspect, since I am largely uninformed in the domain of the spiritual. The human psyche, unlike the body, is not particularly sensitive to geographical conditions. A writer's psychological state, depression, or cheerfulness may fluctuate, yet the writer's inner disposition—their speaking heart (*del-e sokhan-gou*)—was formed prior to migration. If we move past the outer shell of a literary work and look deeply, the imprint of the writer's foundational identity is clearly observable within it. Fortunately, the migrant writer's heart holds primacy over the circumstances and place of their dwelling.

The speaking heart? I do not understand this. Please explain further.

I have addressed this concept in a detailed essay [10] and have sought to demonstrate that *del* (the heart) in Persian culture corresponds to the unconscious as defined by Sigmund Freud. I shall include this essay in the appendix to our conversation. I wrote the essay in French and then translated it. It attracted the attention of the Swiss German-language specialist journal *ANRISS*, which translated and published it in German. In summary, the structure of our unconscious is formed during those very first few years in the mother's embrace and within the maternal culture, and all our subsequent languages pass through the filter of that mother tongue. The speaking heart is none other than our unconscious. [11] Psychoanalysis regards the human being as a symbolising, speaking, desiring, and split being.

What are the effects of migration on the writer and on the structure of literary works? How and from what perspective do you examine these effects?

I know writers who, after several decades, have learned the language of the host country merely enough to meet daily needs, yet have never read a single book or even a single page of a newspaper in another language. Even when they engage with the literature of the host country or host continent, they have read it in Persian translation. These writers have remained within the very same style, manner, and structure they had prior to migration. Another spectrum consists of writers who have been integrated into academic environments; they have translated books from the host country's language into Persian and vice versa, and have written books in their second language. They have experimented with styles and structures other than their own and attained a richer depth. Reading writers in their original mother tongue undoubtedly leaves a far deeper mark on any writer's style and craft.

At times, there is also the danger that the writer becomes submerged in the literature of the host country and forgets how to walk in their own stride! On the whole, however, the most constructive impact on the style, mode of thinking, and working methods of Iranian men and women of letters in Europe and America may be seen as a movement towards a kind of Cartesianism—encompassing precision, documentary rigour, and the presentation of clean, high-quality work. Yet this very tendency is a double-edged sword, as it can strip us of that Iranian mythological world, that dreamlike poetic realm. If a writer succeeds in taking the constructive element from each culture and synthesising them, they create masterpieces.

Are you saying that only the physical location of these writers has changed, whereas they continue to live in the clime of their previous cultural geography? What about Sa'edi? As the saying goes, he kept himself waiting at the station for the train home. He did not even learn French to the minimal degree you mentioned, nor did he have any inclination to learn it—whereas, as you put it, the writer's speaking heart has a different nature and a different atmosphere…

Yes! How beautifully the noble Hafez has prepared the answer to your question: *"The stranger's bewildered heart remains in the homeland."* We do not all endure separation from the beloved in the same way. Sa'edi consumed himself; others found different paths. As Nietzsche says, *"What does not kill me makes me stronger."* Art, poetry, and literature mean sincerity—opening one's heart and sharing its contents with others. They are not commercial commodities to be packaged and placed on the market. They are the fruit of the heart, of our innermost being. If our heart dies far from the homeland, what remains for us to offer?!

How do you view the translatability of literary works by Iranian migrant writers? Most works by migrant writers have been translated either by themselves or by acquaintances. Public reception tends to favour the writings of those Iranian authors written in the linguistic domain of the host country. Conversely, good translations of writers inside Iran also occasionally meet with warm reception. You yourself have written books in French. How does French society regard you as an Iranian thinker, artist, and man of letters, and what is your scholarly standing?

My works—whether articles, books, or paintings—have received recognition commensurate with their merit. Twenty-seven exhibitions of calligraphy and painting in various countries—most notably at UNESCO in Paris, by UNESCO's invitation, as well as the International Exhibition of Calligraphy in Novgorod, Russia, the Contemporary Museum of Calligraphy in Moscow, the Saint Petersburg Library, the San Francisco Library, and the Kyiv Library, together with UNESCO's invitation to present my views on *Nasta'liq* calligraphy and its relationship to Iran's culture and geographical space alongside *Master Fan Zeng*, China's foremost painter, calligrapher, and poet—may serve as signs of recognition of my artistic work. My lecture in French at UNESCO has been published as a book. One can still wait patiently until art and literature in exile are invited back to the homeland.

My scholarly works, like those of all my French colleagues, have been published in specialist journals. As for my books: *Knowing Hafez Through Hafez*, centred on a psychoanalysis of Hafez's ghazals, is counted among reference works. Recently, the Paris-based Syrian singer Abed Azrié produced an album of his songs centred on the poetry of the noble Hafez and asked me to introduce Hafez; in this album, I speak for ten minutes about Hafez. Another example is the Parisian psychoanalytic journal *Célibataire*, which, in an issue series entitled *Islam*, published my article *"Topography of Shi'a Sacred Sites"* at the editor-in-chief's request.

In your opinion, how do audiences from other cultures respond to Iranian literary works?

The success achieved today by cinema, the visual arts, and translations of great poets of the past such as Hafez, Khayyam, and Rumi has not yet fallen to contemporary Iranian literature and poetry. My own personal experience may serve as an example in this regard: my works on Hafez and Khayyam have had a wider reach than translations of contemporary poets (undertaken with the assistance of other friends).

I have heard about your work on Hafez. My father was one of the old architects and stonemasons of Shiraz; the paving of the Hafezieh—its older section—is his handiwork. The pools, the stone edging of the garden beds, and so forth—for me, these are part of Shiraz, Hafez, and the Hafezieh. How did it come about that you thought of presenting Hafez and Khayyam to the French? Surely Hafez holds his own intimate *Hafez-esque* resonances in your solitude...

Perhaps it would be fitting to summarise my view of Hafez and his poetic world for you as follows: «Hafez undoubtedly touches the collective memory (collective memory, historical memory, ethnic spirit, spirit of the language, shared historical essence, shared ethnic essence) of the Persian-speaking Iranian, to such a degree that after the passage of centuries his poetry remains inextricably bound to this memory. They find their articulate voice in "Hafez", and in a sense Hafez serves as a mediator between the collective-imaginary memory of the Iranian peoples and their historical movement. This is the secret that Hafez carries in his breast, and this is the secret of Hafez's profound and enduring presence for Iranians».

As for the secret of my acquaintance with Hafez, it goes back to when I was fourteen years old, ranked first in my class, and received his *Divan* of poetry as a gift. In those days, neither I, nor those around me, nor my teachers understood anything of the ghazals. From that day to this, I have lived with Hafez. I have also recounted this lifelong companionship in the introduction to the book *Another Look at the Secret of Hafez*. [12]

What are the principal themes addressed in the literary works of Iranian migrant writers within American and European cultural spheres?

My answer will be very personal and limited. The phenomenon of migration itself; the cultural, economic, and political causes connected to socio-political transformation in Iran; and encounters with the cultures of the host countries—their differences and similarities—form the predominant axes. Efforts to re-examine one's own culture and society, the lives of migrants in Iran both prior to migration and during migration, and introducing these to the host country are likewise prominent themes.

How do you assess the degree of attention paid by the host countries of Iranian migrant literature to Iranian intellectual productions in literary form?

Iran's intellectual productions up to five centuries ago are regarded with interest and respect. Unfortunately, however, for reasons we all know, a few decades into the Safavid dynasty and up to the present day, those intellectual productions that constitute the great treasure of our culture ceased to be generated. We fell behind in science, knowledge, and technology; all of them were replaced by the teaching of superstitions and matters devoid of universal or vital value, and until roughly one hundred and fifty years ago, with the beginning of the Iranian awakening, we endured three centuries of slumber and regression. From the onset of the Constitutional Revolution to the present day, only in cinema and the visual arts have we occasionally managed to make up for some of our backwardness. Ultimately, our intellectual productions have focused on finding ways to understand Iranian culture better and to introduce it better to the world—an endeavour exemplified in the research of Dariush Shayegan. Naturally, the literary forms of our thought cannot attract the attention they deserve, because the short story, the novel, and similar genres arrived from the West after the Iranian awakening.

In your view, what has caused the Iranian human being to falter in confronting and encountering modernity and the modern world, and to suffer fragmentation? Living in Tehran and Shiraz, I observe this rupture and fragmentation deeply: severing oneself from oneself and remaining adrift in self-alienation! Yet modernity relies primarily on deep attentiveness to one's own heritage. As Hafez says, let us not beg from strangers for what we ourselves possess… Is that possible?

Here, my heart is brimming with things to say—both as a lover of the culture of Iran-zamin, as a psychoanalyst, as an active participant in various fields of art and literature, and as a researcher on the role of culture in strategic services, in the service of organisation or cultural leaps. Would that there were time to speak of thirty years of activity in upholding and observing the provisions of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights; of thirty years of experience in strategic services in France and the publication of the fruits of those experiences in three books in French and three in Persian on that very subject; of my research on applied psychoanalysis and Iranian public culture, summarised in the book *Listening Differently and Psychoanalysis in Iran*; and finally, of twenty years of teaching psychoanalysis and training dozens of psychoanalysts. Briefly put, we must first re-read our own history so as to obtain an image of it that corresponds more closely to reality. Then, on the basis of such a history, we must proceed to diagnosis: accurately and clearly evaluate strengths and weaknesses, achievements and shortcomings, and then, in light of today's world as it actually is, identify solutions for our problems that are both desirable and feasible, and put them into practice.

In the meantime, until that day arrives, we are gripped by disorientation. We wish to have wings so as to fly faster, yet instead we suffer major ruptures and irreparable regressions. Nevertheless, one must not despair; it is fitting that we take flight from the platform of what we are and soar in proportion to our own wings. Undoubtedly, there is a way. In two books—*A Strategic Look at the Future of Iran* and *Another Look at the Cultural Land of Iran*—I have set out thoughts on this matter. I am deeply hopeful, provided that we choose the Cultural Land of Iran as the axis of our national solidarity; the remedy does not lie in excess and deficiency, nor in delusions of superiority.

What is the most widely read genre among the works of Iranian migrant writers? Fiction, poetry, drama, literary criticism, or theoretical literary debates?

One can only offer a sense of the Iranian audiences abroad for these works. In my view, first and foremost literary criticism and theoretical literary debates, followed perhaps by the short stories and novels of second-generation writers inside and outside the country, attract the attention of Iranians abroad.

It would be worthwhile if you could say something about the psychological perspective and Jacques Lacan's psychoanalytic approach to issues of human culture and literature. Lacan has been influential above all in three vast domains of the human and empirical sciences: literary criticism and theoretical debates on criticism; philosophy and the examination of human worldviews and ideological fixations; and a profound semiotic understanding of existence, life, woman, gender, and sex. His deep reflections on paranoid human behaviour have, in their own right, brought about an astonishing revolution in artistic imagination. Today, one cannot speak of psychological criticism and overlook him, or fail to weigh his thought alongside the works of Poulantzas or Julia Kristeva. Yet in our Iran, whenever global thinkers are discussed, it seems to me that everything remains at the surface. What I have just remarked may also carry this message: in order to be present in today's world, we have no choice but to know the equations of today's world, come to terms with them, and contribute our share… Is that not so?

Let me put it plainly: the "correct" translation of writings produced by a world in motion is the shortest path to understanding this world and finding a worthy place in which to settle and dwell; yet attaining that word "correct" demands immense effort. Proper translation itself requires an entire world of culture. The three essential conditions for a correct translation are these: first, the translator must be an expert in the subject matter they intend to translate—holding specialisation and professional mastery in that field, having worked in it, poured heart and soul into it, and paid their dues in practice—rather than simply hearing the name of Marx or Freud and setting out to translate *Capital* or *The Interpretation of Dreams*.

Second, they must be intimately acquainted with the nuances and turns of the author's language; and third, they must be able—provided they have understood the concepts well—to render them in clear, accessible language for readers, so that full comprehension is achieved, rather than misunderstanding or partial understanding.

I have translated two books from French into Persian, both pertaining to my profession. When I translated them, every single line was revised with multi-member teams of Persian-speaking and French-speaking specialists. We also published both books in bilingual editions so that scholarly readers could point out their flaws to us. For a proper presence in the world, we must make our own language authentic and understand the language of others authentically. No secure future will ever be built upon hasty, half-baked efforts.

Translation is the foundation of cultural transmission. The predicament of superficial readings of today's progressive global culture will persist in our Iran until a major, foundational movement of "correct translation" is established. Genuine communication with the Other is possible only when we recognise the Other, in another position, as one of our own. This holds true in person-to-person relations, in culture-to-culture relations, and in relation to the human world at large.

What is the state of the press and its media capacities for migrant writers (both inside and outside their own country)?

On the whole, the press and media inside Iran ignore writers, men and women of letters, and thinkers residing abroad. Let us look at the proportion of writings by thinkers abroad relative to total output in Iran's cultural sphere, and then look at the proportion of articles, interviews, and book reviews concerning those thinkers in domestic media—such a comparison can be highly instructive. Outside Iran as well, apart from what circulates on the internet, the reach of serious periodicals is very limited. Fortunately, online media, Facebook, and Telegram have generated enthusiasm for disseminating writings at every level.

One of the initiatives undertaken in the Iranian press over at least the past two decades has been the publication of dozens of interviews with contemporary Iranian writers and thinkers. In my view, recognition is a prerequisite for proper introduction. What is your own assessment of presenting your works on the internet? How would you prefer to be introduced in Iranian society—in the field of literature and culture, or psychoanalysis?

I believe the depth of the issue goes far beyond the efforts of thoughtful, hardworking journalists, publishers, and critics. Let me give an example. My daughter wrote a book in French that was published by a reputable publisher in France. The publisher promoted the book very well, and several journals even awarded it prizes. Three months later, the French Embassy in India invited her for one month to present the book at various Indian universities. The fruit of that one-month residency was the translation and publication of the book in English by an Indian publisher. I expect to be given the opportunity to present my books, ideas, and experiences at the universities of my motherland. Via Skype, I am prepared to deliver ten lectures a week on my findings at Iranian universities. I expect that out of twenty-seven exhibitions of my work, at least one would be held in my homeland. I expect to serve on the examining committee of dozens of doctoral theses in my homeland. I expect to pass on all my clinical knowledge one day a week to hundreds of psychiatrists and psychoanalysts. I expect to direct dozens of scholarly book-publishing series. I expect…

Expectation… is a fine thing. How do Iranian migrant writers deal with the issue of censorship and self-censorship?

That is a subtle point. The phenomenon of censorship is meaningless abroad. Self-censorship occupies its greatest space along two axes: fear of physical elimination on account of political opposition, and fear of being judged or targeted by a fatwa for crossing ideological red lines. Yet there is also an inner torment that constantly keeps us in flight from ourselves: we continually push certain things to the recesses of our minds. Do we not also practise self-censorship in order to push away the Other? At the same time, I do not think fear can simply be equated with constructs of censorship. The mechanism of fear is a kind of prejudgement: for instance, out of fear that such-and-such might happen, we refrain from doing such-and-such! Censorship, in the sense of deterrence and suppression, is the concealment of the distance between the reality and the truth of a matter.

Look! In one sentence, and with an example from my own experience, I will try to convey the heart of the matter. Anthropology and psychoanalysis have a great deal to say about tradition and religion. It is not that they are necessarily right, but they have things to say. Come, without censorship, allow me to examine and present scientifically the dangers of displacing celebration with mourning that has taken place over the past five hundred years in Twelver Shi'ism—whereas Freud came from a Jewish family and was raised in Jewish culture, yet in his book *Moses*, he demonstrates that historically we have two Moseses, not one.

What do you consider to be the primary mental taboos of Iranian migrants?

A taboo is an unspoken piece of knowledge that itself generates cultural cohesion. One might regard disparaging Iran and Iranian culture as a kind of taboo that has remained taboo even among the second and third generations. To a certain extent, Iranian migrants have preserved in migration their self-esteem, lofty ambition, keeping up appearances despite hardship, refraining from laying bare their inner sorrows, preserving honour and reputation, and even at times a fierce sense of honour—traits characteristic of our temperament.

Fascinating! Disparagement—a sense of shame? Over being Muslim or Iranian, for example?! Are loneliness and a phobia of fear taboos for us Iranians outside our country?

My meaning is quite the opposite. The taboo exists because we are extraordinarily sensitive lest others fail to speak properly and favourably of our culture, our society, or our history—that is, we do not permit the name of Iran and everything connected with it to be spoken of disparagingly.

What is the impact of geographical and cultural constraints abroad on the process of producing literary works?

The fundamental constraint is, first and foremost, migration itself. Creative production requires time, peace of mind, a lighter burden of earning one's daily bread, and a venue in which to present one's work. I personally know many Iranian writers who spent a lifetime in major cities of Europe and America driving taxis ten hours a day. To produce literary and intellectual work under such hardship, to face the even greater hardship of finding a publisher, and—most painful of all—to get bogged down in book distribution! One prominent Iranian writer, an old friend of mine, produced scarcely five hundred pages in total during thirty years of driving a taxi, yet since retiring—in less than five years up to today—he has published more than five thousand pages.

Well, these matters are important! We have four million migrants, at least one million of whom hold degrees above a bachelor's—why do they lag behind in reading books, or why do published books fail to reach a second printing? Is it true that Iranians generally do not welcome reading books? In Iran, for example, Saint-Exupéry's *The Little Prince* has thirteen or fourteen translations and editions on the market; the latest edition I saw cost nearly fifty thousand tomans. That book sells, whereas works by Iranian authors do not receive such reception. What, in your view, is the point here? One of the finest works I have ever seen and read on the subject of migrant literature is the collection of articles in the journal *Arash*, published by Parviz Ghelichkhani. It is extraordinary. In that special issue I read essays far better argued and more profound than the propositions of Edward Said, Nabokov, Solzhenitsyn, Bulgakov, or Milan Kundera. Where does the problem lie? Continuing along the tracks of an oral culture…

There are several points here: reading books is like observing hygiene of body and mind, and it begins in childhood within the family, at school, and among playmates. The second generation of Iranians abroad are in fact avid readers. Regarding the esteemed journal *Arash*, you are right; I myself have published several articles there. When I say that the achievements of Iranians abroad are ignored, I mean precisely what you have just described. Do you know that across the world's universities, without exaggeration, a doctoral thesis of a very high calibre on Iran is defended every single week? A two-page introduction of each on radio, television, in the press, and on websites could showcase Iranian achievements; then we would no longer have much need to idolise second-rate foreign thinkers. Do you not think that the immense global stature of contemporary Iranian cinema is the fruit of Iranians' own work, yet the labour of introducing this precious treasure was shouldered either by the filmmakers themselves or by festivals outside Iran?

Iranian memoir-writing is an emerging literary genre. How do you view this field?

Memoir-writing, from a psychoanalyst's perspective, is listening to stories told by a narrator that everyone already knows—especially in a culture of concealment and keeping up appearances. A genuine memory is recounted in the psychoanalyst's consulting room, and even then only after the narrator has attained trust. In which of these memoirs have we ever been able to find something that we could place in the negative column of the narrator's own conduct? Memoir-writing is the review of a lifetime's endeavour through the narrator's conscious filter.

Can we re-read the genre of Iranian migrant literature through the model of a culture of concealment? What is your suggestion? Literature of exile, literature of escape, prison literature, and literature of flight are parts of a body of writing that grows tall in migration. How do you view the totality of works produced in these memoir sub-genres? Another element I notice in memoirs is the re-reading of the memoirists' partisan pasts—for instance, revisiting the Tudeh Party, the left, the right, the religious right, and other factions active in those years. In your view, where in Iranian migrant literature do these belong?

Without exaggeration, the bulk of articles, stories, even historical writings and documentary films are, directly or indirectly, memoirs brought into migration—a great treasure trove for writing an accurate and impartial history of post-revolutionary Iran. Yet the culture of concealment in memoir-writing has two important facets: one is traditional concealment, which is simply preserving honour, putting on a brave face, and holding one's head high; the other is strict observance of security concerns. Concerning the culture of concealment, let me tell you an anecdote about the publication in Europe of my second, very slim book of Persian fiction. The first time I read *One Hundred Years of Solitude* in Persian, I was a doctoral student; I fell ill for a week. The book's eerie atmosphere affected me so deeply that I longed to write a novel like *One Hundred Years of Solitude*. Later I read that nearly all the characters in the story had actually existed and, as Gabriel García Márquez's mother put it, most of the villagers knew them. Well, I too wrote a short novel whose protagonist was an acquaintance, and, like a psychoanalyst, I turned the character inside out. After the book was printed, mischievous people passed copies to my relatives, and such an uproar broke out that I was forced to buy up every remaining copy of the book—and to this day it sits in a storeroom.

Since long ago, the question of tradition and modernity has been one of the central issues confronting Iranian writers and thinkers. In your view, what position does the Iranian migrant writer occupy in this encounter?

Migration renders both perspectives more balanced: it makes tradition more respected and strips modernity of its absolute desirability. Living in migration is the experience of living within the clime of another tradition. The migrant strives to understand the existential roots of tradition, because respect for tradition is respect for the people. The thoughtful migrant lives within modernity; the absolute ideal gives way to an ideal that requires adaptation to traditions. Yet this question calls for a very detailed essay; perhaps it is precisely this shift in the idealising gaze towards modernity and the return of a kind of respect for tradition that will be able, after the return of the host of migrant thinkers to our beloved homeland Iran, to invent a fresh perspective on the model of development and progress.

Does Iranian migrant literature hold a place in literary and academic circles outside Iran?

Iranian migrant literature is the youngest member of the global community of migrant literature. Before us, North African Arabs, Turks from Turkey, Pakistanis, and Indians arrived on these shores with their literary works. We are guests with a history of barely a third of a century. On the other hand, our beloved Iran, despite the extensive presence of Europeans, was never a colony of any superpower. For this reason too, deep familiarity with our culture among people here is very limited. We need time.

What a striking point! In your opinion, what can time do for us and for our culture?

Time means an opportunity for several generations of Europeans and Americans to gradually become acquainted with our little-known culture and its profound, astonishing dimensions. It is not we who need this time; they need it in order to come to know us. Let me give an example: the translation of the priceless ghazals of the noble Hafez into French. Just two weeks ago this was the subject of my lecture in Paris. You mentioned Charles-Henri de Fouchécour, the distinguished figure who in 2006 finally translated all of Hafez's ghazals into French for the first time. The first ghazal of Hafez reached Europe in the seventeenth century via Bosnian Turks and was translated into Polish; twenty years later it was translated into Latin; a century later, seventeen ghazals were translated into Latin and one ghazal into English.

By the end of the eighteenth century, all the ghazals were translated into English, and at the beginning of the nineteenth century into German. In France, two hundred years elapsed between the first translation at the end of the eighteenth century and the translation of the complete ghazals. In short, they need time so that, through everyone's concerted effort, we may introduce to the world at least ten world-class poets of the first rank, seven hundred poets of the second rank, and seven thousand poets of the third rank, all of whom possess published *Divans* of poetry. The only path is sustained presence in the everyday and cultural life here, and that requires both time and immense work. Let us allow time to do its work.

In your view, what problems do Iranian writers and thinkers face in publishing their works abroad?

The question ought to be asked the other way round: at which stage of production, printing, and distribution does the Iranian thinker *not* encounter difficulties? If they write in the host language, they lag behind their peers by the entire depth of a mother tongue. If they write in their mother tongue, the entire cycle—typesetting, printing, and distribution—is beset with problems. They are strangers even in their own homeland. The sole privilege that has come our way in recent years is the appearance of pirated photocopied editions of our books in Iran after they are published abroad—which, moreover, abides by no copyright law whatsoever!

In this regard, why do writers not lodge complaints themselves? Can I file a complaint on your behalf against a street-corner bookseller or peddlers selling pirated books? That group has now inflicted indescribable problems upon publishing inside the country as well. My suggestion is that this issue requires all writers to support one another—not to mention that we writers have no guild! In your view, are the rights of the Iranian author respected outside Iran?

Within the system of production and distribution, the Iranian author's rights are respected to the exact same extent as any other citizen's. The problem is not legal rights; the problem is getting the product to the consumer, a wheel whose very axle is broken at the foundation.

Could you describe a day in the life of an Iranian migrant writer?

Rarely can an Iranian writer sit at their desk from morning until dusk and simply be a writer. At least half of their time is spent on daily necessities. Maintaining contact with the homeland and compatriots, as well as presenting and securing access for earlier works, takes up another quarter of the time. What remains are three or four hours that can be put to productive use. Research in one's mother tongue is harder; access to sources is time-consuming; and, most importantly, a sphere for intellectual coordination with speakers of the same language is rarer. Today, the internet has solved half of these problems. Unfortunately, working extensively on the internet also brings its own plagues and afflictions. As for my own personal experience, I spend six to eight hours a day working with a computer in various ways, half of that time on Skype with people across the world.

How do you see the future prospects of Iranian migrant literature?

In all likelihood, our literature and poetry will, with the passage of time, follow in the footsteps of cinema and the visual arts. Yet until then, I hope that literature returns from migration to the embrace of the homeland so that, together with literature inside the country, it may build the flourishing literature of Iran-zamin.

[1]. Serge Rezvani (Cyrus Rezvani) was born in Iran in 1928 (1307 SH). His father was [Majid Rezvani](https://fa.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=%D9%85%D8%AC%DB%8C%D8%AF_%D8%B1%D8%B6%D9%88%D8%A7%D9%86%DB%8C&action=edit&redlink=1), a researcher, stage actor, and author of [*Theatre and Dance in Iran*](https://fa.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=%D9%86%D9%85%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%B4_%D9%88_%D8%B1%D9%82%D8%B5_%D8%AF%D8%B1_%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%B1%D8%A7%D9%86&action=edit&redlink=1). His mother was of [Caucasian](https://fa.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D9%82%D9%81%D9%82%D8%A7%D8%B2) migrant origin. In childhood he moved with his family to [Moscow](https://fa.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D9%85%D8%B3%DA%A9%D9%88) and from there to France. Cancer took his mother from him in his youth, and he was obliged to spend his childhood and adolescence in boarding schools for Russian émigrés. At fifteen he ran away from those boarding schools to pursue painting. He painted for twenty years and thereafter turned to writing plays and fiction. In 1950 Serge married the French actress [Évelyne Lanzmann](https://fa.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=%D8%A7%DB%8C%D9%88%D9%84%DB%8C%D9%86_%D9%84%D8%A7%D9%86%D8%B2%D9%85%D9%86&action=edit&redlink=1), though they soon divorced, and he married Danièle—or Lula (the name Serge gave Danièle and by which he called her)—the daughter of the French Prime Minister of the time. Danièle's family was displeased with the union, yet Danièle left everything behind and moved in with Serge. Lula left a vital and profound imprint on Serge Rezvani's life and work. Lula died in 2004 from [Alzheimer's disease](https://fa.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D8%A2%D9%84%D8%B2%D8%A7%DB%8C%D9%85%D8%B1). He now lives in Paris and is a well-known name and figure in French cinema, music, and literature. He has published more than forty novels, fifteen plays, two poetry collections, and several philosophical essays in French, and his plays have repeatedly been staged in French theatres by himself or others. Among his novels and plays may be mentioned [*The Years of Enlightenment*](https://fa.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=%D8%B3%D8%A7%D9%84%E2%80%8C%D9%87%D8%A7%DB%8C_%D8%B1%D9%88%D8%B4%D9%86%DA%AF%D8%B1%DB%8C&action=edit&redlink=1), [*The Story of a House*](https://fa.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=%D8%AF%D8%A7%D8%B3%D8%AA%D8%A7%D9%86_%DB%8C%DA%A9_%D8%AE%D8%A7%D9%86%D9%87&action=edit&redlink=1), [*The Eclipse*](https://fa.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=%DA%A9%D8%B3%D9%88%D9%81_(%DA%A9%D8%AA%D8%A7%D8%A8), [*The Eighth Whip*](https://fa.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=%D8%AA%D8%A7%D8%B2%DB%8C%D8%A7%D9%86%D9%87_%D9%87%D8%B4%D8%AA%D9%85&action=edit&redlink=1), [*Human Law*](https://fa.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=%D9%82%D8%A7%D9%86%D9%88%D9%86_%D8%A7%D9%86%D8%B3%D8%A7%D9%86%DB%8C&action=edit&redlink=1), [*The Asphalt Table*](https://fa.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=%D9%85%DB%8C%D8%B2_%D8%A2%D8%B3%D9%81%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%AA&action=edit&redlink=1), [*Elliptical Portraiture*](https://fa.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=%DA%86%D9%87%D8%B1%D9%87_%D9%86%DA%AF%D8%A7%D8%B1%DB%8C_%D8%A8%DB%8C%D8%B6%D9%88%DB%8C&action=edit&redlink=1), [*An Amorous Testament*](https://fa.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=%D9%88%D8%B5%DB%8C%D8%AA_%D8%B9%D8%A7%D8%B4%D9%82%D8%A7%D9%86%D9%87&action=edit&redlink=1), [*The Inhabitants of Potemkin*](https://fa.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=%D8%B3%D8%A7%DA%A9%D9%86%D8%A7%D9%86_%D9%BE%D9%88%D8%AA%D9%85%DA%A9%DB%8C%D9%86&action=edit&redlink=1), [*Crossing the Black Hills*](https://fa.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=%DA%AF%D8%B0%D8%B1_%D8%A7%D8%B2_%D8%AA%D9%BE%D9%87%E2%80%8C%D9%87%D8%A7%DB%8C_%D8%B3%DB%8C%D8%A7%D9%87&action=edit&redlink=1), and [*The Origin of the World*](https://fa.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=%D8%B1%DB%8C%D8%B4%D9%87_%D8%AF%D9%86%DB%8C%D8%A7&action=edit&redlink=1). (Abridged from the Wikipedia entry on Serge Rezvani)

[2]. Wise human, sapient human, or modern human, or by its [scientific name](https://fa.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D9%86%D8%A7%D9%85_%D8%B9%D9%84%D9%85%DB%8C) *Homo sapiens*: this name was chosen by Carl Linnaeus in 1758 CE to designate the intelligent human being. It is the name of a [species](https://fa.wikipedia.org/wiki/%DA%AF%D9%88%D9%86%D9%87_(%D8%B2%DB%8C%D8%B3%D8%AA%E2%80%8C%D8%B4%D9%86%D8%A7%D8%B3%DB%8C) of the [genus](https://fa.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D8%B3%D8%B1%D8%AF%D9%87) [*Homo*](https://fa.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D8%A7%D9%86%D8%B3%D8%A7%D9%86_(%D8%B3%D8%B1%D8%AF%D9%87). According to the theory of [evolution](https://fa.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D9%81%D8%B1%DA%AF%D8%B4%D8%AA), *Homo sapiens* is an evolved descendant of *Homo erectus*. From a [palaeoanthropological](https://fa.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D8%AF%DB%8C%D8%B1%DB%8C%D9%86%E2%80%8C%D9%85%D8%B1%D8%AF%D9%85%E2%80%8C%D8%B4%D9%86%D8%A7%D8%B3%DB%8C) standpoint, two foundational hypotheses exist regarding the origin of *Homo sapiens*. The first view holds that modern humans multiplied from a common ancestor that diverged from [*Homo erectus*](https://fa.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D8%A7%D9%86%D8%B3%D8%A7%D9%86_%D8%B1%D8%A7%D8%B3%D8%AA%E2%80%8C%D9%82%D8%A7%D9%85%D8%AA) in [Africa](https://fa.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D8%A2%D9%81%D8%B1%DB%8C%D9%82%D8%A7). The other hypothesis contends that *Homo sapiens* underwent its evolutionary course from *Homo erectus* not only in Africa, but also in other regions of the world. Since 2010 CE, [genetic](https://fa.wikipedia.org/wiki/%DA%98%D9%86%D8%AA%DB%8C%DA%A9) studies have established an intermediate view, whereby the gene pool of *Homo sapiens* derives predominantly from an African ancestor, although admixture in the course of evolution indicates that evolution also occurred in other parts of the globe. *Homo* is a Greek word meaning human and humankind, and *sapiens*, a Latin word, means wise.
