en.body_markdown:
### https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/01/CX-062.jpg

### I am in love with the I without I

### Abhar al-'Ashiqin (The Jasmine of the Lovers)

### Ruzbihan Baqli Shirazi

## Preface

Examining the discourse of prophets, Illuminationist (*Ishraqi*) mystics, and that group of individuals who have approached physical death and returned by chance leads us to recognise the close resemblance among these three discourses. Our aim is to investigate such discourses without sitting in judgement on the truth or falsity of these statements. In other words, we consider discourse to be the product of the individual's own internal processes and interactions. Speech (*kalam* / the word) is the axis of this inquiry. Our field of investigation extends from mythological sources to psychoanalytic hypotheses and the experiences of those who have returned from physical death. At the same time, speech is our working instrument: speech illuminates these diverse experiences—an experience of which each person speaks in their own language.

"I am in love with the I without I"

The first *I*: the conscious, loving *I*. The second *I*: the universal *I*, the comprehensive *I*, the singular *I*, the *I* within and the *I* without—provided we strip away from it the third *I*: the external *I*, the reflection of the *I* in the mirror of others. Is the *I* that is here the object of love not the very same *I* of which the thirteenth-century mystic Najm al-Din Kubra speaks in his book *Fawa'ih al-Jamal*? "Know that the soul, Satan, and the angel are not realities outside of you; you yourself are these. Likewise, heaven, earth, and the realm of divine majesty (*jabarut*) are not outside of you; paradise, hell, death, and life are within you as well. Once you have completed the mystical journey, at the moment of purity, you shall attain such awareness." This very "I" forms the axis of al-Hallaj's poem: "I am He whom I love, and He whom I love is I; we are two spirits dwelling in one body. If you see me, you see Him, and if you see Him, you see me." Let us observe to what extent love and unity are intertwined. Borne upon the vessel of this phrase—"I am in love with the I without I"—let us journey through the valley of Iranian mysticism in an endeavour to find an answer to these three questions:

- What is the Other World, and what are its traces?

- How far back does human memory reach, and from "when" does it remember?

- What impact has the emergence of speech had upon us?

The concepts of "light", "love", and "the other side of the I" serve as historical bridges spanning from primordial mythological-religious elements to the residual experience of those who have approached physical death and returned. "Discourse" in our inquiry is merely the medium that makes close dissection possible; it is a sign of the reflection of reality upon the individual, not an instrument for passing judgement.

On the one hand, the discovery of the concept of the unconscious within the *I* as the other side of the *I*, and on the other hand, the significance of the word and the structure of language as the foundation of the unconscious, demonstrate that the deployment of speech is the event that made the human being "human". This event gave rise to our verbal memory, oriented our emotions, and led to the production of new "concepts" situated at the "border" of speech.

The rediscovered key is the word. Our verbal memory (in the sense of drawing what lies outside us into conceptual form through space–time) makes use of speech. Likewise, the relation between the "I" and the "I" passes through the medium of "speech". How did it transpire in the intermediate state, on the border between the animal condition and the discovery of speech? Why do we perpetually need something other than speech for "expression"—for instance, music, dance…? Why have great mystics always felt unable to capture their Illuminationist experiences in words? This same feeling is also echoed in the discourse of those who have returned from near physical death.

These questions lead us to a pivotal point. In the intermediate era, on the border of the invention of speech, on the border between verbal memory and pre-verbal memory, has a "stratum" of human memory pertaining to the era prior to the discovery or invention of speech not remained within us? (Perhaps what Freud refers to in his Schema of Letter 53 as "Mother", "Pre-Mother", or "Eternal Mother"). A stratum that knows neither time nor space—in other words, time is always, "pre-eternity and the eternal present", and space is everywhere. This "place" of memory lies in the neighbourhood of "speech" and "God", where everything is fashioned through "God–the Word": absolute light, absolute love, bordering on the other side of the I (Figure 1 — Appendix 3).

Have prophets and mystics not drawn singularly close to this border of the intermediate era of the invention of speech? Accessing once again a memory that dwells within us—let us recall the saying of Najm al-Din Kubra: "Know that the psyche, Satan, and the angel are not realities outside of you; you yourself are they."

Or al-Hallaj's *"Ana al-Haqq"* ("I am the Truth").

Commentary: "The reliving of primordial historical time in the 'historiography of the psyche' does not take place in a determinate location, but unfolds in the enchanted space of the imagination, between pre-eternity and eternity" (Appendix 1 – 2). Pre-eternity and post-eternity, before and after time: one may readily accept that human beings lived in a space that did not separate time and space from one another; in other words, the invention of concepts stretched out "time" and "space" into linear extension.

"As soon as lover and beloved are united through love, within this union remain sounds, colours, delight, space, and time, enveloped in a state of ecstasy" (Appendix 1 – 3). "In reality, the divisions of time, space, and causality in the mythological outlook bore no relation to contemporary scientific modes of cognition. Mythical thought points to a world possessing its own distinctive divisions of time, space, and causality: if time is reversible and if space is a quality governed by the events that transpire therein, causality is far more the simultaneity of occurring events than a causal relation in the form of a linear chain of cause and effect" (Appendix 1 – 2). In other words: "Because the psyche has its own singular history, it is always in the present." One of our present difficulties is gaining access to the trace of the concepts of "space–time", place, time, and causality before, during, and after the interval in which the invention of speech occurred. Bearing in mind that our memory is "blind" outside its field of operation, this observation enables us to distinguish the concept of time founded upon verbal memory from the concept of primordial time, mythical time, or natural (biological) time.

Henry Corbin, in his book *Creative Imagination in the Sufism of Ibn 'Arabi*, speaks of discontinuous qualitative time: "By whatever name we call them, the events that mark the relation with the 'invisible personal guide' do not occur in quantifiable material time. These events cannot be measured by the continuous, uniform unit of time regulated by the revolution of the planets; they do not fit within the bounds of continuous, irreversible events. Beyond doubt, these events take place in 'time', yet in their own singular time—this discontinuous time of pure quality, whose moments cannot be measured save by their own unit, a unit that alters each time with its own density, a density that measures time while the past is present in the future and the future is present in the past, like the notes of a musical phrase that follow one after another, yet are all in the present so as to be able to compose precisely that musical phrase" (Appendix 1 – 4).

The concept of Paradise—a realm where neither the concept of time nor the concept of space exists—is found in nearly all cultural and religious mythologies. Across diverse texts, Paradise is an eternal, pre-eternal place, an environment of blossoms and greenery in which birds sing. Was this not an image of the space of human life prior to the invention of the word? It is here that the imagery of Eden, Paradise, pre-eternity, and eternity converge—in other words, an alternative vision of cyclical time:

Paradise — the end — the beginning of Eden.

For the Celtic peoples, the concept of Paradise is expressed by the word *síd* or *sídh*: the visible portion of the Other World. It may be situated beyond the ocean, upon islands. *Síd* signifies peace, and all the "ever-present" dwell in *sídh*, which naturally lies beyond time and space (Appendix 1 – 5). Such a concept of the Other World, in which "time and space" are other, resides within us, in such a way that human faculties of perception do not recognise them. The question arises as to how these concepts came to be present within us. In Zoroastrian culture, this image of the "Other World" manifests in the Avesta thus: "This homage is for the Earth, which is an angel" (Appendix 1 – 1). A historian of Zoroastrian culture naturally reconstructs this thought as follows: "The Earth is an angel—an angel as real as a flower" (Appendix 1 – 1). Henry Corbin interprets the presence of the Angel of the Earth in these terms: "The process of perceiving the Angel of the Earth in the imagination as 'unreal' demonstrates that such a conception of the Earth pertains to the 'psycho-spiritual' structure" (Appendix 1 – 4). From a psychoanalytic perspective, may we not conclude that such an association of meanings intertwines the concepts of angel, earth, woman, mother, homeland, paradise, Eden, birth, and life? Nevertheless, employing the concept of the structure of memory appears more fitting than the concept of a psycho-spiritual structure.

The structure of memory enables us to reconstruct its cognition and evaluate it.

Where Henry Corbin speaks of the "hidden depth of the psyche", is this not an interpretation of the structure of memory: "An encounter with the Earth, not as an aggregate of material impressions, but in the person of its Angel, is a 'psychic' event that can occur neither in the impersonal abstract world nor in the domain of sensory data. The Earth must be perceived not through the senses, but through a primordial image; and precisely because this image bears the contours of an individual design, it manifests as a sign of an image of the self that the psyche holds in its ultimate depth" (Appendix 1 – 4).

If this hidden depth is not in our memory, then where is it? It lies here, alongside our faculty of perception and our sensory faculties, unable to express itself through words.

The surviving traces of this no-where – no-when—in brief, this placeless realm of "Eden – Celestial Earth – Paradise"—manifest themselves from mythical times to the present day through two other concepts: love and light.

Light stands in opposition to darkness, whereas the basis of our perception operates through "opposition". Love is a state of ecstasy in Eden–Earth, the present, eternity, and pre-eternity. Henry Corbin writes: "The Mazdean vision divides the totality of what is conceivable between an infinite height of light, where Ahura Mazda, the Lord of Wisdom, dwells for ever, and darkness, the negative power of death and fragmentation, Ahriman" (Appendix 1 – 2). Such a sensation of rapture and bliss, love for the beloved, leads to union. Let us recall Ruzbihan's phrase: "I am in love with the I without I." The bliss of the moment manifests as light, devoid of the concept of time. As Ibn 'Arabi puts it: "Celestial love is spirit without body; earthly love is body without spirit; divine love possesses both body and spirit" (Appendix 1 – 2).

Darkness undergoes a shift of foundation in mysticism: Najm al-Din Kubra says: "…whereas this veil is not outside of them; it is a part of them; this veil is the darkness of their primordial existence."

In the Gospel of John, the four concepts of light, love, the Word, and union are centred in Christ: "As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world" / "I and the Father are one" / Jesus speaks to them again: "I am the light of the world" / "Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will attain the light of life."

In response to the question of how and since when we separated the two concepts of time and space, Henry Corbin writes: "Orientation in time: the various ways in which human beings demonstrate their presence upon the earth, and the continuity of this presence in something called history, and the question here is to know whether this matter has meaning… whereas one of the driving forces of Iranian mystical literature is the attainment of the Orient—an Orient that we know well is situated neither on a geographical map nor anywhere else; it is an Orient that lies in none of the seven climes" (Appendix 1 – 6). "Orientation is one of the primary phenomena of our presence in the world. Human presence is the spatialisation of the world outside oneself, and such a phenomenon requires a relation with one's world; indeed, such a relation is defined by one's mode of presence in the world. The four cardinal directions—east and west, north and south—are not things towards whose recognition this presence moves, but directions that signify orientation and familiarity with one's world. Having these directions means guiding oneself in this world" (Appendix 1 – 6). Henry Corbin demonstrates the role of human memory in the invention of time and space, though he does not specify which memory he is speaking of; and the organisation, the mapping of this network from the primordial evening that lies outside human memory, is a singular point: "The point of orientation, the celestial north, the Pole Star, where the various modes of perceiving this vertical dimension do not exist—so alien that it rectifies space, yet within time" (Appendix 1 – 6). Let us unpack the concept of the Pole, a concept that simultaneously gathers within itself the origin of human emergence in time (one's past) and human emergence in space (whence one came and whither one goes): "It forms the eighth land… this absent mystical Orient, the possibility of origin and the principle of return, the object of perpetual quest, is the Celestial Pole" (Appendix 1 – 6).

The East is the border of speech, and the West is the cognition of speech.

In their culture, the Icelanders hold an interpretation close to this theme: orientation or the quest for the east, in northern conceptions, rests close to notions of festivals or the public calendar; they use a single word for north and below, and for south and above. North is on the left and south is on the right. The sun moves from east to west and remains in the south throughout the day. The bright half of the world belongs to the living and the lords of light; the special half, of the dead and the gods of mysteries, is darkness (Appendix 1 – 2).

The foundation of the structure of our memory lies in words; words have enabled us to expand concepts, to establish relations between these concepts, and likewise to bring about the emergence of intelligence.

Zoroaster's spiritual journey in *Eran-Vej* (*Airyanem Vaejah*) leads to the Mazdean vision; the Prophet of Islam interprets his Ascension (*Mi'raj*) thus: "I beheld my Lord in the fairest of forms." Mystics recount their experiences of upward journeying. For example, Mulla Sadra of Shiraz, in the seventeenth century CE, in his book *Entry into the Unseen*, describes his journey as follows: "When I attained this state and detachment from the world, over a long period after my interior, my psyche, and my heart caught fire from the supreme flames as a result of prolonged and intricate spiritual exertions, the lights of the angelic realm (*malakut*) shone upon my psyche. All the mysteries of the unseen, which I previously knew only through logical reasoning, I suddenly apprehended in a single integrated grasp and direct vision" (Appendix 1 – 2). Najm al-Din Kubra says: "I was in seclusion; I was lifted upwards, and before me the sun was rising. They carried me into the sun… Through long nights I contemplated the sky until I saw it both beneath me and above me. Throughout the nights I observed the earth and sought to discover it as it truly is, until it dissolved itself into a tree of light" (Appendix 1 – 6). Another mode of the intuitive journey of those who have approached death and returned was described by Dr Moody in 1955 and has since been the subject of extensive research. This phenomenon is lucidly summarised in the book *An Inquiry into the Existence of Guardian Angels*:

- The individual invariably states that what they have seen cannot be expressed through words.

- The individual hears people saying that they have died; everything appears strange to them, and they feel themselves to be dead.

- The individual feels no pain whatsoever and experiences total calm and serenity.

- The individual exits their body and observes what is transpiring around them.

- The individual is drawn into a "tunnel".

- The individual beholds a brilliant light.

- The individual encounters a kind of boundary.

To better understand the expressions of a person who has undergone this experience, let us read the following passage together: "I was filled with the knowledge of God, and in that precious domain of His being I was one with Him. My attention was drawn upward, where a great door stood open, leading to another circular door. A white light was shining and breathing into the darkness… It was the most beautiful light I had ever seen. It seemed to me that I was moving very rapidly, yet everything was outside time… There before me stood the living presence of light. Within, I felt intelligence, reason, understanding, love, and truth." Comparing these utterances—spoken by prophets, mystics, and those who have undergone a near-death experience—suffices for us to recognise their identity. Whereas a near-death experience comes only to those who have been declared medically dead, the visionary (intuitive) experience of mystics requires will and the execution of a direct or indirect method. Without endorsing the veracity or degree of practicality of this method, we quote one of those rare treatises that speaks simultaneously of a method, the testing of its application, and its outcome: "Our method is the method of alchemy, and it consists in liberating the rare luminous organ (*latîfa*) imprisoned beneath the mountains… It may happen that you see yourself at the bottom of a well, a well affected by a downward movement from top to bottom (while in reality it is you who are ascending)… Your inner states affected by this emergence include seeing deserts, cities, and countries coming towards you from above and then disappearing beneath you… just as if you were watching a boat appear and vanish upon the waves of the sea… You behold with your eyes what until now you had apprehended with your faculty of understanding." (Appendix 1 - 6). Finding the common factors among the three types of "journey" is scarcely difficult: the prophetic state (Zoroaster, Buddha, Muhammad, Christ), the mystical visionary state (across various schools: Jewish, Christian, Islamic, and Iranian), and the near-death experience of those who have returned from physical death. These common factors are light, a state of ecstasy and bliss, love, and a sense of the void of time and space. In all cases, the individual faces the difficulty of describing and expressing their state through words and has no recourse other than to articulate it using the words they know.

The state of these travellers—in a world that belongs neither to the sensible world (directly knowable through our senses) nor to the world of concepts (known through words), but to the imaginal world—is, in the case of a near-death experience, accessible to everyone (regardless of gender, age, culture, religious beliefs, or historical date). This journey may be voluntary, as Suhrawardî states:

"Read the Qur'an in such a manner as though it had been written for you alone."

And Mowlavi (Rûmî) says:

I am a mute who has seen a dream, and all the people are deaf;

I am powerless to speak it, and they to hear it.

This is a journey outside time, outside space, outside speech, outside sensation, and far from the concept.

The verb, the word, *logos* possesses diverse aspects:

- It is my means of communication with the other.

- It is the foundation of our memory structure, enabling us to have an "unconscious".

- It is our means of identification.

- It has enabled us to attain the concept of the "Pole" and its division into the two concepts of time and space.

In a single word lies everything.

"In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God / Verily, verily, I say unto you, he who keeps my word shall never die / Christ said unto the twelve:

Will ye also go away? Simon Peter answered him: Lord (Master), to whom shall we go? Thou hast the words of eternal life." Gospel of John.

Thus are things created, because we name them; the beginning, the origin, is the moment we became aware of the presence of the word and the "God-Word" was present. This "God-Word" is both within us and outside us—within us and at the same time the agent of relation. It is always here, for through its presence the word "time" exists. It is this "Word-Language" that has made us human—like the positioning of the word *Hû* ("He") in Sufism in place of God.

Dâwûd Qaysarî, the celebrated commentator on Ibn 'Arabî's *Fusûs*, says: "Every being of this world is a sign of the Eternal Name, and since every Eternal Name knows an essence that gathers all names within itself, this name too must encompass all names.

Just as the creature, among creatures, is a state through which it shall know the totality of names. Viewed in this way, the worlds are infinite." (Appendix 1 - 2). Is it not for this very reason that we say God placed His spirit (which is the Word itself) in the human being?

Without the memory of words, the word could not exist. In other words, "Speech-Logic-God" is the capacity to commit the word to memory. Before the presence of the word, who were we? Another memory was active in us, and remains active through image and sign. Does another deep layer of memory exist in direct relation with physical factors in the brain? Accessing the presence of this layer beyond the memory of the word is perhaps possible through analysing the utterances of those who have returned from the visionary journey.

The soul (*psyche*), the absent part of our being, stands in direct relation with this memory beyond the word, "*huk*" (for convenience, we shall henceforth denote memory beyond the word in this article by "*huk*" [Persian acronym *ḥ-v-k*]). *Dhikr* (invocation), as a spiritual method, performs an essential function. The spiritual energy dispersed through *dhikr* permits the ascent from the well; sometimes, indeed, through the repetition of a single word, the effect of the word is erased, the veil rises, and we gain access to the other world. In mysticism, the concept of *latîfa* (subtle organ) is precisely *huk*! "…It takes place neither in the world perceptible through the external senses nor in fantasy, but in the imaginal world, the imaginal world that has the *latîfa* as its corresponding organ in the human creature." (Appendix 1 - 6).

In other words, our understanding of the world before the invention of the word cannot be articulated through words. "A dual union that escapes the divisions of human language" (Appendix 1 - 6). Another world, another memory, and another language exist.

"To speak is to translate from the language of angels into human language." All strange architecture passes through this frontier; this point is expressed by Mollâ Sadrâ as follows:

"Know that a substance has three states of existence, such that some possess a stronger and denser presence. Then there is another world, an interval between the two preceding worlds, a world that the soul creates and establishes because it is the image of the Creator, whether in its essence, in its signs, or in its conduct." (Appendix 1 - 2). If the Creator is "Speech", the soul is memory beyond speech. Najm al-Dîn Kubrâ indicates this difference of place: "The Eternal Being has various places for His indwelling; the existing places are signs that you shall distinguish through your mystical experience, for when you turn to this or that place, you involuntarily utter the name of this or that place…" (Appendix 1 - 6). Let us pay heed to this intimate connection between name, word, and place. The sole factor that makes possible the construction of a memory beyond the word passes through the duality of "presence and absence".

Another element of expression, music, is one of the earthly signs of the other world: "The birds all sing an eternal music, and when the people of the *síd* assume human form, they too become masters of this difficult art." (Appendix 1 - 11).

Having God within oneself, having Him with oneself, or being God are subjects most frequently discussed. "I have said: Ye are gods," Gospel of John.

"For God cannot see other than Himself, nor be observed by other than Himself" (Appendix 1 - 6). It is clear that we cannot see inside another except inside ourselves; this union—word, God, human—is in their birth. We find the same thought in the Gospel of Luke: "If someone who is your guide says to you that the Kingdom is in heaven—yet the Kingdom is inside you and outside you."

What manifests sometimes as a "journey", sometimes as an encounter with the "Other", and sometimes as a manifestation of the Supreme Essence, spirit, soul, or psyche, may share a single root. This root is simultaneously within us—a page of the book of our memory—and outside us, in the collective human heritage prior to our memory and also outside us, in the collective human heritage prior to the invention of speech. Accessing this root (*huk*) is a journey, an encounter with another from the "other world", an essence outside time and space. The hypothesis may be summarised as follows: a memory dwells within us; accessing this memory is the subject of a potential journey. That is why we employ signs, sounds, colours, and so forth.

"…But imagination is a spiritual agent, the subtle envelope of the soul and the musical element from which colours, sounds, and musical elements are fashioned." (Appendix 1 - 2). In other words, "things take place neither in the sensible world, through the external senses, nor in the imaginary world, but in the 'imaginal world', a world that has the *latîfa* as its corresponding organ in the human being." (Appendix 1 - 6).

Let us trace the footsteps of the concept of the imaginal world from Zoroastrian culture down to the era of Iranian Illuminationism: "For a long time, 'official philosophy', caught in the trap of the positive sciences, has permitted only two bases of knowledge: perception through the senses, which produces data, and concepts, which produce the laws governing those data." (Appendix 1 - 1). It is noteworthy that in both the world of the senses and the world of concepts, the instrument is the word. Yet between sensory perception and the rational strata there lies an empty space. What could take place between these two, and has done so, is active imagination or "agent imagination". The empty space is not between these two worlds, rather it precedes them—prior to the invention of the word, the word that moulds sensation and concept.

"Active imagination or agent imagination is not an instrument for fabricating fantasy, the unreal, the mythical, or futurology. A world cannot be revealed to anyone or become known until we have found a name for it" (Appendix 1 - 1). In other words, presence exists when it finds a name. Concerning God's creation of the world, a verse of the Qur'an states: "*Kun fa-yakûn*"—"Be!" and it was.

"The key name of the imaginal world governs the entire network of commanding concepts of the individual and what pertains to their cognition, such as imaginal perception, imaginal cognition, and imaginal consciousness" (Appendix 1 - 1). This sentence demonstrates the difficulty of finding exact words. On the one hand, between the concepts of the imaginal world and the world of imaginal consciousness, the boundary of precision breaks down. How are we to relate this inner awareness (or imaginal consciousness) to this outer world (the imaginal world)? *Huk* is a memory within us that carries an image of the outside: a world beyond human perception or an inner superconsciousness. Henry Corbin summarises the Mazdean view in this sentence: "In the vital energy of the human being there is a thought, the abode of *Spenta Ârmaiti*; in this thought there is a word, the abode of *Ashi Vanuhi*, a female angel (sister of *Daênâ*); and in this word there is an action, the abode of *Daênâ*." Into the sacred Zoroastrian triad—good thought, good word, good deed—three mighty feminine angels enter.

We draw close to the triad Father–Son–Holy Spirit, where the Father represents the wisdom of thought, the Holy Spirit the word, and the Son the deed. Islamic mystics employ the concept of the Holy Spirit as the guardian angel. These notions lead us back to *huk*.

In cultures close to mythical time, awareness of the presence of the "Word-God" was clearer than today. The conception of the "I", the celestial I, is a sign from afar guiding us toward the presence of an "other I" distinct from the "I".

Is it through thought or through excavation that one may hope to reach the trace of this inner paradise, this celestial Earth at the centre of a world that preserves the essence of bodies on the Last Day—whereas the definition of "within the ARCHETYPE" according to Voltaire is: "A world made, according to Plato's account, of the stuff of thought and always situated at the centre of the brain"? Henry Corbin links Iranian myth to the Mazdean vision and leads us to Iranian Illuminationism: "In twelfth-century Iran, Suhrawardî re-establishes the philosophy of light and the angelology of ancient Iran; the schema he presents is founded upon the world of imaginal forms, an intermediate world that transforms phenomena into spiritual signs, and which is for that reason the world through which the resurrection of bodies is accomplished."

We conclude this point with an excerpt from the *Treatise on the Perfect Man* by 'Alî Hamadânî, the Iranian mystic: "In every purified part of the human being, an opposite part thinks in harmony with it, for nothing can be seen except by its counterpart. Thus, when the illuminative symbol is purified, it fashions within it its counterpart, and likewise for the soul, the heart, the spirit, and so on, up to the hidden secret (*khafiya*), up to the inner abode where the veil is lifted: the eternal entities of which I am the expression; I am its voice…"

The presences of memory beyond words—"*huk*"—manifest in diverse forms: the celestial I, the guardian angel, the unseen presence, the supreme presence, the Holy Spirit, the universal human, the philosopher's angel, the perfect nature, the active intellect, the angel of knowledge, the active intelligence, the angel of humanity, the man of light, the guide of light, the spiritual twin, the unseen guide, the celestial witness, the saviour and spiritual guide, the organ of inner vision of the soul.

Examining each of these names of the "*huk*" phenomenon lies beyond the scope of this article, yet one may in a certain manner compare these names with the set of definitions of contemporary psychoanalysis. A brief definition of the "soul–inner self" (*nafs*) in the view of Islamo-Iranian mystics has three dimensions:

- *Nafs-e ammâreh*, the lower soul, that which commands.

- *Nafs-e lawwâmeh*, that which warns and criticises.

- *Nafs-e mutma'inneh*—the pacified / reconciling soul.

Henry Corbin emphasises: "Our insistence upon preventing any confusion of concepts stems from the fact that something here is inescapable. It is indeed difficult to fit the three concepts of *nafs-e ammâreh*, *lawwâmeh*, and *mutma'inneh* in any way into the mould of the 'conscious' and the 'unconscious'." Instead, he employs the concept of the "superconscious": "On the other hand, this human soul dawns like the light of consciousness into the darkness of the superconscious."

Superconscious: an unconscious phenomenon serving as the agent of active mental functions. This definition links the superconscious to the unconscious, yet does not enable us to understand further. If we turn to the psychoanalytic concepts of the Id, the Ego, and the Superego, we arrive at an approximate parallel between mystical concepts and psychoanalytic concepts. The Id is the ensemble of conscious or concealed inner drives; that which in the individual adapts the body to reality controls the drives (the Id is condemned by the Superego).

Superego: the element of the psychic structure that acts unconsciously upon the "Ego" as a means of defence against drives that generate feelings of guilt within us—feelings of guilt cultivated in us from childhood through the image of the parents.

The Id may serve as *nafs-e ammâreh*, the Ego as *nafs-e mutma'inneh*, and the Superego as *nafs-e lawwâmeh*. A summary of our understanding of the human book may be condensed in the outline of Diagram 2 in Appendix 3.

The Book of Man, or the layers of memory in its broad sense, or inner data:

1. The layer of vital memory: the layer we carry with us at birth; memory of the animal era.

2. The layer of imaginal memory, the Eighth Continent: the layer of "I without I", the imaginal world, the celestial I, and the other names denoting the agent of the celestial I that we listed earlier.

3. The layer of acoustic memory: the frontier layer prior to the birth of the word.

4. The layer of verbal memory: Logic—God—Word.

5. The layer of conceptual memory—the domain of intelligence.

6. The next layer of memory: the future, perhaps one day.

If we turn to the elaboration of psychoanalytic theory, we arrive at another cross-section of this book (Diagram 3, Appendix 3).

These explanations are highly condensed and require deeper elaboration, particularly in the following areas:

- Analysis of the concept of paradise across the whole of human mythology.

- Analysis of the concepts of love (*mehr*), light, time, and space.

- Deeper analysis of the material put forward through the experience of those who have returned from physical death.

- Analysis of the functioning of the data-management systems that human beings have invented thus far, which in another account enables us to understand this book better.

Appendix 1

1. Henry Corbin: *Corps spirituel et Terre céleste : de l'Iran mazdéen à l'Iran chiite*, Buchet/Chastel, 1979.

2. D. Shayegan: *Henry Corbin : La topographie spirituelle de l'islam iranien*, La Différence, 1990.

3. Rûzbehân: *Le Jasmin des fidèles d'amour*, Librairie d'Amérique et d'Orient, 1981.

4. H. Corbin: *L'Imagination créatrice dans le soufisme d'Ibn Arabi*, Aubier, 1958.

5. J.-P. Persigout: *Dictionnaire de mythologie celte*, Éditions du Rocher, 1985 and 1990.

6. H. Corbin: *L'Homme de lumière dans le soufisme iranien*, 2nd edition, Paris, Éditions de Médicis, 1971.

7. L. Massignon: *Le Dîwân de Hallâj*, Éditions du Seuil, 1981.

8. F. Le Roux: *La civilisation celtique*.

9. Pierre Jovanovic: *Enquête sur l'existence de l'ange-gardien*, Filipacchi.

Appendix 2

Biographical References

1. Shihâb al-Dîn Suhrawardî — Shaykh al-Ishrâq

Shaykh al-Ishrâq was born in Iran in 1155 CE and was martyred in 1191 by fatwa of the religious authorities.

His great life's work was in fact an Islamic and Islamic-Illuminationist re-reading of ancient Iranian sources. His writings bring together the names of Plato and Zoroaster in a metaphysics of light, wherein Platonic ideas are interpreted within Zoroastrian angelology.

2. Muhyî al-Dîn Ibn 'Arabî

Born in Moorish Andalusia in 1165, he died in 1240 in Damascus, and is one of the greatest Illuminationist mystics.

3. Sadr al-Dîn Muhammad Shîrâzî, Mollâ Sadrâ

His works stand at the intersection of the thought of Avicenna, the Illuminationism of Suhrawardî, the mysticism of Ibn 'Arabî, and Shi'ism.

4. Henry Corbin

In 1935, the Bibliothèque nationale de France sent him to the French Institute in Berlin. He produced the first French translation of Heidegger's *What Is Metaphysics?*. He subsequently received missions to Turkey and Iran, and founded the Department of Iranian Studies at the French Institute. He is the author of *Fundamental Currents of Islamic Intellectual Movement in Iran from the First Day to the Safavid Period* [*En Islam iranien*], a four-volume history of Islamic philosophy in Islam and Iran devoted to Iranian thinkers, Shi'ism, and mystics. He died in Paris in 1978 CE.

5. Dâwûd Qaysarî

His origins trace back to Anatolia, and he lived in Cairo. He is one of the greatest mystics of the fourteenth century CE and died in 1350 CE. He is renowned for the commentary he wrote on Ibn 'Arabî's *Fusûs*.

6. Najm al-Dîn Kubrâ

Born in 1149 CE, he spent the early part of his life travelling. In 1184 CE he came to Khwarazm and subsequently became active in Central Asia. His heroic death took place during the Mongol invasion.

7. Rûzbehân Baqlî Shîrâzî

'Alî Muhammad ibn 'Alî Nasr Rûzbehân was born in Fasâ in 1128 CE; his death occurred in 1209 CE.

8. Hallâj

Abû Majîd Husayn ibn Mansûr Hallâj was born in 857 CE and died in 922 CE. He is renowned for his love of eternity, which was regarded as "heresy".

https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/01/DSC0678-Copier.jpg

et proposition de définition d'indicateurs de mesure du rôle des femmes

Notre propos dans ce texte est de tenter d'offrir un regard nouveau. Ce regard pourrait peut-être aider l'ensemble des forces progressistes, à l'intérieur comme à l'extérieur de l'Iran, sur la voie de la convergence des revendications et, en définitive, de la convergence dans le champ de l'action ; ou tout au moins contribuer à généraliser le recours à ce triple instrument — stratégique, structurel et psychique — aux côtés d'autres moyens tels que la création d'associations, le développement des médias, les efforts éducatifs, la sensibilisation de l'opinion publique mondiale, les défenses juridiques à l'échelle internationale… Commençons par mieux cerner ces trois regards. Observons ensuite le rôle des femmes, de la Révolution constitutionnelle à nos jours, à la lumière de ces outils, et efforçons-nous enfin de dégager pour l'avenir, dans la mesure des moyens de cet écrit, une stratégie efficace et rigoureuse fondée sur des indicateurs de mesure.

Notre dessein, dans ce bref exposé, n'est pas de retracer l'histoire de la pensée structuraliste dans les champs de la psychanalyse et des sciences sociales, ni de ce que l'on appelle le regard structurel. Le regard structurel exige avant toute chose d'examiner les phénomènes dans un champ pluridisciplinaire, et cela sur le temps long. Les travaux de Darwin, Marx, Freud et Claude Lévi-Strauss peuvent être considérés comme des exemples éclatants de cette approche structurelle. Bien que le structuralisme ait été systématisé à la suite de Ferdinand de Saussure (né en 1857, mort en 1913), linguiste suisse, avant de se diffuser dans d'autres disciplines, de grands esprits tels que Darwin, Marx et Freud avaient déjà mis en œuvre ce regard structurel dans la pratique. En considérant la structure de la langue comme principe fondamental en linguistique, Saussure fit de celle-ci une branche du savoir général. On tient communément Saussure pour le père de la linguistique du XXe siècle.

Le regard que nous portons sur le psychisme est lui aussi un regard structurel. Jacques Lacan, psychiatre et psychanalyste français, s'appuyant sur les découvertes de Freud et de Saussure, jeta un regard structurel sur l'inconscient. Il formula ainsi sa grande découverte : l'inconscient de l'être parlant, de l'être désirant, est structuré comme un langage. Au fil de plus de quarante années d'enseignement, il reconnut et mit au jour la formation et le fonctionnement de l'inconscient. Il identifie comme facteurs déterminants de la formation de l'inconscient la mère — tout particulièrement la langue maternelle —, le nom et la présence du père dans le désir de la mère, ainsi que le facteur de la différence des sexes, c'est-à-dire la forme manifeste de cette différence. La formation de l'inconscient de la femme et de l'homme se différencie à partir de cette différence biologique.

Et c'est à partir de là que la vie de l'être parlant, de l'être symbolisant, se trouve confrontée à la plus grande contradiction de son existence. La femme et l'homme, en tant que deux êtres parlants, communiquent l'un avec l'autre par la voie de la symbolisation, tout en demeurant, en tant que deux structures biologiques et psychiques distinctes, frappés d'étrangeté l'un pour l'autre. Et ce sont ces deux-là qui fondent la famille, qui instaurent la division du travail — tant au sein de la famille qu'au sein de sociétés plus vastes — depuis l'aube de la vie communautaire : époque pré-cynégétique, époque de la chasse, époque de l'agriculture et de l'élevage, et époque de l'urbanisation. Le rôle de la femme et de l'homme, à l'intérieur comme à l'extérieur du foyer, se transforme et s'adapte au fil de l'évolution du mode de vie. Pour assurer la survie, ces rôles se transmettent d'une génération à l'autre sous forme de traditions, évoluant et s'ajustant à la réalité.

Les traditions se transmettent de génération en génération sous les espèces de la religion et des croyances ethniques et culturelles. Le brassage des cultures entre elles, d'une part, et l'effort de l'être humain pour tirer le meilleur parti de son environnement en vue d'une vie plus propice, d'autre part, transforment et élèvent les traditions, soit graduellement, soit par la contrainte et d'un seul coup. Et c'est alors que survient la deuxième grande contradiction de l'existence humaine. À certaines époques de l'histoire, et pour plusieurs composantes de la société, les traditions figées ne répondent plus aux besoins ; c'est là que se creuse et culmine le fossé entre deux générations, entre les partisans de la tradition immuable et ceux qui aspirent au renouveau. Et nul doute que la pression sur le psychisme et sur le corps s'intensifie pour cette part de la société qui se trouve le plus directement exposée au mouvement des transformations.

Par ailleurs, en ce qui concerne notre Iran, le grand choc d'interférence culturelle auquel on a donné le nom de modernisation débute dès l'orée du XIXe siècle, en 1803, avec la série des guerres irano-russes et les défaites iraniennes. Cette interférence culturelle s'est poursuivie sans interruption jusqu'à aujourd'hui et, tout naturellement, elle ne pouvait être identique pour les nomades, les habitants des villages et les habitants des villes.

Comme nous l'avons rappelé, au début du XIXe siècle, le rôle des femmes en tant que citoyennes en Iran n'était pas uniforme dans ces trois modes de vie. Dès lors, compte tenu de cette dimension « culturelle — mode de production » en Iran et de la tradition de vie des citoyennes et des citoyens, comment examiner de manière structurelle les transformations intervenues depuis le début du XIXe siècle jusqu'à nos jours ? Et comment tenter de dresser une vue d'ensemble permettant de tirer de ces mutations et de ce panorama des enseignements pour le progrès, et singulièrement pour le rôle des femmes à l'avenir ? Ma proposition est de comparer deux tableaux : un tableau du début du XIXe siècle et le tableau d'un idéal possible pour les décennies à venir. Pour ces deux tableaux, nous avons besoin d'indicateurs qui soient à la fois suffisamment éloquents, mesurables et porteurs de sens. En dernier ressort, ces indicateurs doivent cheminer sur la voie du progrès et des normes des droits humains.

Commençons par le tableau de l'idéal possible du rôle des femmes en Iran dans les décennies à venir. Cette proposition peut constituer une première ébauche et requiert assurément de nombreuses analyses et une large concertation. Mais il faut bien commencer quelque part. Représentons-nous l'idéal possible — les conditions optimales des femmes iraniennes dans les décennies futures — à l'aune des normes de la Déclaration universelle des droits de l'homme, augmentées de deux caractéristiques supplémentaires : d'un côté, un environnement plus sain, propice à l'existence des mères et des enfants, et, de l'autre, de meilleures conditions sanitaires et d'existence, assorties d'assurances sociales adaptées aux mères et aux enfants.

Le second tableau correspond aux conditions de vie des femmes au début du XIXe siècle dans les trois « cultures — modes de production » : nomade, rurale et urbaine.

Mais comment choisir nos indicateurs ? Après un examen approfondi et des entretiens avec des personnes avisées, je propose les quelques indicateurs fondamentaux suivants :

1- Le rôle de la femme dans la famille et la vie conjugale
2- Le rôle de la femme dans la société, incluant : le milieu professionnel, l'encadrement et la direction, l'activité politique et sociale
3- Le rôle des femmes dans les productions scientifiques, artistiques et culturelles
4- L'autonomie et la vie privée des femmes
5- Le rôle des femmes et leurs droits civiques et citoyens.

Je vais tenter d'évaluer de façon très succincte et rapide l'évolution de ces cinq indicateurs au cours de ces deux siècles. Ces indicateurs reposent principalement sur la vie urbaine. Je suggère à ceux que la question intéresse de s'efforcer tout à la fois de perfectionner ces indicateurs et de les étendre aux deux autres milieux « culturels-productifs ».

Dans cette perspective structuro-culturelle, je fais délibérément abstraction des périodes politiques afin de mesurer les changements indépendamment des régimes politiques et de porter un regard objectif exclusivement centré sur le rôle des femmes. Certes, en deux siècles, l'évolution de nos indicateurs a connu des hauts et des bas et, selon la conjoncture politique en Iran et dans le monde ainsi que le rythme du progrès technologique — notamment les technologies du traitement de l'information et de la communication —, ces indicateurs ont plus ou moins progressé vers notre idéal possible. Penchons-nous sur chacun de ces indicateurs :

Dans cette approche stratégique, nous laissons naturellement de côté les cas d'exception, tout en sachant que, de manière générale, jusqu'à vingt pour cent d'exceptions à la règle restent négligeables dans les analyses globales.

1- Le rôle de la femme dans la famille et la vie conjugale : c'est là que résidait le rôle principal des femmes citadines au début du XIXe siècle. Les femmes assuraient la gestion domestique du foyer, l'hygiène et la santé de la famille, les relations familiales ainsi que les premiers apprentissages. La maison tenait lieu, à cette époque, d'un grand nombre des institutions sanitaires, médicales et de services d'aujourd'hui. D'un côté, le rôle des femmes s'exerçait pour l'essentiel entre ces quatre murs ; de l'autre, les services dispensés à l'intérieur de ces quatre murs étaient d'une extrême diversité.

Aujourd'hui, l'on peut affirmer que, mis à part les droits citoyens — tels que le droit au divorce, la garde des enfants, le droit de choisir d'avoir des enfants, le droit à la monogamie —, le rôle des femmes au sein de la famille a connu un progrès notable : non seulement les femmes n'ont pas perdu la gestion du foyer, mais elles conservent généralement une réelle maîtrise du suivi de l'éducation et de l'instruction des enfants ainsi que de la santé familiale. Sur le plan culturel et traditionnel, les femmes iraniennes ont également su préserver aujourd'hui la pérennité du rôle maternel, de la tendresse et de l'affection. À jeter un regard rapide sur cet indicateur, on peut dire que, hormis les droits civiques — lesquels, alors même qu'ils tendaient dans les années précédant la révolution vers une forme d'équilibre très tardif, ont de nouveau subi un recul sévère, dont témoignent par exemple la question de la monogamie ou le divorce soumis à l'autorisation du tribunal —, dans tous les autres domaines et globalement par rapport aux sociétés comparables, les femmes ont accompli une progression raisonnable et équilibrée.

2- Le rôle des femmes dans la société, incluant : le milieu professionnel, l'encadrement et la direction, l'activité politique et sociale :

On peut dire qu'en ce domaine nous sommes partis à peu près du barreau le plus bas de l'échelle. Depuis qu'elles ont conquis le droit de vote et d'éligibilité, les femmes l'ont fermement préservé. Elles se sont adaptées à la quasi-totalité des milieux professionnels. Dans l'action politique, en particulier aux niveaux de la résistance et de l'opposition, tant à l'intérieur qu'à l'extérieur du pays, elles ont joué des rôles essentiels. Face aux pressions des traditionalistes, tout particulièrement au cours des trente-trois dernières années, elles ont résisté avec constance, jour après jour. Aujourd'hui, à l'exception de quelques domaines tels que la magistrature, la fonction présidentielle et, semble-t-il, certaines branches des soins médicaux, les femmes ont su imposer leur présence féconde. D'une manière générale, on peut estimer que la présence des femmes sous cet indicateur poursuit son cours ascendant et global.

3- Le rôle des femmes dans les productions scientifiques, artistiques et culturelles :

Cet indicateur, à lui seul, peut s'avérer des plus révélateurs. Car la production culturelle, artistique et scientifique exige des moyens particuliers ainsi qu'une disposition psychique et intellectuelle telle que son taux de croissance reflète l'évolution de nombreux autres indicateurs. Point n'est besoin de statistiques : aujourd'hui, dans tous les domaines susmentionnés, malgré toutes les pressions politiques et le manque de moyens, la part des femmes à l'université, parmi les écrivains et poètes, les cinéastes, les peintres et les calligraphes ne cesse de croître. On peut sans doute affirmer qu'au cours des deux derniers siècles, la production culturelle des femmes a incontestablement suivi, en toutes circonstances, une courbe favorable et ascendante. Malgré la pression directe exercée sur les femmes dans le domaine de la musique, et singulièrement du chant, les concerts clandestins ou donnés sur les toits ne manquent pas. On peut raisonnablement espérer qu'une fois levé l'obstacle politico-religieux, nous assisterons à une véritable explosion de la création artistique féminine. À notre sens, la croissance de cet indicateur est plus porteuse d'espoir encore que celle de tous les autres.

4- L'autonomie et la vie privée des femmes : le libre choix du conjoint et des conditions du mariage, le choix vestimentaire, le choix des loisirs, du sport et des activités artistiques, l'indépendance financière, le choix de la manière d'accueillir et de vivre le désir et le besoin sexuels, la liberté de voyager, la liberté d'aller et venir, la liberté de participer aux rituels traditionnels et religieux : sur ce terrain, nous sommes confrontés à trois ordres de difficultés — traditionnelles, politiques et sociales. Le libre choix du conjoint, bien qu'il requière l'avis favorable du père lors du premier mariage, relève avant tout de la tradition et des mœurs populaires elles-mêmes. La liberté de voyager à l'intérieur du pays demeure surtout une question traditionnelle et, sous l'angle de la sécurité des femmes, un enjeu social. En revanche, le voyage des femmes à l'étranger subordonné à l'autorisation du mari relève d'un choix politique. Cette question cruciale n'a été résolue à aucune époque. Ce qui revêt par-dessus tout une portée symbolique et constitue, dès le lendemain de février 1979 (bahman 1357) et jusqu'à aujourd'hui, le champ de bataille quotidien entre les femmes et le pouvoir politique en Iran, c'est la question de la liberté vestimentaire des femmes. Avant cette date, la liberté de choix vestimentaire connaissait surtout des limitations d'ordre traditionnel et social.

L'indépendance financière est directement liée au droit au travail, acquis qu'il convient également de compter au nombre des conquêtes des femmes. Les activités collectives, sportives et récréatives sont, comme chacun le sait, poursuivies par les femmes hors du regard des agents de la « promotion de la vertu et de la prévention du vice », dans toute la mesure du possible et tant qu'elles n'entrent pas en contradiction frontale avec le principe du voile islamique. Autrement dit, elles tirent parti de chaque interstice et repoussent chaque jour les frontières de l'interdit.

5- Le rôle des femmes et leurs droits civiques et citoyens : l'évolution de cet indicateur peut être examinée à travers trois périodes distinctes : avant l'existence d'un droit civil codifié et d'une justice moderne dans les années 1920 (décennie 1300 du calendrier solaire iranien), de cette période à février 1979 (bahman 1357), et de cette date à nos jours. Durant la première période, ce qui touchait aux droits des citoyens, femmes comme hommes, relevait de la coutume, fortement imprégnée de la charia, et le juge était lui-même le juge religieux (*hâkem-e shar'*). Durant la deuxième période également, malgré l'existence d'un Code civil écrit, les droits fondamentaux des femmes continuaient pour l'essentiel de graviter autour de cette même coutume islamique, à cette différence près que les lois codifiées ne laissaient pas aux magistrats non cléricaux la latitude d'une interprétation individuelle.

Tout au long de cinquante années d'application des lois civiles codifiées, de menus progrès ont été accomplis. Mais, sur le fond, tant durant la deuxième que durant la troisième période, les droits fondamentaux des femmes — tels que le droit à l'héritage, le droit au divorce, le droit de choisir de ne pas être vierge sans perdre les avantages du mariage, le droit de bénéficier d'un temps égal d'accueil et de garde des enfants après la séparation, et d'autres dispositions du même ordre — sont demeurés captifs des limites du droit coutumier fondé sur la charia ; avec cette nuance que, dans la troisième période, les juges cléricaux eurent les mains plus libres qu'auparavant, tant pour interpréter en faveur des femmes qu'à leur détriment.

Ce que l'on peut affirmer en ce domaine, et avec une entière certitude, c'est que les lois sociales et civiles sont profondément marquées par l'empreinte de la tradition, de la coutume et de la charia. Cette réalité appelle une solution tripartite : politique, sociale et traditionnelle. Le rôle de l'élévation culturelle de la société s'avère, sur chacun de ces trois plans, absolument fondamental.

Ici, avant de conclure, je souhaiterais formuler trois remarques. Premièrement, les traditions, telles les couches sédimentaires des fonds océaniques qui, au fil de millions d'années, se transforment en montagnes, régissent dans la longue durée les relations entre citoyens, groupes sociaux, classes productives et cultures diverses. Ces traditions passent d'une génération à l'autre par la voie de la langue, des us et des coutumes. On ne saurait bouleverser d'un seul coup les traditions sans substitution ni adhésion collective, sans engendrer des blessures psychiques incurables. Les traditions s'inscrivent profondément, par la langue et la culture, dans la structure de notre inconscient, et leur transformation est l'œuvre de plusieurs générations. Au regard des liens étroits qui unissent les choix politiques, l'organisation sociale et la circulation des traditions, il convient de mener avec une délicatesse singulière un jeu chorégraphique et artistique entre ces trois facteurs fondamentaux et fondateurs de la société, afin que, dans le cours du temps et grâce à l'élévation progressive de la culture générale, les citoyens soient amenés en douceur sur la voie de l'accueil du neuf.

Deuxièmement, s'agissant du rôle des femmes, prêtons attention à la subtilité de la contradiction fondamentale de l'être parlant dans la vie de chaque jour. Femmes et hommes sont les plus proches de tous les êtres vivants par l'instrument de communication qu'est le symbole et le langage, et les plus étrangers les uns aux autres dans leur fonctionnement biologique et psychique.

Troisièmement, fort heureusement, les prodigieux moyens de communication d'aujourd'hui, les voyages et les migrations tempèrent les « difficultés chronophages » d'hier. En fin de compte, il importe d'en faire un usage optimal.

Ainsi qu'il ressort de ce regard très rapide et pris avec du recul, à travers cinq indicateurs et deux tableaux — le début du XIXe siècle et l'idéal possible des décennies à venir —, on peut conclure ceci :

Dans l'ensemble, et indépendamment des séquences politiques, principalement grâce à la détermination et à l'effort quotidien des femmes, pour autant qu'il s'agisse des citadines, tous les indicateurs — à l'exception de celui des droits civils et citoyens — se situent peu ou prou dans la zone verte, ou ont la possibilité d'y accéder. Malheureusement, dans le domaine des droits civiques et en raison de sa dépendance à l'égard des trois facteurs politique, social et traditionnel, nous avons besoin de davantage de temps, de patience, de résistance, de persévérance, d'endurance et d'opiniâtreté. C'est ici que l'effort de chaque citoyen, dans chacun de ses gestes quotidiens pour la défense des droits civiques en général et des droits civils des femmes en particulier, devient indispensable et nécessaire.

Nous venons de loin ; nous avons traversé bien des hauts et des bas. Nul doute que cette épine douloureuse sera elle aussi arrachée du pied de nos mères, de nos sœurs, de nos épouses et de nos filles, sous leur propre conduite et avec le concours des hommes épris de liberté et adversaires de toute discrimination.

en.title: A "Structural-Cultural" Perspective on the Role of Women, from the Constitutional Revolution to the Present Day

en.body_markdown:
https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/01/DSC0678-Copier.jpg

and a proposal for defining indicators to measure the role of women

Our aim in this discourse is to endeavour to offer a fresh perspective. This perspective may perhaps assist the constellation of progressive forces inside and outside Iran on the path towards the convergence of demands and, ultimately, convergence in the sphere of action; or at the very least help to popularise the use of this threefold set of instruments—strategic, structural, and psychological—alongside other tools such as establishing organisations, creating media outlets, educational initiatives, raising awareness among global public opinion, and mounting legal defences at the international level. Let us first become better acquainted with these three perspectives. Next, let us examine the role of women from the Constitutional Revolution to the present day in the light of these instruments, and finally endeavour, insofar as lies within the scope of this essay, to identify an effective and rigorous strategy for the future using measurable indicators.

It is not our intention in this brief study to recount the history of structuralist thought in psychoanalysis and the social sciences, nor what is termed the structural perspective. Above all else, a structural perspective requires examining phenomena within a multidisciplinary field and over the long term. The works of Darwin, Marx, Freud, and Claude Lévi-Strauss may be regarded as prime exemplars of the structural perspective. Although structuralism was formally codified after the Swiss linguist Ferdinand de Saussure (born 1857, died 1913) and spread to other fields, towering figures such as Darwin, Marx, and Freud had already put the structural perspective into practice. By viewing the structure of language as the foundational principle of linguistics, Saussure defined linguistics as a branch of general knowledge. Saussure is widely regarded as the father of twentieth-century linguistics.

Our perspective on the psyche is likewise a structural one. Drawing upon the findings of Freud and Saussure, the French psychiatrist and psychoanalyst Jacques Lacan cast a structural gaze upon the unconscious. He articulated his great discovery thus: the unconscious of the speaking human being, the desiring human being, is structured like a language. Over more than forty years of teaching, he identified and elucidated the formation and functioning of the unconscious. He identifies the formative factors of the unconscious as the mother—especially the mother tongue—the name and presence of the father in the mother's desire, and the factor of sexual difference, namely the manifest form of that difference. The formation of the unconscious in women and men diverges on the basis of this biological difference.

From this point onward, the life of the speaking human being, the symbol-making human being, becomes caught in the greatest contradiction of its existence. Women and men, as two speaking beings, communicate with one another through symbolisation, yet as two distinct biological and psychic structures they experience mutual estrangement. It is these two who lay the foundations of the family and divide labour—both within the framework of the family and within broader societies—from the dawn of communal life: the pre-hunting era, the hunting era, the era of agriculture and animal husbandry, and the era of urbanisation. The roles of women and men inside and outside the household change and adapt as modes of life evolve. For the sake of continued survival, these roles are transmitted from generation to generation in the form of traditions, evolving and adapting to reality.

Traditions pass from one generation to the next in the guise of religion and ethnic and cultural beliefs. On the one hand, the mingling of cultures with one another, and on the other, humanity's effort to make optimal use of its surroundings in pursuit of a more suitable way of life, refine and elevate traditions—either gradually or forcefully and all at once. And it is here that the second great contradiction of human existence arises. At certain junctures in history, and for several pillars of society, static traditions cease to meet existing needs; at such moments, the rift between two generations—between the defenders of static tradition and the seekers of renewal—reaches its peak. Beyond doubt, the pressure upon both psyche and body grows all the more acute for that segment of society most directly in the path of change.

Furthermore, as regards our Iran, the great cultural interference that has been given the name of modernisation began at the dawn of the nineteenth century, in 1803, with the series of Russo-Persian wars and Iranian defeats. This cultural interference has continued uninterruptedly down to the present day and, quite naturally, could not be the same for nomadic tribes, village dwellers, and urban residents.

As noted above, at the beginning of the nineteenth century the role of women as citizens in Iran was not uniform across these three ways of life. Now, taking into account this "cultural–mode of production" dimension in Iran and the lived tradition of female and male citizens, how can we examine in a structural manner the changes from the early nineteenth century to today, and attempt to present a comprehensive overview from which lessons may be drawn for progress, and particularly for the future role of women? My proposal is to compare two pictures: a picture of the early nineteenth century and a picture of the possible ideal in the coming decades. For these two pictures we require indicators that are at once sufficiently expressive, measurable, and meaningful. Ultimately, these indicators must advance along the path of progress and human rights standards.

Let us begin with the picture of the possible ideal for the role of women in Iran in the coming decades. This proposal may serve as an initial blueprint and undoubtedly requires extensive scrutiny and collective reflection. Yet one must begin somewhere. Let us conceive the possible ideal—the optimal conditions for Iranian women in the coming decades—as the standards of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, augmented by two further characteristics: on the one hand, a cleaner environment suited to the life of mothers and children, and on the other, better health and living conditions backed by appropriate social insurance schemes for mothers and children.

The second picture depicts the living conditions of women in the early nineteenth century across the three "cultures–modes of production": nomadic, rural, and urban.

Yet how ought we to select our indicators? Following closer examination and interviews with knowledgeable individuals, I propose the following foundational indicators:

1- The role of women in the family and marital life
2- The role of women in society, including: the workplace, management, and political and social activity
3- The role of women in scientific, artistic, and cultural production
4- Women's autonomy and private life
5- The role of women and their civic and citizenship rights.

I shall endeavour, in a very brief and condensed manner, to assess the changes in these five indicators over the course of two centuries. These indicators are grounded primarily in urban life. My suggestion is that interested researchers strive both to refine and improve these indicators and to extend them to the other two "cultural-productive" environments.

From this structural-cultural standpoint, I deliberately omit political eras so as to measure changes independently of political regimes and to cast an objective gaze solely upon the role of women. Undoubtedly, over two centuries the trajectory of our indicators has experienced peaks and troughs, and in accordance with prevailing political conditions in Iran and the world, as well as the rate of technological advancement—particularly information-processing and communications technologies—these indicators have moved more or less towards our possible ideal. Let us examine these indicators:

In this strategic perspective, we naturally pass over exceptional cases, while bearing in mind that, as a rule, up to twenty per cent of exceptions to the norm may be discounted in broad analytical frameworks.

1- The role of women in the family and marital life: this was the principal role held by urban women at the start of the nineteenth century. Women bore responsibility for the internal management of the household, cleanliness and family health, kinship relations, and early education. In that era, the home fulfilled the functions of many of today's health, medical, and service institutions. On the one hand, women's role was essentially enacted within those four walls; on the other, the services provided within those four walls were remarkably diverse.

Today, it may be said that, setting aside citizenship rights—including the right to divorce, child custody, the right to choose whether to bear children, and the right to monogamy—the role of women within the family has seen substantial progress. Not only have women not lost management of the home, but they also generally maintain firm oversight over the upbringing and education of children as well as health and well-being. From a cultural and traditional standpoint, Iranian women today have likewise admirably preserved the continuity of the maternal role, tenderness, and affection. Casting a swift glance at this indicator, one may state that—apart from citizenship rights, which even as they were moving towards a much-belated equilibrium in the pre-revolutionary years suffered another severe setback, exemplified by the right to monogamy or divorce requiring court permission—in all other respects, and overall in comparison with similar societies, women have achieved reasonable and balanced progress.

2- The role of women in society, including: the workplace, management, and political and social activity:

It may be said that in this area we began virtually from the lowest rung. From the moment women secured the right to vote and to stand for election, they safeguarded it well. They have adapted to nearly every kind of working environment. In political activity, particularly at the levels of resistance and opposition both inside and outside the country, they have played pivotal roles. Against the pressures of traditionalists, especially over the past thirty-three years, they have resisted admirably, day after day. Today, save for a few domains such as the judiciary, the presidency, and seemingly certain branches of healthcare services, women have succeeded in imposing their constructive presence. On the whole, it may be stated that women's presence under this indicator continues along its broad and general upward course.

3- The role of women in scientific, artistic, and cultural production:

This indicator alone can be exceedingly revealing. For cultural, artistic, and scientific production demands specialised facilities and a degree of psychological and intellectual readiness such that its growth rate reflects the advancement of many other indicators. No statistics are required: today, across all the aforementioned fields, notwithstanding all political pressures and lack of resources, the share of women in universities, and among writers and poets, filmmakers, painters, and calligraphers, is steadily rising. One might well say that over the last two centuries, women's cultural production has undeniably maintained a positive and upward trajectory under all circumstances. Despite direct pressure upon women in music, and especially singing, underground or rooftop concerts are far from rare. One may readily hope that once the politico-religious obstacle is removed, we shall witness an explosion of women's artistic production. In our estimation, the growth of this indicator is more encouraging than that of any other.

4- Women's autonomy and private life: choice of spouse and conditions of marriage, choice of dress, choice of leisure, sport, and artistic pursuits, financial independence, choice of how to attend to sexual desire and need, freedom to travel, freedom of movement, and freedom to participate in traditional and religious rituals. Here we confront three types of obstacle: traditional, political, and social. Free choice of spouse, though it requires the father's favourable consent for a first marriage, is governed primarily by the people's own tradition and custom. Freedom to travel within the country is largely a traditional issue and, in terms of women's safety, a social one. By contrast, women travelling abroad with their husband's permission is a political choice; this vital issue has never been resolved in any era. What carries the greatest symbolic weight—and has constituted, from the very first day after February 1979 (Bahman 1357) down to the present, the daily battleground between women and Iran's political establishment—is the issue of women's freedom of dress. Prior to that date, freedom of choice in dress faced predominantly traditional and social constraints.

Financial independence is directly tied to the right to work, an achievement that may likewise be counted among women's gains. Collective, sporting, and recreational activities—as we all know—are pursued by women out of sight of the agents of the "promotion of virtue and prevention of vice", insofar as possible and provided they do not directly contravene the principle of Islamic dress. In other words, they seize every opportunity and break through forbidden boundaries every single day.

5- The role of women and their civic and citizenship rights: the trajectory of this indicator may be examined across three distinct periods—prior to the existence of codified civil laws and a modern judiciary in the 1920s (the 1300s SH), from that juncture to February 1979 (Bahman 1357), and from that date to the present day. In the first era, matters pertaining to the rights of citizens, whether female or male, were governed by custom heavily shaped by sharia, and the judge was himself the religious magistrate (*hakem-e shar'*). In the second era as well, despite the existence of a codified civil code, women's fundamental rights still revolved largely around that same Islamic custom, with the difference that codified statutes did not permit non-clerical judges individual interpretation.

Over fifty years of implementing codified civil laws, modest progress was achieved. Yet in essence, in both the second and third eras, women's fundamental rights—such as inheritance rights, the right to divorce, the right to choose not to be a virgin without forfeiting marital entitlements, the right to equal time in caring for and hosting children after separation, and similar matters—remained imprisoned within the confines of customary law grounded in sharia; the difference being that in the third era clerical judges enjoyed far greater latitude than before, whether to interpret in favour of women or to their detriment.

What can be stated in this regard, and with complete certainty, is that social and civil laws are intensely shaped by tradition, custom, and sharia. This crucial matter demands a threefold solution: political, social, and traditional. The role of society's cultural growth is paramount in all three spheres.

Here, before concluding, I wish to point to three considerations. First, traditions—like sedimentary layers on the ocean floor that over millions of years turn into mountains—regulate over long stretches of time the relations among citizens, social groups, productive classes, and diverse cultures. These traditions pass from generation to generation through language, manners, and customs. Traditions cannot be fundamentally altered overnight without replacement and public acceptance, lest we inflict incurable psychological wounds. Traditions are deeply lodged in the structure of our unconscious through language and culture, and changing them is the work of several generations. Given the intimate links between political choices, social structure, and the circulation of traditions, one must engage with these three foundational pillars of society with exceptional delicacy—like a dance, with artistic finesse—so that over time, through the gradual elevation of general culture, citizens are gently guided towards embracing what is new.

Second, concerning the role of women, let us heed the subtlety of the fundamental contradiction of the speaking human being in everyday life. Women and men are the closest of all living beings in the medium of communication—namely symbol and language—and the most estranged of all in their biological and psychic functioning.

Third, fortunately, today's miraculous means of communication, together with travel and migration, moderate the "time-consuming difficulties" of yesterday. Ultimately, we must put them to optimal use.

As has emerged from this very swift, panoramic overview employing five indicators and two pictures—the early nineteenth century and the possible ideal of the coming decades—we may conclude that:

On the whole, and independently of political eras, chiefly through the daily resolve and efforts of women—insofar as urban dwellers are concerned—all indicators, with the exception of civil and citizenship rights, stand more or less in the green zone or possess the potential to enter it. Unfortunately, in the realm of citizenship rights, owing to their dependence upon the three factors—political, social, and traditional—we require greater time, patience, resistance, perseverance, forbearance, and tenacity. It is precisely here that the effort of every citizen, in every daily gesture in defence of citizenship rights in general and women's civil rights in particular, is indispensable and necessary.

We come from afar; we have witnessed many peaks and troughs. Beyond doubt, this painful thorn too will be drawn from the foot of our mothers, sisters, wives, and daughters under their own leadership and with the solidarity of freedom-loving men who oppose all discrimination.

fr.title: Entre la méthode de Descartes et les croyances surnaturelles
fr.executive_summary: https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/03/AA3.jpg Descartes et le cartésianisme considèrent, dans la logique, les relations de cause à effet observables, mesurables et tangibles, perceptibles directement et indirectement par nos sens et obéissant aux lois naturelles, telles que les lois de mesure…
fr.body_markdown:
https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/03/AA3.jpg

Descartes et le cartésianisme considèrent, dans la logique, les relations de cause à effet observables, mesurables et tangibles, perceptibles directement et indirectement par nos sens et obéissant aux lois naturelles, telles que les lois de mesure de la relation entre le poids, la surface et le volume. D'un autre côté, dans le domaine du surnaturel, nous tombons dans des relations de cause à effet dont les racines ne sont ni homogènes, ni expérimentables, ni tangibles. La racine des relations surnaturelles remonte à la continuité qui va de l'invention de l'esprit jusqu'aux dieux et au Dieu unique. Dans le premier système de traitement des données de l'être humain, après la nomination, il nous fallait que la relation d'un être vivant nommé — qui, dans ce système de traitement des données, est en relation avec d'autres êtres nommés — fût également préservée après sa mort. Par conséquent, nous comblions la place vide des disparus par ce « présent absent », par exemple l'esprit du père… Cela s'est progressivement étendu, et ce présent absent s'est propagé aux corps, aux objets et aux phénomènes naturels, inventant les dieux et leur volonté pour expliquer les relations de cause à effet. Et c'est dans l'évolution de ce même phénomène que nous sommes parvenus à un Dieu absolu qui est unique et échappe à tous les moyens et instruments de connaissance individuels et collectifs de l'être humain, de sorte qu'en s'accomplissant ainsi, nous revenons de nouveau au non-savoir absolu originel.

Dans l'intervalle entre la méthode directe de Descartes et les croyances surnaturelles, c'est-à-dire entre ces deux extrêmes, on peut aujourd'hui évoquer la découverte et la mise en œuvre de trois autres logiques ou de trois outils complémentaires dans la compréhension et l'analyse de l'être. La première logique renvoie au cours du mouvement de la culture humaine : appelons-la la *paléoculture*, la culture de l'essence de l'être humain — une logique inscrite dans l'institution même de la culture humaine depuis l'époque où l'homme a commencé à recourir à l'outil de la symbolisation, il y a environ un million d'années. La deuxième logique renvoie à la culture dans laquelle le « je » est entouré ; elle remonte à l'essence de ses symboles linguistiques et traditionnels, une culture enracinée dans la mère, dans la langue maternelle, dans les dialectes, les locutions familières, les poèmes et les modes de relation culturelle traditionnelle avec autrui, avec la société et avec l'être, avec leurs prescriptions et leurs interdits. Et la troisième logique est cette logique même enfouie dans l'identité intérieure du « je », fondement de l'inconscient, qui constitue la logique interne du fonctionnement de cet inconscient. Dans la première logique — la paléoculture — nous trouvons la trace de Jung ; dans la deuxième logique, celle d'Eliade ; et dans la troisième logique, celle de Freud et de Lacan.

Le fonctionnement de ces trois logiques est caché et latent.
