L'interaction entre toutes les voies de la connaissance réside dans le respect de leur continuité, condition qui rend possible leur enrichissement. Le temps permet de revisiter et de revivre le passé au présent. Les écrits, les peintures, les photographies, la récitation des mythes, le cinéma, le théâtre, le roman, la nouvelle… constituent tous les archives des traces de notre effort, les effets réciproques de la compréhension de notre passage dans l'existence à l'aide du progrès scientifique et technique. Dans le même temps, la connaissance du passé contribue à la connaissance de soi et de l'autre. Plus je connais ma propre manière d'être, plus je puis connaître mon monde et, par conséquent, davantage innover. Ce processus prend une accélération croissante, au point que l'on peut dire que la moitié des scientifiques que la planète Terre ait jamais portés sont vivants aujourd'hui.

Les disciplines scientifiques elles-mêmes sont immergées dans cet océan de signifiants, une prison qui nous enferme dans les signifiés. Hafez a pressenti cette difficulté à sa manière :

Lave les feuillets si tu es notre compagnon d'étude,

car la science de l'amour ne se trouve point dans les registres.

Toutefois, quelle règle directrice convient à nos laboratoires ?
La Déclaration universelle des droits de l'homme, avec son préambule et ses trente articles, structure le cadre de notre société : fruit du long cheminement de la vie collective de nos ancêtres, de la caverne jusqu'à la Lune. De la première empreinte de symbolisation jusqu'à la Déclaration universelle des droits de l'homme s'étend une distance d'environ quarante mille ans, un long chemin fait d'efforts et de labeur pour accroître notre connaissance et notre bien-être. Quatre-vingt mille sites d'art pariétal préhistorique (environ 40 000 à 8 000 avant notre ère) témoignent de la diversité des symboles et de leurs instruments de tracé, présents sur les cinq continents ; ils parlent d'espérance, de voyage, d'espoir de paix, de vie familiale, de découvertes, d'émerveillement face à l'existence et enfin de relation à l'autre et à la nature. En contemplant les peintures préhistoriques, j'entends la même voix qu'à la lecture de la Déclaration universelle des droits de l'homme : la voix du premier être humain qui se redressa. Nous observons ce même effet saisissant dans le *Shahnameh* de Ferdowsi de Tous. Après un propos sur l'existence, il relate ainsi le récit de l'apparition de l'être humain :

Lorsque tu dépasses cela, l'être humain apparut — il devint la clef de toutes ces entraves.
Sa tête se dressa droite tel un haut cyprès — par la belle parole et la sagesse agissante.
Réceptacle d'intelligence, de discernement et de raison — les bêtes sauvages et le bétail lui obéissent.
Si par la voie de la raison tu médites un instant — sur ce que signifie l'être humain en son unité :
On t'a élevé des deux mondes — on t'a nourri à travers maintes médiations.
Tu es le premier par la nature originelle, le dernier par le décompte — ne te tiens donc pas toi-même pour un jeu.

On peut se demander comment Ferdowsi a pu formuler de telles intuitions jusqu'à l'évolution de l'être humain, et cela il y a mille ans, sans disposer du savoir scientifique contemporain.

En guise de conclusion :
Les laboratoires de la connaissance et de l'édification de soi et de l'autre sont infinis. N'hésitons pas à créer de nouveaux laboratoires ; sans aucun doute, ils se frayeront eux-mêmes une place dans l'avenir. L'œuvre et la quête de nouveauté ne se perdent jamais. Vivons avec nous-mêmes afin de devenir.

Qu'est-ce donc que cette voûte élevée, simple et richement ornée ?

De cette énigme, nul savant au monde n'a connaissance.

en.body_markdown:
https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/01/peinture-300706-143.jpg

Become a lover, lest one day the work of the world come to an end,

Without your having read the design of purpose from the workshop of existence.

I have endured a pain of love of which ask not; I have tasted a poison of separation of which ask not.
I have wandered through the world and, at the end of the quest, chosen a beloved of whom ask not.
So greatly do the tears of my eyes flow in longing for the dust of His threshold, ask not.
Last night, with my own ears, I heard words from His lips of which ask not.
Why do you bite your lip at me, saying "speak not"? I have tasted a ruby lip of which ask not.
Without You, in my beggar's hut, I have suffered hardships of which ask not.
Like Hafez, a stranger on the path of love, I have attained a station of which ask not.

Permit me to draw a little closer to this station of Hafez, the stranger on the path of love:

Although he says we should not ask, let us ask nevertheless, just as he himself advises:

Like Mansour, those who raise up from the sought aim raise high;

At this threshold, when they summon Hafez, they drive him away.

In this sacred court, when the ardent bring their need, they bring coquetry;

For with this pain, if they remain captive without remedy, they remain so.

· Who is Hafez?

Hafez, like the first anthropologist, carries the relativity of knowledge into the depths of human gaze. He expands the field of inquiry beyond the conventional and known world of his time and lends it depth. He cleaves open the limits of perception, thought, imagination, and phantasy. He tramples upon the intellectual tradition of his era. He joins new elements to the old. He brings together the world of sleep, the world of dreams, and the world of reality alongside the world of illusion and imagination. It is as though he recognises every world of the human being. He gives dimension to humanity. He places human dignity above all else. He makes tolerance the guiding principle of his work. He recognises the real human being, with all their passions, desires, and needs, in their corporeality, in their thinking, and in their need for joy and pleasure. He shatters artificial boundaries: he accepts neither physical and earthly borders nor boundaries across the innumerable worlds of the human being.

Speak not to the pretender of the secrets of love and intoxication,
Lest he die in ignorance in the pain of selfishness.
Become a lover, lest one day the work of the world come to an end,
Without your having read the design of purpose from the workshop of existence.

Around two enchanting couplets of Hafez of Shiraz, we embark together upon a journey: from the cave paintings of early humans to the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

We shall endeavour together to discover and comprehend the subtle, hidden, and profound relationship between "love", "the work of the world", "the design of purpose", and "the workshop of existence". Over more than hundreds of thousands of years, humanity created "symbolisation". Speech separated human beings from the animal. Through speech and symbol, humanity created writing, civilisation, culture, and diversity.

The diversity of language, script, customs, and culture upon a small Earth amidst billions of galaxies and planets bears witness to plurality within unity. From the earliest beliefs down to the present day, humanity has stood before an agonising and perennial question: its place in existence. Hafez of Shiraz calls the path of inquiry becoming a "lover", and doing so before "the work of the world" comes to an end. Let us regard "the workshop of existence" as both a laboratory and a manufactory, both a site of knowledge and a place of creation.

Traversing life from the first human being to the present day alongside Hafez of Shiraz—as the first "anthropologist"—and drawing upon his other ghazals, we shall review the harmony and consonance of the diverse paths of knowledge.

Can all such laboratories be permitted to pursue their inquiry side by side?

What universal charter grants humanity this possibility?

Do the answers of Hafez of Shiraz and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights move in the same direction?

Together, we shall go in search.

What is this lofty dome, simple yet richly patterned?

Of this enigma no sage in the world is aware.

And now, our discussion today:

Speak not to the pretender of the secrets of love and intoxication,
Lest he die in ignorance in the pain of selfishness.
Become a lover, lest one day the work of the world come to an end,
Without your having read the design of purpose from the workshop of existence.

Between bacteria and the human being, *Homo sapiens*, there lies a span of more than three billion years, and from *Homo sapiens* to our time, forty thousand years. Life continues, and the more the years accumulate, the greater grows the resistance against death—"something" which, for the sake of simplicity, we call "life". And in the end, a day arrives when we write the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and humanity stands proud as a worthy witness to three billion years. Such a trajectory has many radiant days ahead of it: we must write the rights of life, bearing in mind that the finest way to write the right to life is to establish it. It is as though the aim of life were "living" against "death". This vast path towards "pleasure", passing through a vital stage which I term the stage of "human rights", cannot halt before attaining the right to life, as our sole foundational right upon "Earth". The testimonies preserved along this path—beyond fossils and the lives of our ancestors—are historical and architectural evidence, prehistoric art, writings, oral culture, and human cultural heritage; all of these are living specimens of our Earth. Perhaps, perhaps this right will guide us beyond this Earth. And perhaps this right will demand of us another space in which to leave behind the heritage of "life" for our children; it is necessary to chart this shared path of life, each according to their own capacity…

Time flows to the length of weariness.

Silence is as vast as the eyes of the blue sky.

The sky sees us just as we see it. Yes, it has eyes. Yes, between us and the sun lies the astonishing grandeur of silence, and there is no occasion to count it. Therefore, a path other than counting is required.

· Become a lover…

Become a lover, lest one day the work of the world come to an end,
Without your having read the design of purpose from the workshop of existence.

The aim is to seek the locus of love—a dual locus, a site of self-intensification and a place to sense presence within the field of change and to guide it. Nothing is pre-written: life innovates, creates, bestows, and endures. In the Persian language, the word *hâl* means the present moment as well as being joyful and well in that state; at the same time, it is the ultimate goal of those who turn to mystical experience. Attaining the present moment—a moment at the intersection of what has been discovered and invented and what is yet to be discovered and invented, between sensing the exterior from within, like this third place, in the midst of a torus: an exterior in the midst of the interior, or an interior in the midst of the exterior.

· Laboratories in the world:

Prehistoric art is one of the earliest testimonies of humanity's struggle to proclaim its rights. Allow me to begin with a poem by Saadi, one of the most renowned Iranian poets of the thirteenth century CE, which is displayed in one of the buildings of the United Nations in New York:

Human beings are limbs of one body,

For in creation they stem from a single essence.

When time brings pain to one limb,

The other limbs can find no rest.

You who are indifferent to the suffering of others

Are unworthy to be called human.

Diverse studies have been conducted on the origins of human emergence, on the roots of the one hundred and forty thousand languages we have created and employed, and on the path traversed between prehistoric art and writing. These studies remind us that "in the beginning" human beings were not as distant from one another as we imagine. In the poem "Human beings are limbs of one body", calligraphy, writing, and symbolism are at once the point of departure and the point of arrival.

The first declaration of human rights was inscribed in the sixth century BCE, under the reign of Cyrus, the first king of Persia. Discovered in Mesopotamia in the nineteenth century, this declaration is engraved in Old Persian cuneiform upon a clay cylinder and is today housed in a museum in England. According to this declaration, people enjoyed full freedom of thought, language, and ritual: "I proclaim that all are free to worship their gods, and I command that no one may be mistreated on this account. I command that no house be destroyed. I establish peace and well-being for all humankind. I decree that every person has the right to live in peace in whatever land they choose…".

From Iran to human rights—like being present in a river that has been flowing for thousands of years—we offered the earliest signs of human rights through the cylinder bequeathed by Cyrus, the founder of Persia 2,500 years ago. Iran is the cradle of administrative organisation, with the invention of the postal, military, and taxation systems; with respect for the beliefs and traditions of diverse peoples; and with continuity in the presence of architecture and the Persian language. A civilisation that has endured numerous cultural earthquakes: from Alexander of Macedon to Islam, from Genghis Khan to Tamerlane and fierce, sweeping religious movements; from Mithraism to Mazdaism, from Sunnism to Shiism, from the discovery of modernity to *laïcité*.

Let us note together several clear traces of the invention of the principles of *laïcité*—equality and liberty grounded in the human being and their presence in the workshop of existence: from Cyrus's cylinder of human rights to Ferdowsi, the sage who observes the world with acuity; to the citizens of England who, in the thirteenth century, established the principle of the jury, according to which a free person can only be judged by free persons—and it was these very people who declared in the seventeenth century: "No one may be held in captivity save by the decision of a judge". In the same vein, let us recall that in 1787, in drafting their Constitution, the Americans adopted the principles of the continuity of human rights. And finally, in 1789, the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen shines forth like a brilliant star.

From this trajectory, let us return to the workshop of existence and pause briefly upon one of these paths amidst all the other paths of the world—my own path: I intend to turn the lens of the camera inwards, to draw out the fruit of my knowledge and understanding—a twofold capacity for instinctive knowledge and scientific knowledge. For psychoanalysis stands at the crossroads of art and knowledge.

With every movement, my hands call their own extension into question: a questioning between this unity with the workshop of existence, the repetition of the breath-movement of life taught to me by the masters, and the discovery of that subtle point which awaits me in the next instant.

A movement that carries me towards another horizon, not only in relation to the dance of words amongst themselves—the play of letters upon a white surface—but in harmony with the relationship to the white space left behind, the unwritten.

Opening a path towards a truth born of an excess of a few millimetres in tracing a letter at the end of a word, in continuation of a phrase from a poem that lives within me and which Hafez recites to saturate me and guide me at the exact moment when I am able to comprehend it:

Ghazal 143

I said: "When did the Sage give you this world-viewing cup?"

He said: "On the day He fashioned this enamel dome."

Yes, it is the heart that is the researcher. The heart seeks an imaginary instrument to find its answer—an instrument not available within reality. In the Elder of the Magi (*Pir-e Moghan*), Hafez sees an imaginary being with an anthropological gaze, one who possesses a profound view of history, one endowed with sight from the very dawn of creation. Such an instrument lies within our observations—observations from across a deep angle and to the full volume of existence.

My birth in Shiraz, near Persepolis—symbol of the pre-Islamic era—and the traces of ruins astonishing to any child. And finally, turning inwards, lifting successive outer masks, transforming the human being into a field of observation, dissecting humanity in diverse directions: in Greek culture, *psyche* and *soma*; in Islam, spirit and body; in Iranian mythology, *ravan* (soul), *badan* (body), and *jan* (vital spirit)—which bears affinity with the Greek *psyche* and the Western *âme*; and in Iranian mysticism and its pre-eminent representative, Hafez of Shiraz.

With his singular anatomy of the human being, Hafez attains a degree of perfection: *ravan* (soul), *jan* (vital spirit), *sar* (head/mind), *del* (heart), *ruh* (spirit), right up to the threshold of *serr-e del* (the secret of the heart). From psychoanalysis to anthropology, from the word to the footprint of knowledge, we must contemplate the depth of this cognitive field that has gathered us together. The speaking being can be cut and stitched, constructed and deconstructed from multiple angles: from the vantage point of an individual, the unity of a bacterium, a living cell, to feeling the speech of the other in one's own flesh and skin; a ceaseless back-and-forth between the individual and the collective; from the family to the tribe, from the nation-state to the community of like-minded and fellow believers; from the individuality of the speaking human to the humans who preceded them, to the animal, to the plant, and simply to life.

And we learn not to become ensnared in the play of our own "signifiers", to allow ourselves to take our worlds seriously—the dreams and phantasies within ourselves and within society—and, advancing further still, to become attuned even to delusions, to lose ourselves in the reality of others as the other of the other. Let us behold this invisible realm within the bubble offered to us by the image of a virtual world, in this grand "masquerade ball", and the networks of invisible relations that unite individuals so as to forge from them other inseparable wholes. Like the ensemble of acoustic images of words invented down to the present day by us, the creators of symbols, which ultimately circulate so freely hither and thither that one cannot know which belongs to whom: it is as though we bring these symbols into being, transmit them to the other, immerse ourselves in them, and ultimately forget them, only to take them up again at another time and carry on the work. And in the end, as a boundary—the familiar boundary—this point of existence which is the ensemble of these symbols, and which, contrary to assumption, is not so fixed.

It is as though this ensemble of our discoveries, inventions, knowledges, and insights has gathered together so that we may understand ourselves and the other, and also grant ourselves the possibility of transformation. Once again, Hafez:

Ghazal 374

Come, let us scatter roses and pour wine into the goblet;

Let us cleave the roof of heaven and cast a new design.

If sorrow raises an army to shed the blood of lovers,

I and the cupbearer will charge together and overturn its foundations.

An alchemical back-and-forth unfolds between this interior and exterior, between this instinct and knowledge, between the freedom of the artist and their scientific rigour.

When we turn to calligraphy, this back-and-forth lies between the artist's precision and their scientific freedom: the language of nature on the one hand, and the human experience of writing on the other.

Twenty years of experience were needed to find another "locus" (*jaygah*)—*jaygah*, a word signifying "time-space"—an experience of duality: East–West, Symbolic–Real, instinct–experience, another line within a four-dimensional volume. What I wish to share with you, in response to your generosity and your presence here, is precisely this experience: that our presence is a passage through a volume, from one point to another, singular; this volume of presence lies within the universal "locus"—at least eleven billion human beings—I am not alone.

Upon encountering psychoanalysis, I gained a different perspective on the multi-millennial cultural movement of Iran. With the prohibition of the outward representation of the body in Islam, art and literature gathered around architecture, poetry, and calligraphy. This threefold knot of architecture, poetry, and calligraphy carries within itself three possibilities of human knowledge:

- First, the imprint of reality (geography, ways of life, climate, nature, plants, flowers, plains, and deserts…)
- Second, the imprint of the world of imagination, dream, hope, and desire
- And finally, the Symbolic imprint, inscribed in culture, in behaviour, in words, in the manner in which we move, in bodily gestures, in the turning of the eyes, in dancing…

With such sensitivity, I seek to reveal the consonance and harmony of the image of the "archetypal world"—a quest that passes through painting, the symbolic presence of architecture in painting, the drawing and curves of calligraphy, the iconography of dome curves in the letters of the alphabet, and perhaps in the future through the traces of the deepest symbolisation introduced by signs and symbols, namely prehistoric art. The multiplicity of the dimensions of my presence in existence, one after another, simultaneously or sequentially, has led me to an alchemy called life. On the one hand, the penetration of scientific precision and its application as an engineer, accompanied by the opening of data-processing systems as a possible model translating a question that springs from within outwards; and on the other hand, instinctive perception and artistic creativity lend their density to my dreams and phantasies in exile. To illuminate these dimensions, I quote a poem of my own, born of my encounter with this verse of T. S. Eliot: "I should be glad of another death":

It learns to fly.

It reaches the height of the roof of self-sufficiency.

Alone, above the possibility of looking back upon time gone by.

The eagle of solitude is born.

A thin membrane is torn.

The free eagle rebuilds its own life anew at every instant, alone.

The instant is time, and the point is existence.

The playful eyes of the eagle, without seeking death, have found the solitude of death.

From this astonishment before the star-filled nights of the Iranian desert, before the grandeur of the blue depths calligraphed with poetry unto infinity, following a trail, until years later at Tehran Polytechnic where I found my scientific guide in Einstein. Later, in Europe, I became acquainted with the disciples of Freud—that magician, the discoverer of the dark recesses of the human psyche. And finally, my hand set out eagerly to write and rewrite the poems of Hafez in *nasta'liq* calligraphy: *nasta'liq*, this summit of Persian calligraphy, which in my view comprises the most harmonious curves that humanity has ever created. These dimensions of rediscovering writing—the workshop of existence, the sky, and the desert—are in fact my body.

The importance of reckoning 14 billion years, 11 billion *Homo sapiens sapiens*, and the passage of more than 3 million years since the emergence of bacteria lies in being able to envisage the movement of life in its totality, to situate every element of life within a universe, with relativism and holism. In this manner, we attend to the relativity of the realms of plants, animals, and human beings, as well as the movement from the static towards the mobile.

The dew awakens,

a lingering purity of the night

washes the leaf.

This brief pause has allowed us to touch more clearly the locus and aims with which I observe existence and grow within it.

The workshop of existence is like an ensemble of laboratories in which we conduct research in order to understand, discover, and invent the other and ourselves. For the continuity of methods and tools, for adaptation, for transforming multidimensional movements—within the locus of 14 billion years, at least 40,000 years of *Homo sapiens sapiens*, and 11 billion human beings born up to the present day—and ultimately for the efficacy of these laboratories, we require fundamental laws to clarify the utmost freedom of each laboratory.
Without a guiding charter, dialogue is impossible. Without freedom, we shall not cross boundaries and experiences. Tolerance and mutual communication require connection and the transmission of messages. We must draw benefit from one another's work. We need a common language, and without imposing any particular orientation, we need a secular (*laïque*) foundation. Even tolerance requires a boundary. How can one be certain that the boundary of tolerance is genuine? Does returning to the boundaries of symbolisation, language, speech, and the purification of their traces not open a path?

The fruit of our presence in this workshop bears arborescent, reciprocal traces—from root to stem—such as: the tree of languages, the tree of scripts, the tree of shared cultures and myths, the migrations and journeys that enrich the deep roots of the laboratories, and ultimately symbols, words, and their effects—not merely the capacity to forge tools of communication with oneself and with the other. For instance, there are the 140,000 languages that our world has witnessed, or the thousands of scripts, amongst which Chinese script is the oldest, whose graphic form and beauty, rooted in prehistoric art, resemble *nasta'liq* calligraphy.

In the search for the value of values, a point of departure, can one explore what lies before and after symbolisation? Imprisoned at the very threshold of symbolisation, access to this value of values becomes impossible for us. It is here that Hafez says:

Ghazal 94

Your love will come to your aid, even if, like Hafez,

you recite the Qur'an by heart in fourteen traditions.

Let us note that for Hafez, in order to understand, love is inescapable; even for grasping the path of a book like the Qur'an, it is love that comes to his aid. To gain an understanding of this workshop of existence and find a starting point, let us attend to resonance with existence, to love as the "state" of the speaking being, in the manner of the early magicians, as resonance with the other, and ultimately to understanding through extension in being—a being without differentiation.

The foundational disciplines of knowledge through symbolisation render the real measurable in the form of intelligible and teachable units. Yet there also exists another laboratory, far removed from any measurability and from the logic of cause-and-effect relations: what we call, outside this field of symbolisation, the inexplicable. How can the work of these laboratories existing within the workshop of existence be made to flourish between the two poles of illuminative love and the scientific path? Between these two poles dwells cultural diversity.

The interplay amongst all ways of knowing lies in respecting their continuity—a fact that makes their enrichment possible. Time enables the revisiting and reliving of past time in the present. Writings, paintings, photographs, the retelling of myths, cinema, theatre, novels, short stories… are all archives of the traces of our endeavour, the reciprocal effects of understanding our passage through existence by means of scientific and technical progress. At the same time, knowing the past aids in knowing oneself and the other. The more I know my own manner of being, the more I can know my world and, consequently, the more I can innovate. This process gathers accelerating momentum, such that one may say that half of the scientists whom the Earth has ever known are alive today.

Scientific disciplines too are immersed in this ocean of signifiers—a prison that confines us to signifieds. Hafez sensed this difficulty in his own way:

Wash clean the pages if you are our fellow-student,

for the science of love is not to be found in notebooks.

Even so, what charter is fitting for our laboratories?
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights, with a preamble and thirty articles, organises the framework of our society: the fruit of the long path of our ancestors' communal life, from the cave to the Moon. From the earliest footprint of symbolisation to the Universal Declaration of Human Rights lies a span of nearly forty thousand years—a long road of endeavour and struggle to increase our knowledge and well-being. Eighty thousand sites of prehistoric painting (circa 40,000–8,000 BCE) bear witness to the diversity of symbols and their drawing instruments, present across all five continents, speaking of hope, travel, the hope of peace, family life, discoveries, awe before existence, and ultimately the relationship with the other and with nature. Looking upon prehistoric paintings, I hear the very same voice as when reading the Universal Declaration of Human Rights: the voice of the first human being who stood upright. We observe this same astonishing effect in the *Shahnameh* of Ferdowsi of Tus. After a discourse concerning existence, he recounts the story of the emergence of humanity thus:

When you pass beyond this, humankind appeared — it became the key to all these fetters.
Its head rose upright like a tall cypress — through fair speech and the practice of wisdom.
Receptive of intelligence, judgement, and reason — wild beasts and cattle alike obey it.
If by the path of reason you reflect a little — on what humankind means in its essence:
You have been brought forth from both worlds — you have been nurtured through many intermediaries.
First in innate nature, last in reckoning — it is you; hold not yourself in jest.

One may ask oneself how Ferdowsi articulated such insights—extending even to human evolution—a thousand years ago, without being acquainted with contemporary scientific knowledge.

By way of conclusion:
The laboratories of knowledge and of the making of oneself and the other are infinite. Let us not harbour doubt in creating new laboratories; without question, they will carve out their own place in the future. Work and the quest for renewal are never lost. Let us live with ourselves in order to become.

What is this lofty roof, simple yet richly patterned?

Of this riddle no wise person in the world is aware.
