en.body_markdown:
https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/03/IMGP0973-Copier.jpg

Prologue:

In this essay I seek to demonstrate that the author of *The Ontology of Hafez*(1) places numerous difficulties in the reader's path:

- The author erases pre-Islamic Iranians from history.

- The author has not grasped the concept of myth.

- The author is unacquainted with the contemporary theories of Freud, Jung, and Eliade concerning the path that leads anthropology towards mythology and oral history.

- The author clings to presuppositions in which he leaves himself no room whatsoever for doubt or hesitation.

- The author contends that Hafez merely expresses and repeats the mystics of the Khorasan school, to such an extent that in his book Hafez is relegated to a footnote.

- That the mystics of the Khorasan school placed the mystical exegesis (*ta'wîl*) of Creation in the Quran at the summit of their ontological knowledge.

- The author lowers the "study of ontology" to the level of examining the genesis of humankind from Hafez's viewpoint.

- The author suffers from a traditional conception of history and historical products and transformations, rather than an effervescent vision that leads to the interpenetration of phenomena and cultures — as though culture in Iran began only with the advent of Islam.

- The author is unaware of Hafez scholars and the work of hundreds of researchers who have investigated Hafez's thought and produced valuable works, and turns only to a narrow branch of Hafez researchers who are under the sway of a religious outlook and base their inquiry and perspective on belief in a "Creator".

- In a scholarly work, diverse opposing and supporting theories ought to be presented and discussed; in many places, the theories of others have been forgotten or passed over in a few brief words.

- Ashouri's endeavour in his writing on Hafez is a continuation of the same endeavour that, in other dimensions, is summed up in the following statement: "Today, contemporary Iranian history has been reduced to three things: the Constitutional Revolution and the leadership of Sheikh Fazlollah, the Oil Nationalisation Movement and the leadership of Kashani, and the Islamic Revolution, whose historical roots of the 1357 [1979] Revolution go back to 15 Khordad 1342 [5 June 1963], and that too under the monopoly of a particular faction." (11)

It may be said that this very same endeavour is underway in its cultural dimensions to give everything a religious, clerical, Islamic, and divine colouring. On page 22 we read:

"The most fundamental feature of Hafez's world in the realm of thought... is that it is a religious world, and he looks upon the world through the lens of religion and religious understanding..."

And it is gratifying that amid this all-encompassing effort by the masters of religion and the state to portray everything and everyone as Islamic, there are those who write in widely circulated periodicals published in Iran: "...the secret of Hafez's endurance and of his becoming a place of pilgrimage for the *rends* of the world lies hidden in the depths of the mysteries of the endurance of Iranian culture." (12)

Preface

Although the author occasionally displays skill in coining equivalents for terms — such as choosing *sarnemoun* for *Archetype*, *mesâlvâreh* for *Paradigmatic*, and *nâsâznemâ* for *Paradoxical* — in choosing the title of his book he indulges in an ambition that complicates both his task and ours. *The Ontology of Hafez*, and that too "by way of" an exploration into the foundations of his thought, leads us into difficulties.

Ontology is the one branch of knowledge that, unless it is all-encompassing, cannot be regarded as a comprehensive inquiry. The work might rather have been titled: *An Attempt at Exploring the Foundations of Hafez's Thought on the Basis of Two Presuppositions: The Archetype and the Mysticism of the Khorasan School*. Had the book borne such a title, the reader would not be crushed beneath the heavy weight of "ontology". For the field of ontology is boundless, and exploring this field requires a lofty vantage point above ontologies — an intricate task, and by no means an easy one.

In the first few pages of the book, under the heading "Hafez's Ontological Model", the researcher introduces his fundamental presuppositions to the reader by drawing upon the data and findings of Berkeley, Jung, and Eliade.

We read: "The fundamental model of ontology in Hafez's world — that is, the civilisation and culture of which he is the heir — is, like all traditional civilisations and cultures, an archetypal model: that is, a world in which, on the basis of myths, archetypes or exemplary models are provided that serve as patterns of behaviour for humankind. At the centre of these myths stands the central myth, namely the myth of Creation, in which the primordial event that is the origin and fountainhead of this-worldly events is recounted." And in the footnote on this same page we read:

"...just as the archetype of the Perfect Human in the mystical understanding of the myth of Creation in the Quran is Adam himself, whose conduct in the myth, according to its mystical exegesis (*ta'wîl*), is also a pattern of behaviour for Hafez."

To put it more plainly, in the author's words: "The entirety of Hafez's discourse lies in the myth of Creation and the primordial event that is the origin and fountainhead of worldly events, according to the mystical exegesis of the myth of Creation in the Quran." The rest of the book is devoted to tracing this very presupposition. Engaging with the ideas of Jung and Eliade bears fruit only when we trace the roots of what they said — for they devoted themselves to human oral culture, which rests upon "language and speech", and drew upon the structure of language and the bonds and essence concealed within language.

Dariush Ashouri cites Jung as saying: "...myths, in their varied narrative forms among different peoples, contain those universal patterns of the mind which, in Jung's view, reside in the collective unconscious and are inherited through procreation and birth." Today we know that this path of procreation and birth is none other than the vast expanse of the field and structure of language and oral culture (2), and therein lies the secret: the archetypal myth of Hafez, which dwells within the expanse of the Dari language, cannot be a Quranic model, still less its mystical exegesis. If we seek an archetype for Hafez, we must look for it in the expanse of Persian oral culture, for the Persian language and myth are older than the Quran. And it is precisely from this point that the researcher goes astray. This is the very same trap that has tainted the oral and written history of Persian speakers — the same trap that substituted Shi'ite history (after the Safavids) for the history of Iranian Islam; the same trap that compelled the great figures of Iranian thought and literature to stitch their discourse — bound to *Mehr* and love — with the garment of the Quran so that they might survive. At times when Hafez says:

Love will come to your rescue, even if, like Hafez,

You recite the Quran by heart in fourteen readings

In other words, Hafez takes his archetype from *Pîr-e Golrang*, Sheikh Ruzbehân, and Sheikh al-Eshrâq [Suhrawardi], where Sheikh al-Eshrâq writes: "Read the Quran as though it were written for you."

Let us return to another passage of the book, where the snare of the "primordial myth of the Quran" repeatedly draws our eye across Ashouri's pages. On page 33 we read: "We know of no other Persian *dîvân* of ghazals that contains so many historical allusions." If we mean the mythological history of the people of the Iranian land and Persian speakers, it is precisely in that direction and presentation that Hafez's *Dîvân* makes the fewest allusions to our mythological history; and if it is the history of a psychic journey, an inner journey, or an illuminationist journey, we cannot call that a historical allusion.

Here, out of the entire oral and mythological history of the Iranian people from ancient times, the researcher contents himself solely with Quranic mythological history, which belongs to the Abrahamic foundational myths. Hafez's repeated returns to Persian mythological figures and concepts such as Jam, Kay, and Kâvus (3) are ignored. In a digression on page 34 of his book, the author refers to the "departing soul" and writes: "Yet this travelogue, even while taking place on earth and during the lifetime of Mohammad Hafez Shirazi and recounting aspects of his life story and that of his contemporaries, because it is a spiritual travelogue, fundamentally recounts the memories, adventures, and experiences of the departing soul whose journey is from eternity without beginning (*azal*) to eternity without end (*abad*), whose story begins with the descent of the 'spirit' (*rûh*) from the spiritual world, from its original birthplace, into the earthly world, and whose culmination is its return once again to the homeland." Here it is not without benefit to dissect the fundamental disparity between the two views of Creation — the "Islamic" and the "Iranian mythological". In Islam, *azal* and *abad* are the two endpoints, beginning and end, of time, and between them flows the time in which our life unfolds; whereas in Iranian myth there exists a world and a time parallel to this time, such that our body is in this world — the earthly globe — while our soul (*ravân*) and the souls of other things are in that parallel world, and our endeavour is to reach that "soul". And it is this journey that forms the basis of the illuminationist experience. What the esteemed researcher calls the "departing soul" has nothing to do with the "spirit" (*rûh*), which is a Quranic and Islamic phenomenon, and this is perhaps one of the points that repeatedly places the author in difficulty when unlocking Hafez's poems.

Human knowledge of myth is remarkably new and recent! Where on page 51 he writes: "A mythological account fundamentally does not possess a rational form and does not stem from human reason, but rather reaches humankind from the unseen source, on the basis of absolute divine authority..." How can one regard myth — "the memory of human oral culture" — as coming from an unseen source, and at the same time claim that one's research is theoretical and scientific? What kind of science is this? On the one hand, Iranian mythology has no place whatsoever in his research; on the other, he begins with Islam, and if on rare occasions cultural influence and reciprocity are at play, even that comes from Greece.

He views the field of research into influences on "knowledge" in the same light as the influences of oral cultures, the effects of language and ethnic history, and their interpenetration and fusion with one another.

In a way, the researcher himself arrives at the question of why "the mysticism of love" takes shape in Iran, yet he passes quietly by it. On page 56 of the book we read: "...which, within the Islamic world, and especially in the Iranian world and in the space of the Persian language, makes possible the emergence of the mysticism of love out of the heart of ascetic Sufism." What he refers to as "the space of the Persian language" is that very essence which has endured within the language. It is that same *Mehr*, which means both "sun" and "love", and that intricate play of Hafez's poetry, which revolves around the two poles of love and light — such that he sees nothing sweeter than the voice of the speech of love (here it is not a matter of mere hearing, for this voice is accompanied by light) as a memorial that might remain eternal. One must ask how this love (*'eshq*), of which there is neither mention nor allusion in any verse of the Quran, can serve as the fundamental basis of Hafez's ontology while never once being mentioned in the Quran. The closest counterpart to the word *'eshq* in the Quran is *mahabbat* (affection), which in none of the verses mentions a romantic/amorous relationship between humankind and "Allah" (5) — to the extent that the author of the book contents himself with a single hadith from the Prophet to substantiate an amorous relationship between humankind and Allah in Islam. The endeavour of twentieth-century researchers such as Sigmund Freud, Jung, Eliade, and others has been precisely to understand why mythological knowledge endures in the mould of languages and is transmitted across the cultural eras of human societies. In this connection, one may recall the invaluable works of Henry Corbin, who over more than thirty years of effort traced the roots of concepts such as "time", "illumination" (*eshrâq*), the imaginal world (*'âlam-e mesâlî*), and the like from early Iranian mystics such as Sheikh al-Eshrâq and Sheikh Ruzbehân down to the Shaykhiyya school — showing how the structures embedded in the words of a language and culture remain the vehicle for mythological concepts and, like subterranean waters, continue their cultivation. And it is for this very reason that over the course of time this fertile subterranean river wells up like spontaneous springs from the hearts of cherished figures such as Hafez.

The author's estrangement from pre-Islamic Iranian culture is such that even in understanding post-Islamic mystical concepts he falls into confusion. Thus, in Iranian mysticism, the imaginal world (*'âlam-e mesâlî*) or *Hurqalyâ* is an intermediate world between the higher world — the world of mysteries, the esoteric world, the world of divine names — on the one hand, and the corporeal world and the world of sense and matter on the other (p. 59). He equates the imaginal world with the world of Ideas. On this point, refer to the introduction of *Spiritual Body and Celestial Earth: From Mazdean Iran to Shi'ite Iran*. Because the author understands myth in its Quranic sense, in order to trace its roots he devotes several detailed chapters to tracking the myth of Creation in the scriptures of Jews and Christians, knowing full well that the mythological or legendary roots of the Quran draw their water from the Torah.

The author puts forward a presupposition to the effect that Hafez's "ontology" revolves around the "creation of Adam", and in order to prove this claim he reads Hafez's poems along these lines and categorises them accordingly, so that through them he might align Hafez's knowledge with two books: *Mersâd al-'Ebâd* by Najm al-Dîn Râzî and *Kashf al-Asrâr* by Abu'l-Fazl Rashîd al-Dîn Meybodî. Previously, in the book *Yek Qesseh Bîsh Nîst* (*It Is Nothing But One Tale*), Hassan Anvari, in dissecting the ghazal beginning "Last night I saw the angels knocking at the tavern door...", referred to Najm al-Dîn Râzî's *Mersâd al-'Ebâd* and the story of Creation and its mystical exegesis. Bearing in mind that Anvari's book was published in 1368 [1989] and Dariush Ashouri's book in 1377 [1998], how fitting it would have been if the author had at least made a brief reference to Hassan Anvari's work. Where the author writes: "The present book is a theoretical and scientific answer to the question 'What does Hafez say?' and an identification of that inner logic which binds together and unifies all his diverse and meaningful symbols, concepts, and expressions — without searching for ideas of our own choosing", it would have been better to say that the present book is *one* of the attempts undertaken, rather than claiming it is *the* theoretical and scientific answer. In the introduction we read: "Hafez is the greatest enigma of our culture." If this statement is true, our culture is undoubtedly conceived as the culture of today's Persian-speaking Iranians, and this culture was not born in a single day. This culture has gathered drop by drop over thousands of years, mingled with other cultures, and existed within the field of the law of mutual influence. And I suspect the author's deviation begins right here: in defining culture, he begins it with Iran's Islamic mystical culture. The author states that among "the multitude of things written about him, I have not found an article or book that truly provides me with a satisfactory answer to the question of what Hafez says." How helpful it would have been had he also introduced his primary research sources to us.

In this introduction we read: "In this book I have endeavoured to approach this *Dîvân* with preconceived methods and principles so as finally to give a scientific and theoretical answer to the question 'What does Hafez say?' Therefore, this work is neither an endorsement of Hafez's thought and worldview nor a refutation of it, but solely a scientific study in the morphology of Hafez's thought. Yet the question that forms the foundation of this research is of fundamental importance not only for Hafez studies, but also for understanding the foundations of our culture and mentality. Indeed, unravelling the *Dîvân* of Hafez and striving to understand it theoretically is essential for unravelling our inherited culture and striving to understand it from a contemporary standpoint."

Upon reading the book, we expect the author to introduce his preconceived methods and principles and then unravel our inherited culture. Our review of this book rests upon these very two points, and we seek to show what this method is, to what extent the author has understood and applied it, and how far it bears any trace of our inherited culture.

Examination of the Ontological Model of Hafez in Dariush Ashouri's Work

The core of the researcher's argument, which forms the basis of his work, appears on page 29:

"The fundamental model of ontology in Hafez's world — that is, the civilisation and culture of which he is the heir — is, like all traditional civilisations and cultures, a mythological-archetypal model: that is, a world in which, on the basis of myths, archetypes or transcendent models are provided that serve as patterns of behaviour for humankind. At the centre of these myths stands the central myth, namely the myth of Creation, in which the primordial event that is the origin and fountainhead of this-worldly events is recounted." At the end of his explanation of the term *sarnemoun* (Archetype) in the footnote on page 29, we read:

"Myths, in their varied narrative forms among different peoples, contain those universal patterns of the mind which, in Jung's view, reside in the collective unconscious and are inherited through procreation and birth.

archetypes such as the archetype of the mother, the father, the hero, and the wise old man appear in various myths in diverse narrative forms and serve, for their believers, as an exemplar and model of behaviour. Thus, the archetype of the Perfect Human in the mystical reading of the myth of creation in the Qur'an is Adam himself, whose conduct in that myth, according to its mystical *ta'wil* [esoteric interpretation], is likewise a model of behaviour for Hafez..." The researcher's fundamental deviation begins precisely at this point. For while the Qur'an may contain part of the mythology of the Arabs of Mecca, it cannot constitute myth for other peoples who converted to Islam—unless, contrary to the research of the scholars cited by Mr Ashouri, such as Jung and Eliade, we were to believe in a single, uniform myth for all the nations of the world, and one revealed to prophets in sacred scriptures at that. Perhaps, ultimately, his understanding of the archetype—as something transmitted through human biological reproduction—amounts to this?

First, Jung's presupposition still has a long way to go before attaining scientific status; second, Jung does not regard myths as originating in a celestial scripture; and third, if an archetype exists for the human being as a speaking living being, it resides in speech and the word. It is language that carries within itself the weight of mythical knowledge, and nothing else. If archetypes pass from one generation to the next, they do so on the foundation of speech. The freight of every word and the relations among words—within the circulation and formation of these words—mean that the perspective of the "mystics of the Khurasan school" rests upon the Persian language, which has carried its essence with it from a past far more remote than five or eight centuries. In his effort to graft the Qur'an onto myth, Illuminationist mysticism onto the Qur'an, and Hafez onto Illuminationist mysticism, the researcher all at once grafts Hafez onto the Qur'an, and in doing so:

- advances a novel claim regarding a scientific and modern method of Hafez scholarship;

- overlooks the difference between Iranian and non-Iranian Islamic mysticism;

- makes no reference to the pre-Islamic cultural-mythical past of Iranians, to such a degree that one is left in two minds as to whether all of this is deliberate or inadvertent. Why does the author distort the meaning of myth to this extent?

On page 37 we read: "On the whole, what has been stated here as the paradigm of Hafez's thought relies upon the entire heritage of mystical thought concerning the descent and re-ascent of the Universal Soul from the spiritual world to the corporeal world and its return once more to its original abode. Therefore, to comprehend the foundation of this ontology, one must study the myth of creation in its religious account and subsequently its mystical *ta'wil*." How can one fall into this trap and fail to see that, fundamentally, if the Qur'anic account of creation were a myth, and if this myth existed naturally in the archetypes of Hafez or other mystics, there would be no need for mystical *ta'wil* and for separating it from the Qur'anic account, nor any need for philosophical polemics between opponents and proponents? The need for coded speech, veiled expression, and esoteric interpretation arises precisely where plain speaking brings trouble—and this trouble is the very contradiction embedded at the core of the mythical thought of Persian speakers, which reaches its peak in the distinction between *rūh* [spirit] and *ravān* [soul]. The principal predicament of Hafez and his predecessors was to convey Iranian mythical concepts in the mould of Qur'anic vocabulary; otherwise, what need would there have been for conflict, cipher, concealment, the candle-torture of Shaykh al-Ishraq [Suhrawardi], and the severing of Hallaj's head and hands? For the spiritual world, according to one account, is that very Celestial Earth (*zamīn-e mīnovī*) from which, according to Iranian myths, our *ravān* descended to earth and to which it shall return. By contrast, within Qur'anic concepts there is neither a "corporeal world" and a "spiritual world", nor a doctrine called the "Universal Soul". On page 40 we read: "Mythical worldviews that were founded in the primordial era of humanity, laid the cornerstone of ethnic cultures, and in the languages of peoples articulated their eternal history." How can one, in the statement above, believe in the intimate bond between ethnic culture, ethnic language, and eternal history within a mythical worldview, and yet on the other hand jumble all these concepts together in one's own writing? If we align his statement with the research he has conducted, we will read that the mythical worldview is articulated in the Qur'an in such a way that this Qur'anic mythical worldview constitutes the cultural foundation and ethnic language of Hafez! What, then, becomes of speaking Dari and his collection of ghazals composed in the Dari language?

Only one is aware of Hafez's heart-captivating poetry

Who knows the grace of temperament and the art of speaking Dari

All this grace, beauty, allusion, and enchanting expression operates through the medium of this language, not the Arabic language of the Qur'an; how, fundamentally, could the Qur'an be Hafez's ethnic myth? Myth dwells at the heart of language. On page 43 it is stated: "With this religion, another myth was added to the myth of the Fall, namely the myth of God's descent into the body of Christ for the salvation of humanity." He persists in his error regarding the relation between religion and myth, calling the religion brought by Christ a myth—and "another myth" at that—oblivious to the fact that myths are created across millennia during the emergence and formation of oral civilisations, not through the utterance of a single individual. An individual such as Homer or Ferdowsi can collect myths, but cannot invent a myth. On page 46 the author quotes Eliade to the effect that:

"...whereas myth is an account of the phenomena and events of the beginning of the world which, in the minds of its believers, expresses the foundation and direction of all things..."

From this apt and accurate statement, one cannot conclude that every discourse containing an account of the phenomena and events of the world's beginning is therefore a myth.

Myths, like sedimentary mountains in the depths of the oceans, have taken shape particle by particle and are the product of millennia and centuries of human life and experience.

Giants, dragons, and Simurghs bear traces of prehistoric animals. They inhabit the poems, parables, proverbs, popular dialects, art, and artistic works of each and every forebear. Had we recognised myth, its profound richness, the role of oral culture prior to the era of written civilisation, and their mutual interplay with culture and language, we would not have succumbed to so colossal a mistake as to confuse the so-called heavenly scriptures with myths, or to define myth outside the bounds of ethnic culture and language. In an extensive article, I have set out the role of mythical knowledge in the poetry of Hafez (3).

On page 50 of the book we read: "In the endeavour made by mystics to interpret myth esoterically, they ultimately transform the pictorial and narrative language of myth more or less into a conceptual and symbolic language that imparts a more or less logical order to myth and renders its fundamental groundlessness somewhat reasoned; and in the Islamic world they accomplished this by discovering an inward realm of meaning over against the outward meaning of the Qur'anic verses. From this relative rationalisation of myth and scripture emerges a meaning which—for instance, in the account of the creation of the world and of Islam, for whose existence there is no reason other than the attachment of the eternal will to this matter—

with the introduction of esoteric interpretation for it, namely the desire for the manifestation of eternal beauty, introduces a logic of creation that, especially in the case of the human being, renders his existential necessity justifiable in relation to that desire for manifestation.

Yet this gaze behind the scenes and this effort to uncover the hidden logic of existence suddenly turns into the discovery of a cipher of the 'world of mysteries' and the 'mysteries of the world', setting in motion a long caravan of saints, shaykhs, and spiritual poles (*aqtāb*), all of whom consider themselves favoured by the Unseen world and possessors of the cipher to those mysteries."

In any case, the endeavour to which Mr Ashouri refers is in truth the endeavour employed by mystics to attain the authentic myth of their own people, not the Qur'anic narrative of creation; for that very reason, they are compelled to posit an inward meaning over against the outward meaning, because Iranian myth does not harmonise with the Qur'an. And because the Unseen world resides within every human being (unlike the manner in which it exists in Islam, where there is only one path to the Unseen world, namely the Prophet—and hence the Sufi *tariqah*), we arrive at that long caravan. For in Illuminationist mysticism ("You, you are the copy of the divine treasure"), or to put it another way, mythical knowledge lies within you and stems from your ethnic and linguistic culture, and it is thus that every human being can stand in relation to such a realm. And it is for this very reason that the author grows agitated and lashes out at all independent thinkers who understand the authority of the Unseen differently; page 51: "...that initial endeavour to render myth intelligible by bestowing an esoteric meaning upon it meets with failure because the mythical account fundamentally lacks a rational framework and does not originate in human reason, but rather reaches humanity from the authority of the Unseen and on the basis of absolute divine authority..." That the mythical account does not originate in reason is a valid statement; however, that it comes from the authority of the Unseen is a grand discovery by the researcher—one which, had the thinkers of the past two centuries who investigated the foundational science of myth, language, and ethnic culture heard this claim, would have made them shudder. Either Greek, Indian, Babylonian, Iranian, Celtic, and other myths are not myths, or if they are myths, the source of these myths too is that very Unseen—and what creativity this absolute divine authority has displayed in fabricating all these diverse myths! It would have been better had we contented ourselves with studying the Qur'an in the manner of theological seminaries rather than pointlessly grafting myth onto the Qur'an. A few lines further down we encounter a new difficulty: "Many of the contradictions and inconsistencies in Hafez's ontology likewise go back to these ambiguities in the tradition of the esoteric interpretation of myth, which is an untieable knot. The mythical world, in its simple narrative, is nothing other than the background of the empirical world." These inconsistencies and ambiguities exist because you, like others, began your research with a presupposition, and since you cannot easily sustain your presupposition, you propose a novel definition of myth whereby, on the one hand, it is nothing other than the background of the empirical world, and on the other hand, myths have arrived in sacred scriptures and from the Unseen. You yourself cite the theories of Eliade and Jung and the significance of myths in human culture and language. Yes, myths reach far beyond "the background of the empirical world" and dwell, in a certain sense, within the very fabric of language and culture. Further on, page 53 states:

"The hermeneutic re-reading of the Qur'an in search of the hidden logic of the myth of creation in the third and fourth centuries AH all at once transformed—and even turned upside down—the perspective on the relations among God, the world, and humanity as it appeared in the ascetic conception. And from within the dualistic perspective of the ascetic worldview emerged a cosmovision in which God, instead of dwelling on the celestial Throne, makes His home in this very earthly world within the heart of the most trembling creature in the universe for Him, namely the human being; and the vast gulf that stood between God and humanity in the earliest account of the creation myth in Christianity and Judaism gives way to a union between Creator and creature—and the thread of all mystical-amorous thought leading down to Hafez lies right here." The author finally turns—while recalling the creation myth in Judaism, which is more or less identical to the Qur'anic account of creation—yet he does not tell us why God suddenly descends from the celestial Throne to the earthly world, nor why in the third and fourth centuries AH the concept of love returns to the mystical-poetic outlook. Had this been a matter of influence from Greek philosophy, Illuminationist mysticism ought to have emerged from Andalusia and the Near East, which were closer to and had earlier access to Greek texts, rather than from the soil of Khurasan, the cradle of the Dari language. Two centuries after the Arab invasion of Iran, Iranian myths are still alive in the thoughts, speech, and daily lives of the people, such that Daqiqi and Ferdowsi fashion masterpieces out of them. At this very same time, Shaykh al-Ishraq Suhrawardi explicitly writes in his works that he studied Zoroastrian texts. Daqiqi openly calls himself a Zoroastrian, and Ferdowsi begins the legends of creation with Jamshid, not with Adam and Eve.

Further on, page 69 states: "As we said in the introduction to this book, the principal source of Hafez's ontology must be sought in the books written in prose concerning mystical theories and hermeneutic ontology." Here too, an error is committed both in methodology and in scholarly execution. It is possible to find similarities to some of Hafez's verses in several works predating Hafez; yet it must be understood, first, that others before Mr Ashouri have already said this, and it is an old project aimed at reducing everything back to Islam; and second, for the ontology of someone like Hafez, one must read Hafez and adduce parallels from others, rather than starting from the works of others, adducing Hafez as corroboration, and relegating Hafez's poetry to footnotes. Such an enterprise cannot be called "the ontology of Hafez". In reality, this research is the verification of the scholar's erroneous initial presupposition, founded upon a flawed grasp of the concepts of myth and archetype. We leave judgement to the readers regarding this hunt for correspondences between two prose works—Maybudi's *Kashf al-Asrar* and Najm al-Din Razi's *Mirsad al-Ibad*—and Hafez's poetry, where time and again, solely on the basis of verbal similarities between the texts of those two books and various poems of Hafez, the author strives to reach his predetermined conclusion. We cite only a single example (page 78): "...that with the foot of ascetic discipline and the footwear of reproach (*malāmat*), you must journey to the horizons of poverty (*faqr*)." From the two phrases "reproach" and "horizons of poverty" in the prose of *Kashf al-Asrar*, the author cites in a footnote the following lines from Hafez:

My heart and faith are gone, and the Beloved has risen in reproach

Against us many a bow of reproach have they drawn

Do not reproach me, the drunkard, for my black ledger of deeds

Grant me, O God, the fortune of poverty

In the garb of poverty I perform the work of people of fortune

If they bestow upon you the sovereignty of poverty, O heart

In a station where primacy is conferred upon the poor

Let us reflect more closely: what connection do we find between the verses above and that prose sentence from *Kashf al-Asrar*? In two sections of *The Ontology of Hafez* entitled "The Mystical Drama: 'The Destiny and Chronicle of the Soul'" and "In Eternity Without Beginning", following what has preceded and on the basis of the same preconceived view, Ashouri attempts to present his claims summarily and directly to us without relying on prior presuppositions of Hafez's ontology. Then, in the section "Adam Confronting the Angel" (*Ādam dar barābar-e malak*), he writes (page 174): "In reality, Adam confronting the angel is none other than Hafez confronting the ascetic (*zāhed*)." And as he gradually runs into interpretive and conceptual difficulties within his prefabricated apparatus, he writes: "Of course, it is difficult, amid Hafez's roguish (*rendāneh*) play with language and the twists and turns he gives to his concepts in order to conceal his ultimate intent, to extract certain things explicitly from his verses; yet within this symbolic and playful language he leaves open the possibility of two or more interpretations, and therefore in his allusions to the ascetic and the Sufi one may well also find an allusion to the angel." First we read that Hafez conceals his ultimate intent, without knowing why! If Hafez's speech, discourse, and intent are identical to the words of Maybudi in *Kashf al-Asrar* and Najm al-Din Razi in *Mirsad al-Ibad*, what need is there for secrecy? If Hafez's ontology is merely a continuation of the mysticism of the Khurasan school—not a single one of whose mystics was ever sent to the gallows or subjected to candle-torture—why would Hafez have had to refrain from openly aligning himself with them?

From the beginning of the book to its end, the author repeatedly reiterates the same mystical interpretation of the myth of Adam's Fall, without any doubt entering his mind, without asking himself that one must also respond to the ontological presuppositions of other Hafez scholars, and without hesitating for a moment to consider that Hafez's foundational terms—such as *pīr-e moghān* [the Magian Elder], *eshq* [love], *rend* [the inspired rogue], *meykhāneh* [the tavern], *mey* [wine], *kharābāt* [the ruin/tavern], *kū-ye dūst* [the lane of the Beloved], and *sāqī* [the cupbearer]—are fundamentally not Qur'anic. And why, fundamentally, would Hafez have needed to employ such "roguish play and labyrinthine language in order to conceal his ultimate intent" merely to interpret and comment upon the Qur'an?

In defining *rendī* [roguish libertinism / free-spiritedness], the author writes: "*Rendī* is that domain of free-spiritedness and free thought which, within a religious culture, can be attained through the esoteric interpretation of scripture and of life." On page 224 we read: "It is here that his 'wine' (*mey*) also displays its two-facedness. This wine too possesses an eternal archetype in which, in the primordial tavern, Adam's clay was kneaded with it and a draught of it was given him to drink so that he might become human." Let us recall that in the opening sections of the book, the author ridicules all those who in any way strive to seek other meanings in the vocabulary of Hafez's poetry (page 15): "The use of wine, tavern, Magian, elder, *kharābāt*, and things of this sort in the earlier tradition of our Sufi poetry is a mechanical affair"—and yet in the end he resorts to this very practice himself. On page 230 it states: "With the emergence of the hermeneutic perspective toward the myth of the Fall and the discovery of its inward meaning by the mystics on the basis of certain verses of the Qur'an... all at once the perspective toward God and humanity is turned upside down and gives way to a monistic view in which the spiritual world and the corporeal world are interwoven, and God is Being itself, and Being is one, manifested in all its appearances." Two perspectives: one ascetic—a moral conception of existence, of absolute good and evil, in which God is a punitive judge and the world is divided into two realms, the pure spiritual world and the defiled corporeal world; and the other, in Ashouri's words: "an aesthetic conception of existence in which good and evil mingle together, and the arid, mechanical world of good and evil gives way to a living, dynamic, and beautiful world in the radiance of the Soul of the World; the universe is flooded with light, the *kharābāt* of the Magians becomes the locus of manifestation of the 'Light of God', and the beauties of nature appear as the manifestation of eternal beauty."

Comparing these two perspectives, the author writes: "The passage from the arid, terrifying moral outlook of the scowling ascetic to the delicate, beauty-beholding outlook of the intoxicated poet-lover entails the overturning of all relations of everything, especially the relation between humanity and God, which transforms from the relation of worshipper and Worshipped (*ābed o ma'būd*) into the relation of lover and Beloved (*āsheq o ma'shūq*)." Compare them: these two perspectives differ fundamentally from one another. In the second type of relation, "the relation of lover and Beloved" and the God of Light cannot fundamentally be Qur'anic. Therefore, this second perspective has its roots elsewhere, and it is largely out of fear—as a protective covering for thought—that this relation has been grafted onto the Qur'an. For in the Islamic worldview, the relation is that of servant (*bandeh*) to Allah and worshipper to the Worshipped, and in not a single verse of the Qur'an is the human being defined, enjoined, or even referred to as "lover of Allah" (*āsheq-Allāh*). These concepts and expressions—the overturning of relations, the relativity of good and evil, and the light of love—must have their roots somewhere other than the Qur'an. Where is that place? How can one overlook so many conceptual, institutional, and semiotic connections between the mythical knowledge of pre-Islamic Iranians and the world of Hafez? How can one be unaware, to this degree, even of the theoretical foundations of the role of symbols and signs? How can one fail to see all the pressure that, from the very onset of the spread of Islam down to the present day, has found expression in diverse forms—in the outward eruption of the institutions, symbols, and signs of pre-Islamic culture in carpet motifs and floral designs, in tales and proverbs, in architecture, poetry, and literature, in beliefs, historical movements, and uprisings, and in the creation and founding of mysticism—and instead reduce everything back once again to that same Qur'an?

On page 232 we read: "It appears that with Hafez we stand at the end of this path and the perfection of this culture, and it is with him that the 'culture of *rendī*' becomes an essential and inseparable part of Iranian culture." In reality, because Hafez at the summit undertakes a re-polishing of the living Iranian culture, this illumination is brought to completion with him, and from then onwards Iranian culture, emerging from beneath the crust of several centuries of pressure, rediscovers the sprout of its ancient culture—which is precisely an amorous, compassionate, loving, and luminous gaze upon the world.

Sweeter than the sound of the word of love I have seen no

Keepsake that might remain within this revolving dome

On page 243 we read: "In any event, the system of hermeneutic thought—albeit unconsciously and consciously—seeks to impart a logical and intelligible order to myth, and humanises God and deifies humanity to such a degree that ultimately it beholds God within itself and itself within God, and the tongue of ecstatic utterance (*shath*) is loosened." If the definition of "unconscious" in Ashouri's statement is the "unconscious" of psychoanalysis, the brainchild of Sigmund Freud, then fundamentally the unconscious cannot make an effort to understand myth. The unconscious has its own logic, structure, and distinctive mode of functioning, in which the notion of comprehension within the structure of consciousness has no place. The unconscious is the manner in which the acoustic images of words relate to one another, nothing else, and it bears no relation to the id (10). Rather, it is myth that, during the era of oral culture, constructs the logic and structure of human comprehension, not the reverse; and it is for this very reason that through a meticulous understanding and examination of myths and the words employed within them, we gain access to the mode of perception of various peoples—even prior to the attainment of script and writing—and learn how popular and human culture exerts its influence in ethnic form across different languages and dialects.

On page 253 we read: "In any case, by living according to the creed and way (*madhhab o mashrab*) of *rendī*, Hafez attained among all mystical poets an individuality that perhaps none other attained, and for that very reason understanding him is more difficult than all others." Here *mashrab* [temperament/way], *madhhab* [creed/sect], and mysticism are placed side by side in a single row. If Hafez is a mystic and belongs to the creed or way of *rendī*, why does he attain individuality? What is the agent of this individuality? With the definition the author gives of *rend* a few lines above, our difficulty deepens: "In any event, *rendī*—whether in its unseemly sense of fraud, dissoluteness, trickery, and... swindling, or in its lofty spiritual sense—is an inseparable part of Iranian culture, and it is this very *rendī* that loosens our social bond..." Although the meaning of the final sentence is unclear, on the one hand the author nevertheless concedes that Hafez—who begins with the mystical interpretation of the Qur'an and advances to the way of *rendī*, a school that is "an inseparable part of Iranian culture"—draws his roots from Iranian culture. Perhaps it would have been better had the author begun his book with that very section on the school of *rendī*, sparing us all his fruitless effort to attach Hafez to Islam and the Qur'an. It is as though, at the end of the book, he regrets what he has done and distances himself slightly from dragging Hafez down into footnotes under the influence of *Mirsad al-Ibad* and the like, writing (page 260): "Yet the most difficult of all is Hafez, whose Divan one must perforce—with a thousand forced exertions and with the help of those couplets of his that carry a scent of asceticism, worship, and Qur'an-recitation—interpret in such a way that it fits neatly into the theoretical apparatus of Sufism; and in this they have indeed succeeded, going so far as to regard every couplet of Hafez as a translation into metaphorical and symbolic Sufi language of a Qur'anic verse or a Hadith." It is as though the author has forgotten that he himself inflicted this very same treatment upon Hafez's poems, to the point of hunting for verbal correspondences between couplet after couplet of Hafez and the prose of those two aforementioned books, devoting over a hundred pages of his book to this task. And as we approach the end of the text, the researcher drifts away from his initial hypotheses (page 276): "Hafez's poetry is reflective in a special sense: that is, a bold rethinking of the entire heritage of mythical thought and esoteric interpretation, carrying it to the utmost limit of its internal logic. In this sense, he is not only the last great poet, but also the last great thinker of this tradition; and if he expresses his thoughts in the mould of poetry, imagery, symbol, and poetic allusions, it is because his thought is poetic-mythical—and for this very reason he fills the entire space of Iranian culture after him."

This conclusion is entirely sound, on the condition that myth be understood in its true sense—and for the Persian language, that means Iranian myths. Because Hafez is a distillation of the cultural movement of a people who have journeyed from afar and mingled with other cultures along the way, the dust of this long road settles upon the heart in his poetry. If Hafez is Hafez, he participates in a cultural totality—a totality rooted in every word, the function of that word, and the relation of those words to one another.

That which Hafez, through immense effort, sets before us under the name of the path and way of love, over against two other paths: the madrasa, book-learning, reason, and the ledger on the one hand, and ascetic mortification, foolish imitation, and blind conformity on the other.

In the closing pages of Mr Ashouri's text, it appears thus (page 282): "If reaching the secret of this universe is possible neither through asceticism and mortification nor through reason and argumentation, but rather through an awakened soul and an aware heart surrendered to the beauty of the Beloved and His contemplative guidance." What distant or close, direct or indirect connection does this awakened soul have with the Qur'an and with the representatives and believers of this book across more than fourteen centuries? How good it would have been had we listened a little to these very people of the aware heart:

Love will come to your rescue even if, like Hafez,

You recite the Qur'an by heart in fourteen variant readings

If we turn to the subsequent pages, we will read:

On page 299, the author transcribes a passage from Nasrollah Pourjavady's book *Bū-ye Jān* [The Fragrance of the Soul] and shows how he has fallen into the trap:

"The shortcoming we wish to explain here stems from the neglect by historians of Islamic philosophy and wisdom (*hikmat*) of a wisdom that Iranian thinkers, inspired by the Glorious Word of God, composed in the Persian language. A wisdom neglected in histories of Islamic philosophy and wisdom is a wisdom of mystical tasting (*hikmat-e dhawqī*) which Iranian shaykhs, in accordance with their own understanding and spiritual taste, adapted from the Qur'an and articulated its themes exclusively in Persian, particularly in their poetry."

It was Iranian shaykhs who, exclusively in the Persian language and in their poetry, articulated a "wisdom of mystical tasting" that is distinctive and singular—and the author insists emphatically that all of this was adapted from the Qur'an! How could one speak otherwise, how could one so lock the great doors of reason and argumentation with antiquated prejudices that, in the face of such patent evidence, one keeps repeating in another guise the very claims that for several centuries have revolved history, writings, and knowledge around the Qur'an? This passage may be placed alongside a passage by Morteza Motahhari in the book *Erfān-e Hāfez* [The Mysticism of Hafez] (page 20): "So far as I have studied, no evidence has come to light that Hafez belonged to the order of Sufis, and indeed the indications are to the contrary... It is evident that his spiritual mentor was not of the type of well-known Sufi shaykhs or from these famous Sufi lineages; and in general Shi'i Sufism enjoys this distinction over Sunni Sufism that it was less entangled in these lineages and formalities" (6). Sometimes Hafez was a Shi'i! Sometimes Hafez followed the Shafi'i legal school, and Shafi'is were mostly Ash'arite in theology! (7) Sometimes "Hafez's ghazals are watered by the pure, limpid spring of the thoughts of Zoroaster, the prophet of ancient Iran, and the Magian Elder (*pīr-e moghān*) in Hafez's poetry is none other than Asho Zarathustra" (8).

Sometimes Hafez is a disciple of Ibn Arabi: "Muhyi al-Din Arabi al-Ta'i al-Andalusi stirred up a mystical tumult in the Islamic world, stretching from Andalusia to Egypt, Syria, and India... Iraqi, Dawud Qaysari... Mowlavi Balkhi [Rumi], Mahmud Shabestari, Hafez, and Jami are all disciples of his school" (page 20, Morteza Motahhari) (6).

On page 301, the author delivers the coup de grâce to his own text and writes: "Thus, what we have termed 'the thought of Hafez' in this treatise is in truth more of a mindset (*dhehniyyat*) than a system of thought (*andīsheh*)..." Let us note that the subtitle of the book is *An Inquiry into the Foundations of Hafez's Thought*.

On page 305:

"The sorrow of love is but a single point, and how wondrous it is

That from every tongue I hear it, it is unrepeated"

"is the very same point heard from many tongues across the space of Islamic-Iranian civilisation."

What the author hears across the pages of the book is Islamic and Qur'anic; the Iranian dimension of "Hafez" he either does not hear or does not speak.

Our endeavour is rather to make our cry heard through reviewing Ashouri's book: "Our knowledge of ourselves stands in need of a fundamental reconstruction so that we may once and for all be liberated from the heavy sediment of one-sidedness that has penetrated the depths of our worldview; and this becomes possible only when we adopt the grounds of scientific and scholarly knowledge—namely documentary evidence, dialectics, deep inquiry, and reasoned demonstration—and refrain from hasty and premature learning. By way of example, consult the bibliographic sources cited in Mr Ashouri's text, which rely predominantly upon encyclopaedias, whereas for profound knowledge and deep understanding one must labour far more than this."

==============================================

Sources and Notes:

1. Ashouri, Dariush: *Hastī-shenāsī-ye Hāfez* [The Ontology of Hafez] or *Kāvoshi dar bonyādhā-ye andīsheh-ye ū* [An Inquiry into the Foundations of His Thought], Tehran, Nashr-e Markaz, 1377 SH [1998].

2. Consult the collected works of Jacques Lacan, French psychoanalyst and psychiatrist, in particular his Seminars I to XXIII.

3. *Rāz-e Hāfez, Hāfez-e Rāz* [The Secret of Hafez, the Keeper of the Secret]: Hassan Makaremi, Hamayesh-e Shenakht-e Farhang-e Iran Publications, Germany, Hamburg, 1998.

4. Written by Henry Corbin, French Iranologist; this book was translated by Mr Dehshiri and published in 1358 SH [1979] in Tehran.

5. Abd al-Baqi, Muhammad Fu'ad: *Al-Mu'jam al-Mufahras li-Alfāz al-Qur'ān al-Karīm*, Dar al-Kutub al-Qariyah, 1364 SH [1985], pp. 191, 192, 193, collection of verses on the theme of love (*hubb*).

6. Motahhari, Morteza: *Erfān-e Hāfez* [The Mysticism of Hafez], Sadra Publications, 1368 SH [1989], Tehran.

7. Mashkur, Mohammad Javad: "Hāfez jabrī-madhhab ast" [Hafez Is a Predestinarian], *Vahid* journal, vol. 9, p. 555.

8. Vahidi, Hossein: *Pazhūheshī dar ārmān-e pārsāyī dar Īrān* [A Study on the Ideal of Piety in Iran].

9. Anvari, Hossein: *Yek qesseh bīsh nīst* [It Is Nothing More Than One Tale], 1368 SH [1989], Tehran.

10. Consult the articles by Mr Molalli in the journal *Dabīr*, issues 1 to 7.

11. *Īrān-e Fardā*, Tir 1375 SH [June–July 1996], "Tārīkh-sāzī barā-ye mellat-e bī-hāfezeh" [History-Making for a Nation Without Memory].

12. Mohammad Qaraguzlu: "Darāmadī bar chīstī-ye rāz-e bozorg-e Hāfez" [An Introduction to the Nature of the Great Secret of Hafez], *Hamshahri* newspaper.

* This text was published for the first time in *Aftab* journal, issue 42, Mordad 1379 SH [July–August 2000].

[TehranReview > Sélections > Un regard sur la mentalité des Iraniens 26 Aug 2013](http://tehranreview.net/articles/13409)

## [Source : BBC Persian](http://www.bbc.com/persian/blogs/2013/08/130817_blog_l44_nazeran_mental_iran.shtml)

https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/03/wsb_426x440_peinture-300706-017.jpg

Une meilleure connaissance de notre culture et de notre psyché, d'une part, et la vigilance collective de nous autres Iraniens, d'autre part, peuvent-elles renforcer nos dispositions constructives et servir d'antidote à nos traits de caractère les moins heureux ?

Depuis les temps les plus anciens, des écrits d'Hérodote il y a vingt-cinq siècles aux divers orientalistes des cinq derniers siècles, des intellectuels de l'époque de la Révolution constitutionnelle tels qu'Akhoundzadeh et Talebof jusqu'à Djamalzadeh et Sadeq Hedayat, et jusqu'aux dernières décennies, de très nombreux ouvrages ont été publiés qui ont interrogé ce que nous sommes et notre manière d'être.

Bien des propos ont été tenus au sujet des particularités et des dispositions psychologiques de nous autres Iraniens ; jusqu'à quel point de tels discours sont-ils fondés ?

Certaines de ces appréciations sont les suivantes : les Iraniens n'ont pas de solidarité nationale ; les Iraniens se considèrent supérieurs aux autres nations ; les Iraniens sont portés sur le paraître, pratiquent le *ta'arof* et sont donc habitués au mensonge ; les Iraniens sont individualistes et n'ont pas l'esprit du travail collectif ; ils érigent en norme ce qui leur plaît à eux seuls ; les Iraniens envient la réussite d'autrui ; les Iraniens sont égocentriques ; les Iraniens se croient touche-à-tout et compétents en tout ; les Iraniens ne sont pas ponctuels ; bien que, sur le plan individuel, notamment à l'étranger, ils réussissent remarquablement, dès qu'il est question de travail d'équipe, ils s'y dérobent.

Des notions telles que l'honneur (*âberou*), le respect, l'honneur familial (*nâmous*) et le culte de cet honneur revêtent pour les Iraniens une importance singulière ; les Iraniens sont très intelligents, cultivés et créatifs ; les Iraniens sont extrêmement hospitaliers et chaleureux.

Les Iraniens sont patriotes et fiers de leur identité iranienne. D'un autre côté, on nous perçoit comme quelque peu mélancoliques, avec des penchants tournés vers le passé.

Ces traits de caractère ne concernent-ils que nous, Iraniens ? Sont-ils intrinsèquement mêlés à notre être ou sont-ils susceptibles de changer ? Nous vivons dans la culture de notre société, tel un poisson dans l'eau. Les générations se transmettent mutuellement leur héritage culturel.

Dans le même temps, chaque génération, sous l'influence des échanges avec d'autres cultures, des transformations environnementales et des progrès scientifiques et techniques, enrichit la culture de la génération précédente afin de la transmettre à celle qui lui succède.

Au sein de ces traditions, de ces croyances, de ces dispositions individuelles et collectives, nos traits de caractère se forgent également. C'est à travers trois facteurs — les potentialités avec lesquelles nous venons au monde, la famille et la culture — que nous devenons ce que nous sommes.

On peut dire que nos dispositions psychologiques d'Iraniens dépendent de manière structurale, indépendamment de la structure de notre psyché individuelle, de nos strates culturelles qui se sont sédimentées les unes sur les autres au fil des siècles, de nos conditions écologiques de vie et de nos grands systèmes de production.

Nous devons envisager l'articulation entre quatre strates culturelles (antérieure à l'islam, de l'islam à l'avènement du chiisme, de cette période jusqu'à la rencontre avec la culture occidentale, et de cette rencontre jusqu'à aujourd'hui), les influences environnementales (zones montagneuses, désertiques, humides, arides) et les macro-systèmes de production (agricole-rural, pastoral-nomade et urbain-industriel-tertiaire) comme les piliers structuraux de la société iranienne. Et nous devons examiner la relation entre traits de caractère et traditions dans ce cadre, en tenant compte de la diversité culturelle, linguistique et religieuse de la population.

Que signifie « structural » dans le champ de la psychologie ? La psyché humaine possède une structure complexe.

Lorsque les êtres humains entrent dans un groupe ou une collectivité, ils deviennent plus complexes encore ; lorsqu'ils s'inscrivent dans le cadre d'une culture, ils partagent une langue commune et cette culture remonte à des centaines d'années ; et, d'autre part, lorsque ces cultures se trouvent juxtaposées telle une mosaïque culturelle et qu'au fil de l'histoire ces cultures subissent des guerres, des occupations, des massacres et des invasions prolongées aux effets profonds, les réalités s'enchevêtrent et se complexifient à un point tel que, si nous voulons les étudier dans le menu détail, le fil nous échappe des mains.

Porter attention à la structure d'ensemble signifie que nous essayons d'observer — qu'il s'agisse de la psyché d'un individu, de la psyché culturelle d'une société ou d'un ensemble de cultures vivant côte à côte — sous un angle plus élevé, dans une portée plus vaste et au sein d'une totalité.

Le regard structural nous permet d'inscrire le sujet particulier qui nous intéresse dans une perspective plus large.

S'agissant d'une société, nous pouvons parler de mémoire historique, d'identité culturelle, de traditions et de coutumes, des mythes d'une société ou des fondements communs de l'existence et de la culture. Tout en étant généraux, ces éléments sont aussi tributaires du temps et de l'espace et se transforment au gré de divers événements.

Notre identité est, en vérité, notre identité culturelle même, et son indice majeur est la langue.

En fait, la démarche qui s'est amorcée avec Freud jusqu'à Jacques Lacan, sur la base des idées de Ferdinand de Saussure, montre que le langage, en tant que structure fondamentale et inaugurale, constitue jusqu'aux assises mêmes de la pensée humaine ; et lorsque cette culture dont l'indice est la langue s'accompagne de l'État, de la nation et de la culture avançant dans une même direction — c'est-à-dire lorsqu'il existe une société dotée d'une culture, d'une langue, d'un État et d'une nation —, cela engendre une identité nationale et culturelle définie, qu'il devient aisé de cerner comme socle et fondement.

La culture est l'ensemble des proverbes, des contes populaires, des recueils poétiques et des jeux traditionnels. Le regard structural repose toujours sur deux principes. Le premier est que nous devons situer chaque phénomène dans son arrière-plan historico-géographique.

Par exemple, considérer la culture du peuple iranien, dans toute la mesure du possible et selon nos connaissances, depuis au moins deux mille cinq cents ou trois mille ans ; c'est-à-dire l'appréhender dans son contexte historique, là où la diffusion de la langue persane et de la culture iranienne a exercé son influence et en a subi en retour.

Un autre aspect consiste à rechercher les assises fondamentales des phénomènes pour adopter une approche structurale. Par exemple, lorsque Darwin, Marx ou Freud nous ouvrent de nouveaux horizons, leur regard est structural.

Darwin embrasse l'ensemble de l'apparition de la vie à travers le monde entier et porte un regard structural. Marx procède de même : il observe l'ensemble de l'histoire. Freud, quant à lui, aborde l'étude de l'être humain à partir de l'anthropologie et de l'ethnographie, puis revient à *Totem et Tabou*. C'est parce qu'avec de tels savoirs, on ne peut opérer autrement que par une approche structurale.

Sur le plan culturel, nous avons une culture préislamique. Entre la présence de l'islam et le chiisme se situe une autre culture. Après l'avènement du chiisme apparaît une nouvelle culture, et avant notre rencontre avec la culture occidentale existait encore une autre culture.

Représentez-vous ces quatre mondes comme quatre strates. Nous pouvons également opérer une autre coupe transversale dans ces cultures : nous avons une culture à strates nomades, une culture à strates rurales et une culture à strates urbaines.

À titre d'exemple simple, à l'époque de Cyrus, vingt-cinq pour cent de notre population était nomade. En 1900 encore, 25 % de la population était nomade. Les nomades ont même atteint jusqu'à 50 %, et bien que la strate nomade ne représente aujourd'hui qu'environ 1 ou 2 %, cette strate demeure une composante importante de notre culture.

La strate rurale constitue une autre strate très importante de notre culture. L'urbanisation dans les petites villes représentait 25 % des strates en 1900 ; elle atteint aujourd'hui 70 %, ce qui forme un socle majeur et fondamental.

Si nous portons le regard d'un autre côté, nous avons une culture qui prévaut dans les régions désertiques. Ce n'est pas la même culture que celle qui règne dans les régions montagneuses, dans les zones à fortes précipitations ou dans les zones arides.

Par ailleurs, la culture est liée aux différentes langues et dialectes : comme au Kurdistan, au Lorestan, au Guilan et au Mazandéran. Toutes ces strates s'entremêlent et prennent une forme complexe.

À côté de tout cela, au cours des deux derniers siècles au moins, trois grands bouleversements ont ébranlé notre socle social. Le premier est l'avènement de la loi constitutionnelle en 1285 (1906) ; le second est la mutation des années 1342 à 1348 (1963-1969), qu'ils appelèrent eux-mêmes la « Révolution du Shah et du Peuple », au cours de laquelle le système de production rural et nomade — un système vieux de six cents ans — fut brisé en l'espace de six ans ; et le troisième est la confessionnalisation des fondements de l'État depuis 1357 (1979) jusqu'à nos jours.

Le regard structural consiste précisément à replacer tout ce que nous savons et entendons dire au sujet de ce peuple au sein de ces strates culturelles, en tenant compte de ces trois grands événements.

En conclusion, on peut affirmer que c'est la langue qui transporte avec elle toutes les catégories culturelles. La langue maternelle est semblable à un navire : c'est par son intermédiaire que des cultures sont transmises à chacun d'entre nous.

C'est pour cette raison que, même selon la définition qu'en donne la psychanalyse, la langue maternelle de la mère est considérée comme la langue maternelle : parce que c'est la mère qui apporte avec elle la culture, qu'elle a elle-même reçue de sa propre mère.

Nous voyons donc qu'il convient ici d'examiner avec prudence la relation entre les comportements et les agissements de chaque individu sur trois ou quatre générations et les transformations environnementales. Autrement dit, il est impossible que la culture d'une société change rapidement et aisément, et que les individus qui composent cette société se transforment tout aussi facilement sur le plan structural.

Version abrégée de l'article présenté lors du deuxième colloque des chercheurs iraniens en psychologie à l'étranger à Cologne, intitulé « Notre culture et notre psyché »

en.title: A Look at the Mentality of Iranians
en.executive_summary: TehranReview Curated A Look at the Mentality of Iranians 26 Aug 2013 Source: BBC Persian https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/03/wsb426x440peinture-300706-017.jpg Can a deeper familiarity with our own culture and psyche on the one hand, and the collective vigilance of us Iranians on the other, enhance…
en.body_markdown:
[TehranReview > Curated > A Look at the Mentality of Iranians 26 Aug 2013](http://tehranreview.net/articles/13409)

## [Source: BBC Persian](http://www.bbc.com/persian/blogs/2013/08/130817_blog_l44_nazeran_mental_iran.shtml)

https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/03/wsb_426x440_peinture-300706-017.jpg

Can a deeper familiarity with our own culture and psyche on the one hand, and the collective vigilance of us Iranians on the other, strengthen our constructive traits and serve as an antidote to our unfavourable dispositions?

From ancient times—in the writings of Herodotus twenty-five centuries ago, through various Orientalists of the past five centuries, to the intellectuals of the Constitutional Revolution era such as Akhundzadeh and Talebof, to Jamalzadeh and Sadeq Hedayat, and down to recent decades—numerous books have been published that have scrutinised our nature and character.

Much has been said regarding the characteristics and mentality of us Iranians; to what extent are such claims valid?

Several of these remarks run as follows: Iranians lack national solidarity; Iranians consider themselves superior to other nations; Iranians are fond of outward show, practise *ta'arof*, and are therefore accustomed to lying; Iranians are individualistic and lack the spirit of collective work, treating whatever pleases them personally as the standard; Iranians are envious of the success of others; Iranians are self-centred; Iranians act as though they are masters of every trade; Iranians are not punctual; although individually, especially abroad, they are successful people, as soon as group work is mentioned, they flee from it.

Matters such as personal dignity (*aberu*), respect, family honour (*namus*), and the veneration of honour hold special importance for Iranians; Iranians are highly intelligent, cultured, and creative; Iranians are exceedingly hospitable and warm-hearted.

Iranians are patriotic and take pride in being Iranian. On the other hand, we are perceived as somewhat melancholic, with tendencies inclined towards the past.

Do these dispositions apply solely to us Iranians? Are these traits ingrained in us, or are they susceptible to change? We live within the culture of our society, like fish in water. Generations transmit their cultural burden to one another.

At the same time, each generation, under the influence of contact with other cultures, environmental changes, and scientific and technical advances, enriches the culture of the preceding generation before passing it on to the next.

Amidst these traditions, beliefs, and individual and group temperaments, our dispositions are also shaped. It is through three factors—the potentialities we bring with us into the world, the family, and culture—that we become who we are.

It may be said that the dispositions of us Iranians depend structurally—distinct from the structure of our individual psyche—upon our cultural strata accumulated one atop another over the centuries, upon our ecological living conditions, and upon our macro-systems of production.

We must regard the interconnection among four cultural strata (pre-Islamic, from Islam to the emergence of Shiism, from that era to the encounter with Western culture, and from that encounter to the present day), environmental influences (mountainous, desert, humid, arid), and macro-systems of production (agricultural–rural, pastoral–nomadic, and urban–industrial–service) as the structural pillars of Iranian society. And we must examine the relationship between dispositions and traditions within this framework, taking into account the cultural, linguistic, and religious diversity of the people.

What does "structural" mean in the field of psychology? The human psyche possesses a complex structure.

When human beings enter a group or collectivity, they become even more complex; when they exist within a shared culture, they possess a common language and that culture stretches back hundreds of years; and, moreover, when these cultures sit side by side like a cultural mosaic and, throughout history, undergo war, occupation, massacres, and prolonged invasions with profound consequences, matters become so entangled and complex that if we attempt to examine them in piecemeal detail, the thread slips from our hands.

Attending to the overall structure means that we strive to view—whether the psyche of an individual, the cultural psyche of a society, or a constellation of cultures living side by side—from a higher vantage point, across a broader scope, and within a totality.

A structural perspective enables us to see the particular subject under consideration within a wider horizon.

In relation to a society, we can speak of historical memory, cultural identity, traditions and customs, a society's myths, or the shared foundations of life and culture. While these are general, they are also subject to time and place and alter in response to different events.

Our identity is, in truth, none other than our cultural identity, and its principal marker is language.

Indeed, the work begun by Freud and carried through to Jacques Lacan, building upon the ideas of Ferdinand de Saussure, demonstrates that language, as a fundamental and foundational structure, forms even the very basis of human thought; and when this culture whose marker is language is accompanied by the state, the nation, and culture moving along a single path—that is, a society possessing one culture, one language, one state and nation—this produces a distinct national-cultural identity that can readily be defined as a foundation and bedrock.

Culture is the sum of proverbs, folk tales, collections of poetry, and popular games. A structural perspective always rests upon two principles. First, that we must view every phenomenon within its historical-geographical background.

For example, viewing the culture of the people of Iran, as far as is possible and known to us, over at least two thousand five hundred to three thousand years; that is, viewing it in its historical context, as far as the spread of the Persian language and Iranian culture has exerted influence and been influenced in turn.

Another aspect is to seek out the foundational underpinnings of phenomena in order to achieve a structural perspective. For instance, when Darwin, Marx, or Freud open new vistas before us, their perspective is structural.

Darwin looks at the entire emergence of life across the whole world and does so structurally. Marx does likewise: he looks at the entirety of history. Freud, too, begins his examination of the human being from anthropology and ethnography and then turns back to *Totem and Taboo*. This is because with such knowledge, nothing can be accomplished except through a structural perspective.

Culturally, we have a pre-Islamic culture. Between the arrival of Islam and Shiism there is another culture. Following Shiism there is yet another culture, and prior to our encounter with Western culture, another culture existed.

Picture these four worlds as four strata. We can also make another cross-section through these cultures: we have a culture with nomadic strata, a culture with rural strata, and a culture with urban strata.

As a simple illustration, in the time of Cyrus, twenty-five per cent of our people were nomads. In 1900 as well, 25 per cent of the people were nomads. Nomads even reached up to 50 per cent, and although the nomadic stratum today stands at 1 or 2 per cent, this stratum remains an important layer of our culture.

The rural stratum is another highly significant layer of our culture. Urbanisation in small towns accounted for 25 per cent of the strata in 1900; today it has reached 70 per cent, and this constitutes a very major and fundamental pillar.

If we look from another angle, we have a culture that prevails in desert regions. This is not the same culture that prevails in mountainous regions, regions with abundant rainfall, or regions with scarce rainfall.

Furthermore, culture depends upon diverse languages and dialects, such as in Kurdistan, Lorestan, Gilan, and Mazandaran. All of these strata merge into one another and assume a complex form.

Alongside all this, over at least the past two centuries, three major upheavals have disrupted our social foundation. One is the emergence of constitutional law in 1285 (1906); another is the transformation of the years 1342 to 1348 (1963–1969), which they themselves named the "White Revolution" (Revolution of the Shah and the People), during which the rural–nomadic system of production—a six-hundred-year-old system—was shattered in the span of six years; and the third is the religious restructuring of the foundations of the state from 1357 (1979) to the present.

A structural perspective means situating everything we know and hear about this people within those cultural strata while taking these three major upheavals into account.

Finally, it may be said that it is language that carries with it all cultural categories. The mother tongue is like a vessel: through it, cultures are transmitted to each one of us.

For this very reason, even according to the definition used in psychoanalysis, the mother's mother tongue is considered the mother tongue—because it is the mother who brings the culture with her, having herself received it from her own mother.

We thus see that here we must examine with circumspection the relationship between the conduct and behaviour of each human being across three or four generations and environmental changes. That is to say, it is impossible for a society's culture to change quickly and easily, and equally impossible for the individuals of that society to change structurally with such ease.

Abridged text of the paper presented at the Second Conference of Iranian Psychological Researchers Abroad in Cologne, titled *Our Culture and Our Psyche*

fr.title: Proposition concernant le projet de sondage du site Melli-Mazhabi
fr.executive_summary: https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/03/DSC04130.jpg Portons un regard plus attentif sur les questions posées par le site Melli-Mazhabi aux acteurs politiques et lisons ensemble les interrogations fondamentales / Posons les questions sous un autre angle et réorientons-les ainsi… Dans les circonstances actuelles,…
fr.body_markdown:
https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/03/DSC04130.jpg
Portons un regard plus attentif sur les questions posées par le site Melli-Mazhabi aux acteurs politiques et lisons ensemble les interrogations fondamentales / Posons les questions sous un autre angle et réorientons-les ainsi…

Dans les circonstances actuelles, il existe sans nul doute suffisamment de signes abondants pour amener tous ceux qui aspirent passionnément à la dignité, à la prospérité, à la liberté et à l'indépendance du peuple iranien à réfléchir sérieusement aux moyens de sauver l'Iran du péril présent. Plus que jamais, au niveau des penseurs et des acteurs politiques à l'intérieur comme à l'extérieur du pays, nous assistons à la publication d'articles, d'entretiens, de débats et de colloques dont l'axe central est cette même préoccupation légitime. En dernière analyse, chacun de ces efforts repose sur la position, le point de départ et la vision de ses auteurs. On peut schématiquement classer ces orientations de la manière suivante :

- Ceux qui cherchent à obtenir une réponse à la question de savoir comment nous en sommes arrivés là, quelles ont été nos erreurs, et comment les conditions régionales et mondiales y ont pris part ?

- Ceux qui se contentent d'examiner et d'analyser la situation présente et jouent surtout le rôle d'analystes politiques.

- Ceux qui s'efforcent de trouver un remède et cherchent une issue à l'impasse dangereuse actuelle.

Il ne fait aucun doute qu'une de ces démarches, ou toutes ensemble et leur interaction réciproque, finira par ouvrir une voie de passage. Toutefois, dans une situation aussi critique, on peut s'attendre à ce que nous orientions nos forces vers le cœur même du problème : c'est à la fois plus fécond et, dès lors que nous réfléchissons tous au fondement du mal et de son remède, cela accroît nos chances de parvenir à une convergence de vues.

Ce bref rappel a pour objet d'orienter l'angle de nos questions davantage vers l'effort d'action que vers la seule analyse. Portons un regard plus attentif sur les questions posées par le site Melli-Mazhabi aux acteurs politiques et lisons ensemble les interrogations fondamentales :

« Site Melli-Mazhabi : Où mènera l'avenir du conflit nucléaire de l'Iran : fermeté de l'Iran, poursuite des sanctions et marche vers la guerre ? Recul de l'Iran et acceptation des conditions de l'Occident ? Jeu gagnant-gagnant au bénéfice des parties au conflit ? Victoire de l'Iran et acceptation d'un Iran nucléaire par l'Occident ? Et… »

Dans ces questions, les parties au conflit sont conçues comme étant l'Iran et l'Occident, et l'axe du conflit comme portant sur les activités nucléaires de l'Iran, les sanctions et, en fin de compte, le déclenchement d'une guerre entre les parties. Plusieurs présupposés sous-tendent la formulation de ces questions, sur lesquels il est peut-être possible de revenir :

- Que désigne-t-on par « l'Iran » dans ces questions ? Le gouvernement de la République islamique d'Iran ? Le peuple iranien ? Le pouvoir de la République islamique, et en particulier la personne du Guide suprême, qui souligne lui-même être le décideur principal, ultime et unique en la matière ?

- Que désigne-t-on par « l'Occident » ? Les États-Unis et leurs alliés ? Israël et ses alliés ? Des forces plus modérées telles que l'Europe ?

- Dans ce soi-disant conflit, les autres pays, l'Organisation des Nations unies ou l'opinion publique mondiale n'ont-ils aucun rôle ?

La nature même de ces questions nous fait passer de la position d'opposants au pouvoir de l'État de la République islamique et d'amis du peuple iranien à celle de journalistes, d'analystes politiques et, en définitive, de spectateurs d'un match de football qui ne s'attribuent d'autre rôle que de crier, d'applaudir ou de commenter.

Posons les questions sous un autre angle et réorientons-les ainsi : dans les circonstances actuelles, quel est notre rôle dans la défense des intérêts à long terme, à moyen terme et à court terme du peuple iranien ? Comment peut-on intervenir dans les échanges et les équations économiques et politiques actuels afin que le peuple iranien en tire le plus grand bénéfice ? À l'évidence, les réponses à ces interrogations passent par d'autres questions qui transforment fondamentalement la classification et la manière même d'interroger.

Notre objectif stratégique est de parvenir à un Iran prospère, libre et indépendant, dont les habitants vivent en paix et en sécurité parmi les peuples du monde, dans le cadre de la Déclaration universelle des droits de l'homme.
