Full Implementation of the Constitution, Holding Free Elections, Demanding the Interpretation of the Constitution: All Three or None

Can the science–art of modern strategy be useful in charting Iran's future,

and if so, in what manner and who is capable of accomplishing this vital task?

He enjoys the fruit of life who, in every undertaking,

First reflects, and only then adopts its path.
(Hafez: Qasideh No. 3)

Foreword: The relative calm of recent months has afforded political actors the opportunity to deepen fundamental discussions concerning the nature and methods of the struggle both inside and outside Iran. Naturally, terms such as strategic direction, strategy, principal slogan, foundational duty, and short- and long-term objectives have once again returned to the forefront of writings and debates.

Beyond the well-known demands that preceded the elections, several new debates have also been added, which may be summarised very briefly as follows:

The principal slogan of all those affiliated with the post-election movement ought to be the demand for "holding free elections".

The principal slogan ought to centre "around changing the Constitution".

Or, fundamentally, if this very Constitution were implemented properly and in full, that would suffice.

What deeply calls for particular rigour regarding this literature, these exchanges, dialogues, and arguments is the misty atmosphere prevailing in the use of language, the mode of reasoning, and the application of the science–art of strategy. Clarifying definitions, insofar as possible, may help in some measure to open up the dialogue further.

We observe that all three slogans under discussion still have a long road ahead before ascending to the level of a strategic objective. They fall far short of the precision and coherence required to become universal and to rally everyone around their axis. These objectives have been put forward first, and only afterwards do we go searching for how they might be implemented in society. As we know, in a scientific process, not only do strategic objectives require measurable quantitative indicators for their implementation, but one must also proceed to translate them into operational objectives and operational plans, organise their progression, and at the very least test the practical feasibility of those plans.

Above all, the science–art of strategy rests upon innovation. Its ultimate endeavour is that the process of designing and executing strategic objectives should culminate in a form of management that we call "innovation management".

The full and complete implementation of the Constitution, the amendment and rewriting of the Constitution, or the holding of free elections is devoid of any form of "innovation", and ultimately reduces society's demands to a bare minimum that may gradually become odourless and colourless. Strategy must be so coherent, practical, precise, articulate, comprehensive, persistent, actionable, intelligible, and teachable that it becomes in itself an educational corpus for political cadres and the public.

Should the science–art of strategy be applied only after seizing power and solely for administering and guiding society? Or

can it also be employed in the struggle to attain power? Or, fundamentally, can these two intertwined categories even be separated from one another? Before entering into the discussion, let us review together several examples of theses recently completed at Iranian universities and what these documents indicate regarding the weakness of our understanding of the science–art of modern strategy.

First example: Thesis title: *The Mechanism of Elite Coalition and the Formulation of National Strategy in Post-Revolutionary Iran*:

By Parviz Dalirpour, University of Tehran, Faculty of Law and Political Science, Doctoral degree, year of graduation: 1384 [2005–2006]. In part of the abstract we read: The formulation of a national development strategy requires the highest degrees of cohesion among decision-makers and consensus among intellectual and instrumental elites on the definition of development and its components. This dissertation argues that the existence of conflicting worldviews and approaches among various socio-political currents in Iran is one of the factors behind the divergence in attitudes towards development and the blocking of the most vital stage of consensus over a national strategy. Social pluralities and the conflicting interests of social forces regarding entry into the process of development and broad consensual change constitute another major factor behind this lack of consensus. This is while Iranian history has shown that a state which casts itself as the agent of social change and advances with a specific definition of development without needing the consensus of major social forces faces the risk of instability. This is due to the diverse social structure and the danger of class displacements and the disruption of the existing equilibrium. In post-revolutionary development programmes, however, social change was not addressed as social transition and remained oriented towards preserving the status quo in the reciprocal relationship between state, economy, and society. Therefore, Iran's diverse social structure is itself one of the major obstacles to the lack of consensus and agreement over a national strategy. This issue demonstrates that Iran has not yet completed the process of transition towards a nation-state in the classical sense of the term.

Second example: Thesis title: *An Examination of the Structure of the Military Strategy of the Islamic Republic of Iran in the New International System: Priorities and Realities*, by Alireza Saeidabadi, Shahid Beheshti University, International Relations, Master's degree, 1379 [2000–2001]. In the abstract we read: Strategy in our country is an underdeveloped concept that remains predominantly monopolised by the military and does not enjoy an independent scholarly standing. Accordingly, in this thesis, an effort has been made, as far as possible free from political considerations, to study and analyse its functioning in Iran in light of the new conditions of the international system from the post-Cold War period to the present through a structural examination of its research dimensions—such that the structure of the domestic political system and the structure of the international system have been treated in the present study as two independent variables, each of which has exerted direct and indirect effects on the internal and external threats and opportunities of the political system of the Islamic Republic of Iran. Yet, nevertheless, consensus has never been reached on the issue of strategic planning at the national level, and the country's decision-making system continues to suffer from structural deficiencies... This constitutes one of the principal reasons for the mismatch between the internal and external threats and opportunities of the political system of the Islamic Republic of Iran and the quantitative and qualitative components of national power, which ultimately results in following action-and-reaction policies and remaining distant from a system of strategic planning at the national level.

Let us also note an example of the use of the word "strategy" in one of the Friday prayer sermons: "The strategy of the Islamic Republic over the past thirty-one years has been a strategy of resistance and steadfastness." *Rahbord* (strategy) has to do with *rah* (the path), and a path has to do with movement. How can resistance be a strategy?

Let us return to our initial question: can the modern science–art of strategy assist in charting Iran's future? And if so, by whom and how?

Let us briefly examine the contemporary definitions of these terms and the process of applying the modern science–art of strategy:

Definitions:

The word *stratège*, meaning military commander, comes from the Greek language and belongs to the vocabulary of war. In practice today, this term is used across all fields of military, administrative, industrial, service, and political management, non-profit organisations (at the national, regional, and international levels), the leadership of political movements and political parties, the preparation of long-term regional, national, and international programmes, the drafting of state budgets, and even research laboratories, educational institutions, and so forth.

— Across different management methodologies, both varied definitions of strategy and general methods for formulating it are offered. Nevertheless, in every case, several general and overarching characteristics exist in the preparation and formulation of a strategy for an operational entity:

Strategic objectives, strategic plans, and indicators for measuring the execution of these objectives.

It is from here that long-term planning is prepared following the precise definition of the three aforementioned factors. In practice, it is in the course of executing long-term programmes that applied plans are defined. Executing applied plans in the field of action requires clarifying tactics, and the overall line connecting tactics is what we call politics—politics, which is the very art of the possible. It is an art because it requires invention, and because it unfolds in the arena of reality, it is therefore the art of the possible.

Strategy is the "science–art" of making optimal use of available resources in attaining predetermined objectives. Hence, the specific and precise determination and definition of objectives is essential. Making use of resources requires knowing them and organising them.
Strategic objectives (*ahdaf-e rahbordi*), and identifying, discerning, and determining them in any field, is a task at once deceptively simple and exceedingly difficult, situated today on the frontier between science, art, and experience. Discerning strategic objectives requires both a precise knowledge of details across the diverse dimensions influencing the field of operation of those objectives, and an extraordinary capacity to free oneself from the snare of those details, to soar, to rise above, and to look ahead.

Formulating a strategic plan and attending to tactical stances bear a logical and structural relationship to strategy.

Strategic objectives must be definable, ambitious, actionable, and measurable.

In determining "definable objectives", we need to assess "needs". We must choose our words accurately and lucidly, and know well the language of society, our audiences, and our colleagues, in such a manner as to create the smallest possible gap between thought, speech, and deed. Words are the essential instruments for conveying our thought in defining and determining "strategic objectives". A prime example of this in the history of the past two centuries are the words "Constitutionalism" (*Mashrutiyat*) and "Republic" (*Jomhuri*) at the two major turning points of the Constitutional Revolution and the February [1979] Revolution.

Assessing needs demands depth of insight and foresight. Needs are undoubtedly assessed in an intimate relationship—whether direct or mediated—with the people. From this arises the necessity of knowing the human being, both individually and collectively. Knowing the human being lies in knowing their body and psyche. And it is here that familiarity with psychology and psychoanalysis comes to our aid. The science of sociology familiarises us further with the movement of peoples. History is the science of phenomena that have occurred—tracing, interpreting, and explaining them. Learning from how human societies have moved from times long past down to the present—their beliefs, desires, wishes, dreams, and imaginings—brings us closer to the human being.

Ambitious goals are the only path that delivers us from stagnation and turning endlessly in circles around ourselves. These goals guide us towards inquiry and innovation. They enable us to draw upon the utmost of our capacities and resources. They compel us into a healthy rivalry with the innate human need for progress and for deeper knowledge of oneself and of existence. These goals transform into a driving force, an agent of our growth and flourishing. Strategic goals must be translated into operational goals. Therefore, it is on the stage of reality, production, and construction—across the expanse of the family, the village, the city, the country, the region, and the world—that these goals can be put into action. The execution of these goals takes place in a specific time and place. The feasibility of implementing these goals within a bounded timeframe is a fundamental condition.

Implementing goals requires not only an executor and a designated time and place, but also instruments. These instruments can be divided into two major groups: technology and research capabilities on the one hand, and management and organisation on the other. In this regard, one may ask oneself whether generating electricity through nuclear technology can be an actionable strategic goal. After all, if the economic, social, and political capacities required for fundamental research or access to modern technology under balanced international relations do not exist, in the medium term we will face immense, irreparable catastrophes, or we will plunge the replacement, maintenance, and continued operation of the installations into fundamental crises. Can the strategic goals of a society be defined separately from the level of competence of its managers and the governability of its people?

Goals can be defined and implemented within a specific spatial domain. Precision in defining the sphere of application and execution of these goals will prevent any deviation or misinterpretation. A striking example of leaving the domain of application of goals distorted can easily be observed in Iran's second Constitution. The conflation and commingling of the two domains of *mellat* (nation) and *ommat* (religious community) is visible at the very core of the definition of this Constitution's goals, in its general principles and in its very fabric; and ultimately, these goals must be tangible and speak to the human soul and psyche. Progress towards them must be felt. They must allow us the possibility of review and revision. For these reasons, these goals must be measurable, so as to absolve us from subjectivism and idealism. From the very outset, one must have both a scale of measurement and instruments of measurement to gauge movement towards them. Strategy is, above all, attaching importance to the future. It is, in a sense, placing the future at the centre. Preparing oneself for the future. Setting goals and programmes for the future, for becoming, for being in the future. Yearning to attain one's aspirations, planning, drawing upon all of one's own and others' resources, knowledge, and art. At times, turning to forces beyond logic, because a better future is our need, our aspiration, and perhaps the very reason for our being. A fundamental study is required to illuminate more clearly the impact of religion on the need for foresight. One might say that perhaps our dreamed-of, paradisiacal utopia lies in another world. For religious believers, sketching an earthly future takes shape solely within the framework of permissible religious aspirations. The fundamental utterances were already brought by the prophets in the past. The future can neither unlock mysteries nor serve as an answer to a longing rising from the heart.

Possessing a strategic goal requires, above all, ambition, faith in human capability, and knowledge of oneself, others, one's surroundings, and history.

Let us return to the article by one of the proponents of the slogan "Free Elections":

We see how the term "strategy" and the "central slogan" have been merged together and how both have been distorted.

A question arising from the above examination that can deeply trouble us is this: do the regression, baseness, cultural poverty, mediocrity, and ignorance of a state and ruling power not gradually drag the opposition to that ruling power down into decline alongside it? Should one not always remain vigilant, and—even though in the field of action one must be present on the scene and act as the "opposition" to a ruling power—refrain from descending into decline with it? Following last year's elections, both inside and outside the country, the energy and attention of many intellectuals, men and women, politicians, and active members of the opposition have—quite rightly—been spent on mocking, deriding, and exposing the absurdity, emptiness, falsehood, and nonsense of the words and deeds of the Islamic Republic's ruling establishment. Matters have reached the point where, even within the ruling establishment itself, reference has been made to the cultural poverty and the penchant for lawlessness of those in charge. Perhaps the time has come for us, with the help of the vast throng of Iranian intellectuals, scholars, and enthusiasts abroad and at home, to devote our utmost effort and concern to discussions examining strategic construction—and doing so by mastering this science–art.

Then, in a clearer atmosphere, with cleaner and more coherent words, we shall turn to choosing and selecting strategic goals, and in a scientific and investigative climate—far removed from personal whims and plausible-sounding "oughts" and "ought-nots"—we shall engage in finding the way forward.

Briefly, I shall address only one of the articles that recently speaks of strategy: "Free Elections: The Political Strategy of the National Republicans of Iran", written by Mr Hassan Shariatmadari. In this text, the intention is not to scrutinise his political viewpoint; our focus is on the method of reasoning. If we test Mr Hassan Shariatmadari's text using the aforementioned method regarding strategy, we can divide its contents into three categories:
1. Assessment of the current situation: In this text it is stated: "From major cities to the most remote villages, people regard participation in public affairs and involvement in political life as their right and duty, and to this day, despite all the restrictions imposed by the rulers, despite repression and killing, the people still have not withdrawn from the political arena... The ties and connections among people in different parts of the country have made politics national and nationwide in the true sense... The media revolution has placed the satellite dish in place of the pulpit and trapped the genie of censorship in a bottle through the internet."
2. Drawing conclusions from the current situation: In this text it is stated: "Consequently, the generalisation of politics has created the popular groundwork for an advanced democracy in society. This groundwork is neither compatible with institutions and ideas that restrict political participation to the 'ommat' and supporters of Velayat, nor receptive to a democracy that excludes a major segment of citizens... The universalisation of politics has also ensured the durability and persistence of the society's major political tendencies... Political forces—whether left or right, pro-government or anti-government—continue, in varying proportions, to maintain a base among the people... The political and intellectual continuity of all these tendencies inside and outside the country demonstrates that each is capable of cultivating its political cadres and taking steps towards forming distinct political parties."

3. Proclaiming a strategy based on this conclusion and its benefits: Further on, it states: "This is the most important foundation of the strategy of free elections, in which no political force—whether pro-government or anti-government—is left out; which recognises neither 'insider' nor 'outsider', neither 'pure' nor 'impure'. A policy that can align all political forces while preserving their distinct programmes, and—regardless of differing programmes and different political systems—turn the struggle for the freedom of political activity into the shared goal of all forces that accept the sovereignty of the ballot box and are willing to challenge one another in a democratic competition."

Later in this text, however, strategy shifts into the central slogan: "Today, free elections are on course to become the principal slogan of the democracy-seeking movement in Iran. What is on the agenda today is organising a joint struggle to realise it. In our view, the first step on this path is initiating an organised dialogue among political forces and figures so that they may formulate appropriate solutions for advancing a coordinated policy."

In this text, strategy is effortlessly transformed into the central slogan—and specifically for the democracy-seeking movement in Iran. Is holding free elections a strategic goal, or is it a central slogan? And they propose the method for reaching this goal as follows: "To achieve free elections and institutionalise them, national resolve and will must be mobilised... organising a joint struggle to realise it... they are capable of cultivating their political cadres and taking steps towards forming distinct political parties..."

Yet if free elections are a strategy—or, better put, a strategic goal—as already noted, one must follow the chain to its very end and demonstrate that this goal is feasible. It is necessary to point out succinctly the conditions for free elections:

What distinguishes genuine elections from a voting spectacle pertains to five fundamental, necessary, and sufficient principles of an election (for unsound, flawed, or incomplete elections cannot be called elections; an election either adheres to its five fundamental principles or it is not an election, and at most constitutes a kind of polling).

These five principles are set out concisely yet completely in Article 25 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights:

"Every citizen has the right and the opportunity, without restriction, to vote or to be elected in periodic and impartial elections conducted on the basis of universal, equal, and pure suffrage, guaranteeing the freedom of expression of the electors."

First Principle: The freedom to be elected and to declare one's candidacy.

Second Principle: Providing the opportunity and possibility to exchange views, receive the opinions of electors, and convey the programmes and views of representatives.

Third Principle: Every citizen, whether candidate or elector, having equal access to the opportunity to exchange views and receive opinions. Without further discussion, it suffices to look at the cohesive and interlocked complex of "Sepah–Basij–Mosques–Seminaries" across the country down to the most remote villages to understand how candidacies backed by this four-legged interlocked network will monopolise all means of opinion-dissemination.

Fourth Principle: The impossibility for individuals to participate in voting more than once, which itself is only achievable by holding the vote through the establishment of electoral rolls so that each individual can vote solely in their own constituency, and only once. Otherwise, there will be no guarantee whatsoever against fraud and abuse.

Fifth Principle: Every election requires an independent and impartial authority to adjudicate complaints, both at the national level and at the international level. At the international level, it is self-evident that since no such request has been made by the Iranian government, this is not possible; and as for a competent and impartial domestic authority, on the one hand, the head of the judiciary is directly appointed by the Supreme Leader.

Even so, one can understand that "Free Elections: The Political Strategy of the National Republicans of Iran" ought to be read thus: "Free elections are the proposed central slogan for gathering Iran's political activists inside and outside the country."

Which, in its own right, is indeed highly valuable, yet it cannot be a political strategy.

Hassan Makaremi

It is, in a sense, placing the future at the centre. Preparing oneself for the future. Setting goals and programmes for the future, for becoming, for being in the future. Yearning to attain one's aspirations, planning, drawing upon all of one's own and others' resources, knowledge, and art. At times, turning to forces beyond logic, because a better future is our need, our aspiration, and perhaps the very reason for our being. A fundamental study is required to illuminate more clearly the impact of religion on the need for foresight. One might say that perhaps our dreamed-of, paradisiacal utopia lies in another world. For religious believers, sketching an earthly future takes shape solely within the framework of permissible religious aspirations. The fundamental utterances were already brought by the prophets in the past. The future can neither unlock mysteries nor serve as an answer to a longing rising from the heart.

Possessing a strategic goal requires, above all, ambition, faith in human capability, and knowledge of oneself, others, one's surroundings, and history.

Let us return to the article by one of the proponents of the slogan "Free Elections":

We see how the term "strategy" and the "central slogan" have been merged together and how both have been distorted.

A question arising from the above examination that can deeply trouble us is this: do the regression, baseness, cultural poverty, mediocrity, and ignorance of a state and ruling power not gradually drag the opposition to that ruling power down into decline alongside it? Should one not always remain vigilant, and—even though in the field of action one must be present on the scene and act as the "opposition" to a ruling power—refrain from descending into decline with it? Following last year's elections, both inside and outside the country, the energy and attention of many intellectuals, men and women, politicians, and active members of the opposition have—quite rightly—been spent on mocking, deriding, and exposing the absurdity, emptiness, falsehood, and nonsense of the words and deeds of the Islamic Republic's ruling establishment. Matters have reached the point where, even within the ruling establishment itself, reference has been made to the cultural poverty and the penchant for lawlessness of those in charge. Perhaps the time has come for us, with the help of the vast throng of Iranian intellectuals, scholars, and enthusiasts abroad and at home, to devote our utmost effort and concern to discussions examining strategic construction—and doing so by mastering this science–art.

Then, in a clearer atmosphere, with cleaner and more coherent words, we shall turn to choosing and selecting strategic goals, and in a scientific and investigative climate—far removed from personal whims and plausible-sounding "oughts" and "ought-nots"—we shall engage in finding the way forward.

Briefly, I shall address only one of the articles that recently speaks of strategy: "Free Elections: The Political Strategy of the National Republicans of Iran", written by Mr Hassan Shariatmadari. In this text, the intention is not to scrutinise his political viewpoint; our focus is on the method of reasoning. If we test Mr Hassan Shariatmadari's text using the aforementioned method regarding strategy, we can divide its contents into three categories:
1. Assessment of the current situation: In this text it is stated: "From major cities to the most remote villages, people regard participation in public affairs and involvement in political life as their right and duty, and to this day, despite all the restrictions imposed by the rulers, despite repression and killing, the people still have not withdrawn from the political arena... The ties and connections among people in different parts of the country have made politics national and nationwide in the true sense... The media revolution has placed the satellite dish in place of the pulpit and trapped the genie of censorship in a bottle through the internet."
2. Drawing conclusions from the current situation: In this text it is stated: "Consequently, the generalisation of politics has created the popular groundwork for an advanced democracy in society. This groundwork is neither compatible with institutions and ideas that restrict political participation to the 'ommat' and supporters of Velayat, nor receptive to a democracy that excludes a major segment of citizens... The universalisation of politics has also ensured the durability and persistence of the society's major political tendencies... Political forces—whether left or right, pro-government or anti-government—continue, in varying proportions, to maintain a base among the people... The political and intellectual continuity of all these tendencies inside and outside the country demonstrates that each is capable of cultivating its political cadres and taking steps towards forming distinct political parties."

3. Proclaiming a strategy based on this conclusion and its benefits: Further on, it states: "This is the most important foundation of the strategy of free elections, in which no political force—whether pro-government or anti-government—is left out; which recognises neither 'insider' nor 'outsider', neither 'pure' nor 'impure'. A policy that can align all political forces while preserving their distinct programmes, and—regardless of differing programmes and different political systems—turn the struggle for the freedom of political activity into the shared goal of all forces that accept the sovereignty of the ballot box and are willing to challenge one another in a democratic competition."

Later in this text, however, strategy shifts into the central slogan: "Today, free elections are on course to become the principal slogan of the democracy-seeking movement in Iran. What is on the agenda today is organising a joint struggle to realise it. In our view, the first step on this path is initiating an organised dialogue among political forces and figures so that they may formulate appropriate solutions for advancing a coordinated policy."

In this text, strategy is effortlessly transformed into the central slogan—and specifically for the democracy-seeking movement in Iran. Is holding free elections a strategic goal, or is it a central slogan? And they propose the method for reaching this goal as follows: "To achieve free elections and institutionalise them, national resolve and will must be mobilised... organising a joint struggle to realise it... they are capable of cultivating their political cadres and taking steps towards forming distinct political parties..."

Yet if free elections are a strategy—or, better put, a strategic goal—as already noted, one must follow the chain to its very end and demonstrate that this goal is feasible. It is necessary to point out succinctly the conditions for free elections:

What distinguishes genuine elections from a voting spectacle pertains to five fundamental, necessary, and sufficient principles of an election (for unsound, flawed, or incomplete elections cannot be called elections; an election either adheres to its five fundamental principles or it is not an election, and at most constitutes a kind of polling).

These five principles are set out concisely yet completely in Article 25 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights:

"Every citizen has the right and the opportunity, without restriction, to vote or to be elected in periodic and impartial elections conducted on the basis of universal, equal, and pure suffrage, guaranteeing the freedom of expression of the electors."

First Principle: The freedom to be elected and to declare one's candidacy.

Second Principle: Providing the opportunity and possibility to exchange views, receive the opinions of electors, and convey the programmes and views of representatives.

Third Principle: Every citizen, whether candidate or elector, having equal access to the opportunity to exchange views and receive opinions. Without further discussion, it suffices to look at the cohesive and interlocked complex of "Sepah–Basij–Mosques–Seminaries" across the country down to the most remote villages to understand how candidacies backed by this four-legged interlocked network will monopolise all means of opinion-dissemination.

Fourth Principle: The impossibility for individuals to participate in voting more than once, which itself is only achievable by holding the vote through the establishment of electoral rolls so that each individual can vote solely in their own constituency, and only once. Otherwise, there will be no guarantee whatsoever against fraud and abuse.

Fifth Principle: Every election requires an independent and impartial authority to adjudicate complaints, both at the national level and at the international level. At the international level, it is self-evident that since no such request has been made by the Iranian government, this is not possible; and as for a competent and impartial domestic authority, on the one hand, the head of the judiciary is directly appointed by the Supreme Leader.

Even so, one can understand that "Free Elections: The Political Strategy of the National Republicans of Iran" ought to be read thus: "Free elections are the proposed central slogan for gathering Iran's political activists inside and outside the country."

Which, in its own right, is indeed highly valuable, yet it cannot be a political strategy.

Hassan Makaremi

Clinical Psychoanalyst and Researcher at the Sorbonne

Can the modern science–art of strategy be useful in finding a way forward for Iran's future?

If so, in what manner, and who can accomplish this vital task?

He reaps the fruit of life who, in every undertaking,

First reflects, and only then adopts its course.
(Hafez: Qasideh No. 3)

Preface: The relative calm of the past few months has afforded political actors the opportunity to deepen fundamental discussions regarding the ways and means of struggle inside and outside Iran. Naturally, terms such as strategic, strategy, central slogan, fundamental duty, and short-term and long-term objectives have returned to the forefront of writings and debates.

Beyond the demands already known prior to the elections, several new discussions have been added, which may be summarised very briefly as follows:

The principal slogan of all adherents of the post-election movement ought to be the demand for "holding free elections".

The principal slogan ought to revolve "around amending the Constitution".

Or, fundamentally, if this very Constitution were implemented properly and in full, that would suffice.

What deeply prompts the need for particular precision in this literature, in these exchanges, dialogues, and arguments, is the misty atmosphere prevailing in the use of language, the mode of reasoning, and the application of the science-art of strategy. Insofar as possible, clarifying definitions may in some measure help open the dialogue further.

We observe that all three slogans under discussion still have a long way to go before ascending to the level of a strategic objective. They are far removed from the precision and rigour required to become universal and to rally everyone around their axis. These objectives have been put forward first, and only afterwards do we go in search of how to implement them in society. As we know, in a scientific process, not only do strategic objectives require measurable quantitative indicators for their implementation, but one must also test their translation into operational objectives, operational plans, and the organisation of progress — at least with respect to the practical feasibility of the plans.

Above all, the science-art of strategy rests upon innovation. Its ultimate endeavour is that the process of designing and executing strategic objectives should culminate in a form of management that we call "innovation management".

The full and complete implementation of the Constitution, the amendment and rewriting of the Constitution, or the holding of free elections lacks any kind of "innovation" and ultimately reduces society's demands to a bare minimum that may gradually become scentless and colourless. A strategy must be so coherent, practical, precise, articulate, comprehensive, persistent, actionable, intelligible, and instructive that it becomes in itself an educational framework for political cadres and the public alike.

Should the science-art of strategy be applied only after seizing power and solely for governing and directing society? Or

can it also be applied in the course of the struggle to attain power? Or, fundamentally, can these two intertwined categories even be separated from one another? Before entering into the discussion, let us review together several examples of theses recently completed at Iranian universities and the reference in these documents to our weak grasp of the modern science-art of strategy.

First example: Thesis title: *The Mechanism of Elite Coalition and the Formulation of National Strategy in Post-Revolutionary Iran*,

by Parviz Dalirpour, University of Tehran, Faculty of Law and Political Science, Doctoral level, year of degree: 1384 (2005–2006). In part of the abstract we read: Formulating a national development strategy requires the highest degrees of cohesion among decision-makers and consensus among intellectual and instrumental elites on the definition of development and its components. This dissertation argues that the existence of conflicting worldviews and approaches across the various socio-political spectra in Iran is one of the factors behind divergent attitudes towards development and the obstruction of the most crucial stage — consensus over a national strategy. Social pluralities and the conflicting interests of social forces regarding entry into the development process and broad consensual change are counted as another major factor in this lack of consensus. This is while Iranian history has shown that a state which casts itself as the agent of social change and advances along this path with a particular definition of development without needing the consensus of major social forces faces the danger of instability. This owes to the diverse social structure and the risk of class shifts and the disruption of the existing equilibrium. In post-revolutionary development programmes, however, social change was not addressed as social transition, and was instead oriented towards preserving the status quo in the reciprocal relationship between the state, the economy, and society. Therefore, Iran's diverse social structure is itself one of the major obstacles to the lack of accord and consensus over a national strategy. This issue indicates that Iran has not yet traversed the transition towards a nation-state in the classical sense of the term.

Second example: Thesis title: *Examining the Structure of the Military Strategy of the Islamic Republic of Iran in the New International System: Priorities and Realities*, by Alireza Saeidabadi, Shahid Beheshti University, International Relations, Master's level, 1379 (2000–2001). In the abstract we read: Strategy in our country is an underdeveloped concept that lies largely under the monopoly of the military and does not enjoy an independent academic standing. Therefore, this thesis has sought, as far as possible free from political considerations, to study and analyse its functioning in Iran in light of the new conditions of the international system from the post-Cold War period to the present through a structural examination from research perspectives, such that the structure of the domestic political system and the structure of the international system are treated in the present study as two independent variables, each of which has exerted direct and indirect effects upon the internal and external threats and opportunities of the political system of the Islamic Republic of Iran. Yet, notwithstanding this, consensus has never been achieved on the issue of strategic planning at the national level, and the country's decision-making system continues to confront structural deficiencies... One of the primary reasons for the mismatch between the internal and external threats and opportunities of the political system of the Islamic Republic of Iran and the quantitative and qualitative components of national power is that it ultimately leads to the pursuit of action-reaction policies and distance from a system of strategic planning at the national level.

Let us also pay attention to an example of the usage of the word "strategy" in one of the Friday prayer sermons: "The strategy of the Islamic Republic, over the past thirty-one years, has been the strategy of resistance and steadfastness." Strategy (*râhbord*) has to do with a path (*râh*), and a path has to do with movement. How can resistance be a strategy?

Let us return to the initial question: can the modern science-art of strategy assist in charting Iran's future? And if so, by whom and how?

Let us briefly examine the contemporary definitions of terms and the process of applying the modern science-art of strategy:

Definitions:

The word *strategos*, meaning military commander, comes from the Greek language and belongs to the vocabulary of warfare. In practice today, this term is used across all domains of military, administrative, industrial, service, and political management, non-profit organisations (at national, regional, and international levels), the leadership of political movements and political parties, the preparation of long-term regional, national, and international programmes, the drafting of state budgets, and even research laboratories, educational institutions, and the like.

- Across various management methodologies, both differing definitions of strategy and general methods for formulating it are offered. Nevertheless, in every case, several general and overarching characteristics exist in the task of preparing and formulating a strategy for an operational ensemble:

Strategic objectives, strategic plans, and indicators for measuring the execution of these objectives.

It is from this point that long-term planning is prepared following the precise definition of the three aforementioned factors. In practice, it is in the course of executing long-term programmes that operational plans are defined. Executing operational plans in the field of action requires clarifying tactics, and the overall line connecting tactics we call politics (*siyâsat*) — politics, which is the art of the possible. It is an art because it requires invention, and because it operates in the arena of reality, it is thus the art of the possible.

Strategy is the "science-art" of making optimal use of resources in attaining predetermined objectives. Hence, the clear and precise determination and definition of objectives is indispensable. Making use of resources requires knowing them and organising them.

Strategic objectives, and identifying, understanding, and defining them in any field, is a task both deceptively simple and arduous, situated today on the frontier between science, art, and experience. Understanding strategic objectives requires both an exact knowledge of details across the various dimensions influencing the field of operation of these objectives, and an extraordinary capacity to free oneself from the trap of those details, to soar, to rise above, and to exercise foresight.

Formulating a strategic programme and adopting tactical positions stand in a logical and structural relationship with strategy.

Strategic objectives must be definable, ambitious, actionable, and measurable.

In determining "definable objectives", we need to assess "needs". We must choose words precisely and clearly. We must know the language of society, our audience, and our colleagues thoroughly, in such a manner as to create the smallest possible gap between thought, speech, and deed. Words are the fundamental instruments for conveying our thought in defining and determining "strategic objectives". Striking examples of this in the history of the past two centuries are the words "Constitutionalism" (*mashrûtiyyat*) and "Republic" (*jomhûrî*) at the two major turning points of the Constitutional Revolution and the February 1979 (Bahman) Revolution.

Assessing needs demands depth of vision and farsightedness. Needs are undoubtedly assessed in close relationship — direct or mediated — with the people. From this point on, knowing the people, both individually and collectively, becomes obligatory. Knowing human beings lies in knowing their body and psyche. And it is here that familiarity with psychology and psychoanalysis comes to our aid. The science of sociology acquaints us more closely with the movement of the people. History is the science of events that have occurred, of tracing, interpreting, and explaining them. Learning from how human societies have moved from ancient times down to the present — their beliefs, desires, wishes, dreams, and imaginings — brings us closer to the human being.

Ambitious objectives are the sole path that delivers us from stagnation and spinning in circles. These objectives guide us towards inquiry and innovation. They enable us to draw upon the utmost of our capacities and resources. They place us in healthy competition with the innate human need for progress and for greater knowledge of oneself and of existence. These objectives become a motive force, an agent of our growth and flourishing. Strategic objectives must be translated into operational objectives. Thus, it is upon the stage of reality — in production, in construction, across the expanse of the family, village, city, country, region, and the world — that these objectives can be carried out. The execution of these objectives takes place in a specific time and place. The feasibility of executing these objectives within a bounded timeframe is a fundamental condition.

Putting objectives into practice requires not only an executor and a designated time and place, but also instruments. These instruments may be divided into two major groups: technology and research facilities on the one hand, and management and organisation on the other. In this vein, one may ask oneself whether generating electricity through nuclear technology can be a viable strategic objective. For above all else, if the economic, social, and political capacities necessary for fundamental research or access to modern technology under balanced conditions of international relations are absent, in the medium term we shall confront vast, irreparable catastrophes, or else face fundamental crises in replacing, maintaining, and continuing the operation of the facilities. Can the strategic objectives of a society be defined independently of the level of capability of society's managers and the governability of the people?

Objectives can be defined and executed within a specified spatial domain. Precision in defining the domain of application and implementation of these objectives will prevent any deviation or misinterpretation. A striking example of the blurring of the domain of application of objectives can easily be observed in Iran's second Constitution. The conflation and commingling of the two domains of *mellat* (nation) and *ommat* (religious community) is visible at the core of the definition of this Constitution's objectives, both in its general principles and in its very fabric. Ultimately, these objectives must be tangible and speak to the soul and psyche of human beings. Progress towards them must be felt. They must afford us the possibility of review and revision. For these reasons, these objectives must be measurable, so as to absolve us of subjectivism and abstract idealism. It must be possible, from the very outset, to possess both a scale of measurement and an instrument of measurement for gauging movement towards them. Strategy is, before all else, attaching importance to the future — in a sense, placing the future at the centre. Preparing oneself for the future; setting objectives and a programme for the future, for becoming, for being in the future; aspiring to attain one's ideals, planning, and drawing benefit from all resources, sciences, and arts — one's own and those of others; and at times appealing to forces beyond logic, because a better future is our need, our aspiration, and perhaps our very reason for being. A fundamental study is needed to clarify more fully the impact of religion on the need for foresight. One might say that perhaps our dreamed-of utopia and paradise lie in another world. For religious believers, charting an earthly future takes place solely within the mould of religiously permissible aspirations. The foundational pronouncements were delivered by the prophets in the past; the future can neither unlock mysteries nor answer a desire rising from the heart.

Having a strategic objective requires, above all, ambition, faith in human capability, and knowledge of oneself, of others, of one's surroundings, and of history.

Let us return to the article by one of the proponents of the "free elections" slogan:

We see how the terms "strategy" and "central slogan" have been merged together, and both have been distorted.

A question that may deeply trouble us from the foregoing examination is this: does the regression, baseness, cultural poverty, mediocrity, and ignorance of a government and ruling establishment not gradually drag the opposition to that establishment down into the abyss alongside it? Ought one not to remain ever vigilant — and even though in the arena of action one must remain present on the stage and serve as the "opposition" to a ruling power, refuse to descend into the abyss with it? Since last year's election, both inside and outside the country, the energy and attention of many intellectuals, men and women, politicians, and active opposition figures have — quite rightly — been spent on mocking, deriding, enumerating the absurdities, emptiness, lies, and nonsense of the words and deeds of the Islamic Republic's ruling establishment. Matters have reached such a pass that even from within the establishment itself, references have been made to the cultural poverty and the habit of lawlessness among those in charge. Perhaps the time has come to devote our resolve and concern, with the aid of the vast multitude of Iranian intellectuals, scholars, and enthusiasts inside and outside the country, to discussions examining strategic construction, precisely through mastering this science-art.

Then, in a clearer atmosphere, with cleaner and more unified terms, we shall proceed to select and choose strategic objectives, and in a scientific, research-oriented space — far removed from personal tastes and credible-sounding imperatives — we shall pursue the charting of a path.

I shall briefly address only one of the articles that has recently spoken of strategy: "Free Elections: The Political Strategy of the National Republicans of Iran", written by Mr Hassan Shariatmadari. In this essay, the intention is not to dissect his political viewpoint; our focus is on the mode of reasoning. If we test Mr Hassan Shariatmadari's article against the method mentioned above concerning strategy, we can divide its contents into three categories:

1. Assessment of the existing situation: The article states: "People from major cities to the most remote villages regard participation in public affairs and involvement in political life as their right and duty, and to this day, despite all the restrictions imposed by the rulers, despite repression and killing, the people still have not withdrawn from the political arena... The ties and connections among people across different parts of the country have made politics genuinely national and nationwide... The media revolution has placed satellite television in place of the pulpit, and the internet has bottled the genie of censorship."

2. Conclusions drawn from the existing situation: The article states: "The conclusion is that the universalisation of politics has created the popular groundwork for an advanced democracy in society. This groundwork is no longer compatible with institutions and ideas that restrict participation in politics to the *ommat* and supporters of *velâyat* (guardianship), nor is it receptive to a democracy that excludes a major segment of citizens... The universalisation of politics has also brought about the durability and persistence of the major political tendencies in society... Political forces — whether left or right, pro-government or anti-government — have continued, in varying proportions, to preserve a base among the people... The political-intellectual continuity of all these tendencies inside and outside the country demonstrates that each is capable of cultivating its own political cadres and moving towards forming distinct political parties."

3. And the proclamation of a strategy based on this conclusion and its benefits: The text continues: "This is the most important foundation of the strategy of free elections, in which no political force — whether supportive of or opposed to the government — is excluded, and no distinction is made between insider and outsider, pure and impure. It must be a policy capable of aligning all political forces while preserving their distinct programmes, so that, irrespective of differing programmes and different political systems, the struggle for freedom of political activity becomes the shared objective of all forces that accept the sovereignty of the ballot box and are prepared to challenge one another in a democratic competition."

Further on in this article, however, "strategy" turns into "central slogan": "Today, free elections are on course to become the foremost slogan of the pro-democracy movement in Iran. What is on the agenda today is organising the joint struggle for its realisation. In our view, the first step on this path is initiating an organised dialogue among political forces and figures so that they may formulate appropriate mechanisms to advance a coordinated policy."

In this article, strategy easily turns into the central slogan — and specifically for the pro-democracy movement in Iran. Is holding free elections a strategic objective or the central slogan? And the method proposed for reaching this objective is framed as follows: "To achieve free elections and institutionalise them, national resolve and will must be mobilised... organising the joint struggle for its realisation... capable of cultivating their own political cadres and moving towards forming distinct political parties..."

Yet if free elections constitute a strategy — or rather, let us say, a strategic objective — just as one set out, one must go all the way to the end of the chain and demonstrate that this objective is actionable. It is necessary to recall, concisely, the conditions for free elections:

What distinguishes elections from a voting spectacle pertains to five fundamental, necessary, and sufficient principles of an election (for unsound, improper, incomplete... elections cannot be called elections; an election either adheres to its five fundamental principles or it is not an election, and at most constitutes a kind of ballot-casting).

These five principles are set forth concisely yet completely in Article 25 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights:

"Every citizen shall have the right and the opportunity, without unreasonable restrictions, to vote and to be elected at genuine periodic elections which shall be by universal and equal suffrage and shall be held by secret ballot, guaranteeing the free expression of the will of the electors."

First principle: Freedom to be elected and to declare one's candidacy.

Second principle: Creating the opportunity and possibility to exchange views, receive the views of voters, and convey the programmes and views of candidates.

Third principle: Having equal access to the opportunity to exchange and receive views for every citizen, whether candidate or voter. Without further argument, it suffices to look at the cohesive, interconnected ensemble of "IRGC – Basij – mosques – seminaries" across the country down to the most remote villages to understand how candidacies backed by this interconnected "four-legged" network will monopolise all means of communicating opinions.

Fourth principle: The impossibility of individuals taking part in the vote more than once, which is achievable only by conducting voting through the establishment of electoral rolls so that each individual may vote solely in their own designated constituency, and only once. Otherwise, there will be no guarantee whatsoever against fraud and abuse.

Fifth principle: Every election requires an independent and impartial authority to adjudicate complaints, both at the national level and at the international level. At the international level, obviously, since no such request has been made by the Iranian government, this is not possible; and as for a competent and impartial domestic authority, on the one hand, the head of the judiciary is directly appointed by the Supreme Leader.

Nevertheless, it becomes clear that "Free Elections: The Political Strategy of the National Republicans of Iran" ought to be read in this light: "Free elections is the proposed central slogan for bringing together Iranian political actors inside and outside the country."
