en.body_markdown:
https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/03/DSC02711.jpg

The bazaar of longing has grown brisk—where is that cypress-statured Beloved,

So that I may offer my soul as wild rue upon the fire of His face?

"Hafez undoubtedly places his finger upon the collective memory (collective memory, historical memory, ethnic spirit, spirit of language, shared historical essence, shared ethnic essence) of the Persian-speaking Iranian, in such a way that across the passage of centuries his poetry remains inextricably interwoven with this memory. They find their own eloquent tongue in 'Hafez', and in a certain sense Hafez is an intermediary between the collective-imaginary memory of Iranian peoples and their historical movement. This is a secret that Hafez carries within his breast, and this is the secret of Hafez's profound and abiding presence for Iranians."

I wrote these letters in such a way that no stranger understood;
Do you, too, out of generosity, read them in the way that you know.

1- I do not intend to speak of that eternal luminary "Hafez of Shiraz" as an expert in Persian literature and poetry. Nor do I possess the capacity to grasp the myths of Iranian peoples to the extent that they have come to be known. Nor have I the strength to gather a worthy provision from the expanse of knowledge in the field of psychoanalysis. Yet, being enamoured of all three, I make a modest attempt in their midst.

Persian poetry, as all agree, shines throughout the East and the world, and its radiant flame, "Hafez", is by some accounts the crowning jewel of world poetry. Myths are the foundation of cultural structure—or, by another account, the memory—of every people. The discovery of the phenomenon of the unconscious and the presence of ethnic memory over the past century has opened a fresh vantage point for our understanding. Our endeavour is, by relying upon these newly discovered insights into the human condition and entering through the gateway of the myths of Iranian peoples, to answer this centuries-old question: Why "Hafez"?

Undoubtedly, on other occasions, scholars who are masters of these three domains will, with more eloquent expression and stronger instruments, expand upon this brief outline and perhaps cast fresh light upon the secret of Hafez's greatness.

Beyond what Persian speakers across many centuries have sought in the "word" of Hafez, there exists a sign loftier than "beauty of imagery and speech", "spiritual and religious sanctity", and "historical and social insight". "Hafez" dwells beside the Qur'an in the homes of Persian speakers. Although he is a *hāfez* [memoriser] of the Qur'an, for Iranians he appears to be the emblem of safeguarding a more precious and deeper phenomenon—namely, "collective and ethnic" memory.

The secret of "Hafez" is undoubtedly no new question. Time and again we have asked and striven earnestly to find the answer: not only why "Hafez", but why and how people of thought (the elite) and others (the common folk)—from every ethnic group, tribe, inclination, social class, creed, and cast of mind (mystic and layperson alike)—as soon as they lie within the sphere of influence of the Persian language, have chosen Hafez as their expressive voice. In sorrow and in joy, in everyday conversation and in nocturnal solitude, he is present. Each person, as it were, is his companion according to their own supposition. He is a diviner of auguries.

In the crystal orb of his *Divan*, hope glimmers, and it is a site of bibliomancy (*istikhārah*). At his tomb, one day the gathering of minstrels is spread out, and on another day people of religion serve in commemoration of him.

2- He used to recite the Qur'an in fourteen variant readings, and it appears he had advanced sufficiently in the sciences of his age. Neither a captivating physical appearance nor an eventful biography has remained of him in memory—only some five hundred ghazals. The works published thus far concerning Hafez may be categorised as follows:

- Establishing critical editions of the ghazals, tracing, emending, and attempting to distinguish the authentic from the spurious, and recovering the original order and arrangement of the verses within the ghazals and early manuscripts.

- Studies surrounding Hafez's life, his era, the manner of his work and conduct, the influences of others upon him or Hafez's influence upon other poets—biographical accounts of Hafez across historical, geographical, social, and ultimately literary terrains.

- Commentaries on the ghazals, interpretation of the poems, elucidation of subtleties, deciphering of symbols, and comparative study of his verses, particularly in relation to Hadiths, Qur'anic verses, and the prevalent ideas of his time; uncovering and unpacking Hafez's thought in the sphere of conceptual analysis represents another effort from another angle, with the idea that by relying on Hafez's poems and classifying them according to concept or chronological order of composition, one may arrive at the key concepts of Hafez's thought and thereby achieve a fresh understanding of Hafez.

- And finally, literary, linguistic, and comparative scholarship—or, in other words, an inquiry into the quintessential essence of Hafez's poems.

Our aim here is rather to find "a fresh perspective on Hafez": why Hafez? Why does the Hindu burn him in fire and the Muslim wash him in Zamzam, and why do only those shaped by Persian culture become so infatuated with him (in comparison with the global renown of Khayyam)? Why have Persian speakers opened such an exalted station for Hafez?

3- Our initial endeavour to find an answer to this question was to render the inquiry more scientific through a structural view of Hafez's thought—by searching his poems for key concepts, treating those concepts as elements of a system of thought, and discerning the manifold relations among these concepts so as to fathom the secret of Hafez's thought (you will find an example of our first effort in Appendix No. 1). Such an effort, without drawing upon foundational hypotheses, will not on its own lead anywhere, for ultimately it will drive us into the cul-de-sac of further "whys", the key to unlocking which lies hidden in the general hypotheses of the circle of human knowledge.

4- The basis of our work here rests, on the one hand, upon the psychoanalytic theory of Freud [1], completed by Lacan [2], and on the other hand, upon the researches of Henry Corbin [3] regarding the roots of Iranian thought. The heart of the hypothesis of contemporary psychoanalysis is this: "Everything is language." The structure of the human unconscious is like the structure of a language (the mother tongue, the infant's relation with the mother, and the formation of the unconscious during the earliest years of life). Signs [4] or acoustic images [5] construct an ensemble which, like a "text", writes our unconscious. These "signs" migrate from one individual to another, such that one cannot properly tell who owns these signs; and it is thus that through "economy of speech", "overdetermination/ambiguity", "condensation and brevity", and the use of "wordplay and conceptual play"—in short, what is known in the literary domain as poetry and the architecture of speech, and in everyday life as proverbs, jokes, riddles, invectives, and the like—in practice a set of "signs" lives within the space circulating between "each and every individual" among us, forming the basis of today's culture and yesterday's myth [6]. (In Appendix No. 2 you will find examples of these influences in contemporary culture.)

The power of Hafez of Shiraz lies in his speech—and specifically "Dari" speech—within the expanse of Persian-speaking culture:

Only one is "aware" of Hafez's heart-captivating poetry
Who knows the grace of temperament and the art of speaking Dari

Or again:

You have conquered Iraq and Fars with your sweet poetry, Hafez;
Come, for now is the turn of Baghdad and the time of Tabriz

(Iraq here refers to the region of present-day Arak. One observes that even in Hafez's own time, the sphere of influence of Hafez's poetry is Persian culture.)

It is in this way that the collective memory of a people is shaped by the mother tongue, and the history latent within culture is transmitted from one generation to the next through the mother tongue by drawing upon myth and legend, playing its part in shaping the unconscious of each one of us and giving rise to cultural distinction and richness. (With the passage of time, we come ever more fully to appreciate the grandeur of the palace-building method chosen by Ferdowsi: a palace built of Persian words and grounded in Iranian myths.)

Hafez undoubtedly places his finger upon the collective memory of Iranian peoples and Persian speakers, in such a way that across the passage of centuries his poetry remains inextricably interwoven with this memory. They find their own eloquent tongue in Hafez, and in a certain sense Hafez is an intermediary between the collective-imaginary memory of Iranian peoples and their historical movement. This is a secret that Hafez carries within his breast, and this is the secret of Hafez's profound and immortal presence for Iranians. (Ferdowsi plays this same role in the historical-social sphere, Sa'di in everyday life, and Mowlavi [Rumi] in philosophical knowledge.)

5- Let us turn to Henry Corbin's insights. Briefly, in Iranian mythology, the "Earth" is an angel (a Yazata) in the heavens (the Celestial Earth, *zamīn-e mīnovī*); our body is on earth, and our soul (*ravān*) is in the Celestial Earth. After death we return to the Celestial Earth. (Apparently, a profound relation exists between the Celestial Earth, the Iranian garden, and the design of the Iranian carpet.) Real geography is established upon seven climes (*haft keshvar*), at the centre of which lies Iran, surrounded by the six other climes.

Hafez came for your sake into the clime of existence;
Step forth to bid him farewell, for he will soon be departing (*ravān*)

(Here *ravān* can carry two meanings: *ravān* as the "celestial I/soul", and *ravān* in the sense of setting out / departing.) Ahura Mazda, the Yazata of Yazatas, is Light and our Creator. The sole path to comprehending existence and the self is communion with the "*ravān*" (that part of the "I" which dwells in the Celestial Earth). Only through this path shall we attain complete knowledge, the "Perfect Human", and the "station of the Elder (*pīr*)". The endeavour to reach and commune with the celestial self through illumination (*ishrāq*) is the very path of Light—or, in other words, "Love". It is not without reason that the word *Mehr* in the Persian language means both the Sun, the generator of light, and Love.

You are no less than a mote—do not be base, practise love (*mehr*),
So that, whirling, you may reach the private sanctuary of the Sun

Ahura Mazda and the six other Yazatas are all deities of wisdom/intellect. ("In the name of the Lord of soul and wisdom" — Ferdowsi.) Ahura Mazda is Light and power. The angel of the Earth, or Celestial Earth—a feminine deity—which bears a distant kinship to the notion of Paradise in the Iranian mind, is in a sense the emblem of nature's beauty and the emblem of feminine beauty. In a certain way, reaching the "other I" dwelling in the "Celestial Earth", which passes through illumination and love, is attained through "unreason" (*bī-kheradī*); and the sign of unreason is intoxication, and attaining intoxication is through "wine" (*mey*). (For further explanation, consult Henry Corbin's introduction to Shaykh Ruzbihan's *Abhar al-Āshiqīn*.) [7]

6- It is thus that, relying upon the cipher of the "Celestial Earth", the relation between Hafez's imaginary Beloved, the rose, garden, meadow, minstrel, and wine, on the one hand, and the Elder (*pīr*) or Magian Elder (*pīr-e moghān*), on the other, is uncovered. In reality, the key to unlocking this secret is the presence of "parallel time" (another life parallel to this mortal world in the Celestial Earth—an image of the Garden of Paradise).

Love—or illumination through uniting with Light—is a path set over against "reason", as well as against all other forms of knowledge, even non-Illuminationist Sufism.

Wash clean the pages if you are our fellow student,
For the science of love is not to be found in the ledger

The mysteries of amorous play do not fit within the Sufi hospice;
The goblet of Magian wine can only be drunk with the Magians

It is thus that imitating Hafez after him becomes practically impossible. With immense effort others have sought to follow in his footsteps by speaking of wine, the Beloved, and the "Elder", yet because their poetry is devoid of the "essence" of mythical backing, it fails to gain acceptance.

Now let us take a stroll through the *Divan* of Hafez so as to gather what benefit we can:

6.1- The longing to return to the Celestial Earth and the melancholy born of this separation—or, as Henry Corbin puts it, the "Celestial Earth" signifies the ultimate homesickness, nostalgia, and estrangement of the human heart [8].

In expectation of Your face, we remain in hope;
In the coquetry of union with You, we remain in fantasy and dream.

Joyous the day when I depart from this ruined abode,
Seek the ease of the soul, and go in pursuit of the Soul's Beloved.

My heart has grown weary of the terror of Alexander's prison;
I shall pack my belongings and depart to Solomon's realm.

The longing for Your lane never leaves our head;
The stranger's wandering heart remains with the homeland.

From the battlement of the celestial Throne they whistle a call to you;
I know not what has befallen you in this snare-ground.

You are afflicted with the sorrow, trial, and anguish of separation;
O heart, this lament and wailing of yours is not without cause.

My purpose in both mosque and tavern is union with You;
No other fancy have I—God is my witness.

The dust of my body becomes a veil over the face of the soul;
Blessed the moment when I cast off the veil from that face.

Such a cage is not worthy of a sweet-singing bird like me;
I shall go to the rose-garden of Rizwan, for I am a bird of that meadow.

(With certainty of returning to the Celestial Earth and a place free from both worlds.)

Where is the glad tiding of union with You, that I may rise above life?
I am a bird of sanctity and would rise from the snare of the world.

6.2- The sole path to knowledge is illumination (uniting with the light of love), and that too is made possible through intoxication and wine. Selflessness (*bī-khodī*) is uniting with the other I, the twin self, the celestial I, or the "Witness" (*shāhed*), the "celestial soul" (*jān-e olwī*). To attain this eighth clime, the Celestial Earth, we require active imagination or the presence of "state" (*hāl*)—concentration in a parallel time, yet an "other" time.

The "celestial soul" conceived a longing for the dimple of Your chin;
It laid its hand upon the ring of those curling, tangled locks.

The beggar of Your lane has no need of the eight Paradises;
The captive of Your love is free from both worlds.

(One must ask: where is this third world?)

Love will come to your rescue even if, like Hafez,
You recite the Qur'an by heart in fourteen variant readings.

(It is fitting here to draw a comparison with Freud's words regarding psychoanalytic treatment; he says: our cure is effected through love.) [9]

Never dies the one whose heart has been brought to life by love;
Our permanence is inscribed upon the scroll of the universe.

I am the physician of love—give me wine, for this elixir
Brings relief and sweeps away erroneous thought.

If the cupbearer pours wine of this kind into the goblet,
He will cast all mystics into perpetual drinking.

Sweeter than the sound of the word of love I have seen no
Keepsake that might remain within this revolving dome.

In this figurative station, take up nothing but the cup;
In this playhouse of trifles, gamble on nothing save love.

(In reality, the figurative station stands in relation to the real station, which is the Celestial Earth.)

Upon the petal of the rose they have written with the blood of the anemone
That whoever became ripened (*pokhteh*) took up wine like the Judas-tree blossom.

(What is "ripening" other than preparing for the journey to the Celestial Earth?)

O Hafez, exalted Paradise is my inherited home;
Why should I make my dwelling in this ruined abode?

(This sentence from the book *Eternal Memory* by Dariush Shayegan [10] comes to mind:
In the poetry of a poet like Hafez, through poetic space, the symmetrical state and dialectic of love—which is like the restless movement of the spirit within the nature of the eternal Beloved—is articulated.)

My purpose in both mosque and tavern is union with You;
No other fancy have I—God is my witness.

I shall not cease my quest until my desire is fulfilled:
Either the body reaches the Soul's Beloved, or the soul leaves the body.

6.3- And here reason leads nowhere:

What is this lofty, plain ceiling of myriad designs?
No sage in the world is aware of this enigma.

If you gain nothing else from wine, is this not enough
That for a moment it leaves you unaware of the temptation of reason?

Untie the knot from your heart and give no thought to the celestial sphere,
For the mind of no geometer has ever untied such a knot.

If reason does not drop anchor into intoxication,
How shall it steer the ship out of this whirlpool of calamity?

The predicament of love lies beyond the compass of our learning;
This subtlety cannot be solved by this erring intellect.

It may be observed that humanity's mode of perceiving the external world can be divided into three methods: direct sensation (unrelated to what we have previously stored within ourselves!); the rational method, namely the simultaneous use of stored data together with logic, reasoning, and direct and indirect empirical methods; and finally "love", "*hāl*" [ecstatic state], and "intoxication"—a relation with the interior (in Henry Corbin's terms, the world of active imagination—hidden within the hidden—access to parallel time), as when Hafez says:

None like Hafez lifted the veil from the face of thought
Since they combed the tress-tips of speech with the pen.

This alludes primarily to the unveiling of "thought", since Hafez has lifted the hijab from its face and rendered it "exposed/disgraced" (*rosvā*). We know that mythical values lose their currency at the point where "script" is invented. Myths function within the sphere of oral exchange. Where the tresses of speech are combed, reason goes to work; myth and "its outlook" fade, and though the Beloved is beautiful, she has been "combed" and exposed.

In the following couplet, Hafez alludes once more to the bestowal of reason upon humanity—by which gift humanity is in reality driven mad, for its mythical power is stolen away:

Heaven could not bear the burden of the Trust;
The lot of the task fell upon the name of mad me.

6.4- On the other hand, the geography of Hafez's knowledge is a mythical geography: seven climes, or seven realms of existence:

Shiraz, the water of Rokni, and this gentle breeze—
Find no fault with it, for it is the beauty-spot upon the cheek of the seven climes.

6.5- The "*rend*" is a free spirit who is liberated from both worlds, dwells in "parallel time", pursues union with the Celestial Earth, and seeks love:

When you pass by our tomb, ask for spiritual resolve (*hemmat*),
For it shall become the pilgrimage-site of the *rends* of the world.

Hypocrisy and deceit bestow no purity upon Hafez's heart;
I shall choose the path of *rendī* and love.

Love, youth, and *rendī* are the sum of desire;
Once the meanings are gathered, one may strike the polo-ball of eloquence.

I am the servant of the resolve of that reckless *rend*
Who, in beggarly guise, knows the art of alchemy.

They bestow the palace of Paradise as reward for deeds;
For us, who are *rends* and beggars, the Magian monastery suffices.

The Beloved is with us—what need is there to ask for more?
The fortune of the companionship of that intimate of the soul suffices us.

For God's sake, do not send me away from Your door to Paradise,
For the head of Your lane suffices us over all being and space.

I am a lover, a *rend*, and a wine-drinker aloud,
And all these ranks I hold from that fairy-faced houri.

6.6- Hafez's historical knowledge—or his grasp of the history of the ancients—possesses a wholly mythical identity. It is as though, apart from myth, human beings had never lived, no great wars had taken place, nor any massacres, slaughter, or rise and fall of kings and dynasties. It is as though Hafez lives in an ethereal—or "Hurqalya"—world. Time is eternal:

Take the goblet on condition of courtesy, for its substance
Is compounded from the skulls of Jamshid, Bahman, and Qobad.

Who knows where Kavus and Kay have gone?
Who is aware how the throne of Jam went to the wind?

The anthem of Jamshid's assembly, they say, was this:
Bring the cup of wine, for Jam shall not remain.

Since the King of the Turks saw fit to cast me into the pit,
If the grace of Tahamtan [Rostam] does not lend a hand, what shall I do?

Cast away the lasso of Bahram's hunt and take up the Cup of Jam,
For I have traversed this desert: neither Bahram is there, nor his grave.

When has fidelity ever existed in this age? Bring the cup of wine,
So that I may recount the tale of Jam and Kay Kavus.

6.7- Hafez dwells in the world of imagination (*‘alam-e takhayyol*), or active imagination—an intermediate realm between the world of the senses and that of concepts, that is, between the empirical world (our sensation of cold and heat, the passage of time, pain, and so forth) and the world of abstract concepts (mathematical and philosophical ideas that exist in abstraction). It is a world that may, in a certain sense, be called the spiritual earth (*zamin-e minavi*) or the celestial realm (*Malakut*). In the *Divan* of Hafez, there is scarcely a trace of the concerns and notions of everyday life; even when he speaks of a 'stipend' (*vazifeh*), it is in relation to the cost of wine.

The dwellers of the sanctuary of modesty and chastity of the celestial realm
Drank intoxicating wine with me, the wayfarer by the roadside.

I am a bird of the garden of the celestial realm; I am not of the world of dust;
For a few days they have fashioned a cage out of my body.

Intoxicate me so that in self-oblivion I may not know
Who came and who departed in the sphere of imagination.

In the workshop of the eye I drew the imagined form of your image;
In beauty of figure I have neither seen nor heard the like.

To behold your face requires a soul-seeing eye—
And how could my world-seeing eye ever attain such a rank?

No more graceful cypress than your stature has grown in the meadow of coquetry;
No fairer form than your image ever existed in the world of depiction.

Where is this 'world of depiction' (*‘alam-e tasvir*)?

You, who in noble virtues are a world apart,
Let not the fidelity of my covenant slip from your memory.

A true human being is not to be found in this world of dust;
Another world must be built, and a human being fashioned anew.

Where is this 'other world'? It is as though Hafez lived in a time between sleep and waking, between being and non-being. Is this not the very time rooted in the depths of the Persian language, its literature, and the cognitive foundations of Persian? Is this not the dreamlike Iranian image of existence? Does not this very life in parallel time (sleep and waking—which is undoubtedly carried indirectly upon 'the wings of the Persian language' in the mind of each of us whose primary mental structure is shaped by Persian) facilitate the presence of belief in the living Unseen or the Hidden Imam (*Imam-e Zaman*)? As Shayegan puts it: '... at the level of mythic vision, the categories of time, space, and causality merge into one another.'

My head bows neither to this world nor to the hereafter;
Blessed be God for these tumults that stir within our head!

Where is that realm outside both this world and the hereafter, where in truth 'the head of Hafez'—or 'the secret (*serr*) of Hafez'—unfolds?

Intoxicate me so that in self-oblivion I may not know
Who came and who departed in the sphere of imagination.

This 'sphere of imagination' (*‘arseh-ye khiyal*) seems to possess a place of its own. Perhaps had Henry Corbin known this expression, instead of the Latin term *Mundus imaginalis* (active imagination), he would have employed this very phrase, 'sphere of imagination'.

At dawn the Elder of the tavern gave me the world-seeing cup,
And in that mirror made me aware of your beauty.

What is this world-seeing cup, or Cup of Jam, wherein we see in another manner, with another eye, and wherein other data reside?

6.8- Wine, intoxication, and mystical state (*hal*), love and illumination (*ishraq*), access to parallel time, and presence in the celestial realm (*Malakut*) attain balance, equilibrium, and harmony through the role of music.

Speak of the minstrel and the wine, and seek less the secret of time;
For no one has solved, nor shall ever solve, this riddle through philosophy (*hekmat*).

On the one hand, this points to the impossibility of unravelling the enigma of existence through philosophical reason; the only method is love.

Give glad tidings, O heart, for once again the minstrel of love
Has struck up an intoxicated melody and cured the hangover of longing.

Be not without wine and minstrel, for beneath the vault of heaven
With this song you may drive sorrow from the heart.

6.9- The Eighth Clime—which Henry Corbin calls the Eighth Earth or Eighth Country, and which Shayegan describes as that northern paradise named the land of *Var* in the sacred scripture of ancient Iran and *Hvar* in Zoroastrian cosmology—manifests clearly in the Eighth Clime of all our philosophers. This spiritual memory serves as a spring from whose waters the Iranian psyche slakes its thirst, drawing upon the spiritual heritage of its forebears. It is a world beheld with the eye and the heart, where words and books have no part:

O God, show unto the soul that station
Wherein speech grows without letters. (Mowlavi)

A wondrous science is the astronomy of love,
Whose eighth heaven is the seventh earth.

Again, as Shayegan states: 'In this world, by virtue of its disposition and metamorphosis, a kind of illuminative geography radiates forth, possessing its own mountains, springs, and rivers,' for in primordial memory these flowers, meadows, stars, moon, sun, and garden are the very images of the Garden of Eden. Thus it is that in the poetry of Hafez we never depart from the Garden of Eden; and in the collective Iranian mind and memory, whenever a poem does not speak of these categories, in popular parlance we do not call it 'poetry'.

6.10- Let us examine the concepts of the angel (*fereshteh*), the witness (*shahed*), and the *izad* (divine being). In Hafez's poetry, these bear a closer resemblance to their Mazdean antecedents—angels who are neither messengers nor servants.

At dawn the unseen herald (*hatef*) of the tavern said to me out of goodwill:
'Come back, for you are an ancient companion of this threshold.'

Indeed, the expressions 'celestial I', 'spiritual self' (*man-e minavi*), 'absent guide', 'Holy Spirit' (*Ruh al-Qodos*), 'angel of knowledge', and 'unseen herald' (*hatef*) undoubtedly spring from a single root: 'This inner guide, this hidden master—whatever the name, the role is ever the same: to awaken the soul exiled in this world and lead it to the encounter with its natural self.' [11]

If the grace of the Holy Spirit should lend aid once more,
Others too would perform what the Messiah used to do.

Come, cupbearer, for the unseen herald brought me the glad tiding:
'Bear the pain patiently, for I am sending you the remedy.'

6.11- The role of light in Persian myths as the manifestation of Ahura Mazda, the God of Wisdom, and of Mithra (*Mehr*), love, with the sun as the embodied manifestation of this light:

O heart, if you gain awareness of the light of guidance,
Like the candle you will be able to give up your head with a laugh.

Until the mote possesses lofty aspiration, O Hafez,
It will not become a seeker of the fountain of the radiant sun.

From the moment I set my face upon this threshold,
High above the throne of the sun has been my resting place.

Since all creatures live by your fragrance,
O Sun, withdraw not your shadow from us either.

Both worlds are a single radiance of his face;
I have told you—both the manifest and the hidden.

Here he speaks of the hidden world—a parallel world alongside the presence of the celestial realm (*Malakut*) and the spiritual earth running parallel to the manifest world.

You are no less than a mote; do not demean yourself—practise love,
So that, whirling, you may reach the sanctuary of the sun.

6.12- Is taking auguries (*fal*) and consulting the *Divan* of Hafez mere coincidence? Or does the widespread practice of the storyteller (*naqqal*) and of turning to Hafez reflect a collective need and belief—a hidden sign of a relationship established in another space and place between the seeker of the augury and Hafez? What reason—or better, what unconscious element—has bound 'Hafez' to this need to know the Unseen or the 'hidden'? Has not all this insistence in Hafez's poetry upon the presence of the witness (*shahed*), upon drinking intoxicating wine with the dwellers of the sanctuary of modesty and chastity of the celestial realm, and upon the dreams of yesternight, over time built the foundation for the collective belief that 'Hafez answers auguries'?

Do not depart from this door in despair; cast an augury—
It may be that the lot of fortune falls in our name.

A heart that reveals the Unseen and possesses the Cup of Jam—
What grief should it feel over a signet ring lost for a moment?

Though I know that solace of the heart will not grant the heart's desire,
I trace an image in imagination and cast a psychic augury.

7- It is time to turn to the ghazals of Hafez and analyse selected examples so that we may further illuminate the two axes in question (mythic foundations and the role of collective memory):

on the one hand, the deep presence of Iranian mythic values in Hafez; and on the other, the deployment of these myths through language and speech, which form the bedrock of a people's collective memory.

7.1- A ghazal opening with the couplet:

I declare it openly and rejoice in what I have said:
I am the servant of love and free from both worlds.

In this ghazal, Hafez is the bird of 'the sacred rose-garden'—let us read: 'the spiritual earth'—burning from separation and distance. The earthly world is 'the snare of contingency'; Adam brought him into this 'ruined abode' (*kharab-abad*). It is striking that if we consider the concept of 'Nowhere-land' (*Na-koja-abad*) coined by Shaykh al-Ishraq Suhrawardi, the relation between the earthly world, the 'ruined abode', and *Na-koja-abad*—or the Eighth Continent, or the spiritual earth—becomes much clearer. The servant of love is free from both worlds: Eden and Paradise, and today's world of life before and after 'life'. Thus love binds me to another place—or, so to speak, to another time—in such a way that it makes Hafez forget 'the shade of the Tuba tree, the blandishments of the houri, and the brink of the heavenly pool'.

In this ghazal, uncovering the direct relation between 'Mother Earth' (*madar-e giti*), 'the *alef* of the Beloved's stature', 'the darling of the people' (*jegar-gusheh-ye mardom*), 'the head of your street', and love requires deeper scrutiny. The concept of love is deployed as a worldview, an outlook on existence, a way of life—'since I became a bonded servant at the door of the tavern of love' and 'I am the servant of love and free from both worlds'. The 'present moment' (*hal*) and presence in the 'now', giving one's heart to 'the darling of the people', and learning only the '*alef* of the Beloved's stature', together with the relation to 'mother' and 'being born'—specifically Mother Earth, the feminine angel of the earth—lead us to some extent toward the locus of the concept of love, which, while immaterial, possesses a bodily and material form: the trace of 'the darling of the people', pointing to a 'human being' in abstract, universal, and material form; 'the *alef* of the Beloved's stature', which has an entirely 'signifying' aspect; and finally Mother Earth, which carries an imaginary aspect.

7.2- A ghazal opening with the couplet:

Joyous that day when I depart from this ruined dwelling,
Seek ease for the soul, and set out in pursuit of the Beloved of souls (*Janan*).

The 'ruined dwelling' or 'ruined abode' (*kharab-abad*) stands unmistakably in contrast to *Na-koja-abad*. Departure—or better, 'wayfaring', 'flowing' (*ravan*), or the union of the soul (*jan*) with the Beloved of souls (*janan*)—this need at once to depart and unite with *Janan*, and on the other hand to follow that 'gracefully swaying cypress', drawing near like a mote to the sun or the fountain of the sun, the source of light, affection (*mehr*), and love, going 'toward the tip of those dishevelled tresses'. Earthly love and love beyond the earth walk side by side.

7.3- A ghazal opening with the couplet:

Speak not to the pretender of the secrets of love and intoxication,
Lest he die unawares in the torment of self-worship.

'Love and intoxication' and their secrets belong to a single bowl, and require one who is 'informed'—'he to whom tidings came, no tidings of him ever returned'. Apart from being a lover, there is no way to read the intended love. And this 'intoxicating love' is bound in a certain manner to the narcissus-eye and the captivating affection (*mehr*) of the Beloved.

Consider the following ghazals:

A greeting like the sweet fragrance of familiarity
To that pupil of the eye of brightness.

O King of the fair ones, I cry out against the sorrow of solitude;
Without you the heart is at its last breath—it is time you returned.

O heart, if you emerge from that dimple of the chin,
Wherever you go, you will soon emerge in repentance.

In these ghazals, if we follow the hidden path of Hafez's movement by means of 'free association' [12] (bearing in mind that these ghazals were certainly composed at different times, since our method of selection follows the final letter of the closing word of the first hemistich), we gain a different view of what passed through Hafez's mind at the time of composition. From familiarity to the seclusion of the pious, disenchantment with everyone until finding the key in the quarter of the Magi, to the world ('the faithless bride'), and finally the complaint against hypocritical ascetics who may be accompanied by 'the covetous ego' (*nafs-e tame‘*), whereas 'the alchemy of felicity' lies in separation from them. It is as though the bride of the world, deceitful companions, hypocritical ascetics, and the covetous ego stand on one side, while the alchemy of felicity, kingship in beggary, and the quarter of the Magi stand on the other. An unbroken line links 'alchemy' and 'the Magi'—another path beyond the bride of the world, faithless companions, and fleeting time. In the second ghazal, the quest for the King of the fair ones is an ardent quest, haunted by the fear of losing patience in this search and by a return to the ancient principle that the pain of separation is itself the cure. In this enamel tavern (*minakadeh*), the path of wine and the hope for the sweet scent of union are the cure for the love-maddened lover. Observe how time in this ghazal has two dimensions: past, present, and future—marked by the verbs of complaining yesternight, the dancing of the morning breeze in the present, and 'favoured be whatever you think, commanded be whatever you decree' on the one hand, and in reply 'being free from oneself and one's own thought', migrating into the receptivity of living in parallel time on the other.

In the third ghazal, the heart and 'the Joseph of affection (*mehr*)' are both in the well; it is better that the former remain without the ear of reason in that Fountain of Life, for the moon, sun, morning, night, morning breeze, stream, and swaying cypress are all that image of the spiritual earth, and abiding therein is a journey through the parallel world of the celestial realm (*Malakut*).

8- Finally, drawing upon what has been outlined, we shall analyse eight ghazals of Hafez. In our view, the soul of all these ghazals bears a trace of the overarching design under consideration:

A ghazal opening with the couplet:

May your beauty be the sun of every gaze;
May it grow fairer still than the fairness of your fair face.

The beauty of the countenance of 'the sun of every gaze', which in a fresh instant creates love, cannot be the subject of a worldly discourse, nor of an earthly 'instant'. The scale of the sun's grandeur, radiance, and boundlessness and of that 'instant' fits along the two axes of the infinitely great and the infinitely small in such a way that it can unfold nowhere save outside earthly time—where the past passes into the future and the future into the present.

A ghazal opening with the couplet:

If the Sufi drinks wine in measure, may it be wholesome for him;
Otherwise, may the very thought of this act be forgotten by him.

The 'Elder' (*Pir*) is a Sufi who takes wine in measure; inevitably, his hand reaches the intended witness (*shahed-e maqsud*). It is here that he becomes forgiving of faults, and it is here that the 'Elder' is praised by Hafez in the final four couplets of the ghazal.

For years the heart begged us for the Cup of Jam,
Entreating from a stranger what it possessed itself.

The world-revealing Cup of Jam is the heart, which is with me and is purified by 'lifting the goblet'. The Messiah and his intermediary went nowhere other than 'purity of heart' or 'intoxication of heart', which is as it were a journey to the parallel world. And that 'I am the Truth' (*Ana al-Haqq*) of that Friend says the very same thing. What else besides another presence—being 'present' in possible time—could impel Hafez so decisively to declare: 'Others too would perform what the Messiah used to do'! There, knowing full well that gallows are raised by such words, the Wise Creator, God of intellect, placed the 'Cup of Jam' inside the heart before 'time and space' (before raising this azure dome). Consider how in this ghazal the Magian Elder, the tresses of idols, the Cup of Jam, the Wise One, God, the staff of Moses, the Messiah, the Holy Spirit, and Hallaj—who seemingly cannot coexist in one place—come together through Hafez's 'free association' with utmost gentleness, delicacy, and harmony to become the architects of 'another world' that, in Hafez's imaginative power, inscribes the image of our distant mythic paradise. 'I myself am that Cup of Kay Khosrow,' says Shaykh al-Ishraq Suhrawardi [13].

What intoxication is this—I know not—that has turned toward us?
Who was the cupbearer, and whence did he bring this wine?

'Intoxication' unfolds across a tableau that stretches from the cupbearer, the wine, the harp, and the sweet-voiced bird to the untying of knots by the morning breeze and the arrival of the rose, the wild rose, and the violet. It is like the image of 'Eden, Paradise', the first and final Garden, to which the guidance of the Magian Elder and his command of intoxication lead Hafez—that very place where the Shaykh, with his promised paradise, remained helpless. How could one fail to recognise in this sequence of 'Hafez's felicitous state' a sign of the lingering psyche, the image of the celestial earth within the expressive depths of Persian literature, speech, culture, and myth—or more simply, the Persian 'word'? Indeed, it is this 'shadow of the jewel of the mother tongue's speech' that, unseen, hidden, and quiet, has forged this bond between earthly history and spiritual history.

I, and the disavowal of wine—what tale could this be?
Usually I possess at least this much reason and competence.
The poet's free 'association' draws him into an 'imaginary quarrel'
with a companion who urges him to renounce wine; and the Magian Elder, love, intoxication, guidance, and *rendi* (inspired nonconformity) are set over against asceticism and formal prayer.

Yesternight at dawn they rescued me from sorrow,
And in that darkness of night they gave me the Water of Life.

It is difficult to add a superfluous word to this ghazal. Dawn, sunrise—where light engenders wine. Thus that long night must bring tidings of the manifestation of the 'Essence'; it obtains the heart's desire, and that unseen herald (*hatef*, the spiritual self) had already brought glad tidings of this union. And Hafez, as the singer of honey and sugar, as the keeper (*hafez*) of presence, as the keeper of the secret, becomes 'the confidant of the secret'—in other words, Hafez becomes 'Hafez'. The next ghazal, opening with 'Yesternight I saw angels knocking at the tavern door', undoubtedly brings the tale to its close.

9- In this section we leave the continuation of the task to the reader, turning to scattered couplets from Hafez's ghazals to question him:

Through hope of his face, the heart does not become the companion of the soul;
Through longing for his street, the soul does not serve the body.

Hope of him and longing for his street obstruct the concord of heart and soul, and the service of the soul to the body. Who is this 'he' who sows division among the three elements—'heart', 'body', and 'soul'—or, so to speak, walks gracefully between I, I, and I? Where is 'his street'? This 'he' is Hafez's own question as well.

Within my weary-hearted interior, I know not who it is
That while I am silent, he is in lamentation and uproar.

Hafez, if you seek the Water of Eternal Life,
Its source is the dust at the threshold of the dervishes' retreat.

Preacher, do not counsel the love-frenzied, for we
Would not glance at Paradise in exchange for the dust of the Beloved's street.

The garden of Paradise, the shade of the Tuba tree, and the palace of the houri
I do not equate with the dust of the Beloved's street.

I, to whom today a ready-money Paradise is granted—
Why should I believe the ascetic's promise of tomorrow?

Is not the dust of the Beloved's street or the retreat of the dervishes that very 'ready-money' Paradise, the Paradise of the 'present', the existing Paradise, or the parallel Paradise—such that he regards the tale of Paradise as an anecdote of his street, or that Hafez's irony speaks of 'others too would perform what the Messiah used to do', and elsewhere:

I have seen no sweeter poetry than yours, Hafez,
By the Qur'an that you hold within your breast.

Through 'free association', he sets his own speech alongside the 'eloquence' of the Qur'an. What could have made him so conscious of 'himself' that 'unconsciously'—through 'free association'—he involuntarily sees his own word as equal in weight to the word of the Qur'an?

Another question:

What marvel of a figure are you, O sweet-skilled master horseman,
That you are right before the eye yet absent from sight?

Save in a world where the encounter takes place in a different space—or, in other words, where two gazes exist at one time, in one place, in the present—what meaning could this verse have?

In the following verses, can the role of 'imagination' (*khiyal*) be understood merely as 'dream and fancy' in everyday speech, or is imagination a power, a possibility realised through effort?

It nurtures the fancy of encompassing the sea—alas!
What ambitions lie in the head of this impossible-dreaming drop!

Or observe the depiction of 'the Beloved's image' in 'the gaze'—what delicacy:

Whenever I long to behold my soul,
In my gaze I depict the image of your fair face.

This gaze, and the power of depiction, stand equal to seeing. Is this seeing the same 'seeing'?

A discussion of 'the mediated relationship between Shaykh Ruzbahan and Hafez' lies beyond the scope of this essay; yet as a fitting close, observe the verb 'to see' in this sentence from the Shaykh in *‘Abhar al-‘Ashiqin*:

'As for me, I beheld his beauty in the form of a red rose; it was like a world within a world from which red roses rained down, and this spectacle had neither limit nor shore.'

Undoubtedly Hafez's seeing is the very speech of Shaykh Ruzbahan, drawn toward the concrete beauty of words, the fresh fragrance of poetry, and the beauty of the image forged by Hafez's supreme taste. Ruzbahan says: '... you are in the veil of your "you-ness"; if you step out of your "you-ness", the veil of wrath will lift...'; and Hafez says: 'You yourself are your own veil, Hafez; rise up from the midst!'

Ruzbahan says: '... show forth the world-displaying cup; how long will you keep us weary? Do you not know that the nest of the bird of the celestial realm (*Malakut*) is in our house?' And Hafez says:

I am that bird whose whistle comes every evening and dawn
From the roof and the Throne...

I am a bird of the garden of the celestial realm; I am not of the world of dust...

I asked: 'When did the Wise One give you this world-seeing cup?'...

Spread your wings and sing from the Tuba tree;
It is a pity for a bird like you to remain captive in a cage.

(Henry Corbin notes that the Tuba tree is the tree of the spiritual earth.)

10- Hafez's message also bears signs of other factors rooted in cultural transformations. Cultural invasions undoubtedly foster an 'inward turn'. The presence of Islamic culture, its concepts, and its beliefs likewise found their place. The synthesis of Iranian mythic vision and Islamic vision in the form of mysticism (*‘erfan*) and its varied hues left its mark upon his poetry.

Our aim here is not to offer one single, exclusive key to unlocking the secret of Hafez, but rather to dwell upon and emphasise one among these keys.

In Hafez's poetry, the beliefs of his era—especially the role of fate and destiny ('What primordial allotment they apportioned in our absence...'), attention to the stars (that is, astrology), and the influence of the stars upon the earth—appear repeatedly. On the other hand, 'self-sufficiency' (*bi-niazi*), renouncing 'the world', and renouncing 'power' during the few brief days of earthly life constitute one of the foundational pillars of his poetry.

The fluctuations of Hafez's thought, like those of any human being, are visible throughout his poems. He lays his perplexity before the Magian Elder and suddenly despairs of finding an answer ('The secret of this veil remains hidden and shall remain hidden'). He mocks those who claim to have found imaginary answers, calling them pretentious physicians. Yet for all that, he never relinquishes the longing for union and the quest to find his own jewel.

Appendix 1

Poems in the *Divan* of Hafez that are in some way connected to the concept of the Magian Elder (*Pir-e Moghan*) may be gathered into four groups:

1- Poems in which the term *Pir-e Moghan* (Magian Elder) is explicitly used.

2- Poems which, through studying their relationships with preceding and succeeding poems, can be confirmed as pertaining to the concept of the Magian Elder.

3- Poems from which the concept of the Magian Elder can be drawn by allusion or by somewhat indirect interpretation and commentary.

4- Poems connected by a shared mediating concept to another poem that contains the term *Pir-e Moghan*.

Furthermore, the relation between the 'Magian Elder' and other concepts in Hafez's poetry may be recognised in two ways: either this relation appears openly in the poem, or it must be extracted from hidden links across the body of his other poems. In any case, given the lack of full access to critical editions of Hafez's *Divan*, minor errors may appear here. This research can achieve its full weight only when the concept of the 'Magian Elder' in the literature of Hafez's era is thoroughly dissected and the role of 'time' is inscribed within it—and, if possible, when the poems containing the concept of the Magian Elder are arranged and analysed in chronological order of composition, reflecting the growth and maturation of Hafez's thought. Here, we have contented ourselves with ordering them according to the final letter of the ghazal's rhyme. Another task that remains to be undertaken is refining the present conclusions in the crucible of criticism, so as to verify whether within the corpus of Hafez's ghazals—among poems unrelated to the 'Magian Elder'—anything can be found that contradicts our theory and conclusions.

Let us proceed to the heart of the matter:

1- Why should we turn away from the threshold of the Magian Elder?
Fortune resides in that abode, and spiritual opening at that door.

(Fortune and spiritual opening come from the Magian Elder; Hafez's attachment to the Magian Elder perhaps answers the critics as to why the Magian Elder—because it is he who grants opening and 'fortune'.)

2- It is I whose cloister is the corner of the tavern;
Prayer to the Magian Elder is my morning litany.

(Hafez prays to the Magian Elder instead of God.)

3- If the Magian Elder became our spiritual guide, what difference does it make?
There is no head in which there is not a secret from God.

(The Magian Elder is a resolver of difficulties and unravels the enigma.)

4- I said: 'Wine and the patched frock are not the rite of religion';
He said: 'This practice is observed in the religion of the Magian Elder.'

(The religion of the Magian Elder is the rite of wine and the patched frock.)

5- They trouble the peaceful hour of the Magian Elder once again;
Behold these wayfarers, see what they do to the Elder!

(These wayfarers vex my Magian Elder.)

6- I am a disciple of the Magian Elder; be not angry with me, O Shaykh,
For you merely made the promise, while he fulfilled it.

(Hafez is a disciple of the Magian Elder. In comparison with the Shaykh, Hafez has chosen the Magian Elder.)

7- I am the servant of the Magian Elder, who frees me from ignorance;
Whatever our Elder does is the very essence of grace.

(Hafez is the servant of the Magian Elder. It is he who frees Hafez from ignorance, and whatever the Magian Elder does is right and pure grace.)

8- Behold the goodness of the Magian Elder: for whatever we, ill-behaved drunkards,
Did, was beautiful in his generous eye.

(The Magian Elder possesses a generosity that sees no sin or wrongdoing—perhaps a rebuke to the worshipper, the ascetic, and the Sufi, who judge human conduct as good or evil.)

9- From eternity I have worn the ring of the Magian Elder in my ear;
We remain as we were, and so it shall ever be.

(I have been and shall remain the servant of the Magian Elder.)

10- If I sought aid from the Magian Elder, do not blame me;
Our Shaykh said there was no magnanimity in the monastery.

(No help can be had from the monastery. I sought aid from the Magian Elder.)

11- Long live the fortune of the Magian Elder, for the rest is easy;
Let another go and blot my name from memory.

(Hafez cares only that the 'Magian Elder' remain enduring, sound, and fortunate, and gives no thought to his standing with others.)

12- Should sorrow spring an ambush from a corner of the heart,
The sanctuary of the Magian Elder's threshold suffices as your refuge.

(Hafez takes refuge from sorrow with the Magian Elder.)

13- I, who wish to drink nothing save the pure wine of the vat,
What can I do if I do not heed the word of the Magian Elder?

(Hafez heeds only the word of the Magian Elder, who bids him drink wine.)

14- More than forty years have passed while I boast
That I am the humblest among the servants of the Magian Elder.

(For years Hafez has been a servant of the Magian Elder, though not a perfected servant.)

15- In this tumult where no one asks after another,
I accept obligation from the Magian Elder.

(Hafez stands in suppliant relation to the Magian Elder in a place where no one bows to another.)

16- I shall not abandon the service of the Magian Elder,
For therein I do not see my true interest.

(Hafez's true interest lies in continuing to serve the Magian Elder, contrary to the counsel of others.)

17- I am a Sufi of the cloister of the sacred realm, yet
At present the temple of the Magi is my appointed abode.

(Now that Hafez lives upon the earth, he prefers to dwell in the Magian temple.)

18- If the Magian Elder grew weary of my repentance,
Tell him: 'Clarify the wine, for I stand ready to apologise.'

(Offering apologies, Hafez seeks to return to the Magian Elder.)

19- If the Magian Elder does not open the door before me,
At which door shall I knock, and where shall I seek a remedy?

(The sole source of remedy is the Magian Elder.)

20- Hafez, the threshold of the Magian Elder is the haven of fidelity;
Go, recite the lesson of the discourse of love, and hear it from him.

(The Magian Elder stays with you, and of love you can speak with him alone.)

21- Stain your prayer mat with wine if the Magian Elder bids you,
For the wayfarer is not unacquainted with the ways and customs of the stations.

(The Magian Elder is a seasoned wayfarer and knows everything; obey—obey utterly.)

From studying the poems above, one may clearly conclude that:

Hafez is the disciple, servant, attendant, dust of the threshold, and obedient listener of the Magian Elder. He holds a dialogue with him, and this bond is ancient and enduring; he heeds him alone; there is great pressure to separate Hafez from the Magian Elder, and if he at times yields, he returns with apologies; in an age when no one bows his neck to another, Hafez bows his neck to the Magian Elder. Nevertheless, the relationship is not wholly one-sided: Hafez too has things to say, and the relationship takes the form of a dialogue. With a somewhat lesser degree of certainty, one may also say that:

- The Magian Elder speaks of love and wine-drinking, resolves difficulties, and dispels sorrow. Regarding the relationship between God, Hafez, and the Magian Elder, one may say that the Magian Elder opposes formal worship, and Hafez chooses the Magian Elder over formal worship. To attain the concept of God, Hafez chooses the path offered by the Magian Elder. Love and finding the way to love, wine, the fact that Hafez has a perplexity, bears sorrow, is downcast, and strives to resolve his perplexity—despite all flights and returns, he chooses the Magian Elder as his spiritual master (*morad*); the Magian Elder is not censorious and follows a method different from others; he speaks of love and recommends wine as the means to comprehend it.

In other words, is Hafez's perplexity not the comprehension of the world and of his own existence? And does he not search for an answer to his question, experimenting with diverse paths? What question, what guide, what path, and what way? This mode of analysis and these questions must be pursued across Hafez's other poems. Yet for all this, the guide and master for Hafez, through every rise and fall, remains ultimately the Magian Elder. Who is the Magian Elder? Where is he, and what did he do? We possess only a delicate, distant outline of him. The path is apparently love. In other poems of Hafez, other paths such as the seminary (*madreseh*), asceticism and worship, and Sufism are also mentioned.

Hafez chooses love. What path is this, and what are its distinguishing features? One must search for it in Hafez's other poems. The vehicle for traversing this path is wine itself. In this brief study, given the limitations of research resources, an effort has been made to extract the concept of the Magian Elder across all of Hafez's poems. As it appears, the Magian Elder is the sole figure who is never subjected to Hafez's sarcasm, invective, or mockery—unlike the ascetic, the devotee, the Sufi, the shaykh, the market inspector (*mohtaseb*), the scholars of the seminary, and the rest...

Appendix 2

A Glance at the Influence of Mythic Concepts on Contemporary Literature

The following examples were gathered quite by chance while reading newspapers and magazines that happened to be at hand. In all likelihood, the authors of these pieces were far removed from any precise 'historical-mythic' knowledge of the concepts they were invoking; yet, as noted, this collective essence keeps itself alive in our 'hidden' depths, lives on, and surfaces here and there.

1- A poem by Pour-Nasirinezhad — *Donya-ye Sokhan* journal, Shahrivar and Mehr 1373 (August–October 1994).

Butterflies and Angels

(My mother, without having composed a poem—spoke in poetic utterance—butterflies are the two wings of angels—with silvery, amber hues—from that time on we—held the butterfly in reverence—within our hearts—and ascribed a kinship between flowers and butterflies—and wherever we saw a flower—of amber yellow or silver hue—we did not find the place of angels empty there—even today we remain that child with a celestial mind—wherever we see a butterfly, we mount its wings up to the sky.)

(Bearing in mind that *parvanak* is a Manichaean term meaning saviour and guide of the soul, or angel), the poet begins through free association with the mother and the mother tongue; like a child with a celestial mind, he everywhere beholds the 'butterfly–angel of the soul' through the teaching of the mother tongue.

2- Throughout Persian songs we see, here and there, the trace of this lost angel of the soul or lost 'spiritual I', both manifest and hidden. One example:

The night I heard the song of your reed-flute, like a thirsty gazelle I ran after you

Running, running, I reached the edge of the spring; I saw no sign of wine or melody

O Peri, where are you, that you show not your face, nor open a door from that hidden Paradise?

Everywhere I have searched for you—from moon and sun I have asked tidings of you—I have caught your scent from the rose—for that reason I have clung to the rose's hem—my heart wanders bewildered by you, my breath is steeped in you—in the garden of dreams I smell you like a rose—in water and mirror I seek you like the moon—O Peri, where are you? On this Yalda night I strive after you—in sleep and waking I speak to you—moon and star know my pain, for like me they wander in search of you—appear one night beside the spring—amid my tears it opened like a rose.

This thirst and longing to find an 'angel' who opens the gate of Paradise and is bound up with the rose, wine, and melody—while moon, star, and sun likewise pursue it—is the very thing Hafez seeks in his 'laments'. The 'free association' of words by the lyricist of a song once so widely popular is noteworthy: his breath is steeped in it; it is far and near, present and absent.

3- A poem by 'Mahyar'

Chiaroscuro

I am heartsick of this earth; where is another sky?
In another sky, where is another galaxy?

My eyes and these stars—how long flickering at one another?
I want another eye in another flickering.

Hafez, what became of wine and goblet, of a new design and another?
What became of the cupbearer, what became of joy, where is another scattering of blossoms?

In the grip and double grip of this time, in every bound and boundless expanse,
I desire another place within another time.

O nomad of the desert, where is the road to the traceless plain?
Perhaps therein I may find of myself another name and trace.

He seeks the promised intoxication in another place that lies in another time—neither in the bounded nor in the boundless, but beyond the traceless plain—so that thereby he may perhaps find another name and trace in this *Na-koja-abad*. We see how this symbol of the 'other I' in the 'celestial earth' lives on amid the folds of poetry.

4- A poem by Mohammad-Baqer Kolahi Ahari, *Negah-e No* journal, Azar–Bahman 1373 (November 1994–February 1995).

The Sublime World

(They are the sparrows of the afternoon—or the spokespersons of the sublime world—a quieter silence and a serene Gabriel—with the parrot of wisdom upon his shoulder—and a green bottle of rain and wind—a snake in the chest and a green parrot in the cage—and the bottle of rain upon this brown pulpit—and a blessed Gabriel who is my guest.)

Where is the 'sublime world' (*jahan-e barin*)? A serene and blessed Gabriel is here the poet's guest: a sublime world parallel to our world, and Gabriel who is not merely the guest of the prophet, but the guest of the poet, accompanied by the snake and the parrot—the symbol of sexuality and the symbol of speech. Is this mere chance?

5- To adorn this appendix, we cite a poem by Allameh Tabataba'i, which opens this hemistich of Hafez: 'From your friends he learned in the path of affection (*mehr*)...':

Ever I say and have said many a time: my faith is the affection of the beloveds.

Worship lies in intoxication in the religion of love; outside this circle are the sober ones.

In the quarter of lovers they raised walls between the heart and desire.

How many Farhads have died in the mountains; how many Hallajs have mounted the gallows!

The noblest lovers, who are free, cast strings into the snare of the soul.

Steeped in themselves they have departed—how many colourful flowers by the streams!

Beware, be not deceived by the world, for at the foot of this flower lie thorns.

6- A section from the narrative poem *Marshes and Waters*, composed by Seyyed Hasan Hoseyni, 1374 (1995–1996).

This is the affair: yes, the affair is repetitive; our wound is ancient, infinitely deep.

I ask you: what became of that Ahuric ardour? What became of the wing of ascension and the imagination that traverses the Throne?

Behind these ruins of the mind, is there a city? There is not. For the venom of this heart-deadness, is there an antidote? There is not.

Ahuric ardour, the imagination that traverses the Throne, and the quest for a city, a place, a *Na-koja-abad* beyond this ruined abode (*kharab-abad*).

* This paper was first presented at the Third Symposium on Research into Ancient Culture and Avestan Studies, organised by the Rudaki Association, in Hamburg.

[1] Sigmund Freud, founder of clinical psychoanalysis.
[2] Jacques Lacan, French psychoanalyst and psychiatrist, died in 1980.
[3] Henry Corbin, French orientalist, founder of the Department of Iranian Studies at the French Embassy in Iran, died in 1979, Paris.
[4] 'Sign' (*neshaneh*) is used here as the equivalent of the French word *signifiant* (signifier). Every word is composed of two parts: one is its sign, which is the same for all, and the other is the concept of the word, which differs for each individual.

[5] 'Acoustic image' (*tasvir-e sowti*) is used as the equivalent of the French *image acoustique*—in effect, signs in their phonic form.
[6] Sigmund Freud, *The Joke and Its Relation to the Unconscious* (*Kalam-e Ravan*).

Freud Sigmund: Le mot d’esprit et la relation á l’inconcient, Folio, France.

fr.title: Compte rendu d'ouvrage : L'ontologie de Hafez
fr.executive_summary: https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/01/DSC0625-Copier.jpg Cet article a été publié pour la première fois dans la revue Âftâb, n° 42, mordâd 1379 (juillet-août 2000).
