en.body_markdown:
https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/01/DSC0625-Copier.jpg

This article was first published in *Aftab* journal, No. 42, Mordad 1379 [July–August 2000].

Preamble:

In this essay, I intend to demonstrate that the author of *The Ontology of Hafez* (1) places a variety of difficulties in his own path:

- The author excises pre-Islamic Iranians from history.

- The author has not grasped the concept of myth.

- The author is unacquainted with the contemporary theories of Freud, Jung, and Eliade regarding the path that leads anthropology towards mythology and oral history.

- The author clings to presuppositions in which he leaves himself no room for doubt or hesitation.

- The author contends that Hafez is merely an exponent and repeater of the mystics of the Khorasan school, to such an extent that in his writing Hafez is relegated to a footnote.

- [Maintaining] that the mystics of the Khorasan school placed the mystical interpretation (*ta'vil*) of Creation in the Quran at the summit of their ontological knowledge.

- The author reduces "ontological enquiry" to the level of examining and studying the genesis of humankind from Hafez's perspective.

- The author suffers from a traditionalist view of history and historical products and transformations, rather than a dynamic vision leading to the interpenetration of phenomena and cultures—as though culture in Iran began only with the presence of Islam.

- The author is unaware of Hafez scholars and the work of hundreds of researchers who have investigated Hafez's thought and produced valuable works, addressing instead only a narrow branch of Hafez researchers who are under the sway of a religious worldview and base their enquiry and outlook on belief in a "Creator".

- In a scholarly work, diverse opposing and supporting theories ought to be presented and discussed; in many places, the theories of others are forgotten or passed over with exceedingly brief remarks.

- Ashouri's endeavour in his writing on Hafez is a continuation of the very same effort summarised in other dimensions by the following statement: "Contemporary Iranian history has now been reduced to three things: the Constitutional Revolution and the leadership of Sheikh Fazlollah; the Oil Nationalisation Movement and the leadership of Kashani; and the Islamic Revolution, whose historical roots in the 1978–79 Revolution go back to 15 Khordad 1342 [5 June 1963], and even that monopolised by a particular faction." (11)

One might say that this very same effort is under way in its cultural dimensions so as to give everything a religious, sectarian, Islamic, and divine colour. On page 22 we read:

"The most fundamental characteristic of Hafez's world in the realm of thought... is that it is a religious world, looking upon the world through the prism of religion and religious understanding..."

And it is gratifying that amidst this all-encompassing campaign by the masters of religion and state to portray everything and everyone as Islamic, there are those who write in widely circulated periodicals published in Iran: "...the secret of Hafez's endurance and his becoming a place of pilgrimage for the *rends* of the world lies in the depths of the enduring mysteries of Iranian culture." (12)

Preface

Although the author occasionally displays skill in coining lexical equivalents—such as choosing *sarnemoun* for *Archetype*, *mesalvareh* for *Paradigmatie*, and *nasaznama* for *Paradoxal*—in choosing the title of his book he indulges in an ambition that complicates both his task and ours. "The Ontology" of Hafez, and presented "by way of" an enquiry into the foundations of his thought, leads "us" into "difficulties".

Ontology is the one discipline of knowledge which, unless it is all-encompassing, cannot be regarded as a comprehensive investigation. The work might better have been titled: *An Attempt at Exploring the Foundations of Hafez's Thought Based on Two Presuppositions: Archetype and the Mysticism of the Khorasan School*. Had the book borne such a title, the reader would not be crushed beneath the heavy weight of the "ontological". For the field of ontology is boundless, and exploring this field requires a lofty perspective soaring above ontologies—an intricate undertaking, and by no means an easy one.

In the opening pages of the book, under the heading "The Ontological Model of Hafez", the researcher introduces his foundational presuppositions to the reader by drawing upon the data and findings of Berkeley, Jung, and Eliade.

We read: "The fundamental ontological model in Hafez's world—that is, the civilisation and culture of which he is the heir—like all traditional civilisations and cultures, is an archetypal model! That is, a world in which, upon the foundation of myths, archetypes or exemplary models are furnished that serve as patterns of behaviour for humankind. At the centre of these myths stands the central myth, namely the myth of Creation, in which the primordial event that is the origin and fountainhead of worldly events is recounted." And in the footnote on the same page we read:

"...just as the archetype of the Perfect Human in the mystical understanding of the myth of Creation in the Quran is Adam himself, whose behaviour in the myth, according to its mystical interpretation, serves as a pattern of behaviour for Hafez as well."

To put it more plainly, according to the author: "All of Hafez's discourse lies in the myth of Creation and the primordial event that is the origin and fountainhead of worldly events, according to the mystical interpretation of the myth of Creation in the Quran." The remaining sections of the work are devoted to tracing this very presupposition. Engaging with the ideas of Jung and Eliade bears fruit only when we examine the roots of what they have said—because they devoted themselves to human oral culture, which is founded upon "language and speech", and drew upon the structure of language as well as the bond and essence embedded within language.

Dariush Ashouri quotes Jung: "...myths, in their diverse narrative forms among various peoples, contain those universal patterns of the mind which, in Jung's view, reside in the collective unconscious and are inherited through lineage and descent." Today we know that this path of "lineage and descent" is precisely the expanse of the field and structure of language and oral culture (2). And herein lies the secret: Hafez's archetypal myth, which dwells in the expanse of the Dari Persian language, cannot be a Quranic model, let alone its mystical interpretation. If we seek an archetype for Hafez, we must seek it within the expanse of Persian oral culture, for Persian language and myth are older than the Quran. It is precisely at this point that the researcher goes astray. This is the very same trap that has tainted the oral and written history of Persian speakers—the same trap that replaced the history of Iranian Islam with post-Safavid Shi'ite history; the same trap that compelled the great figures of Iranian thought and literature to stitch their discourse, bound as it is to *Mehr* and love, into the shirt of the Quran in order to survive. At times, when Hafez says:

Love will come to your rescue even if, like Hafez,
You recite the Quran by heart in fourteen canonical readings

To put it differently, Hafez draws his archetype from the rose-hued elder (*Pir-e Golrang*), Sheikh Ruzbahan, and the Master of Illumination (*Sheikh-e Eshraq*, Suhrawardi), where Suhrawardi writes: "Read the Quran as though it were written for you."

Let us return to another passage of the book, where the trap of the "primordial myth of the Quran" pulls Ashouri's writing in every direction. On page 33 we read: "We know of no divan or collection of Persian ghazals containing so many historical markers." If we mean the mythological history of the people of the land of Iran and Persian speakers, it is precisely in that direction and presentation that Hafez's *Divan* contains minimal reference to our mythological history; and if it is the history of a psychic journey, an inner journey, or an illuminative journey, we cannot call that a historical marker.

Here, out of the entirety of the oral and mythological history of the Iranian people from time immemorial, the researcher contents himself solely with Quranic mythological history—which is none other than the foundational Abrahamic myths. Hafez's repeated returns to Persian mythological figures such as Jam, Kay, and Kavus (3) have been ignored. In a digression on page 34 of his book, the author refers to the "wayfaring soul" and writes: "Yet this travelogue, while unfolding upon earth during the lifetime of Mohammad Hafez of Shiraz and recounting aspects of his life story and that of his contemporaries, insofar as it is a spiritual travelogue, fundamentally recounts the memories, adventures, and experiences of the wayfaring soul, whose passage runs from pre-eternity (*azal*) to post-eternity (*abad*)—a story that begins with the descent of the 'spirit' (*ruh*) from the spiritual realm, from its original homeland, into the earthly world, and whose culmination is its return once more to its homeland." Here it is not without merit to dissect the fundamental disparity between the two outlooks—"Islamic" and "Iranian mythological"—towards Creation. In Islam, *azal* and *abad* are the beginning and end of time, and between them flows the time in which our lives unfold; whereas in Iranian myth, a world and a time exist parallel to this time, such that our body resides in this world—the earthly globe—while our soul (*ravan*) and the souls of other things reside in that parallel world, and our striving to attain that *ravan* forms the basis of the illuminative experience. What the esteemed researcher refers to as the "wayfaring soul" has nothing to do with the *ruh* (spirit), which is a Quranic and Islamic phenomenon—and this is perhaps one of the points that repeatedly places the author in difficulty when unpacking Hafez's poems.

Humanity's understanding of myth is exceedingly new and modern! Yet on page 51 he writes: "The mythic account essentially possesses no rational form and does not originate from human reason, but reaches humankind from the unseen realm, on the basis of absolute divine authority..." How can one treat myth—"the memory of human oral culture"—as stemming from the unseen realm while simultaneously claiming that one's research is a theoretical and scientific work? What sort of science is this? On the one hand, Iranian mythology has no place whatsoever in his research; on the other, he begins from Islam, and if cultural influence and cross-fertilisation are occasionally acknowledged, even that comes from Greece.

He views the sphere of studying influences of "cognition" in the same light as the influences of oral cultures, the effects of language and ethnic history, and their mutual absorption and fusion.

In a way, the researcher himself arrives at the question of why "loving mysticism" (*erfan-e asheqaneh*) takes shape in Iran, yet he passes quietly by it. On page 56 of the book we read: "...which in the Islamic world, and especially in the Iranian world and within the space of the Persian language, prepares the ground for loving mysticism to emerge from the heart of ascetic Sufism." What he calls "the space of the Persian language" is that very essence preserved within language: it is *Mehr*, which is at once "sun" and "love", and it is that intricate play of Hafez's poems revolving between the two poles of love and light—such that he sees no sweeter memorial capable of enduring than the voice of the speech of love (here it is not a matter of mere hearing, for this voice is accompanied by light). One must ask how this love (*eshq*)—which is neither named nor even alluded to in any verse of the Quran—can serve as the fundamental basis of Hafez's ontology while not once being mentioned in the Quran. The counterpart of the word *eshq* in the Quran is *mahabbat*, a concept which in none of the verses mentions an amorous relationship between humankind and "Allah" (5)—so much so that the author of the book contents himself with a single hadith from the Prophet as documentary proof of an amorous relationship between humankind and Allah in Islam. The endeavours of scholars such as Sigmund Freud, Jung, Eliade, and others in the twentieth century were aimed at understanding precisely why mythic cognition endures within the mould of languages and is transmitted across the cultural epochs of human societies. In this connection, one may recall the invaluable work of Henry Corbin, who over more than thirty years traced the origins of concepts such as "time", "illumination" (*eshraq*), the imaginal world (*alam-e mesali*), and so forth among early Iranian mystics from Suhrawardi and Sheikh Ruzbahan down to the Shaykhiyya—showing how structures latent within the words of a language and culture remain the vehicles bearing mythic concepts and, like subterranean waters, continue their cultivation. It is for this very reason that over the course of time this fertile earthly river bursts forth like artesian wells from the hearts of beloved figures such as Hafez.

The author's estrangement from pre-Islamic Iranian culture is such that even in understanding post-Islamic mystical concepts he falls into conflation. Thus, in Iranian mysticism, the imaginal world (*alam-e mesali*) or *Hurqalya* is an intermediary world between the higher world, the world of mysteries, the esoteric world, and the world of Divine Names on one side, and the corporeal world and the world of sense and matter on the other (page 59). Yet he aligns the imaginal world with the Platonic world of Ideas. On this matter, one should consult the introduction to the book *Spiritual Body and Celestial Earth: From Mazdean Iran to Shi'ite Iran* (*Zamin-e Minavi, Kalbod-e Ensan dar Ruz-e Rastakhiz, az Iran-e Mazda'i ta Iran-e Shi'i*). Because the author understands myth in its Quranic sense, he devotes several lengthy sections to tracing the myth of Creation in the scriptures of Judaism and Christianity, knowing full well that the mythic or legendary roots of the Quran draw from the Torah.

The author advances a presupposition to the effect that Hafez's "ontology" revolves around the "Creation of Adam", and in proof of this claim he reads Hafez's poems along these lines and categorises them accordingly—in such a manner that through them he may harmonise Hafez's cognition with two books: Najm al-Din Razi's *Mersad al-Ebad* and Abu al-Fazl Rashid al-Din Meybodi's *Kashf al-Asrar*. Earlier, in the book *Yek Qesseh Bish Nist* (*It Is But One Tale*), Hasan Anvari, in dissecting the ghazal opening with "Last night I saw angels knocking at the tavern door...", had already referred to Najm al-Din Razi's *Mersad al-Ebad* and the story of Creation and its mystical interpretation. Bearing in mind that Anvari's book was published in 1368 [1989] and Dariush Ashouri's book in 1377 [1998], how fitting it would have been if the author had made at least a brief mention of Hasan Anvari's work. Where the author writes: "The present book is a theoretical and scientific answer to the question 'What does Hafez say?' and an identification of that inner logic which binds together and unifies all his diverse and richly meaningful symbols, concepts, and expressions—without seeking ideas of our own choosing," it would have been better to say that the present book is one of the attempts made, rather than claiming it is a theoretical and scientific answer. In the prologue we read: "Hafez is the greatest enigma of our culture." If this statement is true, our culture is undoubtedly conceived as the culture of present-day Persian speakers of Iran, and this culture was not born overnight. It has gathered drop by drop over thousands of years, mingled with other cultures, and existed within the field of the law of mutual influence. And I suspect the author's deviation begins precisely here: in defining culture, he starts it from the Islamic mystical culture of Iran. The author states that amidst "the vast mass of things written about him, I have found no article or book that truly brings me a satisfying answer to the question 'What does Hafez say?'". How helpful it would have been had he also introduced his primary reading sources to us.

In this prologue we read: "In this book I have endeavoured to approach this *Divan* with a preconceived method and set of principles so as ultimately to give a scientific and theoretical answer to the question 'What does Hafez say?'. Accordingly, this work is neither an endorsement of Hafez's thought and worldview nor a refutation of it, but solely a scientific enquiry into the morphology of Hafez's thought. Yet the question underlying this study is of fundamental importance not only for Hafez studies, but also for understanding the foundations of our culture and mentality. Indeed, unlocking the *Divan* of Hafez and striving to understand it theoretically is indispensable for unlocking our inherited culture and striving to understand it from a contemporary perspective."

Upon reading the book, we expect the author to introduce his preconceived method and principles and then to unlock our inherited culture. Our review of this book rests upon these very two points, and we endeavour to show what this method is, to what extent the author has grasped and applied it, and how far it bears the imprint of our inherited culture.

An Examination of the Ontological Model of Hafez in Dariush Ashouri's Writing

The gist of the researcher's argument, which forms the foundation of his work, appears on page 29:

"The fundamental ontological model in Hafez's world—that is, the civilisation and culture of which he is the heir—like all traditional civilisations and cultures, is a mythic-archetypal model. That is, a world in which, upon the foundation of myths, archetypes or transcendent models are furnished that serve as patterns of behaviour for humankind. At the centre of these myths stands the central myth, namely the myth of Creation, in which the primordial event that is the origin and fountainhead of worldly events is recounted." At the end of his commentary on the term *sarnemoun* (Archetype) in the footnote on page 29, we read:

"Myths, in their diverse narrative forms among various peoples, contain those universal patterns of the mind which, in Jung's view, reside in the collective unconscious and are inherited through lineage and descent."

"Archetypes such as the archetype of the mother, father, hero, and wise old man appear in various myths in diverse narrative forms and serve, for their believers, as an exemplary model of conduct. Just as the archetype of the Perfect Human [insan-e kamel] in the mystical interpretation of the myth of creation in the Qur'an is Adam himself, whose conduct in that myth—according to its mystical hermeneutics [ta'wil]—likewise serves as a model of conduct for Hafez..." The researcher's fundamental deviation begins at this very point. For while the Qur'an may contain a portion of the mythology of the Arabs of Mecca, it cannot serve as myth for other peoples who were converted to Islam—unless, contrary to the research of scholars cited by Mr Ashouri such as Jung and Eliade, we were to believe in a single identical myth for all the nations of the world, and moreover a myth revealed to prophets in heavenly scriptures. Perhaps, ultimately, his understanding of the archetype—as something transmitted in human beings through biological reproduction—amounts to this?

First, Jung's presupposition still has a long way to go before becoming scientific; second, Jung does not regard myths as originating from a heavenly scripture; and third, if an archetype exists for the human being as a speaking living being, it resides in speech and the word. It is language that carries within itself the weight of mythical knowledge, and nothing else. If archetypes are transmitted from one generation to the next, it is on the basis of speech. The weight of each word and the relation of words to one another, in the circulation and formation of these words—the conception of the "mystics of the Khorasan school"—rests upon the Persian language, which has carried its essence from a past far more remote than five or eight centuries. In order to fasten the Qur'an to myth, Illuminationist mysticism [irfan-e ishraqi] to the Qur'an, and Hafez to Illuminationist mysticism, the researcher abruptly fastens Hafez to the Qur'an, and in doing so:

- puts forward a novel claim regarding a scientific and modern method of Hafez scholarship;

- ignores the difference between Iranian and non-Iranian Islamic mysticism;

- makes no reference to the pre-Islamic cultural-mythical past of Iranians, to the extent that we are left in doubt as to whether all this is deliberate or inadvertent. Why does the author distort the meaning of myth to such a degree?

On page 37 we read: "On the whole, what has been stated here as the paradigm of Hafez's thought relies upon the entire heritage of mystical thought concerning the descent and re-ascent of the Universal Spirit from the spiritual world to the corporeal world, and its return once more to its original abode. Therefore, in order to understand the foundation of this ontology, one must study the myth of creation in its religious account and then its mystical hermeneutics [ta'wil]." How can one fall into this trap and fail to see that, fundamentally, if the Qur'anic account of creation is a myth, and if this myth exists in its natural form within the archetypes of Hafez or other mystics, there would be no need for a mystical reinterpretation separating it from the Qur'anic interpretation, nor any need for philosophical polemics between opponents and proponents? The need for cryptic speech, veiled expression, and esoteric hermeneutics arises precisely where speaking openly lands us in trouble—and this trouble is none other than the contradiction lying at the heart of the mythical thought of Persian-speakers, which reaches its culmination in the distinction between "spirit" [ruh] and "soul" [ravan]. The major predicament of Hafez and his predecessors was conveying Iranian mythical concepts within the mould of Qur'anic vocabulary; for otherwise, what need would there have been for conflict, ciphers, concealment, the candle-piercing execution [sham'-ajin] of Shaykh al-Ishraq [Suhrawardi], and the severing of Hallaj's head and hands? For the "spiritual world" is, according to one tradition, that very celestial earth [zamin-e minavi] from which, in Iranian myths, our soul [ravan] descended to earth and to which it shall return—whereas in Qur'anic concepts there exists neither a corporeal world and a spiritual world, nor a doctrine known as the Universal Spirit. On page 40 we read: "Mythical worldviews, which were founded in the primordial era of humankind, laid the foundation of ethnic cultures and, in the languages of those peoples, expressed their eternal history." How can one affirm in the passage above the intimate connection between ethnic culture, ethnic language, and eternal history in a mythical worldview, while simultaneously conflating all these concepts in one's own writing? If we align his statement with the research he has conducted, we would read that: the mythical worldview is expressed in the Qur'an in such a way that this Qur'anic mythical worldview constitutes Hafez's cultural foundation and ethnic language. What then becomes of speaking Dari and his collection of ghazals composed in the Dari language?

He alone appreciates the captivating poetry of Hafez who knows grace of temperament and the speaking of Dari.

All this grace, beauty, allusion, and enchanting expression is achieved through this language, not the Arabic language of the Qur'an; how, fundamentally, could Hafez's ethnic myth be the Qur'an? Myth dwells in the very heart of language. On page 43 it is stated: "With this religion, another myth was added to the myth of the Fall, namely the myth of God's descent into the body of Christ to save humanity." He persists in his error—concerning the relationship between religion and myth—by calling the religion brought by Christ a myth, and indeed "another myth", oblivious to the fact that myths are created over the course of the emergence and formation of oral civilisations, across millennia, not through the utterance of a single individual. An individual such as Homer or Ferdowsi can collect myths, yet cannot invent a myth. On page 46, the author quotes Eliade as follows:

"...whereas myth is an account of the phenomena and events of the beginning of the world which, in the minds of its believers, expresses the foundation and direction of all things..."

From this apt and accurate statement, one cannot conclude that every discourse containing an account of the phenomena and events of the beginning of the world is a myth.

Myths, like sedimentary mountains in the depths of the oceans, have taken shape particle by particle and are the product of millennia and centuries of human life and experience.

Giants, dragons, and Simurghs bear traces of prehistoric animals. They inhabit the poems, parables, proverbs, popular dialects, art, and artistic works of every single one of our forebears. Had we understood myth, its profound richness, the role of oral culture prior to the era of written civilisation, and their mutual interplay with culture and language, we would not have succumbed to so colossal an error as to confuse so-called heavenly scriptures with myths, or to define myth outside the bounds of ethnic culture and language. In an extensive essay, I have examined the role of mythical knowledge in the poetry of Hafez (3).

On page 50 of the book we read: "In the effort mystics make to interpret myth esoterically [ta'wil], they ultimately transform the figurative and narrative language of myth more or less into a conceptual and symbolic language, imparting a more or less logical order to myth and rendering its fundamental groundlessness somewhat reasoned; and in the Islamic world they accomplished this by discovering a realm of inner [batini] meaning over against the outer [zahiri] meaning of the verses of the Qur'an. From within this relative rationalisation of myth and Scripture emerges a meaning—for instance, in the account of the creation of the world and of Islam—for whose existence there is no reason other than the eternal will having ordained it.

With the introduction of an inner interpretation for it—namely, the desire for the manifestation of Eternal Beauty—a logic of creation emerges which, particularly with regard to the human being, makes his existential necessity justifiable in relation to that desire for manifestation.

Yet this gaze behind the scenes and this endeavour to uncover the hidden logic of existence suddenly turns into the discovery of a cipher of the 'world of mysteries' and the 'mysteries of the world', setting in motion a long caravan of saints [awliya], shaykhs, and spiritual poles [aqtab], all of whom consider themselves favoured by the unseen world and keepers of the key to those mysteries."

In short, the endeavour to which Mr Ashouri refers is in reality the effort made by mystics to gain access to the genuine myth of their own people, rather than the Qur'anic narrative of creation; for that very reason they are compelled to posit an inner [batini] meaning against the outer [zahiri] meaning, since Iranian myth is not consonant with the Qur'an. And because in order to reach the unseen realm that resides within every human being (unlike in Islam, where only a single path to the unseen exists—namely the Prophet—whereas here it is the spiritual path [tariqat]), we arrive at that long caravan. For in Illuminationist mysticism ("You, you are the manuscript of the divine treasure")—or, in other words, mythical knowledge—it resides within you and stems from your ethnic and linguistic culture, and it is thus that every human being can stand in relation to such a realm. And it is for this very reason that the author grows indignant and lashes out at all dissenters who understand the source of the unseen differently; page 51: "...that initial effort to render myth intelligible by bestowing an inner meaning upon it meets with failure because the mythical account fundamentally lacks a rational framework and does not spring from human reason, but rather reaches humankind from the unseen source and on the basis of absolute divine authority..." That the mythical account does not originate from reason is a valid statement; however, that it comes from the unseen source is the researcher's grand discovery—one that, had the thinkers of the past two centuries who investigated the foundational relation between myth, language, and the culture of peoples heard such a claim, might well have made them shudder. Either Greek, Indian, Babylonian, Iranian, Celtic, and other mythologies are not myths, or, if they are myths, the source of those myths too must be that same unseen realm—and what creativity this absolute divine authority has displayed in fashioning so many diverse myths! It would have been better had we contented ourselves with studying the Qur'an in the manner of theological seminaries, rather than needlessly grafting myth onto the Qur'an. A few lines further down we encounter a new difficulty: "Many of the contradictions and inconsistencies in Hafez's ontology likewise trace back to these very ambiguities in the tradition of the hermeneutics of myth, which is an untiable knot. The mythical world, in its simple narrative, is nothing other than the background to the empirical world." These inconsistencies and ambiguities arise because you too, like others, began your research with a presupposition, and since you cannot easily sustain your presupposition, you propose a novel definition of myth according to which, on the one hand, it is nothing more than the background to the empirical world, and on the other, myths have arrived in heavenly scriptures and from the unseen. You yourself cite the theories of Eliade and Jung and the significance of myths in human culture and language. Indeed, myths go far beyond "the background to the empirical world" and are, in a profound sense, embedded within the very institution of language and culture. Further on, on page 53, we read:

"The hermeneutical rereading of the Qur'an in search of the hidden logic of the myth of creation in the third and fourth centuries AH abruptly transformed—and indeed turned upside down—the horizon of the relations between God, the world, and the human being as they appeared in the ascetic conception. From within the dualistic perspective of the ascetic worldview there emerged a world-embracing perspective in which God, instead of dwelling upon the heavenly Throne, makes His home in this very earthly world, within the heart of the creature most trembling before Him—namely, the human being; and the vast gulf that separated God and humanity in the earliest narrative of the creation myth in Christianity and Judaism gives way to a union between Creator and creature, and here lies the thread of the entire mystical-amorous thought that culminates in Hafez." The author finally addresses the creation myth in Judaism—which is more or less identical to the Qur'anic account of creation—yet he fails to tell us why God suddenly descends from the Throne to the earthly world, or why in the third and fourth centuries AH the concept of love returns to the mystical-poetic outlook. Had this been a matter of influence from Greek philosophy, Illuminationist mysticism would have emerged from Andalusia and the Levant, which stood in closer proximity and had earlier access to Greek texts, rather than from the soil of Khorasan, the cradle of the Dari language. Two centuries after the Arab conquest of Iran, Iranian myths remain vividly present in the thought, speech, and lives of the people, to such an extent that Daqiqi and Ferdowsi fashion masterpieces out of them. At this same time, Shaykh al-Ishraq Suhrawardi explicitly writes in his works that he engaged in studying Zoroastrian texts; Daqiqi openly declares himself a Zoroastrian; and Ferdowsi begins the legends of creation with Jamshid, not with Adam and Eve.

Continuing on page 69, we read: "As we stated in the introduction to this book, the primary source of Hafez's ontology must be sought in prose works written on mystical hermeneutical theories and ontology." Here too, an error occurs both in methodology and in scholarly practice. It is certainly possible to find similarities to certain verses of Hafez in several works preceding him, yet it must be understood that, first, others had already said this before Mr Ashouri—and it is an old project aimed at reducing everything back to Islam—and second, to establish the ontology of someone like Hafez, one must read Hafez himself and draw corroborating evidence from others, rather than beginning with the works of others, summoning Hafez merely as corroboration, and relegating Hafez's poetry to footnotes. This cannot be called the ontology of Hafez. This study is in fact the demonstration of the researcher's initial false presupposition, grounded in a flawed grasp of the concepts of myth and archetype. We leave it to the readers to judge this correlation-hunting between two prose works—Maybudi's Kashf al-Asrar and Najm al-Din Razi's Mirsad al-Ibad—where, passage after passage, solely on the basis of lexical similarities between the texts of the two aforementioned books and various poems of Hafez, the author strives to reach his desired conclusion. We cite just a single example (p. 78): "...that with the foot of ascetic discipline and the sandals of blame [malamat] you must journey to the horizons of poverty [faqr]." From the two terms "blame" [malamat] and "horizons of poverty" [afaq-e faqr] in the prose of Kashf al-Asrar, the author cites the following lines from Hafez in a footnote:

Heart and faith are gone, and the beloved has risen in reproach [malamat]

Many a bow of reproach [malamat] have they drawn against us

Reproach [malamat] not this intoxicated one for his dark scroll of deeds

O God, bestow upon me the fortune of poverty [faqr]

In the garb of poverty [faqr], I perform the work of kings

If the sovereignty of poverty [faqr] be granted to you, O heart

In a station where pre-eminence is bestowed upon the poor [faqiran]

Let us reflect more closely: what connection do we find between the verses above and that prose sentence from Kashf al-Asrar? In two sections of The Ontology of Hafez—entitled the mystical drama "The Destiny and Story of the Soul" and "In Pre-Eternity"—following what came before and on the basis of that same preconceived view, Ashouri attempts to present his claims summarily and directly without relying on the prior premises of Hafez's ontology. Then, in the section "Adam versus the Angel", he writes (p. 174): "In fact, Adam versus the Angel is none other than Hafez versus the ascetic [zahed]." And as he gradually runs into difficulties of interpretation and hermeneutical comprehension within his pre-fabricated system, he writes: "Admittedly, it is difficult to extract certain things plainly from Hafez's couplets amidst his rogue-like [rendaneh] wordplay and the twists and turns he gives his concepts in order to conceal his ultimate intent; yet within this symbolic and playful language he leaves open the possibility of two or more interpretations, so that in his allusions to the ascetic and the Sufi one may well discern an allusion to the Angel as well." First we read that Hafez conceals his ultimate intent, without being told why! If Hafez's discourse, speech, and intent were identical to the words of Maybudi in Kashf al-Asrar and Najm al-Din Razi in Mirsad al-Ibad, what need would there be for concealment? If Hafez's ontology were merely a continuation of the mysticism of the Khorasan school—none of whose mystics were sent to the gallows or executed by candle-piercing—why should Hafez have avoided aligning himself openly with them?

From the beginning of the book to its end, the author repeatedly reiterates the same mystical interpretation of the myth of Adam's Fall, without allowing a single doubt to enter, without asking himself that one ought also to respond to the ontological presuppositions of other Hafez scholars, and without hesitating for a moment over the fact that Hafez's foundational terms—such as Pir-e Moghan [Elder of the Magi], love [eshq], rend [inspired rogue], tavern [maykhaneh], wine [may], the quarter of ruins [kharabat], the alley of the Friend [kuy-e dust], and cupbearer [saqi]—are fundamentally non-Qur'anic. And fundamentally, why would Hafez have needed to employ such "rogue-like wordplay and convoluted language to conceal his ultimate intent" merely in order to interpret and expound the Qur'an?

In defining rendi [inspired roguery], the author writes: "Rendi is that realm of free-spiritedness and free-thinking which, within the context of a religious culture, can be attained through the hermeneutical interpretation of Scripture and existence." On page 224 we read: "It is here that his 'wine' [may] also reveals its two-faced character. This wine too has a pre-eternal archetype, in which, in the pre-eternal tavern, Adam's clay was kneaded with it and a draught of it was given to him to drink so that he might become human." Let us recall that in the opening sections of the book the author mocks all those who attempt in any way to seek other meanings in the vocabulary of Hafez's poetry (p. 15): "The use of wine, tavern, Magus, elder, quarter of ruins, and things of that sort in the antecedent tradition of our Sufi poetry is a mechanical affair"—yet in the end he resorts to this very practice himself. On page 230 it appears: "With the advent of the hermeneutical perspective towards the myth of the Fall and the discovery of its inner meaning by the mystics on the basis of certain Qur'anic verses... the outlook towards God and humanity is suddenly turned upside down and gives way to a monistic perspective in which the spiritual world and the corporeal world are intertwined, and God is Being itself, and Being is one, manifested in all its appearances." Two outlooks—one ascetic: a moralistic conception of existence, of absolute good and evil, in which God is a punitive judge and the world is divided into two realms, the pure spiritual world and the defiled corporeal world; and the other, as Ashouri writes: "an aesthetic conception of existence in which good and evil commingle, and the dry, mechanical world of good and evil gives way to a living, dynamic, and beautiful world in the radiance of the World-Soul; the cosmos is flooded with light, the tavern of the Magi [kharabat-e moghan] becomes the locus of manifestation of the 'Light of God', and the beauties of nature are beheld as the manifestation of Eternal Beauty."

Comparing these two outlooks, the author writes: "The passage from the dry, terrifying moralistic outlook of the dour ascetic to the tender, beauty-beholding outlook of the intoxicated lover-poet entails the overturning of the entire set of relations among all things—especially the relation between humanity and God, which transforms from the relation of worshipper and Worshipped into that of lover and Beloved." Consider how fundamentally these two outlooks differ from one another. In the second type of relation—"the relation of lover and Beloved" and the God of Light—it cannot fundamentally be Qur'anic. Therefore, this second outlook has its roots elsewhere; and it is largely out of fear—as a protective cloak for thought—that this relation has been grafted onto the Qur'an. For in the Islamic worldview the relation is that of servant [bandeh] to Allah and worshipper to Worshipped, and in none of the verses of the Qur'an is the human being defined, enjoined, or even alluded to as "lover of Allah" [ashiq-Allah]. These concepts and expressions—this overturning, the relativity of good and evil, and the light of love—must have their roots somewhere other than the Qur'an. Where is that place? How can one overlook so many conceptual, institutional, and semiotic connections between the mythical knowledge of pre-Islamic Iranians and the world of Hafez? How can one be ignorant to such a degree even of the theoretical foundations of the role of symbols and signs? How can one fail to see all the pressure that, from the onset of the spread of Islam down to the present day, has erupted in myriad forms through the outward expression of pre-Islamic cultural institutions, symbols, and signs—in carpet motifs and floral designs, tales and proverbs, in architecture, poetry, literature, beliefs, historical movements, uprisings, and in the creation and founding of mysticism—and instead reduce everything back to the Qur'an once again?

On page 232 it is stated: "It seems that with Hafez we stand at the end of this path and the perfection of this culture, and it is with him that the 'culture of rendi' becomes an essential and inseparable part of Iranian culture." Indeed, because Hafez at his zenith undertakes the re-polishing of the living Iranian culture, this luminosity reaches completion with him, and thereafter Iranian culture, from beneath the crust of several centuries of pressure, recovers the sprout of its ancient culture—which is none other than a loving, compassionate, affectionate, and luminous gaze upon the world.

Sweeter than the sound of the word of love I have seen no keepsake to endure beneath this revolving dome.

On page 243 we read: "In any case, the system of hermeneutical thought—albeit unconsciously and consciously—seeks to impart a logical and intelligible order to myth, and renders God so anthropomorphic and humanity so theomorphic that ultimately it beholds God in itself and itself in God, and the tongue of ecstatic utterance [shath] is unsealed." If the definition of "the unconscious" in Ashouri's statement is the same "unconscious" as in psychoanalysis, nurtured by Sigmund Freud, then the unconscious fundamentally cannot make any effort to understand myth. The unconscious has its own distinct logic, structure, and mode of functioning, within which the concept of conscious understanding has no place. The unconscious is the manner in which the acoustic images of words are linked to one another—nothing else—and it bears no relation to the Id [nahad] (10). Rather, it is myth that, during the era of oral culture, constructs the logic and structure of human understanding, not the reverse; and it is for this very reason that through a meticulous study and examination of myths and the words employed within them, we gain access to the mode of perception of diverse peoples prior to the acquisition of script and writing, and learn how popular and human culture, shaped ethnically across different languages and dialects, exerts its formative influence.

On page 253 we read: "In any event, by living according to the creed and way of rendi, Hafez achieved an individuality among all mystical poets that perhaps none of the others attained, and for this very reason understanding him is the most difficult of all." Here, "way" [mashrab], "creed" [mazhab], and "mysticism" [irfan] are placed on the same footing. If Hafez is a mystic and follows the creed or way of rendi, why does he attain individuality? What is the factor behind this individuality? With the definition the author offers of the rend a few lines above, our difficulty deepens: "In any case, rendi—whether in its unworthy sense of deceit, debauchery, trickery, and... fraud, or in its lofty spiritual sense—is an inseparable part of Iranian culture, and it is this very rendi that weakens our social bond..." Although the meaning of the last clause is unclear, on the one hand the author nonetheless concedes that Hafez—who begins with the mystical hermeneutics of the Qur'an and advances to the school of rendi, a school that is "an inseparable part of Iranian culture"—draws his roots from Iranian culture. Perhaps it would have been better if the author had begun his book directly with the section on the school of rendi, sparing us all his fruitless efforts to fasten Hafez to Islam and the Qur'an. It is as though towards the end of the book he repents of what he has done and distances himself somewhat from dragging Hafez into footnotes under the influence of books such as Mirsad al-Ibad, writing (p. 260): "Yet the most difficult of all is Hafez, whose Divan one must often force with a thousand contortions—and with the help of those couplets of his that carry a scent of asceticism, worship, and Qur'an-recitation—to be interpreted so as to fit neatly into the theoretical apparatus of Sufism; and in this they have even succeeded, going so far as to regard every couplet of Hafez as a translation into metaphorical and symbolic Sufi language of a Qur'anic verse or a Hadith." It is as though the author has forgotten that he himself has inflicted this very treatment upon Hafez's poetry, to the point of hunting for lexical correspondences between each couplet of Hafez and the prose of the two aforementioned books, devoting over a hundred pages of his book to this task. And as we approach the end of the text, the researcher drifts away from his initial hypotheses (p. 276): "Hafez's poetry is philosophical [andisheh-garaneh] in a specific sense: namely, a bold rethinking of the entire heritage of mythical thought and hermeneutics [ta'wil], pushing it to the furthest limit of its inner logic. In this sense, he is not only the last great poet, but also the last great thinker of this tradition; and if he expresses his ideas in the form of poetry, imagery, symbol, and poetic allusion, it is because his thought is poetic-mythical—and for this very reason he fills the entire space of Iranian culture after him."

This conclusion is entirely sound, provided that "myth" is taken in its true sense—and, for the Persian language, drawn from Iranian myths. Because Hafez is a distillation of the cultural movement of a people who have come from afar and mingled along the way with other cultures, the dust of that long journey settles upon the heart in his poetry. If Hafez is Hafez, he participates in a cultural totality—a totality rooted in every word, the function of that word, and the relation of those words to one another.

What Hafez sets before us with strenuous effort under the name of the path and way of love, over against two other paths: the seminary [madreseh], book-learning, reason, and ledger on the one hand, and ascetic mortification and dull-witted, blind conformity on the other.

In the closing pages of Ashouri's work, we find the following (p. 282): "If gaining access to the secret of this world is possible neither through asceticism and mortification nor through reason and argumentation, but rather through an awakened soul and a perceptive heart surrendered to the beauty of the Friend and His contemplative guidance..." What remote or close, direct or indirect relation does this awakened soul bear to the Qur'an and the representatives and believers of that book over more than fourteen centuries? How good it would be if we listened a little to these very people of the perceptive heart:

May Love come to your aid, even if, like Hafez, you recite the Qur'an by heart in all fourteen canonical readings!

If we turn to the subsequent pages, we shall read:

On page 299, the author reproduces a passage from Nasrollah Pourjavady's book Buy-e Jan [The Scent of the Soul], revealing just how thoroughly he has fallen into the trap:

"The deficiency we wish to explain here stems from the neglect by historians of Islamic philosophy and wisdom of a wisdom that Iranian thinkers, inspired by the Glorious Word of God, composed in the Persian language. The wisdom neglected in histories of Islamic philosophy and wisdom is an intuitive [zawqi] wisdom which Iranian shaykhs, in accordance with their own understanding and taste, adapted from the Qur'an and expounded exclusively in Persian, particularly in their poetry."

It was these Iranian shaykhs who, exclusively in the Persian language and in their poetry, expressed an "intuitive wisdom" that is singular and unique—yet the author insists emphatically that all of this was adapted from the Qur'an. How can one speak otherwise? How can one lock the great doors of reasoning with worn-out prejudices so tightly that, in the face of such patent evidence, one keeps repeating in another guise the very claims that for several centuries have forced history, writings, and knowledge to revolve around the Qur'an? One may set this passage alongside a passage from Morteza Motahhari in his book Irfan-e Hafez [The Mysticism of Hafez] (p. 20): "So far as I have studied, no evidence has come to light that Hafez belonged to the garb of the Sufis; indeed, the evidence points to the contrary... It is clear that his spiritual mentor was not of this type of well-known Sufi shaykhs or of these famous Sufi orders, and in general Shi'i Sufism enjoys the distinction over Sunni Sufism of having been less entangled in these orders and formalities" (6). Some claim Hafez was a Shi'i! Others claim Hafez followed the Shafi'i school, and Shafi'is were predominantly Ash'ari in theology! (7) Still others hold that "Hafez's ghazals drank deep from the pure and limpid spring of the thoughts of Zoroaster, the prophet of ancient Iran, and the Pir-e Moghan [Elder of the Magi] in Hafez's poetry is none other than Asho Zarathustra" (8).

And others claim Hafez was a disciple of Ibn Arabi: "Muhyi al-Din Arabi al-Ta'i al-Andalusi stirred a mystical ferment across the Islamic world from Andalusia to Egypt, Syria, and India... Iraqi, Dawud Qaysari... Mowlavi Balkhi [Rumi], Mahmud Shabestari, Hafez, and Jami are all disciples of his school" (Morteza Motahhari, p. 20) (6).

On page 301 the author delivers the coup de grâce to his own text, writing: "Thus what we have termed Hafez's 'thought' in this treatise is in reality more of a mentality than thought..." Let us note that the subtitle of the book is "An Inquiry into the Foundations of Hafez's Thought".

On page 305:

"The sorrow of love is but a single point—and how wondrous that from every tongue I hear it, it is ever unrepeated:
It is that very same point heard from many tongues within the expanse of Islamic-Iranian civilisation."

What the author hears across the pages of the book is Islamic and Qur'anic; the Iranian dimension of "Hafez" he either fails to hear or leaves unspoken.

Our primary endeavour, through this review of Mr Ashouri's book, is to make our cry heard: our knowledge of ourselves requires a fundamental rethinking so that we may once and for all be liberated at the root from the heavy sediment of one-sidedness that has penetrated the depths of our worldview. This becomes possible only when we adopt the foundations of scientific and scholarly inquiry—documentary evidence, dialectics, probing depth, and rigorous reasoning—and refrain from hasty and premature learning. By way of example, consult the bibliography of works cited in Mr Ashouri's book, which relies largely on encyclopaedias, whereas deep knowledge and profound understanding demand far more labour than this.

Sources and Notes:

1. Ashouri, Daryoush: *Hasti-shenasi-ye Hafez* [The Ontology of Hafez], or *Kavoshi dar Bonyadha-ye Andisheh-ye U* [An Inquiry into the Foundations of His Thought], Tehran, Nashr-e Markaz, 1377 SH (1998).

2. See the Collected Works of Jacques Lacan, French psychoanalyst and psychiatrist, in particular his *Seminars*, Nos. 1 to 23.

3. *Raz-e Hafez, Hafez-e Raz* [The Secret of Hafez, Hafez of the Secret]: Hassan Makaremi, Hamayesh-e Shenakht-e Farhang-e Iran Publications, Hamburg, Germany, 1998.

4. Written by Henry Corbin, French Iranologist; this book was translated into Persian by Mr Dehshiri and published in Tehran in 1358 SH (1979).

5. Abd al-Baqi, Muhammad Fu'ad: *Al-Mu'jam al-Mufahras li-Alfaz al-Qur'an al-Karim*, Dar al-Kutub al-Qariyah, 1364 SH (1985), pp. 191, 192, 193, compilation of verses on the theme of love (*hubb*).

6. Motahhari, Morteza: *Irfan-e Hafez* [The Mysticism of Hafez], Sadra Publications, 1368 SH (1989), Tehran.

7. Mashkur, Mohammad Javad: "Hafez Jabri-Mazhab Ast" [Hafez Is a Predestinarian], *Vahid* Journal, Vol. 9, p. 555.

8. Vahidi, Hossein: *Pazhuheshi dar Arman-e Parsa'i dar Iran* [A Study on the Ideal of Piety in Iran].

9. Anvari, Hossein: *Yek Qesseh Bish Nist* [It Is But One Tale], 1368 SH (1989), Tehran.

10. See the essays of Dr Molali in *Dabir* journals, Issues 1 to 7.

11. *Iran-e Farda*, Tir 1375 SH (June–July 1996), essay "Tarikh-sazi baray-e Mellat-e Bi-Hafezeh" [History-Making for a Nation Without Memory].

12. Mohammad Qaragozlu: "Daramadi bar Chisti-ye Raz-e Bozorg-e Hafez" [An Introduction to the Nature of Hafez's Great Secret], *Hamshahri* newspaper.

* This essay was first published in *Aftab* journal, No. 42, Mordad 1379 SH (July–August 2000).
