en.body_markdown:
https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/03/DASTHA.gif

[Read on Roozonline](http://www.roozonline.com/persian/news/newsitem/article/-fb12e910ad.html)

Tuesday, 25 December 2012 (5 Dey 1391)
In the following sections of this article, we shall examine several examples of what have become known in Iranian political literature as discourses surrounding "strategy". Reference to these discourses and the use of diverse texts serve solely to illuminate this general problem: that strategic services do not hold their rightful place in our political literature. The aim is in no way to conduct a deep critical scrutiny or to demonstrate the superiority of one discourse over another. The objective is neither judgement nor refutation; pointing to existing examples is intended merely to assist a deeper understanding.

Several years ago, I asked permission from one of the prominent figures of Iranian Marxist thought—with a long record spanning more than sixty years in theoretical and political arenas both inside and outside the country—to speak with him about my dissertation and the advances achieved in the field of strategic services in the contemporary world. I can say that he listened to my remarks with magnanimity and kindness, and in reply asked me with great astonishment: "Why do you raise these matters with me?" And he added: "The ideal-possible of the future society is clear to every communist, as is the path to reach it." I resolved to consult the existing literature to learn his view on strategy. Fortunately, in one of the texts in whose preparation and drafting he had played a role, written a year and a half after Bahman 1357 (February 1979), I was able to find a chapter on the strategy and tactics of struggle, opening with the following introduction: "Strategy must be formulated with due regard to the historical stage, the level of relations among the classes of society, and at the same time international relations, an assessment of the forces of revolution and counter-revolution, and the stance of the government towards the revolution." The term *râhbord* or "strategy" is used in two ways. Initially, the concept of strategy meant the art, guidance, adaptation, and harmonisation of forces towards achieving objectives. Elsewhere, strategy is understood as a set of principal objectives, policies, and general programmes aimed at attaining those objectives in a manner capable of explaining these matters. This latter definition is far more comprehensive and useful.

In the above definition, strategy is scarcely close to strategic objectives. One must extract the strategic objectives from between the words. Does it mean that the strategic objective is the victory of the forces of the revolution? Is this victory against the existing ruling power? We see that this introduction states the conditions for formulating strategy, yet makes no mention of its objectives. At the end of this chapter we read: "...such is the path for the masses to attain sovereignty, and such is the path for realising the lofty ideals of the communists." Even supposing we regard the masses' attainment of sovereignty as a strategic objective, out of the four components of a strategic objective—definability, measurability, ambition, and feasibility within a limited timeframe—this objective shares only in its ambition. How is progress towards this strategic objective to be measured?

We observe that in explaining strategy in its first sense, no role whatsoever is accorded to the cultural dimensions and cultural foundations of the people. Equally absent in the above-mentioned text is the question of around which axis of national solidarity or national consensus such a people can be gathered. Further on in the same piece we read: "Another factor is the active presence of the clergy in the struggle, who, across different class positions yet under an outwardly uniform culture and attire, blend class characteristics with cultural characteristics..." One might perhaps understand from this that cultural characteristics cannot be uniform across different classes.

Let us now turn together to another text entitled *The National Solidarity Pact*... In this text, fortunately, the strategic objective for reaching the ideal-possible—based on the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the role of the nation-state—is well and clearly defined. In the same document, at the end, a section is also included under the heading "Our Political Path and Method", which may be termed operational objectives. These objectives are harmonised neither with one another nor with the strategic objectives. By way of example, in order to achieve the ideal-possible society, any foreign intervention and any cooperation with foreign governments are opposed on the one hand, leaving the task entirely to the people, their awareness, and freedom-seeking forces; on the other hand, the entirety of the Islamic Republic system is rejected, violence is eschewed both within society and in confronting the Islamic Republic system, and peaceful political struggle is chosen as the method of struggle. In practice, these operational objectives allow no room to exploit the internal and external contradictions of the Islamic Republic. In other words, in this document the operational objectives of the transitional period and those of the consolidation period have been conflated. One can readily accept that after the period of stability, no violence should be countenanced and no foreign force permitted to intervene. Yet how, in the face of the monolithism and violence of the Islamic Republic, can one rely solely on political methods from within? We see that dividing the period under consideration into three phases—pre-transition, transition, and consolidation—is indispensable.

In another text, which is a proposal for convening a symposium to "Present Tomorrow's Strategy Regarding the Main Issues and Problems Before Us", we see that strategy is defined in terms of strategic objectives, operational objectives, and action plans for achieving those strategic objectives. In the programme of this symposium, three sections are envisaged: a look at yesterday's successes, failures, and efforts; "Where are we today?"; and proposals and plans for tomorrow's Iran. In the first section it states: "To what extent have we succeeded in raising public awareness? What mistakes have occurred in the struggle for democracy and equality in Iran?" Many unspoken presuppositions lie embedded in these two questions. Without naming strategic objectives, achieving democracy and equality is our strategic objective; and when we introduce raising public awareness as an operational objective, what relationship exists between the two? It is as though, on the basis of a precise prior assessment, we already know that our failure stems from a low level of public awareness. Is it not necessary, prior to such a diagnosis, to take a comprehensive snapshot of Iran's economic, cultural, social, and political dimensions within the region and the world, so as to base our diagnosis upon it? In the second section, "Where are we today?", the assessment begins from the 1388 (2009) elections, and following the assessment of today's issues and problems, tomorrow's solutions—the practical paths, namely the operational objectives—are addressed.

In the third section, the proposals and plans for tomorrow's Iran are divided into cultural, social, economic, security, and political domains, and in each domain, by way of a preamble emphasising today's problems, a path for tomorrow's Iran is sought. It is as though, in the proposed programme and in the planners' analysis, the three fundamental stages of change in a society have been tangled together. This lack of precision in separating the three interconnected stages—pre-transition, transition, and post-transition—in the practical arena leaves us wavering in choosing the applications and the policy for achieving our objectives. It is not at all unlikely that our allies in the pre-transition stage will not be the same as our allies in the other two stages. Clarity of vision regarding the future requires, above all, a sound and profound grasp of the stages of passage from today to the future.

Allow me, in the same vein, to examine the definition of strategy in yet another text. First, let us read the definition provided:

"Strategy is a comprehensive and integrative programme for linking objectives, policies, and active chains in the field of social and political action. Within such integrative linkages, the task of policymaking is nothing other than concentrating the political capacity of effective social forces—through the deployment of politico-propaganda instruments and horizontal and vertical organisation—to launch an assault upon the weak points of the ruling authoritarian power, and, by shifting the balance of power in favour of the opposition forces and taking advantage of the convergence of domestic and international crises, to bring about the conditions for the transfer of power to forces emerging from the democratic political movement."

Let us dissect this definition together: to arrive at a shared definition, we must begin with the most central part of strategic services, namely strategic objectives. According to the science-art of strategic services, a strategic objective requires four attributes: definability, feasibility, measurability, and ambition. In the text above, the strategic objective may be construed as: "bringing about the conditions for the transfer of power to forces emerging from the democratic political movement." Let us read "power" as the existing political sovereignty of Iran. We cannot today identify the forces emerging from the democratic political movement. The presupposition for reaching our goal is that a democratic political movement must first take shape in Iran. Thus we have two strategic objectives: one is the establishment of a democratic political movement in Iran, and the other is the transfer of political sovereignty to the forces emerging from this movement.

Does there exist today an acceptable, universally understood, and widely endorsed definition of a "democratic political movement"? Must we assume that a political movement stands in contrast to a military movement, a street movement, a civil war...? Does the word "democratic" carry the sense of "popular"? Thus we require a movement with popular participation in the political sphere. Does this not mean pursuing the initiatives of civil society until political sovereignty changes? With these presuppositions, we have two clear strategic objectives: striving towards the formation of civil society, and transferring political sovereignty to the leaders of civil society.

Now I must turn to explaining the operational objectives, that is, how to achieve these objectives. Let us read together: "concentrating the political capacity of effective social forces through the deployment of politico-propaganda instruments and horizontal and vertical organisation to launch an assault upon the weak points of the ruling authoritarian power, and, by shifting the balance of power in favour of the opposition forces and taking advantage of the convergence of domestic and international crises". Who are the actors? Effective social forces, the ruling authoritarian power, and the opposition forces. First, we must identify the effective social forces, then assess their capacities, and then, using the science of organisation, place these forces at the disposal of the opposition forces, so that under the leadership of the opposition forces and by capitalising on domestic and foreign crises, we may launch an assault upon the weak points of the ruling authoritarian power. Accordingly, to reach the two strategic objectives above, let us add three operational objectives: 1- identifying effective social forces, assessing their capacities, and organising them; 2- establishing a joint leadership of the opposition forces and effective social forces; 3- assaulting the weak points of the ruling authoritarian power at opportune moments.

Suppose an organ (a party, group, collective...) intends to pursue these strategic and operational objectives. In that case, with due regard to its own resources, it formulates practical and executable plans with indicators for measuring progress; and then, in view of its own forces and the conditions of time and place, it organises itself to execute its plans. Internal organisation and policymaking both demand knowledge, experience, and perseverance. Yet without taking into account resources and temporal and spatial conditions, they cannot be taken for granted. How can one formulate plans, organisation, and execution schedules for building a hospital without considering time, place, financial resources, and the required human capital? Nevertheless, in architectural consultancy offices specialising in hospital construction, general methods, calculation formulas, and planning outlines do exist.

To summarise: under present conditions and concerning our homeland Iran, two strategic objectives and three operational objectives may be put forward as a proposal for evaluation and dialogue—and no more. One may say that strategic planning exists, yet strategy is not a plan. Strategic planning likewise proceeds through to the end of defining strategic objectives, operational objectives, and their measurement indicators. From that point onwards, planning takes shape in the form of action plans. The passage in question could perhaps be reformulated as follows: "A proposed comprehensive and integrative strategic plan for linking objectives in the field of social and political action in today's Iran, comprising two strategic objectives:

The establishment of a democratic political movement in Iran

and the transfer of political sovereignty to the forces emerging from this movement.

From these objectives, under today's conditions in Iran, three operational objectives follow:

1- Identifying effective social forces, assessing their capacities, and organising them

2- Establishing a joint leadership of the opposition forces and effective social forces

3- Assaulting the weak points of the ruling authoritarian power at opportune moments.

Taking into account the capacity of opposition forces inside and outside the country and their convergence around these objectives, we can draw upon scientific principles of organisation, organise ourselves, and—in pursuit of these objectives and in accordance with available forces and the conditions of time and place—formulate and implement the necessary policies."

Let us examine another perspective in the writings of the opposition: "Now, thinking about tomorrow's Iran without negating the past—indeed, by re-reading it—a platform had been prepared that sought to walk in the sphere of ideals yet upon the ground with an expert gaze. This meant proposing possible justice, reasonable democracy, and sustainable development among elites, intellectuals, and students... which bypassed the politico-cultural deadlock by introducing a national expert perspective... This intersection formed a new triangle, within which freedom drew closer to democracy and equality to possible justice." You will note that democracy, as a definable political system, can serve as a strategic objective. Freedom, however, can assume diverse definitions across different social and cultural spheres. The above text's reference to knocking at the door of the politico-cultural deadlock indicates that, in defining strategic objectives, familiarity with world history and culture on the one hand, and innovation on the other, are foundational pillars.

In the same vein, one may ask whether "possible justice" is definable as a strategic objective. How is the attainment of this possible justice to be measured? Increasing the number of literate people, or the number of pupils and university students, or lifting a substantial percentage of Iranians out of poverty... Similarly, with what tools do we measure the attainment of sustainable development? The level of domestic and foreign investment, environmental indicators such as air pollution or healthy agriculture... Although the three strategic objectives in the text above appear reasonable, without a precise definition of measurement indicators they leave us in confusion.

Another text, by comparing the manner of defining and applying the strategic objectives of Turkish society with recent movements in the Middle East and North Africa, turns to "assessing the likelihood of implementing the Turkish model in Iran". Although in providing strategic services, looking closely at other societies is one of the appropriate ways to learn from experience, doing this very task without a methodology leads us astray. In this text, the comparison is conducted solely along a cultural-religious axis and from a secularist perspective (*laïc-secular*). This is a comparison between strategic objectives grounded in an ideal society and what has been realised within the possible of a given society. In the comparative method within strategic services, one can only compare the ideal-possible with reality and draw conclusions. Under this approach, most of our criticisms in the two realms of the possible and the ideal will fail to intersect. For in the aforementioned text, there is fundamentally no mention of strategic objectives and their indicators in the fields of economics, international politics, or resolving problems related to cultural diversity.

In a document published at the conclusion of one of the recent conferences entitled "The Strategic Choice of the Future", we read that projects can be divided and evaluated into three categories: first, reforms from within, democracy from within, the plan for the return of the reformists, elections with the participation of the reformists; second, the project of civic siege, the strategy of free elections and structural reforms, an organised transition beyond the Islamic Republic, and building democracy through the sovereignty of the ballot box; and third, the project of constructing an alternative and organising forces outside the country. At the end of this document comes the question: "Which project and strategy can realise democratisation and prepare the ground for dismantling the apparatus of despotism?".

It is here that the strategic objective is declared—namely, the seizure of political power by whatever means possible. In the drafting of this document, we see that the logic of Strategic Services has moved directly from the bottom upwards. We begin with the strategic objective, translate it into operational objectives, and then proceed to propose projects aimed at achieving these operational objectives. Here, however, they begin with the projects and only at the very end unveil their strategic objective. Should we not, at the outset of the meeting, first seek to bring strategic objectives onto the table, so that we at least know what our analysis of the concrete situation is, and exchange ideas on the nature and scope of these strategic objectives? How can one treat the operational objective of building an alternative abroad as if it were on the same plane as the strategic objective of seizing political power inside the country? If the strategic objective is the establishment of a political system within a democratic framework, then all the operational objectives set out above can be pursued in parallel and simultaneously. We see that the absence of a Strategic Services methodology entangles us in unnecessary complexity during negotiations and drives us apart from one another.

In another article we read: "Forecasting and determining the probable future political trajectory of any society is one of the analytical foundations for discussing how to confront various political events and for determining political strategy and tactics." The author then proceeds to depict several conceivable scenarios and, on the basis of the more probable scenario, points out a number of solutions. Here, all at once, in the domain of Strategic Services, the author begins from the final step. What the author terms "forecasting and determining the probable future trajectory" can only be addressed after the stages of understanding the society and identifying its strengths and weaknesses, which lead to strategic objectives, operational objectives, and only at that stage to the definition of possible scenarios. Towards which strategic objectives is this "determination of political strategy and tactics" directed? How can one, in a single text, offer prescriptions for selecting future political tactics while remaining oblivious to strategic objectives and their measurable indicators?

With another example from one of Mr Banisadr's articles in *The Huffington Post*, we conclude our brief tour of Strategic Services from the perspective of the opposition. In this article, with the utmost goodwill, he proposes fourteen measures to Western governments so that the Iranian people may attain democracy on their own and suffer no harm or loss either from economic sanctions or from an unwanted war. Without examining these measures or passing judgement on their effectiveness, we ask ourselves: how did these proposals come to his mind? Undoubtedly he was mindful that such measures fall within the broad framework of strategic objectives, even though he makes no explicit mention of those strategic objectives. Undoubtedly the strategic objectives he has in mind for the future of the Iranian people are their happiness and prosperity. Why did this simple and elementary question not occur to him: that the strategic objectives of the Iranian people and those of the decision-makers of Western societies cannot be one and the same? This was the very same mistake he made in his initial collaboration with Khomeini. He assumed that Khomeini's strategic objective was aligned with his own. Khomeini's strategic objective was to realise "pure Muhammadan Islam" by establishing an Islamic government founded upon the absolute guardianship of the jurist (*Velayat-e Motlaqeh-ye Faqih*).

Today, the strategic objectives of the West are to overcome the deep financial and economic crisis that has engulfed it. Repaying the massive debts of governments, resolving the challenges posed by the growing competition of China and countries such as Brazil, India, and Turkey, protecting and preserving the environment, and utilising cleaner energy stand at the forefront of the West's strategic objectives. This is the very same West which, unfortunately, over the past two centuries, wherever its short-, medium-, and long-term interests have been at stake, has shown no regard for any humanitarian or human-rights consideration. We see that putting forward such proposals is nothing more than evidence of our naivety in the arena of politics and Strategic Services.

Strategic Objectives in the Discourses of Those Close to the Leadership of the Islamic Republic

Without doubt, the actions and performance of a governing regime—particularly after three decades—can be examined through the models of Strategic Services. Spoken or unspoken, through writings, discourse, documents, and conduct, one can attempt to elucidate the strategic objectives and operational objectives of the Islamic Republic's ruling system. An accurate understanding of a regime that claims to be "ideological-religious" is essential. This examination must be conducted in its expert, analytical dimension, which requires patience, impartiality, knowledge, and the requisite craft. In such endeavours, judgement regarding the human and social dimensions of strategic objectives must be deferred to a subsequent stage. Just as on a battlefield, the assessment of both friendly and enemy strategic objectives takes place in a professional, expert setting so that it remains free of any prejudice. Striving to understand the strategic objectives of the Islamic Republic's ruling system makes us better prepared for the future and enables us to scrutinise our own foundational plans in this regard with greater precision. Such preparation will certainly not make us immune to future errors. In today's interconnected and turbulent world, one must always be ready, like a skilful dancer in the political arena, to adapt with agility and speed to the course of events. This vital capacity is possible only if our foundations of knowledge also come to our aid—and one such foundation is awareness of the objectives of ruling powers.

We shall endeavour, using what is accessible to us, to probe—albeit in passing, and drawing upon the statements of figures close to the leadership of the Islamic Republic of Iran—and outline the initial contours of strategic modelling. Undoubtedly, the critique and scrutiny of political actors and experts in strategic affairs can bring this brief sketch to perfection. Let us begin with the remarks of Ahmad Jannati, one of the key and influential figures at the leadership level. Ahmad Jannati, Secretary of the Guardian Council, stated at a gathering of provincial heads of election supervision offices: "The power of Islam grows day by day, yet unfortunately Islamic values are not spreading... It may be that a minority in society harbours enmity towards Islam and a majority falls into heedlessness, yet if a group is prepared for self-sacrifice and struggle, the banner of Islam will not fall to the ground... If justice is harmed in its economic, cultural, and political dimensions, the very same calamity will befall the Islamic Republic as befell Imam Ali and the House of Ali in early Islam." From this discourse one may infer that, in his mindset, the strategic objective is the propagation of Islamic values throughout the world, and power is an instrument in the service of this objective. According to him, the instrument—namely power—is steadily being consolidated, yet the strategic objective, the spread of Islamic values, remains unattained. He divides the people into three categories: a majority afflicted by heedlessness—meaning indifference towards Islamic values; a hostile minority; and another minority who, provided they are willing to carry the banner of Islam upon their shoulders, will ensure these values do not fall to the ground. In this regard, he draws upon the experiences of all those countries that have diverged from the path of human rights and progress in the twentieth century; for we know that in such countries, under ordinary conditions, possessing the instruments of governance—security, the economy, communications, education, and the like—together with roughly ten per cent of the population is sufficient to sustain rule.

He concludes that even if power is attained, should justice be harmed, the fate of the Islamic Republic will resemble that of "Imam Ali and the House of Ali". Thus, by his own account, "Imam Ali and the House of Ali" lost political power. This comparison, contained in that brief phrase, can assist us greatly. If "Imam Ali and the House of Ali" are the symbol of justice in Shiite culture, how then did they lose political power? At the same time, he acknowledges that attaining the absolute power of *Velayat-e Faqih* has failed to bring about the expansion of Islamic values. In other words, the growth of power is not aligned with the strategic objective of spreading Islamic values. In a sense, beneath the words and deep down, for the speaker himself, the future of this power is already defeated; for he knows well that, according to his own beliefs, the governance of the Islamic Republic cannot rise above that of early Islam, and we all know the fate of the justice of "Imam Ali and the House of Ali". Here, this authoritative representative of Twelver Shiite *Velayat-e Faqih* thought speaks simply and plainly of the strategic defeat of "Imam Ali and the House of Ali" in maintaining their hold on power. We know that in practice, after that period, Umayyad rule continued to govern with entirely different values. The ideals of "Imam Ali and the House of Ali" in their strict and original form were never realised—not only after them, but in none of the direct or indirect governments across the lands under the influence of Islam.

Now consider another report by Hassan Abbasi, Head of the Centre for Doctrinal Studies, as quoted by the Student News Agency (Daneshjoo): "...There is scarcely any field in which the Supreme Leader has not established a trend [strategic planning]; he has defined all fields... The bulk of the Supreme Leader's trend-setting is affirmative: the movement for the production of knowledge and the software movement... The strategic literature put forward during his [Khamenei's] presidency and leadership has rendered us [the Islamic Republic], I say without exaggeration, self-sufficient in strategic thinking for the next hundred years... None of the country's officials has the capacity to reach his level in the realm of macro-policymaking." First, Strategic Services are provided by the Leader, over an exceedingly long-term horizon, and the Leader possesses a systematic intellectual framework. Yet what domains do these Strategic Services encompass? Only with great effort can one extract a few strategic objectives and operational objectives from his lengthy address. Defining strategic objectives is regarded as the Leader's duty, while defining operational objectives is seen as the government's responsibility. For this reason, he is pleased that the leadership of *Velayat-e Faqih* can guarantee the continuity and coherence of strategic objectives. He articulates the Leader's first strategic objective as follows: "The movement for the production of knowledge and the software movement: the point is that if we strive for fifty years, we shall become exporters of science; thus we have a trend for which we must labour for fifty years. Since 1381 (2002–2003), when this trend was introduced, as the Leader instructed, you must produce science in such a manner that others are compelled to learn the Persian language." This first objective is definable, time-bound, actionable, and possesses a measurable indicator for determining its success: namely, within the next fifty years, the Persian language must become one of the scientific languages of the world.

He continues: "The most important mega-trend that he has put forward is the category of society-building. I shall refer to his most significant trends in this area from 1360 to 1390 (1981–2011), over these twenty years. In 1359 (1980–1981), following Ayatollah Taleqani, he raised for the first time in Friday prayers the concept of the Mahdavi society in opposition to civil society. In 1360 (1981–1982), for the first time, he put forward the theory that our society must become the living embodiment of the Quran, and he has repeatedly stated that we remain far from it. In 1368 (1989–1990), the society of justice; in 1369 (1990–1991), the Alavid society; in 1371 (1992–1993), the divine society; in 1375 (1996–1997), the society of Imamate, and in the same year 1375, the society of the common people and the elite; in 1376 (1997–1998), the luminous society... Our comprehensive and strategic plan is the Quran; we must Quranise society." The second strategic objective is somewhat vaguer. One can infer that the Quranic society is to be brought into being gradually, and that it also differs from civil society. In the remainder of his remarks, several operational objectives for attaining this strategic objective can be extracted: "The first step is familiarising everyone with the outward text of the Quran... The sources of society-building: the first layer is the Quran, then the Hadiths, and then reason... The value of Quran reciters, memorisers, and teachers must be made manifest." These three operational objectives likewise fit within the general framework of operational goals: to bring the outward text of the Quran to the general public; to utilise its inner meaning in law-making; and simultaneously to honour the promoters of the Quran.

In the same discourse, several other important points are noted: that our strategic outlook up to the year 2050 is to become a superpower, and that the Leader has defined the doctrine of foreign and domestic policy: "When asked about foreign policy, the Supreme Leader stated: dignity (*ezzat*), expediency (*maslahat*), wisdom (*hekmat*). Regarding domestic policy, he stated: dignity (*ezzat*), mercy (*rahmat*), authority (*eqtedar*). Dignity is the common denominator of both; join these two statements together at the hinge of dignity." In Strategic Services, such factors are termed the foundational cultural pillars. Whatever the case, through these behavioural pillars one may infer that expediency signifies the pursuit of interests; wisdom signifies foresight; dignity signifies preserving outward appearances; mercy signifies clemency towards the insider minority; and authority signifies the exercise of power against outsiders.

Does there exist in the Islamic Republic today an authoritative document formulated and implemented on the basis of the science–art of Strategic Services? Is such a document respected by the entirety of the system? Beyond cultural strategic objectives, does this document address political, economic, and social strategic objectives across domestic, regional, and global dimensions with a ten- or twenty-year horizon?

Our purpose in this brief excursion through the strategic literature of both the opposition and the ruling establishment was primarily to illustrate the application of Strategic Services methodologies and to invite political actors to avail themselves of this body of knowledge.

Examining the history of at least the past two centuries of Iran through a strategic lens—extracting the strategic objectives of movements, uprisings, and insurrections, and gaining an accurate understanding of the outcomes achieved, as well as the strengths and weaknesses of the measures taken to reach those objectives—is profoundly illuminating and instructive for our future. A strategic perspective enables us to observe the actions of political figures with greater detachment and precision, and to assess the validity and credibility of political movements both in their mode of operation and in their resulting outcomes compared against predetermined objectives. With this preamble, we may examine the Constitutional Movement: identify the strategic objectives of this movement in its Constitution, and assess the extent to which those objectives were realised.

In highly condensed form, the strategic objectives of that Constitution may be summarised as follows: the separation of government from the monarchy, the codification and institutionalisation of the judicial system, the enactment of laws by the representatives of the people, and the delivery of civic services by the government under the oversight of the people's representatives. At that time, according to available statistics, only one-quarter of Iran's population lived in small towns, half lived in villages, and one-quarter were nomadic tribes. In defining strategic objectives, the dimension of feasibility of implementation and achieving results carries particular weight. Was an answer given to that fundamental question at the time? Was voting and electing the people's representatives truly feasible for more than seventy-five per cent of the population, especially under the sway of landlords, tribal khans, and feudal structures across parts of Iran? In practice, up until the referendum of 1342 (1963), the proportion of tribal khans and landlords among parliamentary deputies, from the very first Majlis until that day, hovered around fifty per cent. Consequently, for nearly sixty years after the ratification of the Constitution, implementing the strategic objectives—namely extending state services to villagers and nomads on the one hand, and overseeing the government's performance through the people's representatives on the other, for more than seventy-five per cent of the population—remained unattainable.

Today, criticising the strategic objectives that laid the foundations of the Constitutional Constitution is straightforward, for those objectives have demonstrated their validity and flaws in the crucible of a hundred-year test. Our aim is not merely to draw lessons from this analysis, but to ensure that in the future, prior to drafting any constitution, we think through strategic objectives in advance and measure them, through rigorous critique, against the conditions of time and place, feasibility, time-boundedness, definability, and ambition.

What has been stated concerning the Constitutional Constitution holds equally true for the Oil Nationalisation Movement, the programme known as the White Revolution, and the Constitution of the Islamic Republic. How can we prevent future errors on the path towards the reconstruction and flourishing of our beloved Iran? In our view, making use of Strategic Services reduces the margin of error, renders the path more reliable, and even strengthens national solidarity across all three stages: prior to the transition, during the transition period, and ultimately in the era of stability.

By employing scientific methods and recognised methodologies in defining, formulating, and implementing strategic objectives towards a free and prosperous Iran, and by convening a seminar of thinkers and activists who propose ways forward, the first bricks of a foundational manifesto for the reconstruction of Iran can be laid.

In such a crisis-ridden and complex world and region, should we not, in order to reach a final solution for liberation from the closed and constricted circle of Iran's existing regime, endeavour to focus all forces upon the primary and foundational question, and in this vein summon the following questions for an answer?
1. Is it not more fitting that we devote our energies to foundational and strategic issues?

The deeper and more far-sighted an objective, the greater the forces it summons to itself over the long term.
2. Is it not more fitting that we return to the terrain of tangible reality and to strategic objectives endowed with scientific characteristics—objectives recognised by realism, definability, and attainability through measurable indicators?
3. Is it not more fitting that we make the betterment of the Iranian people's lives, and the strategic questions required to achieve it, the central axis? For the borders and frontiers of Iran, the definition of the Iranian people, and the definition of welfare, freedom, progress, and a better life are clear both from the perspective of the people and from that of experts.

4. Is it not more fitting that we avail ourselves of the scientific and accepted methodology for defining strategic objectives and all commit ourselves to it? It is under the shelter of a prosperous, free, thriving, and knowledge-seeking Iran that one can cultivate diverse strands of thought and schools of philosophy—and not the reverse.
If our answer to these questions is yes, we can introduce further related questions and speak of the ways and methods of tracing the answers. And the first step undoubtedly returns to the reality of what we are.

In a scientific process, not only do strategic objectives require measurable quantitative indicators for their implementation, but one must also test their translation into operational objectives, operational plans, and the organisation of progress—at the very least from the standpoint of the practical feasibility of those plans.

Above all, the science–art of strategy rests upon innovation. The ultimate endeavour is that the process of designing and executing strategic objectives leads to a form of management that we term "innovation management".
Strategy must be so coherent, practical, precise, articulate, comprehensive, sustained, executable, intelligible, and teachable that it becomes in itself an educational corpus for political cadres and for the public.

Should the science–art of strategy be applied only after seizing power, and solely for the administration and guidance of society? Or can it also be employed in the struggle to attain power? Or, fundamentally, can these two intertwined categories be separated at all? Let us return to the very first question: can the modern science–art of strategy assist in charting Iran's future? And if so, by whom and how?
