en.body_markdown:
The Role of the Regime's Opponents: Replacement or Opening the Way?

(Applying Modern Findings in Finding a Path Through Tradition)

June 11, 2010 by makaremi | Edit

We are speaking of the people of Iran, across the expanse of an ancient land, amidst those countries that have given themselves the name of the Middle East, in a world where advances in communication are coming ever closer to demonstrating, in a singular way, the interconnectedness of more than six billion human beings on planet Earth. This shared sense of membership in the global community on the one hand, and attachment as a citizen to a particular land and culture on the other, outside the bounds of theoretical knowledge and in everyday life itself, renders the human being at least "two-dimensional". Looking at the world as a moving and tangible reality on the one hand, and turning towards a future along the continuous axis of historical movement on the other, places the human being upon a stage with the depth of historical-vital knowledge and the breadth of a planet named Earth.

Thus, the human being is on the one hand a product of the history of their birthplace, and on the other lives within the expanse of a six-billion-strong world. Their standpoint is neither detached from their historical-cultural-geographical past nor from the unified movement of the globe. We are speaking of the Iranian citizen amidst very ancient neighbours, in a world that is changing with astonishing speed and drawing closer to convergence and unity. The roots of the efforts of our forebears, from one hundred and fifty years ago up to the present—following the discovery of the new Western world, which was the product of the Renaissance and the Industrial Revolution—are manifested in actions and reactions that concisely trace the political, social, and economic history of the Iranian people. One of the simple and effective ways of classifying these efforts—and perhaps one of the most useful—is to employ the provisions of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as the arbiter of the people's will and the symbol of their triumph in attaining a superior life.

On the one side, believers in the provisions of this Declaration—whether they named it explicitly or not—and on the other side, three currents—statists (*dolat-madaran*), ideologues (*maktab-madaran*), and theocrats (*din-madaran*)—have been and remain present on Iran's socio-political stage. The first group makes its operational plan conditional upon observing four fundamental forms of upholding the provisions of this Declaration:

— Respect for human rights between nations and states

— Respect for these provisions in all written laws and regulations of society

— Practical observance of these laws and regulations in the relationship between the state and citizens

— And finally, the day-to-day observance of these laws in the relationship of citizens with one another.

In the other group, one may place the ensemble of individuals who supported a prefabricated blueprint whose doctrinal, governmental, economic, and religious dimensions had been selected in advance.

Put another way, the programme presented by these figures did not see the remedy in placing the cultural-historical-geographical coordinates of Iranian society and citizens along the historical path of movement towards modernity, but rather confined their attachment to already-tried paths and solutions.

In three foundational and profound movements of the Iranian people after encountering the West—the Constitutional Movement, the Oil Nationalisation Movement, and the Bahman 1357 (1979) Uprising—we advanced right up to the threshold of victory in upholding the provisions of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and in all three cases we failed to cross that threshold. In all three cases, dependence upon and attachment to a particular doctrine, system of governance, or religion, and a one-dimensional outlook, held our movement back from final victory. For the fourth time, do we not need a fourth method?

This path undoubtedly demands the establishment of the provisions of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, in all their dimensions, as its existential axis. Over the past two centuries, the principles of this Declaration have not only weathered numerous challenges, but have today become the grammar of interaction among nations and states—both in relations between them and in relations between citizens and states, as well as with one another. Iranian citizens have demanded democracy at three specific historical junctures. Let us not forget that, setting aside the European countries born of the Renaissance, the United States, Canada, and Australia, the Constitutional Law in Iran was ratified and put into effect earlier than in other nations—earlier than Japan, Russia, and others. There is no need to remind ourselves that our country lies in a region that has profound and comprehensive transformations ahead of it, and at this juncture of time and space, Iran—drawing upon its natural resources, its special strategic and geopolitical position, its cultural and human backing, its young and constructive workforce, and its experience of more than one hundred and fifty years of seeking modernity and democracy—has something to say.

Regarding these two principles—the demand for democracy and bringing into effect the provisions of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights on the one hand, and Iran's elevated standing for the ultimate attainment of its aspirations (a fitting and worthy potential) on the other—no room for doubt remains. What is seen and heard in the mass media in recent months is a general agreement upon these two axes: we both want democracy and human rights, and we are capable of achieving them.

This time, and for the fourth time, must we once again make ideal blueprints—such as the form of government, the type of ruling ideology, or the economic system—our primary principle as in previous opportunities, or can we seek methods of greater effectiveness? In answering the question of how, once and for all and in our fourth attempt, to free ourselves from the three models of absolute guardianship—statism, theocracy, and ideological doctrinarism—we can in a sense also draw benefit from the advances of new human knowledge.

Must ready-made, clear-cut answers be tested once again? Must we once again resort to founding political, ideological, and religious parties and groups? How can the fragmented ensemble of Iranian citizens—who inside the country grapple with the hardships of daily life and strive to open up a stifled and dormant socio-political and cultural space, or abroad contend with the difficulties of migration or come to terms in one way or another with the values of host societies—be placed on a trajectory where, for the fourth time, they reach their lofty destination? How can one draw upon the totality of experiences and scientific, psychological, anthropological, economic, political, and organisational knowledge, and arm oneself with a superior weapon—a different, contemporary, and effective weapon? Put differently, how can one employ modern instruments to achieve a modern society?

What Is the Question?

The hearts of Iranians far from their homeland beat in their chests with the memory of Iran and its pride, and for the life of Iranians in a free and prosperous land amongst neighbours with a vision of "inter-popular" coexistence—and that in a lasting manner. Although after two decades Iranian emigrants and refugees have managed in every corner of the globe to carve out a foothold and a dignified life through hard work, on the whole, individually or collectively, under cultural, artistic, professional guises or within political parties and groups, they have deadened within themselves and around them this burning question: how can one, once and for all, turn the wheel of the land of Iran towards democracy and meritocracy, and towards the prosperity and welfare of the people of this land? And set Iran, after a century and a half of relentless effort by diverse generations—from their earliest encounters with modern culture to the present day—onto the irreversible path of human civilisation?

Modernity, and forging a bond with it, is a deep and long-term path that cannot be applied by decree; one must move towards it with patience and perseverance, with due regard for understanding the foundational cultural values existing in each society—and this without turning the people back to their traditions. The artful role in applying modernity lies in ensuring that incompatible traditions are themselves pushed back, while cultural-historical legacies are naturally and gradually placed in their proper place, without becoming tools in the hands of reactionaries.

Although the current of modernisation has 150-year-old roots in Iran, it is today that this confrontation between tradition and modernity is unfolding across all its dimensions. Individual, group, ethnic, and cultural obstacles and resistances to attaining a modern space must be precisely analysed, and a specific solution conceived for each of its dimensions.

Opposition to ruling apparatuses and regimes sometimes becomes an end in itself and holds us back from the foundational idea, which is guiding Iranian society onto a modern path. Overthrowing and replacing the ruling system and establishing a regime built on new foundations, without acquiring the modern strategic instruments of today's world, does not necessarily bring us to our goal. One of the difficulties of persisting over the long term in playing the role of "subversive opponent" is that the "ins and outs" of subversion keep us from the fundamental role, which is building a modern society.

One can play the role of a "proposing opponent" who, with seriousness and perseverance, reflects upon the strategies and applications of moving towards modernity, puts these ideas forward on a broad scale, adopts coordinated stances in response to domestic and external events, and expects that over the long term the proposing opponents themselves—or a part of them—whether through overthrow, infiltration, or transformation, will in one way or another put their strategies and solutions into practice.

The sole condition for the victory of constructive, proposing opponents lies in choosing the soundness, precision, and universality of their strategies and solutions; and this vital task cannot be carried out unless we make deep and comprehensive use of contemporary achievements in theoretical and practical knowledge, and of modern communication tools—communication networks, the internet, satellite broadcasting, mobile communication systems, and the like.

The vast ensemble of efforts by enlighteners and thinkers—especially over the past two centuries—across every corner of the globe who have played a role in bringing their societies to the elevated level of human civilisation and the observance of all dimensions of human rights, we classify perforce, given the limited scope of this article, as follows:

— Societies that have striven to accelerate the modernisation of their production system and economic flow

— Societies that have striven to model themselves on modern systems without paying attention to the compatibility of those models with their own realities

— Societies that have turned to foregrounding only one of the dimensions—economic, industrial, cultural, political (mode of governance), modernisation of the administrative system, and so forth—without paying attention to harmony among them.

Another dimension of this classification may pertain to the theoretical aspects and foundations of a movement, such as philosophical idealism, magnifying and foregrounding the people's aspirations and hopes, foregrounding the burning problems and issues of the day (war, disease...), or foregrounding the existing culture in society.

Likewise, diverse strategies and solutions have been put to the test. At times the welfare of the present generation has been foregrounded, and at times the welfare, comfort, and progress of children and future generations have been prioritised. Some have pinned their hopes on the self-sacrifice of several generations to reach the goal, while others have foregrounded ideological and non-material dimensions over worldly well-being and spoken of other-worldly values.

The cultural leap, in the sense in which we speak of it here, requires a profound understanding of the internal cultural foundations of our society (from an anthropological, sociological, and psychological perspective). This leap, which begins with foundational culture, will extend to all dimensions of modernity; it depends on the growth of each individual's outlook towards the future, on the capacity for individuation, on the creativity of our imagination regarding our own future and that of our society, and on our efficacy and inventiveness in forging new paths and bypassing internal and external obstacles.

This text forms the basis of a study that can undoubtedly be published in the future in a richer and more expansive form.

This text has the capacity to serve as the starting point for exchange, questioning, and dialogue in the arena of thinkers who:

— On the one hand wish a better future for the people of our land, and on the other are ready to listen with an open ear to what is new.

— On the one hand regard the knowledge and learning of peoples across diverse fields as a source of intellectual enrichment, and on the other leave the path open to every experiment.

— On the one hand do not imprison research, cognition, and knowledge within the boundaries of language, culture, territory, and the depths of millennia, centuries, years, and months, and on the other seek specific answers to specific questions.

— On the one hand continuously commit themselves to finding strategies, viewing it as an ongoing, complex, and long-term endeavour, and on the other make "situational specificities" foundational in finding solutions, employing flexibility and attention to detail as the instruments of their work.

— On the one hand view the people of Iran as a distinct part of the peoples of the world, with all their cultural richness and diversity, and on the other see Iran as a colourful land of diverse cultures, languages, and customs.

— On the one hand regard individual, group, and cultural freedoms as the source of flourishing, and on the other view human beings as equal before the achievements of life and do not imprison life's share within the walls of futile "oughts" and "ought-nots".

If we assume that an economic revolution (creating equality) and a revolution in social relations lead to freedom, our problem is creating a kind of harmony between equality and freedom. My freedom stops where your suffering begins. I am free insofar as my actions and words do not bring you pain and suffering. That pain and suffering of yours may be the product of my excess in exercising my freedom or my resources. Perhaps in this way we can find the very compatibility, harmony, and union that we seek.

Is revolution necessary? And is it always necessary? Or which dimension of revolution is necessary at which juncture? Must one of the political, social, economic, or cultural dimensions be foregrounded in a revolution? Can one begin from only one of these dimensions? Can all of this be called a revolution of life or harmony with the existing world? In response, can one not conceive strategies and solutions that, by drawing upon all human achievements on a global scale, attain harmony and unison amongst people, groups, the nation, the region, and the world?

In seeking our remedy, we need "multi-question", "multi-dimensional", or "multi-branch" thinkers—"multi-disciplinary", "inter-disciplinary", and reflective scholars. Put another way, the practical role of pathfinding and strategy-making becomes foundational, in a sense, through establishing specialised networked communication. Here, the value of scholars and enlighteners lies not only in their particular role within their own specific expertise; rather, within the networked interaction of these disciplines, new questions are born that transform the field of work and thought into a grand laboratory across the expanse of a nation and land. And this ferment will not only yield the share of insight and questioning of each specialist, but from the sum of networked dynamism, each question will take on new dimensions and create an opening in other fields of thought. Here, that theoretical coalition which political units formally pursue takes root.

The discourse of tradition and modernity has preoccupied thinkers in Iran and in countries outside the sphere of the Industrial Revolution for more than two centuries; and the discussion of the failures of the Constitutional Movement of 1285 (1906), the failure of Khiabani in 1299 (1920), the failure of Colonel Mohammad Khan Pasyan, the failure of Mosaddegh in 1332 (1953)... and their recurrence points to a fundamental and underlying problem that lies either in grasping the fundamental questions or in answering them. Examining and scrutinising their historical and social sequence requires widening our field of vision. This field—not only with the two dimensions of time and space, but by adding concepts such as myth, mythic memory, archetypes, meta-archetypes, multiple layers and their interpretations in relation to time and the influence of various and invading cultures, historical memory, history, culture, and geopolitical analysis—can be studied in a highly complex and expansive matrix with the following dimensions:

— On the one hand, deepening our historical time dimension, moving from centuries to millennia.

— On the other hand, placing the geographical expanse into possible categories—land, country, ensemble of culturally kindred countries, and economic pacts—and opening it up further.

— And finally, opening up the various economic, political, social, and cultural dimensions of the field of inquiry of "tradition–modernity".

Along this path, one can benefit from the experiences of others and examine the solutions proposed, implemented, or abandoned mid-way by others. These solutions can be categorised as follows:

— Transformation and change must come from within, taking place in ideas and cultures.

— By changing the mode of everyday life, changes in thought and ideas will follow.

— By changing the political model of society—constitutionalism, a council system, a democratic republic, an Islamic government, the dictatorship of the proletariat...—the movement towards modernity will take place.

— Eradicating the old modes of production and replacing them in an autonomous manner (transforming feudal lords into capitalists of state-owned factories) will guide us towards modernity.

Many thinkers likewise conclude at the end of their investigations that the equation between tradition and modernity is insoluble; deeming them fundamentally incompatible, they leave the solution to the passage of time. Another group speaks in their writings of a "cultural leap", without either defining it precisely or demonstrating how it is to be achieved. These thinkers have grasped the profound complexity of the relationship between tradition and modernity in its cultural, traditional, and historical dimension, and have recognised the significance of what lies buried in the depths of a people's language and culture; at times they prescribe as a remedy the highly diligent learning of a foreign language from childhood, and at other times they pin their hopes on a form of social psychotherapy (addressing the severe cultural complexes that paralyse us). In our literature, references to "pains that, like leprosy, gnaw at the soul of society and cannot be spoken of to anyone" abound.

Between this recourse to urgent questions, one-sided answers, and a resolute will to apply pre-prescribed remedies on the one hand, and despair, deprivation, and a corrosive despondency—or the recourse to patience, time, or a return to one's own self out of hopelessness—on the other, thinkers have never abandoned the effort to untie the knot of "tradition and modernity" in the face of the depth and complexity of the questions, answers, and remedies.

One of the deepest afflictions in this regard is the challenge of importing ideas from the other side wholesale. Undoubtedly, the translation of these bodies of knowledge without an accurate understanding of their application, on the one hand, and the transformation of these "poorly translated and poorly understood" ideas into second-, third-, and multi-hand currency, on the other, not only diminishes the depth of the transmitted thought, but gradually turns our oral knowledge into a kind of cultivation of banal clichés whose traces can be seen in speech, in writing, and likewise in practical remedies. "It is all their doing"—wherein for each of us, *their* refers to yet another *Other* among others, and without dissecting it, everyone assumes that yes, this *they* is that same perennial proper noun that changes its face yet never loses the power to pre-write what is "already written". Abundant signs of this can be offered in the examination of Iranian mysticism, the examination of class and productive dynamics from the past to the present, and the examination of religious, Shi'i, and superstitious beliefs—clichés such as: "Iranian mysticism has been the finest remedy after every bitter defeat", "Our stock has already rotted away"...

Another question that preoccupies thinkers is the regressive trajectory in the observance of the Declaration of Human Rights: how certain fragments of its principles were put into practice after the Constitutional Revolution, and how these foundational principles have today undergone distortion and followed a path of regression.

On the one hand, an accurate knowledge of ourselves—of our past and our present—with contemporary instruments requires time, energy, and tools of inquiry: contemporary self-knowledge such as gaining access to economic and cultural figures and statistics, precise knowledge of natural endowments such as mines and oil, and obtaining an exact, illuminating picture in the cultural and economic spheres. On the other hand, mythical, historical, and cultural self-knowledge pursued in a manner free from prejudices and futile archaism—understanding waves of migration, the cultural proportions and affinities among nomadic tribes, and ethnic, national, and cultural minorities—remains essential; yet knowledge of our historical-cultural image is itself afflicted by the same blight of "cliché-ism". The intermingling of historical myths throughout successive waves of invasion not only permeates the depths of culture and language, but also confronts our thinkers with grave challenges, thereby contaminating both our questions and answers and our search for remedies.

Our knowledge of ourselves, of our culture, and of the self within the expanse of sociological and anthropological inquiry has also been acquired through translation, and this in turn plunges us into a fresh alienation and duality, to the point where we even behold ourselves in the mirror of the West.

In a word, the transparent knowledge and application of the tools for understanding ourselves and the West—tradition and modernity in both of their historical-cultural depths—is on the one hand the sole remedy, and on the other so remote, intricate, and profound that at first glance it brings thinkers nothing but despondency and depression, especially in a terrain where every backwardness is squared or cubed. The elusiveness of these instruments of knowledge also prevents us from applying them to the understanding of tradition and modernity. In this connection, one may cite the belatedness of our intellectuals in the domain of applied psychoanalysis, applied anthropology, and the ancillary instruments derived from these two fields. Where the combination of "applied anthropology and psychoanalysis" has become a practical instrument elsewhere, the discoveries of Freud and his followers—and their fields of application—still end for a substantial portion of our intellectuals in simplistic clichés such as "Not everything is sexuality and sexual drives." Modelling of "social" groups today is carried out by employing systematic knowledge, structuralism, and the formation of early societies (anthropology), with the aid of sociology, social psychology, organisational sciences, and geopolitical studies.

When one dimension of modernity passes beyond the intellectual stratum and enters everyday life, if there is no sustained, foundational vigilance and ongoing work in safeguarding the values of modernity, there is no guarantee of its continuity.

The gaze of ordinary people in the streets and bazaars upon Iran's first Constitution could not prevent its several reactionary supplementary articles, because the foundational principles of that law did not penetrate into the soul, flesh, skin, and everyday life; and soon, of all those poems, songs, articles, and popular fervour in the public mind, scarcely a trace remained—so much so that the verse by the late Bahar, *Either death or modernity and reform / No path save these two lies before the homeland*, fell into oblivion, and a short while after the bombardment of the National Consultative Assembly, Sheikh Fazlollah Nouri fiercely attacked the two principles of liberty and equality as the foundational pillars of constitutionalism, declaring them incompatible with Islam.

Human needs are as vast and abundant as human attachment to aspirations and the breadth of human culture. On the one hand, human beings bring with them the capacity to build and cultivate the world; on the other hand, if this same human being remains unorganised, they remain turbulent, destructive, and bound to the past. Examining the comprehensive text of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights is one of the avenues that can reveal to us the abundance and depth of human needs and aspirations.

Undoubtedly, in future eras our descendants will enrich this Declaration still further, for creative humanity expands its world and enriches its aspirations with every passing moment. In that day as well, to the measure of their constructive imaginative capacity, they will bestow upon this Declaration fresh colour, fragrance, breadth, depth, and beauty. Examining the Preamble and the thirty articles of this Declaration—within the field of human vision and existence, as far as the penetrating gaze of contemporary human beings can reach, fourteen billion years after the emergence and explosion of our present cosmos, within the depth of several hundred million years of life and more than forty thousand years of modern humanity (*Homo sapiens sapiens*)—calls for a different interpretation, commentary, and perspective. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights is a distilled text that represents the fruit of all human striving to live together, on the one hand, and of the endurance of life upon planet Earth, on the other. The word *life*, insofar as the present author has scrutinised it across various dictionaries and cultures, is synonymous with *continuation*. *Life* stands opposite *death*, opposite *ending*, opposite *termination*. In its depth and in its very essence, life is continuation itself; and from this vantage point too, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights is the concentrated fruit of the continued presence of life on Earth and of that life's noble achievement: the human being.

In the midst of this, what is the foundational question? If we imbue at least our ancient society with the fragrance and colour of the universal dimensions of the Declaration of Human Rights, which question will be more fundamental than the others? How do we arrive, out of tonnes of strategies, methods, theories, and foundational political principles, at a fundamental question and strive to answer it?

The Universal Declaration of Human Rights situates humankind within a field at least forty thousand years deep and among the multitude of eleven billion human beings who have been born into the world up to the present day—a humanity that has created more than thousands of languages and dialects and, through institution-building and self-representation, invented the means of exchange with one another, and that in a world where today the volume of communicative data doubles every seven years and which holds within itself and before it half of all the scientists ever born up to the present.

It is remarkable that the first Declaration of Human Rights was translated into Persian in the closing years of the eighteenth century by one of the professors of the Collège de France in Paris. If we look once more, with sufficient patience, at the corpus of speeches, articles, poems, and utterances of our forebears before and after the Constitutional Decree, we shall readily observe that all of them can be classified on the basis of those very thirty articles of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights—as though, by way of example, the sermons of Seyyed Jamal Va'ez Esfahani dissected one of those provisions in each of his discourses.

Globalisation began with human rights and extends to economics, language, art, and literature. In a sense, the acceptance and spread of human rights in human societies may be reckoned the first global movement of modernity. In the existential depth of this idea (the Universal Declaration of Human Rights), the establishment of a democratic institution within human society is commended. On the other hand, the concept of the ruler—the sovereign, in whatever form or content it assumes and under whatever name or title such as *Shah*, *Emir*, *Caliph*, *President*, *Supreme Leader*, *Führer*—has the final word, in such a way that it defines states of exception and emergency and, in those critical moments, decides and determines the course. It is the relationship between such an individual or group and the people that renders the social institution democratic; and it is for this reason that *Velayat-e Faqih* and its constitutional form bear no affinity whatsoever with democracy.

On the other hand, many thinkers point in various ways to structural and infrastructural reforms—such as balance between state and private ownership, transformation of the monetary and banking system, and overhaul of the judicial apparatus—and regard these as indispensable to the modernisation of Iran. At times, too, they hasten to propose amending the Constitution. Although such transformation is infrastructural and necessary, one cannot address the aforementioned reforms solely by amending the Constitution, which sets forth the political configuration of society and the balance of powers within it. This is the very shortcut that can lead us astray from the foundational goal.

A dialogue of cultures—a dynamic give-and-take in which each side places its discoveries in the field of knowledge and submits them to translation, transmission, and critique—returns to the "field of the possible" only when both parties are not merely conscious of mutual respect and of the need for each other's knowledge, but when the open arena of such dialogue is made possible through freedom of expression, critique, and thought on both sides. Until complete conditions of freedom to publish, critique, and translate all ideas and bodies of knowledge—opposing and concurring, contradictory and harmonious—are achieved, and until the translation and authoring of opposing and concurring works take place in a free atmosphere with full respect for the rights of authors and thinkers and under their careful oversight and authorisation, we shall either remain passive, second- and third-hand consumers of the newly discovered ideas of others—and that through irresponsible translations by individuals who present themselves in the field of translation solely on the pretext of knowing two languages, divorced from deep knowledge of the subject being translated—or else remain in regret over the absence of sustained, living communication, yearning for a healthy dialogue with thinkers of other cultures. A further sorrow and regret lies in the fact that since epochs of thought—from the Enlightenment and the Renaissance to modernity and postmodernity—surge forward at great speed, with every fertile idea drawing upon new discoveries and, in the crucible of labour and effort, giving birth to another idea, our belatedness in the foundational arenas of these ideas makes our task exceedingly arduous. To the extent that one cannot traverse a hundred-year road in a single night, one cannot universalise four centuries of Enlightenment, modernity, and postmodernity in a society whose scientific infrastructure lacks the foundational readiness.

On the other hand, traditionalism—resting on the belief that the basis of truth, power, and all laws lies in the past, that everything has already been written, that the world has already been made—stands in contrast to the view that the world can be invented and can be discovered, and that these two categories become one with respect to existence. In a sense, we gradually discover the world and invent it at every moment; whereas for traditionalists even the discovery of the world merely adds astonishment before it, for to them the invention of existence is impossible, because existence has already come into being and cannot come into being anew, existence has already been written and cannot be written.

Knowledge of history—our mythical history and its roots—on the one hand, and knowledge of the contemporary science of organising modern societies, on the other, both of which are mutually indispensable to any profound and comprehensive movement for Iran's future, demand a comprehensive, all-encompassing, and profound effort. Understanding pre-Islamic myths, the contemporaneity and convergence of these myths across Zoroastrianism, Manichaeism, Islam, and its Shi'i branch, together with tracing the spread of Sufism and its roots, is necessary for comprehending the standing of contemporary Iranian society. The deep cultural foundations of a people cannot be observed solely in what transpires on the superstructure of their lives. Anthropological modelling of complex societies of deep antiquity such as Iran—whose culture has been subjected to numerous upheavals and turbulences—requires possessing the instruments of this knowledge, sufficient time, and patience.

Intellectuals and enlighteners—those who turn towards the great laboratory of life with their multi-questioning world—are both engaged in discovering it and committed to inventing the future: discovering what has passed, and inventing what lies ahead.

Humankind created the concepts of future and past and extended their span from days to months, years, centuries, and millennia. It expanded the depth of its projects from storing food for two days (forty thousand years ago) to long-term designs spanning centuries for the discovery of existence. The freedom of the "conscious" human being is complete only when they regard themselves as the creator of their own future, not puppets who confine the depth of their freedom to a "blind-groping" discovery of existence.

Not few were those who regarded economic reform—and specifically in the form of an industrial revolution—as the primary condition for political and administrative reform, and that at times by despotic means for the sake of educating and advancing the nation. Not few were, and not few are, the advocates of liberty who, by reducing the concept of a "cultural leap" to a single dimension, effectively withdraw into seclusion and become isolated elements.

In modernity, the "individual" is born, and relativity (being relative) fills the place of the absolute, for the "individual" sees themselves within the expanse of social contracts rooted in at least 40,000 years of group life and eleven billion other human beings.

Taxation, administrative, and legal systems, as well as the form, power, and sphere of action of administrative, policing, and military forces, likewise serve as a mirror of this tradition and modernity—to such an extent that compulsory education in state-supervised schools, by comparison with traditional *maktab-khaneh*s, or sending seminary students into military conscription, is itself a stark symptom of this duality. Although one may at times, by force of the lash, impose the outward forms of modernity upon tradition, trampling upon the concepts and established findings of anthropology, sociology, and psychology—above all the unconscious and cultural memory—will inevitably manifest its return one day.

If we understand *modernisation* as change in organisation, mode of life, mode of production, transformation of economic and social superstructures, and forms of assembly, *modernity* is a fundamental transformation of society's values that acts not only upon the mode of thought, but upon the foundations of the individual's unconscious.

Undoubtedly, elements of endurance have taken root in the depths of our culture, rendering us since antiquity resilient against rapid cultural shifts—to such a degree that, despite everything, the Persian language survived and many pre-Islamic customs, rites, and traditions have been preserved to this day and sedimented within Shi'i Islam; and in the same way we were able to resist the attacks of the Ottomans, the Portuguese, the British, and the Russians and, by whatever means, not lose our independence to this day.

This very culture likewise calls, in a different way, for its own distinctive needs, methods, techniques, and strategies along the path towards modernity. Those elements which, as the inner values of our culture, generated resistance remain actively present today. Perhaps we ought to harness these factors for the sake of national unity, social cohesion, and popular solidarity, and invent out of their resistance to change a strategic ally on the road to modernity.

The critique and assault upon tradition must be rescued from the narrow confines of religion, creed, and social, productive, and economic relations, and, by situating Iranian society as a whole within human-historical society, be harmonised and aligned with the contemporary world. Put differently, so long as we do not view the trajectory of Iranian society amidst all other trajectories and do not demonstrate that the movement of modernity is a global trajectory extending that very 40,000-year movement of our ancestors, we cannot distinguish Westernisation, Western mimicry, Western veneer, or modernisation from modernity.

The difference between modernity and modernisation is the very fundamental difference between casting a ballot and choosing. The primary conditions of choosing not only provide the social, political, and economic conditions of freedom for both the voter and the candidate, but also summon the human conscientious responsibility of every chooser and every chosen, one by one, for their own generation and for generations to come. They endow the acts of choosing and being chosen with human and historical meaning and significance. Casting a ballot, by contrast, is an outward act that can be deployed in any deviant and dependent assembly for any anti-human deed. Thus, not every recourse to selection by majority vote can be deemed modernity.

Another question is whether, over the course of the two centuries that have elapsed since our encounter with modernity, our modernist intellectuals and thinkers have succeeded in agreeing upon a minimum common ground so as to share it with the people and thereby make these values enduring.

A further question concerns the pathology of Iran's movement towards modernity—the calamities and obstacles that have arisen and will arise along this path. Are these crises and resistances foreseeable? Can models of progress and renewal be examined in relation to Iran's anthropological and sociological structure, and can steps be taken towards harmonising and integrating the movement of the various economic, social, cultural, and political dimensions of modernity?

One must also answer this question: should we allow time to do its work so that through "trial and error" a synthesis of "tradition and modernity" emerges, or should we draw upon all contemporary lights, experiences, and technologies and nip waiting and its school of thought in the bud? Must we wait yet again for a newer Shi'ism to be born from the process of early Islam and pre-Islamic Iranian myths, or can we take a shortcut?

Put differently, in modernity the individual is an individual and is separate from their presence in existence, whereas in tradition the individual is a continuation of the world. In modernity the individual stands alone before existence, even though they remain a continuation of life.

Reinventing modernity for ourselves and our society, by drawing upon the values of modernity for us and in the present day, means inventing a new mode of possible life in today's world whose aim is human happiness and one's consonance and companionship with the surrounding world.

How can we profit from the trials, errors, and experiences of the past two centuries in attaining modernity?

How can we separate the depth of modernity from modernisation and its superficial shell?

How can we elevate the social (cultural and economic) achievements of modernity in Iran to the level of the individual achievements of renewal (modernisation), which has advanced far further?

How can we guard against fear of the future and flight into the past under various guises of "what it already possessed..."?

How can we prevent futile and unwarranted leaps and haste in traversing the path of modernity?

How can we reconstruct the intimate and foundational relations of *laïcité* (*laos*—the people, the general public, the human being), democracy (government of the people by the people), and the radical and enduring observance of the provisions of human rights at their various levels, alongside reconstruction, modernisation, economic progress, and the establishment of at least basic human needs across all strata of urban and rural society, as well as nomadic and ethnic communities?

How can we attain the outlines and chapters of a scientific society—a society in which scientific thought, scientific exchange of views, and the presence of thinkers at various levels guarantee the survival of popular decision-making with the participation of experts; a society in which the respective roles of politicians, managers, and specialists are each accorded their proper place?

How can we achieve indicators of health in the Iranian society of tomorrow and benefit from social, political, and cultural health and their harmony and consonance with one another? Economic health—as a thriving, vibrant economy in which the flourishing individual, amidst a healthy and cultured people and within a dynamic cultural arena, engages in cultural exchange: a harmony between what has come down to me from my forebears and what I receive from universal human culture.

Before presenting my concise proposal regarding Iran—which is the fruit of a body of experiences and the distillation of knowledge acquired in the political and social spheres, in activism for the defence of human rights on the one hand, in clinical psychoanalysis on the other, and in the experience of modernising a French state administration from 2003 to the present day—I shall limit myself to mentioning a small example of the application of applied anthropological and psychoanalytic knowledge in the domain of social action.

By way of example, one may offer the following brief outline merely to open the discussion on this matter, if we reduce the cultural foundations of a society to three elements:

_ Attitude towards beliefs: absolutising or relativising beliefs,

_ Belief in the value of the individual and individualism as the foundations of society, or the dissolution of the individual into society and the absolutisation of society,

_ And finally, the role of the human being in discovering the past and inventing the future.

https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/08/Sans-titre.png

https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/08/Sans-titre1.png

Contemporary Iranian society can readily be categorised among those societies we have termed "expectant traditionalists", and to elevate this society into a modern society (with the cultural, social, political, and economic dimensions of modernity), one may have recourse to three methods:

— Transition through democracy with a religious populace (foregrounding individualism)

— Transition through a planning dictatorship (foregrounding the relativity of beliefs)

— And a direct, simultaneous movement towards modernity (foregrounding both the relativity of beliefs and individualism at the same time).

Choosing any one of these methods, and the precise reasons for that choice, is an exceedingly complex undertaking that requires a comprehensive, complete, and long-term plan.

Proposed Plan:

We may establish two general preconditions as the groundwork for our action:

— A national movement of Iranian citizens for the establishment of the provisions of the Declaration of Human Rights

— Drawing upon all contemporary scientific and technical achievements, we place this "Cultural–Organisational Leap" programme as the basis of a public dialogue: a programme employed today in modern societies, using modern instruments, to modernise organisations, administrations, factories, and even the structure of cities, at times yielding remarkable results. The theoretical foundation of this programme rests upon anthropological studies and behavioural and psychological studies of human beings from early societies to the present day.

The "Cultural–Organisational Leap" programme comprises three fundamental stages:

— Defining the cultural–organisational model

— Defining the prerequisites necessary to reach the said model

— Organising for the implementation of the said programme and model.

The first stage itself comprises four fundamental phases:

In the first phase, a complete snapshot is taken of the cultural, political, economic, and social (structural) dimensions of society. In this examination, we place the problems and core axes of weaknesses and deficiencies, on the one hand, and the points of strength, on the other, under the magnifying glass—like looking into a clear mirror, or like examining a patient through various medical tests.

In the second phase of the first stage, drawing upon the analysis of weaknesses and strengths, we strive to provide an answer to a foundational question: how do we wish to see our Iran ten or twenty years from now? In seeking an answer to this question, we tread within the realm of the possible on the one hand and the field of our ideals on the other—casting an eye towards the feasibility of attaining our ideals in view of the direction of history and today's potential.

In the third phase of the first stage, drawing upon these two achievements—now that we possess a picture of our present and have identified our possible ideal—we shall answer another question: what are our strategic objectives? What is our position, where do we stand, from where do we speak, and within what framework are we situated? Such strategic objectives can today be found in some of the aims and charters of parties and groups—with the difference that the objectives of organisations and parties rest mostly upon hypothetical ideals rather than possible ideals, and stand far removed from a realistic picture of the existing state of society.

In the fourth phase of the first stage, we strive to articulate, in line with our strategic objectives and their framework, a cultural–organisational model of society. In this model, the share of creative imagination, the utilisation of effective and constructive emulation, and foresight is of great importance. This model is defined in a very broad and open manner so as to leave room for every kind of modification and reform in the course of movement.

Now the second stage may begin. In this stage, tasks are entrusted to various groups. Within the framework of the aforementioned cultural–organisational model, they strive to translate strategic objectives into operational objectives. Then, for each of these operational objectives, practical levers can be defined, by setting which in motion we draw closer to the operational objective. At this same time, we must also define indicators of attainment and measures of success for our operational objectives. The aforementioned practical levers are, in fact, the very implementation plans within whose framework public and specialist debate and exchange of views can be set in motion.

Disseminating these plans and conducting debate and exchange of ideas require deploying all modern communications capabilities. Groups and advisers, through tireless labour, breathe life into the plans and strive to bring them to completion. Throughout the second stage, the following objectives are pursued:

— Convergence of thought and harmony among the actors involved

— Generating momentum and raising fundamental issues within society

— Taking positions on world issues and events both abroad and at home

— Bringing closer together the groups and individuals who will later shoulder the practical execution of the plans.

And finally, in the third stage, through organisation at the level of society as a whole and upon assuming political and executive power, all or part of these plans become executable.

What must be added to this ensemble is the cultural dimension of this programme. In this dimension, by applying contemporary knowledge, efforts are made to bring the foundational cultural infrastructure of society to light and put it to the test. On the other hand, by defining a new cultural model and fresh cultural foundations, efforts are made through the dissemination and expansion of these foundations over the long term to prepare the ground for the execution of foundational programmes. In the long term and gradually, within a reciprocal (cultural–organisational) relationship, the human being becomes more fertile and citizenship likewise attains its growth.

The cultural dimension in this movement serves, as it were, as the guarantor of progress and the coordinator of our behaviour; for rather than predetermining the will and the path of movement in advance, it is the movement of heart, soul, and desire—and the attainment of the cultural desire for popular sovereignty—that supplies the requisite fire and energy, and not the reverse. This programme and its servants are like instruments in the hands of citizens.

fr.title: La situation dans la région, l'Iran et la dépression d'Ahmadinejad

fr.body_markdown:
https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/01/ENSANE-KAMEL.gif

www.akhbar-rooz.com
[Samedi 10 ordibehesht 1390 – 30 avril 2011, Akhbar-Rooz :](http://www.akhbar-rooz.com/news.jsp?essayId=37624)

En l'absence de données dignes d'être tenues pour fiables, on ne peut que s'appuyer sur ce qui parvient aux oreilles — rumeurs, « on-dit », sous-entendus, allusions, silences… — pour tenter de reconstituer une forme de réalité empreinte de prudence et la soumettre au jugement de chacun, afin que se laisse peut-être entrevoir une parcelle de ce qui se trame. Le vent des mouvements sociaux et politiques, avec plus ou moins d'intensité, balaie une vaste partie des pays de la région. Et, comme toujours, les acteurs intérieurs et extérieurs y jouent leur partition.

Notre propos n'est pas ici de repeindre ce tableau. Ce qui nous intéresse, c'est ce qui se joue dans notre Iran au cœur de ces vents contraires. Les mouvements sociaux de protestation dans les usines, les difficultés économiques quotidiennes de la population, la pression croissante sur les prisonniers politiques, les dissidents et leurs familles, les restrictions médiatiques et le bridage de l'espace Internet constituent aujourd'hui les couleurs dominantes du fond sur lequel se dessinent les figures de la vie des Iraniens. Au milieu de cette conjoncture, de nombreuses nouvelles font état de l'absence d'Ahmadinejad dans l'exercice de son rôle habituel.

Ces informations ont également trouvé écho dans les médias crédibles hors d'Iran, annonçant qu'il s'adresserait prochainement au peuple dans une allocution télévisée. Comme si, au sommet de la direction politique iranienne, une profonde fracture se faisait jour. Et l'axe de cette fracture s'est cristallisé autour de l'un des proches d'Ahmadinejad, Esfandiar Rahim Mashaei. Encore une fois, à distance et avec la plus grande prudence

en.title: The Situation in the Region, Iran, and Ahmadinejad's Depression
en.executive_summary: https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/01/ENSANE-KAMEL.gif www.akhbar-rooz.com Saturday, 10 Ordibehesht 1390 – 30 April 2011 (Akhbar-Rooz): In the absence of data worthy of acceptance, one can only rely upon what reaches the ear—rumours, "they say"s, insinuations, asides…
en.body_markdown:
https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/01/ENSANE-KAMEL.gif

www.akhbar-rooz.com
[Saturday, 10 Ordibehesht 1390 – 30 April 2011, Akhbar-Rooz:](http://www.akhbar-rooz.com/news.jsp?essayId=37624)

In the absence of data worthy of acceptance, one can only rely upon what reaches the ear—rumours, "they say"s, insinuations, asides, silences…—to strive to reconstruct a cautious form of reality and submit it to the judgement of the public, so that perhaps a glimpse of what is unfolding may come into view. The wind of social and political movements has swept across a vast swathe of the countries of the region with varying intensity; and, as ever, both internal and external actors are playing their parts.

Our aim here is not to repaint that canvas. What concerns us is what is unfolding in our Iran amidst these winds. Social protest movements in factories, the everyday economic hardships of the people, mounting pressure upon political prisoners, dissidents, and their families, media restrictions, and the curbing of the Internet space constitute today the primary colours of the ground and figures of the Iranian people's lives. Amidst all this, abundant reports speak of Ahmadinejad's absence from performing his accustomed role.

These reports have also found their way into credible media outside Iran, stating that he will soon address the people in a televised speech. It appears as though a deep rift is emerging within Iran's political leadership; and the axis of this rift has crystallised around one of Ahmadinejad's closest associates, Esfandiar Rahim Mashaei. Once again, from afar and with the utmost caution, let us dissect the root of this duality. Where do the fundamental differences of view lie?

- Iranian Islam or the "Iranian School", glorification of pre-Islamic Iran, and an Islam with a diminished role for the clergy, on the one hand, versus insistence upon the role of *Velayat-e Faqih* and "pure Muhammadan Islam", on the other.
- Relative freedom in women's attire, their presence in sports arenas, and relative moderation in enforcing outward appearances, on the one hand, versus ever-increasing pressure to enforce outward observances and incessant criticism of the failure to deal decisively with "deviants", on the other.
- An interpretation premised upon accommodation with the United States and the West in the current regional conjuncture, on the one hand, versus hardline confrontation and unilateralism based on force and the continuation of past policies, on the other.
- An interpretation of the nature of the winds of regional events grounded in data indicating popular demands for freedom and democracy, on the one hand, versus an interpretation maintaining that the people's demands are Islamic, on the other.

Over the next two years, two pivotal elections will be held in Iran. History holds lessons regarding these two elections: namely, that Khamenei, in view of the conclusion of each president's two permitted terms, effectively casts him aside prior to the parliamentary elections during his second presidential term (recall the eras of Rafsanjani and Khatami) and seeks to configure the next presidency and its coexistence with the parliament. In such a conjuncture, following the natural course, both factions will view capturing the parliament next year as the gateway to the presidency. And this point too is worth learning from past experience: in Iran's method of staging electoral spectacles, intelligence and its ministry play a foundational role; the roles of the Ministries of Intelligence, Interior, and Defence become ever more decisive.

Meanwhile, numerous whispers are circulating regarding Ahmadinejad's unaccounted handling of oil revenues, and it has been reported that Khamenei has appointed a three-member committee chaired by his son to oversee these revenues.

Amidst all this, sanctions are tightening the pressure; the subsidy-elimination scheme and the plan to remove several zeroes from Iran's currency are fuelling economic chaos. Ahmadinejad stands before a wall of unfeasible, illusory promises. He has seen the fate of others in the final two years of the presidency; he knows that he is no longer the Master's court favourite (*Malijak*); and he sees that the winds are rising. For someone like him, with a psychic structure very close to that of a mythomaniac (one who alters reality in appearance and has scant conscious awareness of doing so), no recourse remains save falling into the pit of depression—what those around him have termed "influenza".

Hassan Makaremi; Sorbonne Researcher, Clinical Psychoanalyst
Paris, 10 Ordibehesht 1390

fr.title: Iran : le voile se lève, le visage d'un coup d'État
fr.executive_summary: https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/01/peinture-300706-193-Copier.jpg Cet article a été publié dans Libération – 3 JUILLET 2009, Libération, Paris. fr.body_markdown:
https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/01/peinture-300706-193-Copier.jpg

Cet article a été publié dans Libération

[3 JUILLET 2009 Libération Paris](http://www.liberation.fr/monde/2009/07/03/iran-le-rideau-tombe_568343)

Le scrutin du 22 khordad de cette année lève le voile sur un coup d'État rampant. L'élection d'Ahmadinejad, il y a quatre ans, a ouvert la voie à l'homogénéisation des leviers du pouvoir en Iran. Jusqu'alors, le Guide, Ali Khamenei, détenait de fait les rênes du pouvoir en nommant directement le chef du pouvoir judiciaire, les commandants de l'ensemble des forces de défense et de sécurité ainsi que la direction de la radiotélévision d'État, et en exerçant, par l'entremise du contrôle discrétionnaire (*nezarat-e estesvabi*) du Conseil des gardiens sur toutes les élections à tous les niveaux, la validation ou le rejet des candidatures.

En 1384, la présidence d'Ahmadinejad a parachevé la pyramide des réseaux des Gardiens de la révolution (*Pasdaran*) et des *Bassidjis* forgés durant la guerre Iran-Irak, à l'image d'une armée qui n'attendait plus qu'un commandant. À l'époque déjà, le scrutin s'était accompagné d'irrégularités et de doutes, à commencer par le taux extrêmement faible de participation. Au cours de ces quatre années, le Guide et le président, désormais pleinement unifiés, ont engagé leur coup d'État par étapes, tandis que le Conseil des gardiens, lors des élections législatives de 1387 à l'Assemblée consultative islamique, rendait de fait le Parlement homogène en disqualifiant les réformateurs. La présidence a ouvert les portes aux *Pasdaran* dans tous les organes exécutifs, les ministères et les préfectures, et, finalement, a progressivement vidé de leur substance les organismes de contrôle de l'action gouvernementale — telle la dissolution de l'Organisation du plan et du budget — ouvrant ainsi aux *Pasdaran* l'accès aux grands projets.

Les objectifs stratégiques de ce réseau mafieux et sécuritaire, produit de ce coup d'État rampant, sont nombreux : unifier les forces dites « des nôtres » (*khodi*) ; écarter les « autres » (*gheir-e khodi*), y compris ceux qui pourraient un jour négocier avec les réformateurs ; accroître la capacité préventive en mettant l'accent sur l'éventualité d'un coup d'État de velours ou d'une attaque extérieure grâce à des actions culturelles et médiatiques, en tentant de supprimer la limitation à deux mandats pour l'élection présidentielle (propos tenus par Ahmadinejad dans son QG de campagne) ; et, enfin, nouer des alliances avec des pays de la région à majorité chiite ou gouvernés, comme l'Iran, par des populistes — autrement dit, gagner du temps sur la scène internationale jusqu'à acquérir la puissance de défense jugée nécessaire.

Cette consolidation et ce verrouillage institutionnel du système s'accompagnent également d'une réorganisation destinée à unifier le système éducatif (le projet « une école, une mosquée ») et à multiplier les associations rattachées aux mosquées. Parallèlement, on s'efforce de s'assurer le contrôle de l'économie en renforçant le pouvoir de fondations telles que la Fondation des invalides de guerre (*Janbazan*), la Fondation des martyrs (*Shahid*) et *Astan Quds Razavi*, dotées de budgets vertigineux hors de tout contrôle parlementaire — des fondations exonérées de tout impôt et placées sous l'autorité directe du Guide.

Les objectifs stratégiques de ce coup d'État à plus long terme consistent à préparer des belligérants idéologiques qui, prenant appui sur leur socle social, briseront la frontière de l'État-nation, déploieront leurs ailes vers l'oumma chiite dans la région et s'empareront ainsi de la direction unifiée du monde islamique.

Un tel programme était déjà inscrit dès 1357 : l'alliance entre une branche du clergé chiite adepte du *Velayat-e Faqih* et sa base sociale, issue d'une culture rurale et orale — une classe sociale née après les réformes agraires des années 1340 avec l'exode des ruraux vers les petites villes et les périphéries densément peuplées des grandes métropoles.

Dès 1357, un autre coup d'État rampant s'était déjà dessiné. Bazargan, premier Premier ministre après l'effondrement du régime impérial, fut contraint à la démission au moment même de l'occupation de l'ambassade des États-Unis. Quelques mois plus tard, Bani-Sadr, premier président de la République, fut écarté du pouvoir, tandis que tous les partis et groupes d'opposition étaient déclarés illégaux. Durant ces mêmes années, le clergé modéré fut réprimé et des figures telles que Shariatmadari furent assignées à résidence. Les minorités religieuses et ethniques n'échappèrent pas non plus à la répression. En 1367, au terme d'une guerre injuste qui dura huit ans, le massacre collectif des prisonniers politiques fut déclenché par une *fatwa* directe de Khomeiny — massacre dont, d'après le seul communiqué d'Amnesty International publié pour le vingtième anniversaire de cette tragédie, plus de 5 000 noms sont recensés. Cette même année, le successeur désigné de Khomeiny, Montazeri, fut écarté de la scène en raison de ses protestations incessantes contre ces exécutions. Enfin, à la mort de Khomeiny, Khamenei accéda au rang de Guide, alors même qu'il ne remplissait pas, aux termes des articles 5 et 110 de la Constitution, les conditions requises pour occuper cette fonction. Cette désignation constitua le premier signe clair et manifeste de l'orientation de ce coup d'État.

L'une des complexités du régime tient au fait que, bien que Khomeiny et son successeur Khamenei soient parvenus au pouvoir par un processus violent et que le système édifié par la Constitution soit fortement déséquilibré en faveur du pouvoir du Guide, le principe de souveraineté nationale et l'élection du président de la République (fût-ce parmi les candidats agréés par le Guide) forment un espace presque protégé et impénétrable — peut-être un legs de la révolution de 1357 ou, plus loin encore, du mouvement culturel de la Révolution constitutionnelle. Peut-être même l'accession de Khatami au pouvoir, avant Ahmadinejad, prenait-elle racine dans ce principe.

Le 22 khordad de cette année, le Guide et ordonnateur du coup d'État tombe le masque et commet par ce geste deux erreurs majeures. Premièrement, il proclame le résultat du scrutin avant le Conseil des gardiens qu'il a lui-même nommé et auquel incombe légalement cette prérogative ; deuxièmement, il ferme la voie à toute contestation légale des résultats électoraux. Ce faisant, il perd toute légitimité en tant que garant du déroulement du scrutin, et avec elle le soubassement même de la fonction de Guide.

Les conséquences de ce dévoilement de la nature du régime et de son coup d'État dépendent des facteurs suivants : jusqu'où les dirigeants, les instigateurs, les exécutants et les donneurs d'ordres de ce coup d'État iront-ils dans les tueries, les pressions, la répression et le crime ? Dans quelle mesure le peuple, étranger aux clientèles inféodées au régime, résistera-t-il au retour de quatre nouvelles années semblables aux quatre terribles années écoulées ? Jusqu'à quel point les candidats à l'élection présidentielle — qui ont tous été des piliers du régime durant ces trente dernières années et n'ont guère les mains propres — sont-ils prêts à accompagner la résistance et à l'approfondir ? Jusqu'où les acteurs du Bazar et le clergé qui lui est lié, lesquels ont été des acteurs socio-politiques majeurs de l'histoire politique iranienne, ne lâcheront-ils pas Khamenei et Ahmadinejad ? N'oublions pas qu'ils n'ont pas répondu à l'appel de Khamenei à organiser une grande fête de la victoire au lendemain de la proclamation des résultats et de la victoire d'Ahmadinejad par le Guide.

Et enfin, comment la communauté internationale et les pays de la région joueront-ils leur rôle constructif — un rôle capable de dénoncer les violations des droits humains en Iran sans s'ingérer dans les affaires intérieures du pays ? C'est une heure historique ; rien n'est encore tranché. Le regard et les méthodes des dirigeants gagnent en maturité, et le peuple joue un rôle immense dans ce moment décisif. Nous avons besoin d'un regard historique et anthropologique capable, par la connaissance des facteurs agissants et déterminants de la situation présente, de fournir une analyse de la conjoncture actuelle — celle d'un peuple issu d'une grande civilisation, doté d'immenses richesses, et qui peut jouer un rôle décisif dans l'avenir de la région et du monde.

L'histoire nous montrera la mesure de cette maturité.

Hassan Makaremi

Psychanalyste clinicien

Chercheur – Sorbonne

Trésorier de la Ligue de défense des droits de l'homme en Iran

Paris, le 10 tir 1388

Cet article a été publié dans Libération

Bienvenu, Welcome, Khosh Amadid

en.title: Iran: The Curtain Lifts, the Face of a Coup d'État
en.executive_summary: https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/01/peinture-300706-193-Copier.jpg This article was published in Libération – 3 JULY 2009, Libération, Paris. The 22 Khordad ballot this year lifts the veil on a creeping coup d'état. Ahmadinejad's election four years ago paved the way for homogenising…
en.body_markdown:
https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/01/peinture-300706-193-Copier.jpg

This article was published in Libération

[3 JULY 2009 Libération Paris](http://www.liberation.fr/monde/2009/07/03/iran-le-rideau-tombe_568343)

The 22 Khordad ballot this year lifts the veil on a creeping coup d'état. Ahmadinejad's election four years ago paved the way for homogenising the levers of power in Iran. Until then, the Supreme Leader, Ali Khamenei, effectively held the levers of power by directly appointing the head of the judiciary, the commanders of all defence and security forces, and state broadcasting, and by vetting or disqualifying prospective candidates across all elections at every level through the approbatory supervision (*nezarat-e estesvabi*) of the Guardian Council.

In 1384, Ahmadinejad's presidency completed the pyramid of the networks of Revolutionary Guards (*Pasdaran*) and *Basij* forces forged during the Iran–Iraq War—like an army that needed only a commander. Even then, the elections were accompanied by irregularities and doubts, such as the very low turnout rate. Over those four years, the Supreme Leadership and the presidency, now wholly unified, launched their staged coup d'état, while the Guardian Council, in the 1387 parliamentary elections to the Islamic Consultative Assembly, effectively homogenised the parliament by disqualifying reformists. The presidency opened the doors to the *Pasdaran* across all executive bodies, ministries, and provincial governorships, and finally hollowed out the institutions responsible for overseeing government performance—such as dissolving the Plan and Budget Organisation—thereby opening the way for the *Pasdaran* in major projects.

The strategic objectives of this mafia–security network, the product of this creeping coup d'état, are manifold: unifying the "insider" (*khodi*) forces; marginalising the "outsiders" (*gheir-e khodi*), even those who might one day negotiate with reformist outsiders; increasing preventive capacity by highlighting the possibility of a velvet coup or foreign attack through cultural and media measures, by attempting to abolish the two-term limit on running for the presidency (a remark Ahmadinejad made at his campaign headquarters), and finally by forging alliances with countries in the region whose populations are predominantly Shi'i or which, like Iran, were governed by populists—in other words, buying time in the international arena until the requisite defence capability is attained.

This institutional consolidation and entrenchment of the system is also accompanied by a form of organisational restructuring designed to homogenise the educational system (the "one school, one mosque" scheme) and establish various associations affiliated with mosques. On the other hand, efforts are under way to seize control of the economy by expanding the power of foundations such as those of the War-Disabled (*Janbazan*), the Martyrs (*Shahid*), and *Astan Quds Razavi*, with staggering budgets beyond parliamentary oversight—foundations exempt from all taxation and administered directly under the Supreme Leader's supervision.

The longer-term strategic objectives of this coup are to prepare ideological warmongers who, anchored in their social base, will break across the boundary of the nation-state, spread their wings towards the Shi'i *ummah* in the region, and thereby seize the unified leadership of the Islamic world.

Such a programme was foreseen as early as 1357: an alliance between a branch of the Shi'i clergy that believed in *Velayat-e Faqih* and its social base, the product of a rural–oral culture—a social class that emerged after the land reforms of the 1340s through the migration of villagers into small towns and the densely populated peripheries of major cities.

From 1357 onwards, another creeping coup d'état had already taken shape. Bazargan, the first Prime Minister after the collapse of the monarchical system, was forced to resign simultaneously with the seizure of the American Embassy. A few months later, Bani-Sadr, the first President, was ousted from power, while all opposition parties and groups were outlawed. During those same years, the moderate clergy was suppressed and figures such as Shariatmadari were placed under house arrest. Religious and ethnic minorities did not escape repression either. In 1367, at the close of an unjust war that lasted eight years, the mass killing of political prisoners began by direct *fatwa* of Khomeini—on the basis of Amnesty International's statement alone on the twentieth anniversary of this tragedy, the names of more than 5,000 victims are documented. In that same year, Khomeini's designated successor, Montazeri, was removed from the scene owing to his persistent protests against these massacres; and finally, upon Khomeini's death, Khamenei ascended to the position of Supreme Leader, even though under Articles 5 and 110 of the Constitution he lacked the qualifications to hold that office. That selection was the first clear and unmistakable sign of the direction of this coup d'état.

One of the complexities of the regime lies in the fact that although Khomeini and his successor Khamenei came to power through a violent process, and although the system constructed under the Constitution is heavily skewed in favour of the Supreme Leader's power, the principle of national sovereignty and the election of the presidency (even from among candidates approved by the Supreme Leader) constitute a nearly protected and impenetrable space—perhaps a legacy of the 1357 revolution or, further back, of the cultural movement of the Constitutional Revolution. Perhaps Khatami's rise to power in the period preceding Ahmadinejad was also rooted in this principle.

On 22 Khordad of this year, the Supreme Leader and orchestrator of the coup drops the mask and, by this move, commits two grave mistakes. First, he announces the election result before the Guardian Council—which he himself appointed and whose legal duty that was; second, he blocks every avenue of legal challenge to the election results. Thus, he forfeits all credibility as the guarantor of the conduct of elections, and along with it the very foundation of the Supreme Leadership's function.

The consequences of this unveiling of the regime's essence and its coup depend upon the following factors: how far will the leaders, perpetrators, executors, and order-takers of this coup go in killing, pressure, repression, and crime? To what extent will the people outside the regime's dependent bases resist the re-imposition of another four years like the terrifying past four? To what degree are the presidential candidates—all of whom have likewise been pillars of the regime over the past thirty years and whose hands are scarcely clean—willing to stand with the resistance and deepen it? How long will the Bazaar elements and the clergy tied to them, who have been major socio-political actors in Iran's political history, refrain from abandoning Khamenei and Ahmadinejad? Let us not forget that they did not respond to Khamenei's call to stage a grand victory celebration the day after Khamenei announced the results and Ahmadinejad's victory.

And finally, how will the international community and the countries of the region play their constructive role—a role capable of protesting human rights violations in Iran without interfering in Iran's internal affairs? This is a historic hour; nothing is yet clear. The outlook and methods of the leaders are maturing, and the people hold an immense role in this juncture. We are in need of a historical and anthropological gaze capable, through knowledge of the active and operative factors of the present situation, of offering an analysis of current conditions—the conditions of a people rising from a great civilisation, endowed with abundant wealth, and capable of playing a decisive role in the future of the region and the world.

History will show us the measure of this maturity.

Hassan Makaremi

Clinical Psychoanalyst

Researcher – Sorbonne

Treasurer of the League for the Defence of Human Rights in Iran

Paris, 10 Tir 1388

This article was published in Libération

Bienvenu, Welcome, Khosh Amadid
