en.body_markdown:
https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/01/MVC-001F.jpg
[Read on Roozonline.](http://www.roozonline.com/persian/news/newsitem/article/-798b99b9d2.html)
Monday, 29 September 2014 (7 Mehr 1393)
Our cultural land encompasses the earth, the mountains, the sky, and the sea; society and "the people who have departed and those who have remained"; all of our oral and written culture; diverse religious beliefs (Shia, Sunni, Ismaili, Zoroastrian, Christian, Jewish, Bahá'í, ...); stone inscriptions, manuscripts, and archaeological artefacts; all infrastructures, bridges, and ports; natural and mineral resources and the richness of nature; wildlife and all plants and trees, far and near; all qanats and rivers; all extinct languages as well as all living languages and dialects such as Kurdish, Turkish, Balochi, Lori, and Arabic...; all modes of production, industry, the arts, and fine crafts; and traditions, dances, games, festivals, and the celebration of Nowruz. All the prestige and value of Iran's cultural name lie within the volume of this cultural land.

The dimensions of the cultural land can be better understood in relation to other concepts such as nation, state, and country. The Cultural Land of Iran exists in a volume rather than on a flat surface, and it encompasses diverse cultures as well as the exchange and communication amongst these cultures. This grand experience is itself the outcome of a multi-millennial process that has exerted a profound influence on the creation and growth of humanity's cultural heritage. This process includes the creation, growth, and expansion of the administrative and bureaucratic system—from Cyrus to the present day—as well as the structure of its languages and the readiness of those languages to coin or adopt words. Within this process, cultural productions ranging from oral culture to the entirety of written culture—from thousands of unpublished manuscripts to the corpus of published works and even translated works, from the earliest Sanskrit translations to the present—have come into being; the corpus of religious beliefs that has settled into the culture since ancient times, down to the body of textbooks of the various religious schools of this land, has likewise taken shape within this very context.

It must be noted that the Cultural Land of Iran also comprises the myths remaining from the earliest inhabitants of the Iranian plateau, down to the mythological strands inherited from the Aryan migrants and their exchange with other surrounding oral cultures. Productive systems—from the invention of the qanat to the chahartaq, the levying of taxes and the establishment of the postal system, the creation of a regular and standing army, the construction of architectural masterpieces, and the achievements of handicrafts and the arts of calligraphy and Nasta'liq penmanship—are likewise inscribed within this wealth of the cultural land. The cultural diversity and richness of our land have been forged by the earliest inhabitants of the civilisations of Jiroft, Lorestan, and Susa, together with contributions arising from Macedonian, Arab, Turkic, Hindu, Armenian, and other lineages. In addition to these, our cultural land encompasses all mystical experiences from the remotest antiquity to the present day, with all their oral and written achievements—whether in millions of couplets of poetry or in the oral traditions of the Naqshbandi, Gonabadi, and other dervish orders.

Let us not forget that our cultural land has also been shaped by migrations—from the migrations of the Parsis to India, to migrations to the Caucasus and the countries around the Persian Gulf, to several waves of migration to Africa, Europe, and America. This migration, which today—for the first time, with a figure approaching four million people—has itself transformed into a considerable economic and social force within host societies, possesses the inner capacity to form part of a contemporary, organised civil society.

Before proceeding, it is essential to recall a fundamental point: we must clarify concepts, definitions, and the role of words, and brush the dust off them. Through clarification and by establishing coherent, shared concepts, we can communicate better; yet one must always bear in mind that during historical crises, revolutions, and great upheavals, new concepts rapidly become widespread, and the relationship between these concepts and the words carrying them and previous concepts suffers disruption. This is what inflicts the greatest damage on the health of communication among the people of a society. Within a very short span of time, people who have lived in their natural, social, and productive environment and established a calm, continuous relationship with words and concepts find that words no longer represent their former meanings. Words such as "republic", "freedom", and "Islam", and concepts such as traditional beliefs and political system, in our Iran, are examples of such a complex situation.

Given the particular importance of this discussion, we shall endeavour to clarify these definitions in relation to one another—not because readers are unaware of them, but rather to enhance clarity and foster collective reflection and empathy. In this essay, our effort is directed towards defining a number of the following concepts in close relation to one another: homeland and native land (mihan and vatan), realm and country (mamlekat and keshvar), regime, system, sovereignty, government, state, uprising, movement, revolution, nation, people, society, ummah, community, population, belief, religion, ideology, tradition, culture, language, script, the corpus of ancestral works, oral culture, myth, history, civilisation, renewal (tajaddod), modernity, modernism, development, progress, programme, strategy—strategic services, popular rule, democracy.

The definitions of these concepts—in everyday language, in academic spheres, or in the language of international relations—may, overtly or covertly, differ from one another. Ultimately, one must submit to a set of consistent definitions. We Iranians live amongst the other peoples of this vast planet Earth and engage in exchange and dialogue with seven billion neighbours; we share land and maritime borders with them; we participate as partners in various regional and international treaties; every day thousands of people pass through Iran's air borders and thousands of vessels ply its coastal waters; every day we supply several hundred thousand barrels of oil and in return receive the bulk of our daily necessities; we establish various media outlets for others and benefit from the media of others; and every day we exchange billions of messages via telephone, the internet, media, and other social networks. By the very nature of human life, these communications are continually increasing. It is on the basis of these exchanges that we endeavour, to the best of our ability, to take as our foundation the common denominator of academic definitions accepted by international convention, so that we may situate the resulting conclusions within the context of the dynamic, contemporary world—even though we are well aware of the difficulties inherent in this presupposition.

On the one hand, the world is constituted by the richness of cultural diversity; words and concepts are forged within the specific history and geography of each era on the basis of the movement of the human beings who create cultures. Yet human communication has, since ancient times, given rise to the science-art of translation; at times, too, finding an accurate and appropriate equivalent separates words from their original context and turns them into counter-definitions....

We know that the growth and development of human civilisation stem from migrations, and civilisations are constructed through the encounter of migrants and the intermingling of cultures[i]. By way of example, the word "Islam" and the concept behind it vary even in societies where the majority of people traditionally consider themselves Muslim. Over these fourteen centuries, across five dimensions, Islam has left numerous deposits within diverse societies and social strata, and across varied aspects of individual and social life. These five dimensions may be summarised as follows: over the span of fourteen centuries, across a vast expanse stretching from North Africa to Central Asia, Central Europe, and beyond Indonesia, Islam has assumed myriad colours in different dimensions. For the sake of continuing our discourse, we may readily agree upon the following dimensions:

- The traditional dimension of Islam—that is, what pertains to people's everyday lives: civil and penal laws applied in practice; various rituals of marriage and divorce; commercial relations and transactions; family and social relations; and beliefs and convictions integrated into daily life, such as dream interpretation and votive offerings (nazr o niyaz). These traditions are a synthesis of what existed in the culture of pre-Islamic peoples and subsequently accepted traditions, behaviours, and discourses. Over the centuries, through the fusion of cultures, traditions have been renewed and have evolved alongside the advancement of science and technology—like every living organism in the struggle for survival.

- Islam in the field of sociology, anthropology, cultural history, history of religions, and history of ideas and its trajectory: let us call "scientific Islam" the examination and deep study of Islam in its diverse colours through recognised scientific methods, based on existing documents and evidence, as is customary in academic spheres—dialogue concerning research methods and instruments, findings, and inviting thinkers from various schools and beliefs of Islam to critique and examine these findings. This is an Islam that, in the long term, can correct many prevailing prejudices; by revealing the diverse hues of Islam, it invites believers to tolerance and moderates violence and insistence on the uniformity of beliefs. Such an Islam belongs to the realm of specialists, and the fruits of its work take a very long time to mature. The sublime value of such an Islam lies in explanation and enlightenment; it requires patience, time, and tolerance. These studies can introduce a measure of relativity into doctrinal boundaries. Such studies familiarise the minds of believers with the "why" of phenomena and help them become better acquainted with the trajectory of how their beliefs evolved. In the relation between diverse Islams, words become more precise and clearer; etymological and historical tracing replaces dogmatic insistence.

- Another is philosophical Islam, which from the very beginning engaged thinkers within Islamic societies. Although this theory has encountered resistance, it has maintained its presence in various forms up to the present day. From Avicenna (Ibn Sina) to Farabi, and from Mulla Sadra to Hajj Mulla Hadi Sabzevari, thinkers endeavoured to preserve the framework of philosophical thought—namely, addressing the foundations of thought and how it operates—and, while transmitting the teaching of ancient Greek philosophy, to draw upon the philosophical foundations of the Far East. With all its variegation, this philosophy also belongs primarily to the domain of knowledge, and its hermeneutic genealogy—situating this thought within the broader corpus of human philosophical knowledge as an effort to unify the history of human philosophy independently of religious inclinations—can render a great service to advancing enlightenment regarding the plurality of Islam.

- Undoubtedly, the mystical current of Islam has, alongside the spread of this religion and from its very inception, maintained a wholly independent presence in the Islamic world. This presence at times assumes an entirely philosophical dimension; at times it goes among the people and alters certain everyday behaviours and practices; and at times, solely in the cultural dimension, it draws poetry, music, and dance into its orbit. In our view, Islamic mysticism is inseparable from the broader phenomenon of mysticism and mystical experience, whose roots began with "shamans" (tribal healers/sorcerers) and progressed alongside the evolution of human culture. The diverse forms of mystical experience and thought—mostly covertly, yet at times overtly—define a particular relationship between the human being and the "Beyond" that cannot always align with the fundamentalist interpretation of the world in Islam. In its philosophical and cultural dimensions, mysticism has rendered immense services to the expansion of thought. Its social dimension continues to live on in a form of mutual tolerance. Mystical thought has been interwoven with human culture since time immemorial and has accompanied it; indeed, one might readily say that its antiquity and presence in human culture transcend formal religion and have themselves become a factor in the emergence of the foundation of cultural tolerance. With their lives, culture, poetry, and music, mystics have enriched our world.

- Finally, let us speak of an Islam that, as a method and pathway, attains the experience of governing society. Tracing the evolution of governmental Islam across the history of diverse societies lies beyond the scope of this brief essay. Our purpose here is to pose the fundamental question concerning the relationship between the citizen and a governance that bestows the name of Islam upon itself, or profits from the name of Islam to secure its own legitimacy and credibility. Indeed, the problem in the daily lives of citizens in such societies with their rulers is neither a traditional problem, nor an anthropological or sociological one, nor historical, nor philosophical or mystical.

Let us begin with the land (sarzamin). A land is a unit of the planet Earth that can be named: an expanse capable of serving as the habitat for a human population, defined under a single name. Over the passage of centuries and millennia, this name can in practice acquire a symbolic meaning. Mythical lands take shape in this manner. A land is a unit of the Earth's surface defined in relation to human life and the time of human existence—a surface that acquires volume in relation to the human being. Within this volume live human beings who are the creators of culture and life in this land. In such a land, political-military-economic units may take shape under various names, and diverse cultures may coexist with one another. One may say that in a cultural land, names derive their power and emblem from history and myth and live in harmony with one another.

Today, with a few exceptions, the dominant political-military unit in territories is called the state. States exercise their political power within precisely demarcated borders and maintain order inside those borders using law-enforcement forces. The totality of people placed under the authority of the state is called the nation. By virtue of this interdependence, today—save in rare cases—the unit of the nation-state is accepted. Sometimes several nation-states lie within a single cultural land, and sometimes several lands lie within a single nation-state. The basic characteristic of a nation-state is the presence of people within the unit of a country. In other words, the nation-state within its defined borders and in its historical presence is what we call a country. Countries generally possess foundational laws—traditional, written, or a combination of both—on the basis of which state structures gain legitimacy. A regime or system (nezam) is an interconnected set of institutions necessary to establish sovereignty and administer a country. The system is independent of individuals. An organisation is a framework in which individuals perform predetermined roles. A single currency, shared official and administrative language or languages, unified representatives in international organs authorised to sign treaties, and banking, commercial, and communication ties all derive from this presence of a country, nation-state, or system.

Yet how did these concepts take shape in our Cultural Land of Iran? Let us acknowledge that the Constitutional Law—establishing a monarchical system in which the Shah reigns rather than rules, and defining the roles of the three branches (legislative, judicial, and executive) separately from one another—laid the first foundations of the state, nation, country, and system of Iran. Reza Shah succeeded, by abolishing feudal regionalism (moluk al-tawayefi), in laying the groundwork for the modern concept of the country. Until 1962 and the start of the Land Reform, this country was governed under the banner of the Constitution, the government, and the administrative, social, productive, and traditional system that defined the role of the state and the three branches—with a few exceptions, each of which is important for our analysis:

- Following the ratification of the Supplementary Fundamental Law, it was stipulated that laws passed by the National Consultative Assembly had to receive the approval of five mujtahids. Gradually, under the interpretation that a sufficient number of qualified mujtahids already sat among the parliamentary deputies, this principle was in practice never implemented, and the hand of the Shia clergy was gradually removed from the legislative branch.

- Although the spirit of penal, civil, and administrative laws was rooted in Shia tradition and religion, in practice the judiciary too gradually came to be administered by trained jurists. One may say that the executive branch was modernised in a certain fashion, yet remained the natural continuation of the ancient bureaucratic system. Although feudal fragmentation was eliminated and central state authority was established uniformly throughout Iran, the productive-financial-property systems known as landlord-peasant (arbab-ra'iyati) and khan-tribal (khan-ashireh'i) continued in both agricultural and pastoral production sectors, with histories stretching back centuries and millennia. Until 1962, the landlord-peasant system was a state within a state.

By examining the percentage of khan and landlord deputies from the First Majles up to the first Majles following the Land Reform, we observe that this proportion stood between 40 and 50 per cent. Even accounting for the half-hearted nature of the electoral system as a whole both before and after this period, Iran's legislative sphere was in practice in the hands of landlords and khans, while the Shah was either linked to a ruling tribe or was himself the greatest landlord—or both. In practice, the Constitutional Law and modernisation yielded no results for the inhabitants of villages and nomadic tribes. During this period, the social, financial, and traditional influence and power of the Shia clergy—especially in villages and small towns, encompassing roughly more than half of the country's population—did not diminish; rather, clerical seminaries gradually grew stronger, and clerics gained access to and maintained a presence in the most remote corners of the realm. The Bazaar, as a foundational pillar of the distributive service system, and the landlords and khans in the two productive systems of agriculture and pastoralism, always maintained close financial and social ties with these religious seminaries. Throughout this interval, the clergy succeeded in preserving the structure and modus operandi of their seminaries—both financially and in terms of communicating with and mobilising supporters and believers, as well as maintaining ties with seminaries outside Iran, for example in Najaf and Karbala. Yet, until the establishment of the Islamic Republic, this state within a state could not affect the concept and presence of the nation-state in the land of Iran.

Between the years 1962 and 1979 (1341 to 1357 SH), the landlord-peasant and khan-tribal systems of production were dismantled, and in practice the influence of landlords and khans declined sharply. For the multitude of rural migrants and landless villagers moving into the cities and transforming into impoverished urban classes, the influence of the Shia clergy continued covertly, and a vast portion of our compatriots found their refuge and backing in them. From this point onwards, the guardians of the concept of the Cultural Land of Iran increasingly became the middle class, the educated stratum, traditional families, and the bazaar merchants—for members of the affluent, non-traditional strata tended rather to move in the direction of a superficial modernisation.

Thus, this concept emerged amidst the overt conflicts of political factions both inside and outside the country. Inside Iran, the adherents of Velayat-e Faqih—with apparent silence yet through daily pressure exerted across the educational, legal, security, and cultural systems, notably the Supreme Council of the Cultural Revolution—waged a struggle against the depth of the concept of the cultural land, to such an extent that in none of the training programmes of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (Sepah) is there the slightest trace of this concept. By way of example, consult the website of the Revolutionary Guards, the Constitution, the article pertaining to the establishment of this corps, and the publications of this institution: the name of Iran has been completely omitted, and everywhere one encounters the concept of the "Islamic Homeland" (mihan-e eslami). This Islamic Homeland is devoid of borders, history, and territorial limits, leaving the hands of the executors of the Constitution free for any form of interpretation or exegesis.

In the clashes amongst the various internal political factions, the concept of the Cultural Land of Iran is fundamentally absent from both theoretical and practical debates. However, this concept exists outside the country, within the sphere of social, political, and cultural activities. Knowledge, dissemination, and efforts towards the expansion and advancement of Iranian culture—particularly ten years after the diaspora and from the 1980s onwards—are clearly evident. Fortunately, everyone takes an interest in the presence of a shared Persian language. One may say that the ensemble of forces believing in the return of the Constitutional Law naturally give a more prominent presence to Cultural Iran from a political-national angle. At the same time, one must not lose sight of the fact that, in our view—given the events in countries surrounding Iran, the region, global policies in support of Israel, and the formation of ideological political forces centred around Islam with diverse orientations—there is a danger that the concept of the Cultural Land of Iran may gradually be consigned to oblivion, even among enlightened commentators. Given the likelihood of prolonged wars in the region and the prominent presence of three monotheistic religions, their sacred sites, and their fervent believers, one may rightly fear that this concept could drop off the agenda of civil and political forces.

In any event, from the perspective of strategic services, we require belief in long-term strategic objectives. If these objectives lack universal inclusivity, and if they do not lead to the creation and expansion of social solidarity, they will damage the historical, long-standing life of a culture. Iran's cultural presence across millennia—and its flexibility, interaction, and coexistence even with invading cultures—gives us the hope that "there is a living essence in this culture that flows so continuously". We can place the preservation, elevation, growth, expansion, and development of this culture within the Cultural Land of Iran—while upholding respect for the diversity of cultures, languages, traditions, and religious beliefs living in this mosaic—among our fundamental strategic objectives.

If we consider the secret of social and national solidarity in every society to lie in pursuing several strategic objectives, then by placing the value of the cultural land in Iran alongside social justice, the preservation, respect, and implementation of the provisions of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and the preservation and elevation of good neighbourly and humane relations with other lands, we can hope to enjoy the broad consensus of political forces and civil society both inside and outside Iran's borders.

Iran as a Cultural Land privileges harmony and agreement in action, in theory, in culture, and in what is rooted in millennia over other factors of national solidarity; hence, it can serve as a foundational factor of national solidarity over the long term and across present and future generations. One can readily hope that in future generations, once the Middle East grows calm, the conflicts amongst adherents of the three monotheistic religions and their internal disputes, as well as international conflicts based on profiteering from natural resources such as oil and gas, will subside, and a union of free human beings will emerge—living in the mould of their ancestral cultures and side by side, much like units that exist today in other regions of the world. And why should there not emerge a union of cultural-economic countries or lands, while upholding compliance with all provisions of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights?

If we yearn for that day—a day that can guide the region not only towards peace, construction, and fertility, but also foster the flourishing and enrichment of the region's multi-millennial cultural diversity—we must from this very moment establish culture, and in our case the Cultural Land of Iran, as the factor of internal solidarity in each society. No collective human political-social movement will triumph unless the strategic objectives of that movement are sound from the standpoint of historical perspective—or, to put it better, move along a historical-cultural-human trajectory, just as at least the past several tens of thousands of years of our existence as Homo sapiens have demonstrated. The path of cultural transcendence may at times have been disrupted for a brief period or even turned backwards, yet it has never abandoned its overarching trajectory of flourishing.

Following the invention of language, out of roughly 140,000 languages we have invented thus far, only 6,000 remain living languages (a living language is one used by more than 3,000 people for their daily communication). Following the invention of script and its stabilisation, we have day by day rendered it more concise, mature, and useful—a long, multi-millennial journey from prehistoric painting to pictographic hieroglyphs, to the Aramaic, Phoenician, and cuneiform scripts. Following the invention of the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen in Paris in 1792 up to the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948 and its acceptance and signature by 52 countries, including Iran, its universality has expanded; even though a very long road still lies ahead of us before reaching our ideal—namely, the observance of the principles of this Declaration everywhere and for everyone—its pace of growth is remarkable.

Under the canopy of the cultural land and respect for cultural diversity, and on the path of construction and dynamism, believers and thinkers will undoubtedly—while upholding observance of Article 1 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights—arrive at a comprehensive and inclusive definition for all human beings.

The human being possesses an identity that represents his or her presence in the world. Such an identity, with its diverse dimensions—such as cultural identity, sexual identity, and social identity—takes shape around the axis of one's life after birth. One's primordial wish, longing, and desire to stay alive gradually transforms over the course of growth and settles at the centre of one's identity. The desiring and speaking human being, through his or her presence, defends this identity and this desire to continue living. In the arena of life, when a human being encounters his or her counterpart—that is, an "I" positioned in a different situation who possesses the same structure of a desiring, identity-bearing "I"—their wishes and needs may, at times, be drawn into confrontation with those identities.

From this moment onwards, we witness two possible scenes: either the principle of rule-governed dialogue and the acceptance of "another reciprocal I" is brought onto the stage, and through tolerance we find an acceptable solution to address the desires and identities of these two "I"s; or we arrive at violence. In its principles, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights defines this "I", takes its freedom, equality, and dignity as the foundation, and establishes rule-governed dialogue between two individuals, two groups, states and peoples, and between states as the basis of relation. One can readily conclude that turning away from the foundational principles of this Declaration—which is the achievement of millennia of human endeavour—constitutes the overarching meaning of violence in all its forms and degrees of intensity. The principles of this Declaration rest on no law other than the acceptance of the identity of the speaking human being, which has taken shape around the axis of his or her right to life.

Footnote

1- More than one hundred and fifty thousand years ago, the first great human migration began. Out of the 13 billion human beings born up to the present day, 7 billion of us are alive today, all of whom are the product of migration. Up to 90,000 years before our time, migrations took place within Africa; then, by 50,000 years ago, we arrived in the vicinity of present-day India. By 30,000 years ago, we had traversed Asia, Europe, and Australia, and from that day to the present, we have trodden across the Americas and the rest of the world. Changing environmental conditions—heat, cold, and drought on the one hand, and the search for more favourable living conditions on the other—turn migration into a necessity. Along the course of these migrations, the human being adapts to the new, and the new shapes the human being.

fr.body_markdown:
https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/01/DSC0073-Copier.jpg

Jeudi 27 février 2014 (8 esfand 1392)

Le captif de ton amour est libre des deux mondes ;

Le mendiant de ta ruelle se passe des huit paradis.

L'importance de telles études réside en ce qu'elles bousculent l'étroitesse d'esprit puérile qui consiste à diviser le monde en cultures, en religions et en traditions, et qu'elles portent ensuite la profondeur du regard humain jusqu'au fondement même de l'apparition de l'être humain sur la planète Terre. Elles montrent encore la profondeur de la dépendance et de la solidarité de l'être humain moderne (*Homo sapiens sapiens*) dès l'instant où il commence à parler. Peut-être l'unique antidote aux vues étriquées de l'être humain consiste-t-il à tourner son regard vers l'universalité de la culture, lorsque nous replaçons l'être humain dans l'étendue de quarante mille ans d'existence, de onze milliards d'individus et d'un être sans frontières.

On dirait que si l'on veut quitter Hâfez pour commencer ailleurs, c'est lui qui se tient embusqué dans un refuge et nous barre la route. Il y a plusieurs années, dans un texte intitulé « La mémoire au-delà du mot », j'avais évoqué une station dans les expériences humaines que l'on désigne diversement comme la « station de l'amour », l'« état » (*hâl*), la « sortie de soi », la « délivrance » ou le « huitième continent ». Dans cet écrit, je m'étais attaché à montrer l'accès à cette station dans les discours de cultures diverses, depuis les temps les plus reculés jusqu'à nos jours. On peut suivre la trace d'un tel discours depuis les chamanes et les « premiers humains », en passant par les textes mythologiques, les recherches récentes des scientifiques sur les « revenants de la mort clinique brève », les mystiques de l'Illumination (*ishrâq*), les paroles rapportées des prophètes, certains états d'extase induits par les stupéfiants, jusqu'à un groupe de sujets psychotiques.

Dans ce texte, je m'efforçais de dégager un fil conducteur commun en explorant ces divers discours à travers leur durée historique et leur épaisseur temporelle, et de montrer que, puisque l'expression de cette station ou de cette expérience demeure, de l'aveu unanime, impossible par les « mots », on peut reconduire cette expérience au vestige d'une mémoire humaine antérieure à l'accès de l'être humain au langage et à la parole.

Un tel retour d'un souvenir lointain qui surgit parfois devant l'être humain — et dont l'avènement et le lieu présentent une forme générale commune par-delà la séparation des cultures, des langues et des époques — peut être tenu pour un événement. Le secret du discours des mystiques de l'Illumination tient à ce que, dans leurs expériences, ils dessinent l'accès à un monde que l'on peut résumer de manière condensée par quatre mots : amour, lumière, unité et universalité.

Cet événement n'est ni la mort, puisqu'il se déroule au sein de la vie, ni la vie, puisqu'en cette expérience la relation avec le monde extérieur se trouve tranchée. Pour ceux qui sont familiers de la culture de la mystique illuminative, multiplier les exemples d'un tel discours reviendrait à porter du cumin à Kermân. On peut se borner à évoquer les paroles de Hallâj et de Cheikh Rûzbehân Baqlî de Chirâz. Dans les paroles rapportées des prophètes, nous rencontrons fréquemment l'Ascension (*mi'râj*) et ses diverses exégèses et interprétations, ainsi que le lien intime du Christ avec la lumière et l'amour. Ceux qui sont familiers du discours des sujets psychotiques ont maintes fois entendu ces derniers parler eux aussi de brefs instants où une jouissance profonde envahit leur âme et où ils accèdent à un autre état.

De telles paroles s'entendent également dans les récits de certaines personnes plongées dans l'extase par des substances stupéfiantes, et parfois aussi dans la bouche d'athlètes de très haut niveau qui poussent leur effort jusqu'aux ultimes limites de leur corps. Dans les études anthropologiques modernes consacrées aux récits d'expériences des sorciers et chamanes des tribus primitives, on perçoit également la trace de telles expériences, car ceux-ci, parfois sous l'effet de stupéfiants et de mouvements monotones, relatent une expérience de voyage et de sortie hors de leur propre corps.

Mais ce qui a le plus profondément ébranlé les études scientifiques de la seconde moitié du XXe siècle, ce sont les travaux du médecin américain le docteur Moody, qui, en publiant un ouvrage consacré à plus de cinq cents expériences de mort clinique brève fondé sur le recueil de leurs témoignages, fit apparaître une concordance inédite. Depuis lors et jusqu'à aujourd'hui, l'expérience de mort clinique brève fait l'objet de recherches et d'examens dans différentes écoles de médecine et de psychologie. Bien que ces personnes appartiennent à des cultures diverses, parlent des langues différentes et aient connu cet événement à des âges variés, elles décrivent généralement un état empreint d'aisance et de sérénité, sans désir de retour ; dans cet état, une lumière singulière est perçue, et leur difficulté fondamentale demeure qu'après ce retour, aucun mot ne parvient à dire ce voyage.

La diversité de ces expériences — des mystiques de l'Illumination aux revenants de la mort clinique brève, aux personnes en proie aux stupéfiants et aux chamanes des tribus primitives — d'une part, et leur présence depuis l'aube de l'histoire jusqu'à nos jours dans des cultures variées, d'autre part, nous ouvrent une porte pour porter un autre regard sur notre propre mystique illuminative et la séparer de manière décisive et définitive de la religion. Car ce phénomène, cette expérience, est infiniment plus profond et plus saisissant que les religions, les cultures et les divers modes de vie. La démonstration de l'hypothèse de la présence de cette station chez l'être humain et de son lien avec le vestige de la mémoire antérieure à l'invention du langage, de la parole et du mot ne devient possible qu'avec l'avancée des recherches scientifiques en anthropologie, en archéologie, en linguistique, en psychanalyse clinique, en psychologie — en particulier dans la branche qui étudie le fonctionnement de la mémoire — et singulièrement dans la recherche sur les modalités d'émergence du langage et de la parole.

Il y a quelque temps, à la suite d'une autre recherche, j'ai parcouru de nouveau d'un bout à l'autre le *Dîvân* de Hâfez. Dans cette recherche, je m'étais proposé de confronter d'une certaine manière la Déclaration universelle des droits de l'homme — avec son préambule et ses trente articles — aux poèmes de Hâfez, ou du moins de trouver en regard de chaque « article » un poème de Hâfez afin de composer une série de calligraphies-peintures. C'est au cours de cette relecture que, soudain, Hâfez me dévoila un autre secret. Dans plus de dix de ses poèmes, Hâfez évoque un lieu et une station extérieurs aux deux mondes, et chaque fois il relie d'une manière ou d'une autre cette station et ce lieu à l'amour. Dans le présent texte, je m'efforce, en analysant ces poèmes, de mettre en lumière cette relation :

Je le dis ouvertement, et de mes propres paroles mon cœur est réjoui :

Je suis l'esclave de l'amour, et des deux mondes je suis affranchi.

Qu'il me soit permis de passer sur l'étude littéraire, esthétique et sur l'art de séduction des poèmes de Hâfez, ce qui nous entraînerait trop loin. Si Hâfez, cette fois, parle ouvertement, c'est à n'en pas douter qu'il avait déjà tenu ce même propos à mots couverts. De cette franchise il se réjouit ; il se réjouit d'avoir ouvert son cœur. La servitude envers l'amour le libère des deux mondes. Quels sont ces deux mondes ? De façon succincte, dans les trois religions monothéistes — le judaïsme, le christianisme et l'islam — il est question du monde passager présent, dans lequel se déroule notre vie quotidienne, et d'un autre monde, qui est le monde d'après la mort, le monde du jugement, le monde perpétuel et éternel (*bâqî*). Bien que les définitions de ces deux mondes ne soient pas identiques dans les trois religions, elles possèdent des traits communs, tels que le rôle du temps, le caractère créé et contingent (*hâdeth*) de ce monde, la création des cieux et de la terre en six ou sept jours, la création d'Adam et Ève, ainsi que des notions comme l'éternité sans commencement (*azal*) et l'éternité sans fin (*abad*), le permanent (*bâqî*) et le périssable (*fânî*). Le phénomène permanent et toujours stable constitue un monde, tandis que le monde contingent et périssable, qui possède un commencement et une fin temporels, constitue l'autre monde.

Les interprétations et exégèses de ces deux mondes dans les trois religions susmentionnées, ainsi que les divergences des commentateurs sur la manière dont advient le monde périssable et sur le rôle du monde éternel, ne sont pas notre propos ici. La structure fondamentale de la connaissance, dès lors que nous croyons en un Créateur unique, nous convoque nécessairement au monde contingent et au monde éternel. Dans le vers cité, Hâfez tient la servitude de l'amour pour la liberté à l'égard des deux mondes. Appelons cette servitude de l'amour une « station » (*maqâm*) ou un « état », car dans d'autres poèmes de Hâfez cette relation est énoncée plus clairement encore :

Je ne céderais cette station ni pour ce bas monde ni pour l'au-delà,

Quand bien même, à chaque instant, une assemblée se lancerait à ma poursuite.

Cette « station » est posée face à ce bas monde (*donyâ*) et à l'au-delà (*âkherat*) ; autrement dit, ce bas monde et l'au-delà relèvent du même jeu des deux mondes et des sollicitations ou incitations de diverses assemblées, chacune prisonnière soit de ce bas monde, soit de l'au-delà. Hâfez porte la station de l'amour si haut qu'il situe sa plénitude dans le cœur comme le rejet de toute dépendance à l'égard du néant et de l'être :

Ô cœur, ne demeure pas un seul instant dépourvu d'amour et d'ivresse ;

Puis va-t'en, car tu es délivré et du néant et de l'être.

Néant et être, périssable et permanent : deux mondes et deux phénomènes tangibles pour l'être humain, à l'instar de la mort et de la vie. Au point que Hâfez considère même la souveraineté de l'univers comme un simple tributaire de l'amour. Là encore, la station de l'amour se tient face au monde éternel et au monde périssable, et en dehors de ces deux-là, si bien qu'il désigne la plus haute dignité — la souveraineté de l'univers — comme attachée au service de l'amour :

Que le monde éphémère et le monde éternel soient sacrifiés au Témoin et à l'Échanson,

Car je vois la souveraineté de l'univers comme un simple tributaire de l'amour.

Tantôt Hâfez oppose « tout ce qui existe » à la station de l'amour, tantôt « le monde éternel et le monde périssable », tantôt encore « l'être et le néant » ; et la contradiction de tout cela avec les deux mondes, éternel et périssable — lesquels tiennent tous deux dans « ce qui existe » — n'a pas échappé à son regard acéré :

À l'instant même où j'ai accompli mes ablutions à la source de l'amour,

J'ai prononcé d'un coup les quatre *takbîr* sur tout ce qui existe.

La libération de tout ce qui existe s'opère ici par le prélude et la préparation à l'accomplissement de la prière, mais cette fois dans la station de l'amour : servitude, *takbîr* et ablutions à la source de l'amour, ce qui, comme nous l'avons vu précédemment, n'est possible pour Hâfez qu'au prix de l'abandon des deux mondes.

Nous retrouvons ces deux mondes — l'un étant ce monde de la vie présente, et l'autre celui vers lequel nous traînons notre âme avec regret — dans un autre de ses poèmes :

Réjouissons-nous, sinon l'on nous entraînera dans le regret,

Le jour où nous transporterons le bagage de l'âme vers un autre monde.https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/01/DSC0073-Copier.jpg

Dans la pensée de Hâfez, « ce qui est », la « Création », est un atelier doté d'une structure, où réside un dessein, et dont l'ouvrage prendra fin un jour. L'unique voie pour déchiffrer l'énigme et le secret de cet atelier demeure, là encore, la station de l'amour :

Deviens amant, sinon un jour l'œuvre du monde prendra fin,

Sans que tu aies lu le dessein voulu dans l'atelier de l'existence.

Pour atteindre au secret des deux mondes et à la lumière de la coupe où se reflète l'univers, il place la voie dans le fait de boire d'un trait. Tenons pour acquis que ce qu'il entend par l'ivresse du vin n'est autre que l'entrée dans l'arène et la station de l'amour. L'essence d'une telle coupe, il la tient pour issue d'un autre monde, qui n'est assurément ni ce monde éternel ni ce monde périssable. Car « l'argile des potiers » fait allusion à la glèbe d'Adam pétrie avec le vin et permettant, par cette voie, d'accéder à la station de l'amour, laquelle constitue un troisième monde :

La gemme de la coupe de Jamshîd provient de la mine d'un autre monde ;

Et toi, tu quémandes cela à l'argile des potiers.

Cet « autre monde », par une allusion directe cette fois, esquisse le dessein d'une troisième station ou d'une autre âme, qui se trouve au cœur même de la vie de l'être humain et avant sa mort. J'ai montré le rôle de ce troisième monde dans une communication présentée au colloque de Hambourg (*Hâfez du secret ou le secret de Hâfez*). Ce monde se situe au-delà de la rétribution et de la récompense du paradis dans l'au-delà que promet Dieu, et au-delà des biens matériels de ce bas monde dont le souverain peut nous combler :

Ne t'accoutume pas à l'obligation envers autrui, car dans les deux mondes,

L'agrément de Dieu et la grâce du roi te suffisent.

Il tient les denrées de ce monde-ci comme de l'autre pour de maigre valeur et se tient en quête d'autre chose :

Ne prise pas même un grain d'orge les délices des deux mondes devant les amants,

Car celles-ci sont une denrée modique et celui-là un don abondant.

Et c'est de là que les glaneurs de la moisson d'amour n'abaissent point la tête devant les profits des deux mondes :

Ils ne s'inclinent point devant la moisson des deux mondes ;

Vois la fierté et la hauteur des mendiants et des glaneurs !

Et ce mendiant est le mendiant de la ruelle de l'amour, qui se passe des huit paradis et est libre des deux mondes :

Le mendiant de ta ruelle se passe des huit paradis ;

Le captif de ton amour est libre des deux mondes.

Et s'il se fait notre compagnon, une porte s'ouvre et une station s'obtient qui vaut bien l'hostilité des deux mondes. La question nouvelle qui se pose est de savoir pourquoi et comment cet autre monde — le monde éternel — pourrait être ennemi, sinon à supposer que le Juge s'érige en adversaire dans l'exercice même de son jugement et qu'au lieu des huit paradis, il inflige à Hâfez le châtiment de l'enfer ? Là encore, Hâfez préfère la station de l'amour :

Dis à l'Ami : sois mon compagnon, et que les deux mondes soient mes ennemis ;

Dis à la Fortune : ne me tourne pas le dos, et que toute la surface de la terre lève une armée.

Et encore, si une tourmente venait à heurter l'un contre l'autre les deux mondes, il compte alors sur la lampe des yeux veillant sur le chemin de l'attente de l'Ami. Dans la station de l'amour et l'attente de l'Ami, la tourmente des deux mondes n'a plus de place :

Si le vent de la discorde venait à bouleverser les deux mondes,

Nous resterions avec la lampe de nos yeux, tournés vers le chemin où l'on attend l'Ami.

Nous achevons notre brève déambulation dans l'univers tridimensionnel des trois mondes de Hâfez par ces trois distiques. Bien qu'il ne s'adresse qu'aux gens de discernement (*ahl-e nazar*), lorsqu'il dit :

Les gens de discernement perdent les deux mondes en un seul regard ;

C'est l'amour, et dès la première mise l'on peut engager le denier comptant de sa vie.

Il perd les deux mondes en un seul regard dans le jeu de l'amour, dans ce bref instant où l'ouverture à l'âme et à la station de l'amour devient possible, et il place dans la mise du pari de l'amour le capital comptant de sa vie :

Au jour de ma mort, accorde-moi le répit d'un souffle pour te contempler,

Afin que, tel Hâfez, je renonce d'un coup à la vie et au monde.

Et comment se fait-il que Hâfez, hormis la station de l'amour, tienne tout ce qui existe dans les deux mondes pour périssable, y compris le monde éternel lui-même !

J'ai exposé les deux mondes devant un cœur éprouvé par l'expérience :

Hormis ton amour, il tint tout le reste pour périssable.

Le cœur éprouvé de Hâfez connaît la station de l'amour, et c'est lui qui distingue le bon aloi du faux et juge périssable toute la moisson de jouissances des deux mondes.

Hâfez n'est pas le seul à dévoiler ainsi, avec tant de franchise, une troisième station ou un troisième monde entre les deux mondes. Mowlavi (Rûmî) fait une allusion rapide à cette notion dans ce distique :

Avec les deux mondes, l'amour entretient une étrangeté ;

En lui résident soixante-douze folies.

Et Ferdowsi, qui compare la délivrance de l'espoir en l'au-delà et de l'espoir en ce monde à l'état d'ivresse :

Ni espoir de l'au-delà, ni ce bas monde en main,

Éperdu, détaché des deux, tel un homme ivre.

Fort de ce préambule, l'on peut concevoir qu'il advienne parfois à l'être humain une station où, au sein de sa vie matérielle et avant la mort, il outrepasse le réel de son corps et, dans l'état d'amour et d'ivresse qui n'est en apparence qu'un souffle, se trouve tout ensemble « dans la vie » et « hors d'elle », sans avoir encore posé le pied de l'autre côté, dans la mort.

en.title: Hafez, Love, and the Two Worlds: The Transient and Everlasting Worlds Sacrificed to the Beloved Witness and the Cupbearer
en.executive_summary: https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/01/DSC0073-Copier.jpg Thursday, 27 February 2014 (8 Esfand 1392): 'Captive to your love, one is free from both worlds; a beggar in your lane stands in no need of the eight paradises.' The importance of such studies lies in shattering the childish narrow-mindedness of dividing the world into cultures, religions, and…
en.body_markdown:
https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/01/DSC0073-Copier.jpg

Thursday, 27 February 2014 (8 Esfand 1392)

Captive to your love, one is free from both worlds;

A beggar in your lane stands in no need of the eight paradises.

The importance of studies such as this lies in the fact that they shatter the childish narrow-mindedness of dividing the world into cultures, religions, and traditions, and then carry the depth of human insight back to the very foundation of humanity's emergence upon planet Earth. They demonstrate once more the depth of interdependence and solidarity of modern human beings (*Homo sapiens sapiens*) from the very moment they begin to speak. Perhaps the sole antidote to human myopia is to draw one's gaze towards the universality of culture, when we situate humanity within the expanse of forty thousand years of existence, eleven billion lives, and boundless being.

It is as though, should you wish to leave Hafez behind and begin elsewhere, it is he who sits in a sanctuary and bars your path. Years ago, in an essay entitled *Memory Beyond the Word*, I pointed to a station within human experience that is variously called the 'station of love', 'state' (*hal*), 'stepping outside oneself', 'deliverance', or the 'eighth continent'. In that essay, I sought to demonstrate access to this station across the discourses of diverse cultures from the remotest antiquity to the present day. One may trace the footprint of such discourse from shamans and 'the earliest humans' to mythological writings, from recent scientific studies on 'those who have returned from brief clinical death' to the mystics of Illumination (*ishraq*), the reported sayings of prophets, certain states of self-transcendence induced by narcotics, and a group of psychotic subjects.

In that essay, I aimed to uncover a common thread by investigating diverse discourses across their historical span and temporal volume, and to show that because expressing this station or experience in 'words' is, by universal consent, impossible, one may trace this experience back to a vestige of human memory predating humanity's access to language and speech.

Such a return of a distant memory that occasionally confronts human beings — and whose occurrence and locus exhibit a shared general form across the divisions of culture, language, and time — may be regarded as an event. The secret of the discourse of the mystics of Illumination lies in the fact that, in their experiences, they chart access to a world that may be concisely associated with four words: love, light, unity, and universality.

This event is neither death, since it unfolds within life, nor life, since within this experience one's relation with the external world is severed. For those acquainted with the culture of illuminative mysticism, offering examples of such discourse would be like carrying cumin to Kerman. One need only mention the sayings of Hallaj and Shaykh Ruzbahan Baqli of Shiraz. In the reported utterances of the prophets, we repeatedly encounter the Ascension (*Mi'raj*) and its varied exegeses and interpretations, as well as Christ's intimate bond with light and love. Those familiar with the speech of psychotic subjects have heard time and again that they too speak of brief moments in which a profound jouissance seizes their soul and they attain another state.

Such accounts are also heard in the recollections of certain individuals entranced by narcotics, and at times from the mouths of athletes at the highest levels of sport who push their exertion to the utmost limits of their bodies. In modern anthropological studies examining the reported experiences of shamans in primal tribes, traces of such experiences are likewise audible, for these figures, sometimes under the influence of narcotics and monotonous movements, speak of an experience of journeying and stepping outside their own bodies.

Yet what shook the scientific studies of the second half of the twentieth century most profoundly were the investigations of the American physician Dr Moody, who, by publishing a book on over 500 experiences of brief clinical death and gathering their testimonies, brought a striking concordance to light. From that date until today, the experience of brief clinical death has been the subject of research and enquiry across various schools of medicine and psychology. Although these individuals hail from diverse cultures, speak different languages, and underwent this event at varied ages, they generally speak of a state characterised by ease and tranquillity with no desire to return; in this state a remarkable light is beheld, and their fundamental difficulty is that, following this return, no words can articulate the journey.

The diversity of these experiences — from mystics of Illumination to returnees from brief clinical death, those entranced by narcotics, and shamans of primal tribes — on the one hand, and the presence of these experiences from the dawn of history to the present across varied cultures, on the other, open a door for us to look anew upon our own illuminative mysticism and to separate it decisively and permanently from religion. For this phenomenon, this experience, is far deeper and more all-encompassing than religions, cultures, and varied ways of life. Proving the hypothesis of this station's presence in human beings and its connection to the vestige of memory predating the invention of language, speech, and words becomes possible only through the advancement of scientific research in anthropology, archaeology, linguistics, clinical psychoanalysis, psychology — especially the branch devoted to the functioning of memory — and above all research into how language and speech came into being.

Some time ago, in pursuit of another study, I read through the *Divan* of Hafez from end to end once more. In that study, I intended to measure the Universal Declaration of Human Rights — with its preamble and thirty articles — in some fashion against the poems of Hafez, or at least to find a poem by Hafez corresponding to each 'article' in order to compose a series of calligraphy-paintings. It was during that re-reading that Hafez suddenly unlocked another secret for me. In more than ten of his poems, Hafez alludes to a place and a station outside the two worlds, and each time he binds this station and place in some way to love. In the present essay, I endeavour to demonstrate this relationship by dissecting these poems:

I declare it openly, and in my own words my heart takes delight:

I am the servant of love, and from both worlds I am free.

Allow me to pass over the literary and aesthetic examination and the art of enchantment in Hafez's poetry, for that would take us too far afield. As to why Hafez speaks openly this time, he had undoubtedly uttered the very same truth behind a veil beforehand. He takes delight in this candid utterance; he delights in having laid bare his heart. Servitude to love frees him from the two worlds. What are these two worlds? Briefly, across the three monotheistic religions — Judaism, Christianity, and Islam — mention is made of the present transient world in which our everyday life unfolds, and another world, which is the world after death, the world of judgement, the perpetual and everlasting (*baqi*) world. Although the definitions of these two worlds are not identical across the three religions, they share common features, such as the role of time, the contingent and created (*hadith*) nature of this world, the creation of the heavens and the earth in six or seven days, the creation of Adam and Eve, and concepts such as eternity without beginning (*azal*) and eternity without end (*abad*), the everlasting (*baqi*) and the transient (*fani*). The everlasting, ever-enduring phenomenon forms one world, while the contingent and transient world, which has a temporal beginning and end, forms another.

The interpretations and exegeses of these two worlds in the three aforementioned religions, and the disagreements of commentators over how the transient world came into being and the role of the everlasting world, are not our concern here. The foundational structure of cognition, whenever we believe in a single Creator, compels us towards the contingent world and the everlasting world. In the verse cited above, Hafez regards servitude to love as freedom from both worlds. Let us call servitude to love a 'station' (*maqam*) or 'state', for in other poems by Hafez this relationship is expressed even more clearly:

I would not trade this station for this world or the hereafter,

Even though an assembly pursue me at every moment.

This 'station' is set over against this world (*dunya*) and the hereafter (*akhirat*); in another guise, this world and the hereafter belong to the same interplay of the two worlds and the encouragements and urgings of various assemblies, each ensnared either in this world or in the hereafter. Hafez elevates the station of love to the point where he identifies its richness in the heart as the casting off of dependence upon non-being and being:

O heart, be not for a single breath devoid of love and intoxication;

Then go, for you have been delivered from non-being and being.

Non-being and being, transient and everlasting: two worlds and two tangible phenomena for human beings, like death and life. So much so that Hafez deems even the sovereignty of the cosmos to be an attendant upon love. Once again, the station of love stands over against the everlasting world and the transient world, and outside both, such that he describes the highest rank — the sovereignty of the cosmos — as girt in the service of love:

May the transient world and the everlasting world be sacrificed to the Beloved Witness and the Cupbearer,

For I behold the sovereignty of the cosmos as a mere attendant upon love.

At times Hafez sets 'all that exists' over against the station of love, at times 'the everlasting and transient world', and at times 'being and non-being'; and the contradiction between these and the two worlds, everlasting and transient — both of which are contained within 'that which exists' — did not escape his piercing gaze:

At the very moment I performed my ablutions at the spring of love,

I pronounced the four *takbirs* at once over everything that exists.

Freedom from all that exists is achieved here through the prelude and preparation for standing in prayer, yet this time in the station of love: servitude, the *takbir*, and performing ablutions at the spring of love — which, as we saw earlier, is possible for Hafez only in the station of renouncing the two worlds.

We find these two worlds — one this world of living, and the other the one towards which we drag our souls with regret — in another of his poems:

Let us make merry, lest they drag us away in regret,

On the day we carry the baggage of the soul to another world.https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/01/DSC0073-Copier.jpg

In Hafez's thought, 'that which is', 'Creation', is a workshop endowed with structure, containing a purpose, whose work will one day come to an end. The sole way to read the riddle and secret of this workshop remains, once again, the station of love:

Become a lover, lest one day the work of the world come to an end,

While you have left unread the intended design in the workshop of existence.

To attain the secret of both worlds and the light of the world-revealing cup, he places the path in draining a draught. Let us take it as understood that what he means by drinking wine is precisely entering the arena and station of love. The jewel of such a cup he holds to come from another world, which is assuredly neither this everlasting world nor that transient world. For 'the clay of the potters' alludes to the clay of Adam and its kneading with wine, and thereby reaching the station of love, which is a third world:

The jewel of Jamshid's cup comes from the mine of another world;

Yet you seek it from the clay of the potters.

This other world, with a direct allusion this time, puts forward the design of a third station or another soul, which lies within the human being's living existence and prior to death. I demonstrated the role of this third world in a paper delivered at the Hamburg conference (*Hafez of the Secret, or the Secret of Hafez*). This world lies beyond the recompense and reward of paradise in the next world promised by God, and beyond the material blessings of this world with which a sovereign may endow us:

Do not accustom yourself to being indebted to others, for in both worlds,

The favour of God and the bounty of the sovereign suffice you.

He regards the wares of both this world and the next as meagre and is in search of something else:

Value the delights of both worlds at a mere barleycorn before the lovers,

For this is a paltry ware and that a boundless gift.

And hence the gleaners of the harvest of love do not bow their heads to the bounties of the two worlds:

They do not bow their heads before the harvest of both worlds;

Behold the pride and loftiness of the beggars and gleaners!

And this beggar is the beggar in the lane of love, who stands in no need of the eight paradises and is free from both worlds:

The beggar in your lane stands in no need of the eight paradises;

The captive of your love is free from both worlds.

And should the Beloved become a friend, a door opens and a station is won that makes the enmity of both worlds worthwhile. The fresh question that arises is why and how that other world — the everlasting world — could be an enemy, unless the Judge takes up enmity in the very act of judgement and, instead of the eight paradises, visits the torment of hell upon Hafez? Here too, Hafez prefers the station of love:

Tell the Beloved: be my friend, and let both worlds be my enemies;

Tell Fortune: do not turn your back, and let the whole face of the earth raise armies against me.

And again, should turmoil dash both worlds together, he counts upon the lamp of the eyes watching along the path of awaiting the Beloved. In the station of love and awaiting the Beloved, the turmoil of the two worlds has no place:

Should the wind of turmoil dash both worlds together,

There remain we, the lamp of our eyes, and the path of awaiting the Beloved.

We bring our brief stroll through the three-world universe of Hafez to a close with these three couplets. Although he turns only towards the people of insight (*ahl-e nazar*), when he says:

People of insight stake and lose both worlds in a single glance;

It is love, and on the very first throw one may wager the ready coin of one's life.

He loses both worlds in a single glance of the game of love, in that brief moment when an opening towards the soul and the station of love becomes possible, and in the wager of love's gamble he stakes the ready coin of his life:

On the day of my death, grant me a single breath's respite to behold you,

So that, like Hafez, I may rise above both life and the world.

And how is it that Hafez, apart from the station of love, deems everything in both worlds to be transient — even the everlasting world itself!

I laid both worlds before a heart seasoned by experience:

Save for your love, it judged all the rest to be perishable.

Hafez's seasoned heart knows the station of love, and it is that heart which distinguishes the genuine from the base and deems the entire harvest of pleasures of both worlds to be perishable.

It is not Hafez alone who so candidly reveals a third station or third world between the two worlds. Mowlavi (Rumi) makes a passing allusion to this concept in this couplet:

With both worlds, love keeps an estrangement;

Within it lie seventy-two madnesses.

And Ferdowsi, who compares deliverance from hope in the hereafter and hope in this world to a state of intoxication:

Neither hope of the hereafter nor this world in hand,

Bewildered, severed from both, like one intoxicated.

With this preamble, one may conceive that a human being occasionally attains a station in which, during material life and prior to death, one passes beyond the Real of one's body, and in the state of love and intoxication — which appears to be no more than a single breath — is at once 'within life' and 'outside it', without yet having set foot on the other side, in death.

fr.title: Le concept de « voir » dans la poésie de Hâfez : la « vision » hafézienne
