en.body_markdown:
https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/01/DSC0076-Copier.jpg
[Read on Gooya](http://news.gooya.com/politics/archives/2014/05/179193.php)

Friday, 12 Ordibehesht 1393

Indifference, which is the flip side of depression, itself generates a form of withdrawal, non-involvement in social issues, and estrangement from collective work, and is one of the scourges of civil society. We see that we are trapped in a vicious circle: economic and social pressures, within an overarching atmosphere of cultural and historical depression, generate depression and indifference, and these two phenomena render civil society listless and numb, thereby enabling the continuation of the current rulers' governance.

Part Three: Depression, Addiction, and Social Indifference in Iran

In the first and second parts of this study, which were published previously, we sought to refine the scope of inquiry by addressing general definitions and, by clarifying those definitions and drawing upon official state data, to explain the structure and system of mental healthcare in Iran. In this section, we shall examine the most significant psychological pathology posing an immense danger to the future of our society—namely, depression, addiction, and social indifference in Iran—placing particular emphasis on the grave consequences of the high rate of individual and social harms associated with depression, or heart-deadness (*del-mordegi*).

According to statistics and available data, among all the psychological pathologies afflicting our society, the most fundamental is precisely this depression, which drags us into a vicious circle: depression, addiction, indifference, disregard for civil society, neglect of national destiny, neglect of national interests, acceptance of the ruling regime, fatalism, belief in the conspiracy theory that "everything is orchestrated by them", submission to a servitude-breeding and depression-inducing tradition and religion, *rowzeh-khani* (ritual mourning recitations), the glorification of weeping, sorrow, and grief, and a perpetual sense of guilt… Within this vicious circle, factors such as Shia Islam, proximity to sources of narcotics production and distribution, and the traditional religious attitude towards narcotics—which is remarkably lenient—compound the layer of historical depression produced by historical wounds, imposing a profound predicament upon our generations and those to come.

From a scientific standpoint, an unusually high prevalence of depression across various societies is linked to war, homelessness, famine, or natural disasters. In Iran, however, the presence of historical depression in Shia-populated regions must be recognised as a fundamental factor in this vicious circle. One need only observe the communal dances, joyful music, and spirit of dialogue, laughter, and celebration among our Kurdish, Baloch, and Turkmen compatriots, and compare them with Yazd and Qom.

A depression rate three times the global average and the affliction of over two million addicts in Iran cannot be attributed merely to poverty and proximity to Afghanistan, for the proportion of addicts in our other neighbour, Pakistan—which has a lower per capita income—is lower than ours. Nor can low literacy or lack of education explain this phenomenon, since more than half of our addicts hold a secondary school diploma or higher: Babak Dinparast, Deputy Head of the Drug Control Headquarters, announced: "22 per cent of addicts in the country hold a bachelor's degree or higher, 15 per cent hold an associate degree, and 38 per cent hold a secondary school diploma." [i]

In Iran today, the foremost psychological pathology—with its direct and indirect effects such as addiction, suicide, low productivity, and indifference towards civil society—is precisely depression. At present, the rate of depression in Iran is three times the global average. Dr Ahmad Hajebi, adviser to the Deputy Minister of Health for Mental Health and Addiction, told a reporter for the *Hamshahri* newspaper: "23.6 per cent of the population in Iran suffer from psychiatric disorders. Based on the findings of this study, the prevalence of psychiatric disorders among Iranian women is 26.5 per cent and among men 20.8 per cent." He identified depression, with a prevalence of 12.7 per cent, as the most common psychiatric disorder in Iran, adding: "15.4 per cent of Iranian women and 10.2 per cent of Iranian men suffer from depression." According to this official, "the results of the latest national survey indicate that the unemployed and incapacitated, women, divorced individuals, the illiterate and semi-literate, urban dwellers, and those of low socio-economic status are more exposed than others to psychiatric disorders." [ii]

Our analysis and examination of the presence of such a high rate of this illness in society leads back to the general roots of depression—such as economic hardship, distrust in the future and the absence of any prospect for it, unemployment, and highly significant, interrelated cultural factors. First and foremost, historical depression—especially over the past five hundred years—is of paramount importance, and today the current closed cultural climate, with the seminary and religious values imposed over the past thirty-five years, further fosters the spread of this illness. The fundamental problem with historical depression is that it becomes transformed into a value: mourning, death, and martyrdom become values; even in the sensibility of intellectuals, and even in modern poetry and literature, this depression makes its presence felt.

The roots of psychological pathologies such as depression, anxiety, stress and strain, duality of personality (*taqiyya* / dissimulation), and historical depression must be examined rigorously and continuously, and decisive action must be taken to eradicate them. An examination of the spectrum of psychological pathologies across different strata of Iranian society reveals that everything crystallising around the axis of depression—such as addiction, disregard for surrounding affairs, turning inward into oneself, low work ethic, and lack of responsibility—collectively exhibits a remarkably high incidence. Fundamental research in this area is exceedingly rare, because on the one hand conducting fieldwork for such studies requires freedom of action, freedom of response, and reliable statistics, and on the other hand it requires the application of scientific method, which is precisely independence from prejudice. One may ask: have these psychological pathologies intensified during the era of Islamic governance?

Nevertheless, a new study conducted by researchers at the University of Queensland in Australia demonstrates that Iranians are among the most depressed peoples in the world, and that overall the inhabitants of the "Middle East" and "North Africa" have been identified as the most depressed populations globally. According to *The Washington Post*, in this study published in the medical journal *PLOS* [Public Library of Science] [iii], researchers examined the scope of depression's spread worldwide using data on prevalence, progression of the illness, and duration of affliction. Based on the researchers' findings, depression is the second most prevalent condition among human beings worldwide, with more than four per cent of the global population suffering from it. According to the latest official state statistics, this rate for Iran stands at 13 per cent.

Among these, the "most depressed" country in the world was Afghanistan, where one in every five people is depressed. The lowest rate of depression was observed in Japan, where prevalence is estimated at under 2.5 per cent. According to one of these hypotheses, "conflict" is one of the drivers of depression in societies; for example, Afghanistan, Honduras, and Palestine were identified as the "most depressed regions". Factors such as unemployment, low wages, and severe economic and financial inequalities have shown a direct correlation with the prevalence of depression among a society's citizens.

In this tangled skein, several indicators are conspicuously absent: social indifference, the role of mourning rituals and self-flagellation such as *zanjir-zani* (chain-beating) and *qameh-zani* (head-laceration with a blade), seminary superstitions, and the presence of the historical depression and wounds of us Iranians.

Indifference, which is the flip side of depression, itself generates a form of withdrawal, a disinclination to engage in social affairs, and distance from collective work, and is one of the scourges of civil society: a vicious circle. Economic and social pressures, within an overarching climate of cultural and historical depression, generate depression and indifference, and these two phenomena leave civil society enfeebled and listless, thereby enabling the continuation of the regime's rule. Another outcome of frustrations is the depression and torpor of individual citizens and, consequently, of society as a whole—an issue that merits reflection in its own right and brings numerous social anomalies in its wake.

After a long silence, an official recently pointed in an article to the root of this destructive and ruinous depression, only to face attacks from all sides, with his remarks dismissed as bizarre. Let us read an excerpt from the article together: "In bizarre remarks, the Governor of Yazd claimed: weeping for Imam Hossein is the cause of depression among the people of Yazd! In this regard, the strange comments of this official met with reactions from Friday prayer leaders. Hojjatoleslam Seyyed Ebrahim Hosseini, the Friday prayer leader of Abarkuh, advised: 'Let us strive through *rowzeh*, weeping, and the recitation of martyrdom tragedies to keep alive the memory of the Imam and the path of the Master of Martyrs; what is sometimes heard—that weeping causes depression among the people—is completely false.' He added: 'Weeping brings about a catharsis and a house-cleaning of the heart from sorrows and distress, and leads to lightness and spiritual expansion; weeping for Imam Hossein (AS), in particular, holds many mysteries and secrets.' Hojjatoleslam Mohammadreza Madih, the Friday prayer leader of Taft, also referring to those who recently claimed that the *rowzeh* of Imam Hossein (AS) causes depression, stated: 'Mourning and weeping over the oppression suffered by the Household of the Prophet, and especially Abi Abdallah (AS) and the dear martyrs of the plain of Karbala, brings vitality and joy to heart and soul; and those who seek to insinuate that mourning causes depression should know that as long as Shia Islam exists, *rowzeh* and mourning will exist as well.' Asserting that depression caused by the *rowzeh* of Imam Hossein (AS) is an outright falsehood, he added: 'On the contrary, sincere mourning actually produces spiritual and psychological vitality.' These remarks are being made at a time when, coinciding with the advent of the Eleventh Government, some imagine that the frameworks and red lines of the system have changed. The Governor of Yazd and those who think like him are ignorant of the religious heritage of the Iranian people and have seemingly forgotten the people's presence in the epic of 9 Dey [30 December 2009], where it was precisely this weeping for Imam Hossein (AS) that mobilised millions of people, resulting in the red line drawn against the sedition of '88 [2009] and its perpetrators. It appears these individuals imagine that the social atmosphere under the Eleventh Government has become conducive to paving the way for events such as the incidents of '78 [1999] and the sedition of '88." [iv]

Let us dissect a portion of these statements further, where one of these turbaned clerics asserts: "Depression caused by the *rowzeh* of Imam Hossein (AS) is an outright falsehood… on the contrary, sincere mourning actually produces spiritual and psychological vitality." This claim rests on no scientific data, no empirical research, and not even common human and traditional intuition. We speak of depression as a psychological pathology—an affliction with specific, observable, and clear symptoms. In Persian, it is more fitting to call depression *del-mordegi* ("heart-deadness") [v]; the heart (*del*) is recognised as the seat of feelings such as attachment (*del-bandi*), courage (*deliri*), cowardice (*boz-deli*), cheerfulness (*del-goshayi*), tenderness (*del-navazi*), love, affection, and dynamism. In a sense, the *del* is like a psychic heart that sustains the continuity of mental life, and once it dies, it drags down into ruin the love of life, constructiveness, and individual autonomy. Our argument does not concern *rowzeh-khani* as such, but rather the elevation of mourning into a supreme value. Mourning differs from commemoration in its foundation, its method, and its consequences alike.

The origin of mourning in humanity goes back to the earliest stages of human cultural production. Across all cultures, mourning serves to soothe the pain and grief of losing a person bound to one's very soul who can never return. In our society, mourning for a departed loved one takes place at intervals of three days, one week, one month, forty days, one hundred days, and one year; and each year thereafter on the anniversary of death, we commemorate that loss. Along this trajectory, the hue of mourning gradually transforms into remembrance and commemoration. Put differently, the period and rituals of mourning constitute a psychological preparation for rising anew and returning to life. The repetitive, annual ensemble of diverse rituals—*rowzeh-khani*, chest-beating (*sineh-zani*), self-harm, *qameh-zani*, rolling oneself and one's young children in the dirt—in Shia Islam, moreover on the occasion of the martyrdom and death of virtually the entire family of the Prophet, cannot fulfil the role of mourning in its anthropological and traditional social sense.

These cyclical rituals, which recur several times nearly every month and reach their climax during the two months of Muharram and Safar, do not constitute traditional mourning aimed at letting go and rising again; they are not for remembering a loss, nor for honouring a departed beloved, because in the course of these formal, repetitive rites the faithful learn no new ethical, human, scientific, artistic, or literary concept through these practices. The turbaned clerics say: "Sincere mourning actually produces spiritual and psychological vitality." The very use of the word "actually" (*ettefaqan*) reveals that their claim runs counter to expectation: what everyone knows full well is that this period of mourning is a season of sorrow, melancholy, and grief. They also append the adjective "sincere" so that if, in practice, the faithful observe effects in themselves diametrically opposed to the clerics' pronouncement, the clerics will already have a pre-emptive retort: "Believer, your mourning was not sincere."

On the other hand, psychological vitality may be conceivable, yet how could another human being perceive or measure "spiritual vitality"? Be that as it may, if their contention is that weeping, wailing, and beating one's head confer psychological vitality, why do the Shia clerics engage in practices intended to bring psychological vitality to the faithful precisely at a time when the revered figures of this faith are portrayed as lying in dust and blood? The reality is that the ensemble of cyclical mourning practices, through its performative tradition, induces in the faithful from earliest childhood a kind of addiction to self-harm and satisfaction in it. Scattering the dust of depression upon oneself, retreating inward, and experiencing a sense of deprivation and helplessness are among the consequences of these rituals as a whole.

It may be stated with certainty that the penetration and persistence of mourning traditions—which form the central axis of clerical Shia Islam—from the full institutionalisation of seminary schools in the seventeenth century CE down to the present day constitute one of the pillars of depression and of disregard for constructiveness and progress among Shia adherents.

One may say that depression, as a psychological pathology, and addiction are twin phenomena: on the one hand, addiction is the product of social conditions and the weakness of society's mental healthcare; on the other, it itself generates social and psychological problems. Indeed, within the organisational structure of Iran's Ministry of Health today, the Office of Mental Health and Addiction is housed within a single body.
When it comes to addiction—and all expert assessments of it—we confront three recurring issues: the scarcity and disarray of statistics, the steadily rising consumption of narcotics, and the absence of sound root-cause analysis and prevention programmes.

Let us examine a few more statements by officials: "Addiction is no longer regarded merely as a social harm, but poses itself as a social crisis." [vi] One publication asks: "What is the exact number of addicts in Iran? Two or four million people?" [vii] The Minister of the Interior and Secretary-General of the Drug Control Headquarters, stating that addiction accounts for 50 to 55 per cent of divorces in the country, "also cited addiction as the cause of 20 per cent of homicides." [viii] Mr Rahmani Fazli stated that the number of addicts in Iran was approximately 1,325,000; yet in the closing days of that very same year, the *Arman* newspaper, quoting Saeed Sefatian, former Director-General of Treatment at the Drug Control Headquarters, reported the actual number of addicts in Iran as "3,600,000." [ix] "The educational profile of narcotics users is as follows: 5.68 per cent are illiterate, 8.03 per cent have primary schooling, 11.76 per cent lower secondary schooling, 37.86 per cent upper secondary schooling, 15.22 per cent an associate degree, and 21.45 per cent a bachelor's degree or higher." [x] Hamidreza Jalaeipour, Professor of Sociology at the University of Tehran, considers the number of addicts in Iran to exceed even that of Pakistan; this sociology professor emphasised:
"The largest, most influential, and best-resourced institutions and organisations in Iran for combating addiction are the state-governing institutions. Yet unfortunately, these institutions—including the Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting (IRIB)—do not operate with a monitoring dashboard for social pathologies." [xi]

"The World Health Organisation (1999) has ranked the narcotics question—encompassing production, transit, distribution, and consumption—alongside three other global issues, namely the production and stockpiling of weapons of mass destruction, environmental pollution, and poverty and class disparity, as among the fundamental challenges posing a grave threat to human life in its social, economic, cultural, and political dimensions on the global stage." [xii]

"Stating that narcotics consumption today has shifted from traditional to synthetic drugs and that the variety of synthetic products is vast, the Minister of the Interior said: 'These substances threaten the entire society.' The Deputy Head of the Drug Control Headquarters cited 'curiosity, recreation, and pleasure' as the reason for young people's turn towards synthetic drugs, adding: 'Unfortunately, the necessary awareness-raising has not been carried out in this regard.' According to the latest statistics from Iran's Drug Control Headquarters and police, more than two million drug users live in the country. The average age of 700,000 of these addicts, who are recreational users, is 21 years. According to Drug Control Headquarters figures, 600 tonnes of narcotics are consumed annually in Iran." [xiii]

Before presenting further figures on the abnormal state of addiction in Iran today, we must note a fundamental point regarding the root causes of this deplorable situation: our traditional, religious attitude towards addiction is remarkably lenient. Although the government announces that civil servants account for half of all addicts [xiv], in practice no serious campaign is waged against this scourge even within the state apparatus itself—a case of the proverb "when the salt itself goes bad". Broadly speaking, the Islamic Republic system reduces the causes of people's turn towards addiction to ease of access to drugs (long, porous borders with Afghanistan, producer of 80% of the world's opium), illiteracy (over ten million illiterate citizens), poverty (over 15 million Iranians below the poverty line; Iranian economist Hossein Raghfar stated: "Statistics show that 12 per cent of the country's population—comprising roughly 17 per cent of the rural population and 8 per cent of the urban population—consists of groups suffering from hunger" [xv]; the Managing Director of the Iran Health Insurance Organisation states: "There are around 8 to 9 million marginalised informal-settlement dwellers in the country" [xvi]), or young people's hedonism and permissiveness.

They blatantly and deliberately evade three major social realities—namely depression, the lack of wholesome recreational avenues for youth, and the indulgent view of addiction held by Shia clerics and tradition—even while close to ten per cent of Iran's population grapple directly with the calamity of addiction: Iran's Minister of the Interior, noting that "if we multiply the number of addicts by household size, six million people are directly affected by the issue of addiction", remarked: "It is worthwhile for us to treat the issue as a thoroughly social one for the sake of the six million people directly involved." [xvii]

Indifference, which is the flip side of depression, itself generates a form of withdrawal, non-involvement in social issues, and distance from collective work, and is one of the scourges of civil society.
We see that we are trapped in a vicious circle: economic and social pressures, within an overarching climate of cultural and historical depression, generate depression and indifference, and these two phenomena render civil society listless and numb, enabling the continuation of the current rulers' governance.

Depression, as a psychological pathology, manifests itself in the overall sense of life, happiness or heart-deadness, in work and productivity, in short stories, poetry, novels, cinema, and theatre, in works of art, and in the everyday language of the people. Should we wish to examine the roots of this malady across recent decades—particularly the past thirty-five years—through artistic works, literature, poetry, novels, cinema, song, and music, we need only quote a passage from an article in the *Kayhan* newspaper, the official organ of the Islamic Republic: "The 32nd Fajr Film Festival must be dubbed the festival of hopeless—and hope-crushing—films: depressed both in structure and narrative, and in content and worldview. Most of the works we see at this year's Fajr Film Festival are contenders in an arena vying to narrate depression and despair—films that, in order not to fall behind their rivals, are willing to sacrifice even dramatic logic and conceal reality just to make their narratives ever more depressing! To such an extent that 90 per cent of the films featured at this year's Fajr Film Festival appear to have been made solely with the aim of dampening the audience's spirits! Some may claim that the depression prevailing over these films merely reflects the country's existing economic difficulties. In principle, were that the case, bleak portrayal ought to be confined to social, economic, and political relations. Yet unfortunately, the bitter development unfolding in our cinema today is the promotion of a negative view of humanity and the world. It is as though in the hearts and vision of many of our filmmakers no ray of hope exists. Even where a path to deliverance is shown, it remains a path shrouded in dust, darkness, and terror. Death runs rampant in the films of this year's festival. Scarcely a film can be found in which someone does not die or get murdered. In some films, death is the very axis and protagonist. In another group of works at this year's festival, man is wolf to man. Virtually nothing worthy of the name human being is to be seen. Tehran is depicted as an asylum in which everyone is bent on tearing apart, plundering, and seducing one another. It is as though in the people of this era nothing called affection exists between family members—so much so that in a large number of films one sees scenes of a wife being beaten by her husband. In the film *The Married Life of Mr Mahmoudi and His Wife* (*Zendegi-ye Moshtarak-e Aghaye Mahmoudi va Banou*), all members of the family lie to and betray one another." [xviii]

The author himself, with simplicity and modesty, offers a sound and apt diagnosis: "That depression and despair have come to dominate our cinema to this extent bespeaks the infiltration of a kind of cultural malady." Yet neither the author nor others pursue scientific research or root-cause analysis of this "cultural malady". By blaming cinema practitioners, *Kayhan* seeks to conceal the fact that the prevailing cultural atmosphere in our beloved Iran, and the upbringing of the present active generation, fall directly under the responsibility of the foundational institutions of the Islamic Republic.

To conclude, we turn to two field examples. Our aim is primarily to delineate the intimate interconnection between depression as a psychological pathology, addiction as a cultural-social calamity, and their political, economic, managerial, and cultural underpinnings. In a word, the foremost psychological pathology in Iran today is depression—occurring at a far higher rate than in other societies worldwide—which has permeated everyday life and all artistic and literary production. This phenomenon resembles a tangled skein formed by cultural depression (the product of cultural wounds, the mourning climate generated by Shia clerics, and the Shia *velayat-e faqih* [Guardianship of the Jurist] foundations of governance) on the one hand, an exceptionally high rate of addiction (which is simultaneously a producer and a consequence of the psychological pathology of depression), and ultimately widespread public indifference to one's own destiny, alongside the cumulative impact of the economic, social, and cultural problems outlined earlier. This very nexus forms the underlying impediment to the emergence of civil society in Iran; and this sluggishness in establishing civil society in turn perpetuates, in a chain-like cycle, the existing cultural pathologies—namely, the cultural ethos prevailing in the seminaries of the Shia clergy. Matters reach the point where we are confronted with 34 per cent of Tehran's residents suffering from psychological pathologies.

First Example [xix]:

The Friday prayer leader of Zehak County in Sistan and Baluchestan Province states: "Over 90 per cent of the people of Sistan live below the poverty line, and more than 50 per cent of the region's population rely on support agencies." According to the state news agency IRNA, Hassan Khedri, speaking on Friday (11 Bahman / 31 January) during a meeting with the Governor of Sistan and Baluchestan Province, identified "migration", "fine dust storms", "tuberculosis", "mismanagement", and "improper management of the border" as the region's foremost threats and challenges, urging officials to "devise solutions to address them".

Mr Khedri noted that given these conditions, "tax exemptions and subsidies on energy carriers" could play a significant role in "encouraging people to remain in the Sistan region".

Concurrent with these remarks, Gary Lewis, the United Nations Resident Coordinator in the Islamic Republic of Iran, published a note—a version of which appeared on Saturday, 12 Bahman on the *Khabaronline* website—recounting his visit to the Sistan region, writing: "More than half of the region's inhabitants survive on assistance from the 'Imam Khomeini Relief Foundation'," and following the desiccation of Lake Hamun, the people "are almost all unemployed and live amid the ruins of abandoned villages".

Referring to his visit to three villages in the province—"Takht-e Dowlat", "Adimi", and "Kuh-e Khajeh"—Mr Lewis wrote: "People were distressed by the lack of water and appealed to the government and the United Nations for help. The people of Sistan feel that nothing is being done to assist them beyond disbursing cash handouts."

According to his report, "a large number of the 400,000 inhabitants of Sistan live 'below the poverty line', and the monthly aid they receive from the government or the 'Relief Foundation' barely exceeds 20 dollars a month."

Earlier, in Dey of that year, the head of the Office of Endowments (*Owqaf*) and Charity Affairs of Zabol County had stated during a ceremony honouring a number of endowment donors that Sistan and Baluchestan Province required endowments for "poverty alleviation", "facilitating youth marriage", and "employment".

Emphasising the lack of state funding for the region, Javad Khalili had stated explicitly that "all development projects" in Zabol County and its surrounding villages are carried out solely through contributions from "philanthropists" and the region's General Office of Endowments. Referring to the poverty of the population, he spoke of the need for land "to build hospitals and clinics" in the area—even as, by his own account, 800 endowed plots in the region had thus far been allocated to "building mosques and *hosseiniyehs*". Mr Khalili specified that from the endowments budget, 37 mosques had so far been constructed in Zabol and 433 million tomans had been spent on building two shrines known as "Bibi Doost" and "Seyyed Baqer".

It is worth noting that Hossein-Ali Shahriari, the Member of Parliament for Zahedan in the Islamic Consultative Assembly, had announced the previous Azar that the unemployment rate in Sistan and Baluchestan Province stood above 50 per cent, adding that "a number of infrastructure undertakings—such as the 'Chabahar–Zahedan–Mashhad railway project', the 'provincial gas-supply project', and the 'Chabahar petrochemical project'—have been halted due to a shortage of funds."

Halimeh Aali, the Member of Parliament for Zabol, had likewise warned the previous Aban—criticising officials' neglect of the desiccation of the Hamun wetlands and its repercussions—that "Sistan, this Pass of Uhud of Iran, is being emptied of its inhabitants owing to poverty and unemployment."

Second Example [xx]: Speaking on Wednesday morning before the Social Affairs Commission of the county's City Council, Mohammad Hadi Balali announced that 722 individuals in the city were undergoing treatment for addiction, stating: "Of this total, 20 are women; 519 are aged 25 to 50, 55 are under 25, and 148 are over 50." Referring to a threefold increase in attempted suicide figures compared with the previous year, he noted: "50 per cent of attempted suicides occur among those aged 20 to 30; those under 20 account for 35 per cent, and individuals over 40 account for 15 per cent."

https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/02/9.jpg
[À lire sur Gooya](http://news.gooya.com/politics/archives/2014/03/177599.php)

Lundi 11 Farvardin 1393

La santé mentale désigne la capacité d'établir des relations harmonieuses et équilibrées avec autrui, de transformer et d'améliorer son environnement individuel et social, et de résoudre ses conflits et aspirations personnels de manière rationnelle, équitable et adaptée. En conséquence, la notion d'hygiène mentale recouvre la garantie du développement et de la santé psychique individuelle et sociale, la prévention de l'apparition des troubles psychiques et, le cas échéant, leur traitement approprié ainsi que leur réadaptation.

## Deuxième partie : le système de santé et la santé mentale dans l'Iran d'aujourd'hui

Dans la première partie de cette étude, parue précédemment, nous nous sommes attachés à poser les définitions générales et à circonscrire le champ d'investigation. Dans cette deuxième partie, tout en précisant ces définitions, nous exposons la structure et le système de santé mentale en Iran à partir des données officielles. Bien que l'accent de cette recherche porte sur les conséquences extrêmement graves du taux élevé de dommages individuels et sociaux liés à la dépression ou à l'abattement (*del-mordegi*), il nous faut avant tout dresser le tableau de l'hygiène et de la santé mentale dans l'Iran d'aujourd'hui.

Commençons par la définition de la santé mentale. Les maladies psychiques ont toujours existé, à des degrés divers, et ne sont l'apanage d'aucune classe socio-économique ni d'aucun âge particulier ; elles constituent néanmoins un péril qui menace l'humanité. Fort heureusement, l'élévation du niveau d'hygiène mentale et l'approfondissement des connaissances ont dissipé les idées fausses et les superstitions entourant ces affections, démontrant que les troubles psychiques sont évitables et que, s'ils sont diagnostiqués à temps et pris en charge, le risque de chronicité et de complications secondaires diminue sensiblement. L'élévation du niveau de santé mentale par la sensibilisation du public aux maladies psychiques constitue l'une des voies fondamentales. L'un des obstacles majeurs de notre société tient à l'image des atteintes psychiques ancrée dans notre mémoire collective : nous assimilons le trouble psychique à la folie et adoptons face à lui la solution la plus courte — nous voulons le fuir, allant parfois jusqu'à nous interdire d'en parler. L'amélioration de la santé mentale repose, d'une part, sur le dépistage et le diagnostic précoces des troubles psychiques ainsi que sur la mise en œuvre de soins adaptés, et, d'autre part, sur la prévention des complications, de l'aggravation de la pathologie et sur la réinsertion des patients. Il va sans dire qu'il convient également d'y contribuer par la prévention et le traitement des maladies somatiques.

L'Organisation mondiale de la santé propose une définition globale de la santé mentale : l'hygiène mentale réside dans la capacité d'entretenir des relations harmonieuses et équilibrées avec autrui, de modifier et d'améliorer son cadre individuel et social, et de résoudre ses conflits et inclinations personnels de façon logique, juste et adéquate. Il en découle que la notion de santé mentale consiste à assurer le plein épanouissement et l'équilibre psychique individuel et collectif, à prévenir la survenue des troubles psychiques et, s'ils se manifestent, à en garantir le traitement approprié et la réadaptation.

Les caractéristiques des personnes jouissant d'une bonne santé mentale peuvent être résumées ainsi : elles éprouvent de la sérénité, ressentent dans une mesure raisonnable un sentiment de sécurité et de compétence, évaluent leurs capacités avec réalisme, se respectent tout en acceptant leurs limites, respectent les droits d'autrui, sont capables de s'attacher aux autres et de les aimer. Elles savent susciter le respect et l'amitié d'autrui, pourvoir aux besoins de leur existence et s'efforcer de trouver des solutions aux difficultés qui jalonnent leur vie. Elles sont aptes à réfléchir et à décider, à assumer leurs responsabilités quotidiennes en se fixant des objectifs raisonnables, sans se laisser submerger par des affects de peur, de colère, d'amour ou de culpabilité au point de bouleverser leur existence.

Il n'est pas inutile de rappeler quelques signes d'alerte témoignant d'une fragilité psychique : une peur injustifiée et permanente, un sentiment d'inquiétude constant, une tristesse chronique et sans motif apparent, une perte aisée de l'équilibre psychique accompagnée le plus souvent d'insomnies répétées, une alternance invalidante de « dépression et d'euphorie », un désintérêt et une aversion persistants envers autrui, l'agitation et le désarroi, l'accès de colère soudain suivi de remords, la propension à s'attribuer systématiquement le bon droit et à juger autrui fautif, ainsi que la plainte de douleurs corporelles multiples sans cause organique identifiable.

Les maladies psychiques, contrairement à certaines affections somatiques, ne conduisent pas directement à la mort. La méconnaissance de la manière dont débutent les troubles psychiques retarde la mise en route des soins, rendant dès lors la maladie chronique et incurable. La prévalence des maladies psychiques est étroitement liée au niveau de connaissance, à la culture, à l'éducation et à la prévention.

L'hygiène mentale est une science du mieux-vivre et du bien-être social qui embrasse tous les âges de la vie, des premiers instants de l'existence jusqu'à la mort — de la vie prénatale, la petite enfance et l'enfance jusqu'à l'adolescence, l'âge adulte et la vieillesse. Elle constitue un savoir et un art qui aident les individus, par l'élaboration de modalités psychiques et affectives saines, à s'adapter à leur environnement et à choisir des solutions plus fécondes face à leurs difficultés.

Les maladies psychiques existent depuis l'Antiquité, à telle enseigne qu'Hippocrate, quatre siècles avant notre ère, soutenait déjà qu'il fallait soigner les malades mentaux au même titre que les malades physiques. Toutefois, ce n'est qu'à partir de 1930, à la suite du premier Congrès international d'hygiène mentale, que cette discipline intégra pleinement les sciences médicales et que les institutions psychiatriques ainsi que les centres de prévention commencèrent progressivement leur action dans les pays avancés. Le premier Congrès international d'hygiène mentale se tint à Washington avec la participation des représentants de cinquante pays ; on y examina les problèmes psychosociaux ainsi que des questions telles que la création d'hôpitaux et de centres de soins ambulatoires, d'établissements dédiés aux enfants atteints de déficience intellectuelle et d'autres dispositifs analogues. En 1948, lors du troisième Congrès international d'hygiène mentale réuni à Londres, furent jetées les bases de la Fédération mondiale pour la santé mentale ; cette même année, la Fédération fut officiellement admise au statut consultatif auprès de l'UNESCO et de l'Organisation mondiale de la santé, l'OMS à Genève assumant le rôle de direction officielle de la Fédération mondiale pour la santé mentale. Depuis cette date, une session internationale se tient chaque année et un congrès mondial tous les quatre ans. À la suite des efforts soutenus de ces organisations, le 18 Farvardin fut proclamé Journée mondiale de la santé, date à laquelle sont examinées à travers le monde les questions sanitaires des différentes sociétés. Il a été demandé aux autorités sanitaires des divers pays d'inscrire les programmes de santé mentale au cœur des programmes de santé publique.

En Iran, la production et la diffusion d'émissions consacrées à la psychologie et à la santé mentale sur les ondes de la radio nationale débutèrent officiellement en 1336 (1957), et le Bureau de la santé mentale fut créé en 1338 (1959) au sein de la Direction générale de la santé du ministère de la Santé publique de l'époque. Bien que la Fédération mondiale pour la santé mentale se considère engagée envers l'ensemble des malades comme des personnes bien portantes, une attention particulière est portée aux groupes et populations qui requièrent davantage de soutien en matière de santé mentale et sont plus vulnérables : les malades et personnes en situation de handicap psychique, les personnes atteintes de déficience intellectuelle, les patients épileptiques, les personnes âgées, les personnes toxicomanes, les chômeurs, les personnes en situation de précarité économique, les enfants et adolescents, les femmes enceintes, les personnes sans soutien familial et les détenus.

## Regard sur les maladies psychiques en Iran et dans le monde aujourd'hui

Selon les estimations de l'Organisation mondiale de la santé, 25 % de la population mondiale souffre aujourd'hui d'une forme ou d'une autre de trouble psychique, neurologique ou comportemental. En Iran, le taux de prévalence des troubles psychiques varie selon les régions de 10 % à 36 %. D'après les études disponibles, 3 % des malades psychiques et 1,6 % de la population iranienne âgée de 15 ans et plus sont gravement atteints sur le plan psychique et nécessitent un traitement psychiatrique sérieux. L'invalidité et l'incapacité engendrées par ces pathologies sont souvent sévères et durables. La charge globale des maladies liées aux troubles psychiques, en intégrant les années approximatives d'incapacité vécues tout au long de l'existence, s'élève à 28 %. Les pathologies majeures ou psychoses comprennent : la schizophrénie — marquée par une dissociation de la personnalité et une perte du sens de la réalité — avec une prévalence mondiale moyenne de 0,3 % et inférieure à 1 % en Iran ; la maniaco-dépression (trouble bipolaire), caractérisée par une dépression profonde et de fortes fluctuations thymiques, présente chez 3 % de la population mondiale ; et la paranoïa, ou suspicion extrême et infondée à l'égard de tout, inscrite dans un cadre délirant.

Les affections relativement moins lourdes englobent les névroses — perte de la capacité de réagir de manière adaptée dans diverses situations et troubles de la personnalité issus d'expériences douloureuses de l'enfance —, les troubles obsessionnels compulsifs avec une moyenne mondiale de 2 %, ainsi que l'ensemble des troubles psychosomatiques, sexuels, thymiques, alimentaires ou du sommeil. Par-dessus tout, la part essentielle dans les atteintes psychiques revient à la dépression, dont la prévalence mondiale avoisine 4 %, mais qui atteint en Iran le chiffre particulièrement alarmant de 12 %. Les statistiques les plus récentes du ministère de la Santé font état d'une prévalence nationale de 25 % de troubles psychiques, proportion qui grimpe à 34 % dans la capitale — soit, rapporté aux 12 millions d'habitants de Téhéran, quelque 4 millions de personnes malades.

La prévalence des troubles psychiques varie de 12 % dans la province de Yazd à 40 % dans la province de Chaharmahal-et-Bakhtiari. Comment interpréter un écart d'une telle ampleur ? On peut avancer qu'indépendamment de la structure psychique individuelle, cette disparité dépend des strates culturelles accumulées au fil des siècles, de nos conditions écologiques de vie et de nos grands systèmes de production. Il convient de considérer comme piliers structurels de la société iranienne l'articulation entre les quatre strates culturelles (antéislamique, de l'islam à l'avènement du chiisme, de cette époque jusqu'à la rencontre avec la culture occidentale, et de cette rencontre à nos jours), les influences environnementales (montagne, désert, climat humide ou aride) et les macro-systèmes productifs (agricole-rural, pastoral-nomade et urbain-industriel-tertiaire), et d'analyser dans ce cadre les rapports entre les tempéraments et les traditions en tenant compte de la diversité culturelle, linguistique et religieuse de la population. Sur le plan culturel, nous portons en nous une culture antéislamique, une culture comprise entre l'arrivée de l'islam et l'installation du chiisme, une culture postérieure au chiisme, ainsi qu'une quatrième culture née après notre rencontre avec l'Occident.

Représentez-vous ces quatre univers comme quatre strates qui constituent les assises de notre culture. Sous un autre angle, l'on peut également envisager cette pluralité culturelle à travers une culture à soubassement nomade, une culture à soubassement rural et, enfin, une culture à fondement urbain. À titre d'exemple, à l'époque de Cyrus, 25 % de notre population était nomade ; en 1900 encore, 25 % des habitants étaient nomades, et la proportion de nomades en Iran a parfois atteint jusqu'à 50 % de la population totale. Bien que la strate nomade ne représente plus aujourd'hui que 1,2 % de la population iranienne, la culture nomade demeure une strate majeure de notre culture, car la formation et la désagrégation des traits culturels dans une société remontent à plusieurs générations. De même, bien qu'au cours des quarante dernières années la proportion de ruraux soit passée de 60 % à 30 %, on constate que l'empreinte de la culture rurale reste très vive dans l'existence des citadins iraniens. L'urbanisation dans les petites villes représentait 25 % des strates en 1900 ; elle atteint aujourd'hui 70 %, constituant le troisième socle de notre culture au regard du mode de production. Ajoutons qu'au cours des deux derniers siècles au moins, trois événements majeurs ont bouleversé notre édifice social : l'avènement de la Constitution en 1285 (1906), la transformation des années 1342 à 1348 (1963-1969) connue sous le nom de réforme agraire, qui bouleversa profondément le système de production rurale, et l'instauration de la République islamique, qui plaça la religion au fondement même du gouvernement et de l'État¹.

Dans ce contexte, quelle est l'architecture du ministère iranien de la Santé et quelles mesures sont en préparation pour améliorer l'hygiène et les soins psychiques ? Parcourons quelques extraits du document relatif au « Programme global de promotion de la santé mentale du pays » couvrant les années 1390-1394 (2011-2015), publié par ce ministère² : « Selon les dernières données et preuves disponibles, la prévalence des troubles psychiques avoisine 20 %, représentant près de 14 % de la charge nationale de morbidité. Or, conformément aux définitions internationales, la santé mentale ne se réduit pas à l'absence de troubles psychiques et englobe d'autres composantes qui, si elles étaient prises en compte, rendraient le poids des problèmes psychosociaux considérablement plus élevé. Messages clés du Programme global de promotion de la santé mentale : selon les rapports publiés par l'Organisation mondiale de la santé en 2004 et 2009, celle-ci définit ainsi les facteurs de risque pour la santé mentale : développement inadéquat durant l'enfance, mariage et procréation inadaptés, violence, violation des droits civiques, troubles psychiques des parents, école inadaptée et injustifiée, faiblesse des compétences psychosociales. La faiblesse du capital social, les comportements sociaux malsains et le déclin des valeurs éthiques en tant qu'élément central de la santé spirituelle sont à l'origine d'une grande part des troubles psychiques, ce qui exige de mobiliser des appuis et de développer la coopération intersectorielle. »

Dans un autre passage de ce même document national sur la promotion de la santé mentale, on lit ceci : « Les troubles psychiques représentent 10 % de la charge totale des maladies, les trois premières causes de la charge des troubles psychiques étant respectivement la dépression (26 % de la charge des troubles psychiques), les addictions (24 % de la charge) et les troubles bipolaires (12 %). Dans l'un des rapports du Bureau de la santé mentale, la population cible de ce service est estimée à plus de 10 millions de malades psychiques nécessitant des prestations de dépistage, de traitement, de suivi et de réadaptation dans les hôpitaux et centres communautaires ; à plus de 15 millions de personnes appartenant à des groupes spécifiques au sein de la population et requérant des interventions ciblées ainsi que des services de prévention des troubles psychiques ; et à environ 40 millions de personnes dans la population générale ayant besoin de services publics de promotion de la santé mentale par l'intermédiaire des médias, des écoles, des lieux de travail et des espaces de rassemblement. »

Nous savons que la maladie dépressive joue un rôle déterminant dans l'expansion de la toxicomanie. En additionnant les pourcentages des trois principales causes de troubles psychiques mentionnées dans ce document — lesquelles sont toutes, directement ou indirectement, liées à la dépression —, on aboutit à un chiffre particulièrement élevé. À travers quelques déclarations de responsables, de chercheurs et de journalistes, je m'efforcerai d'esquisser très succinctement le climat actuel de l'hygiène et de la santé mentale : « La dépression, avec une prévalence de 13 %, constitue le trouble psychique le plus répandu en Iran » ; « 15 % des femmes iraniennes et 10 % des hommes iraniens souffrent de dépression » ; « Les résultats de la dernière enquête nationale montrent que les chômeurs et les personnes en incapacité de travail, les femmes, les personnes divorcées, les personnes analphabètes ou faiblement instruites, les citadins et les personnes de statut socio-économique modeste sont plus exposés que les autres aux troubles psychiques » ; « 50 % des personnes ayant ressenti le besoin de consulter pour des troubles nerveux et psychiques ont cité la difficulté à acquitter les frais de soins parmi les motifs de leur renoncement, et 51 % de celles qui ont consulté tardivement dans les centres médicaux ont également rencontré des difficultés de paiement, dont 27 % ont mentionné les problèmes d'assurance maladie comme facteur de retard. Selon ce rapport, les personnes aux prises avec des troubles psychiques en Iran sont confrontées à des dépenses catastrophiques — expression qui signifie concrètement que ces patients ont dû soit vendre leurs biens, soit emprunter de l'argent à autrui pour se faire soigner. »

Selon le Dr Hajebi, 18 % des patients souffrant de troubles psychiques en Iran se heurtent à des difficultés liées au paiement de frais exorbitants. Il estime nécessaire de repenser en profondeur la couverture assurantielle des personnes atteintes de troubles psychiatriques, tant pour celles qui doivent être hospitalisées que pour celles qui requièrent des soins ambulatoires, psychologiques, de conseil ou non médicamenteux, car la couverture d'assurance est insuffisante et les prestations non médicamenteuses ne sont généralement pas remboursées.

Le règlement des frais médicaux constitue une crise qu'évoquait récemment le Dr Sayyari, vice-ministre de la Santé. Il chiffrait le coût annuel du traitement des troubles psychiques à plus de 960 milliards de tomans. Selon lui, le ministère de la Santé ne peut assumer les dépenses du secteur thérapeutique des troubles psychiques, les hôpitaux fonctionnant en autonomie financière et ne disposant d'aucune autre source de recettes.

Dans la suite de ces déclarations, on lit encore : « Le nombre de lits disponibles dans l'ensemble des hôpitaux psychiatriques publics, privés et relevant d'autres organismes et institutions s'élève à peine à huit mille lits, ce qui constitue une pénurie grave ; conformément au système de hiérarchisation des soins, ce parc devrait être porté à onze mille lits, ce qui n'est pas réalisable. »

Seyed Hassan Hashemi, ministre de la Santé et de l'Éducation médicale, a déclaré : « Le ministère de la Santé est aujourd'hui un ministère accusant un déficit budgétaire de sept à huit mille milliards de tomans… » Indiquant que 50 % des effectifs du ministère chargé de la santé publique ne possèdent qu'un niveau d'études équivalent ou inférieur au baccalauréat, le ministre a ajouté : « Au début du neuvième gouvernement, le ministère de la Santé comptait 230 000 agents ; ce chiffre est passé à 420 000 personnes. La composition des effectifs actifs dans ce ministère spécialisé, directement en prise avec la vie des citoyens, revêt une importance capitale. Or, 50 % des personnels de ce ministère technique ont un niveau égal ou inférieur au baccalauréat³. » Une autre donnée permettant d'établir une comparaison éloquente réside dans les statistiques de la base de données de l'Organisation mondiale de la santé : le ratio moyen de personnels soignants dans le champ des troubles psychiques pour cent mille habitants est 15 fois supérieur à celui de l'Iran en France, 10 fois supérieur au Japon, 4 fois supérieur aux États-Unis et égal à la moitié en Turquie ; en définitive, l'Iran occupe en la matière le cent deuxième rang mondial.

Dans le quotidien *Hamshahri*, on peut lire : en raison de l'insuffisance du soutien des organismes d'assurance et du coût élevé des traitements, cette catégorie de patients ne peut accéder aux soins ; il ne faut donc pas s'étonner de croiser dans la rue ou sur les lieux de travail des personnes privées de santé mentale et livrées à elles-mêmes. D'après les résultats de la dernière enquête nationale communiqués à *Hamshahri* par le Dr Ahmad Hajebi, conseiller du vice-ministre de la Santé pour la santé mentale et les addictions, 24 % de la population iranienne souffre de troubles psychiques. Selon les conclusions de cette étude, la prévalence des troubles psychiques s'élève à 26,5 % chez les femmes iraniennes et à 20,8 % chez les hommes… Il a désigné la dépression, avec une prévalence de 13 %, comme le trouble psychique le plus fréquent en Iran, précisant que 15 % des femmes iraniennes et 10 % des hommes iraniens souffrent de dépression⁴.

Par ailleurs, le Dr Taghi Aboutalebi Ahmadi, conseiller du directeur général de la Santé de la municipalité de Téhéran, estime que la personne jouissant d'une bonne santé mentale interagit harmonieusement avec autrui dans les diverses situations de l'existence et maîtrise efficacement les pressions de la vie. Ces personnes font preuve de souplesse et de créativité et entretiennent de bonnes relations sociales. Elles réussissent immanquablement tant dans la sphère familiale que dans le monde du travail. Ce psychologue social déclarait à *Hamshahri* : « Les responsables doivent impérativement, au moyen d'une planification cohérente visant à former des individus psychologiquement sains, consentir des investissements sérieux depuis la famille jusqu'aux jardins d'enfants et aux universités, car la productivité appartient à celles et ceux qui jouissent de la santé mentale⁵. »

Et pour finir, un autre responsable porte le coup de grâce au bilan de la santé publique en Iran : le ministre iranien de la Santé a affirmé que « la garantie d'une assurance chômage et d'une assurance maladie figure parmi les besoins les plus pressants de la population du pays, car à l'heure actuelle, en raison des coûts écrasants des soins médicaux, sept pour cent de la population nationale bascule chaque année sous le seuil de pauvreté⁶. »

Dans la troisième partie, nous aborderons la pathologie psychique la plus lourde de périls pour l'avenir de notre société, à savoir la dépression, la toxicomanie et l'indifférence sociale en Iran.

https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/02/9.jpg
[Read on Gooya](http://news.gooya.com/politics/archives/2014/03/177599.php)

Monday, 11 Farvardin 1393 (31 March 2014)

Mental hygiene consists in the capacity to relate harmoniously with others, to modify and improve one's individual and social environment, and to resolve personal conflicts and inclinations logically, justly, and appropriately. Consequently, the concept of mental hygiene denotes ensuring individual and social psychological growth and health, preventing the onset of mental disorders, and, should they arise, providing appropriate treatment and rehabilitation.

## Part Two: The Health System and Mental Health in Today's Iran

In the first part of this study, published previously, we endeavoured to address general definitions and clarify the scope of inquiry. In this part, by further elucidating those definitions, we explain the structure and system of mental health in Iran drawing upon official state data. Although the emphasis of our study lies on the grave consequences of the high incidence of individual and social harm caused by depression or despondency, we first need to sketch a portrait of mental health and hygiene in today's Iran.

Let us begin with the definition of mental health. Mental illnesses, to a greater or lesser extent, have always existed and are not confined to any particular socio-economic class or age group. Yet they constitute a danger that threatens humankind. Fortunately, rising standards of mental hygiene and deeper understanding have dispelled erroneous and superstitious notions surrounding these illnesses, demonstrating that mental illnesses are preventable and that, if diagnosed in a timely manner and placed under treatment, the likelihood of chronicity and secondary complications is diminished. Raising the level of mental hygiene through enhancing public awareness of mental illnesses is one of the fundamental pathways. One of the major problems of society is the image of psychological afflictions preserved in our collective memory. We equate psychological affliction with madness and take the shortest route in response to it: we seek to flee from it. At times we do not even deem it permissible to speak of it. Raising the level of mental hygiene—alongside the timely identification and diagnosis of mental disorders and action to treat them on the one hand, and efforts to prevent complications and worsening of illness as well as the rehabilitation of patients on the other—is among the core duties of mental hygiene. Of course, it must not be forgotten that we must also assist this endeavour through the prevention and treatment of physical illnesses.

The World Health Organisation offers a comprehensive definition of mental hygiene: mental hygiene consists in the capacity to relate harmoniously with others, to modify and improve one's individual and social environment, and to resolve personal conflicts and inclinations logically, justly, and appropriately. Consequently, the concept of mental hygiene denotes ensuring individual and social psychological growth and health, preventing the onset of mental disorders, and, should they arise, providing appropriate treatment and rehabilitation.

The characteristics of psychologically healthy individuals may be summarised as follows: they possess inner calm; they feel reasonably secure and capable; they assess their own abilities realistically; they respect themselves while also accepting their shortcomings; they respect the rights of others; they are able to take an interest in others and love them; they can earn the respect and friendship of others; they are able to meet the needs of their lives and strive to find solutions to the difficulties that arise in their lives. Such individuals are capable of thinking and making decisions; they are able to discharge their daily responsibilities by setting reasonable goals; and they are not so overwhelmed by emotions of fear, anger, love, or guilt as to throw their lives into turmoil.

It is not out of place to recall several warning signs of psychological vulnerability as well: groundless and persistent fear; a constant sense of anxiety; chronic and unwarranted unhappiness; losing one's psychological balance easily; frequent bouts of insomnia most of the time; alternating "depression and euphoria" that brings debility in its wake; a persistent feeling of indifference and aversion towards others; agitation and distress; becoming angered quickly and feeling remorse thereafter; insisting that one is always in the right and others in the wrong; and complaining of innumerable bodily pains for which no physical cause can be found.

Mental illnesses do not lead directly to death in the manner of certain physical diseases. Ignorance of how psychological afflictions begin delays the initiation of treatment, as a result of which the illness becomes chronic and incurable. The prevalence of mental illnesses depends upon knowledge, culture, education, and prevention.

Mental hygiene is a science for living better and achieving social well-being, encompassing every aspect of life from the earliest moments of existence until death—from the foetal stage, infancy, and childhood through adolescence, adulthood, and old age. Mental hygiene is both a body of knowledge and an art that helps individuals, through cultivating psychologically and emotionally sound methods, to adapt to their environment and choose more desirable solutions for resolving their difficulties.

Mental illnesses have existed since antiquity, to the extent that Hippocrates, four centuries before Christ, held that mentally ill patients ought to be treated in the same manner as physically ill patients. Yet it was only from 1930 onwards—following the convening of the First International Congress on Mental Hygiene—that this discipline became an established branch of medical science, and psychiatric organisations and prevention centres gradually commenced their activities in progressive countries. The First International Congress on Mental Hygiene was convened in Washington with representatives from fifty countries, where psychosocial problems and issues such as the establishment of hospitals and outpatient treatment centres, specialised centres for intellectually disabled children, and the like were examined. In 1948, at the Third International Congress on Mental Hygiene held in London, the foundation of the World Federation for Mental Health was laid, and in that same year the Federation became an official member of UNESCO and the World Health Organisation, with the World Health Organisation in Geneva assuming official leadership of the World Federation for Mental Health. Since that date, an international meeting has been held every year and a world congress once every four years. As a result of the sustained efforts of these organisations, 18 Farvardin (7 April) was proclaimed World Health Day, on which the health challenges of diverse societies are examined across the globe. Health authorities in various countries have been called upon to incorporate mental hygiene programmes into their public health programmes.

In Iran, the production and broadcast of psychology and mental hygiene programmes on Iranian radio officially began in 1336 SH (1957–1958), and in 1338 SH (1959–1960) the Office of Mental Health was established within the General Directorate of Health of the then Ministry of Health. Although the World Federation for Mental Health considers itself committed to all patients and all healthy individuals alike, groups and populations with greater need for mental hygiene and heightened vulnerability receive particular attention. These include psychiatric patients and persons with psychological disabilities, persons with intellectual disabilities, patients with epilepsy, the elderly, persons struggling with addiction, the unemployed, the economically disadvantaged, children and adolescents, pregnant women, persons without guardians, and prisoners.

### A Look at Mental Illnesses in Iran and the World Today

According to World Health Organisation estimates, 25 per cent of the world's population today suffers from one of the various mental, neurological, or behavioural disorders. The prevalence rate of mental disorders in Iran varies across different regions from 10 to 36 per cent. According to studies, 3 per cent of psychiatric patients and 1.6 per cent of Iran's population aged 15 and over are severely ill psychologically and require serious psychiatric treatment. The disability and incapacitation resulting from these illnesses are frequently severe and prolonged. The overall burden of disease associated with mental disorders—when approximate years lived with disability over the lifespan are calculated—rises to 28 per cent. Major illnesses, or psychoses, include schizophrenia—that is, splitting of personality and loss of the sense of reality—with a global average prevalence of 0.3 per cent and a prevalence in Iran of under 1 per cent; bipolar disorder ("depression–euphoria"), marked by deep depression and severe, fluctuating emotions, with a global prevalence of 3 per cent; and severe, groundless suspicion towards everything within a delusional framework (paranoia).

Relatively less severe illnesses include neurosis—the loss of the capacity to respond appropriately in various situations and personality disorders stemming from regrettable childhood experiences; obsessive-compulsive disorder, with a global average prevalence of 2 per cent; and a group of disorders that may be psychosomatic, sexual, mood-related, or connected to eating or sleeping. Most important of all, accounting for the principal share of psychological afflictions, is depression, with a global prevalence of around 4 per cent and, in the case of Iran, a remarkably high figure of 12 per cent. The latest statistics from the Ministry of Health report that 25 per cent of the country's population suffers from mental disorders, a figure that reaches 34 per cent in the capital—amounting, given Tehran's population of 12 million, to 4 million people.

The prevalence of mental disorders varies from 12 per cent in Yazd Province to 40 per cent in Chaharmahal and Bakhtiari Province. How can such a vast disparity be interpreted? It may be said that, apart from our individual psychological structure, this disparity depends on the cultural strata accumulated over centuries, on our ecological conditions, and on our macro-systems of production. We must consider the interplay among four cultural strata (pre-Islamic, from Islam to the emergence of Shiism, from that era to our encounter with Western culture, and from that encounter to the present day), environmental influences (mountainous, desert, humid, arid), and macro-systems of production (agricultural–rural, pastoral–nomadic, and urban–industrial–service-based) as the structural pillars of Iranian society, and examine the relationship between dispositions and traditions within this framework while taking into account the cultural, linguistic, and religious diversity of the people. Culturally, we possess one culture from before Islam; another culture between the advent of Islam and Shiism; another following Shiism; and yet another following our encounter with Western culture.

Consider these four worlds as four strata forming the foundations of our culture. From another angle as well, one may view these multiple cultures: a culture with a nomadic substructure, a culture with a rural substructure, and ultimately a culture grounded in urban life. By way of example, in the era of Cyrus, 25 per cent of our people were nomads. In 1900 too, 25 per cent of the population were nomads. In Iran, the proportion of nomads even reached 50 per cent of the total population. Today, the nomadic stratum constitutes 1.2 per cent of Iran's population; nevertheless, nomadic culture remains an important layer of our culture, since the formation and disintegration of cultural patterns in society reach back further than a few generations. Although over the past forty years the proportion of rural inhabitants has fallen from 60 per cent to 30 per cent, the influence of rural culture on the daily life of urban Iranians remains visibly substantial. Urbanisation in small towns accounted for 25 per cent of the population strata in 1900; today it has reached 70 per cent, forming the third pillar of our culture in relation to the mode of production. Let us also add that, over at least the past two centuries, three major events have disrupted our social foundation: the advent of the Constitution in 1285 SH (1906), the transformation of 1342–1348 SH (1963–1969) known as the Land Reform—which profoundly altered the rural system of production—and the emergence of the Islamic Republic, which made religion the foundation of the structure of government and the state.[1]

Amid this landscape, what is the structure of Iran's Ministry of Health, and what measures are under preparation to improve mental hygiene and psychological treatment? Let us review several passages from the *Comprehensive National Mental Health Promotion Programme* document for the years 1390–1394 SH (2011–2015), published by this Ministry:[2] "According to the latest available evidence and documentation, the prevalence of mental disorders is around 20 per cent, accounting for approximately 14 per cent of the country's total burden of disease. This is despite the fact that, in accordance with international definitions, mental health is not merely the absence of mental disorders, and encompasses additional components which, if included, would render the burden of psychosocial problems far greater. Key messages of the Comprehensive Mental Health Promotion Programme: based on reports published by the World Health Organisation in 2004 and 2009, the Organisation describes the risk factors for mental health as follows: inadequate childhood development, inappropriate marriage and reproduction, violence, violation of civil rights, parental mental disorders, unsuitable and unwarranted schooling, weak life skills, low social capital, unhealthy social behaviours, and the decline of ethics—as the most central element of spiritual health—are responsible for a large share of mental disorders, necessitating advocacy and the expansion of intersectoral cooperation."

In another passage of the *Comprehensive National Mental Health Promotion Programme* document, we read: "Mental disorders account for 10 per cent of the total burden of disease, with the three leading causes of the burden of mental disorders being, in order, depression (26 per cent of the burden of mental disorders), addiction (24 per cent of the burden), and bipolar disorders (12 per cent)… In one of the reports of the Office of Mental Health, the target population of this office is stated to comprise more than 10 million psychiatric patients requiring identification, treatment, follow-up, and rehabilitation services in hospitals and community-based centres; more than 15 million people belonging to special groups in the community requiring targeted interventions and mental-disorder prevention services; and approximately 40 million members of the general population requiring general mental health promotion services through the media, schools, workplaces, and community gatherings."

We know that depressive illness plays a fundamental role in the prevalence of addiction. When we sum the percentages of the three principal causes of mental disorders cited in the aforementioned document—each of which is directly or indirectly linked in some way to depression—we arrive at an alarming figure. Drawing on several statements by officials, researchers, and journalists, I shall endeavour to sketch, in highly condensed form, the current landscape of mental health and hygiene today: "Depression, with a prevalence of 13 per cent, is the most common mental disorder in Iran"; "15 per cent of Iranian women and 10 per cent of Iranian men suffer from depression"; "The results of the latest national survey indicate that the unemployed and incapacitated, women, divorced individuals, the illiterate and those with low literacy, urban dwellers, and persons of low socio-economic status are more exposed to mental disorders than others"; "50 per cent of individuals who felt the need to seek care for neurological and psychological problems cited difficulty in paying medical costs as one of the reasons for not seeking treatment, and likewise 51 per cent of those who presented to treatment centres with delay faced difficulties in paying costs, of whom 27 per cent cited insurance problems as the cause of their delay in seeking care. According to this report, individuals grappling with mental disorders in Iran are trapped by catastrophic healthcare expenditures." In plain terms, this phrase means that in order to obtain treatment, these individuals have been forced either to sell their assets or to borrow money from others.

According to Dr Hajebi, in Iran 18 per cent of patients suffering from mental disorders face problems associated with paying exorbitant costs. He believes that serious thought must be given to insurance coverage for individuals afflicted with psychiatric disorders—both those requiring hospitalisation and those needing outpatient, psychological, counselling, and non-pharmacological services—because insurance coverage is inadequate and non-pharmacological services are largely excluded from insurance cover.

Paying for treatment costs is a predicament of which Dr Sayyari, Deputy Minister of Health, also spoke recently. He put the annual cost of treating mental disorders at more than 960 billion tomans. According to him, the Ministry of Health cannot shoulder the costs of the mental-disorder treatment sector because hospitals are operated on a self-financing basis and possess no other source of revenue.

Continuing these remarks, we read: "The total number of beds available across all public, private, and other organisational psychiatric hospitals is only eight thousand beds—which itself represents a severe shortage—and according to the tiered referral system this ought to be increased to 11,000 beds, a goal that is not feasible."

Seyyed Hassan Hashemi, Minister of Health and Medical Education, stated: "The Ministry of Health is now a ministry with a budget deficit of seven to eight thousand billion tomans…" Noting that 50 per cent of the workforce of the ministry responsible for the public's health hold only a high-school diploma or less, the Minister added: "At the beginning of the ninth administration, the Ministry of Health had 230,000 personnel, a figure that has now risen to 420,000. The composition of the workforce active in this ministry, as a specialised ministry directly concerned with people's lives, is of utmost importance. Yet 50 per cent of the staff of this specialised ministry hold a high-school diploma or lower qualification."[3] Another statistic that may serve as a basis for comparison in this regard is that, according to the World Health Organisation database, the average clinical workforce in the field of psychological disorders per 100,000 inhabitants is 15 times higher than Iran in France, 10 times higher in Japan, 4 times higher in the United States, and half that of Iran in Turkey—leaving Iran ranked 102nd in the world in this respect.

In the newspaper *Hamshahri*, we read: "Owing to inadequate support from insurance organisations and high treatment costs, this group cannot afford to pursue treatment; do not be surprised, therefore, if in the streets or in your workplaces you encounter people who lack mental health and have been left to fend for themselves." Based on the results of the latest national survey, announced to *Hamshahri* by Dr Ahmad Hajebi, Adviser to the Deputy Minister for Health on Mental Health and Addiction, 24 per cent of people in Iran suffer from mental disorders. According to the findings of this study, the prevalence of mental disorders among Iranian women is 26.5 per cent and among men 20.8 per cent… He identified depression, with a prevalence of 13 per cent, as the most widespread mental disorder in Iran, adding that 15 per cent of Iranian women and 10 per cent of Iranian men suffer from depression.[4]

On the other hand, Dr Taghi Aboutalebi Ahmadi, Adviser to the Director-General of the Health Directorate of Tehran Municipality, maintains that an individual who enjoys mental health interacts well with others across diverse life situations and manages life's pressures effectively. Such individuals are flexible and creative and maintain healthy social relationships with others. They will certainly be successful both within the family environment and at work. This social psychologist told *Hamshahri*: "Undoubtedly, officials must, through coherent planning, undertake serious investment—from the family through to kindergartens and universities—to nurture mentally healthy human beings, for productivity belongs to those who enjoy mental health."[5]

And finally, another official delivers the *coup de grâce* to healthcare and public health in Iran: the Iranian Minister of Health has stated that "the provision of unemployment and health insurance is among the most urgent needs of the country's people, because at present, owing to the crushing costs of medical treatment, seven per cent of the country's population fall below the poverty line every year."[6]

In Part Three, we shall examine the most critical psychological affliction posing a grave danger to the future of our society—namely depression, addiction, and social apathy in Iran.
