en.body_markdown:
https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/01/peinture-300706-151.jpg
[Read on Gooya](http://news.gooya.com/politics/archives/2013/10/168681.php)

Sunday, 13 October 2013 (21 Mehr 1392)

In the book *National Security and the Economic System*, although across various chapters proposals are put forward for moving towards the progress and development of other security, economic, and social dimensions, it is as though — within a single model, and quite apart from the repetition of familiar platitudes — the cultural-doctrinal foundation of Islam and its values are soaring in the heavens, while the actual, proposed model for Iran sits upon the earth among Iranian citizens.

*Special to Gooya Newsletter*
**Part Two: An Examination of Methodology in Strategic Services and in the Book Under Review**

Although the history of management strategy[3] and the definition of the strategist[4] are rooted in war, warfare, and its functioning, from the early twentieth century onwards — at the very moment when the science of management separated from economics and became an independent discipline — strategy acquired diverse meanings. The primary aim of strategic services in management affairs is to chart the overall course and pattern of movement across large-scale human enterprises of labour and production. A clear definition of actionable, measurable, and corrigible objectives helps managers and decision-makers to see the future more transparently and to guide the present more appropriately. Management science operates across multiple dimensions, in both empirical and theoretical fields. Its sphere of application extends to medium and small units, and at times even to the family; it penetrates administrative structures, states, and international organisations. Management science and strategic services draw upon the findings of numerous disciplines in the human sciences, such as sociology, psychology, anthropology, and ethnopsychology. On the other hand, the range of factors influencing the determination of strategy is continually expanding. Time, in its dual dimensions of future and past, reaches beyond one or two years, such that a ten- or twenty-year horizon serves as the baseline. Technology, research, human resources, logistical factors, finance, raw materials, energy, and sustainable development become fundamental determinants of strategy. Geographical and military maps gradually give way to other models and formulae. From the start of the second half of the twentieth century, strategic services were also incorporated into university curricula; research institutes affiliated with major corporations were established; and, most importantly of all, the human being — human culture, the human psyche and unconscious, and human linguistic symbols and values — likewise gradually entered this expanse.

Thus, from the second half of the twentieth century to the present day, strategic services have expanded in an astonishing manner, which may be summarised very concisely as follows:
- Growth in scope of operation: from small working groups to states and international organisations, over half of the US states, and the United Nations.
- Strategic services have become one of the decisive factors in the functioning and success of an organisation.
- Their research domain has expanded, moving from economics to management and thence to sociology, psychology, and anthropology...
- Parameters and variables have multiplied, extending from financial and economic elements towards culture, human needs, desires, and aspirations, as well as artistic and literary dimensions...

It is precisely here that, following ever deeper research and application of strategic services, operational models and diverse, comprehensive techniques are brought into use.

Although strategic services have been designed in manifold ways by practitioners and researchers, on the whole these services encompass three fundamental stages: first, defining and formulating principles, objectives, and a roadmap; second, planning the foundations of the first stage, down to establishing timetabled programmes and indicators of project success; and finally, the stage of executive management. Accompanying these three stages are ongoing evaluation and performance measurement, and at the conclusion of all three stages a comprehensive assessment is conducted, the outcome of which prepares the ground for commencing the next planning cycle.

The book under critique — namely *National Security and the Economic System of Iran* — may be regarded as a document containing only the first stage of strategic services. Although methods differ in this regard as well, all of them nonetheless rely upon shared elements. Taking a snapshot of the existing situation across various economic, financial, logistical, and human-resource dimensions, with due attention to strengths and weaknesses, and carefully analysing this information constitute the initial task. Following this diagnosis, one must proceed to define strategic principles, visions, and objectives, which is among the most vital stages of the strategic-services cycle. Translating these strategic objectives into operational objectives within an atmosphere of social solidarity, while attending to the ideal versus the possible, is a highly technical undertaking requiring specialist expertise. It is from this point onwards that one may embark upon reorganisation and the definition of new projects.

Differences in methodology and theoretical foundations relate chiefly to the degree of importance accorded to what in strategic services is termed 'the depth of the strategic-services domain'. By way of example, one of the most authoritative methods in strategic services is a model known as the 'Strategy Map', devised at Harvard University and continuing to spread rapidly across the globe.

In this method, the depth of the service domain begins from the financial perspective, moves towards the perspective of services, products, and the users of those products, as well as logistics and production capacities, and advances towards human resources — and in particular preparing such a workforce for the future, including training and developing the capacity for innovation and invention.

What forms the core of my own research in the Chair of 'Reorganisation' at Sorbonne University is adding the dimension of human culture and psyche to the aforementioned model — in one account, a rewriting of this model with due attention to the human being, the structure of the human psyche, and collective culture. This presence stems from my two areas of specialisation and is the product of two research disciplines: psychoanalysis and strategy.

With these preliminaries in mind, let us turn together to the book *National Security and the Economic System* and examine this time the methodological aspects employed in this document.

How does the author present the objective of writing this book? On page 34 of the book, we read: 'In the present work, after summing up the investigations carried out, the concluding passage arrives at the following conclusion: under the country's current conditions, safeguarding and enhancing national security in line with the supreme objectives of the system — such as the Constitution and the Twenty-Year Vision Document of the Islamic Republic of Iran — will be possible through designing and formulating an indigenous model of development, a model shaped by taking into account the cultural, geographical, and historical exigencies of the country and paving the way for achieving all religious ideals and national and revolutionary goals, including national security. Hence it is an Iranian-Islamic model. And subsequently, it places the model at the service of faith-centred human development based on a strategy of competitive production, utilising economic, scientific and technological, social, political, defensive-security, and cultural-religious dimensions, centred upon sustainable development and the optimal and comprehensive utilisation of resources and the environment.'

The novel and perhaps foundational point in the stated aim of authoring this document lies precisely in its reference to three simultaneous objectives: first, that this document and its model stand above the system's strategic documents such as the Constitution...; second, that the primary basis for preparing this document is safeguarding national security; and third, that it constitutes an indigenous model on the path to development. It is therefore an entirely strategic document, standing outside the confines of existing recognised and applied models or academic frameworks, with a security-oriented trajectory. As the title of the document indicates — and as is stated repeatedly throughout the chapters of the book, especially its first chapter — it also addresses development on account of its importance in preserving national security in developing countries.

In this model, without explicitly naming strategic objectives, two very clear strategic goals stand out: attaining national security and faith-centred human development. A substantial portion of this document is devoted to dissecting the dimensions of national security and its relationship with economic, social, and cultural dimensions... The book essentially regards the goal of development as one of the pillars of national security, thereby placing the two strategic objectives in a hierarchy and relationship wherein national security takes precedence over development. Within national security, protecting the borders and preserving the system of the Islamic Republic and the values of the Islamic Revolution are likewise treated simultaneously as interconnected elements. One may alter the governing system of a nation, transform its constitution, and replace a previous revolution with another revolution without inflicting harm upon the territorial integrity of the country. The history of the past three centuries bears witness to numerous instances of such transformations.

In defining the second strategic objective — namely faith-centred human development — a fundamental problem exists. Here, the classification of the countries of the world in terms of development, comparing Iran with these countries on the one hand, and the document's independent, self-devised definition of development on the other, plunge us into difficulty. Here too, scientific rigour has been set aside. On the one hand, the document speaks of 'Third World countries' and 'developed countries', and on the other, it addresses 'underdeveloped', 'developing', and 'developed' countries, without specifying precisely where present-day Iran stands within this categorisation. On page 788, we read: 'Whereas the country's attainment of developed status and its establishment in the foremost economic position on the 1404 horizon requires achieving continuous and accelerated economic growth, an examination of the performance of Iran's economy, particularly during the years of implementing the Fourth Plan, indicates the reality that the target of an average eight per cent annual growth... has not only failed to materialise in any recent year, but for various reasons — including limited investment resources and low productivity — has exhibited a downward trend.'

The term 'Third World' came into use after the Second World War and the onset of the Cold War — when the world was divided into two blocs or two worlds, East and West — to designate underdeveloped and developing countries that lay outside the two power blocs. With the collapse of the Second World, the concept of the Third World automatically loses its significance, and employing this term becomes meaningless. What remains is the second classification: that is, dividing countries in terms of development into developed, developing, and underdeveloped countries. Regrettably, in the document under discussion, our present-day Iran is not defined in these terms. On the other hand, strategic objectives must be intelligible and clear, and movement towards them must be measurable in some manner. If we do not know which category of countries we belong to — underdeveloped or developing — how can we define the goal of becoming developed and possess a yardstick for attaining it?

In defining faith-centred human development — whose cultural dimension this document describes as its superior and exceptional feature — the book locates the difference between this model and other models that speak of development solely in political, economic, and social dimensions precisely in this cultural prominence.

The authors of this book criticise development models that have recently incorporated cultural dimensions from an educational angle as well, holding that their conception of faith-centred human development transcends even the sphere of development in the field of education. On page 791, we read: 'Although the category of culture had been neglected in the view of first- and second-generation theorists, in the conception of development from the standpoint of third-generation theorists, culture has been accepted as one of the pillars of development... Statistics on social and cultural indicators have been confined merely to educational indicators such as primary school enrolment rates, the percentage of literate adults... Thus culture in its broad sense — such as beliefs, convictions, values, and traditions... — has not found concrete determination in the proposed cultural and social indicators, such that one might largely regard the educational dimension of culture in this outlook as synonymous with cultural generalities.'

In critiquing the method and model employed, from the standpoint of defining strategic objectives, we must point out that the dialectical relationship between these objectives and their indicators, on the one hand, and the systematic relationship between these objectives and the stage of examining current conditions in Iran, the region, and the world — together with the primary diagnosis aimed at identifying cause-and-effect links among shortcomings, deficiencies, and distortions, and demonstrating these systematic relationships by reference to statistics and data — on the other, constitute the essential, foundational work of any method. And it is at this very juncture that the book's proposed model suffers a deficit, and the authors, perhaps without realising it themselves, forget the elementary principles of their own craft. The book defines the strength of its indigenous development model as attention to culture — and not merely from the angle of education and culture, but from the angle of beliefs, convictions, and traditions.

Let us honestly endeavour to enter into this game and accompany the book in order to see how, even by the book's own definitions, the dimension of comprehensive cultural development is defined and how it harmonises with the other dimensions of development and national security. Fortunately, in the other dimensions, particularly the economic one, the general method of applying dialectical and systematic relationships has been observed; our purpose here is to examine the methodology rather than the outcomes derived from that methodology, which we shall address in forthcoming essays.

From the book's perspective, let us pursue the question of why the model of faith-centred human development is superior. On page 792, we read: 'In the Human Development Index put forward by the United Nations Development Programme, merely the component of education is placed alongside economic and health components. Although recently a human-ethical development index... has been proposed for Islamic countries so that values such as equality, freedom and autonomy, justice, environmental concerns, and sustainable development may be added to the three aforementioned components, culture in the view of the elites and leaders of the system of the Islamic Republic of Iran possesses a broader concept, such that the cultural dimension not only appears alongside other dimensions of development and within the structure of comprehensive and balanced development, but also acts as the infrastructure of development in generating and fostering the growth of other dimensions of development.'

Thus, in the eyes of the framers of this model, the cultural dimension surpasses both the United Nations indicators and the indicators proposed for Islamic countries. Yet a dimension so fundamental ought to possess a clear definition, carry clear measurable indicators, and play an important and foundational role in taking stock of the country's present situation. There ought to be foundational programmes for advancing this dimension and its indicators, placing it at the very centre. Unfortunately, the reader encounters nothing regarding the cultural dimension of development apart from unintelligible generalities that are neither actionable nor measurable. Even in the educational dimension, not a single clear picture — whether in quantity, quality, or character of this educational dimension — is provided on even one page of the book, whereas, according to the book's own claim, in more secondary dimensions such as the economic, social, and security spheres, or foreign relations, more than seven hundred pages of material, interspersed with statistics, maps, and data, are to be found.

If beliefs and convictions form the foundational pillar of the cultural dimension, how can one pass judgement on the failure of economic progress to function without genuinely examining and analysing this dimension? How can one be certain that it is not branches of this very cultural dimension that have instigated and caused corruption, rent-seeking, addiction, hypocrisy, and brain drain? How can one, in a strategic text — and from the perspective of a strategist — content oneself with a few remarks from eminent figures regarding the main foundation of all dimensions of development, which according to the book itself is Islamic belief and conviction? It is as though there were no possibility of any scientific research into the solidity of beliefs and convictions, the penetration of these beliefs, and the functioning of social relations among citizens, between citizens and the system, and between the system and its international relations. It is as though, in the proposed model, the slogans of the cultural dimension serve merely as ornament for the book and bear no living, organic, or systematic relationship with everyday life and the presence of citizens and the system.

In the book *National Security and the Economic System*, although across various chapters proposals are put forward for moving towards the progress and development of other security, economic, and social dimensions, it is as though — within a single model, and quite apart from the repetition of familiar platitudes — the cultural-doctrinal foundation of Islam and its values are soaring in the heavens, while the actual, proposed model for Iran sits upon the earth among Iranian citizens.

Within this very model, using the book's own definition, one may study cultural development in three parts. That is to say, one may accept the objectives and measurement indicators pertaining to the United Nations and Islamic countries, and likewise define objectives and indicators for the dimension that, in the book's own parlance, lies beyond these — namely faith and belief.

In order to conclude our critique and examination in this section — without myself believing in the cultural dimensions defined in this model or considering myself competent in that domain, but solely as a specialist in the cultural aspect of strategic services and with a view to the future — I propose that, now that the authors of the book all stand at the apex of executive power, they complete their model and endeavour to explain the relationship of weaknesses and shortcomings to this same important factor as well. Along this path, perhaps the following objectives and indicators could be proposed for the superior cultural-faith dimension:
- The growth rate of attendance at holy shrines and mosques
- The growth rate of various votive *sofreh* gatherings for Hazrat Abbas, Ruqayyah, and others
- The growth rate in the number of recitations of the *adhan* and *iqamah*
- The growth rate of Quran-recitation competitions, especially from memory
- The growth rate in the number of women appearing in full Islamic-Shiite covering
- The growth rate in the collection of *khums* and *zakat*
- The growth rate in the printing of seminary books
- The growth rate of seminary students in terms of numbers, religious knowledge, and social influence and employment.

To examine scientifically the dialectical relationships between the above indicators and development, in accordance with the definition provided by the United Nations, and to complete the research, one would also need to demonstrate the growth rate of the indicators listed above and their statistical correlation with indicators of social life, social relations, and the physical and psychological health of society — in particular, the rate of increase or decrease in divorce, suicide, delinquency, drug and alcohol addiction, severe and acute depression, the enhancement of a sense of responsibility, increased efficiency per hour of labour, the rate of increase in administrative and financial corruption, and so forth. Only in that case will the model presented in this book, centred upon faith-centred human development, be transformed from an idealised model into an actionable one.

In the forthcoming article, we shall examine and scrutinise the book's data and statistics, how they were obtained, and their degree of accuracy and practical value.

________________________________________
[1] The book *National Security and the Economic System of Iran* (*Amniyat-e Melli va Nezam-e Eqtesadi-ye Iran*) was written by Hassan Rouhani and published by the Centre for Strategic Research of the Expediency Discernment Council: first printing in Mordad 1389 (July–August 2010), and fifth printing in Khordad 1391 (May–June 2012), one year prior to the election. Mohammad-Baqer Nobakht, Mohammad Nahavandian, Mohammad-Hossein Malayeri, and Akbar Torkan collaborated with Hassan Rouhani in writing this book.
[2] Dr Hassan Makaremi; clinical psychoanalyst, researcher in the Chair for the Study of the Role of Innovation and Preparedness in Organisational Leaps — Special Section on Culture and Strategic Services — Sorbonne University, Paris.
[3] Makaremi, Hassan: *A Strategic Look at the Green Era* (*Negahi Rahbordi beh Dowran-e Sabz*), 2012, H&S Media Publications, London.
[4] Makaremi, Hassan: *Several Strategic Perspectives on the Future of Iran* (*Chand Negah-e Rahbordi beh Ayandeh-ye Iran*), 2013, H&S Media Publications, London.

Lundi 8 mehr 1392 (30 septembre 2013)
Critique du livre « Sécurité nationale et système économique de l'Iran » de Hassan Rohani (première partie), Hassan Makaremi

Notre choix d'examiner et de critiquer cet ouvrage s'inscrit dans le prolongement d'un effort pluriannuel visant à développer et à généraliser le rôle des idées stratégiques, tant au niveau de la réflexion que de l'action, à tous les échelons de la société iranienne — à l'intérieur comme à l'extérieur du pays — parmi les chercheurs universitaires, les femmes et hommes politiques et les acteurs civiques et sociaux. Pourquoi l'axe des échanges et des discours ne s'élèverait-il pas au niveau stratégique ? Pourquoi les fondements essentiels ne retiendraient-ils pas l'attention ?
Spécial pour Gooya News

### Première partie : Avant-propos et rôle des mots

#### Avant-propos

L'ouvrage *Sécurité nationale et système économique de l'Iran* (*Amniyat-e melli va nezam-e eqtesadi-ye Iran*), écrit par Hassan Rohani, a été publié par le Centre de recherches stratégiques du Conseil de discernement de l'intérêt supérieur du régime ; sa première édition remonte à mordad 1389 (juillet-août 2010) et sa cinquième édition à khordad 1391 (mai-juin 2012), soit un an avant l'élection présidentielle. Ont collaboré avec Hassan Rohani à la rédaction de cet ouvrage : Mohammad Bagher Nobakht (né en 1329/1950, vice-président chargé de la planification et de la supervision stratégique, directeur par intérim de la vice-présidence au développement de la gestion et du capital humain, porte-parole du gouvernement, secrétaire général du Parti de la modération et du développement, député de Rasht durant les troisième à sixième législatures du Parlement et vice-président chargé des recherches économiques au Centre de recherches stratégiques du Conseil de discernement), Mohammad Nahavandian (né en 1333/1954, chef de cabinet du président de la République et directeur de l'institution présidentielle, ainsi que président de la Chambre de commerce, d'industrie, des mines et de l'agriculture), Mohammad Hossein Malaeri (membre du corps académique du Centre de recherches stratégiques) et Akbar Torkan (vice-présidence aux affaires internationales de la présidence et secrétariat du Mouvement des non-alignés, membre fondateur du Parti de la modération et du développement, conseiller principal du président de la République, secrétaire du Conseil de coordination des zones franches commerciales, industrielles et économiques spéciales, directeur par intérim de l'Agence spatiale iranienne et du Conseil supérieur des affaires des Iraniens de l'étranger).

Nous constatons que tous ces collaborateurs forment aujourd'hui le premier cercle exécutif le plus proche du président de la République. On peut aisément en conclure que les fondements de cet ouvrage constituent peut-être non seulement l'œuvre commune de l'équipe dirigeante du gouvernement actuel, mais qu'il est également possible d'extraire de ce document la ligne de pensée stratégique qui gouverne l'action de ce gouvernement. Il y a lieu de se réjouir que, pour la première fois, soit parvenu au pouvoir un gouvernement qui avait présenté un document stratégique dix ans plus tôt et vient de le réactualiser, et — fait plus important encore — qu'une équipe composée des auteurs mêmes de ce document détienne aujourd'hui le pouvoir exécutif. Ce phénomène est sans précédent dans l'histoire de l'Iran. Par ailleurs, cette planification offre pour la première fois au gouvernement la possibilité de ne pas laisser le gouvernail des objectifs stratégiques échapper des mains du président.

Dans mes deux ouvrages précédents, *Un regard stratégique sur l'ère verte* (1) et *Quelques regards stratégiques sur l'avenir de l'Iran* (2), je me suis efforcé d'éclairer, dans toute la mesure du possible, l'esprit de la pensée stratégique, les services stratégiques et les éléments structurels mis en œuvre dans ces services, à la lumière des études et des méthodes les plus avancées, en lien avec l'Iran et son avenir. À la suite de ces deux livres s'est présentée l'occasion d'accéder à un document dont les rédacteurs détiennent aujourd'hui le plus haut pouvoir exécutif de la société. La critique et l'examen scientifique de ce document, et en dernier ressort sa réécriture selon les méthodes scientifiques contemporaines et depuis une perspective extérieure au régime en place, peuvent nous guider vers un rapprochement des pensées stratégiques en vue d'édifier un Iran libre et prospère.

Auparavant, mon estimé collègue le docteur Fereydoun Khavand avait également souligné, dans un article (3), deux points essentiels de cet ouvrage d'un point de vue économique, dont il ne paraît pas nécessaire de répéter la teneur. En substance : pour la première fois, nous disposons d'un document reposant sur des bases réalistes, permettant d'espérer que les pilotes de l'économie nationale ont conscience des enjeux et des difficultés ; et, d'autre part, comment se fait-il que, malgré la teneur de ce même document, nous n'ayons pas su, au cours des trente-quatre dernières années, apporter de réponse aux problèmes économiques ni mettre concrètement à profit les ressources humaines et naturelles du pays sur la voie du bien-être et de la reconstruction ?

Du point de vue des services stratégiques, la question peut être posée en ces termes : lors de l'élaboration de documents stratégiques, il convient impérativement et préalablement de procéder à l'examen et à l'analyse de la situation présente et d'établir un diagnostic clair des points faibles ainsi que de leur genèse, afin de pouvoir, en s'appuyant sur ce diagnostic, définir de nouveaux objectifs stratégiques et les voies d'action qui en découlent. Le docteur Khavand demande à juste titre : « L'auteur et ses collaborateurs, qui analysent si profondément les concepts économiques et géoéconomiques fondamentaux, à quoi pensent-ils lorsqu'ils confrontent leur savoir aux conditions actuelles de l'Iran ? Comment se fait-il qu'un pays doté de toutes les conditions requises pour s'élever sur la scène économique internationale ait sombré dans un isolement aussi déplorable ? Pourquoi un pays qui se situe au premier rang mondial pour ses ressources gazières (selon les données les plus récentes publiées par British Petroleum) est-il importateur net de gaz ? Pourquoi un pays qui détient les deuxièmes réserves mondiales de pétrole a-t-il été relégué en marge de la production et du négoce de l'or noir ? Pourquoi les structures du commerce extérieur de l'Iran stagnent-elles au niveau des pays les plus arriérés du tiers-monde ? Pourquoi l'Iran détient-il, aux côtés du Soudan, le record du taux d'inflation ? Pourquoi la monnaie nationale iranienne s'est-elle avilie à ce point, même par rapport à l'afghani et au dinar irakien ? Et enfin, cette question fondamentale : au regard de la position extrêmement faible de l'Iran dans le système commercial, monétaire et industriel international, et du lien tout à fait exact que M. Rohani établit entre l'économie et la sécurité nationale, quelle est la situation actuelle du pays du point de vue de la sécurité nationale ? »

Certes, il serait peut-être beaucoup plus aisé, à l'instar de nombreux compatriotes partageant notre affliction, de se contenter face à de tels documents du discours habituel — juste mais insuffisant — selon lequel « … tous ces malheurs proviennent de la structure de la République islamique, du principe de la tutelle absolue du juriste-théologien (*velayat-e motlaqeh-ye faqih*), de l'étroitesse de vue et des superstitions des fils, petits-fils et arrière-petits-fils de Majlesi, Nouri et Kashani… ». Mais nous sommes convaincus que le dialogue fondé sur les connaissances scientifiques, les sciences économiques, l'organisation et la lucidité — jusque dans les niveaux les plus fins et détaillés, et simultanément — clarifie l'espace du discours, dote l'ensemble des forces d'aujourd'hui et de demain d'un outil plus efficace et nous transforme toutes et tous en citoyens plus responsables.

Par cet avant-propos, nous nous proposons de livrer aux lecteurs l'examen de cet ouvrage en plusieurs exposés : d'abord un propos sur la lexicologie et les difficultés actuelles des discours stratégiques ; puis un propos sur la méthodologie, son besoin et sa carence ; ensuite l'examen du dernier chapitre du livre en tant que condensé des positions de ses rédacteurs ; et enfin une réécriture de ce document mettant en lumière ses forces et ses faiblesses. Nul doute que la critique et l'analyse de ces textes, ainsi que la mise au jour de leurs contradictions intrinsèques et internes, puissent constituer le socle d'une réflexion partagée et d'un rapprochement collectif pour celles et ceux des acteurs qui se préparent à assumer les responsabilités de demain.

### Propos sur le rôle des mots

L'une des difficultés de la culture orale et écrite dans les environnements clos tient à l'impossibilité d'y voir s'ancrer une relation précise entre le signifiant et le signifié. Car c'est dans le dialogue, dans l'échange entre écrire et répondre, et au sein d'un milieu vivant, effervescent et continu que ce lien se consolide et se généralise ; dans la pratique, la fréquence de circulation des mots et de leurs charges sémantiques est telle que la langue et les vocables demeurent vivants et que leurs significations tendent vers une plus grande harmonie et homogénéité chez les locuteurs de cette langue — même si nous savons que les signifiés ne coïncideront jamais totalement dans les esprits des êtres humains. Les signifiants et les signifiés sont accordés au sein du système d'information interne de chaque individu (à l'exception des personnes atteintes de troubles psychotiques sévères). Ce phénomène permet à chaque citoyen, dans son rapport aux autres citoyens, de recourir à des normes acceptées de tous. C'est précisément là que les frontières de la liberté de chaque citoyen reçoivent une définition acceptable pour lui-même comme pour autrui, et que la coexistence devient possible.

Notre système d'information interne est peut-être le seul être vivant immatériel. Bien que son fonctionnement et sa survie dépendent de notre existence biologique, il poursuit sa vie indépendamment de nous et se transforme jusqu'au dernier instant de notre vie — plus ou moins, lentement ou rapidement, continûment ou graduellement. En conséquence, la mise en relation de nos systèmes d'information — constitués d'ensembles de signifiants et de signifiés accordés et reliés — maintient ceux-ci actifs et les harmonise dans leur interaction mutuelle.

Un exemple vivant et contemporain en est la culture écrite et orale en République islamique d'Iran. Nous nous souvenons tous qu'après la guerre Iran-Irak parut un ouvrage intitulé *Lexique du front* (*Farhang-e loghat-e jebheh*). Sans nul doute, la nécessité d'un tel livre s'était imposée à l'époque parce que, dans le domaine de la guerre, des termes étaient employés et s'étaient répandus sans être compréhensibles de tous. Un autre exemple est celui du lexique propre aux jeunes des grandes villes en Europe, qui n'est pas intelligible par tous et exige un dictionnaire spécifique. Dès l'avènement de la République islamique, de nombreux termes issus des sphères de l'enseignement religieux chiite se sont infiltrés dans les domaines sociaux et s'y sont installés durablement. L'isolement de la République islamique sur la scène mondiale a également contribué à cette unidimensionnalisation de la langue et de son vocabulaire. Dans les divers domaines économique, culturel et des sciences humaines, ce problème majeur — fruit du développement unilatéral de la culture interne du régime et de ses appareils de communication tels que l'administration, les médias audiovisuels d'État, la presse, le cinéma, les prêches du vendredi ou les entretiens des responsables — a uniformisé la culture du régime de la République islamique et rendu la communication avec elle difficile pour quiconque se situe hors de cette sphère.

Par exemple, pour plus de quatre millions d'Iraniens vivant à l'étranger, indépendamment de la contrainte de vivre dans l'environnement oral et écrit de la société d'accueil, la nouveauté des vocables forgés en Iran et au sein du système de la République islamique aggrave encore leur difficulté de communication. J'ai éprouvé ce problème de près lors de mon séjour à Cuba l'année dernière : notre traducteur de l'espagnol vers le persan était un jeune Cubain qui avait effectué ses études universitaires en Iran. À plusieurs reprises, j'ai constaté une divergence de compréhension entre lui et moi à propos d'un seul et même mot. L'ouverture de l'espace médiatique, administratif, scientifique et politique de l'Iran est l'unique voie vers une réconciliation linguistique de part et d'autre des frontières. À défaut, les Iraniens de l'étranger — et tout particulièrement les deuxième et troisième générations — se trouveront progressivement confrontés au grave problème d'une rupture linguistique, prélude à une rupture culturelle.

Notre choix d'examiner et de critiquer cet ouvrage s'inscrit dans le prolongement d'un effort pluriannuel visant à développer et à généraliser le rôle des idées stratégiques, tant au niveau de la réflexion que de l'action, à tous les échelons de la société iranienne — à l'intérieur comme à l'extérieur du pays — parmi les chercheurs universitaires, les femmes et hommes politiques et les acteurs civiques et sociaux. Pourquoi l'axe des échanges et des discours ne s'élèverait-il pas au niveau stratégique ? Pourquoi les fondements essentiels ne retiendraient-ils pas l'attention ? Pourquoi les regroupements ne s'ordonneraient-ils pas autour d'objectifs stratégiques, ce qui aurait pour résultat pratique des convergences d'action plus aisées, plus durables et plus fécondes ?

La première difficulté pour lire avec exactitude le texte du livre qui nous occupe tient précisément à cette dispersion des termes et à l'effort requis pour saisir le sens des mots utilisés. On ne saurait parvenir à une compréhension juste d'un texte — a fortiori d'un texte stratégique — si l'on est contraint de définir soi-même les mots clés et de les employer par conjecture. Dans cet ouvrage, les définitions (concepts – signifiés), qui constituent les éléments fondamentaux d'une analyse stratégique, sont tenues pour acquises. En avançant dans la lecture du livre, on aboutit à la conclusion que les définitions proposées ne concordent guère avec ce qui figure dans les textes stratégiques selon l'usage international : des termes tels que *arman* (idéal), *barayand* (résultante), *keramat-e ensani* (dignité humaine), *ta'ali-ye ejtema'i* (élévation/transcendance sociale), *towse'eh-ye ensani-ye din-mehvar* (développement humain centré sur la religion)… Pour approfondir l'analyse de cette lacune, considérons les deux signifiants *AIDS* et *SIDA* en anglais et en français : bien que les deux signifiants soient totalement différents, il est clair pour tous, et sans aucune ambiguïté, que le signifié de l'un comme de l'autre est la maladie virale due au VIH.

Ou encore les deux signifiants *NATO* et *OTAN*, derrière lesquels chacun placera l'organisation du traité régional de défense collective entre plusieurs pays. Là où la parole, l'écoute et la circulation des mots et des concepts sont libres, les termes s'affinent, s'uniformisent et accomplissent aisément leur fonction première, qui est de transmettre des concepts. L'un des bienfaits des organisations internationales et des efforts déployés par les États et les nations en faveur d'un dialogue constant autour de questions d'intérêt commun réside précisément dans cette harmonisation du rôle des signifiants. Et lorsque, sur le terrain de l'action, les négociations s'étendent au champ social, il en résulte nécessairement un rapprochement culturel.

En 2009, j'ai été invité par les responsables de l'UNESCO à participer à une table ronde consacrée à la calligraphie. L'autre intervenant était Maître Fan Zeng, peintre, calligraphe et poète chinois. Avant la conférence, au cours de deux séances de dialogue, nous nous sommes efforcés d'harmoniser nos interventions. Fan Zeng m'a rendu attentif à ce principe de la culture chinoise selon lequel le poète, le peintre et le calligraphe ne font qu'un : nul ne peut devenir calligraphe sans atteindre l'harmonie de la peinture et sans connaître en poésie la racine des mots. Ce dialogue m'a davantage familiarisé avec le lien étroit unissant les arts préhistoriques et la symbolisation. Ces arts (datant de 4 000 à 7 000 ans avant notre ère) sont à l'origine de toutes les écritures inventées par l'humanité et préparent l'avènement des premiers arts visuels, de la symbolisation ainsi que de la présence et du rôle des signifiants — ou des mots, qui sont des signes sonores. Assurément, c'est par de tels dialogues que les cultures, aussi riches soient-elles, sortent de leur isolement et se relient à la chaîne de l'accomplissement le plus précieux de l'être humain à travers les millénaires : la culture humaine.

Revenons à l'ouvrage étudié. À la page 805, dans un schéma que l'on peut considérer comme le condensé des fondements théoriques et stratégiques du livre, à la question « Quel idéal (*arman*) ? », il est répondu : « La dignité humaine, l'élévation sociale, la satisfaction des besoins matériels et spirituels de l'individu et de la société. » Et en réponse à « L'objectif final », il est indiqué : « Le développement de l'être humain centré sur la religion (*towse'eh-ye ensan-e din-mehvar*). » Puis les dimensions de l'objectif final sont définies comme suit : « développements économique, scientifique et technologique, social, défensif-sécuritaire, culturel-religieux ».

Nous réservons à l'exposé suivant l'analyse du modèle, de la méthode et de son efficacité. Efforçons-nous ici, en tirant parti de notre connaissance des mots et de leurs rapports mutuels, d'atteindre une compréhension plus précise de ces notions : que peut désigner le concept spécifique d'« idéal » (*arman*) dans un document stratégique ?

Tentons de parvenir à une sorte de langage commun. Le mot *arman* en persan, compte tenu de ses diverses acceptions (idéal ; cité idéale — appelée en philosophie islamique *madineh-ye fazeleh* [cité vertueuse] ; cité idéale que l'on conçoit, à l'instar de l'utopie idéale de Platon, de Thomas More et d'autres…), dont les équivalents dans la terminologie technique des services stratégiques en anglais et en français se rapprochent de la notion de *vision*, désigne en quelque sorte le point même où nous nous tenons et d'où nous contemplons l'être : notre horizon de regard. Que peut signifier « l'objectif final » ? Là où, en définitive, nous voulons parvenir ? Ne s'agit-il pas ici de cette même société idéale ?

La « dignité humaine » (*keramat-e ensani*) est également interprétée et définie en langue persane comme l'honneur, la noblesse, l'éminence et la grandeur humaines. Le terme *ta'ali* (élévation/transcendance) désigne dans notre langue contemporaine ce qui est élevé et supérieur (s'élever, s'exhausser et s'épanouir). Peut-on déduire de l'association de « société » et de « transcendance/élévation » (*ta'ali*) qu'elle désigne une société dans laquelle prévalent des valeurs supérieures ? Dès lors se pose la question : quelles sont ces valeurs supérieures ? Des valeurs humaines selon quelle définition ? Les valeurs supérieures universellement partagées de l'humanité, les valeurs fondamentales de la Déclaration universelle des droits de l'homme, ou les valeurs supérieures rapportées à l'islam, au chiisme ou à l'interprétation contemporaine du chiisme du *velayat-e faqih* ? Et, dans la suite du contenu attribué à l'« idéal », nous lisons : « la satisfaction des besoins matériels et spirituels de l'individu et de la société ». S'agit-il des besoins définis par l'individu ou la société eux-mêmes, ou bien les représentants élus de l'individu ou de la société les expriment-ils ? S'il en est ainsi, pour parvenir à définir ces besoins, les représentants directs du peuple doivent pouvoir les formuler de manière continue et sans préjugés — ce qui n'est réalisable que par la voie d'élections sans filtre de validation préalable (*nezarat-e estesvabi*) !

L'« objectif final » est le développement humain centré sur la religion. Prenons « développement » (*towse'eh*) comme équivalent d'expansion ou de progrès, ou des deux à la fois ; et « centré sur la religion » (*din-mehvar*) comme gravitant autour de la religion (entendons le chiisme duodécimain dans son interprétation du *velayat-e motlaqeh-ye faqih*, la tutelle absolue du juriste-théologien), ce qui, en résumé, revient à orienter l'être humain autour des valeurs du chiisme duodécimain tel qu'interprété par le *velayat-e motlaqeh-ye faqih*. L'objectif final correspond en quelque sorte, peut-être, à notre mission pour atteindre la société idéale. S'il en est ainsi, tenons l'objectif final pour ce lieu ultime auquel l'ensemble des efforts du modèle résumé dans l'ouvrage entend nous conduire.

Quoi qu'il en soit, poursuivons notre effort pour comprendre la culture de l'ouvrage. Si nous le concevons comme constitué de deux volets imbriqués — l'idéal (*arman*) et l'objectif final — que nous assimilons à l'horizon de vision et à l'idéal vers lequel nous cheminons, on peut en déduire que ce qui est visé est un être humain croyant en l'islam — plus précisément le chiisme duodécimain selon l'interprétation de la tutelle absolue du juriste-théologien (*velayat-e motlaqeh-ye faqih*) — appelé à vivre dans une société où l'ensemble de ses besoins auront été satisfaits, dès lors qu'une telle société est une société supérieure — transcendante (*mote'ali*) — et qu'un tel être humain est revêtu de dignité. Ne s'agit-il pas là de cette même société de l'Imam du Temps (*Emam-e Zaman*) à laquelle on s'est efforcé, par le choix des termes et du discours, de conférer la teinte et le parfum de la littérature sociologique, du management et des services stratégiques ?

Dans les écrits qui suivront, nous nous attacherons à approfondir la connaissance de la méthode et des modèles de cet ouvrage.

Hassan Makaremi

[Read on Gooya](http://news.gooya.com/politics/archives/2013/09/167918.php)

Monday, 8 Mehr 1392 (30 September 2013)
A Critique of *National Security and the Economic System of Iran* by Hassan Rouhani (Part I), Hassan Makaremi

Our choice to examine and critique this book follows a multi-year endeavour that seeks to cultivate and universalise the role of strategic thought—both conceptually and operationally—across all strata of Iranian society, inside and outside the country, among academic thinkers, politicians, and civil and social activists. Why should the axis of exchanges and discourses not ascend to the strategic level? Why should fundamental premises not receive due attention? (Special for Gooya News)

Part I: Preface and the Role of Words

Preface
*National Security and the Economic System of Iran* is a book authored by Hassan Rouhani and published by the Centre for Strategic Research of the Expediency Discernment Council—first printed in Mordad 1389 (July–August 2010), and in its fifth printing in Khordad 1391 (May–June 2012), one year prior to the election. In writing this book, Hassan Rouhani was assisted by Mohammad Bagher Nobakht (born 1329/1950, Vice-President for Planning and Strategic Supervision, Acting Vice-President for Management Development and Human Capital, Government Spokesperson, Secretary-General of the Moderation and Development Party, Member of Parliament for Rasht in the third through sixth terms of the Islamic Consultative Assembly, and Deputy for Economic Research at the Centre for Strategic Research of the Expediency Discernment Council), Mohammad Nahavandian (born 1333/1954, Chief of Staff to the President and Head of the Presidential Office, and President of the Chamber of Commerce, Industries, Mines and Agriculture), Mohammad Hossein Malaieri (faculty member of the Centre for Strategic Research), and Akbar Torkan (Vice-President for International Affairs and the Secretariat of the Non-Aligned Movement, founding member of the Moderation and Development Party, Senior Adviser to the President, Secretary of the Supreme Council of Free Trade-Industrial and Special Economic Zones, Head of the Iranian Space Agency, and Secretary of the Supreme Council of Iranians Abroad).

We observe that all of these collaborators now constitute the President's closest executive circle. One may readily conclude that the foundations of this book are perhaps not merely the collective product of the current administration's executive team, but that the strategic line of thought governing this administration's conduct can also be extracted from this document. It is a matter of satisfaction that, for the first time, an administration has taken office having presented a strategic document ten years earlier and now updated it—and, more importantly, that a team composed of the very drafters of this document today holds executive power. This phenomenon is unprecedented in Iranian history. Moreover, this planning enables the government, for the first time, to ensure that the helm of strategic objectives does not slip from the President's hands.

In my two previous books, *A Strategic Look at the Green Era* (1) and *Several Strategic Perspectives on the Future of Iran* (2), I have endeavoured to elucidate, insofar as possible, the ethos of strategic thought, strategic services, and the structural elements deployed within those services, drawing upon the most advanced studies and methodologies in relation to Iran and its future. Following those two volumes, the opportunity arose to gain access to a document whose drafters hold the highest executive power in society. A scholarly critique and examination of this document—and ultimately its rewriting using contemporary scientific methods and from a vantage point outside the ruling system—can guide us towards a convergence of strategic thought for achieving a free and prosperous Iran.

Previously, my esteemed colleague Dr Fereydoun Khavand also pointed out in an article (3) two fundamental aspects of this book from an economic standpoint, whose substance need not be repeated here. In short, for the first time we have in hand a document grounded in realistic premises, allowing one to be optimistic that those steering the country's economy are aware of its problems and challenges. The other point is how it comes to be that, on the basis of the contents of this very document, over the past thirty-four years we have been unable to address economic difficulties and effectively harness the country's human and natural resources for prosperity and reconstruction.

From the standpoint of strategic services, this question may be framed as follows: in preparing strategic documents, one must necessarily begin by examining and analysing present conditions and establishing a clear diagnosis of weaknesses and how those weaknesses arose, so that upon this foundation one may define fresh strategic objectives and the solutions deriving from them. Dr Khavand rightly asks: "What do the author and his collaborators—who examine fundamental economic and geo-economic concepts so profoundly—think when applying their knowledge to Iran's present circumstances? How is it that a country possessing all the necessary conditions to ascend on the international economic stage has fallen into such deplorable isolation? Why is a country that ranks first globally in gas reserves (according to the latest figures published by British Petroleum) a net importer of gas? Why has a country holding the world's second-largest oil reserves been marginalised in the production and trade of black gold? Why have Iran's foreign trade structures stagnated at the level of the most backward Third World countries? Why does Iran hold the record, alongside Sudan, for inflation rates? Why has Iran's national currency become so debased even in comparison with the afghani and the Iraqi dinar? And finally, this fundamental question: given Iran's exceedingly weak position in the international commercial, monetary, and industrial system, and the entirely valid link Mr Rouhani establishes between the economy and national security, what is the country's current condition with respect to national security?"

Of course, it might be far easier, like many sympathetic critics confronted with such documents, to absolve ourselves with the pertinent yet insufficient and perennial refrain: "...All these calamities stem from the structure of the Islamic Republic, the principle of the Absolute Guardianship of the Jurist, and the short-sightedness and superstitions of the sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons of Majlesi, Nouri, and Kashani..." Yet we are convinced that dialogue grounded in scientific knowledge, economic science, organisation, and critical enlightenment—even at micro and granular levels simultaneously—will render the discursive space more transparent, equip the totality of today's and tomorrow's forces with more effective instruments, and transform all of us into more responsible citizens.

With this preface, we endeavour to place our examination of this book before readers in several discourses: first, a reflection on terminology and the current problems of strategic discourses; a reflection on methodology, its necessity and its absence; an examination of the final chapter of the book as a distillation of the drafters' views; and finally, a rewriting of this document attentive to its strengths and weaknesses. Undoubtedly, critiquing and examining these texts and exposing their inherent, internal contradictions can serve as a basis for intellectual convergence and collective alignment among those activists preparing themselves to assume future responsibilities.

A Discourse on the Role of Words
One of the problems of spoken and written culture in closed environments is that there is no possibility for a precise relationship between signifier (*dāl*) and signified (*madlul*) to take root. For it is through speaking and listening, writing and responding, within a living, vibrant, and continuous environment, that communication grows robust and universal, and in practice the circulation of words and their semantic loads keeps language and vocabulary alive, guiding their meanings towards greater harmony and homogeneity among speakers of that language—even though we know that signifieds will never become entirely identical across human minds. Signifiers and signifieds are aligned within the informational system of each individual (with the exception of individuals afflicted by severe psychotic disorders). This phenomenon enables every citizen, in relating to fellow citizens, to draw upon norms accepted by all. It is precisely from this that the boundaries of each citizen's freedom acquire a mutually acceptable definition for oneself and others, rendering coexistence possible.

Our internal informational system is perhaps the sole immaterial living entity. Although its functioning and survival depend upon our biological life, it continues to live independently of us and transforms until the very last moment of our existence—more or less, slowly or swiftly, continuously or gradually. Consequently, through their interaction with one another, our informational systems—composed of coordinated and interconnected ensembles of signifiers and signifieds—remain active and attuned.

A living contemporary example is the written and spoken culture of the Islamic Republic of Iran. We all recall that after the Iran–Iraq War, a book was published titled *Dictionary of the Frontline*. Undoubtedly, the necessity of such a book was felt at the time because, within the wartime sphere, words were used and had gained currency that were not universally intelligible. Another example is the lexicon specific to youth in Europe's major cities, which is not comprehensible to everyone and requires a dedicated dictionary to understand. From the very inception of the Islamic Republic, numerous terms from the spheres of Shiite religious instruction infiltrated the social domain and became entrenched. The Islamic Republic's isolation on the global stage has also contributed to this unilateral narrowing of language and its vocabulary. Across diverse fields—economics, culture, and the humanities—this major problem, resulting from the one-sided growth of the regime's internal culture and its communication apparatuses (such as the administrative bureaucracy, state mass media, newspapers, cinema, Friday prayer sermons, and interviews of officials), has homogenised the culture of the Islamic Republic system and rendered communication with it difficult for those situated outside that sphere.

For instance, in the case of the more than four million Iranians living abroad, quite apart from the necessity of living within the oral and written environment of the host society, the novelty of new terms inside Iran and within the Islamic Republic system further compounds their communicative difficulties. I experienced this problem at first hand during my stay in Cuba last year. Our interpreter from Spanish into Persian was a young Cuban who had completed his university studies in Iran. On several occasions I noticed a divergence between his understanding and mine of one and the same word. Opening up Iran's media, administrative, research, and political spheres is the sole path towards linguistic reconciliation across both sides of the borders. Otherwise, Iranians residing abroad—and especially the second and third generations—will gradually confront the grave problem of linguistic rupture, which is the prelude to cultural rupture.

Our choice to examine and critique this book follows a multi-year endeavour that seeks to cultivate and universalise the role of strategic thought—both conceptually and operationally—across all strata of Iranian society, inside and outside the country, among academic thinkers, politicians, and civil and social activists. Why should the axis of exchanges and discourses not ascend to the strategic level? Why should fundamental premises not receive due attention? Why should alignments not take shape around strategic objectives, the practical outcome of which would be easier, longer-lasting, and more fruitful coalitions in action?

The foremost difficulty in conducting a close reading of the book under review lies precisely in this semantic dispersion and the struggle to ascertain the meanings of the terms employed. One cannot arrive at a sound comprehension of a text—particularly a strategic text—if one is forced to define key terms oneself and deploy them through guesswork. In this book, definitions (concepts—signifieds), which constitute the core elements of a strategic study, are taken for granted as self-evident. As we advance in reading the book, we come to the conclusion that the definitions presented bear little alignment with those found in international strategic literature: terms such as *ārmān* (ideal/vision), *barāyand* (outcome/resultant), human dignity (*kerāmat-e ensāni*), social transcendence (*ta'āli-ye ejtemā'i*), faith-centred human development (*towse'eh-ye ensāni-ye din-mehvar*), and so forth. To dissect this flaw further, let us consider the two signifiers *AIDS* and *SIDA* in English and French. Although the two signifiers are entirely different, it is clear to all, without the slightest ambiguity, that the signified of both is the viral disease HIV.

Or take the two signifiers *NATO* and *OTAN*, behind which everyone immediately places the regional treaty organisation for collective defence among several states. Wherever dialogue and the circulation of words and concepts are free, words are polished, standardised, and effortlessly perform their primary role, which is the transmission of concepts. One of the benefits of international organisations and the efforts of states and nations towards continuous dialogue around matters of common concern is precisely this standardisation of the function of signifiers. And when, in the realm of practice, negotiations extend into the social sphere, cultural rapprochement inevitably ensues.

In 2009, I was invited by UNESCO officials to take part in a round-table on calligraphy. The other speaker was Master Fan Zeng, the Chinese painter, calligrapher, and poet. Prior to our addresses, we endeavoured over two preparatory conversations to harmonise our remarks. Fan Zeng drew my attention to the principle in Chinese culture that the poet, the painter, and the calligrapher are one: one cannot become a calligrapher without attaining the harmony of painting and being versed in the roots of words through poetry. This conversation deepened my acquaintance with the intimate relationship between prehistoric arts and symbolisation. Those arts (dating between 4,000 and 7,000 years before our era) lie at the root of all scripts invented by humankind and paved the way for the earliest visual arts, symbolisation, and the presence and role of signifiers—or words—which are acoustic signs. Undoubtedly, it is through such dialogues that cultures, however rich, emerge from isolation and connect to the chain of humankind's most precious achievement across the millennia: human culture.

Let us return to the book under consideration. On page 805, in a model that may be regarded as the distillation of the book's theoretical–strategic foundations, in response to the question "Which ideal (*ārmān*)?", it states: "human dignity, social transcendence, and the fulfilment of the material and spiritual needs of the individual and society." And in response to "What is the ultimate goal (*hadaf-e nahāyi*)?", it states: "the development of the faith-centred human being." It then defines the dimensions of the ultimate goal as follows: economic, scientific and technological, social, defence–security, and religious–cultural development.

We shall leave the analysis of the model, its methodology, and its efficacy to the next discourse. Drawing upon our understanding of words and the relationships between them, we shall endeavour to arrive at a more precise grasp of these concepts. What can the specific concept of *ārmān* (ideal) mean within a strategic document?

Let us strive towards a shared language. Considering the various meanings of the word *ārmān* in Persian—ideal; *ārmān-shahr* (ideal city), which in Islamic philosophy is termed *Madineh-ye Fāzeleh* (the Virtuous City), an imagined ideal city akin to the ideal utopia of Plato, Thomas More, and others—its equivalents in the technical vocabulary of strategic services in English and French lie close to the term "vision": in a sense, the very vantage point upon which we stand and from which we gaze upon existence; our horizon of sight. What might be meant by "ultimate goal"? The destination we ultimately wish to reach? Is that not itself the ideal society?

Human dignity (*kerāmat-e ensāni*) is likewise interpreted and construed in Persian as human honour, nobility, worthiness, and esteem. Transcendence (*ta'āli*) in our contemporary language signifies elevation and superiority (rising, rising exceedingly high, ascending). From the pairing of "society" and "transcendence", can one infer a society in which superior values prevail? Which raises the question: what are these superior values? Human values according to what definition? Shared universal human values, the foundational values of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, or superior values defined in relation to Islam, Shiism, or the contemporary *Velāyat-e Faqih* interpretation of Shiism? Further on in the content of the ideal, we read: "the fulfilment of the material and spiritual needs of the individual and society." Are these needs defined by the individual or society themselves, or articulated by the elected representatives of the individual or society? If the latter, then in order to arrive at a definition of these needs, the unmediated representatives of the people must articulate them continuously and without prejudice—which is impossible save through elections free of approbatory vetting (*nezārat-e estesvābi*)!

The ultimate goal is "faith-centred human development". Let us take "development" to mean expansion, progress, or both together; and "faith-centred" to mean revolving around religion (read: Twelver Shiism in its *Velāyat-e Motlaqeh-ye Faqih* interpretation), which, summarised, amounts to orienting the human being around the values of Twelver Shiism as construed under the Absolute Guardianship of the Jurist. In a certain sense, the "ultimate goal" is perhaps our mission for attaining the ideal society. If so, let us understand the ultimate goal as that final destination towards which the entire effort of the book's summarised model seeks to carry us.

In any event, let us continue our effort to comprehend the lexicon of the book. If we view it as consisting of two interconnected parts—the ideal (*ārmān*) and the ultimate goal (*hadaf-e nahāyi*), which we equate with the horizon of vision and the ideal towards which we move—we may deduce that what is intended is a human being devoted to Islam, specifically Twelver Shiism under the *Velāyat-e Motlaqeh-ye Faqih* interpretation, living in a society in which all of his needs have been met, for such a society is a superior—transcendent—society, and such a human being possesses dignity. Is this not that very Messianic society of the Hidden Imam (*Imām-e Zamān*) onto which an attempt has been made, through words and phrasing, to impart the hue and flavour of the literature of sociology, management, and strategic services?

In subsequent writings, we shall endeavour to explore further the methodology and models of the book.

Hassan Makaremi
