en.title: The Necessity of Rewriting the History of Iran for Iranians
en.executive_summary: https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/02/11.jpg Read on Gooya Historians align the continuity of historical and cultural events with words in use and with the growth and transformation of those words, employing etymology as an instrument alongside archaeological excavations, archival documentation,…
en.body_markdown:
https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/02/11.jpg

[Read on Gooya](http://news.gooya.com/politics/archives/2014/01/174426print.php)

Historians align the continuity of historical and cultural events with words in use and with the growth and transformation of those words, employing etymology as an instrument alongside archaeological excavations, archival documentation, mythological analysis, and the like. On the other hand, a close scrutiny of the discourse of historians familiarises us with the manner of collective and popular development and, perhaps, with a people's historical wounds. Our endeavour in this essay is to open a window onto this mutual influence through several brief inquiries and examples which are, without doubt, neither exhaustive nor exclusive.

Summary: The rich and ancient history of the land of Iran, with all the varied events that have passed over it through the unceasing efforts of the peoples of this land — both before and after the arrival of the Aryans, both prior to the invasions of the Arabs, Mongols, and Timurids and following those onslaughts — still has a long road ahead before it is fully and scientifically understood. The history of the cultural growth and progress of a land's inhabitants is accompanied, on the one hand, by their daily struggle for survival and well-being, and, on the other, by their intermingling with neighbouring cultures through migrations, wars, victories, subjugations, and conquests. This struggle and cultural cross-pollination leave their footprints in language, culture, oral history, customs, and dialects, emerging across the centuries and millennia.

The individual unconscious, as defined by clinical psychoanalysis, consists of a person's accumulated memories, structured like a language; and through the words of each individual's speech, the individual unconscious makes itself known. This insight may be extended to the scale of a nation: one may say that the collective memory of a land's inhabitants is condensed within the speech and traditions of the people of that realm.

Listening closely to historians — those who have observed the struggles of a land's inhabitants at close quarters and followed their movements — serves as a bridge towards uncovering hidden secrets, the concealed secrets buried within the collective memories of the peoples of this land. This reciprocal interplay of mutual influence is extraordinarily fertile and gives rise to a new mode of historiography.

Historians align the continuity of historical and cultural events with words in use and with the growth and transformation of those words, employing etymology as an instrument alongside archaeological excavations, archival documentation, mythological analysis, and the like. On the other hand, a close scrutiny of the discourse of historians familiarises us with the manner of collective and popular development and, perhaps, with a people's historical wounds.

Our endeavour in this essay is to open a window onto this mutual influence through several brief inquiries and examples which are, without doubt, neither exhaustive nor exclusive.

Preface: In this essay, we shall not touch upon the various schools of historiography, whether classified by their mode of viewing the human story or by the methods and instruments they employ — especially given that, following the theories of Michel Foucault since the 1970s, an objective and independent knowledge of history, free from the intervention of its authors, has been called into question. History is the story of human beings who have lived within their biological and geographical milieu and, in doing so, have acted upon themselves and their surroundings, organised their collective life, witnessed institutions act upon one another, and, through these interactions with the surrounding environment, seen both collective organisation and the individual transformed.

History, in the sense used in this essay, rests upon the following diverse foundations:
- Mythological and legendary history
- History concealed within popular dialects and vernacular speech
- History embedded in literature, poetry, song, art, and culture
- History gleaned from travelogues, notebooks, and memoirs
- History grounded in ancient texts

These are the interconnected and inseparable foundations of history. Conversely, history may also be structured around its diverse branches, such as the social, economic, scientific, cultural, political, ideological, religious, and others.

Before entering the subject proper, let us cast a glance at the sources and origins of contemporary Iranians' knowledge of their history and past:
- Family culture: what reaches us from generation to generation through the family via tales, proverbs, and diverse dialects as the story of our ancestors, forming the earliest foundations of our historical awareness.
- School culture: at all levels, from primary school to university. In the present century, this "school historical culture" has attained a remarkable uniformity and become deeply etched into our collective memory.
- The culture of the mosque and Islamic religious seminaries (Shi'i, Sunni) as well as other religions of Iran: this culture, insofar as it concerns Muslims and Shi'ites, is confined within the closed circle of the Arabian Peninsula and present-day Iraq during the first and second centuries of the Hijra. Time and space possess their own distinctive character within this culture. Historical figures therein enjoy an intermediate existence (half-dream, half-reality). For Shi'ites, this characteristic is clearly observable particularly in the lives of the Prophet, the Imams, and their companions, as well as in the historical literature.
- The culture of the mass media — newspapers, radio, television, cinema, and so forth: although over the past century these have been subjected to narrow-mindedness, censorship, self-censorship, and various forms of control, one can nevertheless trace the transmission of historical knowledge through their overall functioning. The aim of those steering these media appears to be to keep the social atmosphere calm and stagnant so that, by muddling through, they neither offend public opinion nor clash with the authorities of the state, official religion, or the general structure of society.

Let us also look at the roots of the historical knowledge held by the people of Iran today. In this survey, we categorise them as follows:
1. The efforts of Iranian historians in editing, publishing, and abridging past texts in various Iranian languages, Pahlavi, Arabic, and others, and drawing upon this knowledge.
2. The translation of works by non-Iranian scholars and historians:
- The West (Europe and America), which accounts for the principal and foundational share of these translations.
- The Eastern Bloc, translated either directly from Russian and Eastern European languages or into Persian via French, English, and German texts.
- Classical sources from the Greek and Roman eras, which have essentially reached us through modern European languages.
3. The collection of folklore and popular culture — an endeavour initiated by the late Dehkhoda and carried forward by eminent figures such as Enjavi Shirazi, Ahmad Shamlu, and others.
4. The interpretation, examination, and comparative reading of ancient Iranian and Arabic texts using modern historiographical hypotheses, such as Marxist, sociological, psychoanalytical, and historical interpretations, among others.
5. Finally, the efforts of Iranian researchers in assembling documents and sources across the four categories enumerated above and composing general histories — whether comprehensive or specialised, regional or chronological (such as *Social History of Iran* by Ravandi, *History of Ancient Iran* by Hassan Pirnia, and the like).

Challenges of Historiography
With this introduction, we are ready to cast a fresh gaze upon the challenges facing contemporary Iranian historiography:
1. Perhaps the most fundamental and conspicuous of all challenges is the penetration of a religious—and specifically Islamic-Shi'i—outlook into the early historiography of the modern era. The historians who compiled textbooks at various levels, from primary schools to universities, were themselves educated in Quranic *maktab* schools, and—wittingly or unwittingly—the influence of Shi'ism and its particular historical perspective was implanted in the very depths of their souls. On the other hand, official school historians could not write and teach an accurate and genuine history, because a degree of harmony had to be maintained across the texts of different subjects such as religious instruction, religious education, the Quran, and so forth within the textbook curriculum. Just as a dry history detached from the culture, beliefs, and traditions of the people fails, by virtue of its separation from everyday life, to acquaint the reader with his own past, so too a history that conceals the realities of events behind traditional and religious beliefs cannot be called history. Examples abound:
- In official history, insofar as possible, no mention is made of the sectarian affiliation of Iran's great figures of science, literature, and art prior to the Safavid era, lest one fall into the Sunni–Shi'i dichotomy; consequently, the people of Iran today do not properly know whether their forefathers six centuries ago were Shafi'i, Hanbali, or otherwise.
- Reference to the burning of books by the Arabs during their invasion of Iran, the scale of those books, and the reason for that book-burning have been kept behind a veil. In many historical texts, the use of the concept of 'invasion' is somehow avoided altogether.
In the preface to *Iran: Bridge of Turquoise* (1), written by Seyyed Hossein Nasr, we read: '...until the period of the migration of the Aryan tribes and the dawn of a new era on the Iranian plateau, and then the foundation of the first imperial order in the world by Cyrus the Great, and the emergence and spread of the Zoroastrian religion in Iran, and afterwards the invasion of Alexander, and then the revival of national life during the Parthian era and the return to the institutions of the Achaemenid era under the Sasanians, and finally the acceptance of the religion of Islam and the dawn of the radiant Islamic era, which in a short span of time transformed Iran into one of the loftiest and most prestigious cultural centres of the world, and the vicissitudes of subsequent centuries such as the incursions of the Turks and the invasion of the Mongols, followed by the revival of national government by the Safavid dynasty...' How is it that for this scholar, the invasion of Alexander, the incursions of the Turks, and the invasion of the Mongols are acknowledged as invasions, while in place of the Arab invasion he cleverly speaks of the 'acceptance of the religion of Islam' and calls the Safavids the founders of national government?
We know that the first individuals who laid the foundations of modern schools and universities in Iran in the early twentieth century had largely acquired their learning in theological seminaries (*hawzahs*) or environments affiliated with them, and it was these very figures who became the founders of Iran's official historiography textbooks. Fortunately, Ms Simin Fasihi, in her research work published as a book entitled *Main Currents of Historiography in the Pahlavi Period* (2), has pointed out many of the problems of contemporary historiography; one may consult this book in particular for a precise understanding of the earliest historians and history instructors following the emergence of the modern educational system at the beginning of the twentieth century in Iran. The cultural-historical geography of those who, from childhood, began reading and writing in Arabic and were shaped by teachers whose bedside books were *Hilyat al-Muttaqin* and *Bihar al-Anwar* cannot undergo a total transformation within a single generation, and such scholars carry their foundational knowledge within themselves. This cultural-historical space begins at the dawn of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula and continues, in a suspended geography outside physical space, down to the Eleventh Imam. In this mode of historiography, documentary evidence, exact dates of events, the identity of the narrator, and cause-and-effect relationships are exceedingly faint. Expressions such as 'the narrator says', 'I heard', 'it has been related', 'in that province', and 'in that realm' take the place of names, dates, and the concrete manner in which events unfolded. Let us cite an example from the book *Kashkul-e Tabasi (Useful Knowledge)* (3): in the miscellany section of this respected Khorasan preacher, under the heading 'A Woman Who Gave Birth to Forty Twins', he quotes the following from *Nuzhat al-Jalis* authored by Sayyid Abbas Makki (Najaf edition): 'Salih ibn Abi al-Rijal was regarded as one of the renowned judges of his time. His offspring consisted of a single son... Through the bite of a snake, the aforesaid child perished... The wife... addressed her husband, saying: "Know that this child was with us as a trust from God, and today God has reclaimed His trust from us. Now we must not show impatience..." Not long after this incident, the woman conceived by her husband, and at the time of her delivery a sac emerged from her. When they opened the sac, to their utter astonishment it was observed that forty infants were nestled within that sac, each of those children measuring one span (*vajab*) in length. Within a short interval, by divine command, the aforesaid children grew to the size of nursing infants... After some time had passed, all of them were counted among the great scholars of their age... On this account their father was given the epithet Abi al-Rijal [Father of Men]... In that land and territory there is not the slightest doubt or uncertainty concerning the truth of this matter.' This imaginary historical-geographical space is such that neither the narrator, nor the author, nor the readers and listeners of these accounts ever ask themselves: which province, on what date—to say nothing of the logical coherence of forty twins or a length of one span.
The oral history of Persian-speaking Shi'ites has rarely been committed to writing. Yet what can be inferred from the written texts that have come down to us—whether Safavid-era texts such as Majlesi's *Bihar al-Anwar* or recent writings such as the works of Dastgheib made accessible to the public—is predominantly historical events occurring outside time and space. History has stepped beyond the geographical boundaries of its earthly occurrence and turned into events situated between dream and waking, between that world and this world. It is as though myths have returned once more, for the logic of events, like a dream, obeys no physical, temporal, or real-world factor. In these texts, the narrator is always an absent presence: the narrator recounts the tale, yet there is no sign of his physical presence. At times, the narrator begins with a historical incident and links its continuation to dream and fantasy.
This mode of discourse can be observed in the phenomenon of Sheikh Ahmad Kafi—one of the celebrated lamentation preachers (*rowzeh-khan*) of the years 1976–1978 (1355–1357)—and in his recorded cassette tapes, showing how from atop the pulpit, for Shi'ites prepared to mourn, he would 'telephone' Karbala, ask the narrator moment by moment how events were unfolding, and reconstruct them with cries and shouts for his eager listeners—so vividly that in their belief the people would suddenly visualise the narrator alive in the desert of Karbala with a telephone receiver in his hand.
What is referred to as the 'realist endeavour' of the new wave of Shi'i thinkers—rooted in the writings of Jalal Al-e Ahmad, Ali Shariati, and others—is not exempt from this problem either. Without attending to the historical foundation of events or the presence, sequence, and causality of Islamic and Shi'i historical occurrences, these thinkers focused chiefly on 'ideological systems or worldviews', and their primary aim was to forge a reconciliation between their traditional-doctrinal worlds and their perceptions of contemporary knowledge and understanding of the modern world. These writings rest upon two pillars: first, that there is nothing of value in the West, and second, that we must rediscover ourselves. In the short term, such outlooks apply a balm to the historical-cultural wounds of those seeking immediate relief from their suffering. From the words and deeds of a single century of one household—from the Prophet down to the Eleventh Imam—and from narrations near and far, real and imaginary, one cannot construct a system of thought and a structure of historical change capable of answering the ontological and worldview needs of those who thirst for meaning. Although such efforts respond at the initial step to the pressing need of thoughtful people searching for something 'beyond', they soon collapse back into a historical void.
2. The influence of Western historiography: a mode of historiography founded upon documents, archival records, tangible historical findings, and archaeological excavations. Such historians do not know the Persian language, are remote from the culture of the street and the bazaar, do not know Persian writings, tales, poetry, and Iranian myths, and have no familiarity with the inner core and depth of Iranian culture; for this very reason, their historiography is dry and devoid of human cultural colour and fragrance. Examples abound: the uncritical repetition of statements by figures such as Herodotus by Western historians, or the failure to grasp differences between sects and intellectual currents, the conflation of the concepts of Muslims and Arabs, the failure to understand the question of *taqiyya* (dissimulation) in Shi'ism, and so forth.
3. The influence of Eastern Bloc historiography: reliance upon modes of production and placing modes, instruments, and relations of production at the centre; primary focus on economic history; and concentration on the physical, bodily, and material pain and suffering of human beings as well as the oppression of landlords and state and religious potentates have kept these historians distant from how culture is formed and from an understanding of cultural civilisation. Consequently, they pay scant attention to language as the foundation of cultural structure and the individual unconscious, and pay little heed to cultural boundaries, difficulties, and differences, or to the formation of these cultures through the intermingling of cultures.
4. Official school historiography: apart from the problem rooted in the *maktab*-school culture of the founders of our modern educational culture at the beginning of the twentieth century—such as Malek o-Sho'ara Bahar, Mohammad Ali Foroughi, Jalal al-Din Homaei, and others—the direct and indirect pressure of politics and religion across various periods of the past century has brought school history textbooks under its sway.
- During the Pahlavi era, a highly superficial and rudimentary return to the pre-Islamic era combined with a very simplistic Westernisation—resting on the twin pillars of the monarchical system on the one hand and the imitation of Western modes of production and living on the other—generated a form of cultural resistance among the people.
- In the post-revolutionary era, one-sidedness and Shi'ism-centrism took hold to such a degree that the concepts of nation, national culture, the Persian language, literature, art, and the cultural past were subordinated to Shi'i unity—and of its militant variety at that. According to an account in one of the journals published in Iran (4): 'Today, contemporary Iranian history is reduced to three things: the Constitutional Revolution and the leadership of Sheikh Fazlollah Nuri, the Oil Nationalisation Movement and the leadership of Kashani, and the Islamic Revolution and the historical roots of the 1357 [1979] Revolution traced back to 15 Khordad 1342 [June 1963]—and even that monopolised by a particular faction.'
5. The impact of these types of historical outlooks is such that it casts us into the arms of futile extremes: unbridled pride in the culture and grandeur of the ancient empire; efforts to 'purify' the Persian language and purge non-Persian words, especially Arabic ones; the excessive revival of forgotten cultures and traditions; 'returning to one's authentic self' while closing one's eyes to the shifting, dynamic world around us; inventing concepts such as 'Westoxication' (*gharbzadegi*) and substituting a brand of Islam and Shi'ism for modern, contemporary sociological concepts; excessive devotion to economic historiography while consigning cultural life to oblivion; and extreme ethno-centrism—Kurdish, Baluch, Turkish. Elevating any one of these concepts in an abstract, isolated form is the outcome of failing to view all of these concepts comprehensively within the historical life of a nation.
It will not be out of place to cite a few books, very briefly, as examples of what has been set out above:
Example 1: A work entitled *The Military Campaign of Alexander of Macedon into Iran and India Is History's Greatest Lie* (5). The scholar's endeavour therein is to demonstrate that 'the delusion of all chroniclers of the Alexander romance, Alexander scholars, admirers of Alexander, and their Westoxicated followers lies in having mistaken the *Hend* of southern Khuzestan for India (*Hendustan*). This delusion afflicts...' In the preface, the scholar alludes in a telling manner to the motive behind his research: 'Wounds inflicted upon the human body heal after a time and are forgotten. Historical wounds inflicted upon the body of a nation grow ever more painful the older they become.'
As we have stated, our purpose here is not to debate the validity or accuracy of such writings; what matters is that the scholar speaks of a historical wound and sees its remedy in declaring one of the historical invasions of Iran to be, from start to finish, a sheer fabrication.
Example 2: A work entitled *In the Darkness of the Millennia* (5 [6]) by the late Iraj Eskandari. First, it is highly intriguing how one of the founders, intellectuals, and history-makers of this century in Iran undertook a profound study of Iranian history, particularly the period prior to the formation of the first great Achaemenid state; and how he strove, drawing upon mythological history, Avestan culture, and the works of historians from Eastern and Western European countries, to answer the following fundamental question: 'For instance, it merits close attention why the village communes (*communes*) of Iran, in the course of their evolution, did not arrive at that form of property which emerged in classical Greece and Rome and paved the way for the generalisation and predominance of the slave system in production—and fundamentally, what factors caused Iran's class society, of which state formation is the most prominent expression, not to rest upon a mode of production akin to the slave-owning society of ancient "Greece and Rome", even from the period when vast, centralised states such as the Achaemenid, Parthian, and Sasanian empires consolidated? If such be the case—and indeed it is—then the question immediately arises: "Upon what factors and what contradictions did the state in Iran emerge and evolve? Upon which class or classes did the primary burden of exploitation predominantly fall in this society, and in what manner and under what forms was the exploitation of human by human exercised?"' The scholar notes that his aim is not model-building. Yet, after all his investigations, on the final pages of his text he returns to that very initial hypothesis and draws out the same 'if such be the case, all the more so is it thus': 'As has been seen, this definition accords with the socio-economic structure of Elam—the particular form that emerged in that society from the intermingling of the relations of production of primitive classless society with the exploitative and domineering relations of production of class society—and therefore entitles us to regard Elamite society as one of the oldest examples of the Asiatic mode of production.'
Although the scholar possesses the answer to his question from the very outset, in his historiographical method he is highly advanced and balanced. Because he is thoroughly conversant with Iran's language and literature, he is able to extract from the mythological verses of Ferdowsi's *Shahnameh* evidence of modes of production and the presence of early human beings (Neanderthals) in the Iranian lands prior to the arrival of the Aryans:
'Ferdowsi, the great national poet of Iran, expressed this transformation in primitive life in a manner which, though not strictly conforming to literal reality, nevertheless illustrates the successive stages of these changes in the living conditions of the people:

First, a wondrous jewel came within reach,
Through knowledge, he separated iron from stone.

He made molten iron his prime resource,
Which he drew forth from the granite rock.

Once he knew it, he took up the blacksmith's craft,
From which he fashioned axe, saw, and adze.

When awakened humanity added further thereto,
The scattering of seed, tilling, and reaping;

Each person then weighed his own bread,
Laboured, and came to know his proper measure.

Before these arts were marshalled and prepared,
There was no food whatsoever save fruit;

The people's whole affair was clad in leaves,
For all their raiment consisted of leaves.' (6)

Example 3: *History of the Ancient Peoples of Western Asia from the Beginning to the Rise of the Persians*, written by Ahmad Bahmanesh (7):
As the author states, the book was written for university students. In the preface we read: 'Those who deal with history are well aware how obscure and dark the history of the "ancient peoples of the East"—the peoples who founded present-day world civilisation—remained until recently. The sources providing information on this matter were confined to the writings of Greek historians and the Torah, all of which were incomplete and of a legendary or religious character; however, from the day foreign scholars began conducting excavations in Mesopotamia, the fragility and inaccuracy of the ancient historians' accounts were proven.' A brief glance at the bibliography and list of sources of this book suffices to reveal that our historian reads overwhelmingly and exclusively from a single side of historiography: out of 46 sources, 43 are French works published between 1860 and 1953.
Before turning to outline and examine our proposal regarding the rewriting of the history of Iranians for Iranians, it is necessary to address the concept of the historical-cultural wound and its effects. For our people's historical understanding can take shape only in the light of a comprehensive externalisation of diverse, abstract preconceptions and presuppositions.
I owe the concept of the historical wound to Surajprasad Naipaul [V. S. Naipaul], and in particular to his book *Beyond Belief* (8).
What in clinical psychoanalysis is termed psychic trauma or psychological shock (*Traumatisme*, from the Greek word *Trauma*, meaning 'wound') can, in a certain sense, be applied to the ethno-historical memory of a people rooted in a shared culture. Psychic trauma is an unpleasant event that plants its roots in the unconscious and lays the groundwork for psychological difficulties, disorders, and disturbances. Although the structure of the unconscious assumes its general form in childhood itself, psychic trauma can implant its poison into the stability and functioning of the unconscious. In the course of psychoanalysis, by recalling and reconstructing the origins that generated psychic wounds, the individual gradually unties the knot woven around the wound. Retelling the event, speaking about it, and repeating and reconstructing the scenes associated with the incident are all effective in unravelling the knot of psychic trauma. It is not for nothing that in everyday life human beings naturally recount distressing events over and over again, dissecting them each time in a new language and from a fresh angle; and it is for this very reason that in mourning rituals, at fixed intervals—three days, one week, one month, forty days, four months and ten days, and one year—people gather together to speak of the loss of a loved one. The intervals between these gatherings gradually lengthen so that the raw freshness of the wound may slowly grow old.
Historical and cultural wounds upon the cultural body of a people behave in the very same way. The sole remedy lies in retelling and opening up these wounds. These wounds are carried within themselves and in their core across culture and language. As regards the culture of the people of the Iranian land, probing the roots of these ethnic and cultural wounds, laying them bare, dissecting and exploring them, and recovering the effects of these wounds will render immense assistance to our cultural self-knowledge.
To clarify our statement, let us dissect together a passage from the writings of one of Iran's contemporary thinkers. Mohammad Ali Eslami Nodooshan, in an essay entitled *Let Us Not Forget Iran* (11 [10]), writes:
'I have a feeling in the depths of my conscience, like a pleasant yet indistinct testimony that passes from time to time through the heart, and it is this: that Iran's mission has not come to an end, and that her splendour and vitality will return to her. I am certain that Iran can stand tall, become a renowned, beautiful, and prosperous country, and, as befits her civilisation, culture, and antiquity, teach many things to the world.'
Regarding a feeling in the depths of one's conscience as a sign emanating from within the unconscious is scarcely far off the mark. Further on, he writes:
'Iran is a wondrous land. Her history is peerless in its colourfulness and diversity. The greatest men and the basest men have been nurtured in this soil and water; the events that have befallen her are such as befit a chosen and great nation: she has known brilliant conquests and shameful defeats, countless calamities and countless triumphs. It is as though fate has tested all its calamities and games upon Iran.' (11)
In this passage, are the words 'calamities and games' that have befallen Iran not, in a sense, an expression of grief over cultural-historical wounds? Here, the discourse concerns another form of mourning; a few lines further, we read:
'Despite bitter disappointments, we have the right to take pride in our country; our backs have bent beneath the weight of history, yet this very history gives us strength and keeps us from collapsing... Tragedy has always been worthy of great destinies.' (11)
What the author refers to as the bending of our backs beneath the weight of history, we term the historical-cultural wound.
A brief dissection of this passage—which is the heartfelt ache and the inner, hidden, secret longing of a cultured son of this people—reveals how this knotted conviction and this congealed heart's blood stand ready to burst open.
Shams Tabrizi expressed this state beautifully in his *Maqalat*:
'The Sheikh said: The Caliph forbade the performance of *sama'* [mystical audition and dance]. A dervish developed a knot inside himself and fell ill. They brought a skilled physician. He took his pulse; he found none of the ailments or causes he had studied. The dervish passed away. The physician cut open his grave and his chest and extracted the knot. It was like carnelian. In a time of need he sold it. It passed from hand to hand until it reached the Caliph. The Caliph had it set as the stone of a signet ring. He wore it on his ring; one day during a *sama'* gathering, he glanced down. He saw his robe stained with blood! When he looked closely, he saw no wound... He saw the ring-stone melted.' (9)
Such heart's blood, knotted across diverse historical-cultural wounds, must be poured out once and for all, openly and without a veil. The Arab invasion of Iran may be regarded as the fundamental witness to this collective wound. For this wound did not merely shatter the people's political, social, and governmental foundations; it penetrated to the very depths of religious convictions, beliefs, everyday life, script, and writing (the modes of production, commodity exchange, buying and selling remained untouched, since in that respect the Arabs had no 'gift' to offer Iranians!). From this vantage point, the Arab invasion of Iran far surpassed the invasions of the Mongols and the Timurids. It is along this trajectory, and in the aftermath of this invasion, that the 'Two Centuries of Silence' are born—the astonishing collective silence of a people who remain unaware of what has transpired upon them. In untying this complex, innumerable questions lie before us:
- How did the cultural and mythological intermingling of Iranians before and after Islam take place, and among the cultural beliefs of today's inhabitants of this land, which portion pertains to the period before this invasion and which portion to the period after it?
Let us cite a few examples. Figures and numbers that have found a secure place in popular belief without leaving any trace in the culture and beliefs of early Islam—such as the 124,000 prophets, or the tiers, houses, and chambers of Hell, of which we offer a mere drop from the ocean out of Mullah Mohammad Baqer Majlesi's *Haqq al-Yaqin*:
'...Hell has seven tiers: *Jahannam*, *Sa'ir*, *Saqar*, *Jahim*, *Laza*, *Hutamah*, and *Hawiyah*. The drink of Hell is scalding *hamim* and tar, and its food is *zaqqum*. Scalding *hamim* consists of pus and suppuration. This scalding *hamim* is such that if a single drop of it were mixed with the water of this world, all the inhabitants of the earth would perish from its stench. In Hell there is a valley wherein lie seventy thousand houses, and in each house seventy thousand chambers, and in each chamber a thousand black vipers, and in the belly of each viper seventy thousand jars of venom. The intensity of the heat of Hellfire is seventy degrees greater than the fire of this world... Upon the feet of each inhabitant of Hell are fiery sandals, from the intensity of whose heat their brains boil inside their skulls.'
- How were the cultural, political, social, and mythological figures of Iranians born and how were they fused together—examples such as Rostam Dastan and Ali ibn Abi Talib, Siyavash and Husayn ibn Ali...
- The emergence and spread of mysticism (*erfan*) and Sufism (*tasavvof*): the various schools, *madrasahs*, and *khanaqahs*, and their relationship to historical-cultural wounds.
Rewriting, tracing the roots of, and meticulously analysing all these events is, on the one hand, essential for the cultural standing-tall of the generations of the Iranian people, and, on the other hand, an exceedingly arduous task requiring comprehensive and knowledgeable historians. Healing such historical-cultural wounds, like psychoanalysis, lies in their accurate historical retelling.
Although equating the destiny of an individual human being with the cultural destiny of a nation departs from scientific caution, as a clinical psychoanalyst I cannot pass over such abundant resemblance and correspondence without comment. Restoring the health of the Iranian people's collective memory becomes possible by tracing the roots of their wounds and pains on the one hand, and by restoring the health of the space in which this people attains historical and cultural self-knowledge on the other.
- Where do the roots of mourning-worship (*sug-parvari*), martyrdom-cult (*shahid-navazi*), hero-worship, and the culture of dissimulation, *ta'arof* [ritualised politeness], and flattery lie?
- From which cultural-historical events do the roots of excessive hatred and affection toward the Arabs on the one hand and contemporary Western culture on the other, as well as destructive grandiosity and aberrant self-belittlement, draw their nourishment?

Proposal: Far from claiming that this set of proposals is either entirely feasible or exhaustive, we set them out very briefly:
- Translation of documented and scholarly histories written in various languages, accompanied by analysis, critique, and illuminating commentary.
- Reprinting of rare historical manuscripts with explanation, elucidation, commentary, and critique.
- Collection of historical narratives, tales, and stories within the culture of the Iranian people today; tracing the roots of these tales, and analysing, recording, and linking them to cultural-historical events.
- Rewriting the history of Islam and the Imams in a comprehensive, rigorous, and unprejudiced manner, recognising that in contemporary Shi'i oral history, history has been presented in a distorted form severed from physical space and time.
- Critiquing, annotating, and reviewing historical books written in the twentieth century across different eras, refining them, and rendering them scholarly.
- Historical cultural lexicography in the fields of art, architecture, technology, literature, and so forth, in such a way that the roots of changes and transformations in each domain and their connection to historical events are clarified. A particularly striking example in this regard is the study of the architecture of sacred sites before and after Islam.
- Impartial examination of the historical-cultural movements of the Iranian people with due attention to the relations of these movements with other nations of the region. Today, regional history has been interpreted to an extraordinary degree across different countries through diverse nationalist readings and interpretations, to such an extent that Nader Shah Afshar is presented in Iranian, Afghan, and Tajik history textbooks as Iranian, Afghan, and Tajik respectively.
- Fostering widespread dialogue in cultural and historical spheres. How is it possible for peoples who live side by side to inhabit each their own separate geographical-historical-cultural world? Without opening up language and speech, and without the freedom to reconstruct, retell, and engage in dialogue, the inhabitants of each world render their own world ever more closed. The historical wound has brought it about that diverse cultures live alongside one another without encountering one another, each regarding the other's presence as an 'existent non-existent'.
A nation can live in peace when, apart from territory, state, flag, and unified borders, it is nourished by a harmonious and cohesive cultural memory. What generates instabilities, maladies, disorders, and various forms of unrest in the psyche of an individual human being is rooted in contradictions arising from psychic trauma experienced during their lifetime. Psychic traumas build a resistant core around themselves that enables the individual to endure the memory of the trauma and somehow render the event bearable.
In short, the deep and deeply rooted history of the people of the Iranian land—embedded in language, dialect, culture, and everyday life—has carried within its riverbed all bitter and sweet, small and great events from distant ages down to the present day. An exact, impartial, documentary, and meticulous knowledge of this history—free from exaggeration, understatement, partisan tastes, and imaginary presuppositions—can establish the necessary harmony and coherence between the socio-economic life of the inhabitants of this land and their cultural, doctrinal, and traditional life. This harmony will better prepare us in today's world for humane coexistence among diverse cultural, religious, and ethno-linguistic groups inside Iran and with neighbouring nations.
Any one-sided endeavour—whether by magnifying one or several historical-cultural events, omitting portions of this history, or erroneously interpreting and substituting events and occurrences—will end in failure.
It seems that the only path is that same persistent, patient, and dignified listening to the cultural murmur of human beings who, even after several thousand years, have distilled light, fire, love, affection, and reconciliation into the words *mehr* [love/sun] and *mehrabani* [kindness].

Hassan Makaremi

-------------------------
Bibliography and Sources

1. Betty Roloff: *Iran: Bridge of Turquoise*, 1978 edition, Ministry of Information and Tourism.
2. *Main Currents of Historiography in the Pahlavi Period*, Simin Fasihi, Navand Publishing, 1372 [1993–1994], Mashhad http://www.takbook.com/Content/838
3. Tabasi Haeri, Sayyid Ali-Naqi: *Kashkul-e Tabasi*, 4th printing, Roshdiyeh Press, 1352 [1973–1974], Tehran.
4. *Iran-e Farda* journal, Tir 1375 [June–July 1996], article 'History-Making for a Nation Without Memory'.
5. Hami, Ahmad: *The Military Campaign of Alexander*, 2nd printing, 1362 [1983–1984], Davarpanah Press.
6. Eskandari, Iraj: *In the Darkness of the Millennia*, 1984 edition, published abroad.
7. Bahmanesh, Ahmad: *History of the Ancient Peoples of Western Asia*, University of Tehran Press, 1339 [1960–1961].
8. NAIPAUL Surajprasad: *Jusqu'au bout de la foi*, traduit de l'anglais par Philippe Delmare, Plon, 390 p.
Naipaul is a writer of Indian origin who has lived in England since the 1950s. In 1979, for the first time, he travelled for seven months to Malaysia, Indonesia, Pakistan, and Iran and turned the account of his journey into a book. Between 1990 and 1991 he repeated the journey for six months, placing greater emphasis this time on his conversations with ordinary people in the streets and bazaars so as better to 'understand the neurosis of people forcibly converted to another religion', presenting the synthesis in *Beyond Belief*. Quoted from *Libération*, Thursday, 17 May 1998.
9. Tabrizi, Shams al-Din Mohammad: *Maqalat*, edited by Ahmad Khoshnevis, Matbu'ati-ye Ataei, Tehran, 1349 [1970–1971].
10. Eslami Nodooshan, Mohammad: *Let Us Not Forget Iran*, collected essays, Tus Publishing, Tehran, Bahman 134[?].

fr.body_markdown:
Ordibehesht 1394 (avril-mai 2015)

[Lire sur Gooya](http://news.gooya.com/politics/archives/2015/05/196736.php)

Monsieur Ganji, à qui vous adressez-vous ? — Hassan Makaremi

« L'invention d'un islam démocratique » dépend du socle traditionnel et des conditions sociales des idées dominantes de chaque société, et se doit d'être dynamique et actuel. Le problème fondamental et structurel qui règne sur l'espace de pensée de nombre de clercs chiites réside dans leur résistance face à une loi codifiée, cohérente, applicable partout et pour tous, sans exception et non soumise à l'arbitraire des fatwas. Dans son récent article intitulé « La nécessité d'inventer un islam démocratique », publié dans le journal anglophone *Huffington Post* (repris par *Gooya News*, mardi 1er Ordibehesht 1394 / 21 avril 2015)¹, M. Akbar Ganji conclut ainsi : « Si des individus et des groupes considèrent la paix, la liberté et les droits humains comme des idéaux majeurs, ils ont le devoir moral de défendre l'invention d'un islam démocratique. » Fort de près de trois décennies d'engagement pour l'application de la Déclaration universelle des droits de l'homme aux côtés de compagnons proches et lointains, je me considère comme destinataire de ce message et je l'accueille favorablement ; permettez-moi cependant de l'analyser plus avant et d'en éclairer les conditions de coopération.

Si telle est notre voie de salut et si, par cette démarche, nous pouvons contraindre les détenteurs du pouvoir au sein de la société iranienne à respecter les droits humains, M. Ganji a pleinement raison : défendre un islam démocratique n'est pas seulement un devoir moral, mais bien un devoir fondamental des défenseurs des droits humains. Mais qu'est-ce que cet « islam démocratique » inventé par M. Ganji, et comment sa défense peut-elle prendre corps dans la réalité ?

Il est exact que, sous un regard scientifique, ethnologique et anthropologique, et en tirant parti de ce que Michel Foucault a nommé l'« archéologie du savoir », l'être humain a lui-même inventé, élaboré et, plus simplement, créé la culture — cela au fil de centaines de milliers d'années, et après l'avènement de la symbolisation. Il est également exact qu'il a engendré, au cours de cette longue durée, l'ensemble des religions, croyances, traditions, coutumes, convictions, prescriptions et interdits comme autant de sous-ensembles de cet accomplissement culturel. Si nous admettons ce principe, nous constatons qu'au cours de cet immense effort multiséculaire — voire multimillénaire —, l'humanité n'a jamais procédé à la réinvention pure et simple d'une tradition, d'une religion ou d'une pensée ; elle a toujours, par l'exégèse, l'interprétation et l'innovation au sein des fondements religieux et traditionnels, frayé la voie à l'adaptation de l'existence au réel.

Dès lors, la question est de savoir ce qu'est l'« islam démocratique » et comment contribuer à son émergence et à sa diffusion. Je rejoins M. Ganji lorsqu'il écrit que plus d'un milliard et demi d'habitants de notre planète vivent dans des pays que nous qualifions, en raison de leur majorité musulmane, de pays islamiques. Mais il convient de garder à l'esprit que l'islam, selon son histoire, les modalités de sa propagation et les cultures qui prévalaient avant lui sur de si vastes territoires, présente une grande diversité d'interprétations, d'exégèses, de traditions d'application et de modes de gouvernement. Au fil d'une si longue temporalité et dans un espace d'une telle ampleur, un tel islam a développé cinq champs et dimensions, colorant la géographie humaine d'un tel monde, et déposant au cours de ces quatorze siècles, au sein de sociétés et de couches sociales variées ainsi que dans les diverses sphères de la vie individuelle et collective, d'abondants sédiments.

— La dimension traditionnelle de l'islam, c'est-à-dire ce qui touche au quotidien des populations : le droit civil et pénal, les divers rituels du mariage et du divorce, les relations commerciales et les échanges, les liens familiaux et sociaux, les croyances et représentations intégrées à la vie de tous les jours, telles que l'interprétation des songes, les vœux pieux, etc. Ces traditions forment une synthèse entre ce qui existait dans la culture des peuples avant l'islam et les coutumes, comportements et discours ultérieurement adoptés. Toutes se sont renouvelées au fil des siècles et se sont transformées avec le progrès de la science et de la technique, à l'instar de tout organisme vivant engagé dans la lutte pour la survie.

— L'islam dans le domaine de la sociologie, de l'anthropologie, de l'histoire culturelle, de l'histoire des religions, de l'histoire des idées et de son évolution : l'étude et l'exploration approfondie de l'islam dans ses multiples nuances selon les méthodes scientifiques reconnues, sur la base des documents et preuves disponibles, conformément aux usages académiques. Appelons « islam scientifique » le dialogue autour des méthodes et des instruments de recherche, la publication des résultats de ces travaux, ainsi que l'invitation adressée aux penseurs des diverses écoles et sensibilités de l'islam à critiquer et examiner ces recherches. Un tel islam peut, sur le long terme, corriger nombre de préjugés courants, inviter les croyants à la tolérance en donnant à voir sa propre diversité dans différents domaines, et tempérer l'usage de la violence comme l'intransigeance autour de l'unicité supposée des croyances. Cet islam relève de la compétence des spécialistes et l'apparition de ses fruits est une œuvre de très longue haleine. Sa haute valeur réside dans l'explication et l'élucidation ; il exige patience, temps et modération. Ces travaux peuvent introduire une certaine relativité aux frontières du dogme. Ils familiarisent l'esprit des croyants avec le pourquoi des phénomènes et les aident à mieux connaître la genèse de leurs propres convictions. Dans les relations entre les différents islams, les termes gagnent en précision et en clarté ; la recherche étiologique et généalogique se substitue à l'obstination dogmatique.

— Un autre champ est l'islam philosophique, qui a mobilisé dès l'origine les penseurs des sociétés islamiques. Bien que cette orientation se soit heurtée à des résistances, elle a maintenu sa présence jusqu'à nos jours sous des formes diverses. D'Avicenne à Fârâbî, de Mollâ Sadrâ à Hâdj Mollâ Hâdî Sabzevârî, ils se sont efforcés de préserver le cadre de la pensée philosophique — à savoir l'interrogation sur le fondement de la pensée et ses modalités — tout en transmettant l'enseignement de la philosophie grecque antique et en puisant aux fondements philosophiques de l'Extrême-Orient. Cette philosophie, dans toute sa richesse chromatique, relève elle aussi principalement du savoir et de son enracinement herméneutique. L'inscription de cette pensée dans l'ensemble de la connaissance philosophique humaine, et de fait l'effort visant à unifier l'histoire du cheminement de la philosophie humaine indépendamment des appartenances religieuses, peuvent rendre un service précieux à la mise en lumière de la pluralité de l'islam.

— Assurément, le courant mystique de l'islam possède, dès l'origine de cette religion et parallèlement à son expansion, une présence tout à fait autonome dans le monde islamique. Cette présence revêt tantôt une dimension pleinement philosophique, tantôt descend parmi le peuple et infléchit certains comportements et pratiques du quotidien, tantôt entraîne dans son sillage, sur le plan culturel, la poésie, la musique et la danse. À notre sens, la mystique islamique n'est pas dissociable du phénomène global de la mystique et de l'expérience mystique dont les racines remontent aux « chamanes » (guérisseurs et devins tribaux) et qui a cheminé avec l'évolution de la culture humaine. Les diverses formes d'expérience et de pensée mystiques définissent, le plus souvent de manière voilée et parfois au grand jour, une relation singulière entre l'être humain et l'« Au-delà » qui ne s'accorde pas toujours avec l'interprétation et l'exégèse dogmatiques fondamentales de l'islam concernant le monde. Dans ses dimensions philosophique et culturelle, la mystique a rendu d'immenses services à l'élargissement de la pensée. Sa dimension sociale perdure dans une forme de tolérance réciproque. La pensée mystique est pétrie avec la culture humaine depuis des temps immémoriaux et l'a constamment accompagnée ; l'on peut sans doute affirmer sans peine que son ancienneté et sa présence dans la culture humaine dépassent celles des religions instituées et qu'elle est devenue elle-même un facteur constitutif du socle de la tolérance entre les cultures. Par leur vie, leur culture, leur poésie et leur musique, les mystiques ont enrichi notre monde.

— Enfin, parlons de l'islam qui, en tant que voie et méthode, accède à l'expérience du gouvernement de la société. Retracer la genèse de l'islam de pouvoir dans l'histoire des diverses sociétés excéderait les limites de ce bref propos. Notre intention est ici de poser la question fondamentale du rapport entre le citoyen et un mode de gouvernement qui se pare du nom de l'islam ou se prévaut de ce nom pour fonder sa légitimité et son autorité. Or le problème de la vie quotidienne des citoyens de telles sociétés avec leurs dirigeants n'est ni un problème traditionnel, ni anthropologique, ni sociologique ; il n'est ni historique, ni philosophique ou mystique.

Dans cette perspective, et dans le bref laps de temps d'une génération, il est possible d'aborder l'islam politique et son renouvellement, tout en laissant sans nul doute à des temporalités beaucoup plus longues les effets de l'innovation sur la tradition, le mode de vie quotidien, les transactions, le mariage et le divorce, ainsi que les relations sociales, culturelles et humaines. En nous appuyant sur la pensée psychanalytique, nous devons être attentifs à la nécessité de prendre en compte la spécificité de la tradition. On ne saurait extirper la tradition de la racine comme une dent cariée ; à l'image d'une dent de lait, il faut attendre qu'une autre dent perce derrière elle afin qu'elle tombe d'elle-même, par nécessité.

Revenons à l'appel de M. Ganji : comment les militants des droits humains peuvent-ils accompagner un tel islam politique démocratique et coopérer avec lui ? Il convient de donner un nom à cet islam politique qui s'inscrit dans la droite ligne des principes des droits humains et s'accorde avec la Déclaration universelle des droits de l'homme : un islam qui conçoit cette Déclaration comme un programme d'action régissant les quatre types de relations qui sont les nôtres en tant qu'êtres humains — les relations des États entre eux, les relations des États avec les citoyens, les relations des divers groupements humains avec les citoyens, et enfin les relations des citoyens entre eux. Un islam qui, au-delà de ses propres lois, reconnaît cette Déclaration comme souveraine dans les rapports entre les cultures et entre les êtres humains. Un islam politique qui accepte de vivre dans le cadre de l'État-nation, qui accepte que cette Déclaration prime sur les constitutions nationales, et qui accepte que, dans les quatre ordres de relations susmentionnés, ce ne soit pas lui qui ait le premier mot. C'est un tel islam politique qu'il convient de définir dans le champ du souhaitable-possible de chaque société et pour la diffusion duquel il faut œuvrer.

On peut en conclure que la définition du souhaitable-possible d'un tel islam politique dépend entièrement de la maturité culturelle des citoyens et des croyants, de leur système de communication avec la société et les citoyens, du régime politique gouvernant la société, ainsi que des conditions géopolitiques de la région et du climat général du monde. Autrement dit, un islam politique à la fois souhaitable et possible doit d'abord être défini dans ses fondements conceptuels avant que l'on s'emploie à l'atteindre et à le généraliser. Gardons à l'esprit que tel a précisément été l'effort d'une partie du clergé iranien au cours des deux derniers siècles, avec des hauts et des bas dont le récit ne saurait tenir dans ce bref exposé. Œuvrer à l'édification d'une telle théorie, susceptible d'être entendue par une fraction des clercs, de les conduire progressivement, eux et leurs partisans, vers les principes des droits humains et, à terme, de pénétrer le corps et l'âme de la société, constituerait un acquis majeur et permettrait de franchir un pas décisif dans les sociétés à majorité musulmane.

La même sollicitation peut être adressée aux penseurs dissidents et aux tenants d'autres visions du monde. Les défenseurs des droits humains doivent, selon la même méthode et à la même échelle, valoriser les efforts de la société civile, les luttes corporatives et juridiques des avocats, des travailleurs, des enseignants et des universitaires, et s'investir de toute leur âme dans l'épanouissement de ce mouvement. Les défenseurs des droits humains ont le devoir de ne jamais relâcher leurs efforts pour tempérer l'« exclusivisme » (*faqat-garâ'î*), qu'il s'agisse du Hezbollah libanais ou des conceptions du sionisme qui sont à l'origine de l'occupation de la terre palestinienne et du déracinement de millions de citoyens de cette terre. Soutenir un tel islam politique qui envisage l'avenir souhaitable dans les voies tracées par la Déclaration universelle des droits de l'homme constitue un devoir stratégique des véritables défenseurs des droits humains, tout comme il leur incombe de soutenir l'innovation au sein de tout socle traditionnel et intellectuel orientant les peuples du monde vers cette Déclaration.

Ainsi que je l'ai souligné dans l'article « Réponse à une question : le rôle de la religion civique dans l'Iran de demain » (*Gooya Newsletter*, samedi 4 Azar 1391 / 24 novembre 2012)² en examinant la requête de M. Eshkevari, il faut non seulement soutenir l'innovation, mais aussi prendre part à son élaboration théorique et à sa mise en œuvre pratique. Nul doute que le regard expert des défenseurs des droits humains versés dans d'autres domaines que les fondements de l'islam peut contribuer efficacement à dénouer ce nœud.

C'est avec un vif enthousiasme que nous attendons la tenue de colloques et d'échanges véritables et concrets entre les clercs qui s'engagent sur cette voie et les autres experts défenseurs des droits humains ; et nous ne ménagerons aucun effort en ce sens. Tout comme, durant toute l'époque constitutionnelle, les clercs (*mo'ammamîn*) dialoguèrent avec les laïcs (*mokallâhâ*), tout comme les plus hautes autorités des séminaires de Nadjaf et de Qom coopérèrent avec les constitutionnalistes contre les partisans de la *machrou'eh* (gouvernance fondée sur la charia), et tout comme, au sein des Assemblées nationales antérieures à l'avènement de la République islamique — malgré toutes les difficultés et des modes de scrutin atypiques —, ce dialogue et cette coopération se poursuivirent.

Le premier geste pour rendre effectif ce « devoir moral » ne consiste-t-il pas, pour les clercs et les partisans d'un islam politique ouvert à la tolérance, à prendre part aux réunions, colloques et rassemblements des défenseurs des droits humains ? C'est avec une profonde tristesse et un vif regret que nous avons dû constater l'absence d'une telle présence et d'une telle participation au cours des trois dernières décennies.

« L'invention d'un islam démocratique » dépend du socle traditionnel et des conditions sociales des idées dominantes de chaque société, et se doit d'être dynamique et actuel. Le problème fondamental et structurel qui règne sur l'espace de pensée de nombre de clercs chiites réside dans leur résistance face à une loi codifiée, cohérente, applicable partout et pour tous, sans exception et non soumise à l'arbitraire des fatwas. Ceux-là ne se sont pas seulement dressés contre la loi lors de la Petite Tyrannie ; ils n'ont pas seulement joué un rôle négatif en insistant pour modifier la Constitution de la République islamique et y faire inscrire le principe de la « tutelle absolue du juriste-théologien » (*Velâyat-e motlaqeh-ye faqîh*) ; aujourd'hui encore, ils font barrage au gouvernement issu de cette même République islamique lorsqu'il manifeste quelque velléité de soumettre certaines relations sociales à l'empire de la loi.

N'oublions pas ce vers plein de mesure de Bâbâ Tâher, issu de notre culture nationale :
*Qu'il est doux que l'affection vienne des deux côtés,*
*Car la tendresse d'un seul bord n'est que tourment.*

en.title: Mr Ganji, Whom Are You Addressing?

en.body_markdown:
Ordibehesht 1394 (April–May 2015)

[Read on Gooya](http://news.gooya.com/politics/archives/2015/05/196736.php)

Mr Ganji, Whom Are You Addressing? — Hassan Makaremi

"The invention of democratic Islam" depends upon the traditional substratum and social conditions of the dominant ideas of each society, and must remain dynamic and up to date. The fundamental, structural problem governing the intellectual space of many Shia clerics is their resistance to codified, coherent law that is enforceable everywhere and for everyone, without exception and impervious to fatwas. In his recent article "The Necessity of Inventing Democratic Islam", published in the English-language *Huffington Post* (reproduced in *Gooya News*, Tuesday 1 Ordibehesht 1394 / 21 April 2015)¹, Mr Akbar Ganji concludes that "if individuals and groups regard peace, freedom, and human rights as important ideals, they are morally obliged to defend the invention of democratic Islam." Having spent nearly three decades striving in defence of the implementation of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights alongside friends near and far, I regard myself as an addressee of this message and welcome it; yet allow me to analyse it further and clarify the conditions for cooperation.

If this is the remedy for our predicament, and if by this means we can compel the custodians of power in Iranian society to respect human rights, then Mr Ganji is entirely right: defending democratic Islam is not merely a moral duty, but a fundamental obligation for human rights defenders. Yet what is this "democratic Islam" invented by Mr Ganji, and how can defending it be translated into practice?

It is true that from a scientific, ethnological, and anthropological perspective, and drawing upon what Michel Foucault termed the archaeology of knowledge, human beings have themselves invented, devised, and, in simpler terms, created culture—doing so over hundreds of thousands of years, and following the advent of symbolisation. It is equally true that they have produced all religions, beliefs, traditions, customs, convictions, and prescriptions and prohibitions as a subset of this cultural achievement over that vast span of time. If we accept this principle, we see that throughout this immense endeavour spanning hundreds of millennia, humanity has never resorted to reinventing a tradition, religion, or body of thought anew; rather, it has invariably paved the way for reconciling life with reality through exegesis, interpretation, and innovation within religious and traditional foundations.

Now the question is: what is "democratic Islam", and how can one assist in its emergence and widespread adoption? I concur with Mr Ganji where he writes that more than one and a half billion people in our world inhabit countries that we call Islamic countries on account of their Muslim-majority populations. Yet we must bear in mind that Islam—owing to its history, the manner of its spread, and the cultures prevailing prior to it across such vast lands—possesses diverse interpretations, exegeses, practical traditions, and modes of governance. Over so long a passage of time and across so vast an expanse, such an Islam has acquired five fields and dimensions, giving colour to the human geography of such a world and, over these fourteen centuries, leaving abundant deposits across varied societies and strata and within diverse dimensions of individual and social life.

— The traditional dimension of Islam, namely that which pertains to people's everyday lives: civil and criminal law, the various rites of marriage and divorce, commercial relations and trade, family and social ties, and beliefs and convictions woven into daily life, such as dream interpretation, votive offerings, and so forth. These traditions are a synthesis of what existed in the culture of peoples prior to Islam with subsequently accepted traditions, practices, and discourses. All of these have been renewed across the centuries and perfected alongside advances in knowledge and technology, like any living organism in the struggle for survival.

— Islam in the domain of sociology, anthropology, cultural history, the history of religions, and the history of ideas and its trajectory: the examination and deep study of Islam in its varied hues by recognised scientific methods, grounded in extant evidence and documentation, as is customary in academic circles. Let us call "scholarly Islam" the dialogue concerning research methods and instruments, the publication of the findings of these enquiries, and the invitation extended to thinkers across the diverse schools and convictions of Islam to critique and examine this research. Such an Islam can, in the long run, correct many conventional prejudices, invite believers to tolerance by displaying its own diversity across different domains, and moderate the resort to violence and insistence upon the uniformity of beliefs. Such an Islam lies within the remit of specialists, and the manifestation of its results is a very protracted undertaking. Its supreme value lies in explanation and enlightenment; it requires patience, time, and forbearance. These enquiries can introduce a degree of relativity across doctrinal boundaries. They acquaint believers' minds with the causes of phenomena and help them become better acquainted with the genesis of their own convictions. In the interplay among diverse Islams, terms grow more precise and lucid; tracing origins takes the place of dogmatic insistence.

— Another dimension is philosophical Islam, which from the very outset engaged thinkers within Islamic societies. Although this current encountered resistance, it has preserved its presence in various forms down to the present day. From Avicenna to Farabi, from Mulla Sadra to Haj Mulla Hadi Sabzevari, thinkers endeavoured to preserve the framework of philosophical thought—namely, inquiry into the foundation of thought and its workings—while transmitting the teaching of ancient Greek philosophy and drawing upon the philosophical foundations of the Far East. This philosophy, too, for all its variety, belongs chiefly to the realm of knowledge and its hermeneutic genealogy. Situating this thought within the broader corpus of human philosophical knowledge—and indeed endeavouring to unify the history of human philosophy independently of religious affiliations—can render a great service in illuminating the plurality of Islam.

— Undoubtedly, the mystical current of Islam has, from the very inception of this religion and alongside its expansion, maintained an altogether independent presence in the Islamic world. This presence at times assumes a wholly philosophical dimension, at times moves among the common people and alters certain everyday behaviours and practices, and at times draws poetry, music, and dance into its cultural orbit. In our view, Islamic mysticism is inseparable from the broader phenomenon of mysticism and mystical experience whose roots begin with "shamans" (tribal medicine-men and seers) and have evolved alongside human culture. The diverse forms of mystical experience and thought, mostly in a veiled manner and occasionally openly, define a distinct relationship between human beings and the "Beyond" that cannot always align with the fundamentalist or orthodox interpretation and exegesis of the world in Islam. In its philosophical and cultural dimensions, mysticism has rendered vast services to the expansion of thought. Its social dimension endures in a form of mutual tolerance. Mystical thought has been interwoven with human culture from remote antiquity and has accompanied it throughout; one may perhaps readily say that its antiquity and presence in human culture transcend those of formal religions and have themselves become a factor in establishing the basis for tolerance among cultures. Mystics have enriched our world with their lives, culture, poetry, and music.

— Finally, let us speak of the Islam that, as a method and pathway, attains the experience of governing society. Tracing the genesis of governmental Islam in the history of diverse societies lies beyond the scope of this brief note. Our purpose here is to pose the fundamental question regarding the relationship between the citizen and a form of governance that assumes the name of Islam, or exploits the name of Islam to secure its own legitimacy and authority. Indeed, the problem of the daily life of citizens in such societies with their rulers is neither a traditional problem, nor an anthropological or sociological one; it is neither historical, nor philosophical or mystical.

With this perspective, and within the brief span of a single generation, one can address political Islam and innovation within it, while undoubtedly leaving to much longer timescales the effects of innovation upon tradition, everyday ways of life, commerce, marriage and divorce, and social, cultural, and human relations. Drawing upon psychoanalytic thought, we must attend to the necessity of taking the specificity of tradition into account. Tradition cannot be yanked out by the root like a decayed tooth; rather, like a milk tooth, one must wait for another tooth to emerge behind it so that it falls out of its own accord, by necessity.

Let us return to Mr Ganji's appeal: how can human rights activists stand alongside and cooperate with such a democratic political Islam? We must give a name to such a political Islam that aligns with human rights principles and accords with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights: an Islam that regards this Declaration as a programme of action across our fourfold human relationships—relations between states, relations between states and citizens, relations between various human collectivities and citizens, and finally relations among citizens themselves. An Islam that, beyond its own laws, recognises this Declaration as governing relations among cultures and human beings. A political Islam that accepts living within the framework of the nation-state, accepts that this Declaration stands above national constitutions, and accepts that in the fourfold relationships above, it is not the one that holds the first word. Such a political Islam must be defined within the sphere of the desirable-possible of each society, and efforts must be made for its widespread adoption.

One may conclude that defining the desirable-possible of such a political Islam depends entirely upon the cultural maturity of citizens and religious believers, their system of communication with society and citizens, the ruling system of society, and the geopolitical conditions of the region and the general climate of the world. In other words, a political Islam that is both desirable and possible must first be defined in terms of its foundational premises, and efforts must then be directed towards achieving and disseminating it. Let us bear in mind that the endeavour of a section of the Iranian clergy over the past two centuries has been precisely this—marked by vicissitudes whose account lies beyond this brief essay. Striving to lay the groundwork for such a theory that can gain a hearing among a section of the clergy, gradually draw them and their followers towards human rights principles, and ultimately permeate the body and soul of society would constitute a major achievement and make it possible to take a decisive step forward in societies where adherents of Islam form the majority.

The same request may be addressed to dissident thinkers and adherents of other worldviews. Human rights defenders must, by the same method and on the same scale, value the efforts of civil society and the professional and legal struggles of lawyers, workers, teachers, and academics, and strive wholeheartedly for the flourishing of this movement. Human rights defenders are duty-bound never to desist from endeavouring to moderate "exclusivism" (*faqat-garā'ī*), whether in Lebanon's Hezbollah or in the beliefs of Zionism that have brought about the occupation of Palestinian land and the displacement of millions of citizens of that land. Supporting such a political Islam—one that envisions a desirable future in the pathways of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights—is a strategic duty of genuine human rights defenders, just as innovation in every traditional-intellectual foundation that guides the peoples of the world towards this Declaration is the duty of these defenders.

As I noted in my article "Response to a Question: The Role of Civic Religion in Future Iran" (*Gooya Newsletter*, Saturday 4 Azar 1391 / 24 November 2012)² when examining Mr Eshkevari's request, one must not only support innovation, but also participate in its theoretical formulation and practical implementation. Undoubtedly, the expert perspective of human rights defenders knowledgeable in fields other than Islamic doctrine can prove effective in untying this knot.

With great enthusiasm we await the convening of conferences and genuine, practical exchanges between clerics who step onto this path and other expert human rights defenders; and in this endeavour we shall spare no effort. Just as throughout the Constitutional era turbaned clerics (*mo'ammamīn*) engaged in dialogue with secular laymen (*mokallāhā*); just as the highest authorities of the seminaries of Najaf and Qom cooperated with Constitutionalists against the advocates of *Mashru'eh* (Sharia-based rule); and just as in the National Consultative Assemblies prior to the advent of the Islamic Republic—despite all difficulties and irregular electoral practices—this dialogue and cooperation continued.

Is not the first step towards actualising this "moral ought" the participation of clerics and adherents of a tolerant political Islam in the meetings, conferences, and gatherings of human rights defenders? With profound sorrow and regret, over the past three decades we have not witnessed such presence and participation.

"The invention of democratic Islam" depends upon the traditional substratum and social conditions of the dominant ideas of each society, and must remain dynamic and up to date. The fundamental, structural problem governing the intellectual space of many Shia clerics is their resistance to codified, coherent law that is enforceable everywhere and for everyone, without exception and impervious to fatwas. Not only did they stand against the law during the Lesser Tyranny, and not only did they play a negative role in insisting on amending the Constitution of the Islamic Republic and preventing the exclusion of—indeed inserting—the principle of the "Absolute Guardianship of the Islamic Jurist" (*Velāyat-e Motlaqeh-ye Faqīh*), but today too they erect barriers against the government born of this very Islamic Republic whenever it shows some inclination to regulate certain social relations by law.

Let us not forget this measured couplet by Baba Taher from our national culture:
*How sweet when affection comes from both sides,*
*For affection from one side alone is naught but heartache.*

fr.body_markdown:
https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/08/vasma.jpg

Présentation du livre « Il y a certainement une voie » de Mme Sedigheh Vasmaghi, suivie de la 102e rencontre de l'Association Dialogue et Démocratie sur le thème « Moyen-Orient : quel brasier le feu de la guerre et de l'ignorance attise-t-il ? », au cours de laquelle trois intervenants — Morad Veisi, Alireza Nourizadeh et Mojtaba Taleghani — ont pris la parole et exposé leurs analyses. Émission *Sous le ciel de Paris*, chaque jeudi à 19 h (heure de Paris) sur la chaîne de télévision Iran Farda.

[Voir la vidéo](/fa/media/videos/moearfi-ketab-htma-rahy-hst-fa)

[Présentation du livre « Il y a certainement une voie »](http://asre-nou.net/php/view.php?objnr=33521)

Bahman Amini (éditeur), Masoumeh Shapouri (correctrice-éditrice), Dr Hassan Makaremi (psychanalyste) et Bijan Hekmat (militant politique)
Réalisation : Farhamand Rokni
Jeudi 2 Bahman 1393 — 22 janvier 2015

La Dre Sedigheh Vasmaghi, poétesse, écrivaine et militante politique, fut membre et porte-parole du premier Conseil municipal de Téhéran. Dans l'introduction de son livre « Il y a certainement une voie » (*Hatman râhî hast*), elle écrit :

« Le destin du premier mandat du Conseil municipal de Téhéran, nous l'avons tous façonné ensemble. Ce destin est le résultat de nos efforts et de nos erreurs à tous : de la gauche à la droite, des partisans aux adversaires des réformes, tant ceux qui étaient sur le devant de la scène et dont le rôle peut paraître plus visible, que les personnes, groupes et institutions qui agissaient en coulisses — et le lecteur constatera que leur rôle ne fut pas moindre que celui des acteurs sur scène. Mais nous n'avons pas été éduqués à chercher nos erreurs pour les identifier et les corriger afin d'assurer plus fermement le pas suivant. Car nous sommes tous égoïstes et obstinés. Sans en avoir le mérite, nous sommes orgueilleux et, nous croyant exempts de faute, nous rions des erreurs d'autrui, ignorant que les expériences et les erreurs appartiennent à toute la société et à la nation entière, et que tous nous devons en tirer des leçons. Si nous admettons que le coût des expériences sociales est payé par la nation bien plus que par des individus ou des groupes, alors nous considérerons ces expériences comme des capitaux nationaux et non comme des déchets bons à jeter.

…

Le présent ouvrage a été rédigé à partir des notes quotidiennes de l'auteure tout au long de l'existence du premier Conseil ainsi que des documents et archives recueillis. Il relate près de quatre années d'expériences et de réalités du premier mandat du Conseil municipal de Téhéran du point de vue de l'auteure. Des expériences et des réalités auxquelles tous ont pris part, et qui ne sont pas le seul fait des membres du Conseil municipal. Des réalités dont l'équivalent, voire pis encore, existe dans toutes les organisations et institutions du pays. Nul ne devrait donc se rengorger en pensant que les personnages de ce livre sont ainsi faits tandis que nous serions autres. Peut-être qu'en exposant et en rappelant ces expériences, ces réalités et ces événements, une issue s'ouvrira. Revenons à nous-mêmes et trouvons la voie. Il faut chercher. Il y a certainement une voie. »

[Watch the video](/fa/media/videos/moearfi-ketab-htma-rahy-hst-fa)

[Presentation of the book "There Is Surely a Way"](http://asre-nou.net/php/view.php?objnr=33521)

Bahman Amini (publisher), Masoumeh Shapouri (editor), Dr Hassan Makaremi (psychoanalyst), and Bijan Hekmat (political activist)
Film by: Farhamand Rokni
Thursday, 2 Bahman 1393 – 22 January 2015

Dr Sedigheh Vasmaghi, poet, writer, and political activist, was a member and spokesperson of the first term of the Tehran City Council. In the preface to the book *There Is Surely a Way*, she states:

"All of us together shaped the fate of the first term of the Tehran City Council. This fate is the result of the efforts and mistakes of all of us—from left to right, from supporters to opponents of reforms, both those who were on the stage and whose role may appear more prominent, and individuals, groups, and institutions who played roles behind the scenes, and the reader will discover that their role was no less than that of the actors on stage. Yet we have not been raised to search out mistakes, find them, and correct them so as to place our next step on firmer ground. For we are all selfish and stubborn. Without deserving it, we are arrogant, and, considering ourselves exempt from error, we laugh at one another's mistakes, unaware that experiences and mistakes belong to the entire society and nation, and that all must learn from these lessons. If we accept that the cost of social experiences is paid by the nation even more than by individuals and groups, then we shall regard experiences as national capital rather than disposable rubbish.

...

The present book has been written on the basis of the author's daily notes throughout the entire term of the First Council, as well as collected documents and records. The present book recounts nearly four years of experiences and realities of the first term of the Tehran City Council from the author's vantage point—experiences and realities in which everyone had a share, and which are not solely the doing of the City Council members; realities of which even worse examples exist in all organisations and institutions of the country. Therefore, no one should boast that the figures in this book are thus and we are otherwise. Perhaps by recounting and recalling experiences, realities, and events, an opening may appear. May we come to our senses and find the way. One must search. There is surely a way."
