How does a Lacanian clinical psychoanalyst work? To answer this question, one must first become acquainted with Jacques Lacan (Jacques Lacan), the French psychiatrist and psychoanalyst, and gain some grasp of his theories through examining his writings, seminars, and clinical, group, and training experiences. Along this path, we need to become better acquainted with his readings of the structuralists of the second half of the twentieth century—figures such as Sigmund Freud and Ferdinand de Saussure—as well as the incomparable French school of psychiatry. And it is here that we realise just how arduous the task is and how much perseverance it demands.

This is the third time that I am confronted with this question before scholars and thoughtful listeners who have taken the trouble to follow these remarks. The previous occasions were far simpler. The first time, at a sociocultural association in France, I had to speak in Persian to fellow compatriots who had little familiarity with the theoretical and practical fields of psychoresearchers, psychologists, psychotherapists, psychiatrists, and psychoanalysts—a setting in which speaking of the psyche is equated with speaking of psychological injury and madness, especially since in the public mind, "madness usually concerns everyone except me and those around me." To be sure, the audience that day listened to me with the subtle and hidden prejudices floating in our cultural atmosphere, and on that occasion I found the opportunity to restore a measure of dignity to the psychological field. The second time was during my teaching at the Faculty of Medicine in Paris, when I addressed the very same subject, with the difference that this time my remarks were delivered in French and addressed to students who had some familiarity with the foundations of sexoanalysis—or psychoanalysis in the service of disorders of sexual relations. Even there, however, I had to clarify the theoretical underpinnings and the subtleties of the methodological divergence between Lacan and other schools of psychoanalysis, such as short and variable-length psychoanalytic sessions, or the role of the analyst's presence and interpretation. This time, however, the absence of face-to-face contact (this lecture was delivered remotely via Skype), the absence of shared foundations of knowledge, language, and terminology, and the absence of our mutual acquaintance compound the two preceding difficulties.

Today, given the limited time and by way of an initial introduction, I shall first address the psychological field and the relation between signifier and signified, since both of these domains are at once the fundamental pillars of psychoanalytic work—especially of the Lacanian school of psychoanalysis—and the central challenge of today's lecture. Then, as a clinical psychoanalyst of the Lacanian school from the second generation, I shall turn to Lacan and his theoretical, clinical, and applied foundations, and unpack the practical bases of his psychoanalysis. Right here I should mention that I am a student of Jean Fourton, who was himself one of Lacan's twelve close disciples.

The complexities of the psychological domain and its spheres of operation: The use of the word *ravan* ("psyche/flowing") in the Persian language as the equivalent of "PSY" in European languages may be regarded as a blessing of the Persian tongue. This word can serve both for the concept of the "psychic apparatus"—or the structure of psychic functioning—and as a suffix or prefix for all concepts that deal in some way with the psyche, such as psychoanalysis (*ravan-kavi*), psychology (*ravan-shenasi*), psychiatry (*ravan-pezeshki*), psychotherapy (*ravan-darmani*), or psychological (*ravan-shenakhti*). Because at the same time this word is also the verbal noun of the verb "to go/flow" (*raftan*), it conveys this relationship in the very fluidity of the concept of *ravan*: in such a way that *ravan* is at once within us, with us, and elsewhere. In Iranian myths, this locus takes a terrestrial-celestial form, and in the contemporary hypotheses of the Lacanian school of psychoanalysis, it is none other than the other, the Other, or others.

Although the complexities of the human psyche are not solely the subject of the sciences in their modern sense, what has been formally defined within the boundaries of the sciences and in the psychological sphere may be divided into four groups: psychiatry, psychology, psychotherapy, and psychoanalysis. This classification provisionally enables us, in this brief presentation, to gain a clearer understanding of the field of psychological practice. Let us call the study of whatever pertains to the psyche "the psychological," on the assumption that we restrict our field of inquiry to everyday life and tangible logic. For the domain of knowing the psyche reaches back, on the one hand, to the study of all human achievements—from the invention of speech and writing to the realms of mythology, art, and literature from the remotest eras to the present day; within this domain, philosophy, mysticism, religion, popular beliefs, and even talismanic writing and magic also find their place. On the other hand, if we do not wish to venture quite so far afield, the scope of the psychological extends to linguistics, anthropology, sociology, and the cognitive sciences. And since the psyche rests upon the body, the psychological also advances as far as neurology; indeed, the human psyche is caught between three principal axes: the human past, the human being in the company of others, and the human body together with its nervous structure.

Let us try to clarify the matter by defining these four concepts of practical psychological application and citing a few examples:

1. Psychiatry, which historically belongs within the domain of medical practice and is a branch extending from neurology and brain medicine. In psychiatry, we deal with classifying illnesses on the basis of their external manifestations. The aim is the diagnosis of the illness and its treatment. Mental illnesses within the purview of psychiatry may derive their roots, in one way or another, from the body, from the nervous system, or from impaired cerebral functioning—illnesses rooted in congenital factors or difficulties that arise after birth, such as brain lesions or the improper functioning of the memory system, the diagnostic system, or cognitive structure.

In contemporary psychiatry, in order to treat disorders, practitioners trace the roots of bodily and neurological problems and employ everything from psychotherapy to environmental modification, art therapy, and the like, while also assigning a special place to chemical medications in calming the patient's mental space.

At the beginning of the twentieth century, hospital departments for neurological, cerebral, and psychiatric illnesses had not yet been separated from one another.

2. In psychology, the individual's behaviour is the object of analysis—the individual's behaviour within the family, in educational settings, in the workplace, and with friends and acquaintances. Consequently, this science is used wherever "individual behaviour" plays a role, such as recruitment in organisations, public relations, educational sciences, or regulating the individual's relations with others in the social environment. In clinical settings, psychology places the individual before a mirror of their behaviour towards society and others. In the rehabilitation of individuals who suffer from behavioural or mental disorders—whether due to congenital defects or to accidents and illnesses—psychology plays a major role. Moreover, studying social issues is not feasible without taking into account the individual's behaviour in relation to society (social psychology); through group work, psychology is highly effective in reactivating patients' mental activities. Another important sphere of psychology lies in research areas linked to the cognitive sciences and the behavioural sciences.

3. Psychotherapy, backed by experience and through the use of dialogue, seeks to bring the individual face to face with their localised disorders and guide them towards an acceptable resolution. In certain institutions (and whenever necessary), psychiatrists draw upon psychotherapy to alleviate disorders such as anxieties, temporary disorientations, and transient states of distress.

4. Psychoanalysis is a recent practice with a history of less than a hundred years. Psychoanalysis attends to the individual's speech upon the couch of the psychoanalyst's consulting room.

The psychoanalyst operates within the individual's relation to their unconscious. Their sphere of action is akin to holding up a mirror to the individual's speech so that, in this way and over the long term (typically between five and ten years), by recounting whatever comes to mind (free association), the individual gains awareness of how their unconscious functions and thereby reaches the roots of potential disorders in their behaviour. Many disorders are "resolved" through recognising their roots. On the other hand, psychoanalysis also assists in discovering the individual's latent inner capacities. Today, one of the most prominent uses of psychoanalysis is widespread in Western societies, functioning as a form of preparation for the individual's movement in a new direction through a deeper knowledge of their own strengths and weaknesses—like a ship's captain who, by sharpening their power of vision, steers the vessel more skilfully through storms.

Psychoanalytic training is most often described as a master-apprentice transmission. For if the psychoanalyst has not personally passed through the stage of lying upon the couch and undertaking the exploration of their psyche—or excavating the roots of their own "unconscious"—how could they serve as a guide for another person? In psychoanalysis we encounter two phenomena: on the basis of psychoanalytic theories, one may also investigate texts, discourse, and works of art, opening a new angle upon the methods of analysing and interpreting art and literature. It is for this reason that today psychoanalysts participate in research groups across numerous educational institutions, universities, and research centres.

Symbolisation, speech, word, and the relation between signifier and signified: A spoken or oral message—or these very letters, these very words, or their signifying form—does not always convert into a signified except within the framework of sender, receiver, and carrier. The "I" cannot speak of anything other than the "self." Every reality passes through the filter of the truth of this "I." In the psychoanalyst's gaze—a gaze that affirms the presence of the "I" within the individual—the foregoing questions grow even more complex. What the foundations of psychic structure, the family environment, school, lane, and street have built within the individual as the identity of the "I" during the first few years of life is a stratum that escapes even the intervention, will, and supervision of the "I." And this is precisely what we call the unconscious.

The role of words: One of the difficulties of spoken and written culture in closed environments is that the precise relation between signifier and signified cannot become firmly established. For it is through speaking and listening, writing and responding, within a living, vibrant, and continuous environment that communication grows sturdy and widespread; indeed, the circulation of words and their semantic charges is such that language remains alive, and the meanings of words among those who speak that language move towards greater harmony and homogeneity—even though we know that signifieds will never become entirely identical in human minds. Signifiers and signifieds are coordinated within each individual's informational system (with the exception of individuals afflicted by severe psychotic disorders). This phenomenon enables every citizen, in relation to other citizens, to draw upon norms accepted by all. It is from this very point that the boundaries of each citizen's freedom acquire an acceptable definition for themselves and for others, making coexistence possible. Our internal informational system is perhaps the only living non-material entity: although its functioning and survival depend upon our life, it continues to live independently of us and keeps changing until the very last moment of our existence—more or less, slowly or rapidly, continuously or gradually. Consequently, through the interaction of our informational systems—which are composed of coordinated and interconnected sets of signifiers and signifieds—they remain active and harmonised with one another.

The boundaries of signifier and signified lie within the institution of symbolisation. From the moment the simplest word, such as "water," evokes thirst in the mind of a child, an irrigation stream in the mind of a gardener, the sea in the mind of a mariner, and its chemical formula in the mind of a researcher, the question "which water are we speaking of?" becomes essential. Likewise, when speaking of concepts such as religion—and, for instance, when speaking of Islam—a question such as "which Islam are we speaking of?" takes on a new dimension. With the succession of generations, the expansion of the cultural world and greater knowledge of humanity and its surroundings, and the widening sphere of our desires and projects, needs also change; new signifiers are created, and as a result the volume of signifieds expands as well. Signifiers merge across different cultures. Prior to the advent of drinking water in municipal plumbing, the signifier "water" did not call to mind the signified of water inside pipes.

If Sigmund Freud studied the human being in domains extending beyond the "body," reaching into the depths of mythology, oral culture, and *Homo sapiens sapiens*, Jacques Lacan made language, its structure, the word, and above all the acoustic image of the word (the signifier) the fundamental element of his work; and through his major discovery and his formulation that "the unconscious is structured like a language," he re-examined the human psyche within the field of the speaking being, the desiring being, the active and agential subject. His acquaintance with the structuralists of the first half of the twentieth century provided him with the initial tools to combine topology (the science of spatial relations, the study of neighbourhood and proximity) and formalisations derived from modern mathematics with his discoveries, as instruments in the service of teaching and learning.

A few examples of the relation between signifier and signified: The crux of the hypothesis of contemporary psychoanalysis lies in this: "Everything is language." The structure of the human unconscious is like the structure of a language (the mother tongue, the child's relation to the mother, and the formation of the unconscious in the earliest years of life). Signs or acoustic images form an ensemble that writes our unconscious like a "text." These "signs" are transmitted from individual to individual in such a way that one cannot rightly know who owns them; and thus, through "economy of speech," "ambiguity and double entendre," "conciseness and brevity," and the use of "wordplay and conceptual play"—in short, what in the literary sphere is known as poetry and the architecture of speech, and in everyday life as proverbs, witticisms, riddles, invectives, and the like—an ensemble of "signs" practically lives in the circulating space between each individual and another, forming the foundation of today's culture and yesterday's myth.

Along this long road we learn not to become ensnared in the play of our own "signifiers," to allow ourselves to take our mental world seriously, as well as our dreams and our phantasms, and, going further still, to become attuned even to delusions, to lose ourselves in the reality of others—as the other of the other. We come to behold this invisible realm inside the bubble that an image of a virtual world bestows upon us, within this grand "masquerade" and web of invisible threads that links individuals together to weave from them other inseparable ensembles; like the totality of acoustic images, words too have been invented to be deployed by us, the creators of symbols. These symbols are fluid and move to and fro with such freedom that one cannot tell which belongs to whom. It is as though we bring these symbols into being, pass them on to the other, immerse ourselves in them, and finally forget them so as to put them to use at another time—and ultimately arrive at that renowned boundary, at that point of being which is the sum of these symbols and which, contrary to assumption, is not nearly as fixed as it seems.

In his thought, Lacan takes as his foundation the three elements of the Real, the Symbolic, and the Imaginary: it is as though the Real is perceptible only through our senses; symbolisation—which begins with gesture and movement and is perfected through the use of objects and the invention of words and language—together with the Imaginary, which is the continuation of the primordial phantasm after birth, enables us to exercise patience and endurance until a response arrives for the needs of the body. Every word is formed of two inseparable parts, like the two sides of a coin: the acoustic image or sound we use to utter the word (the signifier), and the concept and meaning concealed behind that word (the signified). A fine example is the Persian word *shir*, which has three signifieds: a water tap (*shir-e ab*), the milk of a camel, cow, or other animals (*shir*), and the lion of the jungle (*shir*).

From what standpoint, however, do I speak? Undoubtedly, the twentieth century was illuminated by two monumental insights. First, Sigmund Freud demonstrated that the human being possesses an "unconscious" which, like a stranger within, operates with a distinct behaviour and mode of functioning. Next, Einstein, by recognising and grasping the lawfulness of the release of energy within the nucleus of the atom, led humanity to the atomic bomb and other uses of this energy. Einstein's discovery easily found its way into the expanse of technology, academic sciences, and public knowledge (for it rested upon straightforward experimentation and the familiar logic of cause and effect); Freud's insight, however, even after a hundred years, still has a very long road ahead before it becomes widespread and properly understood. In countless societies, owing to religious, traditional, political, doctrinal, and ideological resistances, this vital theory has remained either unknown or misunderstood. Undoubtedly, an accurate and profound understanding of the insights of Freud and his followers such as Jacques Lacan—with the aid of translations of their works by clinical psychoanalysts who work closely with these concepts, as well as clinical experience (between the individual and the psychoanalyst and in relation to the individual's speech)—is one of the principal ways of introducing this theory in societies such as Iran. Indeed, right here I wish to mention the translation of the book *Television*, an interview with Jacques Lacan, which was published for the first time last year by Ebtekar-e No Publishers in Tehran in a bilingual Persian and French edition. (This book is introduced in the footnote.)

I have spent half of my life in Iran and the second half in France. During the first half, I had two scientific mentors: Einstein and Freud. At that time, the opportunity to become acquainted with Freud did not materialise; neither were adequate translations available, nor was the academic environment receptive. I recall that on Iranian Radio programmes I first became acquainted with the concept of the unconscious through the radio broadcast of Dr Nasseroddin Sahebozzamani, who always opened his discussion by reciting this couplet of Hafez: "Within my weary heart, I know not who dwells / For I am silent, yet he is in clamour and lamentation." In France, upon gaining access to the world of psychological knowledge, I pursued Freud with tremendous ardour. Today I can articulate the fruit of more than twenty years of learning and familiarity with psychoanalysis, with Freud and Lacan, and of experiences gained through years of continuous work in this field. After ten years of personal psychoanalysis and traversing the passage from analysand to clinical psychoanalyst under the direct supervision of one of Lacan's close disciples, ten years of serving as training director for the Association of Psychoanalysts of the Limousin region in France, several years of training and diverse experiences in the International Association of Lacanian Psychoanalysts, and training in case-presentation and patient-review seminars at Hôpital Sainte-Anne in Paris, I succeeded in completing my university thesis on psychoanalysis in the service of sexology at the Faculty of Medicine in Paris. Now, after training several psychoanalysts, organising colloquia and lectures in Persian and French, and collaborating in the founding of the Association of Psychoresearchers of France, I can summarise my views as follows:

– First, clinical psychoanalysis is the crossing of a desert under the guidance of a psychoanalyst who takes the individual by the hand to traverse its various stages, until the individual becomes independent, continues on their own path, and is able to bestow inner peace and serenity upon themselves, their loved ones, and those around them—or even take their seat in the psychoanalyst's chair. In this relationship, the psychoanalyst is compelled each time to cross the desert alongside the patient, and it is in this crossing that the psychoanalyst discovers another self each time. For every human being is like an iceberg whose larger portion lies beneath the water, invisible unless one is a diver. Every human individual is a singular jewel, born once and living once within the volume of space and place. This volume is singular, and so too is its experience.

– Second, by gaining access to the richness of accompanying others—entering the world of their sleep, dreams, phantasies, and everyday lives, and coming to recognise their frustrations—the psychoanalyst discovers how these phenomena take shape and interrelate from the very innermost depths, across all manner of human beings: young and old, women and men, small and great; and thus the psychoanalyst expands the volume of their own presence in existence. Conversely, others and the volume of their presence in existence also enter into the volume of the analyst's life.

– Thanks to Freud's discovery, we know that over the course of their life from birth onwards, every human being experiences the totality of human genesis; by accompanying hundreds of "others," the psychoanalyst traverses this volume time and time again. The psychoanalyst's presence gradually becomes interwoven with human presence in existence; they experience foresight, depth of reflection, tolerance, and love, and gain the capacity to grasp at once their singular presence as an unrepeatable presence and their universal existence as one member among the thirteen billion human beings born thus far—and thereby attain what Freud calls sublimation, cultural elevation, for fortunately in the eloquent Persian language *farhang* ("culture") signifies ascending knowledge.

Who Is Jacques Lacan?

Jacques Lacan (1901–1981), the French psychiatrist and psychoanalyst, is undeniably one of the most eminent continuators of Sigmund Freud's path. As he himself put it, he is "someone who has read Freud." Lacan's works have exerted their greatest influence upon schools of psychoanalysis in France and subsequently in Latin America. He places emphasis upon the formation and functioning of the unconscious. In 1953, Jacques Lacan separated from the Paris Psychoanalytic Society and founded a school named the "French School of Psychoanalysis," which was later renamed the "Freudian School of Paris." From that date onwards, debate and controversy between followers of Lacan and other adherents of Freud have continued.

The basis of the divergence between these two currents of thought has both theoretical foundations and clinical, operational foundations. Jacques Lacan enumerated the importance of the signifier and its symbol in the unconscious and emphasised the presence of the speaking and desiring human being. He advances the formula: "The unconscious is structured like a language." Like Sigmund Freud, Lacan also rests the structure of the unconscious upon the same three pillars: neurosis, psychosis, and perversion.

In the operational stages of psychoanalysis, the frequency and duration of sessions may appear to differ across various schools. After training several generations of clinical psychoanalysts, Lacan dissolved his school in 1980. Since that date, his students have established numerous psychoanalytic associations across France and around the world. His invaluable collected oeuvre comprises his medical thesis, more than twenty-seven seminars, several lectures and an interview, and a collection of writings and essays published in two volumes under the titles *Écrits* (*Writings*) and *Autres écrits* (*Other Writings*). Jacques Lacan's seminars, all of which are transcriptions of his oral teachings, have for the most part been published. His intended audience consists of psychoanalysts, yet his teachings extend well beyond that circle; one need not necessarily be a psychoanalyst to understand Lacan's discourse.

Today, his ideas are taught worldwide across diverse academic disciplines, including philosophy, linguistics, literary and art criticism, aesthetics, architecture, and law. In the first half of the twentieth century, his acquaintance with the structuralists furnished him with the initial tools enabling him to draw upon topology and the application of modern mathematical formalisations as instruments and a working method in the service of his teaching and discoveries. On the one hand, Lacan emphasises empirical and clinical work as a physician and psychiatrist; on the other, he relies upon a penetrating reading of the writings of Freud, the structuralists, and linguists.

In his work, the imprint of Freud's clinical and theoretical findings is clearly visible. His genius lies in a modern re-examination of Freud's ideas. He interconnected phantasm, speech, need, desire, and the word (signifier and signified) through precise, formalised definitions. And because he placed language, speech, the word, and their relation to each individual's unconscious at the centre, wordplay, etymologies, linguistic structure, and writing serve as the principal tools of his work. Beyond university and academic settings and clinical care of the psyche in psychiatric hospitals and psychotherapeutic institutions, a wide network of associations is also devoted to Jacques Lacan's oeuvre. Comparing the works of Jacques Lacan with those of other psychoanalysts and putting them to the test in clinical practice is likewise a subject of study at research centres throughout the world. Literary and artistic criticism grounded in Jacques Lacan's thought has today become widespread. Jacques Lacan's ideas are alive. His complex, indefatigable, and singular personality has been revealed in the brief anecdotes recounted here and there by his students. His storyteller-like idiom and intricate theory present this psychiatrist like a painter working in an abstract style.

Tracing Lacan's findings by reading his works in chronological order of production may be useful to a historian of human achievements, yet for enthusiasts of the humanities and for psychoanalysts it can hardly prove fruitful. At the outset of his career, he drew upon concepts and terms current in the French school of psychiatry of the early twentieth century. Later, through his encounter with Freud's works—and above all through his personal psychoanalysis with one of Freud's direct students, Rudolph Loewenstein—his thought gradually acquired a Freudian cast. His encounter with the Swiss linguist Ferdinand de Saussure brought about a major transformation in Lacan's thought: "The unconscious is structured like a language"—this is the master key to his teachings.

The distinctive features of Lacan's teachings may be enumerated as follows:

– Lacan succeeded in apprehending and expounding Freud's discovery, the unconscious, in two stages: first, how the unconscious is formed, its structure, and the foundational elements of that structure—namely the Real order, the Symbolic order, and the Imaginary order; and second, how this unconscious functions and coexists within the individual—or, in his own terms, the divided subject, the barred subject, the subject split in two, the dual subject. Here, "subject" signifies an agent, an active actor or grammatical subject endowed with will, intelligence, and speech—a hidden, perpetual, and powerful drive that serves as the basis of the individual's movement throughout the entire span of life and is rooted in the primordial desire of every living being to continue living.

– Lacan advanced his teachings simultaneously along three axes in order to bring greater clarity and precision to his work, for he had profoundly grasped that words, owing to the property of signifier and signified, are not faithful representatives for transmitting a message. For this very reason, he delivered the bulk of his teaching orally in the form of twenty-seven annual seminars, so as to maintain a direct, spoken presence—with all its advantages and pitfalls, including slips of the tongue, substitutions, ellipses, homophonies, rhetorical figures, and at times poetic devices—in order that his audience might reach Lacan himself by the closest possible route. To that end, he operated simultaneously along three axes: theoretical exposition, modern mathematical formalisations and topology (the science of spatial relations), and the synthesis of these two with a third instrument, namely the analysis of individual lives such as Hamlet and others previously examined by Freud. Indeed, even in his psychiatric doctoral thesis, Lacan analysed the psychological condition of "Madame Aimée."

– Choosing these three instruments to articulate his teachings caused Lacan considerable trouble and rendered the task of explaining and disseminating his ideas deceptively elusive. One group sought to transpose all of his teachings into mathematical formulas and topology in an effort to complete his formal modelling, and by making this choice drifted away from clinical, investigative, and experiential work. Another group selected solely the clinical and applied facets of his teachings, notably in English-speaking countries. In German universities, the philosophical dimension of his work attracted the greatest attention; in America, it was taken up primarily in art, literary, and film criticism; in France, across every domain—especially law, architecture, and cinema (screenwriting); and in Latin America, in the management of therapeutic institutions. The essential transmission of Lacan's clinical teachings took place directly within the analytic process of those individuals who were psychoanalysed by him and attended his school. To this day, those psychoanalysts transmit what they learned by the very same method. I, too, count myself among these second-generation clinical psychoanalysts. The fruit of the continuity of these schools is the existence of dozens of associations of Lacanian psychoanalysts around the world.

– Lacan repeatedly insists that the psychoanalyst must first of all arrive at their own madness—that is, traverse the stages of psychoanalysis upon the couch in full, just like an analysand; this is the very first step along the intricate and arduous path towards attaining this standing. Then training begins, initially within small groups known as "foursomes" (*cartels*). These groups continue their work under the supervision of those schools and senior psychoanalysts, within schools composed of psychoanalysts, through protracted labour and by arriving at self-discovered insights—just as the noble Hafez says:

Last night I carried my perplexity to the Elder of the Magi,

Who by his confirming gaze would unravel every riddle.

For Lacan, the stages of the unconscious's formation during the first years of an individual's life rest upon the gradual emergence of the three orders—the Real order, the Symbolic order, and the Imaginary order—and upon the relation between the individual and whatever binds them to their presence in existence, to staying alive, to the will to live, which crystallises in an instrument he terms the object-cause of desire (*objet petit a*). Through a logical relation of cause and effect, the subject comes to desire an object-instrument: the will to continue living, which forms the foundation and backbone of all other desires. It is the relation between this subject and this object that awakens the infant to self-recognition—and it is precisely here that complexity begins: the newborn infant's relation to the first object that, in the initial stage, comes to stand in for the concept of longing and desire, for here the relation of subject and object—the very relation of agent and object—comes into being. Lacan names this object the object-cause of desire (*objet petit a*), an object which on the one hand bears a relation to reality and stands at the intersection of the Real, the Symbolic, and the Imaginary orders: the Real order, or the body and the five senses that connect us to the external world—a reality that passes through the Real (the body) and enables the infant to reinvent and rediscover the Symbolic and Imaginary orders. Lacan locates the mediators of this reality in the gaze, the mouth and the mother's breast, or the voice and the infant's faeces—in other words, the entrances and exits directly bound up with the continuation of life. To clarify this section, I include here a diagram that, in my view, summarises Lacan's Seminar on *Anxiety* (please refer to the attached file).

Grasping the foundations of Lacan's thought requires an understanding of the following concepts: the formation of the unconscious and its functioning in clinical psychoanalysis and applied psychoanalysis; the significance of signifier and signified in the structure of language and the structure of the unconscious; the three interdependent categories of the Real, the Symbolic, and the Imaginary; the four discourses; the Big Other; the object-cause of desire; the Name-of-the-Father; and the three structures of the unconscious—neurosis, psychosis, and perversion. These are the practical pillars of Jacques Lacan's psychoanalysis. Right here it can be shown that the practical stages of Lacanian psychoanalysis likewise consist in traversing the reverse path of this very process of the genesis and formation of the unconscious, in such a manner that the dual subject, the barred subject, the divided subject winds along this path in a spiral until reaching its own object-cause of desire.

In a very brief and schematic outline, the stages of clinical psychoanalysis may be summarised as follows: first comes the stage of choosing a psychoanalyst, the individual's consultation with the analyst, and the emergence of the affective attachment of transference between the person and the psychoanalyst—positioned as a subject supposed to know "everything". Not only what the consulting subject knows about himself or herself, but also what the subject does not know, the psychoanalyst is presumed to know. Here the psychoanalyst plays the role of the Big Other, the role of the mother—the one who, if she speaks, if it is brought into speech, will reveal the hidden secret. It is here that demand—that is, the subject's request addressed to the psychoanalyst—plays the central role, and the preliminaries of the infant–mother relationship, or the state of oneness and fusion underlying transference or identification, are established. From this point onward, the unconscious opens up, places trust, and unfolds. In this state, as illustrated in the diagram as well, the subject's desire and demand play the fundamental part; without his or her own will, wish, and movement towards the psychoanalyst, the necessary bond cannot be formed. One of the chief reasons for the sustained functioning of psychoanalysis is precisely this bond—which, for instance, does not form in young children, or in bureaucratic, coercive relationships and environments dependent on closed systems. One might say that the first six months are devoted to seriously establishing this relationship. During this period, a pact is concluded between the subject and the psychoanalyst—or symbolically between the couch and the armchair—within a calm setting where the subject lies upon the couch; the very arrangement Freud ultimately adopted after testing various methods, and which Lacan adopted likewise. It is preferable that the personal presence of the psychoanalyst remain as unobtrusive as possible, or that physical contact and direct visual observation of the analyst be kept to a minimum. The subject attends two or three times a week at a fixed hour; this regularity greatly assists the opening of the unconscious. Usually, during the first few sessions, the subject may sit face to face with the psychoanalyst so that, on the one hand, the subject grasps the stages, functioning, and manner of the work, and on the other, the psychoanalyst ensures that the subject is ready to begin serious work.

Here one may refer to the ethical contract between the subject and the psychoanalyst, which may be understood as comprising five elements: first, strict adherence to attendance—two or three sessions per week at pre-arranged hours—such that this attendance becomes an invariable principle in the subject's life. The duration of sessions may vary according to the course and progress of the work, as well as the subject's speech and whether the essential point has been articulated, and in each session depends upon the psychoanalyst's decision. Second, the subject pays the psychoanalyst's fee for each session so as not to remain indebted to the analyst, thereby addressing from the outset the sense of guilt and its presence in the subject. The fee for missed sessions is also paid, even if the absence is justified.

Thus, a fee is paid in exchange for the psychoanalyst's services, laying the groundwork for a social relationship founded on exchange—the presence of the I and the other on equal terms. Without deeply knowing why, the subject usually tends to be absent precisely at the moments when the greatest possibility for opening the unconscious arises. In the third part of this ethical contract, the subject and the psychoanalyst confine their relationship strictly to the parenthesis of the couch and the armchair—no more and no less; there is no place for physical contact outside this parenthesis, nor for expressing this relationship outside the psychoanalytic axis. Speaking about and repeating what transpires in psychoanalytic sessions with others is, in practice, harmful. Once the unconscious has opened, if it targets someone other than the psychoanalyst, the subject gradually lays bare his or her inner table everywhere, and this can yield nothing but harm.

The fourth clause concerns the contract of free association of thought and the uninhibited utterance of whatever comes to mind during psychoanalytic sessions. This is a very ordinary and effortless matter once the subject's resistance has been broken, yet exceedingly difficult so long as resistance persists. Such resistance manifests itself in diverse ways: preparing material prior to the session—such as recounting a story—prolonged silences, unwarranted repetitions, fabricated tales, narrating films and other people's stories; in short, filling the space of the sessions with anything other than the individual's free association of thought. The principle of uninhibited speech, or free association, is the very principle upon which Freud's psychoanalysis was founded: speaking of everything and everywhere—the past and memories, wishes, hopes, and fantasies; pains, sufferings, and pleasures; disappointments, hatreds, and loves; last night's dreams, childhood dreams, and recurring, ordinary, or strange dreams; and the connection of all these with everyday life, waking and sleeping, work, relationships, groups, neighbours, and comings and goings… in short, whatever crosses the mind as though in the depths of human solitude.

The fifth and final clause is bringing major life decisions onto the couch. For during the stages of psychoanalysis, an individual may, under the sway of circumstances, take decisions that in practice are scarcely in his or her best interest. By examining and scrutinising these decisions on the couch, not only do the manner of their emergence, origin, and outcome become clear to the person, but pointless haste is also prevented. The psychoanalyst takes the necessary care so that the individual's inner journey across the desert of the self exerts the least possible disruption upon his or her daily life.

If, during the first six months of analysis, the individual has entered the stage of transference and situated himself or herself within the conditions described above, we may say that we have entered psychoanalytic work proper. From dream to dream, from wish to fantasy, from fantasy to memory, from memory to everyday occurrences, a vast volume of speech pours forth. At this stage, perseverance, tireless follow-through, repetition upon repetition, and never growing weary either of repeating or of continuing are what make progress possible. It is precisely these repetitions, forgettings, slips of the tongue, modes of pronouncing words, tears, and laughter that produce sparks of the individual's awareness regarding the workings of his or her own psyche. The psychoanalyst's task at this stage—apart from sustaining and managing the period of transference—is to guide the individual towards greater purity of speech and freer, more unguarded association, without reticence or holding back. Through conduct and speech, the psychoanalyst makes it clear that he or she has no intention whatsoever of offering moral guidance or lessons, nor of advising, directing, or judging the subject. For any judgemental or advisory intervention by the psychoanalyst fosters a desire in the subject to present himself or herself in a favourable light, and gradually the subject tailors his or her behaviour and speech to the psychoanalyst's theories, steering the psychoanalytic process towards a kind of play-acting.

Lacan maintains that during the first several months the psychoanalyst must be like a dead person who is nonetheless present—that and nothing more—and content himself or herself with minimal intervention. Parsimony in speech and action and the use of subtle cues can bring the subject to the starting point of understanding. Herein lies the psychoanalyst's art in what we call interpretation: leading the subject towards insight at the opportune moment—neither later nor earlier than the right time—occurs naturally through the psychoanalyst's prolonged listening to the subject's signifiers and entry into the field of those signifiers. Lacan proposes that the psychoanalyst formulate a structural hypothesis for each subject and endeavour, throughout the stages of psychoanalysis, to confirm or revise that hypothesis. At this stage, like an archaeologist excavating hundreds of tonnes of earth to reach an object hidden deep within the soil, the psychoanalyst enables the subject, through the outpouring of words, to draw gradually nearer to the object-cause of desire. At critical and difficult junctures, the psychoanalyst may at times offer solace, encouragement, and affirmation to the subject. As Freud himself declares, our cure operates through love—the very love that arises in the subject as transference. After this stage, it is preferable that this transference turn back towards the subject; the subject needs to reach the stage of narcissism and pass beyond it in order to attain love of the other and enter the civic world, the chain of generations and human beings: the other is an I in another position.

The subject learns to speak with his or her ears and listen with his or her mouth. The psychoanalyst's prolonged silence and occasional interventions engender this very attentiveness and sensitivity towards others and oneself in the subject as well. The subject comes to recognise his or her own share and the other's share in relation to reality, and to traverse each individual's existential truth in order to reach this rediscovered reality. The subject attains lucid oversight of his or her deep, inner identity—neither deeming himself or herself superior nor inferior. From this point, that inner filter of truth formed around the individual's identity becomes visible to him or her, and it is fitting to examine and test it against the touchstone of others' truths. It is here that the subject realises that the reality derived from his or her Real has passed through the filter of his or her truth-identity and is neither so singular, nor eternal, nor beyond doubt. And it is here that Lacan states that there is no Big Other of the Big Other for any subject.

In the final stage, the beginning of the subject's autonomy arrives. As psychoanalysis continues, the subject wishes, is able, and indeed has the right to engage with theoretical foundations, so as to link the personal experience of crossing the desert with theoretical principles. From time to time, the psychoanalyst may direct the subject towards educational tools such as books, films, lectures, and symposia, and occasionally a dialogue may take place concerning them. The subject draws closer to his or her own identity and grasps its share in relation to the other and the surrounding world, becomes able to name his or her psychic wounds and bring them into equilibrium. Should the subject wish, he or she may pursue a path of deeper knowledge and understanding—ordinarily continuing by enrolling in associations, working in groups with others, attending university courses, and sometimes aspiring to move towards assuming the responsibility of a psychoanalyst in the future. After several years of sustained commitment, the subject may take his or her place in the psychoanalyst's armchair.

Lacan holds that in order to begin practising, a psychoanalyst need only obtain authorisation from himself or herself and from a few other psychoanalysts. This statement follows the view of Freud, who for the first time opened the doors of psychoanalytic training and freed it from bureaucratic and academic formalities.

Clinical psychoanalysis is neither for cure nor for recovery; clinical psychoanalysis is for lucid insight (*eshrāf*), whereby the subject gradually advances towards culture, ascending knowledge, sublimation, and transcendence, while bodily needs take a lower rank relative to cultural needs. The subject himself or herself notices sooner and better than anyone else that he or she has undergone transformation.

In closing, I wish to add that numerous questions still remain unanswered and call for further dialogue:

- Is psychoanalysis possible for every subject, of every structure, in every culture, time, and place?

- Who is a psychoanalyst?

- What are the fundamental differences among the schools of clinical psychoanalysis?

- What are the domains of applied psychoanalysis, and how far does their scope extend?

- What are the boundaries separating psychoanalysis and Lacanian psychoanalysis from other fields of psychological knowledge?

- Is psychoanalysis possible in a language other than one's mother tongue?

- Can modern technology be used to extend psychoanalysis into the non-in-person (remote) sphere?

- How can one reach the end of psychoanalysis and recognise it?

- What is the theoretical relationship between psychoanalysis and the beliefs and religion of the individual and society?

1 — Presentation of the book *Télévision* by Jacques Lacan, French psychiatrist and psychoanalyst, translated by the Association of Persian-Speaking Psychoresearchers in France.

This book was published in a bilingual Persian–French edition in Tehran by Rokhdad-e No. The team of translators comprises: Houshang Giliardi, Bijan Hekmat, Hassan Makaremi, Nader Aghakhani, Fouad Saberan, Minou Eshghi, Akbar Pouyanfar, Valentine Shaouli, and Shiva Forouzan. One may say that the text of *Télévision* represents the essence of Lacan's work—the essence of his thought, his eloquence, and at the same time his relationship with others.

As recounted in the preface by the Association and the translators, the idea of translating the book began with this question: what can be done for psychoanalysis in Iran? That question, which was the starting point of our work, gradually evolved into: what can be done for psychoanalysis in the Persian language? We thought the first step was to bring together several Persian-speakers interested in researching the psyche. The transcript of Lacan's interview (*Télévision*) was an apt choice and kept our nine-member group busy and vibrant for two years. May it also encourage some of you, dear readers, to undertake such collaborative endeavours, so that psychoanalytic analysis may likewise contribute to the advancement of the human sciences, which enjoy such keen interest among Iranians. Answering the question "Why Jacques Lacan's *Télévision* in Persian?", they write: above all, why choose Jacques Lacan's *Télévision* instead of a glossary of terms, a lexicon, a guide to psychoanalytic concepts, or a textbook of psychopathology? Here, like Jacques Lacan himself, we selected a powerful and effective text so as to step directly into a major work in which one sees the crossroads of concepts upon which Lacan focused and which are, at the same time, highly advanced.

It must be admitted that even if approaches to psychoanalysis exist in the Persian language, such approaches are not numerous, and remain far behind its growth and expansion in France or other countries. The Persian-speaking world is brimming with the complexities of the thought of the ancients; so much so that, despite its distance from the past, it still possesses a subtlety, patience, and intelligence that have traversed millennia. It is the cradle of an underestimated—or better said, unknown and often misconstrued and indistinctly interpreted—civilisation, a civilisation that flourished across a vast territory, amidst contemplation and discernment. With such philosophical, poetic, and mystical traditions, this culture can undoubtedly today, relying upon science, absorb the achievements of psychoanalysis and benefit from its assistance. An event, a work: *Télévision* is truly a guide—brief, singular, and precise. A work that conceals neither theory, nor difficulties, nor conflicts. If this work was an event at the time of its appearance, it remains so today. It is a unique opportunity in which Jacques Lacan agrees to take part in a television programme and submit to the camera—he who, until shortly before then, had even fled from the microphone of a tape recorder.

An unconventional text of astonishing richness that strikes like a hammer, containing a century of psychoanalytic knowledge—its very first century. Unlike his seminars, where he delivered his remarks slowly and with pauses, here he speaks with unusual rapidity; Lacan does not summarise his work here, but rather circles within it by sketching a tableau and offering a fierce, incisive appraisal. In a language which, contrary to appearances, does not possess an ornate or pretentious syntax, yet upon closer inspection is simple and forceful—visible, illuminating, and trailblazing. Lacan traverses varied lines and influences with intense concentration and nervous, taut attention. Is it out of anger? In one scene, he points with his finger, clenches his fist, and makes the words tremble. All of these are certainly signs of immense tension. Taut, striving. Taut? Yes, at least so it appears. Small, arduous advances made alone across an imaginary ocean. Authoritative and haughty. He speaks of serious work. Lacan hammers away, strips bare, provokes, and summons—and calls this "monkey business". He is no clown; rather, he accentuates and sharpens the features, gives "form", and cries out against the backdrop he has constructed.

In the introduction to Jacques Lacan, French psychiatrist and psychoanalyst, we read: he is undoubtedly one of the continuators of Sigmund Freud's path in the twentieth century. As he himself puts it, "a Lacanian is someone who has read Freud." His works have exerted their greatest influence first upon the French school of psychoanalysis and subsequently in Latin America. His theory rests upon the functioning of the psyche, the presence of the unconscious within it, and its formation and operation. Jacques Lacan enumerated the importance of the signifier and its symbol in the unconscious, emphasised the presence of the unconscious in the "speaking and desiring being", and advanced the formula that "the unconscious is structured like a language". Like Sigmund Freud, Lacan bases the structure of the unconscious upon the same three pillars of neurosis, psychosis, and perversion. At the same time, in clinical practice, the number and duration of sessions may appear different across different schools. His invaluable body of work comprises his medical thesis, more than 27 seminars, essays and articles in two volumes entitled *Écrits* and *Autres Écrits*, lectures, and an interview (whose translation is presented to you here). Jacques Lacan's seminars, all transcribed from his oral teachings, have mostly been published to date.

His addressees are psychoanalysts, yet his teachings extend far beyond them. One need not necessarily be a psychoanalyst to understand his discourse. Today his ideas are taught across the world in diverse academic and non-academic disciplines, such as philosophy, linguistics, literary and art criticism, aesthetics, architecture, law, and more.

His familiarity with the structuralists in the first half of the twentieth century placed in his hands an instrument enabling him to press topology (the science of spatiality, the study of neighbourhood and proximity) and formalisations derived from modern mathematics into the service of teaching and transmitting his discoveries. On the one hand, Lacan relies upon empirical and clinical work as a physician and psychiatrist; on the other, upon deep study of the writings of Freud, the structuralists, and the linguists. In his work, the imprint of Freud's clinical and theoretical findings and concepts is clearly visible. His art lies in structuring Freud's ideas. He viewed the unconscious as a structure and thereby ascribed to it both formation and functioning. He linked fantasy, speech, need, desire, and the word (signifier and signified) to one another through precise, formalised definitions. Because he made language, speech, the word, and their relationship with each individual's unconscious the foundational principle, play with words and etymologies, linguistic structure, and writing serve as the principal instruments of his work. Beyond university settings, training and clinical-care environments—such as psychiatric hospitals, psychotherapy institutes, and networks of associations devoted to Jacques Lacan's work—are engaged across various countries in advancing his thought.

On the other hand, comparing Jacques Lacan's works with those of other psychoanalysts and putting these works to the test in the field of clinical practice is likewise a subject of study at research institutes worldwide. Literary and artistic criticism grounded in Jacques Lacan's ideas has today become widespread, meaning that Jacques Lacan's thought is alive. His complex, prolific, and distinctive personality is revealed in the short anecdotes his students recount of him here and there. Towards the end of his career, his language and theory attain a singular complexity—as though, like painters, he gravitates towards a kind of abstract art in formulating his thought.

Translating a major work by Jacques Lacan—one of the most influential psychoanalysts after Freud—by a group of specialists, and publishing it in a bilingual edition in the original French alongside Persian, can represent a significant step towards continuing such initiatives.

This note is a descriptive report of the lecture *How Does a Lacanian Psychoanalyst Work? (Clinical Psychoanalysis from Lacan's Perspective)*, delivered on 18 Mehr 1393 (10 October 2014) at the Siavashan Centre. The translation of Lacan's book *Télévision* was also presented:

How Does a Lacanian Psychoanalyst Work? (Clinical Psychoanalysis from Lacan's Perspective)

Dr Hassan Makaremi: clinical psychoanalyst, researcher at the Sorbonne University, Paris; Vice-President of the Association of Psychoresearchers and Director of Training of the Association of Psychoanalysts of the Limousin region in France. He has participated to date in fifty symposia on psychoanalysis and applied psychoanalysis and published more than ten books in French and Persian.

fr.title: Le mariage blanc en Iran
fr.executive_summary: En Iran, l'expression « mariage blanc » désigne la cohabitation d'un homme et d'une femme sous un même toit sans que leur union ait été enregistrée comme mariage temporaire ou permanent, ni qu'un contrat religieux (sigheh) ait été prononcé. Il n'existe aucune statistique officielle sur ces cas de cohabitation, mais depuis quelques années, les médias consacrent des reportages à ce…
fr.body_markdown:
En Iran, l'expression « mariage blanc » désigne la cohabitation d'un homme et d'une femme sous un même toit sans que leur union ait été enregistrée comme mariage temporaire ou permanent, ni qu'un contrat religieux (*sigheh*) ait été prononcé. Il n'existe aucune statistique officielle sur ces cas de cohabitation, mais depuis quelques années, les médias consacrent des reportages à ce phénomène — ou « mode de vie » — et font état de son essor dans les grandes villes. Les autorités gouvernementales iraniennes ont elles aussi évoqué ici et là l'existence d'une telle forme de vie commune.

Ainsi, en Dey 1391 (décembre 2012 – janvier 2013), Morteza Talaei, alors président de la commission culturelle et sociale du Conseil municipal de Téhéran, avait qualifié, dans un entretien accordé à l'agence ILNA, la vie commune de jeunes femmes et de jeunes hommes sans mariage dans le nord de Téhéran de « constitution de vies de célibataires » et de « nouvelle forme de fléau social aux conséquences dangereuses ».

Ces dernières années, le nombre de mariages en Iran a amorcé une baisse, hommes et femmes ne parvenant plus, en raison de difficultés économiques et sociales, à fonder un foyer. Selon les statistiques de l'Organisation de l'état civil, au cours des cinq premiers mois de l'année en cours, 288 183 mariages ont été enregistrés, soit une diminution de 4,6 % par rapport à la même période de l'année précédente. Dimanche également, l'agence ISNA a rapporté que Mohammadi Golpayegani, chef de cabinet d'Ali Khamenei, avait « critiqué » le mariage blanc.

Selon ISNA, lors de la cérémonie d'inauguration des projets de la Fondation Barakat dans le village de Soulghan, Mohammadi Golpayegani s'est interrogé sur le sens du mariage blanc et sur ce qu'il advient de la descendance d'une telle union, déclarant : « Il ne faudra pas longtemps pour que la lignée légitime de ceux qui choisissent ce mode de vie disparaisse et qu'ils engendrent des enfants illégitimes. Le souverain islamique doit combattre avec fermeté ce mode de vie. »
L'émission d'analyse de l'actualité d'aujourd'hui, en compagnie de Hassan Makaremi, psychanalyste et chercheur, se penchera sur les causes du choix de ce mode de vie ainsi que sur les racines de la sensibilité des autorités à son égard.

en.title: White Marriage in Iran
en.executive_summary: In Iran, 'white marriage' refers to a woman and a man cohabiting under the same roof without their union being registered as a temporary or permanent marriage, and without a religious marriage formula (sigheh) having been recited. While no official statistics exist regarding this form of cohabitation, media reports over the past several years have addressed this…
en.body_markdown:
In Iran, 'white marriage' refers to a woman and a man cohabiting under the same roof without their union being registered as a temporary or permanent marriage, and without a religious marriage formula (*sigheh*) having been recited. While no official statistics exist regarding this form of cohabitation, media reports over the past several years have addressed this phenomenon—or 'lifestyle'—and noted its growing prevalence in major cities. Iranian state officials have also occasionally referred to the existence of this form of shared living.

For instance, in Dey 1391 [December 2012–January 2013], Morteza Talaei, then head of the Cultural and Social Commission of the Tehran City Council, in an interview with the ILNA news agency, described unmarried men and women living together in northern Tehran as "forming single-person households" and "a new type of social pathology with dangerous consequences".

Marriage rates in Iran have been declining in recent years, as women and men are unable to start families due to economic and social difficulties. According to statistics from the National Organisation for Civil Registration, 288,183 marriages were registered during the first five months of the current year, representing a 4.6 per cent decrease compared with the same period last year. On Sunday, the ISNA news agency also reported that Mohammadi Golpayegani, Chief of Staff to Ali Khamenei, had "criticised" white marriage.

According to ISNA, speaking at the inauguration ceremony for Barakat Foundation projects in the village of Sulqan, Mohammadi Golpayegani asked what white marriage meant and what would become of the offspring of such unions, stating: "Before long, the legitimate lineage of those who choose this way of life will perish, and they will become illegitimate. The Islamic ruler must confront this lifestyle forcefully."
Today's news commentary programme, featuring Hassan Makaremi, psychoanalyst and researcher, will look at the reasons behind choosing this lifestyle as well as the roots of the authorities' sensitivity towards it.

fr.title: Deuxième colloque des chercheurs iraniens en sciences du psychisme à l'étranger
fr.executive_summary: Notre culture et notre psychisme. Une connaissance plus approfondie de notre culture et de notre psychisme, d'une part, et la vigilance collective de nous autres Iraniens, d'autre part, peuvent-elles développer des dispositions constructives et constituer un antidote à nos traits de caractère inappropriés ? Depuis fort longtemps, des écrits d'Hérodote il y a vingt-cinq siècles jusqu'aux divers orientalistes des cinq derniers siècles,…
fr.body_markdown:
Notre culture et notre psychisme

Une connaissance plus approfondie de notre culture et de notre psychisme, d'une part, et la vigilance collective de nous autres Iraniens, d'autre part, peuvent-elles développer des dispositions constructives et constituer un antidote à nos traits de caractère inappropriés ?
Depuis fort longtemps, des écrits d'Hérodote il y a vingt-cinq siècles aux divers orientalistes des cinq derniers siècles, des intellectuels de l'époque de la révolution constitutionnelle tels qu'Akhundzadeh et Talibov jusqu'à Jamalzadeh et Sadegh Hedayat, et au cours des dernières décennies dans de nombreux ouvrages publiés, notre manière d'être a été mise en question. Beaucoup de propos ont été tenus sur nos traits de caractère et nos dispositions psychiques en tant qu'Iraniens ; dans quelle mesure de tels discours sont-ils fondés ? Voici un aperçu de ces jugements :

Les Iraniens manquent de solidarité nationale ; les Iraniens se croient supérieurs aux autres nations ; les Iraniens sont portés à l'ostentation et pratiquent le *ta'arof* [politesse cérémonielle], d'où une habitude du mensonge ; les Iraniens sont individualistes et dépourvus d'esprit de travail collectif, érigeant ce qui leur plaît en critère ; les Iraniens éprouvent de la jalousie face à la réussite d'autrui ; les Iraniens sont égocentriques ; les Iraniens se prétendent touche-à-tout ; les Iraniens ne sont pas ponctuels ; bien qu'ils réussissent individuellement, notamment à l'étranger, dès qu'il est question de travail d'équipe, ils s'y dérobent. Des notions telles que l'honneur (*aberu*), le respect, l'honneur familial (*namus*) et sa sacralisation revêtent pour les Iraniens une importance particulière ; les Iraniens sont très intelligents, cultivés et créatifs ; les Iraniens sont très hospitaliers et chaleureux ; les Iraniens sont patriotes et fiers d'être iraniens. Par ailleurs, on nous juge quelque peu mélancoliques, enclins à une nostalgie passéiste, convaincus d'un destin préétabli selon lequel nous ne sommes que des hôtes de passage en ce monde éphémère, au point d'en venir parfois à conclure que les jeux sont faits et qu'il n'y a plus aucun espoir d'aucun côté.
Ces traits de caractère sont-ils propres aux seuls Iraniens ? Dans quelle mesure renvoient-ils à notre culture et jusqu'à quel point procèdent-ils du fonctionnement de notre psychisme ? Ces traits sont-ils consubstantiels à notre être ou susceptibles de transformation ?
Pourrons-nous, au cours de ce colloque, et tout particulièrement dans l'espace de la diaspora iranienne, apporter des éléments de réponse à certaines de ces questions ? Nous le verrons ensemble.

en.title: Second Symposium of Iranian Psychological Researchers Abroad
en.executive_summary: Our Culture and Our Psyche. Can a deeper familiarity with our own culture and psyche on the one hand, and the collective vigilance of us Iranians on the other, foster constructive dispositions and serve as an antidote to our unhelpful traits? From ancient times—in the writings of Herodotus twenty-five centuries ago, to various Orientalists over the past five…
en.body_markdown:
Our Culture and Our Psyche

Can a deeper familiarity with our own culture and psyche on the one hand, and the collective vigilance of us Iranians on the other, foster constructive dispositions and serve as an antidote to our unhelpful traits?
From ancient times—in the writings of Herodotus twenty-five centuries ago, to various Orientalists over the past five centuries, to intellectuals of the Constitutional Revolution era such as Akhundzadeh and Talibov, through to Jamalzadeh and Sadegh Hedayat, and in recent decades numerous books—works have been published that have challenged our ways of being. Much has been said about the characteristics and temperament of us Iranians; to what extent are such claims valid? Here is an outline of these assertions:

Iranians lack national solidarity; Iranians consider themselves superior to other nations; Iranians are given to pretence and practise *ta'arof* [ceremonial politeness], and are therefore accustomed to lying; Iranians are individualistic and lack a spirit of collective endeavour, making whatever suits them the standard; Iranians are envious of others' success; Iranians are self-centred; Iranians claim to be jacks-of-all-trades; Iranians are unpunctual; although individually successful—especially abroad—the moment teamwork is mentioned, they flee from it. Matters such as honour (*aberu*), respect, family honour (*namus*), and the cult of honour hold special importance for Iranians; Iranians are highly intelligent, cultured, and creative; Iranians are remarkably hospitable and warm-hearted. Iranians are patriotic and take pride in being Iranian. On the other hand, we are perceived as somewhat melancholic, inclined towards the past, believers in a primordial fate according to which we are merely fleeting guests in this transient world—at times even concluding that it is too late and there is no hope from any quarter.
Do these traits apply solely to us Iranians? To what extent do these dispositions stem from our culture, and how far do they originate in the workings of our psyche? Are these traits ingrained in us, or are they capable of change?
Can we, at this symposium—particularly within the space of Iranians living abroad—answer even a portion of these questions? Together, we shall see.
