en.body_markdown:
[Psychoanalysis and Culture 2](http://www.radiozamaneh.com/52550)

Undoubtedly, two great discoveries illuminated the twentieth century. First, Sigmund Freud demonstrated that the human being possesses an "unconscious" that operates like a stranger within, with a behaviour and functioning all its own. Then Einstein discovered the laws governing the release of energy within the nucleus of the atom. Just as Einstein's discovery, owing to straightforward experimentation and the familiar logic of cause and effect, easily found its way into the realm of technology, the university, and subsequently general public knowledge, Freud's discovery travelled a long road before becoming widespread and properly understood. Freud's great discovery and its consequences still remain unknown or misunderstood in many societies on account of religious, traditional, political, and ideological resistances.

A precise and profound understanding of the discoveries of Freud and his followers such as Jacques Lacan, along with the translation of their works by clinical psychoanalysts who engage closely with these concepts and with clinical experience (between the individual and the psychoanalyst, and in relation to the individual's speech), is one way to disseminate this knowledge in societies such as Iran. Until that time, however, perhaps by applying the implications of Freud's findings in the fields of sociology, history, anthropology, and mythology, a modest path may be opened towards clearing away the tarnish of misunderstanding surrounding the phenomenon of Freud's discovery, and our compatriots—albeit very late, after the passage of a century—may be introduced to a small part of how his great discovery works.

The Achievements of Sigmund Freud

Sigmund Freud was born in 1856 in what is now the [Czech Republic](http://fa.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D8%AC%D9%85%D9%87%D9%88%D8%B1%DB%8C_%DA%86%DA%A9) and was then the [Austrian Empire](http://fa.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D8%A7%D9%85%D9%BE%D8%B1%D8%A7%D8%AA%D9%88%D8%B1%DB%8C_%D8%A7%D8%AA%D8%B1%DB%8C%D8%B4), and died in 1939. He was a psychiatrist and neurologist and the founder of the discipline of [psychoanalysis](http://fa.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D8%B1%D9%88%D8%A7%D9%86%E2%80%8C%DA%A9%D8%A7%D9%88%DB%8C). His family were [Ashkenazi](http://fa.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D8%A7%D8%B4%DA%A9%D9%86%D8%A7%D8%B2%DB%8C) [Jews](http://fa.wikipedia.org/wiki/%DB%8C%D9%87%D9%88%D8%AF%DB%8C%D8%AA). His father was a wool merchant who, three years after Sigmund's birth, moved with his family to Leipzig because of financial difficulties and shortly thereafter emigrated to Vienna. Freud entered the Faculty of Medicine at the [University of Vienna](http://fa.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D8%AF%D8%A7%D9%86%D8%B4%DA%AF%D8%A7%D9%87_%D9%88%DB%8C%D9%86) in 1873 and obtained his medical degree in 1882. At that same time he married Martha Bernays and began working at the Vienna General Hospital. In 1885 he travelled to [Paris](http://fa.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D9%BE%D8%A7%D8%B1%DB%8C%D8%B3) for neurological research and at the [Salpêtrière Hospital](http://fa.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=%D8%A8%DB%8C%D9%85%D8%A7%D8%B1%D8%B3%D8%AA%D8%A7%D9%86_%D8%B3%D8%A7%D9%84%E2%80%8C%D9%BE%D8%AA%D8%B1%DB%8C%D9%87&action=edit&redlink=1&preload=%D8%A7%D9%84%DA%AF%D9%88:%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%AF+%D9%85%D9%82%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%87/%D8%A7%D8%B3%D8%AA%D8%AE%D9%88%D8%A7%D9%86%E2%80%8C%D8%A8%D9%86%D8%AF%DB%8C&editintro=%D8%A7%D9%84%DA%AF%D9%88:%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%AF+%D9%85%D9%82%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%87/%D8%A7%D8%AF%DB%8C%D8%AA%E2%80%8C%D9%86%D9%88%D8%AA%DB%8C%D8%B3&summary=%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%AF+%DB%8C%DA%A9+%D9%85%D9%82%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%87+%D9%86%D9%88+%D8%A7%D8%B2+%D8%B7%D8%B1%DB%8C%D9%82+%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%AF%DA%AF%D8%B1&nosummary=&prefix=&minor=&create=%D8%AF%D8%B1%D8%B3%D8%AA+%DA%A9%D8%B1%D8%AF%D9%86+%D9%85%D9%82%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%87+%D8%AC%D8%AF%DB%8C%D8%AF) became acquainted with [Jean-Martin Charcot](http://fa.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=%DA%98%D8%A7%D9%86_%D9%85%D8%A7%D8%B1%D8%AA%D9%86_%D8%B4%D8%A7%D8%B1%DA%A9%D9%88&action=edit&redlink=1&preload=%D8%A7%D9%84%DA%AF%D9%88:%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%AF+%D9%85%D9%82%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%87/%D8%A7%D8%B3%D8%AA%D8%AE%D9%88%D8%A7%D9%86%E2%80%8C%D8%A8%D9%86%D8%AF%DB%8C&editintro=%D8%A7%D9%84%DA%AF%D9%88:%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%AF+%D9%85%D9%82%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%87/%D8%A7%D8%AF%DB%8C%D8%AA%E2%80%8C%D9%86%D9%88%D8%AA%DB%8C%D8%B3&summary=%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%AF+%DB%8C%DA%A9+%D9%85%D9%82%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%87+%D9%86%D9%88+%D8%A7%D8%B2+%D8%B7%D8%B1%DB%8C%D9%82+%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%AF%DA%AF%D8%B1&nosummary=&prefix=&minor=&create=%D8%AF%D8%B1%D8%B3%D8%AA+%DA%A9%D8%B1%D8%AF%D9%86+%D9%85%D9%82%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%87+%D8%AC%D8%AF%DB%8C%D8%AF), who was regarded as the greatest psychiatrist of the age. Charcot was working on the application of [hypnosis](http://fa.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D9%87%DB%8C%D9%BE%D9%86%D9%88%D8%AA%DB%8C%D8%B2%D9%85) in the treatment of [hysteria](http://fa.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D9%87%DB%8C%D8%B3%D8%AA%D8%B1%DB%8C).

Freud then returned to Vienna, opened a practice, and began treating psychiatric patients using hypnosis. In 1896, following several investigations, he began examining, researching, and treating patients together with [Josef Breuer](http://fa.wikipedia.org/wiki/%DA%98%D9%88%D8%B2%D9%81_%D8%A8%D8%B1%D9%88%DB%8C%D8%B1) by a method he himself termed psychoanalysis. Freud later decided to employ [free association](http://fa.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=%D8%AA%D8%AF%D8%A7%D8%B9%DB%8C_%D8%A2%D8%B2%D8%A7%D8%AF&action=edit&redlink=1&preload=%D8%A7%D9%84%DA%AF%D9%88:%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%AF+%D9%85%D9%82%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%87/%D8%A7%D8%B3%D8%AA%D8%AE%D9%88%D8%A7%D9%86%E2%80%8C%D8%A8%D9%86%D8%AF%DB%8C&editintro=%D8%A7%D9%84%DA%AF%D9%88:%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%AF+%D9%85%D9%82%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%87/%D8%A7%D8%AF%DB%8C%D8%AA%E2%80%8C%D9%86%D9%88%D8%AA%DB%8C%D8%B3&summary=%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%AF+%DB%8C%DA%A9+%D9%85%D9%82%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%87+%D9%86%D9%88+%D8%A7%D8%B2+%D8%B7%D8%B1%DB%8C%D9%82+%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%AF%DA%AF%D8%B1&nosummary=&prefix=&minor=&create=%D8%AF%D8%B1%D8%B3%D8%AA+%DA%A9%D8%B1%D8%AF%D9%86+%D9%85%D9%82%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%87+%D8%AC%D8%AF%DB%8C%D8%AF) and the analysis of dreams and sleep, instead of hypnosis, for diagnosing and treating psychiatric patients. At first, holding patients' heads, he would ask them to say whatever came into their minds. After a time, he discontinued physical contact and left the patient lying freely on the couch. Freud recounts that it was the patients themselves who, through their behaviour, taught him: "Be quiet and listen to me. I know better myself where my suffering comes from."

In 1901 Freud founded the [International Psychoanalytical Association](http://fa.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=%D8%A7%D9%86%D8%AC%D9%85%D9%86_%D8%A8%DB%8C%D9%86%E2%80%8C%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D9%84%D9%84%DB%8C_%D8%B1%D9%88%D8%A7%D9%86%E2%80%8C%DA%A9%D8%A7%D9%88%DB%8C&action=edit&redlink=1&preload=%D8%A7%D9%84%DA%AF%D9%88:%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%AF+%D9%85%D9%82%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%87/%D8%A7%D8%B3%D8%AA%D8%AE%D9%88%D8%A7%D9%86%E2%80%8C%D8%A8%D9%86%D8%AF%DB%8C&editintro=%D8%A7%D9%84%DA%AF%D9%88:%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%AF+%D9%85%D9%82%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%87/%D8%A7%D8%AF%DB%8C%D8%AA%E2%80%8C%D9%86%D9%88%D8%AA%DB%8C%D8%B3&summary=%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%AF+%DB%8C%DA%A9+%D9%85%D9%82%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%87+%D9%86%D9%88+%D8%A7%D8%B2+%D8%B7%D8%B1%DB%8C%D9%82+%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%AF%DA%AF%D8%B1&nosummary=&prefix=&minor=&create=%D8%AF%D8%B1%D8%B3%D8%AA+%DA%A9%D8%B1%D8%AF%D9%86+%D9%85%D9%82%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%87+%D8%AC%D8%AF%DB%8C%D8%AF), and in 1902 he established the Wednesday Psychological Society, which carried out its work by holding meetings every Wednesday at his home. In 1909, accompanied by [Carl Jung](http://fa.wikipedia.org/wiki/%DA%A9%D8%A7%D8%B1%D9%84_%DB%8C%D9%88%D9%86%DA%AF) and [Sándor Ferenczi, he travelled to America at the invitation of Clark University in Massachusetts. Freud](http://fa.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=%D8%B3%D8%A7%D9%86%D8%AF%D9%88%D8%B1_%D9%81%D8%B1%D9%86%D8%B2%DB%8C&action=edit&redlink=1&preload=%D8%A7%D9%84%DA%AF%D9%88:%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%AF+%D9%85%D9%82%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%87/%D8%A7%D8%B3%D8%AA%D8%AE%D9%88%D8%A7%D9%86%E2%80%8C%D8%A8%D9%86%D8%AF%DB%8C&editintro=%D8%A7%D9%84%DA%AF%D9%88:%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%AF+%D9%85%D9%82%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%87/%D8%A7%D8%AF%DB%8C%D8%AA%E2%80%8C%D9%86%D9%88%D8%AA%DB%8C%D8%B3&summary=%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%AF+%DB%8C%DA%A9+%D9%85%D9%82%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%87+%D9%86%D9%88+%D8%A7%D8%B2+%D8%B7%D8%B1%DB%8C%D9%82+%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%AF%DA%AF%D8%B1&nosummary=&prefix=&minor=&create=%D8%AF%D8%B1%D8%B3%D8%AA+%DA%A9%D8%B1%D8%AF%D9%86+%D9%85%D9%82%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%87+%D8%AC%D8%AF%DB%8C%D8%AF) had to undergo surgery in 1923 to remove a cancerous tumour from the roof of his mouth, during which a major portion of the right side of his palate was removed.

With the [Annexation of Austria](http://fa.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%AD%D8%A7%D9%82_%D8%A7%D8%AA%D8%B1%DB%8C%D8%B4&action=edit&redlink=1&preload=%D8%A7%D9%84%DA%AF%D9%88:%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%AF+%D9%85%D9%82%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%87/%D8%A7%D8%B3%D8%AA%D8%AE%D9%88%D8%A7%D9%86%E2%80%8C%D8%A8%D9%86%D8%AF%DB%8C&editintro=%D8%A7%D9%84%DA%AF%D9%88:%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%AF+%D9%85%D9%82%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%87/%D8%A7%D8%AF%DB%8C%D8%AA%E2%80%8C%D9%86%D9%88%D8%AA%DB%8C%D8%B3&summary=%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%AF+%DB%8C%DA%A9+%D9%85%D9%82%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%87+%D9%86%D9%88+%D8%A7%D8%B2+%D8%B7%D8%B1%DB%8C%D9%82+%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%AF%DA%AF%D8%B1&nosummary=&prefix=&minor=&create=%D8%AF%D8%B1%D8%B3%D8%AA+%DA%A9%D8%B1%D8%AF%D9%86+%D9%85%D9%82%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%87+%D8%AC%D8%AF%DB%8C%D8%AF) to Germany in 1938 and the escalation of [anti-Semitism](http://fa.wikipedia.org/wiki/%DB%8C%D9%87%D9%88%D8%AF%DB%8C%E2%80%8C%D8%B3%D8%AA%DB%8C%D8%B2%DB%8C) in Vienna, Freud resolved to emigrate. With the assistance of the American diplomat William Bullitt and Princess Marie Bonaparte, the French psychoanalyst, he left Vienna with his family in 1938 bound for Paris, and shortly afterwards moved from there to [London](http://fa.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D9%84%D9%86%D8%AF%D9%86).

[The Interpretation of Dreams](http://fa.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=%D8%AA%D8%B9%D8%A8%DB%8C%D8%B1_%D8%AE%D9%88%D8%A7%D8%A8&action=edit&redlink=1&preload=%D8%A7%D9%84%DA%AF%D9%88:%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%AF+%D9%85%D9%82%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%87/%D8%A7%D8%B3%D8%AA%D8%AE%D9%88%D8%A7%D9%86%E2%80%8C%D8%A8%D9%86%D8%AF%DB%8C&editintro=%D8%A7%D9%84%DA%AF%D9%88:%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%AF+%D9%85%D9%82%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%87/%D8%A7%D8%AF%DB%8C%D8%AA%E2%80%8C%D9%86%D9%88%D8%AA%DB%8C%D8%B3&summary=%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%AF+%DB%8C%DA%A9+%D9%85%D9%82%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%87+%D9%86%D9%88+%D8%A7%D8%B2+%D8%B7%D8%B1%DB%8C%D9%82+%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%AF%DA%AF%D8%B1&nosummary=&prefix=&minor=&create=%D8%AF%D8%B1%D8%B3%D8%AA+%DA%A9%D8%B1%D8%AF%D9%86+%D9%85%D9%82%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%87+%D8%AC%D8%AF%DB%8C%D8%AF) (1900); In this section we merely name thirteen achievements of Sigmund Freud, leaving further elaboration and explanation for another occasion:

– The discovery of the unconscious.

– Defining the stages of psychoanalysis.

– The discovery of the unconscious as a locus within the human psyche grounded in repressions from birth.

– The discovery of the relationship of the unconscious with repressions and unfulfilled wishes. The word "unconscious" had been employed before Freud and existed in ancient cultures as well. Writers such as Shakespeare, Balzac, Tolstoy, Dostoevsky, and Chekhov alluded to the unconscious in their works. Hafez, too, leads us to the threshold of the unconscious:

Within my weary heart I know not who it is / That I am silent while he is in lamentation and uproar.

– Placing the human being on a mobile path and in continuous transformation after birth.

– Bringing the human being into the field of human culture. Freud was a courageous physician who broke the boundaries of the mechanical, biological, anatomical, social, and administrative body, and restored the precise demarcation between human and animal. In his second topography, he centred the division of the psyche on three agencies—the "Superego", the "Ego", and the "Id" (which is our animal part)—and on speech, discourse, and language within the structure of the unconscious.

– Carrying culture into the depths of the human being, from the very dawn of humanity's emergence; he accomplished this vital work by two means: employing anthropology and ethnology, and attending to oral culture, or myth, such that he drew upon the myths of Oedipus and Eros. With *Totem and Taboo*, Freud demonstrated that every human being, from birth to adulthood, traverses the developmental stages of *Homo sapiens*. For example, a child of six or seven becomes ready to read and write in the same manner as our ancestors seven or eight thousand years ago.

– Gathering human pleasures from infancy around a single foundation and daring to speak of infantile sexuality. He became the founder of the role of sexuality in the formation of the psyche and, as the father of sexology and sexotherapy, provoked intense hatred in his own time by discovering and insisting upon the presence and importance of sexuality in children.

– Founding literary and artistic criticism through close attentiveness to speech, writings, and so forth. Today, in many academic environments—especially in art and literature—psychoanalysis holds a special place.

– Conducting profound work on the phenomenon of dreams, both on the history of dreams and on separating dreams from the supernatural, as well as discovering the role of dreams in deciphering the functioning of the unconscious.

– Demonstrating that the concept of God is likewise a human invention, and carrying out deep investigations into the history of the emergence of the Jewish religion.

– Setting aside hypnosis and medication in the treatment of neuroses.

– Deep respect for *laïcité* (secularism) and calling into question human and administrative systems of organisation.

– Expanding the human being across the three worlds of sleep, dream, and reality.

Hafez says: Shall I go mad in this obsession that night till day / I see a peri in my dream and converse with the moon?

The Achievements of Jacques Lacan

Jacques Lacan (1901–1981), French psychiatrist and psychoanalyst, is beyond doubt one of the continuators of Sigmund Freud's path in the twentieth century. He himself declares that he is "one who has read Freud". His works exerted their greatest influence first upon the French school of psychoanalysis and subsequently in Latin America. His theory rests upon the psyche, the presence of the unconscious within it, its formation, and its functioning. Above all, he regarded himself as the discoverer of the "object-cause of desire" (*objet petit a*). In 1953 he founded his school under the name Société française de psychanalyse in Paris, and after training hundreds of clinical psychoanalysts, dissolved it in 1980. Since that date, his disciples have established diverse associations of psychoanalysts across France, Europe, and the world.

Lacan's collected works comprise more than twenty-five seminars, essays and articles (in two volumes, *Écrits* and *Autres écrits*), and various interviews. Jacques Lacan's Seminars, all of which are transcriptions of his oral lectures, have for the most part been published to date and are taught as the foundations of his thought in various schools of psychoanalysis. The oral language of these seminars, which adds to the complexity of his presentation of the functioning of the psyche's structure, poses considerable difficulty for readers and especially for translators of his works.

Some hold that understanding Lacan's works is possible only on condition that one is active in the field of clinical psychoanalysis—as though one must already know him in order to understand his words!

Lacan's ideas have extended beyond the field of clinical psychoanalysis and are taught in various university faculties of philosophy, linguistics, literary and art criticism, aesthetics, architecture, and law.

Whereas Sigmund Freud studied the human being beyond the "body", down into the depths of mythology, oral culture, and *Homo sapiens sapiens*, Jacques Lacan made language and its structure, the word, and above all the acoustic image of the word (the signifier) the fundamental element of his work; and with his major discovery—"the unconscious is structured like a language"—he re-examined the human psyche within the field of the "speaking human", the "desiring human", and the "acting and agentive human". His acquaintance with the structuralists in the first half of the twentieth century placed in his hands the initial tools to combine the use of topology (the science of spatiality and proximity) and formalisation derived from modern mathematics with his discoveries as an instrument at the service of teaching and learning.

Lacan's empirical and clinical work as a physician and psychiatrist as the bedrock of his thought, on the one hand, and his familiarity with Freud together with his contemporaneity and intellectual kinship with the structuralists, on the other, enabled him to construct his thought upon these three axes. Lacan also chose three modes of expression—oral, written, and topological-mathematical—to articulate his ideas. Thus he became at once a researcher of the psyche, an empirical clinical psychoanalyst, and a teacher of his findings, such that in his works three dimensions coexist simultaneously side by side: clinical experience, oral-written discourse, and formalisation employing topology and the language of modern mathematics.

These three dimensions enable students to follow Lacan's studies on clinical cases, his explication and analysis of literary and artistic works, historical realities, and fundamental philosophical theories. In Lacan's writings, the traces of Freud's clinical and theoretical ideas and findings are clearly visible. His art lies in giving structural form to Freud's ideas. He viewed the unconscious as a structure and therefore ascribed to it a genesis and a mode of functioning. He linked phantasm, speech, need, desire, and the word (signifier and signified) to one another through precise, formalised definitions. Because he made language, speech, and the word primary, play on words and etymologies, the structure of language, and writing became the principal instruments of his work—which is precisely why translating his work is all the more difficult.

Several Examples of the Relationship Between Signifier and Signified

The essence of the hypothesis of contemporary psychoanalysis is that "everything is language". The structure of the human unconscious is like the structure of a language (the mother tongue, the infant's relation to the mother, and the formation of the unconscious in the first years of life). Signs or acoustic images form an ensemble that, like a "text", writes our unconscious. These "signs" migrate from one individual to another, such that one cannot truly know who owns these signs; and thus it is that through "economy of speech", "polysemy", "condensation and conciseness", and the use of "wordplay and conceptual play"—in short, what in the literary arena is known as poetry and the architecture of speech, and in everyday life is called proverbs, jokes, riddles, curses, and the like—an ensemble of "signs" practically lives within the fluid space between each and every one of us, forming the foundation of today's culture and yesterday's myth.

Along this long road we learn not to become ensnared in the game of our own "signifiers", allowing ourselves to take our worlds—including our dreams and phantasms—seriously. Going further still, we become sensitive to delusions as well: losing ourselves in "the reality of others", as the other of the Other; beholding this invisible thing in the bubble offered to us by the image of a virtual world; looking into this grand "masquerade" and the invisible networks of relations that unite individuals to make of them other inseparable wholes. Like the ensemble of acoustic images of words invented up to the present day by us, the creators of symbols, which ultimately circulate so freely to and fro that one cannot tell which of them belongs to whom. It is as though we bring these symbols into existence, pass them on to the other, immerse ourselves in them, and eventually forget them, only to take them up again at another time and carry on the work until the end—like the boundary, that well-known boundary, that point of being which is the totality of these symbols and which, contrary to supposition, is not so fixed after all.

Lacan takes three elements—the Real, the Symbolic, and the Imaginary (conjecture)—as the basis of his work, such that the Real is perceptible only through our senses; symbolisation, which began with gesture and movement and was completed through the use of the object and finally the invention of the word and language; and the Imaginary, which is the continuation of the primordial phantasm after birth that enables us to endure and wait until the response to the body's need arrives. Let us cite an example from the noble sage Ferdowsi and read together his opening verses:

In the name of the Lord of Soul and Wisdom, beyond whom thought cannot pass,

Lord of Name and Lord of Place, Lord who grants sustenance and guides the way,

Lord of the cosmos and the revolving firmament, illuminator of the moon, Venus, and the sun.

He is above name, sign, and conjecture; He is the painter of the exalted jewel.

With bodily eyes you shall not see the Creator; do not vex your two seeing eyes.

Nor can thought find a path unto Him, for He is beyond name and beyond place.

Whatever speech passes beyond these jewels, neither soul nor wisdom can find a path to Him.

In the first hemistich of the first verse, from "Lord of Soul and Wisdom", to the second hemistich of the final verse, "neither soul nor wisdom can find a path to Him", we have completed a seamless circle. Between thought—along with its instrument, speech—and God lies an impassable wall. Elsewhere, in praise of wisdom, Ferdowsi esteems it superior to all else that God has bestowed:

Know wisdom to be eternal life; know wisdom to be the very substance of living.

Seven centuries before Descartes, Ferdowsi arrived at the chain linking thinking and being. Soul situates the human being among living creatures, while wisdom elevates the human being above all other life, and he calls God the painter of this "exalted jewel"; elsewhere, in defining the moving creature—the animal—he says:

Neither an articulate tongue nor a seeker of wisdom, nourishing the body on thorns and chaff.

God, quite apart from being Lord of the cosmos, the firmament, the moon, the sun, and Venus, is the Lord who grants sustenance and guides the way. Ferdowsi's God is the Lord of Name and Place. Speech is, in a sense, the bestowing of names upon things and concepts, and likewise the naming of conjecture, imagination, illusions, supposition, and mental imagery. Speech takes shape from institutionalising past words. Every institutionalised element, fertilised over the course of time, grows richer and deeper. The consonance of institutionalised elements leads to the invention of new ones, and it is thus that from a few initial sounds people create words and speech. Initially, people had a single word for time and space—place.

The invention of time and space took a long time. Thereafter, the various directions in space and the times of past, present, and future were constructed: for early peoples, "up" and "north" were one and the same; "late" (*dir*) and "far" (*dur*) were one and the same. Even today, in many villages of Iran, these two words are used interchangeably; instead of saying "it got late" (*dir shod*), they say "it got far" (*dur shod*).

Words have enabled us to separate time and space from one another and construct distinct segments for each. When we look closely, for the human unconscious the mode of functioning of time and space—that is, place—is one. In the research of the French psychoanalyst and psychiatrist Jacques Lacan, who considers himself a continuator of Sigmund Freud's path, we discover that the psychic structure of the human unconscious is formed of three factors—name, imagination (conjecture), and symbol or sign—and these are like three interwoven rings such that if any one breaks, the other two come apart. With every naming, the human being expands the "Real"; through imagination and conjecture, opens the world of the Real ever wider; and through symbols, signs, and words, is able to transmit the grasp of the Real from one generation to the next.

Carl Gustav Jung, the Swiss psychoanalyst and father of analytical psychology, goes very far in employing signs and symbols, to the point where he converges with the borders of alchemy.

Saadi, too, has a verse to the same effect in the preface to the *Golestan*:

O Thou who art beyond imagination, analogy, conjecture, and illusion, and beyond all that has been spoken, all that we have heard and read.

Ferdowsi's keen insight lies in assigning to "name and place" a rank alongside the cosmos, the revolving firmament, soul, wisdom, and the means of human life—namely sustenance and guidance. And it is from this point that he suddenly parts ways with all others:

He is above name, sign, and conjecture.

Ferdowsi demonstrates that human beings do not possess the necessary instrument to go beyond thought. Speech, name, sign, and conjecture represent the summit of human reach. God is above name and place. And it is on this very account that he says:

With bodily eyes you shall not see the Creator; do not vex your two seeing eyes.

The imprint of Jacques Lacan's thought can be seen today in diverse ways across the world of clinical psychoanalysis, philosophical inquiry, and literary and artistic criticism. Beyond university settings, training institutions and centres devoted to the care of the human psyche—such as psychiatric hospitals and psychotherapeutic institutes—and a network of associations interested in the works of Jacques Lacan in various countries are engaged in developing his thought. Indeed, the training of clinical psychoanalysts of his school likewise takes place in the schools of these very associations.

From the standpoint of theoretical work, Lacan's ideas are put to the test every day in the domain of clinical practice, and a body of writings by psychoanalysts examining and comparing the longitudinal psychoanalysis of analysands is made available daily to those interested. On the other hand, comparing the works of Jacques Lacan with those of other psychoanalysts and testing these works in the field of clinical practice are also subjects of study at research institutes around the world. The critique and analysis of literary and artistic works on the basis of Jacques Lacan's thought have today become widespread.

In 1953 Jacques Lacan was expelled from the psychoanalytical association founded by Sigmund Freud. From that date onwards, debate and controversy continued between the followers of that association—known as the Freudians—and Jacques Lacan. The root of the divergence between these two currents of thought has both theoretical foundations and clinical, operational grounds.

The word—and specifically the signifier (the acoustic image of the word)—as the foundation of the structure of the unconscious forms the axis around which Jacques Lacan's theory takes shape. Although Lacan, like Sigmund Freud, bases the structure of the psyche on the same three clinical pillars of neurosis, psychosis, and perversion, he attaches special value to the psychoanalyst's interpretation during psychoanalytic sessions and deems the analyst's silence for prolonged periods mandatory. Lacan believes in short and variable-length psychoanalytic sessions and limits the number of sessions to two or three per week. Although Jacques Lacan's early training was influenced by psychiatrists of the French school of psychiatry, in shaping his own thought he did not carry much baggage from that school.

The complex, prolific, and singular personality of Lacan is revealed in the brief anecdotes his students recount of him here and there. Towards the end of Lacan's work, his language and theory attain a distinctive complexity, as though—like painters of the abstract school—he arrives at a kind of abstract art in the formulation of his thought. Explicating and elucidating his final seminars is no simple task.

To be continued

fr.body_markdown:
[Psychanalyse et culture](http://www.radiozamaneh.com/52353)

Dans les trois textes que vous lirez sous le titre « Psychanalyse et culture », je me propose d'explorer les domaines psychologiques — incluant la psychanalyse, la psychiatrie, la psychologie et la psychothérapie — ainsi que le rôle de la culture dans leurs dimensions théoriques et cliniques. Ces trois essais comprennent les sections suivantes : Avant-propos, les quatre champs psychologiques de la psychanalyse, l'apport de Sigmund Freud, l'apport de Jacques Lacan et la psychanalyse appliquée. Dans une prochaine série d'articles, je m'efforcerai également d'aborder le rôle et les influences réciproques des recherches en sciences humaines, en psychologie et en psychanalyse en Iran et dans le monde, ainsi que leurs rapports avec les États et les structures administratives.

Avant-propos : Sans aborder les notions de psychologique et de culture, il est pratiquement impossible de parler de psychanalyse. C'est pourquoi, après un bref examen des différents champs de connaissance de la psyché, j'aborderai de manière concise la psychanalyse théorique et clinique, pour enfin analyser les rapports entre la psychanalyse et la culture. En ouverture, et pour éclairer mon propos, il convient de nous pencher sur la correspondance entre Einstein et Freud.

En 1932, Albert Einstein, qui avait derrière lui l'expérience de la Première Guerre mondiale, exprime à Sigmund Freud, dans une lettre, son inquiétude face à l'état du monde : « Cher Monsieur Freud, existe-t-il pour l'humanité un moyen de salut face au sinistre fléau de la guerre ? Pourquoi faut-il que les hommes s'entre-tuent avec une telle cruauté ? Pourquoi tous les efforts en faveur d'une paix durable ont-ils abouti à l'échec ? Pourquoi les êtres humains sont-ils si sanguinaires et impitoyables ? Pourquoi les peuples permettent-ils à des dictateurs criminels et insensés d'exploiter leurs passions et de les entraîner jusqu'au bord de la folie et du meurtre de leurs voisins ? Est-il possible d'orienter le développement de la psyché humaine dans une direction qui lui donne la force de résister à la folie de la haine et de la destruction ? »

Après une discussion sur l'histoire de la guerre, Freud développe l'analyse de sa propre théorie et écrit : « Les pulsions humaines sont de deux ordres : celles qui tendent à la conservation de soi et à l'unification de la vie — on les nomme pulsions érotiques ou sexuelles — et celles qui tendent à l'anéantissement et à la mort, que nous résumons sous le nom de pulsion d'agression et de pulsion de destruction. Il semble qu'aucune de ces pulsions n'agisse isolément. Par exemple, chez une personne qui tombe amoureuse, la pulsion de possession, d'emprise et d'agressivité s'intensifie également ; mais la pulsion de destruction, ou de mort et de ravage, est à l'œuvre au sein de tout être vivant et s'efforce de détruire et de désagréger progressivement cet être vivant afin de ramener la vie à l'état inorganique. À l'inverse, la pulsion d'amour et de désir, qui en constitue le pôle opposé, représente les efforts de la vie. Notre but n'est pas d'anéantir totalement les penchants agressifs des hommes ; il faut seulement tenter de les canaliser de sorte qu'ils ne se manifestent pas sous forme de guerre. Certes, la situation idéale et souhaitable serait une société composée d'hommes ayant soumis et assujetti leur vie pulsionnelle à la souveraineté de la raison et de l'intellect.

On ne peut condamner par principe toutes les guerres. Tant qu'il existera des puissances prêtes, sans merci, à anéantir les autres, ces dernières devront elles aussi s'armer pour la guerre. Parmi les traits psychologiques de l'évolution culturelle, deux caractéristiques revêtent une importance majeure : d'une part, le renforcement de l'intellect qui parvient à dominer la vie pulsionnelle, et d'autre part, l'intériorisation des penchants agressifs, avec toutes ses conséquences bénéfiques et tous ses périls. Combien de temps faudra-t-il attendre pour que les peuples du monde deviennent pacifiques ? Je l'ignore. Mon seul espoir réside dans l'attitude culturelle et dans la crainte légitime des effets et des conséquences de la guerre. Tout ce qui favorise l'évolution culturelle, la renforce et l'accélère exerce à coup sûr une action positive contre la guerre… »

Dans ce bref passage se révèlent déjà la profondeur et l'ampleur du regard de Freud. En réponse à l'interrogation d'Einstein, Freud entreprend un examen en profondeur de l'existence, considérant que l'histoire, l'émergence et le développement de l'être humain s'accompagnent simultanément de l'avènement d'une strate qu'il nomme la cristallisation culturelle de l'homme. Freud renvoie à ce qui fait retour chez l'être humain dans sa psyché, ce qu'il désigne lui-même comme l'inconscient. Ce n'est pas en vain qu'en 1930 la société finit par s'éveiller et que Freud reçoit le prestigieux prix officiel Goethe pour l'ensemble de son œuvre — un prix décerné une fois par an à celles et ceux qui ont contribué à l'enrichissement de la culture. Mais bientôt, en Allemagne, les ouvrages de Freud connaissent le destin ardent des livres de Marx, de Bertolt Brecht et d'autres encore.

Freud est convaincu qu'en accroissant la culture de l'homme, on peut partir en guerre contre la guerre. Dans sa théorie, il recourt au concept de sublimation ou « élévation culturelle » (*bâlâ bar-shodan-e farhangi*). J'ai retenu le terme *bâlâ bar-shodan* (« élévation ») plutôt que celui de *tassâ'od*, car le mot *sublimation* au sens d'élévation s'emploie aussi bien dans son acception scientifique en chimie et dans les disciplines connexes que dans le champ de la clinique psychanalytique.

Par ailleurs, le mot même de *farhang* (« culture ») en langue persane exprime à lui seul cette notion d'élévation de la connaissance : *farhang* est formé du préfixe *far*, qui signifie splendeur, noblesse et élévation, et de *hang*, qui signifie gravité, dignité, puissance, capacité, force et vigueur — telle une puissance et une capacité hautes et élevées.

C'est la première fois que Freud a fait usage de ce terme afin de montrer qu'au fil des différentes étapes du cheminement psychanalytique, le sujet atteint le stade de la « sublimation », de sorte que ses besoins corporels — sexuels, alimentaires… — cèdent la place à des aspirations plus hautes (psychiques) ou proprement culturelles, dans toutes leurs dimensions. Mais quel peut être le rôle de l'élévation culturelle dans le domaine de l'art ?

Qu'entend l'oreille du psychanalyste clinicien devant le regard épris ? L'artiste demande : « Cela vous plaît-il ? C'est mon œuvre. » Quel lien existe-t-il entre une œuvre d'art et la sublimation culturelle ? Les impulsions qui régissent notre vie psychique surgissent d'une source et s'acheminent vers un but, poursuivant leur cours jusqu'à la satisfaction de leurs racines productrices. Ces pulsions corporelles qui s'élèvent de notre corps vers notre psyché, lorsqu'elles atteignent leur maturité, changent de but. Le but se situe alors à un niveau supérieur au corps, et la satisfaction du besoin dépasse la vie corporelle quotidienne. Ces messages cherchent un « lieu nouveau » afin d'offrir un message nouveau, et peut-être une trouvaille nouvelle. Autrement dit, cet « autre but, plus élevé » appelle d'autres mots et d'autres concepts.

Les exemples abondent. Picasso, dans ses œuvres, recrée d'une certaine façon le regard des premiers hommes sur eux-mêmes et sur l'existence. Dans les visages humains qu'il façonne, aussi bien en dessin qu'en sculpture, il semble ressusciter ce regard ancestral sur soi et sur les autres hommes, comme s'il avait trouvé ce « lieu nouveau ». Salvador Dalí donne à voir dans ses œuvres la magie de rêves chatoyants et somptueux. Avant lui, on n'eût guère pu croire que l'homme pût être à ce point magicien dans ses songes — des songes qui déploient devant nos yeux l'espace et le temps tels qu'ils s'écoulent dans le rêve même, comme le rêve lui-même. À la sortie d'une exposition de ses œuvres, il semble que l'on s'éveille d'un doux et délicieux sommeil.

Van Gogh attire sur ses toiles cette force intérieure du monde réel. Tout — une table, une fleur, un arbre, une chemise — tout irradie une force vitale. Dans ses œuvres s'impose au regard l'union de la matière et de l'énergie. Goya, le peintre espagnol à l'œuvre si éclatante, commence par la vie de cour, les chasses collectives et la beauté des scènes de nature, puis, dans son tableau majeur *Les Fusillades du 3 mai*, sans même dessiner les yeux du fusillé, il nous donne à voir son « regard ». À y regarder de près, à la place des yeux de cet homme, Goya n'a posé que deux taches noires. Son art sublime réside précisément dans cette « mise en place » : un regard suspendu entre la mort et la vie à travers deux taches noires.

En analysant le phénomène de la sublimation culturelle, Sigmund Freud explique qu'il s'agit d'une activité qui prend racine dans la sexualité tout en en étant vidée. Cette énergie traverse le narcissisme et se dirige vers l'Idéal du Moi ou l'ultime du Moi. Les besoins corporels s'élèvent et cheminent vers cet ultime que le « Moi » a nourri dans son imaginaire. Ce Moi est l'objet de notre désir — hors d'atteinte — que l'on rejoindrait dans un état de perfection du Moi ; et nul doute qu'un tel être relève de l'imaginaire et non du réel. C'est comme si le corps et ses besoins cédaient la place, en deux temps, au narcissisme, puis à un émerveillement plus haut et ultime, à l'image de l'expérience de Narcisse s'éprenant de son propre reflet dans l'eau. Cette image du Moi dans le miroir place en quelque sorte l'artiste en position d'appareil photographique, et son œuvre, telle une photographie, est le produit de cet appareil — si bien que la qualité du cliché témoigne de la qualité de l'appareil. Ainsi, le narcissisme désigne l'élévation et l'anoblissement des productions de ce « Moi ».

C'est peut-être là ce qui s'est inscrit de manière « métaphorique » dans le sourire de la Joconde de Léonard de Vinci. Avant l'émergence des artistes contemporains, durant les époques des arts visuels antérieures à la nôtre, l'accomplissement de l'art consistait peut-être à représenter le monde extérieur de la façon la plus réaliste possible — en portant en quelque sorte l'appareil photographique à sa perfection. Ici, l'image inconsciente que l'artiste se fait de son propre corps est directement exposée au regard, telle une réponse qu'il apporte à cette interrogation sans fin : « Comment suis-je ! »

Les quatre champs psychologiques

Les complexités psychologiques et leurs domaines d'action, abordés de manière très brève et rapide : la psychanalyse, la psychiatrie, la psychologie et la psychothérapie. Ce qui relève du champ psychologique peut être présenté ainsi : l'emploi du mot *ravân* (« psyché / âme / esprit ») en persan, équivalent de « PSY » dans les langues européennes, peut être considéré comme une richesse de la langue persane. En effet, ce mot peut désigner aussi bien la notion d'« appareil psychique » — ou de structure du fonctionnement de la psyché — que servir de préfixe ou de suffixe pour l'ensemble des concepts qui touchent, d'une manière ou d'une autre, au psychisme : tels que *ravân-kâvi* (psychanalyse), *ravân-shenâsi* (psychologie), *ravân-pezeshki* (psychiatrie), *ravân-darmâni* (psychothérapie) ou *ravân-shenâkhti* (psychologique). Car le mot *ravân*, qui est en même temps le nom verbal du verbe *raftan* (« aller, couler »), exprime par là même la fluidité et le mouvement continu de la notion de « psyché » — de telle sorte que la « psyché » est à la fois en nous, avec nous et ailleurs. Ce lieu est, dans les mythes iraniens, une sorte de terre céleste, et dans les hypothèses modernes de la psychanalyse d'orientation lacanienne, c'est précisément l'autre, le Grand Autre ou les autres.

Bien que les complexités de la psyché humaine ne relèvent pas exclusivement des sciences au sens moderne du terme, ce qui est officiellement défini dans le cadre scientifique du cercle psychologique peut être divisé en quatre groupes : la psychiatrie, la psychologie, la psychothérapie et la psychanalyse. Cette classification provisoire nous permet, dans ce bref exposé, de mieux cerner le champ d'action psychologique. Appelons « psychologique » la connaissance de ce qui touche à la psyché, en supposant que nous limitions notre champ de travail à la vie quotidienne et à la sphère du tangible. Car le domaine de la connaissance de la psyché renvoie d'un côté à l'ensemble des productions humaines, depuis l'invention de la parole et de l'écriture jusqu'aux champs de la mythologie, de l'art et de la littérature, des temps les plus reculés à nos jours — domaine où trouvent également place la philosophie, la mystique, la religion, les croyances populaires, les talismans et la magie. D'un autre côté, sans même aller si loin, le champ psychologique s'étend jusqu'à la linguistique, l'anthropologie et la sociologie ; et comme la psyché repose sur le corps, il s'étend jusqu'à la neurologie. En réalité, la psyché humaine est prise entre trois repères majeurs : le passé de l'individu, l'individu au sein de la collectivité des autres, et le corps de l'individu avec sa structure nerveuse.

Essayons d'éclairer notre propos en définissant les quatre concepts d'application pratique du champ psychologique, accompagnés de quelques exemples :

1 - La psychiatrie, qui s'inscrit historiquement dans le cadre de la pratique médicale et constitue une branche dans le prolongement de la médecine du cerveau et des nerfs (neurologie). En psychiatrie, nous avons affaire à la classification des maladies selon leurs manifestations extérieures. L'objectif est de diagnostiquer la maladie et de la traiter. Les troubles mentaux relevant de la psychiatrie peuvent puiser leurs racines dans le corps, dans le système nerveux ou dans un fonctionnement déficient du cerveau : des affections d'origine congénitale ou des troubles survenus après la naissance, tels que les lésions cérébrales, le dysfonctionnement du système mnésique, du système perceptif ou de la structure cognitive. Aujourd'hui, pour traiter ces troubles, la psychiatrie recherche les causes somatiques et neurologiques, recourt à la psychothérapie, au changement de cadre de vie, à l'art-thérapie, etc., tout en accordant une place particulière aux médicaments chimiques pour apaiser l'espace mental du patient. Au début du XXe siècle, les départements des maladies nerveuses, cérébrales et psychiatriques n'étaient pas encore séparés.

2 - En psychologie, c'est le comportement de l'individu qui fait l'objet d'une analyse : le comportement de la personne dans sa famille, en milieu scolaire, au travail, avec ses amis et ses connaissances. Cette science est donc utilisée partout où le « comportement de l'individu » joue un rôle : dans le recrutement au sein des institutions, les relations publiques, les sciences de l'éducation ou la régulation des rapports de l'individu avec autrui et dans le milieu social. Dans les situations cliniques, la psychologie place l'individu devant le miroir de son comportement envers la société et les autres. Elle joue un rôle majeur dans la rééducation des personnes qui, en raison d'une déficience congénitale ou à la suite d'accidents et de maladies, souffrent de troubles comportementaux ou mentaux. Une autre activité majeure de la psychologie concerne l'ensemble des recherches liées aux sciences cognitives et aux sciences du comportement ; par ailleurs, l'étude des questions sociales n'est guère praticable sans prendre en compte le comportement de l'individu face à la société (psychologie sociale). Par le travail en groupe, la psychologie s'avère très efficace pour réactiver les fonctions mentales des patients.

3 - La psychothérapie. S'appuyant sur l'expérience et recourant au dialogue, la psychothérapie s'efforce de placer ponctuellement l'individu face à son trouble localisé et de l'orienter vers une solution acceptable. Dans certains cas (et lorsque cela s'avère nécessaire), les psychiatres font appel à la psychothérapie pour remédier à des troubles tels que les angoisses, les égarements passagers ou les désarrois temporaires.

4 - La psychanalyse est une pratique récente, vieille de moins d'un siècle. La psychanalyse porte son attention sur la parole du sujet allongé sur le divan. Le psychanalyste intervient dans le rapport de l'individu à son inconscient, et son champ d'action consiste en quelque sorte à placer un miroir devant la parole du sujet afin que, par cette voie et sur la longue durée (généralement entre 5 et 10 ans), l'individu, en énonçant tout ce qui lui vient à l'esprit (association libre), prenne conscience du mode de fonctionnement de son inconscient et accède ainsi aux racines d'éventuelles anomalies de son comportement. Bien des troubles se « résolvent » par la connaissance de leur origine. D'un autre côté, la psychanalyse aide à découvrir les forces intérieures latentes de l'individu et constitue aujourd'hui, dans les sociétés occidentales, l'un de ses usages les plus importants : comme une préparation permettant d'aller vers une autre direction grâce à une connaissance plus profonde de ses propres faiblesses et de ses propres forces, à l'image du marin qui, en aiguisant sa vue, gouverne mieux son navire dans la tempête.

La formation psychanalytique est le plus souvent comparée à une transmission de maître à disciple. En effet, si le psychanalyste n'est pas lui-même passé par l'épreuve du divan et n'a pas entrepris l'exploration de sa psyché — ou la fouille des racines de son propre « inconscient » —, comment pourrait-il être le guide d'un autre être ? En psychanalyse, nous sommes confrontés à deux réalités : la psychanalyse clinique et la psychanalyse appliquée. À partir des théories psychanalytiques, on peut explorer des écrits, des discours et des œuvres d'art, ouvrant ainsi un angle neuf pour l'analyse et l'interprétation de l'art et de la littérature. C'est pourquoi, aujourd'hui, dans de nombreux établissements d'enseignement, universités et centres de recherche, des psychanalystes sont membres d'équipes de recherche.

Prenons un exemple : considérons la vie quotidienne d'une famille, Monsieur et Madame « M. » et leurs deux enfants, l'aîné et le cadet. Le père de Monsieur M. souffre d'amnésie ; suivi par un psychologue spécialisé, il s'efforce trois jours par semaine, par des exercices, de lutter contre ce trouble.

Madame M., depuis quatre ans, à la suite de symptômes de névrose — une peur constante et sans objet —, suit une cure psychanalytique ; elle voit son psychanalyste trois fois par semaine et consacre concrètement ses séances, sur le divan, à dire ce qui lui vient à l'esprit. L'enfant aîné, âgé de vingt ans et ayant un âge mental de huit ans, souffre d'une déficience intellectuelle ; un psychologue le suit et reste en contact avec ses éducateurs. Monsieur M., pour vaincre une dépendance à l'alcool, consulte son psychothérapeute deux fois par semaine afin de traverser, par le dialogue et le soutien « verbal », l'étape difficile du sevrage.

Le second enfant, âgé de quinze ans, éprouve des difficultés à écrire les mots ; le psychologue de son école examine son cas afin de l'orienter vers un service de neurologie et de psychiatrie pour des examens plus approfondis, afin de s'assurer que l'origine de son trouble ne relève pas d'une atteinte des organes nerveux. Nous voyons ainsi comment l'individu, le corps, la psyché et le milieu environnant forment un ensemble complexe où, à chaque degré de trouble et de difficulté, nous avons besoin d'une compétence spécialisée.

Comment peut-on aujourd'hui acquérir une spécialisation dans les domaines évoqués ci-dessus ? Pour répondre à cette question, il convient de diviser les champs psychologiques en sous-domaines de recherche théorique, clinique et comportementale. Le psychiatre est actif dans les deux domaines de la recherche et de la clinique. Le psychologue intervient dans les trois domaines, à cette différence près qu'au stade clinique, il requiert la collaboration du psychiatre. Le psychothérapeute ne joue pas de rôle dans les champs de la recherche et de l'étude comportementale, et n'aborde les troubles psychiques que de manière ponctuelle. Le psychanalyste est avant tout actif dans le champ clinique, et son rôle dans les domaines comportemental et de la recherche repose principalement sur la transmission des expériences cliniques. Le psychanalyste s'attache à la structure de l'inconscient de l'individu, avec des effets à long terme.

On a souvent comparé les psychanalystes à des archéologues qui, outre un savoir théorique et scientifique, ont besoin d'une grande patience, de persévérance, de constance ainsi que d'une vaste culture générale. Les relations de la psychanalyse, des psychiatres, des psychologues et des psychothérapeutes avec les organismes administratifs et les institutions de soins varient d'une société à l'autre. À titre d'exemple, la psychanalyse figure en Allemagne parmi les prestations remboursées par les assurances maladie. Aux États-Unis, de nombreux instituts mènent des recherches en psychanalyse parallèlement aux institutions officielles d'enseignement et de recherche médicale. En revanche, en France par exemple, non seulement la psychanalyse n'est pas prise en charge par l'assurance maladie, mais le nombre d'instituts de recherche existants ne dépasse guère les doigts d'une main.

La psychologie analytique : les disciples de Jung qui, en s'appuyant sur la notion de l'homme et de ses symboles et en postulant l'existence d'une sorte d'inconscient collectif, s'efforcent, à l'aide de la remémoration des rêves et de l'interprétation des symboles liés à l'être humain, d'explorer en quelque sorte les tréfonds de l'intériorité.

La sexologie : la sexologie, que l'on désigne en pratique sous le nom de sexothérapie, traite des troubles du comportement sexuel et, au-delà de l'aspect physiologique, rattache l'essentiel du fonctionnement à la psyché et à la culture, en partant du postulat que le comportement sexuel de l'homme est, sur le plan biologique, identique à celui de ses anciens cousins, et que toute cette diversité, cette variété et cette richesse des rapports sexuels sont le fruit de centaines de milliers d'années de travail culturel de l'humanité. Dès lors, la majorité des difficultés et des troubles trouvent leur racine dans la psyché et dans la culture. Sigmund Freud est parfois reconnu comme l'un des fondateurs de la sexologie.

Dr Hassan Makaremi

Paris, automne 1391

en.body_markdown:
[Psychoanalysis and Culture](http://www.radiozamaneh.com/52353)

In the three essays that you will read under the title "Psychoanalysis and Culture", I intend to examine the psychological fields—including psychoanalysis, psychiatry, psychology, and psychotherapy—and the role of culture in their theoretical and clinical dimensions. These three discourses comprise the following sections: Preface, The Four Psychological Fields of Psychoanalysis, The Legacy of Sigmund Freud, The Legacy of Jacques Lacan, and Applied Psychoanalysis. In forthcoming series of articles, I shall also endeavour to address the role and mutual influences of research in the human sciences, psychology, and psychoanalysis in Iran and in the world, as well as their relationship with states and administrative structures.

Preface: Without addressing psychological concepts and culture, speaking of psychoanalysis is virtually impossible. For this reason, after a brief discussion of the various domains of understanding the psyche—and doing so in a concise manner—I shall turn to theoretical and clinical psychoanalysis, and at the end examine the relationship between psychoanalysis and culture. In opening my remarks and in order to clarify what I wish to say, it is fitting to turn to the correspondence between Einstein and Freud.

In 1932, Albert Einstein, who had lived through the experience of the First World War, expressed his concern over the state of the world in a letter to Sigmund Freud: "Dear Mr Freud, is there any way of delivering humanity from the fatal calamity of war? Why must human beings slaughter one another so mercilessly? Why have all efforts towards a lasting peace ended in failure? Why are human beings so bloodthirsty and ruthless? Why do people allow criminal and mad dictators to exploit their feelings and drive them to the brink of madness and the killing of their neighbours? Is it possible to guide the development of the human psyche in a direction capable of withstanding the madness of hatred and destruction?"

Following a discussion of the history of war, Freud turns to an analysis of his theory and writes: "Human instincts are of two kinds: those which seek self-preservation and the unity of life—these are called erotic or sexual inclinations—and those which seek destruction and death. We summarise the latter under the instinct of aggression and the instinct of destruction. It appears that neither of these instincts operates in isolation. For instance, when a person falls in love, the instinct of possession, mastery, and aggression is also intensified within them; yet the instinct of destruction, or death and devastation, is active within every living organism and strives gradually to destroy and disintegrate the living being and return life to an inanimate state, whereas the instinct of love and eros, which is its opposite pole, represents the efforts of life. Our aim is not the complete eradication of human aggressive tendencies; we must only endeavour to channel this inclination in such a way that it does not manifest itself as war. Certainly, the ideal and desirable condition is a society in which there are people who have subordinated and subjected their instinctual life to the sovereignty of reason and intellect.

One cannot condemn all wars in principle. So long as powers exist that stand ruthlessly ready to annihilate others, those others must also arm themselves for war. Among the psychological characteristics of cultural evolution, two features are of great importance: one is the strengthening of the intellect, which has gained mastery over instinctual life, and the other is the internalisation of aggressive tendencies, with all its beneficial consequences and all its perilous repercussions. How long must we wait until the peoples of the world become peace-loving? I do not know. My sole hope lies in the cultural attitude and, secondly, in a justified fear of the effects and consequences of war. Anything that assists cultural evolution and strengthens and accelerates it undoubtedly has a positive application against war…"

Even in this brief passage, the depth and breadth of Freud's outlook become clear. In reply to Einstein's question, Freud conducts a profound examination of life and views the history, genesis, and growth of humankind as simultaneous with the presence of a stratum called human cultural crystallisation. Freud points to the repressed remnants returning within the human psyche, which he calls the unconscious. It is not for nothing that in 1930 society finally awakens and Freud receives the prestigious Goethe Prize for his collected works—a prize awarded once a year to individuals who have contributed to the advancement of culture. Yet soon thereafter, Freud's works in Germany suffer the fiery fate of the books of Marx, Bertolt Brecht, and others.

Freud believes that by increasing human culture, one can wage war against war. In his theory, he makes use of the concept of sublimation, or "cultural elevation". I have used "elevation" (bālā-bar-shodan) in place of the word "ascension" (tasa'od), because the word sublimation, in the sense of rising upwards, is employed both in its scientific usage in the fields of chemistry and allied sciences and in the field of clinical psychoanalysis.

On the other hand, the word farhang ("culture") in the Persian language by itself conveys the concept of the elevation of knowledge: farhang is formed from the prefix far, meaning splendour, dignity, and loftiness, and hang, meaning gravity, poise, power, capacity, and vigour—that is, lofty and elevated power and capacity.

Freud first made use of this term in order to show that, across the various stages of the psychoanalytic journey, the individual reaches the stage of "sublimation" (rising upwards), such that their bodily needs—sexual, alimentary, and so forth—give way to higher (psychical) or, in a sense, cultural needs, in all their dimensions. Yet what can be the role of cultural sublimation in the domain of art?

What does the ear of the clinical psychoanalyst hear from the enraptured gaze? The artist asks: "Do you like it? It is my work." What relationship exists between a work of art and cultural sublimation? The impulses that regulate our psychical life arise from a source, flow towards an aim, and continue until the satisfaction of their productive roots. These bodily impulses, rising from our body towards our psyche, change their aim once they reach maturity. The aim is situated at a stage higher than the body, and the satisfaction of the need transcends everyday bodily existence. These messages search for a new "place" in order to present a new message, and perhaps a new discovery. Put differently, this "higher aim" calls for other words and other concepts.

Examples abound. Picasso, in his works, reconstructs in a certain way the gaze of early human beings upon themselves and upon existence. In the faces he creates of human beings—both in drawing and in sculpture—it is as though Picasso brings back to life that ancestral gaze upon themselves and upon other people, as though he has found that "new place". Salvador Dalí displays the magic of colourful and beautiful dreams in his works. Before him, one could scarcely have believed that a human being could be such a magician in their dreams—dreams that lay before us time and space just as they unfold in sleep. It is as though, upon leaving an exhibition of his works, we awaken from a sweet and gentle dream.

Van Gogh draws that inner force of the real world onto his canvases. Everything—table, flower, tree, and shirt—everything radiates the force of life. In his works, the bond between matter and energy meets the eye. Goya, the Spanish painter of such brilliant works, begins with court life, collective hunts, and the beauty of natural scenes, and in his celebrated work "The Firing Squad", without painting the eyes of the man being shot, he shows us his "gaze". Looking closely, in place of the man's eyes, Goya has placed merely two black spots. His sublime art lies in this very "placement": a gaze suspended between death and life through two black spots.

In dissecting the phenomenon of "cultural sublimation", Sigmund Freud states that it is an activity rooted in sexuality yet emptied of it. This force passes through narcissism and moves towards the ego-ideal, or the ultimate ego. Bodily needs ascend to a higher plane and journey towards that ultimate image which the "ego" has nurtured in its imagination. This is the ego we long for—distant and out of reach—which I shall attain in a state of perfection, and undoubtedly such a being exists in imagination rather than in reality. It is as though the body and its needs give way, in two stages, to narcissism and then to a loftier, ultimate fascination, like the experience of Narcissus who falls in love with his own reflection in the water. This mirror-image of the ego places the artist, as it were, in the position of a camera, and their work, like a photograph, is the product of this camera—just as the quality of the photograph speaks of the quality of the camera. Thus narcissism signifies the elevation and ennoblement of the productions of this "ego".

This is perhaps what is "metaphorically" inscribed in the smile of Da Vinci's Gioconda (Mona Lisa). That narcissism of the artist upon sublimation: perhaps before the rise of modern artists, during the eras of visual art prior to our own time, the perfection of art lay in depicting the external world ever more realistically—in perfecting, so to speak, the camera. Here, the artist's unconscious image of their own body is placed directly on display: an answer that the artist gives to the unending question: "How am I?"

The Four Psychological Fields

Psychological complexities and their spheres of operation—very briefly and in passing: psychoanalysis, psychiatry, psychology, and psychotherapy. What pertains to the psychological field may be presented as follows: the use of the word ravān ("psyche") in the Persian language as the equivalent of "PSY" in European languages may be regarded as a blessing of the Persian tongue. For this word can be used both for the concept of the "psychical apparatus"—or the structure of psychical functioning—and as a suffix or prefix for all concepts that deal in some way with the psyche. Among these are psychoanalysis (ravān-kāvī), psychology (ravān-shenāsī), psychiatry (ravān-pezeshkī), psychotherapy (ravān-darmānī), or psychological (ravān-shenākhtī). Because the word ravān is at the same time the verbal noun of the verb raftan ("to flow / to go"), it conveys this relationship through the fluid, ongoing nature of the concept of "psyche"—in such a way that the "psyche" is at once within us, with us, and elsewhere. In Iranian mythology, this place is in a sense the celestial earth, and in the modern hypotheses of the Lacanian school of psychoanalysis it is the other, the Other, or others.

Although the complexities of the human psyche are not solely the subject of the sciences in the modern sense, what has been formally defined within the bounds of the sciences in the psychological circle may be divided into four groups: psychiatry, psychology, psychotherapy, and psychoanalysis. This division temporarily enables us, in this brief overview, to become better acquainted with the field of psychological operation. Let us call the knowledge of what pertains to the psyche "psychological", on the assumption that we restrict our field of work to everyday life and the tangible sphere. For the domain of knowing the psyche extends, on the one hand, to knowledge of all human achievements—from the invention of speech and writing to the realms of mythology, art, and literature, from the remotest times to the present day. In between lie philosophy, mysticism, religion, popular beliefs, talisman-writing, and magic. On the other hand, if we do not wish to stray too far, the psychological extends as far as linguistics, anthropology, and sociology; and because the psyche rests upon the body, the psychological reaches all the way to neurology. Indeed, the human psyche is caught between three major axes: the human past, the human being in the company of others, and the human body with its neurological structure.

We shall endeavour to clarify this matter by defining the four concepts of practical psychological application and offering a few examples:

1. Psychiatry, which historically lies within the scope of medical practice and is a branch continuing from neurology. In psychiatry, we deal with the classification of illnesses on the basis of their external manifestations. The aim is the diagnosis and treatment of illness. Mental illnesses within the domain of psychiatry may derive their roots in some manner from the body, the nervous system, or impaired brain function—illnesses rooted in congenital factors or difficulties arising after birth, such as brain lesions or the improper functioning of the memory system, the diagnostic faculty, or the cognitive structure. Today in psychiatry, for the treatment of disorders, clinicians trace the roots of bodily-neurological problems and make use of everything from psychotherapy to environmental change, art therapy, and so forth, while also giving chemical medications a special place in calming the patient's mental state. In the early twentieth century, the departments of neurology, brain diseases, and psychiatry were not yet separated from one another.

2. In psychology, the behaviour of the individual is analysed—the individual's behaviour in the family, the educational setting, the workplace, and with friends and acquaintances. Hence this science is utilised wherever "individual behaviour" plays a role, such as recruitment in institutions, public relations, educational sciences, or regulating the individual's relationship with others or within the social environment. In clinical settings, psychology places the individual before a mirror of their behaviour towards society and others. Psychology plays a major role in the rehabilitation of individuals who, whether due to a congenital defect or accidents and illnesses, suffer from behavioural or mental disorders. Another major activity of psychology lies in all research questions dependent upon the cognitive and behavioural sciences; on the other hand, the study of social issues is impracticable without considering individual behaviour in relation to society (social psychology). Through group work, psychology is highly effective in reactivating patients' mental functions.

3. Psychotherapy. Backed by experience and through the use of dialogue, psychotherapy seeks to place the individual locally in front of their specific disorder and guide them towards an acceptable solution. In certain cases (and when necessary), psychiatrists make use of psychotherapy to alleviate disorders such as anxieties, temporary bewilderment, or transient distress.

4. Psychoanalysis is a modern practice with a history of less than a hundred years. Psychoanalysis attends to the individual's speech upon the couch. The psychoanalyst operates within the individual's relationship with their unconscious, and their sphere of action is like placing a mirror before the individual's speech so that, in this way and over the long term (usually between 5 and 10 years), the individual—by recounting whatever comes to mind (free association)—gains awareness of how their unconscious operates and thereby arrives at the root of any possible behavioural disorders. Many disorders are "resolved" in recognising their root. On the other hand, psychoanalysis assists in discovering the individual's dormant inner strengths, and today this is one of the most important uses of psychoanalysis in Western societies: as a kind of preparation for moving in a new direction with a deeper knowledge of one's weaknesses and strengths, like a sailor who, by sharpening their range of vision, steers their ship more skilfully through storms.

Training in psychoanalysis is most often likened to master-apprentice instruction. For if the psychoanalyst has not themselves passed through the stage of the couch and undertaken the exploration of the psyche—or the excavation of the roots of their own "unconscious"—how could they serve as a guide to another person? In psychoanalysis, we encounter two phenomena: clinical psychoanalysis and applied psychoanalysis. On the basis of psychoanalytic theories, one can examine texts, speech, and works of art, opening a new perspective on the interpretation and analysis of art and literature. It is for this reason that today, in many educational institutions, universities, and research centres, psychoanalysts are members of research teams.

Let us take an example: consider the everyday life of a family—Mr and Mrs "M." and their two children, the elder and the younger. Mr M.'s father suffers from amnesia. Under the supervision of a specialist psychologist, he tries to combat this problem through exercises three days a week.

For the past four years, following the appearance of symptoms of neurosis—persistent and groundless fear—Mrs M. has been undergoing psychoanalytic treatment; she sees her psychoanalyst three times a week, and her time is spent essentially on the couch speaking whatever comes to her mind. The elder child, aged twenty with a mental age of eight, suffers from intellectual disability; a psychologist monitors him and remains in contact with his educators. Mr M., in order to overcome alcohol addiction, sees his psychotherapist twice a week so as to pass through the difficult stage of recovery by means of dialogue and "verbal" support.

The younger child, aged fifteen, experiences difficulty in writing words. His school psychologist is assessing him in order to refer him for more thorough examinations to the neurology and psychiatry department, to ensure that the root of his difficulty does not lie in neurological organs. We see how the individual, the body, the psyche, and their surrounding environment form a complex ensemble in which, at each stage of disorders and difficulties, we require a distinct expertise.

How can one attain specialisation in the aforementioned fields today? To answer this question, it is appropriate to divide the psychological domains into the research-theoretical, clinical, and behavioural sub-fields. The psychiatrist is active in both the research and clinical domains. The psychologist is active in all three domains, with the difference that at the clinical stage they require the collaboration of a psychiatrist. The psychotherapist plays no role in the research and behavioural domains and addresses psychological disorders only locally. The psychoanalyst is practically active in the clinical domain, and their role in the behavioural and research domains is primarily based on the transmission of clinical experience. The psychoanalyst engages with the individual's unconscious structure, with results unfolding over the long term.

Psychoanalysts have most often been compared to archaeological excavators who, in addition to theoretical and scientific knowledge, require a certain patience, perseverance, and tenacity, as well as a rich general culture. The relationship of psychoanalysis, psychiatrists, psychologists, and psychotherapists with administrative and healthcare organisations and institutions is not the same across different societies. By way of example, in Germany psychoanalysis forms part of health insurance services. In the United States, numerous institutions alongside official medical teaching and research establishments conduct psychoanalytic research; whereas in France, for instance, not only does psychoanalysis not fall within health insurance coverage, but existing research institutes also do not exceed the number of fingers on one hand.

Analytical Psychology: Followers of Jung who, relying on the concept of the human being and their symbols, and believing in the presence of a kind of collective unconscious, endeavour—through the recall of dreams and the interpretation of symbols associated with humankind—to delve into the innermost depths of the psyche.

Sexology: Sexology—which in practice we call sex therapy—addresses disorders of sexual behaviour and, beyond the physiological dimension, attributes the greater part of its functioning to the psyche and to culture, on the premise that human sexual behaviour is biologically the same as the behaviour of humanity's earlier cousins, and that all this diversity, variety, and richness of sexual relations is the product of hundreds of thousands of years of human cultural work. Consequently, the majority of problems and disorders are rooted in the psyche and in culture. Sigmund Freud is sometimes recognised as one of the founders of sexology.

Dr Hassan Makaremi

Paris, Autumn 1391
