https://www.makaremi.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/01/8-Copier.jpg

An Attempt to Unpack the "Heart" (*Del*): An Example of Applying Clinical Psychoanalytic Knowledge to the Understanding of Wisdom.

"What reveals the wisdom of ancient cultures

is precisely this maturity of their understanding of the human being.

The future of humanity will endure only through the application of two pillars: modern sciences

on the one hand, and the wisdom of ancient cultures on the other."

"Within my weary-hearted interior, I know not who dwells,

For I am silent, while he is in lamentation and uproar."

Hassan Makaremi

Clinical Psychoanalyst

October 2001, France

An Introduction to Hafez and the Heart (*Del*)

Hafez and dynamic love: Through this concept, Hafez opens a new door upon love—namely, the ceaseless, reciprocal striving of lover and beloved. In the arena of love, *"the nightingale's sole thought is that the rose has become his companion; the rose ponders how to weave coquetry into his affair."* The effort and preoccupation of the nightingale in winning the rose's heart on the one hand, and the rose's refusal to sit idle as she raises her demands—which naturally draws the nightingale into renewed exertion—mean that both strive, through this mutual exchange, to elevate the arena of love higher and further. And it is through this passion of lover and beloved that the arena of love grows ever deeper. In this continual striving, lover and beloved become ever richer, reach their utmost limit, and through their mutual growth enrich the arena of love.

And thus it is that reading and re-reading "Hafez" is deemed infinite. In this very striving, admirers of Hafez likewise endeavour, like the nightingale, to attain Hafez's thought; and he, Hafez, has already crafted and refined his own coquetry, constructing a deeper inner layer within his poetry and inviting you into that innermost stratum.

Through the beauty of his choice of words, the power of words and their interconnections, and by deploying every literary and poetic subtlety alongside cultural and psychological allusions to the human condition, Hafez strives to fathom existence and the fundamental relations governing life and humanity, drawing us into multiple worlds.

Each word acquires a distinct force and depth in relation to other words; each hemistich is in itself a jewel that polishes itself within a poem; each ghazal builds a garden of thought. And each verse and each ghazal within Hafez's *Divan* attains such a profound and boundless dimension that with every re-reading of Hafez, the enraptured nightingale awakens and says to himself that surely our rose, Hafez, has concealed yet another hidden layer of the coquetry of his thought, another gem somewhere, so that I must seek him out once more to discover it.

Hafez and his singular existence within being—like the presence of the very essence of humanity in existence—are so profound that one can grasp the vast volume of his *Ghazaliyat* only through both a horizontal and a vertical perception simultaneously: horizontally from words to hemistich and poem, and vertically from poem to ghazal across the breadth of his collected ghazals.

Thus, with each renewed return to him, Hafez unveils a hidden glance to us; and once we have discovered these initial manifest layers, he invites us to the richer, deeper banquet of the underlying strata, declaring:

"Companions, untie the knot from the beloved's tress; / It is a joyous night—prolong it with this tale."

In the first layer, he summons fellow revellers to untangle the knot of the beloved's tress, which will undoubtedly prolong the pleasant night of revelry with friends. No sooner have you emerged from this layer than the beloved's tress itself is a joyous night—dark and sweet—whose untying and uncurling lengthens the tress. And before we have even stepped out of the second layer, Hafez draws his enraptured readers—these intoxicated nightingales, this choicest flower of knowledge—into a third world:

Untying the knot from the tress, unravelling a knot, like unravelling the knot of a riddle, a mystery, and a perplexity. This tress of the beloved set amidst us companions is that very joyous night constituting the enigma of existence and of our presence in this world, which we must unravel together so that the tale of existence may be prolonged—for only through expanding the understanding of existence can its mystery be unlocked.

In this dynamic and elevating love, Hafez does not lightly accept even the subtle play of becoming dust upon the path, stipulating instead the condition that the beloved must behold that dust:

"It is no proper way to leave me upon the dust and flee; / Pass by and inquire after me once more, that I may become the dust of your path."

The first *râh* ("way") refers to manner and conduct; the second—which denotes the place of passage—carries within this second *gozâr* ("passing") the sense of inquiry and return. And he makes the beloved's "inquiring after" him the condition for the lover to become "dust of the path": until you see me, I am not the dust of your path, even though I lie fallen upon the earth. It is your inquiry that makes me "that dust of the path" worthy of you.

Yet for all that, this very dust of the path knows its own human worth, dignity, and station in existence; it knows the pearl of its poetry and the socio-historical standing of its thought:

"You have composed a ghazal and pierced pearls—come and recite it sweetly, Hafez, / For upon your verse the heavens scatter the necklace of the Pleiades."

Though others who compose poetry and recite it before rulers have necklaces and jewels cast at their feet, Hafez receives from the celestial sphere the necklace of the Pleiades. He recognises his own art of the ghazal—in which every word, drawn like a rare pearl from the depths of the ocean, has blossomed and been arranged in matchless harmony into a necklace of verse and ghazal. And worthy of such a necklace is nothing less than the cluster of the Pleiades—bestowed by a gaze like Hafez's upon this order, beauty, power, and boundless mystery of existence and the heavens, and from the celestial sphere itself. Thus, in a single couplet, by mocking the worthless gifts of rulers, Hafez elevates his human dignity from the ocean floor—in quest of the rarest pearl—beyond the sky of imagination to the contemplation of the stars. He opens to us both the infinite expanse of his vision across the heights and depths of heaven and ocean, and teaches us a fresh, profound, and self-sufficient gaze. Such dynamic love, within an endless universe whose every ghazal crossroads opens a new dimension—and before you reach the depths of that dimension, another ghazal arrives to draw you into an uncharted world—means that Hafez's love contends with great complexities. Although melody and beauty of image, vision, colour, and song pour forth from every ghazal, such as:

The *radif* and repetition of the letter *s* in this couplet:

"If the string of my rosary snapped, hold me excused; / My hand was caught in the skirt of the silver-limbed cupbearer."

Or the repetition of the letter *sh* in this other couplet:

"Alas, those saucy, sweet-acting, city-rousing beauties / Have carried patience from the heart as the Turks carried off the banquet of plunder."

Yet Hafez's multidimensional universe not only traverses from the ocean's depths to the necklace of the Pleiades within a single couplet, but also lends another dimension to sleep and dream, summoning moon, star, sun, and firmament:

"Surely I shall go mad in this passion, for from night till day / I converse with the moon and behold fairies in my dreams."

Upon the frontier of reason and madness, love and existence, sleep, dream, and wakefulness—wandering and, for want of an answer, opening discourse with the moon. The multidimensional world of the human being is an exceedingly intricate and interwoven ensemble, immersed like a network of image, imaginary, symbolic, and real, of past, present, and future, of assigning names to the real and uniting names within the realm of concepts. And Hafez dwells simultaneously in all these dimensions, weaving them together with his finesse to find an answer—and out of anguish, at the end, he speaks with the "moon", which, though distant, wordless, and unresponsive, is at least beautiful.

For all that, Hafez's daily life remains concealed—Hafez stays hidden, and at times one can sense that his era too remains veiled. Across more than five hundred surviving ghazals, in fewer than a hundred—in their closing couplets—does he speak of himself, and even then with such humility, modesty, and detachment that the sole memory he leaves upon hearts is a shadow: a bird yearning to take flight from another garden, not from this realm of dust.

"I am a bird of the angelic garden, I belong not to the realm of dust; / For a few days they have fashioned a cage out of my body."

In this detachment, he cuts ties with both worlds and regards "rulers"—the quintessential emblem of this worldly realm—as companions to the darkest blackness:

"The company of rulers is the darkness of Yalda night; / Seek light from the sun—bid it rise."

He even mocks the elixir of eternal life—the unattainable prize pursued by those very rulers—for he is merely dusted with poverty:

"I, who am dusted with poverty—shame upon my aspiration / Should I ever wet my hem in the waters of the sun's spring."

Even though this very dustiness—this dust of the body—torments him too, because it forms a veil over the "face of his soul":

"The dust of my body becomes the veil over the face of my soul; / Blessed the moment when I cast the veil aside from this face."

*

And amidst all of this, Hafez possesses a "heart" (*del*), the understanding of which can bring us somewhat closer to him.

1 – Preface: In concise summary, the opening thesis of this essay is as follows:

- The wisdom of ancient cultures lies above all in the experience transmitted from generation to generation over centuries in the speech and way of life of a people. In a sense, culture is a system that historically transmits meanings embedded within symbols.[1] Since the emergence of clinical psychoanalysis up to the present day, the close analysis of discourse across different cultures—attending to symbols and the meanings concealed behind them—reveals this precious heritage of past culture most vividly hidden within the folds of speech. In its circulation, speech carries wisdom—both overtly and covertly—in proverbs, everyday idioms, prayers, curses, insults, legends, and parables. In this essay, I address just one instance of such wisdom: the cultural achievement of the "heart" (*del*).

- In re-reading, dissecting, interpreting, and construing the writings of the ancients, a major snare lies before our feet. Re-reading our predecessors through contemporary beliefs and prejudices distances us from them. Thus, a single poem from the past is often deployed in disparate analyses simultaneously to buttress opposing and conflicting viewpoints. An accurate understanding of the writings of earlier generations is achieved only when one succeeds in situating oneself within the atmosphere of that era, amidst its utterances, its words, and the interconnection of those words with one another. In clinical psychoanalysis, the subject, by listening to their own speech over the course of years, comes to recognise the utterance of their own unconscious—an unconscious that is nothing other than these very words and the manner in which they are linked together. In this essay, by working upon a single word—"heart" (*del*)—I demonstrate this very method of re-reading as an illustration and a representative sample.

- Between two opposing poles—on the one side, forgetting oneself and one's own culture and circling like a moth around the candle of modern culture and discoveries, and on the other side, turning inward upon oneself, clinging to oneself, gazing only at oneself, and aggrandising oneself—there undoubtedly exists a space that can be rediscovered. This rightful ground for any people lies in walking harmoniously upon the two feet of past and future. The past is within us: in speech and dialect, in every single word of our discourse—like the mother tongue, which imprints its structure within us for all time. Beyond childhood, whatever other language we may speak, write, and conduct our daily lives in, it is the structure of the mother tongue that holds our "unconscious" bound to itself and forms the basis of our wishes, impulses, desires, depressions, joys, sorrows, affections, inscriptions, and our inner condensation. One cannot sever the "cultural mother" from oneself as though she were a "foreign mother". Since she dwells within us, it is far better to understand her properly and draw upon her constructively. On the other hand, human knowledge in recent centuries has furnished instruments that make excavating the past easier. Between those two opposing poles—an uncritical return to an imaginary paradise of the past, or casting aside one's roots to drown in the current of new discoveries—lies a "middle way": confidence in oneself and a renewed self-understanding, situated right in the midst of a new world with new insights. It is this harmony and integration of the historical continuity of human knowledge that awakens openness of thought and the capacity to listen. Without losing ourselves, we stand alongside others: we contribute according to our own worth to advancing universal human culture, and we draw from this ocean according to our own cultural capacity.

- This essay does not claim that our forebears knew everything, still less that they knew it earlier and better than all others. The aim of this essay is to examine an example of applying modern insights to the re-comprehension of the past. Such studies serve as models for those who still believe in ancient cultures and their achievements.

- Like other inquiries addressing diverse domains of human understanding, this essay cannot develop every aspect exhaustively all at once, as that would exceed the reader's patience. No child learns to speak by studying grammar and constructing proper sentences; a child begins with half a word and progresses over years to full words, phrases, sentences, and the articulation of a comprehensive subject. Illuminating the long path of exploring and educating the inner psyche of the human being proves far easier through exemplification, symbol-making, and comparing past understandings. For Persian speakers, who know the "heart" (*del*) in their very soul, entering the realm of the "unconscious" with the key of *del* is far simpler than traversing the labyrinthine paths of complex psychoanalytic hypotheses.

- Clinical psychoanalysis opened a new window onto an ancient world; in a sense, it added a new dimension to human knowledge. In a world where the foundations of thought had been narrowly demarcated under the name of science, the "unconscious"—like a stranger within—reawakened the human being, conferred a new dimension upon humanity and its self-knowledge, and prepared the ear to listen anew to the past. Applying clinical psychoanalytic insight across other fields of knowledge—such as sociology, anthropology, architecture, criminology, cultural studies, lexicology, and so forth—led to a re-reading of other disciplines. This essay seeks to place before the reader an example of such close inquiry in the field of "lexicology".

I – "*Del*" (Heart) and the Persian Language:

Whether in everyday speech or in Persian literature, *del* occupies so singular a place that at times we forget which *del* we are speaking of. Every word is formed of two inseparable halves, like two sides of a single coin: the acoustic image or sound we employ to utter the word (the signifier) and the concept or meaning concealed behind that word (the signified). A fine example is the word *shir*, which carries three signifieds: a water tap (*shir-e âb*), camel's milk (*shir-e shotor*), and the lion of the jungle (*shir-e jangal*). The word *del* follows this very same process. Which *del* are we speaking of? At first glance, more than 150 words are used in the Persian language in which *del* takes on a distinct colouring. I have examined the functioning of the word *del* across various cultures of the world elsewhere [2]. One may say that, apart from ancient Egypt—where the heart was recognised as the seat of thought—across other ancient cultures, *del* possessed much the same character.

The word *del* and its derivatives appear more than 850 times, the word *âb* (water) nearly 800 times, and the word *âftâb* (sun) more than 200 times in Rumi's *Masnavi-ye Ma'navi*. In the *Divan* of the Master of Shiraz, the word *del* and its related terms appear more than 700 times (Appendix I), whereas *jân* (soul/life) and its derivatives appear over 300 times, the name "Hafez" over 500 times, and *mehr* (affection) and *'eshq* (love) with their related terms over 500 times.

On the other hand, at times two words with two distinct phonetic signifiers convey a single concept. Such are the words *del* and *qalb*. However, *qalb* is used as the anatomical name for the blood-pumping organ of the body and is employed in only a few instances in its metaphorical senses, such as *qovvat-e qalb* (encouragement/fortitude) or *nâ-khâles va vârâneh* (impure/counterfeit and inverted).

The Middle Persian (Pahlavi) word for *del* is *dil*. That testimony alone suffices to establish this word within Old Persian. In regional dialects such as Natanzi, Semnani, and Tabari, *del* is used with closely related pronunciations in this very same sense. The oldest text I have found is stanza 12 of the Gathas, where the equivalent term for *del* is used metaphorically: "Therefore, let every person—whether liar or truthful, whether learned or unlearned—reveal what they hold in their heart and mind."

One may well ask why so many other words have sprung from the word *del*. In this study, and for greater clarity, in addition to Persian dictionaries [3], I have drawn upon the *Divan* of the Master of Shiraz, since his poetry may be recognised as an eloquent emblem and representative of Persian culture—and in the words of Hasan Anvari: "Hafez employs the word as a living, autonomous entity with all of its attributes; to him, the word carries authority with all of its phonetic and semantic properties, not merely the meaning of a word and only one single meaning" [4].

The word *del* is used in three broad senses:

1 – In the sense of middle, centre, interior, inside, the very midst—such as *del-e âsemân* (heart of the sky) or *del-e shab* (dead of night / heart of the night). The Master says [5]:

"Last night in our circle, the tale was of your tresses; / Until the very heart of the night, the talk was of the chain of your locks."

Although one could reflect upon every poem of the Master and fill pages with its subtleties, insights, and beauties, I must perforce pass on so that the discourse does not grow unduly long.

2 – The Moïn Persian Dictionary (*Farhang-e Moïn*) states: "The heart (*del*) is a divine and spiritual subtlety; it is the reality of the human being, and it is what perceives, knows, attains gnosis, and loves." It appears that the late Moïn borrowed this definition from the *History of Sufism* (*Tārikh-e Tasavvof*) written by the late Qasem Ghani, for under the corresponding entry for *qalb* (heart), he cites the full passage as follows: "… This *qalb* maintains a mysterious bond and relationship with the physical heart, the nature of which cannot be clearly described…" Such an employment of the word *del* has deep roots in Iranian mystical culture, which forms the subject of another research study [6]. In the *Borhān-e Qāte'* it is written: "It denotes that divine subtlety which cannot be put into words, like the treasury of the secrets of the Real…" In this same tradition, mystics are called *sāheb-del* (masters of the heart), and *del-parvar* refers to one who cultivates the heart or inner being. In most places, when commentators on Hafez refer to *del*, they have only this meaning of the heart in mind. A few examples:

- Zaryāb Kho'i writes: "… It is a world in which God manifests Himself in His attributes of beauty and perfection, and in which there is no trace of demon, Satan, or Ahriman. Because the poet possesses a heart purer than limpid water, he is worthy of witnessing and contemplating such a world [7]." Elsewhere, whenever this same scholar encounters the word *del*, he equates it with the owner of the heart and passes lightly over metaphors such as "the bird of the heart" (*morgh-e del*), "the blood of the heart" (*khoun-e del*), and "the feeble heart" (*del-e za'if*).

- Anvāri states: "*Del* means the inner consciousness of Khājeh [Hafez], which was worthy of harbouring the subtlety of eternal love."

- Zaryāb Kho'i, across more than 400 pages of his work entitled *Āyineh-ye Jām* (*The Mirror of the Cup*), devotes only a single page to the relationship between "the blood of the heart" and "the mark upon the brow" in the ghazals of Hafez, and in his commentary on this couplet:

(478) Trace upon my brow a mole from the blood of my heart,
So that they may know I am of pagan creed, sacrificed to thee.

after offering apt observations on the poem, he concludes: "… and in this poem too, Hafez expresses this very point: trace a mark upon my brow from my own blood… [8]". How effortlessly "the blood of the heart" gives way here to "my own blood", as though there were no trace of the countless metaphors linking the heart, love, affection, and self-sacrifice upon the path of love and the Beloved.

- Khorramshāhi refers our "*del*" to the Cup of Jam (*Jām-e Jam*) and, in his discussion of the Cup of Jam, writes: "The Cup of Jam is the pure, luminous, and refined heart of the mystic, which is considered the theatre of manifestation of the beauty of Truth, the epiphany of the Eternal Beloved, and the all-reflecting mirror of all the unsolvable and obscure mysteries of creation." Elsewhere, quoting Abū Hāmid al-Ghazālī, he writes: "… One is that which all creatures may know, and the other is that which is veiled and known by none… And more wondrous still is that from within the heart a window opens unto the heavenly kingdom [9]."

- At times, Hafez scholars have taken knowledge of *del* so much for granted that they have not spoken of it at all, as in a work entitled *Farhang-e Ash'ār-e Hāfez* (*Dictionary of Hafez's Poetry*), in which more than fifty terms such as *dalq* (dervish cloak), *vajd* (ecstasy), *mohabbat* (affection), and *sabr* (patience) are discussed, whilst *del* is consigned to oblivion [10].

- In the ghazals of Hafez, in our estimation, *del* in its mystical sense is used explicitly more than fifty times [11], with expressions such as: "the speech of the people of the heart" (*sokhan-e ahl-e del*), "of the mystics", "the heart as a mirror", "the mole of wonder upon the face of the heart…", "the heart emerging from behind the veil", "that day the door of meaning opened unto my heart", and finally this couplet like an eloquent mirror:

(27) For this reason they hold me dear at the Magians' monastery:
A fire that never dies is ever burning in our heart.

or:

(25) When thou hearest the speech of the people of the heart, say not it is an error;
O connoisseur of speech, may my soul be sacrificed to thee—the error lies right here.

3 – Yet what chiefly concerns us in this essay is the third *del*: a *del* that functions as an interlocutor, as the other side of the ego, the other side of logic, reason, argument, and calculation; as the counterpart of soul, body, custom, and religion.

II – "Del" (the Heart) and the "Unconscious":

At the outset we confront a striking duality: on the one hand, the link between the two concepts of "*del*" and the "unconscious" is so self-evident that everyone seems to recognise it in their own symbolism; on the other hand, it seems that until now no one has cast a scientific eye upon this connection. Sigmund Freud himself casts, as it were, a sidelong glance at this link. Someone like him—who traces his grasp of the "unconscious" to the workings of words in jokes and witticisms, who regards speech, the word, the proverb, and everyday street parlance as the basis of his work, and who selects the names of his discovered phenomena from mythology—does not ask himself: what is the bond between the "heart" (*del*), known across all cultures of the world from ancient times, and the phenomenon of the "unconscious"? That "heart" whose emblem, pierced by an arrow, we have seen carved upon the trees of every village and the walls of every city. In his text *An Autobiographical Study*, Freud writes: "For the 'unconscious', no anatomical connection with the brain can be found; this link is a conceptual one, like the link with the heart."

["He who listens to the voice of his heart rather than the confused clamour of the street, the market, and the tavern, and has the courage to bring the teachings of his 'heart' into the arena, is ever a proud man."]

Quoting this remark by Börne, Freud writes: "This saying may well be the origin of my innovation." We know that his innovative achievement was the invention of clinical psychoanalysis and the discovery of the "unconscious" as a place within the human psyche. It appears that the term "unconscious" (*inconscient*) was recorded in the Dictionary of the French Academy for the first time in 1878. Our fundamental question is this: does Sigmund Freud bestow a new concept upon an already known word, or does he grant a new presence to an ancient concept—the "heart"? Our endeavour in this essay is to find an answer to this question.

Joël Dor writes in his book *Freud's Achievement*: "In proposing a topical psychic notion such as consciousness applied to the 'unconscious', Freud did not discover a new concept, but rather conferred a new meaning upon an existing word."

I hold a different view: Freud avails himself of this term in order to give a specific structure to his personal investigations and to his observations of what in everyday life escapes the field of our conscious perception—such as ruptures in thought and logic, slips of the tongue, lapses of memory in speech and behaviour, dreams, and, on the whole, the symptoms of the recognised illness of neurosis. Prior to Freud, the word "unconscious" was used in the sense of "non-conscious", just as it continues to be used in everyday speech today.

Around the two concepts of "*del*" and the "unconscious", one almost invariably encounters notions such as wish, desire, memory, speech, love and affection, pleasure, joy, and poetry…

In his *New Introductory Lectures on Psycho-Analysis*, Freud states: "Psychoanalysis has placed the unconscious somewhere between body and psyche." In the eighteenth century, Mesmer, with his hypothesis of animal magnetism for treating patients, fashioned a magnet in the shape of a "heart" and placed it upon the hearts of patients in order to cure hysterical sufferers; here, the heart and the ailments of neurosis are already linked together. In the book *Hysteria Salutes You*, Chauvelot notes: "In Chinese belief, the individual and his organs do not exist; only function is at issue—the functions that govern the body… The axis around which everything (in a country) revolves is the Emperor; in the body, this axis is the 'heart', which maintains the same relationship with the other functions as the Emperor does with his subjects." A Persian proverb says: "The heart is the king of the body" (*del shāh-e badan ast*).

Further on in the same book we read: "… The heart is like a host, and the others are guests. It remains still, and it is through its support that everything operates; it radiates light like the sun and, through its representatives—the eye, the ear, perception, and the tongue—enters into relation with others… When the heart-Emperor is afflicted, it loses the intelligence and perception of what transpires in the body; if the affliction intensifies, symptoms arise such as heaviness in the chest, absent-mindedness, a state between sleep and waking, mad laughter, anger, and gradually fever, pains in the region of the heart and brain, nausea, even unto the death of the patient. When the energy of the heart diminishes, the complexion turns yellow, dejection and withering ensue, and an inflammatory state sets in. In a word, the worst affliction of the heart is psychic: anxiety, suicidal impulses, and amnesia, as though the pathways of the heart's connection had been closed."

The Chinese conception of the heart is psychosomatic. For them, there is not one anatomical heart and another metaphorical heart; both are one and the same heart. It is as though they compressed at a single stroke all the terms of clinical psychoanalysis into their manner of conceiving the functioning of the heart.

Let us return to the "unconscious". Sigmund Freud draws the human world and its interiority down into the depths of myths, poetry, literature, the vernacular of the street and marketplace, popular speech, folk tales, proverbs, legends, stories—in short, everything that has dealings with the human word—like a realm awaiting rediscovery, like ancient ruins requiring excavation and retrieval, like an eloquent museum.

To clarify the concept of the "unconscious" further, let us turn to Freud's own writings.

- In his paper entitled *The Unconscious* (in *Metapsychology*), he writes: "Instinctual representatives that seek to discharge their cathexis—a charge brimming with 'desire'. Coordinated instinctual impulses operate alongside one another, independent and without mutual influence."

- Elsewhere in the same work he writes: "The unconscious knows neither time nor contradiction, neither negation nor doubt, neither substitution nor the difference between the two sexes (woman and man). It transforms the reality of the external world into an internal reality. The unconscious obeys its own laws—laws that recognise neither the conscious logical relations of non-contradiction on the one hand, nor the relation of cause and effect on the other."

In his various reflections and findings, Freud goes further and reveals the unconscious as a phenomenon beyond mere blind submission to desire and whim.

- In his text entitled *Five Psychoanalyses*, he notes: "The ego can have unconscious desires; here, instead of contrasting the conscious and the unconscious, one ought to speak of the contrast between the 'ego' and that which is 'repressed'." Freud readily views the unconscious as accumulated memories, of which repressed desires form a part.

- In another work entitled *On Dreams*, Freud reminds us: "If we merely say that the conscious is the commanding part and the unconscious the emotional, obedient part, we have doubtless stated the matter far too simply; yet this very point forms the essential core of this highly complex phenomenon." Doubtless, in this same connection, one may recall expressions such as: "Listen to what your heart says", "It is the command of the heart; nothing can be done about it", or "Let your heart choose."

- In his 1915 *Note on the Unconscious*, Freud says: "Every psychical act is composed of two phases, between which an examination and elimination take place. First, the unconscious process, which, if eliminated during the test, is called repressed and does not reach the second phase." In the same paper we also read: "The use of phrases such as unconscious affect or unconscious feelings generally leads us to the quantitative operation of an instinctual impulse that is the product of repression."

By employing the expression "unconscious feelings", Freud repeatedly underscores the relationship between these two phenomena and strives, in the passage cited above, to dissect this bond.

- In *The Interpretation of Dreams*, we read: "The path of unconscious thoughts leading to their 'release' opens once they have become sufficiently charged." How beautiful it is that in everyday conversation we too say: "The floodgates of his heartache opened" (*sar-e dard-e delash bāz shod*). And surely the floodgates of heartache open when sufficient pressure has built up; or we say: "Come now, do not keep what is in your heart bottled up—do not hold it inside your heart, speak out!" It is striking that heartache (*dard-e del*) is "spoken". And once again, in clinical psychoanalysis, the sole exit for unconscious material is precisely speaking—and doing so upon the couch, in the presence of the clinical psychoanalyst who sits as an attentive companion.

- In his *Introductory Lectures on Psycho-Analysis*, he writes: "The unconscious in psychical life is nothing other than this earliest, infantile portion of life." In his letters to Karl Abraham, he notes: "The division between conscious and unconscious does not exist in the earliest period of a child's life." In the minutes of the Vienna Psychoanalytic Society, it is recorded: "Drawing a distinction between the conscious and unconscious feelings of children is exceedingly difficult."

From these statements, one may extract the link between the earliest period of childhood and the child's psychical unity. What we say in our daily lives regarding children—"purity of heart" (*del-pāki*), "whatever they have in their heart is on their tongue", "truth comes from the mouths of children", "having a childlike heart" (taking offence at the slightest remark), "their tongue rests upon their heart"—all bear witness to this. Finally, Freud writes in his paper *The Unconscious*: "The primary processes of the unconscious obey the pleasure principle." In Persian, the words *del-khāstan* (to desire from the heart) and *del-khāh* (according to the heart's wish) are not unrelated to this concept.* Among the terms formed from *del* in the Persian language, I have thus far found more than 150 words. All of these words are used in everyday life. From what has been presented, the esteemed reader may follow these words independently and trace their footprints in folk sayings, proverbs, popular dialects, and especially in Persian poetry and songs. Research on this subject could furnish topics for many university theses. Each of the ancient compound words formed with *del* is in itself a complete and distinct exposition of a function of the "heart". These words demonstrate that Persian speakers have accorded a most precious place to the "heart". *Del* appears as something distinct from the ego; there is a perpetual dialogue between the ego and the heart. Freud says: "The ego is not even master in its own house."

The heart chooses a path that is not always the path of the "ego". I weep for my heart, whilst my heart laughs at my plight. The evidence is so abundant that it would unduly lengthen this essay—such as what pertains to *del-khāstan* and *del-khāh* and their bond with desire and wish. Boldness and fear are bound to the heart, as in *por-del* (intrepid, lit. full-hearted) and *kam-del* (timid, lit. faint-hearted); *del-bar* (heart-ravisher) and *del-dār* (heart-holder, beloved); love and affection, that separate logic of heart and head which constitutes the pervasive and primary play of Persian poetry, as in *del-dādeh* (having given one's heart), *del-bar* and *del-robā* (heart-stealing)… Hesitation is expressed as *do-deli* (lit. two-heartedness); depression, languor, and joy as *del-mordeh* (dead-hearted), *del-shād* (glad-hearted), and *del-gereftegi* (heavy-heartedness)… Inner purity and inner impurity in Persian also revolve around the heart: *del-pāk* (pure-hearted), *bad-del* (suspicious or ill-hearted), taking offence as *del-gir shodan* (to become heavy-hearted/hurt), generosity and open-handedness as *dast-o-del-bāzi* (open-handedness and open-heartedness), humanitarianism and altruism, having a kind heart (*del-e mehrabān*), a great heart (*del-e bozorg*), and a generous heart (*del-e bakhshandeh*). Melancholy and separation from beloved and homeland, longing and exile, as *del havā kardan* (the heart yearning). Having a close bond with another is *ham-deli* (shared-heartedness, empathy), "which is sweeter than sharing the same tongue (*ham-zabāni*)". And marriage has also been called "the union of hearts" (*peyvand-e del-hā*). It is as though the Persian language derived all its vocabulary for the functions of the psyche from *del* and called it "the work of the heart" (*kār-e del*). How lovely is this hemistich by Ferdowsi: "One night among nights, he lay asleep, scarred of heart (*dāgh-del*)."

Poetry is described as a kind of opening of the doors of the unconscious, or poetic speech as the fruit of the unconscious. The connection between poetry, music, love, and the "heart" is visible everywhere. Internally, the functioning of the unconscious rests upon three pillars: condensation (conciseness), metaphor, and metonymy (allusion). One can observe the extent to which these three phenomena operate in poetry and song. Dreams, reverie, and wish are the expression of poetic and lyrical feeling; and in clinical psychoanalysis, as Freud stated, the dream is the royal road of access to the unconscious.

On the other hand, the "unconscious" constructs an image for the organs of the body, which is called the unconscious body image. This image plays a very substantial role in mediating psychosomatic disorders. It is noteworthy that human beings have conceived a similar functioning for the heart as well, such as "the eye of the heart" (*cheshm-e del*), "the head of the heart" (*sar-e del*—"The game of love is no idle game, O heart, stake thy head!"), "the mouth of the heart", "the foot of the heart", "the lane of the heart" (*kuy-e del*)…

Of Gobineau, one of the great admirers of Iranian culture, it has been said: "… For him, his beloved Persia was a geography of the heart." People have spoken of the borders of the heart, just as in clinical psychoanalysis we speak of the borders of the unconscious. In his book *47 Days in a Coma*, Chauvelot, the French psychiatrist and psychoanalyst, speaks of the borders of the unconscious, which are precisely the words accumulated in the unconscious and their interconnection with one another. The use of expressions such as "the house of the heart" (*khāneh-ye del*), "the quarter of the heart" (*kuy-e del*), "dweller of the heart" (*sāken-e del*), and proverbs such as "Home is where the heart is" (Swiss) and "The heart is not a knee that can be bent" (African), all follow this very same line.

In the Persian language we have two exceedingly valuable expressions, reflecting upon which is deeply instructive. The expression *dard-e del kardan* (literally "to speak the ache of the heart", meaning to pour out one's heart), signifying an opening of one's inner self or "spreading out the tablecloth of the heart"—that is, bringing one's interiority outward without any boundary or self-restraint. On the other hand, there is the term *sang-e sabour* (literally "the stone of patience"), which we sometimes apply to a friend, neighbour, colleague, or close acquaintance who listens with patience and forbearance to the words of our "heartache", and who, through silence and confidentiality, makes it possible for us to return to them on other occasions to unburden our heart. The *sang-e sabour* embodies that capacity to endure listening to the heartaches of others—that space an individual finds among those around them, such that the listener neither exploits what they hear (the confidences of others) for their own or anyone else's benefit or harm, nor engages in judgement, arbitration, or lecturing. Put differently, the *sang-e sabour* is a patient, neutral confidant who possesses the stamina to hear everything. This remarkably fine bond of pouring out one's heart before a *sang-e sabour* may be seen as closely akin to the function of the clinical psychoanalyst. It is as though human beings quite naturally apprehended and practised this relationship and this need for a clinical psychoanalyst, and as though clinical psychoanalysis were nothing other than the systematisation, theorisation, and pedagogical codification of the concept of *sang-e sabour*. I recall that many years ago one of the residents of our neighbourhood was renowned for being a *sang-e sabour*, and I heard another elderly woman say: "I do not know what he possesses, yet the moment I sit with him for a while, I grow calm." Without entering here into the fundamental discussion of clinical psychoanalysis known as "transference" (*enteqāl-e ehsāsāt*) between the clinical psychoanalyst and the subject, we know that both concepts are intensely close to one another, for "transference" is precisely that state of needing the psychoanalyst's presence. A question may also arise here: what connection exists between the physical heart, which supplies blood to the various organs, and *del*, and whence does it come that the metaphorical word *del* derives from the heart (the cardiac organ)? It seems that the relationship between child and mother—which consists precisely in the mother's supply of blood to the child over many months—is not absent from this metaphor. Maternal love and tenderness on the one hand, and the primary structure of the formation of the "unconscious" out of the manner in which the child separates from the mother on the other, constitute one of the very first foundations of clinical psychoanalytic theory regarding the formation of the unconscious in human beings. Among adolescents in various cultures, there is a custom whereby, to achieve greater closeness and a sense of friendship, they make a small cut on their hands and mingle one another's blood, which for them is a sign of the depth of their bond and friendship. In this metaphorical gesture, one may discern the footprint of that very same blood-tie.

III – Some Examples of the Companionship between "Del" and the "Unconscious":

12 – *Del* as the other side of me, as an addressee and interlocutor, as that which is within me yet separate from me, as an active agent with which dialogue is possible and which is ever present—as when I say: "I was telling a story for my own heart" or "He is speaking to his own heart." The esteemed Hafez, across his collection of ghazals, engages with his own heart more than fifty times [12], with expressions such as: "Whither goest thou, O heart?"; "O heart, youth has departed"; "Until when, on the path of old age, wilt thou follow what custom, O heart?"; "Not just now is the heart of Hafez…"; "O heart, this lamentation and…"; "The game of love demands endurance, O heart…"; "In her lasso-like tresses, O heart…"; "Wish for the spring of life, O heart"; "O heart, the way of…"; "O heart, come so that…"; "Didst thou see, O heart…"; "Bring glad tidings, O heart…"; "One must not grieve at the taunt of the envious, O heart"; "O heart, if today's revelry…"; "From her playful eye, O heart…"; "In the ambush of the glance, I am at war with my own heart"; "O heart of vain covetousness…"; "O heart, from the flood of annihilation…"; "The game of love is no idle game, O heart, stake thy head!"; "Though the company of ease fell pleasantly, O heart…"; "Seek aid from the spirit of the *rend*s, O heart"; "O heart, in vain thy knowledge and life have gone to the wind"; "Thou knowest not the worth of time, O heart"; "Strive for patience, O heart"; "O heart, if thou emergest from that dimple-well of the chin…"; "The path of love is full of tumult and strife, O heart…"

13 – *Del* as the other side of logic, reason, calculation, study, and schooling. As Saadi says:

At first I was on my guard to surrender my heart to none;
I beheld thy likeness: neither reason remained nor wit.

This is what today, in understanding unconscious functioning, we call the "logic of the unconscious", inasmuch as this logic and its mode of operation do not accord with logic based upon concepts and conceptual relations—especially where longing, desire, gratification, and being drawn towards that beyond are concerned. In everyday parlance, the "heart" (*del*) is set in opposition to the "head" (*sar*) and reason. Examples in the poems of Hafez [13]: "the bewildered heart" (*del-e sargashteh*), "like a heart that has lost its head" (*del-e sar az dast dādeh*), "the caravans of heart and knowledge", where the heart stands alongside knowledge:

(600) The tale of how and why brings headache, O heart;
Take up the cup and rest a moment from thy life.

Ferdowsi declares: "Keep heart and brain far from haste; wisdom, in haste, falls asleep."

14 – *Del* as the other side of body and soul (*tan o jān*): in the classification of pathology, illnesses are divided into three categories: psychic, somatic, and psychosomatic. In the early twentieth century, extensive research was conducted on psychosomatic disorders, and in particular the effects of hysteria upon various organs of the body were studied. Examples from the poems of Hafez in which *del* appears distinct from body and soul, and alongside them [14]: "May heart and soul be sacrificed to thy face"; "From heart and soul, the honour of the Beloved's company is the aim"; "Thou hast burned my soul, yet with my heart I love thee"; "The soul melted that the work of the heart might be completed, and it was not"; "the tablet of heart and soul"; "soul upon the lips and the regret of the heart"; "a hundred scars upon soul and heart". In this couplet, with a characteristic roguish wit (*rendi*), Hafez presents the psyche (*ravān*) as a synthesis of heart and soul:

(578) Demand soul and heart from this servant, and take his spirit (*ravān*),
For thy command holds sway over the heads of the free.

In two other couplets, the latent relationship in pathology between *del* and the body is expressed:

Ghazal 139 (G12S)

(157) Therefore my feeble heart draws me towards the meadow,
That the soul may snatch a remedy from death through the zephyr.

(496) Like the zephyr, with an ailing body and an impatient heart,
I shall go in devotion to that gracefully swaying cypress.

In this couplet, Hafez gathers at once everything dear to him:

Ghazal 122 (G118B4)

(142) May my head, gold, heart, and soul be sacrificed to that friend
Who upholds the duty of companionship, affection, and fidelity.

15 – *Del* as the other side of religion and custom (*din o ā'in*), understood here as a mode and tradition of living, and the repetition of behaviour and conduct grounded in habit. Examples from Hafez [15]: "My heart and religion are gone…"; "He who stole the heart and is now bound to religion…"; "Now he is the ruiner of my heart and religion"; "He staked heart and religion on pride"; "the highwayman of religion and heart". And in this couplet, how beautifully he joins heart, religion, reason, and wisdom:

Ghazal 371 (G364B7)

(514) Praise be to God! Like us, he was devoid of heart and religion—
The one whom we had dubbed wise and sagacious.

16 – *Del* as the unconscious, that part of the human psyche from which wisdom and madness, feelings, behaviour, and conduct arise, and to which music, poetry, sleep, imagination, longing, and dreams return. In clinical psychoanalytic knowledge, words and their usage, their consonance, their juxtaposition, and the manner in which they are strung together form the very foundation of the unconscious—such that it is the chain of acoustic images of words (signifiers) that shapes the structure of the unconscious. The effort to catalogue and investigate words stems from this very fact. Few words in the Persian language have gathered around themselves such diverse metaphorical concepts as *del*; perhaps only words such as *āb* (water) or *mehr* (affection/sun) can stand on a par with *del*. Hafez declares:

(26) Within my broken-hearted self, I know not who dwells;
For I am silent, whilst he is in lamentation and uproar.

Undoubtedly, this inner stranger appearing alongside the term "broken-hearted" (*khasteh-del*) is inseparable from *del*. In dictionaries, alongside the metaphorical meaning of *del*, the word *zamir* (inner mind/conscience) has also been used, and in the earliest Persian translations of clinical psychoanalytic sources, the term *zamir-e nākhod-āgāhi* ("unconscious inner mind") was employed. Similarly, dictionaries have defined *del-shodegi* not only as being infatuated, but also as folly, ignorance, and madness. Examples in the poems of Khājeh [Hafez] [16]: "feeble of heart" (*za'if-e del*), "mad heart" (*del-e divāneh*), "distraught/scattered heart" (*parishān-del*—in the coinage of specialised psychology and psychiatry dictionaries, translators coined the term *ravān-parish* to correspond to [psychose] / psychosis); "wise heart" (*del-e dānā*), "the affair of the heart" (*kār-e del*), "sympathetic heart" (*del-e ham-dard*), "being at war with one's own heart", "sorrow-stricken heart" (*del-gham-dideh*), "frenzied/enraptured heart" (*del-shurideh*), "weary/broken heart" (*khasteh-del*), "melancholy-stricken heart" (*del-sowdā-zadeh*), "the heart emerging from the veil", "brooding over the heart's sorrow", "every fragment of my heart holds a tale of grief", "the experience of the heart", "attending to the counsel of the heart", "surrendering the reins of the heart to someone". The consonance of music, the unconscious, and the heart lies concealed in this couplet:

(594) When the nightingale's song took effect within my heart,
I became such that no endurance remained in me.

Dictionaries have also glossed *del* as "the locus of attaining meanings" (*mahall-e tahsil-e ma'āni*) or "the rational/speaking soul" (*nafs-e nāteqeh*). In clinical psychoanalysis, the individual's "speech" is the fundamental element; for this reason, the human being is termed a "speaking being".

17 – The human unconscious possesses a structure. Recent knowledge has shown that one may speak of two phenomena: the formation of this structure and its functioning. The groundwork for the formation of this structure is laid with the birth of the child and continues through the early years of life. This formation depends upon hereditary foundations, the mother, the father, the family, and the surrounding culture. Sweet and bitter events contribute to its shaping—events that sometimes persist for a long time like psychical wounds. In the formation of the unconscious and its structure, maternal love, the child's dependence upon the mother, the figure of the father, and what of the father is inscribed in the mother and in her image play a foundational role. The duality of this dependence-oneness of the child with the mother, on the one hand, and the necessity of separating oneself from the mother and stepping into the world—which is precisely the paternal or separating role of the father—on the other, provides the functional foundation or dialectic of the formation of the unconscious.

Once formed upon the basis of its structure, the unconscious exercises specific functions that govern the individual's daily life. These functions are, in simpler terms, the very centre of human feelings. In this study, I endeavour to examine in two distinct categories those *del*-derived words that relate either to the formation of the unconscious or to its functioning.

1 – Affection and love, whose simple and primary prototype—the foundation of all the child's future loves—is precisely maternal love and affection. Expressions such as "withdrawing one's heart from someone's affection" or "giving one's heart", *del-shifteh* (enamoured), *del-bākhtan* (to lose one's heart), *del bar-dāshtan* (to detach one's heart), *del bordan* (to captivate the heart), *del bar-kandan* (to tear away one's heart), *del-bar* and *del-bari* (heart-ravishing/charm), *del-bastegi* (attachment), *del bastan* (to attach one's heart), *del-basteh* (attached), *del-band* (dear one/beloved child), *del-shodegi* in the sense of being in love, *del-navāz* meaning beloved, cherished, compassionate, and kind, *del-ārām* (heart-soother), *del geravidan* (to incline one's heart), *del-dār* (beloved), *del-khāsteh* (heart's desired, beloved), *del-āvizidan* and *del-āvikhtan* meaning emotional attachment—all stem from the root of affection or rancour arising from the heart. In the ghazals of Khājeh [Hafez], a large proportion of the words derived from *del* appear in this sense [17], such as: "What shall the heart of enemies perceive from the Friend's face?"—here *del* as the locus of perception and distinguishing friend from foe; "My heart is slipping from my hands"; "If that Shirazi Turk captures our heart"; "the heart of lovers"; "heart-illuminating" (*del-afrouz*); "withdrawing the heart"; "giving the heart"; "tying a knot upon the heart"; "paying the coin of the heart"; "the burden of Majnun's heart"; "the heart, royal pavilion of the Friend's love"; "Without dispute, thy tress draws the heart"; "surrendering the heart to coquetry"; "surrendering the heart to love"; "Though the heart conceals the pain of love from the people…"; "giving the treasury of the heart"; "loving with the heart"; "prizing the heart as naught"; "the heart being empty of love"; "hunting the heart"; "the heart departing"; "companion of the heart"; "heartless/enraptured" (*bi-del*); "guarding the heart"; "the heart running in pursuit of…"; "the heart being in someone's hands"; "plundering the heart"; "lying in ambush for the heart"; "setting one's heart upon someone"; "capturing the heart"; "admitting love into the heart"; "leading the heart astray"; "stealing the heart"; "descending into the heart"; "the fallen heart, like Farhād of the fallen heart". In this couplet, Hafez brings the work of the heart to completion with love:

(613) O heart, thou dost not pass through the lane of love;
Thou hast all the provisions gathered, yet thou doest nothing.

18 – One of the domains of clinical psychoanalytic research is the concept of the unconscious body image. More than anyone else, Madame Dolto, psychiatrist and clinical psychoanalyst, strove to popularise this concept. The "unconscious" constructs an image in relation to human organs that comes into play in many instances such as dreams, reveries, behaviour, conduct, and psychological disorders. Particularly towards the end of the stages of psychoanalysis, the individual gradually becomes aware of this unconscious image, feels their presence among others more acutely, pays greater sensitivity to their behaviour and conduct, and completes their self-discovery of their body in space and place. In the poetry of Khājeh [Hafez], the relationship between *del* and other organs of the body appears more than sixty times [18], such as: "the eye of the heart" (*cheshm-e del*), "the sense of smell of the heart" (*mashām-e del*), "the heart trembling like a willow", "the heart entangling in tresses", "my heart, like the cypress, bound by the foot", "the darkened eye of the heart", "the smoke of the heart", "bearing the mole of wonder upon the face of the heart", "the ear of the heart", "the heart said: I shall alight in this city for its fragrance", "the groaning of the heart", "the heart raining tears", "the advice-heeding heart", "the foot-bound heart".

19 – *Del* as the seat of longing, desire, wish, want, gratification, and receiving pleasure: in the formation of the child's unconscious structure, the shaping of desire occupies a special place. For human "individuality" and agency are formed through "wanting". This wanting is born in connection with the first lack of nourishment—hunger and thirst in the infant—such that the balanced relationship among three elements—wish and desire, the articulation or enactment of this wish, and finally real need and necessity—is effective in forming and balancing the child's unconscious structure. Let us note the compound words formed from *del* along these lines, such as: "setting one's heart upon something", "turning the heart's attention", "developing attachment", *del-khāstan* (to desire from the heart), *khāst-e del* (the heart's wish), *kām-e del* (the heart's gratification/fulfilment), *del-gerāni* meaning reluctance and disinclination. Examples from the poetry of Khājeh [Hafez] in this same vein [19]: "the heart in longing for thy face"; "I told thee the state of my heart—it is desire"; "my heart yearning for the joyful face"; "of whom shall I ask the heart's desire?"; "grant the heart's wish of Hafez"; "may the brand of thy grief be forbidden to our heart"; "mayest thou be the fulfiller of my restless heart's wish". And an eloquent example such as this couplet:

(480) Although I know that that solace of the heart will grant the heart's desire,
I sketch an imagined portrait and cast an omen of permanence.

showing how in this poem love, the pursuit of fulfilment, and fantasy—which are among the pillars of the unconscious—are gathered together in one place around the word *del*.

20 – *Del* as the locus of dialogue or the locus of secrets: the sole path for opening the unconscious is speech or the discourse of the friend/other. This sealed secret is opened only with difficulty. The clinical psychoanalyst's endeavour in traversing the long road of an individual's psychoanalysis is, as it were, to create a safe and calm space in which the individual's unconscious may open itself and lift the veil from accumulated memories and hidden psychical wounds. In Persian, *dard-e del kardan* means speaking the innermost depths, and the saying that "the heart is not a tablecloth to be spread before every Tom, Dick, and Harry" points to the complexity and necessary conditions for unburdening one's heart. Through the intricate stages that the individual traverses until, after years, they inevitably lay bare their innermost self without resistance, they keep their unconscious concealed. This resistance operates through various avenues: speaking of other things, speaking of everything, drawing the psychoanalyst into pity, speaking out of turn, storytelling, repetition, and idle chatter. In this regard, this verse from the book *History of the Seljuks* (*Tārikh-e Salājeqeh*) is most apt:

If the heart be not companion to the tongue,
Whatever the tongue utters shall be in vain.

Examples from the ghazals of Khājeh [Hafez] in this regard [20]: "the confidant of the secret of one's frenzied heart"; "the lament and outcry of the heart"; "the heart said his union might be regained through prayer"; "and that secret which I hid within my heart fell out into the open"; "my heart, which boasted of detachment"; "uttering the tale of the heart"; "upon my tongue was what lay in thy heart"; "not only from the secret of my heart has the veil been lifted"; "I have tales enough of the heart for the morning breeze"; "come, let me tell thee the sorrow of the heart's weariness"; "when I count the heartaches".

(213) What need to declare yearning, when the burning of the heart's fire
Can be recognised by the ardour that resides in speech?

21 – *Del* as the locus of a mode of perception, a kind of premonition without proof, logic, or reason—such as "falling into the heart" (*be-del oftādan*), "being inspired to the heart" (*be-del barāt shodan*), "casting into someone's heart", "crossing the heart", and phrases like: "You spoke the very words of my heart", "It is as though you were inside my heart", "You spoke from my heart", or "Our hearts have a pathway to one another." In a portion of his investigations, Freud pursued such workings of the unconscious in relationships and intuitions of this kind. Perhaps events or heard words arrange themselves side by side and forewarn us of a future to which we would have arrived by the same deductions had those words or events not been erased from memory—like knowledge that conceals itself and, when it surfaces, its logical connections or reasons for emerging have been forgotten.

- Pure heart (*del-pāk*), heart like a mirror (*del chon āyineh*), sincere heart (*del-sādeq*): at the very beginning of the formation of the unconscious in children, the "inhibiting filter" has not yet come into operation. Desire, whim, and wish, the utterance of the tongue, and the inner self are one. For children, desire, wish, and want stand in the same place as the real, becoming, and the possible. It is in this way that children dream their daytime desires at night in an unveiled and real manner. In adults, whenever this covering veil and filter is drawn aside, the unconscious manifests its desire; slips of the tongue and unintended, involuntary gestures are of this order. Having a childlike heart, speaking one's heart, or "a word that arises from the heart settles upon the heart", all follow this same path. Examples from the ghazals of Khājeh [Hafez] [21] include: "an unguarded heart" (*del-e bi-hefāz*), "purity of heart" (*safā-ye del*), "simplicity of heart" (*sādeh-deli*), "pure heart" (*del-pāk*), and this lucid, beautiful couplet concerning the mirror of the heart and the image of beauty:

Before the mirror of the heart, whatever I hold,
Save the image of thy beauty, is reflected no more.

- *Del* is also linked to will and resolve. Expressions such as *dar del dâshtan* (to hold in one's heart), meaning inwardly to intend or resolve upon something, or *del âmadan-e kasi* (for someone's heart to come round), meaning to agree to a matter or to give or receive heart (*qovvat-e qalb*), speak of moral backing and the strengthening of will.

22 – One of the foundational pillars of clinical psychoanalytic practice is the stage of transference between the patient and the psychoanalyst. Like an adhesive, this phenomenon serves as the bond of the relationship and guarantees the continuity and perseverance of the psychoanalytic work. For the patient's transference of feelings to the psychoanalyst—as a distinctive kind of affection and attachment—one might perhaps employ the term *ham-deli* (sharing of heart / empathy).

In the poems of the Master (Hafez), we read [22]: *hâl-e del goftan o khabar-e del shenoftan* (telling the state of the heart and hearing news of the heart), *sar-e peyvand-e to tanhâ na del-e Hâfez râst* (not Hafez's heart alone holds the thread of union with you), or *ham-neshin-e del* (companion of the heart).

- *Del* as the seat of dream and fantasy; the Master says: *nakhofteh-am ze khiyâli ke mipazad del-e man* ("I have not slept for the fantasy that my heart is brewing"), or *Hâfez cho minehi del-e to dar khiyâl-e khubân* ("Hafez, as you set your heart upon the image of the fair ones").

23 – *Del* and anxiety, restlessness, fear, agitation, calm, tranquillity, and solace, such as: *shur zadan-e del* (pounding/agitation of the heart), *delhoreh* (apprehension/anxiety), *qarâr gereftan-e del* (calming of the heart), *del-âzordegi* meaning anxiety and restlessness, *del-âsâ* (that which brings solace to the heart), *delshureh* (nervousness/worry), *delgarm* (encouraged/warm-hearted), *delvâpas* (anxious/concerned). In the Master's poems we find [23]: *sabr az del bordan* (stealing patience from the heart), *del-kharâbi kardan* (ravaging the heart), *del-negarâni* (heartfelt worry), *qarâr az del bordan* (taking calm from the heart), *del-sukhteh parvâneh-ye nâparvâ bud* (the burnt-hearted one was a fearless moth), *qarâr beh del bâz âmadan* (calm returning to the heart), *ârâm-e del* (peace of the heart), *del-ramideh* (startled/frightened heart), *del-e bi-qarâr* (restless heart), and this couplet:

(379) Tie a goblet to my shroud so that at the dawn of Resurrection / With wine I may drive from my heart the terror of the Day of Judgement.

24 – *Del* and depression, ardour, liveliness, and excitement, such as: *az del oftâdan* (falling from the heart / losing enthusiasm), *del beh kâr nadâdan* (not putting one's heart into work), *del-oftâdeh* (disheartened), *shekasteh-del* (broken-hearted), *del-afruzandeh* (that which kindles joy), *del-afsordeh* (dejected/depressed), *del-afkâr* (wounded-hearted), *del-angiz* (delightful/stirring), *del-negarâni* (worry), *ranjidegi* (hurt), *âzordegi* (offence/vexation), *delshâd* (glad-hearted, joyful and lively), *del-mândegi* (sorrow and *del-mordegi* / deadness of heart). In the Master's poems we find [24]: *del-ghamzadeh* (sorrow-stricken heart), *del-shekasteh* (broken-hearted), *del-mordeh* (dead-hearted), *mordeh-del* (dead-hearted), *del khosh budan* (to be glad of heart), *za'if-del* (faint-hearted), *mozhdeh ey del* (glad tidings, O heart!), *goshâyesh-e del* (opening/expansion of the heart), *khosh-deli* (cheerfulness), *del-garmi* (warmth/encouragement), and with this couplet in which, with his characteristic subtlety, the Master carries the opening of the heart all the way to the threshold of beholding bodily beauty:

(287) Unfasten the clasp of your robe so that my heart may open / For whatever opening I ever knew came from your side.

25 – *Del* and the relation of hurt and kindness, especially in relation to other people, such as: *beh del gereftan* (to take to heart), *del bar kasi larzidan* (a metaphor for sympathy and compassion), *del nemudan* (a metaphor for showing humanity), *delsuz* (sympathetic/kind), *del beh dast âvardan* (winning someone's heart), *del ranjidan* (taking offence / feeling hurt). In the Master's poems we find [25]: *del beh dast âvardan* (winning the heart), *bahr-e del-e digarân* (for the sake of others' hearts), *del shâd kardan* (gladdening the heart), *del kharidan* (purchasing/winning the heart), *del-e mehrabân* (kind heart). How sweetly is this human need for another human being expressed:

(598) My breast is brimming with pain—alas, for a balm! / My heart has grown weary of solitude—for God's sake, a confidant!

26 – *Del* as the dwelling place of grief and sorrow: on the one hand, sadness in its varying degrees occupies a special place in psychopathology—the closing in of the human being upon oneself, withdrawal from others, despair, hopelessness, and seclusion, which undoubtedly stand on the opposite shore from joy, openness, release, and, in short, truly living. In the Master's poems, this metaphorical sense of *del* is used repeatedly [26], such as: *khun dar del oftâdan* (blood falling into the heart), *del jâ-ye gham* (the heart as the seat of grief), *del-e meskin* (wretched heart), *az del gereh goshudan* (untying a knot from the heart), *ganj-e gham dar del-e virâneh* (the treasure of sorrow in the ruined heart), *del-e khorram* (joyous heart), *hâl-e del-e tang* (the state of the constricted heart), *suz-e del* (burning of the heart), *dard-e del* (heartache), *gereh az del goshudan* (untying the knot of the heart), *del-e majruh* (wounded heart), *del-rish* (sore-hearted), *del-shekasteh* (broken-hearted), *khun dar del oftâdan* (blood falling into the heart), *del-sukhteh* (burnt-hearted), *del khosh dâshtan* (keeping the heart glad), *del shâd kardan* (gladdening the heart), *tireh-del* (dark-hearted), *bâr-e gham-e del* (the burden of the heart's sorrow), *del-khasteh* (weary-hearted), *anduh-e del* (grief of the heart), *del-shâd* (glad-hearted), *nâvak-e del-duz* (heart-piercing arrow), *del-bimâr* (sick-hearted), *del-e meskin* (poor/wretched heart).

27 – Courage and audacity on the one hand, and faint-heartedness and lack of daring on the other, appear in close connection with *del*, such as: *boz-del* (cowardly, lit. goat-hearted), *delir* (brave), *kam-del* (timid), *del beh daryâ zadan* (to throw one's heart into the sea / take the plunge)—as though *del* were the centre of a force that impels the individual to live and to stand upright. The proverb *"delir tigh râ farmâyad va bi-del zabân râ"* ("the brave commands the sword, and the faint-hearted the tongue") beautifully illustrates the role of courage and speech. In the Master's ghazals we find [27]: *shir-del* (lion-hearted), *del qavi dâshtan* (having a stout heart), *mey-e delir nushidan* (drinking bold wine).

- Hesitation, wavering, and lack of firm resolve are likewise linked to *del*. One of the hallmarks of the hysterical psychic structure is precisely this indefiniteness and vacillation in desire, wish, and longing, flitting from branch to branch. In such individuals, it is as though wish and desire have gone missing, and the person runs from door to door in search of them, always having hidden the object of desire in another corner. Expressions such as *do-deli* (double-heartedness / hesitation), *del-del kardan* (dithering), *del yektâ kardan* (making the heart single), and *del yek-deleh kardan* (making up one's mind) belong to this same nexus.

28 – Effervescence, ardour, excitement, and the will to live also emanate from *del*. In the Master's ghazals we find [28]: *del-e doshmanân cherâgh-e mordeh* (the enemies' heart an extinguished lamp), *âtash-e del* (fire of the heart), *sham'-e del* (candle of the heart), *suz-e del* (ardour/burning of the heart), *del-foruz* (heart-illuminating), *âtash-e del-e suzân* (fire of the burning heart), *sobh-e rowshan-del* (bright-hearted dawn), *del-shurideh* (passionate/frenzied heart), *nur-e del* (light of the heart).

29 – In human psychology, and especially in behavioural studies, factors such as envy, rancour, hatred, habit, oversensitivity, loyalty, compassion, and responsiveness to external stimuli such as aesthetics are recognised as traits of an individual's personality. In Persian, we express many of these traits through the word *del*, such as: *del bâ khod nabudan* (one's heart not being with oneself, indicating distraction of the senses), *del-mordeh* (dead-hearted, indicating [...]), *del-suz* (indicating envy [*hasudi*, or compassion]), *del-siyâh* (black-hearted, indicating malice), *del-shekastegi* (broken-heartedness, indicating hurt), *del-shekar* or *del-shekan* (heart-breaker, indicating causing hurt), *del-gerâni* and *del-âzordan* (resentment and hurting someone's feelings), *del az âz por kardan* (filling the heart with greed), *del negâh dâshtan* (keeping the heart, as loyalty), *del-kur* (blind-hearted, as ignorant and ill-intentioned). In the Master's poems we find [29]: *del-sangin* (stony-hearted), *del-omidvâr* (hopeful heart), *del-nâzok* (tender-hearted), *del-zendeh* (lively-hearted), *del-shekasteh* (broken-hearted), *del-siyâh* (black-hearted), *del-mehrabân* (kind-hearted), *âhan-del* (iron-hearted), *del yâd kardan* (the heart remembering), *del-birahm* (merciless heart), *hasrat dar del* (regret in the heart), *del-khorsand* (contented heart), *del-kur* (blind-hearted), *del por-omid* (heart full of hope), *del [...] ferâq* (heart [...] of separation), *del-sabur* (patient heart), *ârezu-ye del* (wish of the heart), *del gereftan* (the heart growing heavy), *del-shâd* (glad-hearted), *del gardânidan* (turning the heart away), *del-kâfar* (infidel/ungrateful heart), *del-sugvâr* (mourning heart), *del-narm* (soft-hearted), *del-darmândeh* (helpless heart), *del-bakhshandeh* (forgiving/generous heart), *del-mokaddar* (troubled/clouded heart):

- Wash the palate of greed and avarice, O heart, from its bitterness and saltiness;

- Do not reproach and oppress our heart any more than this;

- Say that my heart owes fidelity to your down and mole.

30 – One of the aims of psychoanalysis is peace and understanding between the individual and their unconscious. Yet the unconscious, as an inner stranger, does not easily come under one's wing; at times it acts in such a way that the individual themselves cannot offer a logical or reasonable explanation for their own action. In psychopathology, what we call an "act of departure" (or fugue)—fleeing, distancing oneself, and abandoning loved ones and homeland without any prior pretext—compares so fittingly with a "heart" that slips from one's grasp like a bird or a gazelle. In the Master's poems we read [30]: *kojâ hami-ravi ey del bedin shetâb kojâ* ("Whither are you going, O heart, in such haste, whither?"), *del miravad ze dastam* ("My heart is slipping from my grasp"), *del andar pas-e havâ-ye to bast* ("The heart bound itself in pursuit of longing for you"), *del chon kabutaram* ("my dove-like heart"), *fetâd dar del-e Hâfez havâ-ye chon to shahi* ("Longing for a king such as you fell into Hafez's heart"), *morgh-e del* (bird of the heart), *del-ramideh* (startled heart), *del-e harzeh-gard* (wandering/aimless heart), *del cho pargâr beh har su davarâni mikard* ("the heart revolved like a compass in every direction"), *eyb-e del kardam ke vahshi-vaz' o har-jâyi mabâsh* ("I reproached my heart, saying: do not be wild-natured and fickle").

31 – Metaphorical *del*, like the unconscious, also possesses a metaphorical space, and the unconscious is conceived as a reservoir of a chain of acoustic images of words; in this vein, we find traces in the *Divan* of Hafez [31]: *del-e virâneh* (ruined heart), *del-sarâpardeh* (pavilion of the heart), *molk-e del* (kingdom of the heart), *khazineh-ye del* (treasury of the heart), *virân-sarâ-ye del* (ruined abode of the heart), *gusheh-ye del* (corner of the heart), *haram-e del* (sanctuary of the heart), *mehrâb-e del* (prayer-niche of the heart).

- "Wine" (*mey*) and *del* in Hafez's poems act as an intermediary that strips away the pressure of what is repressed and forbidden from the unconscious. It is as though wine assaults the filter of the unconscious, and the unconscious, like a liberated child, reveals its true self. From Hafez we have examples [32]: *beh mey emârat-e del kon* ("rebuild the heart with wine", meaning to forget sorrow), *sharâb nush o gham-e del bebar ze yâd* ("drink wine and banish the heart's grief from memory"), *delash bas tang mibinam ke gar sâghar nemigirad* ("I see his heart sorely constricted if he does not take the goblet"):

(611) Bind your heart to wine so that, bravely, / You may break the neck of hypocrisy and false piety.

It is as though, by deploying such vast concepts around the word *del* and applying it across all the diverse angles we have seen, Persian speakers have felt Descartes' famous dictum *"I think, therefore I am"* in this way:

*"I have a heart (del), therefore I am."*

This short essay seeks only to demonstrate that human culture is ancient: whatever is bound to culture and the human being comes from distant pasts. With a little effort, the footprints of newly discovered phenomena can be traced in earlier ages.

For human culture, like streams joining one another, flows from afar. To understand it, one cannot isolate and examine only a single segment of a stream or river. It is this wholeness and universality of human culture that constitutes its richness. It is this way of thinking about human beings and their achievements that reveals human greatness and refinement, and delivers us from narrow-mindedness, one-sidedness, crooked thinking, and self-conceit.

In the domain of knowing the human psyche and its manifold dimensions—as Freud understood—one must begin from anthropology prior to the emergence of speech, the emergence of writing, and the emergence of the earliest human societies. It is here that myths and all human creations, great and small—poetic literature, prose literature, folk tales, and street proverbs—constitute vast, inexhaustible mines for clinical psychoanalytic research.
